entries.nuance: ㅋㅋ is the texted shape of the snicker 크크/큭큭 (the ㅋ is the consonant for the 'k' giggle), and among Korean 20-30s it is the default 'I'm-relaxed-and-friendly' marker — even more than a genuine laugh, it signals you are at ease. Length is meaning: ㅋㅋ is a polite chuckle, ㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋ is real laughter. The near-rival ㅎㅎ is its softer cousin (a smile, not a laugh), so swapping them changes tone — ㅋㅋ is funny, ㅎㅎ is gentle. The English-speaker pitfall is the lone ㅋ: in English 'lol' is harmless solo, but a single ㅋ (or ㅋ.. / ㅋ?) can read as cold, sarcastic, or even passive-aggressive to a sensitive reader, the texting equivalent of a flat 'ha.' When unsure, never go below ㅋㅋ. And keep all of it out of messages to a boss, professor, or stranger — there it looks unserious.

entries.nuance: ㅎㅎ comes from the soft breathy chuckle 흐흐/하하 (the ㅎ is the 'h' breath), and its real job in Korean chat is not 'this is funny' but 'I'm being warm and gentle.' That is the sharp line vs its rival ㅋㅋ: ㅋㅋ = amused/laughing, ㅎㅎ = smiling/softening. Because it reads as polite rather than rowdy, Koreans sprinkle it onto otherwise bare replies (넵 ㅎㅎ, 알겠습니다 ㅎㅎ) so they don't land as curt — and it slips into friendly-coworker messages where ㅋㅋ would feel too loose. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming ㅎ = strong laughter like 'haha'; it does NOT scale to big laughter the way ㅋㅋㅋ does, so reacting to a hilarious meme with only ㅎㅎ can read as polite-but-unmoved, even a little cold. For genuine funny, switch to ㅋㅋㅋ. And in a strictly formal note to a boss or stranger, still drop it.

entries.nuance: ㅇㅇ is the texted form of 응 (eung, casual 'yeah'), doubled to 응응, so it carries pure banmal — the informal register you use with people you'd speak 반말 to out loud. Its near-neighbor is the polite 네/넵, and the gap between them is exactly the politeness gap, which is why the English-speaker pitfall here is severe: English 'yeah' is fine to almost anyone, but firing ㅇㅇ at a boss, professor, or older stranger skips every layer of politeness and reads as blunt, even disrespectful — like grunting 'uh-huh' at a superior. The safe upgrade ladder for seniors is 네 (polite) → 넵 (cheerful-polite) → 네네 (warm). Also don't confuse ㅇㅇ (yes/agreement, from 응응) with ㅇㅋ (okay/got it, from 오케이): you can answer a yes/no question with ㅇㅇ, but you confirm an instruction with ㅇㅋ.

entries.nuance: ㄴㄴ comes from the doubled English-borrowed 노노 ('no-no'), and the doubling is what makes it playful and soft rather than a hard rejection — it lands like 'nah' or 'nope,' not a stern 'No.' Its polite counterparts are 아니요 / 아니에요 (and very formal 아닙니다), and the whole point of ㄴㄴ is that it lives only in the casual zone with friends and peers. Pair ㄴㄴ with a quick reason or a ㅠ and it stays warm.

entries.nuance: ㄱㄱ is the texted form of 고고, Korea's reading of the English 'go-go,' and it spread from gaming ('go go!' to launch a match) into all of casual life: heading out, ordering food, starting a task, kicking off a plan. It's energetic and breezy — closer to 'let's GO / let's do this' than a neutral 'okay.' The nearest sober alternatives are 가자 (let's go) and the work-safe 바로 진행하겠습니다 (I'll proceed right away). It loves to ride after ㅇㅋ or ㅇㅇ to seal a decision.

entries.nuance: ㅈㅅ is the initials of 죄송 (Sino-Korean 罪悚, literally 'sin + dread/fear' — i.e. 'I feel the weight of having done wrong'), the same word inside the full apology 죄송합니다/죄송해요. entries.nuance: ㅠㅠ is pure visual: the Korean vowel letter ㅠ is reused as a picture of two eyes with tears streaming down (its twin ㅜㅜ is the same face with eyes scrunched), so it's read with the EYES, not pronounced — there's no spoken 'yuyu.' It's one of the most common feeling-markers in Korean chat, and crucially its range runs from genuine sadness all the way to playful, exaggerated 'aw man / waaah' whining; more letters = more drama, often tongue-in-cheek. The English-speaker pitfalls are mostly mechanical and tonal. Mechanically: Koreans usually attach it with NO space, fused to the last word (취소됐어ㅠㅠ), where English would float an emoji after a space. Tonally: because it's text and a little cute, English speakers sometimes deploy it in semi-professional messages thinking it's neutral like 🙁 — but in a formal or work note it reads as childish and unprofessional, so leave it for friends and dating partners. And don't read every ㅠㅠ as real tears; very often it's just light 'ugh, bummer.'

entries.nuance: ㄹㅇ is the consonant skeleton of 리얼, Korea's borrowing of English 'real,' and it works two ways: as a reply it's emphatic agreement ('for real / no joke / facts'), and dropped inside a sentence it's an intensifier meaning 'genuinely/seriously' (이거 ㄹㅇ 웃겨 = 'this is genuinely funny'). It's very current 20-30s slang, at home in friend chats and comments, and frequently fused with ㅋㅋ as ㄹㅇㅋㅋ. Its native-Korean cousins are 진짜 and 정말 ('really/truly'), which carry the same meaning but sound a notch less slangy — and those are what you'd upgrade to in polite contexts (진짜요/정말요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't decode ㄹㅇ as 'right now' or any English-acronym guess — it's strictly '리얼/real (for real).' Second, ㄹㅇ overlaps heavily with the agreement word ㅇㅈ (인정, 'agreed'), but they aren't identical: ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's TRUE,' while ㅇㅈ concedes 'I ADMIT/agree' — close enough to stack (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but ㄹㅇ also works as a standalone intensifier where ㅇㅈ can't.

Treating ㄹㅇ and ㅇㅈ as identical — ㄹㅇ asserts 'that's true / genuinely' (and can intensify mid-sentence), while ㅇㅈ specifically means 'I agree/admit it'; only ㄹㅇ works as a plain intensifier

entries.nuance: ㅇㅈ is the consonant frame of 인정 (Sino-Korean 認定, 'recognize + fix/settle'), literally 'to acknowledge/admit something as so' — and as slang it became young Koreans' punchy way to say 'agreed, that's facts.' Its polite equivalents are 맞아요 ('that's right'), 동의해요 ('I agree'), and very formal 동의합니다, which are what you'd use with seniors. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the literal core is 'acknowledge/admit,' so beyond agreement it can carry a faint flavor of conceding a point ('okay, I'll grant you that') — and the bare-noun 인정 even works as a real verb (그 실수는 인정 = 'I admit that mistake'); reading it as only cheerful 'yes!' misses that edge. Second, don't blur it with ㄹㅇ: ㅇㅈ = 'I agree/admit (인정),' a stance toward what you said; ㄹㅇ = 'for real/genuinely (리얼),' a claim about truth that can also intensify a sentence. They pair (ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ) but aren't swappable everywhere. As always, keep ㅇㅈ casual — to a boss write 맞습니다 / 동의합니다.

entries.nuance: ㄱㅊ is the initials of 괜찮아 ('it's okay'), and it inherits that word's famously wide three-way range: (1) reassuring — 'it's fine, don't worry'; (2) self-report — 'I'm okay'; and (3) soft declining — 'I'm good' (i.e. 'no thanks'). Its polite forms are 괜찮아요 / 괜찮습니다, which is what seniors get. The standout English-speaker pitfall is sense (3): when someone offers you food or a drink and you reply 괜찮아요/ㄱㅊ, a Korean hears 'no thanks, I'm fine WITHOUT it' — a polite refusal — whereas English speakers, hearing 'it's okay,' often think they just ACCEPTED. So 'ㄱㅊ' to '커피 마실래?' means you're declining, not saying yes. If you actually want it, say 응 줘 / 네 주세요. The second pitfall is the usual register one: ㄱㅊ is friends-only, so don't reassure a boss with it — write 괜찮습니다. It naturally follows apologies like ㅈㅅ/미안 to brush them off kindly.

entries.nuance: Polite/formal 존댓말 lead-in (실례 失禮 = 'lose courtesy', 失 lose + 禮 courtesy/manners) said right before you impose on a stranger or ask something slightly personal; it openly admits 'I know I'm being rude by interrupting.' The dividing line vs 죄송한데요 is the feeling: 실례지만 is courteous and a touch formal (you're being proper before a request), while 죄송한데요 leads with an apology and feels softer, almost guilty — you'd use 실례지만 to ask a stranger's name but 죄송한데요 to complain about your food. Habitual partners are 실례지만 + 길 좀, 성함이, 시간 괜찮으세요. Pitfall: English speakers blur it with 실례합니다, which is a standalone 'excuse me' to get attention; 실례지만 ends in -지만 ('but…') so it CANNOT stand alone — you must attach your actual question, or it dangles unfinished.

Don't use 실례지만 as a standalone 'excuse me' — the -지만 means 'but…', so it grammatically demands a request after it. To just get someone's attention, say 실례합니다 or 저기요.
It's 존댓말 only; saying 실례지만 to a close friend sounds stiff and oddly formal. Among friends use 저기 or 미안한데.
Don't follow it with 반말 — 실례지만, 너 이름이 뭐야? clashes in register. Keep the whole sentence polite: 실례지만, 성함이 어떻게 되세요?

structuredNuance.t: Polite/formal 존댓말 lead-in said right before you impose on a stranger or ask something slightly personal; it openly admits 'I know I'm being rude by interrupting.' Habitual partners are 실례지만 + 길 좀, 성함이, 시간 괜찮으세요.

The dividing line vs 죄송한데요 is the feeling: 실례지만 is courteous and a touch formal (you're being proper before a request), while 죄송한데요 leads with an apology and feels softer, almost guilty — you'd use 실례지만 to ask a stranger's name but 죄송한데요 to complain about your food.
실례 失禮 = 'lose courtesy' (失 lose + 禮 courtesy/manners).

English speakers blur it with 실례합니다, which is a standalone 'excuse me' to get attention. 실례지만 ends in -지만 ('but…') so it CANNOT stand alone — you must attach your actual question, or it dangles unfinished.

entries.english: The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)
entries.shortExplanation: 다름이 아니라 is a practical expression meaning "The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)".
entries.explanation: "The thing is… / Actually, the reason I'm asking is… (lead-in before getting to your real point/request)" — that is 다름이 아니라 (dareumi anira). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다름이 아니라, 부탁이 하나 있어서요. ("The thing is, I have a favor to ask."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: Polite set phrase, literally 'it's nothing other (than this)' from 다르다 ('to differ') → 다름 ('difference') + 이 아니라 ('it's not'), that buys a beat before you reveal why you really called or approached someone. It frames what follows as 'the actual matter,' so the listener braces for a request or announcement. The near-synonym is 저기요 / 저, but those just flag 'um, hey' to open a turn, whereas 다름이 아니라 specifically promises 'here comes my real point,' so it's heavier and more formal — perfect for phone calls, emails, and talking to seniors. 다름이 아니고 is the looser conversational form. Pitfall for English speakers: it is a lead-in, NOT a complete sentence, so you must attach your point after it; and the spelling is 다름이 (from 다르다), never 다림이 (which would evoke 다리미, 'an iron').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's a lead-in, not a full sentence — 다름이 아니라. on its own says nothing. Always attach your actual point: 다름이 아니라, 부탁이 하나 있어요.
Spelling: 다름이 (not 다림이). It comes from 다르다 (to differ), so the noun is 다름. 다림이 wrongly suggests 다리미 'an iron'.
Don't drop the connective and say 다름 아니라 in careful writing; standard is 다름이 아니라 with the subject 이.

entries.english: Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)
entries.shortExplanation: 죄송한데요 is a practical expression meaning "Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)".
entries.explanation: 죄송한데요 (joesonghandeyo) = "Sorry, but… / Excuse me, but… (apologetic softener before a request, complaint, or refusal)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 죄송한데요, 이거 환불 가능할까요? ("Sorry, but is this refundable?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 죄송한데요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

entries.nuance: Polite 존댓말 cushion built on 죄송 (罪悚 = 罪 'sin/guilt' + 悚 'fear/awe', so literally 'I feel guilt and trepidation') plus -ㄴ데요 ('…, and so'), opening with an apology so it feels softer and more deferential than 실례지만. The contrast with 실례지만 is the lead emotion: 죄송한데요 apologizes first and works for complaints, refusals, AND small favors, while 실례지만 is courteous-but-not-sorry and is mainly for asking a stranger something. Koreans reach for 죄송한데요 constantly because leading with 죄송 keeps friction down. 죄송한데 (no 요) is the same in casual-polite speech. Pitfall: don't write 죄성한데요 (the syllable is 죄송), and remember this is a SOFTENER, not a genuine apology for wrongdoing — if you actually did something wrong, you need a real 죄송합니다, not just this lead-in.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't spell it 죄성한데요 — the word is 죄송 (罪悚). Listen for the ㅗ: 죄송.
It's a softener, not a real apology. If you genuinely wronged someone, 죄송한데요 sounds too light — use a full 정말 죄송합니다.
Avoid stacking it with a blunt demand: 죄송한데요, 빨리 해요 clashes. Keep the request equally polite: 죄송한데요, 조금만 빨리 해 주실 수 있을까요?

entries.english: Yeah, right? / I know, tell me about it / You're so right (agreeing, often with a sigh)
entries.shortExplanation: 그러게요 is a practical expression meaning "Yeah, right? / I know, tell me about it / You're so right (agreeing, often with a sigh)".
entries.explanation: 그러게요 (geureogeyo) means "Yeah, right? / I know, tell me about it / You're so right (agreeing, often with a sigh)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러게요, 요즘 왜 이렇게 덥죠? ("I know, right? Why's it so hot these days?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 그러게요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

entries.nuance: Conversational agreement from 그렇다 ('to be so') + -게(요), meaning 'I feel exactly the same, you're right' — usually said with empathy or a shared sigh, and it often implies you'd been quietly thinking the same thing. The key contrast is with 맞아요: 맞아요 neutrally certifies a fact as correct ('that's right'), but 그러게요 emotionally COMMISERATES or marvels along with the speaker, so you say 맞아요 to confirm an address but 그러게요 to sigh along with a complaint. It pairs habitually with 말이에요 (그러게 말이에요 = 'tell me about it') and 내 말이. 그러게요 is casual-polite; 그러게 / 그러게 말이야 among close friends. Pitfall: it is NOT a question, so English speakers must not use it to ask 'why?'; and don't use it to accept a compliment about yourself — it agrees with the other person's observation, not with praise of you.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's not a question. English speakers hear 'right?' and try to ask 'why is it like that?' with it — but 그러게요 only AGREES; to ask why, use 왜 그럴까요?
Don't use it to accept praise about yourself. If someone says 'you did great,' replying 그러게요 sounds like 'yeah, I know I'm great.' Use 감사합니다 or 아니에요 instead.
Don't confuse it with 그래요 ('oh, is that so / okay'). 그래요 can be neutral or even doubtful; 그러게요 is warm, felt agreement.

It is NOT a question, so English speakers must not use it to ask 'why?'. Don't use it to accept a compliment about yourself — it agrees with the other person's observation, not with praise of you.

entries.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for gracefully accepting something you can't change — a verbal shrug, built from 어찌하다 ('to do how/what') contracted to 어쩌다 → 어쩔 수 없다 ('there's no way to do anything about it'). The -죠 ending makes it 'well, that's just how it is, right?', softer and more communal than the bare statement. Its closest synonym, 할 수 없죠 ('nothing to be done'), is nearly interchangeable — they swap freely in most contexts. The sharper dividing line is against 포기하다 ('to give up'): 어쩔 수 없죠 is passive ACCEPTANCE of a situation whose outcome was never in your hands, whereas 포기하다 is the ACTIVE choice to quit something you could have kept pursuing — so you say 어쩔 수 없죠 when the train's already sold out, but 포기했어요 when you decide to stop trying. Said calmly it signals mature acceptance; said sharply it tips into passive-aggressive 'fine, whatever,' so tone matters. Pitfall: don't apply it to things you actually control (it claims your hands are tied), and don't swap the two forms — 어쩔 수 없죠 accepts a situation, while 어쩔 수 없이 is an adverb meaning 'unavoidably' that modifies a verb (어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't use it about things within your control. Saying 어쩔 수 없죠 about a choice you could make sounds like a dodge — it claims the situation is genuinely out of your hands.
Don't confuse the two forms: 어쩔 수 없죠 (a standalone 'it can't be helped') vs 어쩔 수 없이 (the adverb 'unavoidably' before a verb, e.g. 어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).
Watch the spelling/sound: it's 어쩔 (double ㅉ), not 어절. And 없죠 is pronounced 'eopjyo', a contraction of 없지요.

entries.nuance: Polite, humble deflection using the honorific 말씀 (the elevated word for 말, 'speech/words'), literally 'what words [are you even saying]!' — i.e., your thanks or praise is so undeserved it shouldn't be spoken. The near-synonym is a flat 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing'), but 무슨 말씀을요 is warmer, more animated, and more deferential, almost protesting on the other person's behalf, so it shines with elders, customers, and anyone you're being courteous to, whereas 아니에요 is the everyday neutral version. The full underlying form is 무슨 말씀을 (하세요/하십니까). Pitfall for English speakers: you MUST use the honorific 말씀, not plain 말 — 무슨 말을요 sounds off and under-polite here; and because the phrase DEFLECTS, never follow it by then accepting the compliment — pair it with a modest add-on like 별거 아니에요 to stay consistent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Use 말씀 (the honorific), not 말. 무슨 말을요 sounds under-polite and slightly wrong; the fixed phrase is 무슨 말씀을요.
Don't deflect and then accept. Saying 무슨 말씀을요 and then 네, 제가 좀 잘하죠 contradicts the humility — follow with modesty like 별거 아니에요.
Don't read it as a literal question demanding an answer. It's a rhetorical deflection, so the other person isn't expected to explain 'what they said.'

entries.explanation: 신경 쓰지 마세요 (singyeong sseuji maseyo) means "Don't worry about it / Don't trouble yourself / Never mind it (telling someone to let something go)". entries.nuance: Polite-casual reassurance built from the idiom 신경(을) 쓰다 — 신경 (神經, 神 'spirit/nerve' + 經 'channel', i.e. the body's 'nerves') + 쓰다 ('to use/expend') — so literally 'don't expend your nerves on this.' It tells someone who feels bad, is fussing over you, or is anxious about others' opinions to stop spending mental energy. The contrast with 걱정하지 마세요 is real: 걱정 is future-facing WORRY ('don't be anxious that something bad will happen'), while 신경 쓰다 is present ATTENTION/bother ('don't fuss over / pay mind to this'), so you'd say 걱정하지 마세요 to someone scared about an exam, but 신경 쓰지 마세요 to someone apologizing over a small spill. 신경 쓰지 마 for friends; 신경 쓰지 마세요 / 마시고 in polite contexts. Pitfall: in careful writing the standard spacing is 신경 쓰지 (two words), not 신경쓰지; and to a senior the bare imperative can feel curt, so soften with 너무 or pair it with 괜찮아요.

In careful writing, space it: 신경 쓰지 마세요 (신경 and 쓰지 are separate words), not 신경쓰지.
Don't confuse it with 걱정하지 마세요. 신경 쓰지 마세요 = 'don't fuss/pay mind to this now'; 걱정하지 마세요 = 'don't be anxious about an outcome.' They aren't interchangeable.
To a senior, the bare command can sound curt. Soften it: add 너무 (너무 신경 쓰지 마세요) or pair with 괜찮으니까 / 괜찮아요.

entries.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for confirming something as approximately true when it isn't 100% exact — 'in effect, that's the case.' It comes from 셈, a native Korean noun meaning 'reckoning/calculation' (from 세다, 'to count'), so X인 셈이다 literally 'it counts/reckons as X.' The -죠 ending invites soft agreement. The sharp contrast is with 맞아요: 맞아요 asserts an exact, factual 'that's correct,' while 그런 셈이죠 always carries an 'approximately / for practical purposes' nuance, letting you agree without overcommitting — answer a quiz question with 맞아요, but answer 'so you've settled into Korea?' with 그런 셈이죠. Pitfall for English speakers: for a firm exact 'yes' do NOT use 그런 셈이죠 (it sounds evasive); and don't mix up the homophones — the phrase uses 셈 (reckoning), not 샘 (a spring, or 'jealousy/envy'), so it's 그런 셈이죠, never 그런 샘이죠.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
For a firm, exact 'yes,' use 맞아요 or 네 — 그런 셈이죠 always means 'roughly/effectively,' so it can sound evasive if the answer is actually definite.
Don't confuse 셈 (reckoning/count) with 샘 (a spring, or jealousy). The phrase is 그런 셈이죠, never 그런 샘이죠.
Keep the modifier 인/은: it's N인 셈이다 and V-(으)ㄴ 셈이다. Dropping it (그런 셈 vs 사장 셈) breaks the structure; say 사장님인 셈이죠.

entries.english: That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)
entries.shortExplanation: 그건 좀… is a practical expression meaning "That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)".
entries.explanation: 그건 좀… (geugeon jom…) = "That's a bit… (uhh) / Hmm, that might be hard… (polite, trailing-off refusal or hesitation)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 음… 그건 좀 어려울 것 같은데요. ("Umm… that might be a little difficult."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 그건 좀… with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.en: Umm… that might be a little difficult.

usagePhrases.note: 그건 좀 그렇다 = the set phrase 'that's kind of iffy'

examples.romanization: A: igeo eottaeyo? B: eum, geugeon jom….
examples.en: A: How about this one? B: Hmm, that's kind of…

examples.romanization: A: oneul bame sigan dwaeyo? B: a, oneureun jom….
examples.en: A: Are you free tonight? B: Ah, tonight is a bit…
examples.note: Declining an invite without a hard 'no'

examples.ko: 같이 투자하자는 건 좀… 죄송해요.
examples.romanization: gachi tujahajaneun geon jom… joesonghaeyo.
examples.en: Investing together is a bit… sorry.
examples.note: Politely refusing a real proposal, then apologizing

entries.nuance: A very Korean indirect refusal: you trail off after 좀 ('a little') and let the silence carry the 'no.' 좀 is the softened contraction of 조금 ('a little'), and here it's a hedging cushion, not a literal quantity — finishing the sentence out loud (…싫어요 'I don't like it' or …안 돼요 'no') would feel too blunt and confrontational, so the UNFINISHED sentence is itself the polite point. The contrast with a flat 안 돼요 is the whole lesson: 안 돼요 is a clear, direct refusal, while 그건 좀… deliberately leaves the refusal unspoken to save everyone's face. It works in both casual and polite speech, with tone, a pause, and a small grimace doing the work. Pitfall: English speakers often DON'T register this as a refusal and keep pushing — in Korea, 그건 좀… almost always means no, and bulldozing past it is pushy. Also resist 'helping' by finishing it bluntly with 싫어요, which destroys the soft purpose.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't finish it bluntly with 싫어요 ('I hate it') or a hard 안 돼요 — that defeats the whole face-saving point. The trailing silence IS the refusal.
Don't miss it as a refusal. English speakers hear an unfinished sentence and keep pushing; in Korea 그건 좀… reliably means 'no, but I'm being polite about it.'
Keep 좀 as the hinge: it's 그건 좀… (with 좀), not 그건… alone. The 좀 is what flags the soft, hedged tone.

entries.english: No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')
entries.shortExplanation: 말도 안 돼요 is a practical expression meaning "No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')".
entries.explanation: 말도 안 돼요 (maldo an dwaeyo) means "No way! / That's ridiculous / You've got to be kidding (disbelief, shock, or 'that makes no sense')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 진짜요? 말도 안 돼요! ("Really? No way!"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 말도 안 돼요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.note: Shocked reaction to surprising news

usagePhrases.ko: 말도 안 돼, 그게 어떻게 가능해?
usagePhrases.romanization: maldo an dwae, geuge eotteoke ganeunghae?
usagePhrases.en: That's absurd — how is that even possible?
usagePhrases.note: 말도 안 돼 = casual
Calling something unreasonable; -죠 invites agreement

usagePhrases.ko: 말도 안 되는 소리 하지 마.
usagePhrases.romanization: maldo an doeneun sori haji ma.
usagePhrases.note: 말도 안 되는 + noun = 'nonsensical ~'

examples.ko: A: 내일 시험이래요. B: 네? 말도 안 돼요!
examples.romanization: A: naeil siheomiraeyo. B: ne? maldo an dwaeyo!
examples.en: A: They say the test is tomorrow. B: What? No way!
examples.note: Quick disbelief at bad news

examples.ko: A: 그 식당 한 시간 기다려야 한대요. B: 한 시간이요? 말도 안 돼요!
examples.romanization: A: geu sikdang han sigan gidaryeoya handaeyo. B: han siganiyo? maldo an dwaeyo!
examples.en: A: They say you wait an hour for that place. B: An hour? That's ridiculous!
examples.note: Indignant disbelief at something unreasonable

examples.ko: 복권 당첨됐다고? 말도 안 돼! 진짜야?
examples.romanization: bokgwon dangcheomdwaetdago? maldo an dwae! jinjjaya?
examples.en: You won the lottery? No way! For real?
examples.note: Excited, happy shock with a friend

entries.nuance: A high-emotion exclamation literally meaning 'it doesn't even become words' (말 'words' + 도 'even' + 안 되다 'doesn't work/come about') — i.e., something is so absurd or shocking it can't be reasoned into language. It covers happy shock, indignation, and 'that's nonsense.' The contrast with 진짜요? / 정말요? matters: those just ask 'really?' to check the truth, whereas 말도 안 돼요 already JUDGES the thing as impossible or outrageous, so you often hear 진짜요? 말도 안 돼요! together — first verify, then react. 말도 안 돼 with friends, 말도 안 돼요 in polite speech; context and tone decide delighted vs angry. Pitfalls for English speakers: watch the spacing and spelling — 안 is a separate word (말도 안 돼요), and it's 돼요, never 되요; and aim it at a STATEMENT or situation, not a person — unlike English 'you're ridiculous,' 말도 안 돼요 targets what was said, not the person's character.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing and spelling: it's 말도 안 돼요 with 안 written separately, and 돼요 (from 되다 + 어요), never 되요.

Don't aim it at a person ('you're ridiculous'). 말도 안 돼요 judges a statement or situation; pointing it at someone's character sounds like an insult — say 그건 말도 안 돼요 ('that's ridiculous') about the claim.
Don't use it as a neutral 'really?'. To simply confirm surprising news, use 진짜요? / 정말요?; 말도 안 돼요 already declares the thing impossible.

entries.english: I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)
entries.shortExplanation: 그럴 줄 알았어요 is a practical expression meaning "I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)".
entries.explanation: "I knew it / I figured as much / I had a feeling (this would happen)" — that is 그럴 줄 알았어요 (geureol jul arasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 거봐요, 그럴 줄 알았어요. ("See? I knew it."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 그럴 줄 알았어요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: 거봐요 ('see, told you') pairs naturally

usagePhrases.ko: 그럴 줄 알았어, 네가 또 늦을 줄.
usagePhrases.romanization: geureol jul arasseo, nega tto neujeul jul.
usagePhrases.en: I knew it — that you'd be late again.
usagePhrases.note: 그럴 줄 알았어 = casual

usagePhrases.en: I knew it would turn out like this.
usagePhrases.note: V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알았다 = 'expected/knew that ~ would happen'
Opposite: 몰랐어요 = 'didn't know/expect'

examples.ko: A: 길이 막혀서 늦었어요. B: 그럴 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: A: giri makyeoseo neujeosseoyo. B: geureol jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: A: I was late because of traffic. B: I figured.
examples.note: Calm 'I expected that'

examples.ko: A: 그 가게 망했대요. B: 그럴 줄 알았어요, 손님이 없더라고요.
examples.romanization: A: geu gage manghaetdaeyo. B: geureol jul arasseoyo, sonnimi eopsdeoragoyo.
examples.en: A: That shop went under. B: I figured — there were never any customers.
examples.note: Confirming a prediction with -더라고요 (recalled observation)

examples.ko: 역시 비가 오네, 그럴 줄 알았어. 우산 챙기길 잘했다.
examples.romanization: yeoksi biga one, geureol jul arasseo. usan chaenggigil jalhaetda.
examples.en: Of course it's raining — I had a feeling. Good thing I brought an umbrella.
examples.note: 역시 ('as expected') reinforces the prediction

entries.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for 'this is exactly what I predicted,' from the grammar V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 ('to know/expect that something would be the case'). Here 줄 is a bound noun meaning roughly 'the fact/way that' — it is NOT the homophone 줄 meaning 'a line/rope/string,' so don't translate it literally. The contrast with 그런 줄 알았어요 is worth knowing: 그럴 줄 알았어요 (with the future-ish 그럴) = 'I expected it would turn out this way' (a correct prediction), whereas 그런 줄 알았어요 (with 그런) = 'I had assumed that was the case' — and the latter is very often used when you were WRONG ('oh, I thought it was like that…'). Pairs naturally with 거봐요, 역시. Pitfall: tone is everything — said warmly it's knowing or sympathetic, but after someone's misfortune a flat 그럴 줄 알았어 lands as a smug 'told you so,' so soften it or add empathy when they've just had bad luck.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
줄 here means 'the fact/way that,' a grammar marker — not 줄 'a line/rope.' Don't translate 그럴 줄 알았어요 literally; it means 'I knew it would be so.'
Don't confuse 그럴 줄 알았어요 ('I correctly predicted this') with 그런 줄 알았어요 ('I'd assumed that — often mistakenly'). The 그럴 vs 그런 flips the meaning.
After someone's bad luck, a flat 그럴 줄 알았어 sounds like a smug 'told you so.' Add empathy (아이고, 그럴 줄 알았어요…) or soften it.

structuredNuance.t: Casual-polite phrase for 'this is exactly what I predicted,' from the grammar V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 ('to know/expect that something would be the case'). Pairs naturally with 거봐요, 역시. Tone is everything — said warmly it's knowing or sympathetic.

The contrast with 그런 줄 알았어요 is worth knowing: 그럴 줄 알았어요 (with the future-ish 그럴) = 'I expected it would turn out this way' (a correct prediction), whereas 그런 줄 알았어요 (with 그런) = 'I had assumed that was the case' — and the latter is very often used when you were WRONG ('oh, I thought it was like that…').
Here 줄 is a bound noun meaning roughly 'the fact/way that' — it is NOT the homophone 줄 meaning 'a line/rope/string,' so don't translate it literally.
After someone's misfortune a flat 그럴 줄 알았어 lands as a smug 'told you so,' so soften it or add empathy when they've just had bad luck.

entries.nuance: Polite-casual phrase that releases the other person from a sense of obligation, built on 부담 (負擔, 負 'to bear/carry' + 擔 'to shoulder a load', so literally 'a load one shoulders' → burden/pressure) plus 갖다 ('to have/hold'), i.e. 'don't hold the burden.' Koreans say it constantly when giving gifts, extending invitations, or asking favors, because in Korea accepting something can feel like incurring a debt (정/체면 dynamics). The contrast with 걱정하지 마세요 is clean: 걱정하지 마세요 calms anxiety about an OUTCOME ('don't worry it'll go badly'), while 부담 갖지 마세요 specifically lifts the weight of OBLIGATION/indebtedness ('don't feel you owe me'). The verb is 갖다, giving the casual 부담 갖지 마 for friends. Pitfall for English speakers: the partner verb is 갖다 ('hold'), so it's 부담 갖지 마세요, not 부담 하지 마세요; and don't over-insist — saying it once warmly is enough, because repeating it can ironically pile on more pressure.

entries.english: to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')
entries.shortExplanation: 눈치가 빠르다 is a practical expression meaning "to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')".
entries.explanation: 눈치가 빠르다 (nunchiga ppareuda) means "to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 눈치가 빠르다 ("to be quick on the uptake"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 눈치가 빠르다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.en: to be quick on the uptake
usagePhrases.note: The whole idiom; 눈치 takes 가, never 를, with 빠르다.

usagePhrases.note: Here 눈치 takes 를 — it means to sense a hidden fact, e.g. 선물인 걸 눈치챘어.
Watching a person's face to gauge their reaction; can sound timid, not a compliment.
The direct opposite — missing social cues entirely.

entries.nuance: 눈치 is the Korean 'social radar' for reading unspoken cues — the mood in a room, what someone really means, when to back off — and 빠르다 ('fast') frames you as catching all that quickly, so it's a warm compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. Distinguish it from 똑똑하다 ('smart/book-clever'): 똑똑하다 is raw intelligence, while 눈치가 빠르다 is interpersonal sensitivity — a person can be 똑똑하지만 눈치가 없다 (brainy yet socially oblivious). The register is casual-to-polite and common at work and among friends. Habitual partners: 분위기를 파악하다 (grasp the atmosphere), 금방 알아채다 (notice right away). The big English-speaker pitfall is treating 눈치 as eyesight because of 눈 ('eye') — it is social awareness, not vision — and using the wrong particle: it must be 눈치'가' 빠르다, whereas 'to catch on' is 눈치'를' 채다, and 'to anxiously gauge someone' is 눈치'를' 보다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't translate it as 'fast eyes' or link it to good vision — 눈치 means reading social atmosphere, despite containing 눈 ('eye').
Particle error: people say 눈치를 빠르다, but the idiom is 눈치'가' 빠르다. Use 를 only with 채다/보다 (눈치를 채다 = catch on).
눈치가 빠르다 (perceptive, a compliment) ≠ 눈치를 보다 (nervously watching someone's reaction, often timid). They are not interchangeable and carry opposite vibes.

entries.shortExplanation: 발이 넓다 is a practical expression meaning "to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')".
entries.explanation: "to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')" — that is 발이 넓다 (bari neolda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 발이 넓다 ("to be well-connected"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Attributive 넓은 + noun; the go-to way to describe a networker.

examples.en: My uncle knows a lot of people.
examples.note: Plain frame: subject + 발이 넓어요.

entries.nuance: Literally 'wide feet,' the image is of feet that have walked into many circles, so it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across different groups. It is a compliment about reach, and its sharper near-synonym is 인맥(人脈)이 넓다, where 인맥 ('person-vein,' a Sino-Korean word picturing connections as veins) names the network explicitly and sounds a touch more formal or business-flavored; 발이 넓다 is the warmer, more idiomatic everyday version. Register is neutral — fine in casual and polite speech alike. Natural partners: 모르는 사람이 없다 (there's nobody they don't know), 소개를 받다/시켜 주다 (get/give introductions). The key English-speaker pitfall is reading it literally (it has nothing to do with foot size) and confusing breadth with depth: 발이 넓다 means you know MANY people, not that you have many CLOSE friends — for true intimacy Koreans would say 친한 친구가 많다 instead. The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다.

Don't use it for close friendships — it means a wide circle of ACQUAINTANCES, not many best friends. For that, say 친한 친구가 많다.
The opposite is 발이 좁다 ('narrow feet'), not 발이 작다 ('small feet'). Mixing the antonym breaks the idiom.

entries.explanation: 손이 크다 (soni keuda) = "to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 손이 크다 ("to be generous (esp. with food/spending)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 손 takes 이, adjective is 크다 ('big').
Attributive 큰 + 사람; common compliment for a host.

usagePhrases.en: to be stingy / always prepare too little
usagePhrases.note: Opposite ('small hands') — skimping on portions or money.
Verb collocation: 크게 쓰다 = lay out money freely on others.

examples.ko: 우리 엄마는 손이 커요.
examples.romanization: uri eommaneun soni keoyo.
examples.en: My mom is generous (cooks a lot).
examples.note: Plain frame; defaults to the cooking-amount reading.

examples.ko: 손이 크신 분이라 선물도 늘 푸짐해요.
examples.romanization: soni keusin bunira seonmuldo neul pujimhaeyo.
examples.en: She's generous, so her gifts are always lavish.
examples.note: Everyday: honorific 크신 + 푸짐하다 (plentiful) for gifts.

examples.ko: 오늘 손 크게 쐈으니까 다음엔 네가 사.
examples.romanization: oneul son keuge sswasseunikka daeumen nega sa.
examples.en: I splurged today, so next time it's on you.
examples.note: Real-situation: 손 크게 쏘다 (slang 쏘다 = treat) when picking up a tab.

entries.nuance: Literally 'big hands,' the picture is of hands that scoop out a lot at once, so it praises generosity — especially cooking in big batches or spending freely to feed and host others. It carries a warm, hospitable glow rooted in Korean food culture's love of abundance (a 손 큰 host would rather over-cater than run short). Contrast it with 인심이 좋다 ('good 인심/人心, human-heartedness'), a near-synonym that stresses a kind, giving disposition in general, whereas 손이 크다 zooms in on the concrete scale of what you make or buy. Register is neutral-to-positive. Natural partners: 음식이 넘쳐나다 (food overflows), 푸짐하다 (lavish/plentiful), 회식 때 많이 사 주다 (treats a lot at company dinners). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about being a big spender on yourself or having literally large hands — it's generosity toward others; and don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = a quick, efficient worker), which is unrelated. Opposite: 손이 작다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Not about literal hand size, and not about splurging on yourself — it's specifically generosity toward others (cooking/giving in big amounts).
Don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = quick, efficient at a task). Different idiom, different meaning.
The opposite is 손이 작다 ('small hands' = stingy/under-prepares), not 손이 짧다 (which evokes 'short arms,' a separate image).

entries.english: to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')
entries.shortExplanation: 입이 무겁다 is a practical expression meaning "to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')".
entries.explanation: 입이 무겁다 (ibi mugeopda) means "to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 입이 무겁다 ("to be tight-lipped / discreet"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 입이 무겁다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 입 takes 이, adjective 무겁다 ('heavy').

usagePhrases.en: a discreet person you can trust with secrets
usagePhrases.note: Attributive 무거운 + 사람; vouches for someone's reliability.
Opposite ('light mouth') — can't keep anything quiet.

usagePhrases.en: to shut one's mouth / keep quiet
usagePhrases.note: Related verb; 다물다 = the concrete act of staying silent.

examples.ko: 우리 형은 입이 무거워.
examples.romanization: uri hyeongeun ibi mugeowo.
examples.en: My older brother is tight-lipped.
examples.note: Plain frame; states a trait.

examples.ko: 이건 비밀인데, 너 입 무거운 거 알아서 말하는 거야.
examples.romanization: igeon bimirinde, neo im mugeoun geo araseo malhaneun geoya.
examples.en: This is a secret, but I'm telling you because I know you're discreet.
examples.note: Everyday: drop 이 (입 무겁다) and use it to vouch before confiding.

examples.ko: 변호사는 기본적으로 입이 무거워야 해요.
examples.romanization: byeonhosaneun gibonjeogeuro ibi mugeowoya haeyo.
examples.en: A lawyer fundamentally has to be tight-lipped.
examples.note: Real-situation: 무거워야 하다 = professional duty of discretion.

entries.nuance: Literally 'a heavy mouth,' the image is that words are too heavy to spill out easily, so it means you can be trusted with secrets — discreet, reliable, not a gossip. It's a compliment, typically used to reassure someone before sharing something private (말해도 돼, 걔 입 무거워). A crucial distinction: 입이 무겁다 is about confidentiality, NOT about being a quiet or shy personality in general — for that you'd say 말이 없다 ('has few words') or 과묵하다 (reserved). Register is neutral, common in both work and personal settings. Natural partners: 비밀을 지키다 (keep a secret), 신뢰를 받다 (be trusted), 믿을 수 있다 (can be relied on). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto general quietness and assuming the opposite is 입이 작다 — the true opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth' = a leaky gossip). Keep the body-part idioms straight: heavy/light mouth = discretion, not mouth size.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about keeping SECRETS, not about being quiet or shy by nature. A chatty person can still be 입이 무거운 if they never leak confidences; for 'quiet,' use 말이 없다 or 과묵하다.
The opposite is 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth'), not 입이 작다. Don't pick the antonym by literal size.
Don't say 입을 무겁다 — 무겁다 is an adjective describing 입, so the particle is 이/은 (입이 무겁다), never the object marker 을.

entries.english: to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')
entries.shortExplanation: 귀가 얇다 is a practical expression meaning "to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')".
entries.explanation: "to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')" — that is 귀가 얇다 (gwiga yalda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 귀가 얇다 ("to be easily swayed / gullible"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 귀가 얇다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 귀 takes 가, adjective 얇다 ('thin').
Attributive 얇은 + 사람; mildly negative.

usagePhrases.en: to be on the gullible side
usagePhrases.note: Softening 편이다 ('tend to be') makes self-criticism gentler.

usagePhrases.en: to be won over / fall for it
usagePhrases.note: Frequent partner verb: 꼬시면 바로 넘어가 = caves the moment coaxed.

examples.ko: 나 귀가 얇아.
examples.romanization: na gwiga yalba.
examples.en: I'm easily swayed.
examples.note: Simplest self-description with 귀가 얇다.

examples.ko: 친구가 좋다고 하니까 귀가 얇아져서 같은 걸 샀어.
examples.romanization: chinguga jotago hanikka gwiga yalbajyeoseo gateun geol sasseo.
examples.en: My friend said it was good, so I caved and bought the same thing.
examples.note: Everyday: 귀가 얇아지다 (become swayed) in a shopping moment.

examples.ko: 주식도 귀가 얇으면 남 말 듣고 손해 봐요.
examples.romanization: jusikdo gwiga yalbeumyeon nam mal deutgo sonhae bwayo.
examples.en: With stocks too, if you're easily swayed you lose money following others.
examples.note: Real-situation: financial warning, 남 말 듣다 = listen to others' talk.

entries.nuance: Literally 'thin ears,' the image is ears so thin that whatever people say passes straight through and persuades you, so it describes someone easily swayed, quick to believe a recommendation, or talked into purchases. The tone is mildly negative or self-mocking, not a harsh insult (Koreans cheerfully admit 나 귀 얇아). Contrast it with 순진하다 ('naive/innocent'): 순진하다 is broad, often sympathetic innocence about the world, while 귀가 얇다 is specifically the trait of being persuaded by others' words — a 순진한 person may still hold firm, but a 귀 얇은 person flips with the last opinion they heard. Register is casual-to-polite. Natural partners: 광고 보면 자꾸 사다 (keep buying from ads), 남 말 듣고 (on others' say-so), 넘어가다 (be won over), 사기당하다 (get scammed). The English-speaker pitfall: it is NOT about hearing ability or literally thin ears, and it must NOT be read as a compliment for being 'open-minded' or 'flexible' — it always implies a lack of one's own judgment.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Not about hearing ability or physically thin ears — it means being easily influenced by what people say.
Don't use it as a compliment for being open-minded or flexible. 귀가 얇다 implies poor judgment/gullibility, which is negative; for genuine flexibility say 생각이 유연하다.
Particle: it's 귀'가' 얇다 (adjective describing the ears), not 귀를 얇다.

entries.english: to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')
entries.shortExplanation: 바람을 맞다 is a practical expression meaning "to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')".
entries.explanation: 바람을 맞다 (barameul matda) = "to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 바람(을) 맞다 ("to get stood up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 바람을 맞다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.note: You are the one left waiting; often written as one word 바람맞다.
Causative 맞히다 — the subject is the no-show who ditched the other.
Totally different idiom! 피우다, not 맞다 — don't confuse the two.

usagePhrases.en: a blind date (set up by someone)
usagePhrases.note: The classic setting where 바람맞다 happens.

examples.ko: 나 또 바람맞았어.
examples.romanization: na tto barammajasseo.
examples.en: I got stood up again.
examples.note: Shortest form; 바람맞다 as one word.

examples.ko: 한 시간 기다리다가 결국 바람맞았어요.
examples.romanization: han sigan gidaridaga gyeolguk barammajasseoyo.
examples.en: I waited an hour and ended up getting stood up.
examples.note: Everyday: 기다리다가 sets the scene before the no-show.

examples.ko: 연락도 없이 바람맞히는 건 진짜 예의가 아니야.
examples.romanization: yeollakdo eopsi barammatineun geon jinjja yeuiga aniya.
examples.en: Standing someone up without even a text is just rude.
examples.note: Real-situation: causative 바람맞히다 to blame the no-show.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to be hit by the wind,' the image is of someone left standing out in the wind, waiting for a person who never came — so it means getting stood up. It is most common for dates and 소개팅 (blind dates) but extends to any no-show, even a business meeting. Register is casual. The make-or-break point is the verb pairing: 바람(을) 맞다 = YOU got stood up (you are on the receiving end), while the causative 바람(을) 맞히다 = you stood SOMEONE ELSE up (you are the no-show) — swapping them reverses who is at fault. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is a near-homonym trap: 바람을 피우다 ('to raise/kindle wind') means to cheat on a romantic partner, a completely unrelated idea — saying 바람피웠어 instead of 바람맞았어 turns 'I got stood up' into 'I cheated.' Natural partners: 한 시간(이나) 기다리다 (wait a whole hour), 연락도 없이 (without even a message).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't confuse 바람을 맞다 (get stood up) with 바람을 피우다 (cheat on a partner). They share 바람 but the verbs and meanings are entirely different — a dangerous mix-up.
바람맞다 (you were stood up) vs 바람맞히다 (you stood someone up): the causative 히 flips who is to blame. Match the verb to who didn't show.
It's about a no-show for a meeting/date, not about literal wind or weather. Never read 바람 here as a breeze.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to not know that time is going,' it means you were so absorbed or having such a good time that you never noticed the hours slip by — English 'time flew.' The load-bearing grammar is the pattern -는 줄 모르다 ('to not realize that…'), so the structure 가는 줄 모르다 must stay intact. The English-speaker pitfall: beginners drop 줄 (saying 시간 가는 모르다) and the 'didn't realize that…' meaning collapses; also avoid using it as an excuse for laziness or neglect — it implies you ENJOYED the time, not that you were careless. Natural partners: 정신없이 (absorbed), 수다 떨다가 (chatting away), 막차를 놓치다 (miss the last train).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Keep 줄 in the structure: it must be 가는 '줄' 모르다. Dropping 줄 (시간 가는 모르다) destroys the '-didn't realize that…' meaning.
It implies pleasant absorption, so don't use it to excuse laziness or neglecting something important — it says you were happily engrossed, not careless.
Don't swap in 시간을 모르다 (which would mean 'not know the time/clock'). The idiom needs the verb 가다: 시간 '가는' 줄 모르다.

entries.english: to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')
entries.shortExplanation: 진땀을 빼다 is a practical expression meaning "to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')".
entries.explanation: "to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')" — that is 진땀을 빼다 (jinttameul ppaeda). examples.note: Simple frame; casual 진땀 빼다 without 을.

entries.nuance: 진땀 is the clammy, sticky 'cold sweat' you break into under pressure — not the healthy sweat of exercise — and 빼다 ('to extract/drain') frames you as having that stress wrung out of you, so 진땀을 빼다 means to struggle through something nerve-wracking, flustered and scrambling. It captures the emotional ordeal, not mere physical exertion. Its closest near-synonym is 진땀(을) 흘리다 ('to shed cold sweat'); the meaning is essentially the same, with 빼다 leaning slightly more toward 'I got put through the wringer' and 흘리다 toward the image of sweat literally pouring. Mind the word itself: it must be 진땀 (the specific stress-sweat), not plain 땀 (ordinary sweat) — 땀을 빼다 would just mean working up a sweat or slimming down. Compare also 식은땀 ('cooled sweat'), which is the cold sweat of fear or shock specifically. Register is casual-to-polite. Natural partners: -느라 진땀 빼다 (sweat it out because of doing X), 어려운 질문을 받다 (get a tough question), 헤매다 (flounder/get lost).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't read it as literal sweating from heat or a workout — it's about a stressful, flustered struggle. For exercise sweat, plain 땀이 나다 fits, not 진땀을 빼다.
Use 진땀, not 땀: 땀을 빼다 means 'work up a sweat / lose weight,' a different idea. The 진 (clammy stress-sweat) is essential.
Don't confuse 진땀 with 식은땀. Both are cold sweats, but 식은땀 is the sweat of fear/shock (식은땀이 나다 = break out in a fearful sweat), while 진땀 빼다 is about laborious struggle.

entries.explanation: 한숨 돌리다 (hansum dollida) = "to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 한숨 돌리다 ("to catch one's breath / get a breather"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Natural lead-in: handle the emergency, then 한숨 돌리다.

examples.romanization: ije jom hansum dollyeosseo.
examples.en: I've finally caught my breath now.
examples.note: Simple frame with 이제 ('now') marking the relief point.

examples.romanization: siheom kkeunnasseunikka jom hansum dollyeo.
examples.en: Exams are over, so take a breather.
examples.note: Everyday: imperative 돌려 telling someone to relax a bit.

examples.note: Real-situation: 급한 불 끄다 pairs naturally before the relief.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to send one breath around,' it means to finally catch your breath and feel relief the moment a hectic or stressful stretch eases — the pressure has just lifted, even if only briefly. It is one of the most useful everyday relief phrases at work and home. Beware the deceptive look-alike: 한숨(을) 쉬다 uses the SAME word 한숨 but means 'to sigh' out of worry, frustration, or weariness (그는 한숨을 쉬었다 = he heaved a sigh) — a heavy, negative breath, the near-opposite feeling. The dividing line is the verb: 돌리다 (relief, you got a breather) vs 쉬다 (a worried/tired sigh). Also distinguish 쉬다 in the sense 'to rest': 한숨 돌리다 is a brief breather right after stress, not a long rest or vacation, for which you'd say 푹 쉬다 (rest fully). Register is casual-to-polite. Natural partners: 이제 (now), 겨우 (barely), 급한 불을 끄다 (put out the urgent fire), 한고비 넘기다 (get past the crisis).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't confuse 한숨 돌리다 (relief, catch your breath) with 한숨을 쉬다 (to sigh out of worry/frustration). Same 한숨, opposite mood — the verb makes all the difference.
It means a BRIEF breather right after a hectic spell, not a long rest or vacation. For real rest, say 푹 쉬다.
Don't insert 을 here — it's idiomatically 한숨 돌리다 (no object marker), unlike 한숨'을' 쉬다 where 을 is natural.

entries.shortExplanation: 김이 새다 is a practical expression meaning "for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')".
entries.explanation: 김이 새다 (gimi saeda) means "for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 김이 새다 ("for excitement/mood to fizzle out"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Full idiom; 김 (steam) + 새다 (leak); 김새다 is the contracted form.

usagePhrases.en: for the buzz to go flat
usagePhrases.note: Near-synonym with 빠지다 ('drain out'); interchangeable.
The everyday contracted spelling you'll hear most.
Common intensifier: 김이 팍 샜어 = the mood totally deflated.

examples.ko: 미리 결말 말하지 마, 김새잖아.
examples.romanization: miri gyeolmal malhaji ma, gimsaejana.
examples.en: Don't spoil the ending — it ruins it.
examples.note: Simple: contracted 김새다 with 잖아 ('you know it does').

examples.ko: 기대했는데 취소돼서 김이 새 버렸어.
examples.romanization: gidaehaenneunde chwisodwaeseo gimi sae beoryeosseo.
examples.en: I was looking forward to it but it got canceled, so the excitement fizzled.
examples.note: Everyday: 새 버리다 ('end up fizzling') adds finality.

examples.ko: 같이 보려고 기다렸더니 혼자 먼저 봤다길래 김이 팍 샜어요.
examples.romanization: gachi boryeogo gidaryeotdeoni honja meonjeo bwatdagillae gimi pak saesseoyo.
examples.en: I waited so we could watch it together, but they'd already watched it alone, so my excitement totally deflated.
examples.note: Real-situation: 팍 (totally) intensifies; -더니/-길래 frame an anticipation spoiled by someone jumping ahead.

entries.nuance: Literally 'the steam leaks out' — picture a hot 만두 or 김밥 going limp as its steam escapes — and it means built-up excitement or a good mood suddenly goes flat. You say it when something spoils the anticipation: a cancellation, a spoiler, a buzzkill comment, plans unraveling. Its near-synonym is 김(이) 빠지다 ('the steam drains out'), essentially interchangeable in everyday speech. Don't confuse it with 흥이 깨지다 ('the festive mood is broken') — that specifically describes a lively, party-like 흥 (merriment) being shattered, whereas 김이 새다 is the broader, quieter deflation of any built-up anticipation. Register is casual; the contracted 김새다 is the form you'll hear most, and 김 빠지다 is its twin. The English-speaker pitfall is a homonym trap: the 김 here is steam/vapor, NOT 김 the edible seaweed (laver) — there is no food in this idiom. And it describes deflated feeling, not a literal leak, so never use it for actual gas or air escaping. Natural partners: 팍 (suddenly/totally), 미리 말하다 (spoil it in advance), 반응이 없다 (no reaction).

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

entries.nuance: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying over something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. It is far stronger and more visceral than plain 걱정하다 ('to worry'): 걱정하다 is the everyday mental act of worrying, while 속이 타다 is the physical, churning agony of it, the way English 'worried SICK' outweighs 'worried.' A close synonym idiom is 애가 타다 (애 = innards/heart-strings), nearly identical in force. The key grammar is the 이/을 voice pair: 속'이' 타다 = YOU feel the burning anxiety (it happens to you), whereas the causative 속'을' 태우다 = to fret, or to MAKE someone else worry (자식이 부모 속을 태운다 = a child makes the parents worry). Register is casual-to-polite; intensify with 속이 타들어 가다 ('burning deeper inward') or the hyperbolic 속이 타 죽겠어 ('dying of anxiety'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't read it as literal heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anguish — and don't swap the particles, or you reverse who is worrying and who is causing the worry.

It's stronger than 걱정하다. Don't downgrade it to mere 'worry' in feel — 속이 타다 is 'worried sick,' the churning, can't-sit-still kind.

entries.nuance: Literally 'there's no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid hyperbole for a place so packed with people that you couldn't even find space to step. Use it for jammed streets, stores, subways, festivals — anywhere overflowing with a crowd — usually with a slightly overwhelmed tone. Its Sino-Korean near-synonym is 인산인해 (人山人海, literally 'people-mountain, people-sea'), a punchier four-character idiom for an enormous throng; 발 디딜 틈이 없다 is the more conversational, everyday way to say it. The single most important thing to get right is spacing and the verb: it is 발 디딜 틈이 없다, where 발 디딜 (from 발을 디디다, 'to set a foot down') modifies 틈 ('gap') — beginners wrongly fuse it as 발디딜. The English-speaker pitfall is scope: this idiom is specifically about a CROWD of people, so don't use it for a room cluttered with objects — for that you'd say 발 디딜 곳이 없다 only loosely, or better 어질러져 있다 (it's a mess). Natural partners: 주말 (weekend), 출근 시간 (rush hour), 축제 (festival), 발 디딜 틈도 없이 (so packed that…).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing/verb error: it's 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (발 디딜 = 'to step,' from 발을 디디다), not the fused 발디딜. Keep the space and the verb 디디다.
It's specifically about crowds of PEOPLE, not a room cluttered with objects. For a messy, cluttered space use 어질러져 있다 or 발 디딜 곳이 없다 (loosely), not this crowd idiom.
Don't drop 틈: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 needs 틈 ('gap'). 발 디딜 데가 없다 exists but shifts nuance toward 'nowhere to step/stand,' so keep 틈이 없다 for the 'jam-packed' meaning.

entries.shortExplanation: 그렇구나 is a practical expression meaning "Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.".
entries.explanation: 그렇구나 (geureokuna) means "Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그렇구나 ("oh, I see"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 그렇구나 (casual) / 그렇군요 (polite) is the 'oh, I see — that's news to me' you breathe out the instant a new fact clicks. It is built from 그렇다 'to be so' + the discovery ending -구나/-군요, which Korean reserves for something you have JUST taken in, so it always carries a faint flavor of fresh realization. The line to draw is against 그러게(요): 그렇구나 receives NEW information ('I didn't know that'), while 그러게 means 'right, I feel the same' about something you already shared — answer a surprising fact with 그러게요 and you sound like you knew all along. Reacting to a past event, shift to 그랬구나 'oh, so that happened.' The English-speaker pitfall is register: 'I see' feels neutral in English, so learners drop plain 그렇구나 on a boss or elder, but the bare -구나 is banmal; with anyone you keep -요 with, it must be 그렇군요, and to a senior even 그러시군요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그렇구나 to a boss, teacher, or elder — the bare -구나 is casual banmal and sounds too familiar; use 그렇군요 (polite) or 그러시군요 (honorific) instead.
Answering surprising NEW info with 그러게요 instead of 그렇군요 — 그러게(요) means 'right, same here' about a shared feeling, so it implies you already knew; for genuinely new facts use 그렇구나/그렇군요.
Using present 그렇구나 for something that already happened — if a friend tells you about a past event, the natural reaction is the past form 그랬구나, not 그렇구나.

entries.nuance: 하긴 is a casual discourse opener that means 'now that you put it that way, you've got a point' — a small step back where you reconsider and half-concede. It is the frozen, idiomatic shortening of 하기는 (하다 'to do' + the topic-contrast -기는), and it almost always opens the reply, usually as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네. The contrast to keep clear is with 그러게(요): 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 하긴 means 'I hadn't thought of it that way — but yes, fair.' That reconsideration nuance is the whole point. Register-wise it is firmly banmal-flavored, everywhere among friends and 20-30s coworkers off the clock, but in formal or business speech it sounds too offhand; there you say 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a full 'yes': 하긴 is a mild 'fair point,' not a strong agreement, and dropping it into a meeting reads as flippant.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 하긴 as full, firm agreement — it is a mild 'fair enough, you have a point,' not a strong yes; for committed agreement say 맞아 / 맞아요 or 그러게.
Using 하긴 in a formal meeting or with a superior — it sounds too offhand and casual; switch to 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요.

entries.nuance: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' you say the moment a small mystery gets solved — you had quietly noticed something off, and the new fact snaps it into place. It is rooted in 어찌 'how/why' + the indefinite -ㄴ지, so under the hood it carries 'so THAT'S why,' and it loves to pair with the retrospective ending -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to replay what you had observed. The dangerous look-alike is 어쨌든 'anyway/regardless': they share the 어쩌- stem and beginners blur them, but 어쩐지 is causal ('that's the reason') while 어쨌든 dismisses the reason ('regardless of the reason'). A second, softer near-synonym is 그래서 그랬구나 'so that's why,' which is more explicit; 어쩐지 keeps it punchy. It works in casual and softly polite speech alike — just surround it with 요-level verbs for politeness. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'why' (왜): 어쩐지 is not a question, it is a satisfied 'ah, no wonder.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 어쩐지 (no wonder, causal) with 어쨌든 (anyway, regardless) — they share the 어쩌- root but are opposites: 어쩐지 embraces the reason, 어쨌든 sets it aside.
Treating 어쩐지 as a question like 왜 ('why?') — it is a reaction meaning 'ah, that explains it,' so it expects no answer.
Forgetting the -더라 that usually follows — saying just 어쩐지 피곤해 (present) loses the 'I'd noticed it earlier' feel; the natural form is 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.

entries.nuance: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and its job is to DROP the current thread and bring up something else you actually want to talk about — a topic switch, not a wrap-up. It comes from 그러나저러나 'this way or that way,' so it literally shrugs off the previous talk to pivot. The contrast you must keep sharp is with 아무튼/어쨌든: those CONCLUDE the present topic and drive to its point, whereas 그나저나 abandons it for a NEW one — answer 'so what's the conclusion?' with 그나저나 and you've changed the subject instead of finishing. It feels casual and warm, like a friendly nudge ('oh, by the way…'), and pairs habitually with 말이야 or a follow-up question (그나저나 밥은?). It is fine in everyday polite talk, but in formal writing or business email it is too chatty; there you use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라. English speakers map all of 'anyway / by the way / regardless' onto one word, so they reach for 그나저나 when they mean to conclude — that is the trap.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그나저나 to wrap up and conclude the current topic — that is 아무튼/어쨌든's job; 그나저나 switches to a brand-new topic, so it derails a conclusion.
Putting 그나저나 in formal writing or a business email — it is conversational and too chatty there; use 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라.
Confusing it with 그러나 'however' because they look alike — 그러나 contrasts ideas within one topic, while 그나저나 leaves the topic entirely.

entries.nuance: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and LAND on what counts — it concludes the current thread rather than opening a new one. It is built from 아무 'any' + the -든 'whichever' ending, so it literally says 'whatever the case, here's the point.' Two contrasts matter. First, against 그나저나: 그나저나 switches to a different topic, while 아무튼 wraps up THIS one — they are not interchangeable even though both translate as 'anyway.' Second, against its closest twin 어쨌든: the two are near-identical and usually swappable, but 어쨌든 leans a hair more on 'no matter what the situation,' often after weighing options, while 아무튼 is the everyday 'anyhow, moving on.' It rides from casual to polite comfortably; 아무튼 간에 adds a touch more 'no matter what.' The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'anyway' to cover both the topic-switch and the wrap-up — in Korean those are 그나저나 and 아무튼, and mixing them confuses listeners.

Assuming 아무튼 and 어쨌든 are always identical — they overlap heavily, but 어쨌든 leans more on 'regardless of the case,' often after weighing reasons, while 아무튼 is the plain 'anyhow, moving on.'
Stretching 아무튼 to mean 'either way both options are fine' — for genuinely weighing two outcomes, 어쨌든 fits better; 아무튼 just signals 'enough detail, here's the point.'

entries.nuance: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was just said, declare it doesn't change the outcome, and move on. entries.nuance: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴 (그렇다 'be so' + the contrast-marking -긴), then -ㄴ데 swings the door open for your reservation. The whole move is a gentle, face-saving disagreement: concede first so the 'but' doesn't sting. The contrast to internalize is with a flat 아니 'no' or 그건 아니지 'that's not it': those reject head-on, while 그렇긴 한데 keeps the other person's dignity by agreeing partway first — Korean conversation strongly prefers this cushioned route. Note also that the -긴 here carries a faint 'true ENOUGH, but…' reluctance that plain 그런데 lacks. It is casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spacing — 긴 attaches to 그렇 (그렇긴), it is never 그렇 긴; and skipping the concession and jumping straight to the objection, which in Korean lands as blunt and a little cold.

entries.nuance: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes — it radiates welcome, not mere consent. It is 그렇다 'to be so' contracted to 그럼 plus the polite -요, so it literally affirms 'it certainly IS so.' Its near-synonym is 당연하죠 'naturally/obviously,' and the two often stack (그럼요, 당연하죠) for extra warmth; the subtle difference is that 당연하죠 stresses 'that goes without saying,' while 그럼요 stresses friendly readiness. The plain-speech version is 그럼 for friends. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is a homograph clash: the SAME letters 그럼 also serve as the transition word 'then / in that case' (그럼 가자 'then let's go'). With the -요 attached, 그럼요 is almost always the emphatic 'of course'; the connective sense is the bare 그럼 plus a clause. Mixing them up makes you answer a yes/no question with 'well then…', which is confusing. Collocations: 그럼요 readily precedes 앉으세요 / 드세요 / 그렇게 하세요 when you grant something.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Confusing 그럼요 (of course) with the transition 그럼 (then / in that case) — 그럼요 with -요 is an emphatic 'yes, of course,' while bare 그럼 + a clause means 'then…'; answering a question with the connective sense sounds off.
Saying plain 그럼 to a customer, senior, or stranger when you mean 'of course' — that is casual; the polite warm form is 그럼요.
Using 그럼요 to mean a neutral, lukewarm 'yes' — it is emphatic and warm ('absolutely!'); for a flat, factual yes use 네 / 예 instead.

entries.nuance: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that signals you feel EXACTLY the same — most often about something mildly annoying, regrettable, or that you half-predicted, so it can carry a soft 'told you so.' It comes from 그러다 'to be/do so' + the -게 ending and works as a fellow-feeling echo. The contrast to fix is against 그렇구나: 그러게 agrees with a feeling you ALREADY share ('yeah, I know, right?'), while 그렇구나 receives a NEW fact you didn't know ('oh, I see') — answer 'it's freezing' with 그렇구나 and you sound like cold weather is breaking news. A second near-synonym is 내 말이(야) 'that's exactly what I'm saying,' which is even more emphatic and pairs with it (그러게, 내 말이). Use 그러게 with friends, 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with, and 그러게 말이야 to ramp the agreement up. The English-speaker pitfall is mishearing the rising tone as the question 'why did you do that?' — it is purely an agreeing reaction, not a 'why.'

Using 그러게 to react to brand-new information — 그러게 echoes a feeling you ALREADY share; for news you just learned, use 그렇구나 / 그렇군요.
Saying plain 그러게 to a senior — it is banmal; with someone you keep -요 with, use 그러게요.

entries.nuance: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the connective -길래, and the defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself: that is exactly what separates it from plain 그래서, which is a neutral 'so' that can take any subject. So 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained, neutral cause) is fine, but to say 'YOU kept saying it's good, so I tried it' you need 하도 맛있다고 그러길래 시켜 봤어 — the cause sits with them. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…). A close cousin is -기에, which means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form. The English-speaker pitfall: learners use 그러길래 for their own internal reason (because I was tired, because I wanted to) — for that you must use 그래서, since -길래 demands an external trigger from someone else.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러길래 (or -길래) for your OWN reason — it must react to someone else's words or actions; for your own internal reason ('because I was tired') use 그래서, e.g. 피곤해서, not 피곤하길래.
Writing -길래 in a formal essay or report — there the more literary -기에 is expected; -길래 is the casual spoken form.

structuredNuance.t: 그러길래 explains YOUR own action as a reaction to what someone ELSE said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. The defining feature is that -길래 always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself. So to say 'YOU kept saying it's good, so I tried it' you need 하도 맛있다고 그러길래 시켜 봤어 — the cause sits with them. It is casual and conversational, the reason frequently trailing off with the result left implied (다들 바쁘다 그러길래…).

What separates it from plain 그래서, a neutral 'so' that can take any subject: 비가 와서 우산을 샀어 (it rained, neutral cause) is fine, but -길래 always points the cause at the other party. A close cousin is -기에, which means the same but is more written/formal; -길래 is the spoken form.
It is 그러다 'to do/be so' + the connective -길래.
Learners use 그러길래 for their own internal reason (because I was tired, because I wanted to) — for that you must use 그래서, since -길래 demands an external trigger from someone else.

entries.nuance: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a SOFT inference from something you observe rather than to state a fact outright. The engine is the ending -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 'it looks like / I guess,' which marks a guess drawn from external evidence, so 그런가 봐요 = 'from what I can see, it seems to be so.' The contrast that matters is against -겠- and against 것 같다. -겠다 (그렇겠어요) is a quicker, more confident 'it must be so' from reasoning, while -나 보다 leans on observed evidence and stays more tentative; 그런 것 같아요 is very close but slightly more subjective ('I think so'), whereas 그런가 봐요 implies 'the signs suggest so.' Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends, and flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.' Two English-speaker pitfalls: spacing — standard is 그런가 봐요, with 봐요 written separately as the auxiliary (not 그런가봐요); and don't use -나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you don't 'guess' your own state, so '배고픈가 봐요' about yourself is odd unless you mean it half-jokingly.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 그런가봐요 — the standard is 그런가 봐요, with the auxiliary 봐요 written as a separate word.
Using -(으)ㄴ가/나 보다 about your OWN feelings or actions — you infer about others/the world, not yourself; for your own state say 그런 것 같아요 or just state it, not 그런가 봐요.
Swapping it for confident -겠어요 when you only have a hunch — 그런가 봐요 is tentative (evidence-based guess); 그렇겠어요 sounds like a firmer 'it must be so.'

entries.english: Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.
entries.shortExplanation: 듣고 보니 is a practical expression meaning "Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.".
entries.explanation: 듣고 보니 (deutgo boni) = "Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 듣고 보니 ("now that you mention it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: 듣고 보니 literally stacks 듣다 'to hear' + -고 보니 'having done and then found,' so it means 'now that I've heard it (and looked back), I realize…' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, almost always ending up agreeing. The -고 보니 frame is a 'do X, then discover' construction (cf. 가 보니 'on going, I found,' 자고 보니 'after sleeping, I realized'), which is why it signals a fresh after-the-fact realization rather than a prior opinion. The contrast to keep is against 그러게: 그러게 means 'right, I already felt the same,' but 듣고 보니 means 'I hadn't seen it that way until you said it — and now I do,' so it foregrounds a CHANGE of mind. It naturally flows into 그렇네 or 맞네 to mark that the penny dropped. It is comfortable in casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause. The English-speaker pitfall is reading -고 보니 as a plain 'after listening' time sequence — in conversation it specifically conveys 'on second thought, I now agree,' not just chronology.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 듣고 보니 as merely 'after listening' (time order) — in conversation it specifically signals 'now that you mention it, I've reconsidered and tend to agree.'
Using 듣고 보니 when you already held that view — it marks a CHANGE of mind prompted by what you just heard; if you already agreed, use 그러게 or 내 말이.
Confusing the -고 보니 'discover after doing' frame with -고 (으)려고 'intending to' — 듣고 보니 means 'on hearing, I found,' not 'in order to hear.'

entries.english: Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)
entries.shortExplanation: 그러게 말이에요 is a practical expression meaning "Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)".
entries.explanation: 그러게 말이에요 (geureoge marieyo) means "Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요. ("Tell me about it — I was thinking the exact same thing."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
