entries.nuance: Whole-hearted, sympathetic agreement that means far more than a flat 네 or 맞아요 — it carries the extra charge 'and I've felt exactly that myself.' Built from 그러게 ('right, isn't it') plus 말이에요 (literally 'it is [my] words'), it's the heavier, more emphatic cousin of plain 그러게요: where 그러게요 is a quick nod, 그러게 말이에요 is a shared sigh that says 'you took the words out of my mouth.' Contrast it with 맞아요, which simply confirms a fact ('that's correct'); 그러게 말이에요 instead bonds you emotionally over a shared feeling, usually a complaint or a 'what can you do' resignation. It is casual-polite (해요체); drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends and go up to 그러게 말입니다 with a boss. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for it to accept a compliment about yourself ('You're so good!' → 그러게 말이에요 sounds like you're agreeing you're great) — it only mirrors the other person's observation, so reserve it for things you both perceive from the outside.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

English speakers use it to accept praise ('You did great!' → 그러게 말이에요), which sounds like smug self-agreement. It's only for echoing a remark about something you both see, not about yourself — for praise say 감사합니다 instead.
It only confirms what was just said, so don't follow it with a counter-argument. To agree-then-disagree you need 그건 그런데… ('that's true, but…'), not 그러게 말이에요.
Don't shorten it to just 말이에요 hoping to keep the meaning — without 그러게 it just means 'I'm telling you / it's true,' losing the empathetic-agreement function.

entries.nuance: An everyday repair phrase you fire off the instant someone misreads your words or your motive: literally '그게 (that) + 아니라 (it is not, and so…).' The 아니라 form is the connective of 아니다 ('to not be'), so the phrase is grammatically unfinished on purpose — it leans forward into the correct version that must follow. Leading with 그게 아니라 softens a correction the way English 'no, what I mean is…' does: you're fixing a misunderstanding, not winning an argument, so it protects the other person's face. Distinguish it carefully from 그게 아니면, which sounds nearly identical but means 'if not that, then…' and offers an alternative rather than denying; and from 그런 게 아니라 ('it's not that kind of thing'), which denies a whole category rather than one specific claim. It rides any speech level — add 요 (그게 아니라요) for extra politeness. The pitfall for English speakers: treating it as a standalone 'No.' Korean expects the true statement attached right after, or you sound like you cut yourself off.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
English speakers use it as a complete reply ('That's not it.') and stop. Korean needs the real meaning attached: 그게 아니라 + your actual point. On its own it leaves the listener waiting.
Confusing 그게 아니라 (denying: 'it's not that') with 그게 아니면 (offering an alternative: 'if not that, then…'). One corrects, the other proposes a plan B — swapping them derails the conversation.
Saying 그것이 아니라 in casual speech sounds stiff and bookish; the natural spoken contraction is 그게 아니라. Reserve the full 그것이 for formal writing.

entries.nuance: A connector for the exact moment a thought clicks into place. It breaks down as 그러고 ('having done/been so') + 보니 ('upon looking,' the -고 보니 'do and then realize' pattern), so literally 'looking at it that way, I now notice…' — the realization is fresh, sparked by what someone just said or by something you glanced at. Compare 그러고 보니 with 알고 보니 ('as it turns out / on closer inspection it was actually…'), which reveals a hidden truth, and with 듣고 보니 ('now that I've heard it'), which is specifically prompted by hearing the other person out; 그러고 보니 is the broadest 'huh, now that I consider it.' The form is identical across speech levels — only the verb ending that follows changes (보니 오늘…네요 vs …네). Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, it marks NEW awareness, so don't use it for facts you already knew. Second, watch the spacing and spelling — 그러고 (from 그러다) is not 그리고 ('and'); a single vowel flips the whole meaning, and it stays two words: 그러고 보니.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it for something you already knew. 그러고 보니 specifically flags a fresh realization; for known facts use 사실은 ('actually') or just state it plainly.
Writing or saying 그리고 보니 instead of 그러고 보니. 그리고 means 'and'; 그러고 (from 그러다, 'to do so') is the correct base. The mix-up is the single most common slip here.
Jamming it into a single word (그러고보니). Standard spacing keeps 그러고 보니 as two words; the 보니 part is a separate verb.

entries.english: Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)
entries.shortExplanation: 그래서 그런지 is a practical expression meaning "Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)".
entries.explanation: 그래서 그런지 (geuraeseo geureonji) means "Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요. ("I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 그래서 그런지 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

entries.nuance: A soft, speculative cause-marker meaning 'I suspect this is the reason, though I'm not certain.' The key is the -ㄴ지 ending (from 그렇다, 'to be so'): 그런지 literally asks-to-itself 'whether it's so,' which is what bakes in the hedge. So 그래서 그런지 = 'so, [maybe] because of that…,' pointing back to a reason you just gave, while -아서/어서 그런지 and -(이)라 그런지 attach the guess directly onto a cause ('because it rained, perhaps…' / 'because it's the weekend, perhaps…'). The sharp contrast to learn is against bare 그래서 ('so, therefore'), which states a cause you're SURE of: 비가 와서 길이 막혀요 ('it's raining so traffic is jammed' — definite) versus 비가 와서 그런지 길이 막히네요 ('maybe because it's raining, traffic seems jammed' — tentative observation). Using plain 그래서 when you're only guessing sounds overconfident; using 그래서 그런지 when the cause is obvious sounds oddly wishy-washy. It describes an observed result, so the English-speaker trap is trying to bolt a command or request onto it (그래서 그런지 + '…please do X') — it can only end in a statement of what you noticed.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그래서 그런지 for a cause you're certain of. It always carries a 'maybe' hedge; for a definite cause-effect, drop to plain 그래서 (e.g. 비가 와서 길이 막혀요).
Attaching a request or command after it ('그래서 그런지 좀 도와주세요'). It links a cause to an OBSERVED result, so it must end in a statement of what you noticed, not an imperative.
Mishandling the connector on a noun: it's 주말이라 그런지 (N+이라), not 주말이어서 그런지 in casual speech. With 이다, the natural form is N(이)라 그런지.

It describes an observed result, so the trap is trying to bolt a command or request onto it (그래서 그런지 + '…please do X') — it can only end in a statement of what you noticed.

entries.nuance: A friendly topic-switcher that literally says 'that — that's so, and…' (그건 = 그것은 'that thing' contracted; 그렇고 = 그렇다 'to be so' + connective -고). It gently certifies the current topic as settled ('right, that's how it is') before swinging to a new one, which is why it never feels abrupt — you're acknowledging, not dropping. Compare three neighbors: 그건 그렇고 closes a topic to open any new one; 그나저나 ('anyway / be that as it may') is an almost interchangeable swap with the same easy register; but 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it's come up') does the OPPOSITE — it segues to a RELATED point rather than away to a new one. So if the next thing connects, use 말이 나왔으니까; if you're leaving the subject behind, use 그건 그렇고. It's casual-polite and extremely common in speech. Pitfalls for English speakers: don't deploy it to disagree — 'by the way' in English can preface a jab, but 그건 그렇고 only steers topics, never pushes back. And mind the spelling: it's 그건 (one contracted word) 그렇고, and 그렇고 keeps the ㅎ (don't write 그러고, which is a different verb).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it to disagree or push back, the way English 'by the way…' sometimes does. 그건 그렇고 only changes the topic; to object you'd say 그건 아니고 ('that's not it') or 그렇긴 한데 ('that may be, but…').
Spelling 그렇고 as 그러고. 그렇고 comes from 그렇다 ('to be so') and keeps the ㅎ; 그러고 comes from 그러다 ('to do so') and means something else. Different verb, different meaning.
Using it to introduce a closely RELATED follow-up. If the new remark grows out of the same topic, the natural choice is 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it came up'); 그건 그렇고 implies you're leaving the topic behind.

entries.shortExplanation: 말이 나왔으니까 is a practical expression meaning "Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)".
entries.explanation: 말이 나왔으니까 (mari nawasseunikka) = "Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요. ("Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too."). entries.nuance: A spoken segue that piggybacks on a topic someone just raised so your follow-up feels invited rather than out of nowhere. It parses as 말이 ('the topic/word,' subject) + 나왔으니까 (나오다 'to come out' in past + -(으)니까 'since/because'), i.e. 'since the subject has come out.' The fuller, very idiomatic 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it's come up, this is what I'll say…') typically front-loads a candid opinion or a small request, cushioning it. Two contrasts sharpen its use: against 그건 그렇고, which switches AWAY to an unrelated topic — 말이 나왔으니까 instead leans INTO the current one; and against the casual cousin 말 나온 김에 (using -(으)ㄴ 김에 'while we're at it'), which stresses convenient timing ('as long as we're on it, let's do it now') more than the candid-remark flavor. Casual-polite, and you can shorten to 말 나온 김에 with friends. The English-speaker pitfall: 'speaking of which…' in English can pivot to anything loosely associated, but 말이 나왔으니까 demands a genuinely related thread that JUST surfaced — for an unrelated jump, you need 그건 그렇고. And like the other lead-ins here, it's incomplete on its own; the real point must follow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it to jump to an unrelated topic, the way English 'speaking of which' can drift. 말이 나왔으니까 requires the point to be genuinely tied to what just came up; for an unrelated switch use 그건 그렇고.
Leaving it dangling as if it were a full sentence. It's a lead-in — you must follow it with the actual remark or request (often via …말인데, …할게요, …물어볼게요).
Mis-conjugating 나오다: it's 나왔으니까 (past + 으니까), not 나오니까. The topic has ALREADY come up, so the past tense is what makes the 'now that it's surfaced' meaning work.

entries.english: Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)
entries.shortExplanation: 다행이네요 is a practical expression meaning "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)".
entries.explanation: 다행이네요 (dahaengineyo) means "Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 다 잘 끝났다니 다행이네요. ("I'm glad to hear it all worked out."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.note: Real situation: relief after a genuine scare

entries.nuance: A warm, sincere reaction of relief. The core noun is Sino-Korean 다행 (多幸), literally 'much (多) good fortune (幸),' so the phrase means 'how fortunate' rather than just 'good.' Aimed at someone else's news it reads as caring ('I'm relieved FOR you'); about your own situation it's a heartfelt 'phew.' The -네요 ending (해요체) adds spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth — a beat more emotional than the flatter 다행이에요. Don't confuse this relief word with two near neighbors: 잘됐네요 ('that turned out well / good for you') celebrates a positive OUTCOME you're happy about, whereas 다행이에요 specifically exhales relief that something bad was AVOIDED; and 축하해요 ('congratulations') honors an achievement someone earned, not a near-miss they survived. Casual form is 다행이다 with friends. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the spelling slip 다행이네요 vs 다행히: 다행이네요 uses the NOUN 다행 + 이다, but 다행히 is the ADVERB 'fortunately' (다행히 늦지 않았어요, 'fortunately we weren't late') and can't end a sentence as a reaction. Mixing them produces ungrammatical Korean.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 다행히네요 or ending a reaction with 다행히. 다행히 is the adverb 'fortunately' and modifies a verb; the relief reaction is 다행이에요/다행이네요 (noun 다행 + 이다).
Using it as congratulations for an achievement. 다행이에요 is relief that something bad was avoided; for an earned success say 축하해요, and for a happy outcome say 잘됐네요.
Saying 다행이네요 about a trivial non-event where nothing was ever at risk. The word implies there WAS a worry or danger that has now passed — without that tension it sounds odd.

structuredNuance.t: A warm, sincere reaction of relief. Aimed at someone else's news it reads as caring ('I'm relieved FOR you'); about your own situation it's a heartfelt 'phew.' The -네요 ending (해요체) adds spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth — a beat more emotional than the flatter 다행이에요. Casual form is 다행이다 with friends.

Don't confuse this relief word with two near neighbors: 잘됐네요 ('that turned out well / good for you') celebrates a positive OUTCOME you're happy about, whereas 다행이에요 specifically exhales relief that something bad was AVOIDED; and 축하해요 ('congratulations') honors an achievement someone earned, not a near-miss they survived.
The core noun is Sino-Korean 다행 (多幸), literally 'much (多) good fortune (幸),' so the phrase means 'how fortunate' rather than just 'good.'

The classic spelling slip is 다행이네요 vs 다행히: 다행이네요 uses the NOUN 다행 + 이다, but 다행히 is the ADVERB 'fortunately' (다행히 늦지 않았어요, 'fortunately we weren't late') and can't end a sentence as a reaction. Mixing them produces ungrammatical Korean.

entries.nuance: A high-alarm reaction that literally says 'a big thing (큰일) has happened (났다).' 큰일 is 큰 ('big') + 일 ('matter/affair'), and 났다 is the past of 나다 ('to occur/break out'), so the whole thing is 'a major affair has broken out' — fired off the moment you realize something's gone wrong or is about to. Tone runs the full range from real panic to a half-joking 'uh-oh.' Mind the tense, because it shifts the meaning: 큰일 났다/났어 (past) = trouble has ALREADY landed; 큰일 나다 in future/conditional (이러다 큰일 나겠다, 큰일 날 뻔했다) warns of trouble LOOMING or narrowly dodged. Contrast it with the gentler 어쩌나 ('oh dear, what to do'), which is soft, sympathetic worry usually on someone ELSE's behalf, whereas 큰일 났다 is an urgent alarm about a concrete problem, often your own. Casual as 큰일 났다/났어; polite as 큰일 났어요, and it loves pairing with 어떡해 ('what do I do'). Two pitfalls: keep 큰일 as ONE noun (write 큰일 났다, not 큰 일 났다 as separate words in this fixed expression), and don't fire it at trivial inconveniences — it implies a real problem, even when you're exaggerating for comic effect.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spacing it as 큰 일 in this fixed expression. Here 큰일 ('serious trouble') is treated as one word; written apart, 큰 일 reads literally as 'a big task' and loses the idiom.

Using the past 큰일 났다 for trouble that hasn't happened yet. For looming danger use the future/conditional: 이러다 큰일 나겠다 ('something bad's going to happen at this rate') or 큰일 날 뻔했다 ('almost went wrong').

Deploying it for minor annoyances (a small typo, a tiny delay). It implies a genuinely serious problem; overusing it for trifles makes you sound melodramatic. For small hiccups, 어떡하지 or 아 이런 fits better.

entries.nuance: A soft exclamation of worry or tenderness — 'oh dear, what's to be done.' It contracts from 어찌하나 ('how shall [I/we] do it'): 어찌 ('how') + 하다 ('do') + the musing -나 ending, which is a question you murmur to yourself rather than ask out loud. That self-directed quality is why it lands as a feeling, not a real request for instructions. It can stand alone as a reaction or nest inside a sentence ('…ㄹ까 봐 / …면 어쩌나 싶다' = 'worried that…'). The crucial contrast is with 큰일 났다: 큰일 났다 is loud alarm about a concrete problem, often your own, while 어쩌나 is gentler, warmer, and typically aimed at SOMEONE ELSE's predicament — concern, not panic. Its near-synonym 어쩌지 leans toward your OWN dilemma ('what should I do?'), whereas 어쩌나 more often sighs over another person's plight; 어쩌니 is a softer, slightly old-fashioned color. The pitfall for English speakers: because it LOOKS like a question (and even ends like one), learners answer it or use it to actually solicit advice. It isn't a genuine question — it's an empathetic sigh. If you truly want guidance, ask 어떻게 하죠? or 어떡하면 좋을까요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating standalone 어쩌나 as a real question and waiting for / giving an answer. It's an expression of feeling, not a request for advice. To actually ask, use 어떻게 하죠? or 어떡하면 좋아요?
Aiming it at someone as criticism ('어쩌나' with a blaming tone). It conveys sympathy and worry, never reproach — pointing it accusingly at a person misreads the warmth built into it.
Confusing 어쩌나 (soft worry, often for others) with 어쩌지 (your own 'what should I do'). They overlap, but 어쩌지 fits self-directed indecision better, while 어쩌나 suits sighing over another's trouble.

entries.nuance: An easygoing, generous phrase meaning 'that falls within the range of normal — no big deal.' It's built from 그렇다 ('to be so') → 그럴 (prospective modifier) + 수도 있다 ('there's even the possibility'), with 수 being the bound noun for 'possibility/ability,' so literally 'there could even be such a case.' The -죠 (from -지요) ending fishes for soft mutual agreement — 'right?' — which is what makes it sound understanding rather than declarative. Its job is to forgive a minor mistake, validate a feeling, or grant that a possibility is reasonable, making it the warm opposite of 말도 안 돼요 ('that makes no sense / no way'). Draw a sharp line against the near-twin 그럴 리가 없죠: identical rhythm, opposite meaning — 그럴 수도 있죠 ACCEPTS that something is possible/understandable, while 그럴 리가 없죠 DENIES it ('there's no way that's true'). One 수 vs 리 flips acceptance into disbelief. Casual as 그럴 수도 있지. The English-speaker pitfall: because it signals 'understandable, no harm done,' don't aim it at something genuinely serious — replying 그럴 수도 있죠 to a real grievance or a big mistake sounds flippant and dismissive, as if you're shrugging off something that actually matters.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Using it to brush off something serious. 그럴 수도 있죠 means 'that's understandable / no big deal,' so applied to a real problem or a hurt feeling it sounds flippant. For weighty matters, acknowledge properly rather than minimizing.
Confusing 그럴 수도 있죠 (accepting: 'it's possible / that happens') with 그럴 리가 없죠 (denying: 'no way that's true'). The 수 vs 리 swap reverses the meaning entirely.
Spacing 그럴 수도 as 그럴수도. 수 is a bound noun and stays a separate word: 그럴 수도 있죠. Writing it joined is a common orthography slip.

It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요. ("Yes, I think that'd be best."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: A polite, gentle recommendation. The engine is the pattern V-는 게 좋겠다 — 는 게 (from 는 것이, 'the act of doing') + 좋겠다 ('would be good'), literally 'it'd be good if [you/we] did ~,' i.e. English 'had better' or 'I think you should.' The all-important -겠- is a softener of supposition here, downgrading a bare fact (좋다, 'is good') into a tentative 'would (probably) be good,' so you advise without bossing. 그러는 게 좋겠어요 specifically endorses a course ALREADY raised in the conversation ('yes — doing that would be best'), with 그러다 ('to do so') standing in for the action just mentioned. Two contrasts matter. First, against the blunt command V-(으)세요 ('do it'): 예약하세요 orders, while 예약하는 게 좋겠어요 merely advises — choosing the imperative where advice is expected can sound pushy to a peer. Second, against V-는 게 어때요? ('how about doing ~?'), which OFFERS an option and leaves the decision open, whereas -는 게 좋겠어요 states your considered RECOMMENDATION. Casual form is 그러는 게 좋겠어. English-speaker pitfalls: don't translate 'you'd better' with its English threat-flavor — Korean -는 게 좋겠어요 is soft, not a warning; and keep the spacing 그러는 게 (게 = 것이 contracted) as a separate word.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using it where a firm instruction is needed. -는 게 좋겠어요 is advice, not a command; for a clear directive (to a subordinate, on a sign, in instructions) use V-(으)세요.
Hearing 'you'd better' as a threat. In English 'you'd better…' can warn of consequences, but Korean V-는 게 좋겠어요 is gentle, considerate advice. Don't add a menacing tone that isn't there.
Spacing 그러는 게 as 그러는게. 게 is the contraction of 것이 ('the thing,' subject) and remains a separate word: 그러는 게 좋겠어요.

entries.english: Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')
entries.shortExplanation: 마음대로 하세요 is a practical expression meaning "Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')".
entries.explanation: 마음대로 하세요 (maeumdaero haseyo) = "Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 편하실 대로 마음대로 하세요. ("Please do whatever's comfortable for you."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: Means 'do it however you wish,' from 마음 ('mind/heart') + -대로 ('in accordance with') + 하세요 ('please do'), so literally 'act according to your heart.' Crucially, tone is the entire message: said warmly it's open-handed generosity ('go right ahead, no need to ask'); said flatly, with a sigh or clipped delivery, it flips into a frosty 'fine, do what you want, I give up' — the same words, opposite feeling, much like English 'suit yourself.' Compare the friendly cousin 마음껏 ('to your heart's content,' as in 마음껏 드세요): it shares the 마음 root but never carries the cold edge, so when you only mean warm encouragement, 마음껏 is the safer pick. Note too that the casual 마음대로 해 and the -든가 variant (마음대로 하든가, 'do whatever, see if I care') lean pointedly annoyed. Register: 마음대로 하세요 is polite-form, 마음대로 해 casual. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, because the icy reading is so easy to trigger, be careful aiming it at a senior or using it during any tension — it can land as dismissive or rude even when you meant it kindly. Second, spelling — it's one word 마음대로 (no space before 대로); the contraction 맘대로 is fine in casual chat but too informal for polite or written contexts.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Using it casually with a senior or in a tense moment without minding tone. The cold 'fine, whatever' reading triggers easily, so to a superior it can sound dismissive — soften with 편하실 대로 하세요 ('do as suits you') when you mean it warmly.
Spacing it as 마음 대로. -대로 is a particle attached to the noun, so it's one word: 마음대로. And 맘대로 (the 맘 contraction) is fine in casual speech but too informal for formal or written use.

Assuming it always sounds generous. Unlike 마음껏 ('to your heart's content,' always warm), 마음대로 하세요 can read as passive-aggressive depending on delivery — if you only mean encouragement, 마음껏 or 편하신 대로 is safer.

entries.english: for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')
entries.shortExplanation: 발등에 불 떨어지다 is a practical expression meaning "for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')".
entries.explanation: 발등에 불 떨어지다 (baldeunge bul tteoreojida) means "for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새 했어. ("It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 발등에 불 떨어지다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; pairs naturally with 코앞 ('right in front')

examples.romanization: dadeul baldeunge bul tteoreojin deusi hoeuisillo ttwieogasseo.
examples.en: Everyone ran to the meeting room like it was an emergency.
examples.note: Real-situation: -ㄴ 듯이 = 'as if'

entries.nuance: Literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot' — when a live ember lands on your foot you jump instantly, so this paints something that has suddenly become so urgent you must drop everything and react now. The near-synonym 코앞이다 ('right in front of your nose') only states that a deadline is close in time; 발등에 불 떨어지다 adds the panic of having to scramble this second, which is why it so often pairs with 부랴부랴 ('frantically') and 밤새다 ('pull an all-nighter'). It carries a self-aware, procrastinator's tone — Koreans say 발등에 불 떨어져야 움직인다 ('I only move once the fire hits my foot') about their own last-minute habit. Register is casual-to-polite and it is everywhere around work and deadlines. The English-speaker pitfall: do not read it literally as a burn injury, and remember 떨어지다 here means 'falls/drops,' not 'runs out' — so 'the fire fell' = the crisis has arrived, not departed.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't read it literally as a burn injury — it is about sudden urgency, not pain, so 'My foot got burned' is a complete mis-hearing.
It's 발등 (the top/instep of the foot), not 발 ('foot') — drop 등 and the vivid image of an ember landing on the exposed instep is lost.
Keep 떨어지다 in the right direction: it means the fire FELL (the crisis is here), so don't confuse it with the meaning 'to run out / be used up.'

entries.shortExplanation: 코앞이다 is a practical expression meaning "to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')".
entries.explanation: "to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')" — that is 코앞이다 (koapida). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 시험이 코앞이야, 큰일 났어. ("The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Casual; time sense, looming pressure

entries.nuance: Literally 'right in front of the nose,' 코앞 (코 'nose' + 앞 'front') frames something as extremely near — either in TIME (an event/deadline almost upon you) or in DISTANCE (a place a few steps away). The dividing line from the near-synonym 가깝다 ('to be close/near') is vividness and immediacy: 가깝다 is the neutral, measurable word ('the station is near'), while 코앞이다 dramatizes 'practically touching your face,' so it feels more pressing for time and more 'right there, no excuse' for distance. With time it loads on pressure (no buffer left); with distance it stresses how convenient/short the hop is. Register is casual-to-polite and it is used constantly. The English-speaker pitfall: 'right under my nose' in English usually means 'overlooked something obvious,' but Korean 코앞 plainly means 'very near' — so don't import the 'missed the obvious' nuance unless context (e.g. 코앞에 두고도 못 찾다) supplies it. Also write it as one word: 코앞, not 코 앞.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Write 코앞 as one word, not 코 앞 — it's a fixed compound noun.

Don't auto-map it to the English idiom 'right under my nose' (= 'missed something obvious'); plain 코앞이다 just means 'very close.'

entries.shortExplanation: 등골이 오싹하다 is a practical expression meaning "to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')".

Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 그 얘기 듣고 등골이 오싹했어. ("I got chills down my spine hearing that."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: 등골 is the line/marrow of the spine and 오싹하다 is that sudden, involuntary cold-shudder, so together they capture chills running down your back from fear, dread, eeriness, or the jolt of realizing you barely dodged disaster. The near-synonym is the listed variant 등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool'): 서늘하다 is a touch quieter and more lingering-dread, while 오싹하다 is the sharper, sudden goose-bump spike — useful when a noise or revelation hits you all at once. Contrast it with plain 무섭다 ('to be scared'), which only names the emotion; 등골이 오싹하다 gives you the bodily sensation, which is why it shines in horror, ghost stories, and near-miss anecdotes. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfall: this is fear-chills, NOT being physically cold from the weather (use 춥다 for that), and you must keep the body-part partner — 등골 goes with 오싹하다/서늘하다, so don't graft on 춥다 ('등골이 춥다' is unnatural).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about fear/dread chills, not feeling physically cold from the weather — for cold air you want 춥다, not 등골이 오싹하다.
Pair 등골 with 오싹하다 or 서늘하다 — don't swap in 춥다 ('cold'); '등골이 춥다' is not idiomatic.
Don't replace it with bare 무섭다 ('scary') when you mean the physical shiver — 무섭다 names the feeling, 등골이 오싹하다 conveys the spine reaction.

entries.english: to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)
entries.shortExplanation: 입에 침이 마르다 is a practical expression meaning "to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)".
entries.explanation: 입에 침이 마르다 (ibe chimi mareuda) means "to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라. ("Mom couldn't stop singing your praises."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: Literally 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — talk up how wonderful someone or something is for long enough and your mouth runs dry, so it means to praise lavishly, tirelessly, without pause. The dividing line from plain 칭찬하다 ('to praise') is intensity and duration: 칭찬하다 can be a single 'good job,' whereas 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다 means going on and on, gushing. It almost never stands alone — it is an adverbial that clamps onto a verb, nearly always 칭찬하다 ('praise'), 자랑하다 ('brag'), or 추천하다 ('recommend'), in the set forms 입에 침이 마르게 or 입에 침이 마르도록. The tone is warm and admiring. Casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfall: it has nothing to do with literal thirst or a dry mouth from dehydration, and you must not drop the partner verb — saying just '입에 침이 마르다' to mean 'I'm thirsty' is wrong; thirst is 목이 마르다 ('throat is dry').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It means praising endlessly, not literally being thirsty or having a dry mouth — for real thirst use 목이 마르다 ('my throat is dry').
Don't drop the verb — it's used as 입에 침이 마르게/마르도록 + (칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다), not as a standalone statement.
Don't conjugate it as a finished action ('입에 침이 말랐다' to describe one compliment); it lives in the adverbial -게/-도록 form modifying the praising verb.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to take off your shoes and step forward' — in old Korea shoes were valuable, so kicking them off to wade barefoot into a muddy job signalled 'I'm all in, no holding back,' hence eagerly stepping up to help, not half-heartedly. The dividing line from plain 돕다 ('to help') is the volunteered, wholehearted energy: 돕다 can be passive or asked-for, but 발 벗고 나서다 praises someone for taking the initiative for others, going out of their way. Compare 앞장서다 ('to take the lead / go in front'), which stresses leading a group from the front, while 발 벗고 나서다 stresses self-sacrificing willingness regardless of rank. It is warm and approving — almost always a compliment. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: watch the spacing, 발 벗고 나서다 is three orthographic words (not 발벗고); and because it implies voluntary, eager involvement, don't use it for reluctant, grudging, or coerced help.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mind the spacing: 발 벗고 나서다, not 발벗고 나서다 — 발 and 벗고 are separate words.
It implies wholehearted, voluntary effort to help — don't use it for reluctant or forced help; for that, plain 도와주다 (with 마지못해 'reluctantly') fits better.
Don't reduce it to 앞장서다 ('take the lead'): leading a group is one thing, but 발 벗고 나서다 highlights self-giving willingness, not necessarily being out front.

entries.english: to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')
entries.shortExplanation: 어깨가 무겁다 is a practical expression meaning "to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')".
entries.explanation: 어깨가 무겁다 (eokkaega mugeopda) means "to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 책임이 커서 어깨가 무거워. ("The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 어깨가 무겁다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.en: The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it.
usagePhrases.note: Casual; 책임 ('responsibility') is the core partner noun

usagePhrases.note: Polite/formal -습니다; staple of work speeches

usagePhrases.note: ~로서 ('in the role of'); family responsibility

usagePhrases.romanization: gidaega keun mankeum eokkaega deo mugeowo.
usagePhrases.en: The bigger the expectations, the heavier the burden.
usagePhrases.note: ~만큼 ('to the extent that') links expectation to pressure

examples.note: New role; -아지다 = 'became'

examples.romanization: dadeul naman minneundago hanikka eokkaega mugeowo.
examples.en: Everyone says they're counting on me, so I feel the weight.
examples.note: Pressure from others' trust

examples.ko: 큰 프로젝트를 혼자 맡아서 어깨가 너무 무거워요.
examples.romanization: keun peurojekteureul honja mataseo eokkaega neomu mugeowoyo.
examples.en: I'm handling a big project alone, so the burden feels heavy.
examples.note: Real-situation heavy workload; 혼자 = 'alone'

entries.nuance: Literally 'heavy shoulders,' it expresses the psychological weight of responsibility or others' expectations pressing down on you — the felt seriousness of a duty. The dividing line from the near-synonym 부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened/pressured') is tone and dignity: 부담스럽다 can be mild, even social (a gift is 부담스럽다 because it's too much), and is more neutrally about discomfort, whereas 어깨가 무겁다 is a humble, slightly noble admission that an important charge rests on you — which is why it is the go-to line in acceptance speeches, new-role announcements, and earnest talk about duty. Habitual partners: 책임 ('responsibility'), 기대 ('expectation'), 맡다 ('to take on'). Register runs casual all the way to formal. The relief counterpart is 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders get lighter'). The English-speaker pitfalls: this is emotional/responsibility weight, NOT literal sore or stiff shoulders (that's 어깨가 결리다/아프다), and don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected, a different emotion.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
It's about emotional/responsibility burden, not literal shoulder pain or stiffness — physical aches are 어깨가 결리다 / 어깨가 아프다.
Don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected, not weighed down by duty.
Don't swap in 부담스럽다 when you want the dignified 'weight of duty' nuance; 부담스럽다 can sound merely uncomfortable or about an over-generous favor.

entries.nuance: Literally 'thick face,' it labels someone shameless or brazen — a person who feels no embarrassment where they should. English actually shares the image in 'thick-skinned,' but beware: English 'thick-skinned' is usually a compliment ('unbothered by criticism'), whereas Korean 얼굴이 두껍다 is most often mildly negative or teasing ('no shame'). It can flip positive only in contexts like interviews or public speaking, meaning 'not easily flustered.' The dividing line from the near-synonym 뻔뻔하다 ('to be brazen/impudent') is bluntness: 뻔뻔하다 is the plain adjective and can sound flatly accusatory, while 얼굴이 두껍다 is the idiomatic, often lighter or jokier phrasing. Blunter, rougher variants are 낯이 두껍다 and 낯짝이 두껍다, and the noun for the trait is 철면피 ('iron face'). Register is casual-to-polite. The pitfalls: it has nothing to do with literal skin thickness, and tone-watch — it can land as an insult, so don't aim it bluntly at someone you must keep polite footing with.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

entries.shortExplanation: 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is a practical expression meaning "to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')".
entries.explanation: 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (nunko tteul sae eopda) = "to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')". entries.nuance: Literally 'no gap (새 = 사이, 'interval') to even open your eyes and nose,' it is a vivid hyperbole for being so frantically busy you can't spare a single second. The dividing line from plain 바쁘다 ('to be busy') is sheer intensity: 바쁘다 covers any level of busy, while 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is the extreme top end — you can't even blink. It functions almost entirely as an adverbial intensifier in the set frame 눈코 뜰 새 없이 + 바쁘다/일하다/지내다, which is why textbooks treat 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다 as one chunk. Note 새 here is the noun 사이/간격 ('gap, interval'), not 새 ('bird') — that homophone trips beginners. Register is casual-to-polite, extremely common for a hectic patch at work or home. The English-speaker pitfalls: keep the spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one word, 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open'), and don't deploy it for a calm, neutral 'I have no time' — there must be genuine, breathless busyness for it to fit.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

It's an intensity phrase usually attached to 바쁘다 — don't use it for a neutral 'I have no time'; it requires real, breathless busyness.
새 here means 'gap/interval' (사이), not 새 ('bird') — don't let the homophone mislead your reading.

entries.english: to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')
entries.shortExplanation: 바가지를 쓰다 is a practical expression meaning "to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')".
entries.explanation: 바가지를 쓰다 (bagajireul sseuda) means "to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')". Say it as one set phrase — for example 관광지에서 완전 바가지 썼어. ("I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 바가지를 쓰다 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

examples.note: 시세 = 'market/going price'; -다가 marks the slip-up

examples.note: Real-situation: 흥정 ('haggling') pairs naturally

entries.nuance: Literally 'to wear a gourd dipper (바가지),' it means to be charged far more than something is worth — to get ripped off. The image is folk: traditionally one was said to overpay a debt 'as if a gourd of charges were dumped on your head.' It thrives in talk of tourist traps, taxis, markets, and festivals. The dividing line from plain 비싸다 ('to be expensive') is fairness: 비싸다 just means the price is high (possibly justified), whereas 바가지(를) 쓰다 implies you were unfairly gouged above the fair rate. The crucial grammar pair: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = YOU, the buyer, overpaid (쓰다 'to wear/put on'), while 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER puts the gouge on someone else (씌우다, the causative 'to make wear'). It is often shortened to just 바가지. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't reverse 쓰다 ('got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('ripped someone off'), and don't use it for poor product quality — that's 별로다 or 안 좋다; 바가지 is strictly about being overcharged.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't reverse the verbs: 쓰다 = you got ripped off; 씌우다 = the seller (or someone) ripped another person off.
It refers to being overcharged, not to a bad-quality product — for poor quality use 별로다 / 안 좋다.
Don't substitute plain 비싸다 ('expensive'): high price alone isn't 바가지; the nuance is being gouged ABOVE the fair rate.

The dividing line from plain 비싸다 ('to be expensive') is fairness: 비싸다 just means the price is high (possibly justified), whereas 바가지(를) 쓰다 implies you were unfairly gouged above the fair rate.
The crucial grammar pair: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = YOU, the buyer, overpaid (쓰다 'to wear/put on'), while 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER puts the gouge on someone else (씌우다, the causative 'to make wear').
Don't reverse 쓰다 ('got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('ripped someone off'), and don't use it for poor product quality — that's 별로다 or 안 좋다; 바가지 is strictly about being overcharged.

entries.english: you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')

entries.explanation: "you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')" — that is 국물도 없다 (gungmuldo eopda). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: Literally 'there isn't even broth (국물),' the image is a shared pot scraped so clean that not a drop of soup is left for you — so it means there is nothing to be gained: no benefit, no leftover, no mercy. Its dominant use is a half-joking warning or threat from someone with the upper hand: '한 번만 더 그러면 국물도 없어' ('do that once more and you'll get nothing from me'). A second use is grumbling that an effort yielded zero reward ('도와줘도 국물도 없더라'). The dividing line from a plainer warning like 가만 안 둬 ('I won't let it slide') is flavor: 가만 안 두다 threatens active punishment, whereas 국물도 없다 threatens withholding any goodwill or payoff — the carrot vanishes rather than a stick appearing. Register is firmly casual and the threat reading is blunt, so it suits friends, family, or clearly informal settings. The English-speaker pitfall: 국물 here is NOT literal soup — it's figurative 'leftover benefit/share,' so don't picture food; and because the tone is so informal and can sting, never deploy it in polite or professional speech where you must stay deferential.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Nothing to do with actual soup — 국물 here means 'leftover benefit/payoff/share,' not broth you can drink.
The threatening tone is informal and can sound harsh; don't use it in polite or professional contexts where you must stay deferential.
It threatens WITHHOLDING any reward or mercy, not active punishment — for 'I'll make you pay' use 가만 안 두다, not 국물도 없다.

entries.english: to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')
entries.shortExplanation: 찬물을 끼얹다 is a practical expression meaning "to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')".
entries.explanation: 찬물을 끼얹다 (chanmureul kkieonda) = "to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 분위기 좋았는데 걔가 찬물을 끼얹었어. ("The mood was great but he threw cold water on it."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: Literally 'to pour cold water over (something hot),' it means to suddenly kill an upbeat mood, excitement, or building momentum — typically with a negative comment or unwelcome news — like dousing a warm fire. The dividing line from the near-synonym 김(을) 빼다 / 김새다 ('to let the steam out / deflate') is agency: 김새다 often just happens (the excitement fizzles on its own), whereas 찬물을 끼얹다 frames an active, deliberate party who throws the buzzkill. It presupposes there WAS heat — enthusiasm, a rising vibe, a plan everyone was hyped about — so it needs momentum to ruin. Habitual partners: 분위기에 ('to the mood'), 좋은 소식에 ('to good news'), 계획에 ('to a plan'). Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: spelling — it's 끼얹다 (kki-eon-da), an easy verb to mangle (the 받침 ㄶ in 얹 → pronounced 언), not 끼언다 or 끼엊다; and don't apply it to just any bad news — there must be a positive mood or built-up excitement present for the 'cold water' image to land.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling: it's 찬물을 끼얹다 (끼얹- has the ㄶ batchim, read 'kki-eon'), not 끼언다 or 끼엊다.
It implies actively spoiling a POSITIVE mood, so don't use it for just any bad news; there must be enthusiasm or momentum to ruin.
Don't blur it with 김새다 ('to fizzle'): 김새다 is the excitement deflating on its own, while 찬물을 끼얹다 points the finger at a deliberate buzzkill.

entries.english: Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?
entries.shortExplanation: 통화 괜찮으세요? is a practical expression meaning "Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?".
entries.explanation: 통화 괜찮으세요? (tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo?) means "Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 통화 괜찮으세요? ("Is now a good time to talk?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: the standard polite opener AFTER you placed the call and they picked up

usagePhrases.note: 지금 = right now; pins the timing so they know you mean this moment

examples.romanization: yeoboseyo? jigeum tonghwa gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: Hello? Is now a good time to talk?
examples.note: the bare minimum polite call opener — 여보세요 then the check

examples.en: Sorry to bother you when you're busy. Do you have a minute?
examples.note: lead with 죄송해요 to soften before the request

examples.ko: 야, 통화 괜찮아? 할 말 있어.
examples.romanization: ya, tonghwa gwaenchana? hal mal isseo.
examples.en: Hey, can you talk? I've got something to say.
examples.note: 반말 between close friends; note no -세요

entries.nuance: This is the reflexive courtesy line the CALLER says the instant the other person answers — you confirm they can actually talk before diving in, the way an English speaker says 'Is this a good time?' 통화(通話) is Sino-Korean, literally 通 'pass/connect' + 話 'speech', i.e. 'a connected conversation', and it always means a phone/voice call — never use it for chatting face-to-face, which is just 얘기/대화. 괜찮으세요? is the all-purpose honorific 'is it okay?'; it scales down to 괜찮아? only with intimates. The big English-speaker pitfall is direction: the person who PICKED UP does not ask this — only the one who dialed does — so don't say it after you answer a call. A second trap is dropping the honorific with a boss or client; 괜찮아? to a 부장님 sounds startlingly familiar, so default to 괜찮으세요?. The nearest rival phrase, 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'), is more general and works off the phone too, whereas 통화 괜찮으세요? specifically asks about THIS call.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking it when YOU received the call. The caller initiates this check; if you answered, you just say 네, 여보세요? — the dialer is the one who confirms it's a good time.
Using 괜찮아? with a boss or client. It is 반말 and sounds too familiar with anyone you'd 존댓말 — the honorific 괜찮으세요? (괜찮- + 으시- + 어요) is the safe default.
Saying 통화 to mean an in-person chat. 통화 is strictly a phone call; a face-to-face conversation is 대화 or just 얘기 — '얘기 좀 괜찮아요?' for talking in person.

structuredNuance.t: The reflexive courtesy line the CALLER says the instant the other person answers — you confirm they can actually talk before diving in, the way an English speaker says 'Is this a good time?' 괜찮으세요? is the all-purpose honorific 'is it okay?'; it scales down to 괜찮아? only with intimates.
The nearest rival phrase, 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'), is more general and works off the phone too, whereas 통화 괜찮으세요? specifically asks about THIS call.
통화(通話) is Sino-Korean, literally 通 'pass/connect' + 話 'speech', i.e. 'a connected conversation', and it always means a phone/voice call — never use it for chatting face-to-face, which is just 얘기/대화.

The big English-speaker pitfall is direction: the person who PICKED UP does not ask this — only the one who dialed does — so don't say it after you answer a call. A second trap is dropping the honorific with a boss or client; 괜찮아? to a 부장님 sounds startlingly familiar, so default to 괜찮으세요?.

entries.nuance: This is what the person holding the receiver says when they must step away briefly but want you to stay on the line — the Korean equivalent of 'please hold.' The grammar stacks two ideas: 끊다 literally means 'to cut/sever,' which is exactly how Korean conceives of hanging up (you 'cut' the call), and -지 말고 ('don't ~ and instead') warns you off doing it, while 기다려 주세요 ('please wait for me') uses the favor verb 주다 to make the wait a kindness you're granting. The classic English-speaker error is mixing 끊다 (hang up a call) with 끄다 (power off a device): phones are 끊어, but a TV or light is 꺼. A near-synonym hold-phrase is 잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment') — that one just asks you to wait, while 끊지 말고… specifically adds 'don't hang up,' so it's the right choice the moment there's a risk the caller gives up and ends the call. Note that to a customer you must keep 주세요; bare 끊지 말고 기다려 sounds like a barked order.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 끊다 with 끄다. A phone call is hung up: 전화 끊어; a device is turned off: 불 꺼 / 휴대폰 꺼. Saying 전화 꺼 means 'turn the phone OFF,' a different action.
Dropping 주세요 with a customer. 끊지 말고 기다려 to a stranger sounds like an order; the favor verb 기다려 주세요 makes it a polite request.
Writing 끊지 as 끈지. The verb is 끊다 (with the ㄶ cluster); 끈 means 'a string,' so 끈지 말고 is a spelling slip.

entries.nuance: Said by whoever answers when the person the caller wants is unavailable, offering to write the message down. The engine is 드리다, the humble verb meaning 'to give / do for' a person you raise, so 남겨 드릴까요? politely volunteers to do you the favor of taking a note — by contrast, 남겨 줄까? (with plain 주다) is the casual version you'd use at home. Note 메모 here is from English 'memo' but in Korean it specifically means a short written message/note, not a corporate memorandum; 메시지 남기다 ('leave a message') is an equally natural near-synonym. The verb is 남기다 ('to leave behind'), and the conjugation trips people up: 남기- + -어 contracts to 남겨, so it's 남겨 (not 남겨다 or 남기어). The main English-speaker pitfall is register: offering 남겨 줄까요? to a customer feels a touch too plain — the humble 드릴까요? matches the service situation, since you're doing the favor for both the caller and the absent party.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 남겨 줄까요? to a customer. The situation calls for the humble 드리다: 남겨 드릴까요?. Plain 주다 (줄까요) is fine at home but under-polite at a reception desk.
Writing 남기다 as 남끼다. The stem is 남기- (남겨 = 남기 + 어). 남끼다 is not a word.
Treating 메모 like an English 'memo' (a formal circular). On the phone 메모 = a quick message/note; the office document is 공지 or 회람, not 메모.

entries.nuance: This is the agent's phrase for transferring your call to another extension or department. 연결(連結) is Sino-Korean, 連 'join' + 結 'tie', literally 'join-and-bind,' i.e. to link two points — so it fits a technical call transfer between lines. -아 드리다 again uses humble 드리다, making it a polite promise to do the routing for you; the most formal centers escalate to 연결해 드리겠습니다, while 연결해 줄게 works casually. The crucial near-synonym contrast English speakers must master is 연결 vs 연락: 연결 ('connect') is wiring two parties together in the moment (transfer the call), whereas 연락(連絡) ('get in touch / contact') is reaching out to someone later — '나중에 연락드릴게요' is 'I'll contact you later,' and you cannot swap in 연결 there. A second contrast is 연결 vs 바꾸다: 연결 is a system transfer to another line/department, while 바꿔 드릴게요 is simply handing the same phone to a person nearby. The common error is the redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 — plain 연결해 already means 'connect (for you),' so 시키다 is unnecessary.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 연결시켜 드릴게요. The causative 시키다 is redundant here; 연결하다 already means to connect a call, so the natural form is 연결해 드릴게요.
Confusing 연결 with 연락. 연결 = link two parties right now (transfer); 연락 = contact someone (later). '담당자에게 연락해 주세요' means have them CALL you, not transfer you.
Using 연결해 드릴게요 to hand a phone to a family member. That household hand-off is 바꿔 드릴게요; 연결 implies a technical transfer to another line.

entries.nuance: A semi-formal word meaning 'absent / away from one's seat,' used both to explain that someone can't come to the phone and, as the set noun 부재중 전화, to label a missed call on your screen. The 한자 makes the register: 부재(不在) is 不 'not' + 在 'be present / exist,' literally 'not-present,' plus 중(中) 'in the middle of' — so 부재중 is 'in a state of being absent,' which sounds officeworthy and official, distinctly more buttoned-up than the everyday 없어요 ('isn't here'). That is the key synonym contrast: with a friend who just stepped out you'd say 잠깐 나갔어요 ('stepped out for a bit') or 자리 비웠어요, never the stiff 부재중이에요. English speakers also slip on 부재중 vs 통화 중: 부재중 means they're AWAY from the phone, while 통화 중 means they're THERE but already on another call — opposite situations. Note the honorific split: about a respected person it's 부재중이세요, but about a line or yourself you keep plain 부재중이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Pronouncing/spelling it 부제중. It is 부재중 — the 한자 is 在 (재 'present'), not 제. 부제 means a 'subtitle,' a totally different word.
Using it for a friend who just stepped out. 부재중 is office/formal; casually say 잠깐 나갔어요 or 자리 비웠어요.
Confusing 부재중 (away from the phone) with 통화 중 (on another call). They describe opposite reasons someone can't take your call.

entries.nuance: The polite way to wrap up or postpone a conversation by promising to reach out again — it works to end a call gracefully or to defer a decision. 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean, 連 'connect' + 絡 'tie/wrap,' literally 'connecting threads,' and crucially it means 'contact' in general: a call, a text, or a message all count, so don't read it as 'phone call' specifically. The honorific engine is 드리다, the humble 'do for you' verb, which raises the listener — with friends it relaxes to 연락할게. Two contrasts English speakers need: first, 연락 (get in touch later) vs 연결 (transfer a call right now) — never interchangeable; saying 연결드릴게요 to mean 'I'll contact you' is wrong. Second, the timing word: 나중에 means 'later' open-endedly (could be tomorrow), while 이따가 means 'a bit later today,' so promising 나중에 연락드릴게요 commits you to less than 이따가. One register caution: 드리다 raises whoever you're speaking to, so using 연락드릴게요 toward someone clearly junior to you can sound oddly over-deferential — plain 연락할게요 fits better there.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 연락 as 'phone call' only. 연락 = contact by any channel (call OR text). '연락 주세요' means 'get in touch,' not specifically 'phone me.'
Swapping in 연결 for 연락. 나중에 연결드릴게요 is wrong — 연결 is connecting a call now; later contact is 연락.
Using 드릴게요 to someone clearly below you in status. The humble 드리다 raises the listener; with a junior, plain 연락할게요 sounds more natural than over-deferential 연락드릴게요.

entries.nuance: Used when the person who answered hands the receiver to whoever the caller actually wanted to reach. The verb is 바꾸다, literally 'to change / swap,' and on the phone it idiomatically means 'swap who is speaking' — so you're not 'changing' anything physical, you're exchanging the voice on the line. -아 드리다 (humble 드리다) makes it a polite favor; 바꿔 줄게 is the home/peer version. The single most useful contrast here is 바꾸다 vs 연결하다: 바꿔 드릴게요 is for handing over the SAME phone to a person right next to you (a family member, a colleague in the room), whereas 연결해 드릴게요 is a technical TRANSFER to another line or department. Use the wrong one and it sounds off — saying 연결해 드릴게요 at home to pass the phone to your mom is comically corporate. The conjugation also trips learners: the stem is 바꾸- and 바꾸- + -어 contracts to 바꿔 (not 바껴, which would come from a non-existent 바끼다).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 연결해 드릴게요 to hand the phone to a family member. At home it's 바꿔 드릴게요; 연결 implies a technical transfer to another line, not passing the same handset.
Writing 바꿔 as 바껴. The stem is 바꾸- (바꾸 + 어 = 바꿔). 바껴 wrongly assumes a stem 바끼-, which does not exist.
Confusing 바꾸다 (swap/change) with 바라다 (hope) or 비꾸다 (no such word). On the phone, 'put someone on' is strictly 바꾸다 → 바꿔.

entries.explanation: "You've got the wrong number" — that is 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (jeonhwa jalmot geosyeosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 전화 잘못 거셨어요 ("You've dialed the wrong number"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: What you say when someone reaches you by mistake. The verb is 걸다, the standard word for placing a call (전화를 걸다, literally 'hang/put up a call'), and here it appears as the honorific past 거셨어요, so you're politely telling the CALLER that they dialed wrong — note you raise them with -시- even while correcting them. Flip the subject and the caller admits it as 제가 잘못 걸었어요 ('I misdialed'), so who 'owns' the error decides the wording: 거셨어요 (you) vs 걸었어요 (I). The headline English-speaker pitfall is the irregular conjugation: 걸다 is a ㄹ-stem verb, so before -시- the ㄹ drops — the honorific is 거시- → 거셨어요, NOT the over-regular 걸으셨어요. A second contrast is 걸다 (place a call) vs 받다 (receive/answer a call): you 전화를 걸다 to dial out and 전화를 받다 to pick up, so 'wrong number' attaches to 걸다, the dialing action. To soften the correction, Koreans love padding it: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('seems you may have the wrong number').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 전화 잘못 걸으셨어요. 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular: the ㄹ drops before -시-, giving 거셨어요. 걸으셨어요 over-regularizes the stem.
Using 거셨어요 about yourself. When YOU misdial, the subject is 제가, so say 제가 잘못 걸었어요 — keep the honorific -시- only for the other person.
Mixing 걸다 (place a call) with 받다 (answer a call). You 전화를 걸다 to dial and 전화를 받다 to pick up; 'wrong number' is about 걸다, the dialing.

structuredNuance.t: What you say when someone reaches you by mistake. The verb is 걸다, the standard word for placing a call (전화를 걸다, literally 'hang/put up a call'), and here it appears as the honorific past 거셨어요, so you're politely telling the CALLER that they dialed wrong — note you raise them with -시- even while correcting them. To soften the correction, Koreans love padding it: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('seems you may have the wrong number').
A contrast is 걸다 (place a call) vs 받다 (receive/answer a call): you 전화를 걸다 to dial out and 전화를 받다 to pick up, so 'wrong number' attaches to 걸다, the dialing action.

걸다 is a ㄹ-stem verb, so before -시- the ㄹ drops — the honorific is 거시- → 거셨어요, NOT the over-regular 걸으셨어요. Flip the subject and the caller admits it as 제가 잘못 걸었어요 ('I misdialed'), so who 'owns' the error decides the wording: 거셨어요 (you) vs 걸었어요 (I).
The headline English-speaker pitfall is the irregular conjugation: don't over-regularize the ㄹ-stem to 걸으셨어요 — the honorific past is 거셨어요.

entries.nuance: A polite way to ask the caller to try again soon instead of holding the line. It breaks into 잠시 후에 ('after a short while': 잠시 from 한자 暫時 'brief time,' + 후 後 'after') and 다시 걸어 주세요 ('please dial again'), where 걸다 is the verb for placing a call and 주세요 frames the redial as a favor you're requesting. This is famously the wording in automated busy-line announcements, so it doubles as a system prompt you'll recognize. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, the voice — 'call back' is the ACTIVE 걸다 → 걸어 주세요, not the passive 걸리다; 다시 걸려 주세요 is wrong because 걸리다 means 'to be caught/take time,' not 'to dial.' Second, don't confuse 잠시 후에 ('after a moment,' a future time when you should ACT) with 잠시만요 ('hold on a sec,' said to freeze someone in the present) — different functions: one sends the caller away to retry, the other keeps them put. A natural near-synonym is 이따 다시 전화 주세요 ('phone again later'), slightly more colloquial than the formal 잠시 후에.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다시 걸려 주세요. The active verb is 걸다 (걸어 주세요 = 'please dial'). 걸리다 is passive ('be caught / take time'), so 걸려 주세요 is wrong here.
Confusing 잠시 후에 with 잠시만요. 잠시 후에 = 'after a short while' (go retry later); 잠시만요 = 'hold on a second' (stay put now). Opposite instructions.
Treating 잠시 후 and 잠깐 as fully interchangeable in formal speech. 잠시 후(에) is the standard announcement register; 잠깐만 is more casual and odd in an automated message.

entries.nuance: The natural way to explain why a call sounds garbled or keeps dropping: the cellular 신호 is 약하다 ('weak'). 신호(信號) is Sino-Korean, 信 'trust/sign' + 號 'mark/signal,' literally a 'sign-mark,' and it covers signals broadly — also a traffic 신호(등) ('traffic light') — so context tells you it's reception. A frequent English-speaker trap is reaching for the loanword 사인 (sign) for 'signal'; on a phone the word is 신호, while 사인 in Korean usually means a 'signature' or a hand 'sign,' not cell reception. The other classic error is the adjective: signal strength is 약하다/세다 ('weak/strong'), NOT 작다/크다 ('small/big') — 신호가 작아요 sounds wrong the way 'the signal is small' does in English. A very common near-synonym is 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 ('the signal doesn't get picked up well'), built on 잡히다 ('be caught'); Koreans use it interchangeably with 약해요. Pair any of these with 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well') to connect the weak signal to the reason you keep saying 'what?'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 사인 for 'signal.' Cell reception is 신호; 사인 in Korean means a signature or a hand sign, so '사인이 약해요' is wrong.
Saying 신호가 작아요/커요. Strength pairs with 약하다/세다 (weak/strong), not 작다/크다 (small/big). '신호가 세요' = 'the signal is strong.'
Confusing 신호 with 신호등. Bare 신호 on the phone = reception/signal; 신호등 specifically is a traffic light. Don't add 등 when talking about a call.

entries.nuance: The flip side of reporting 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well'): instead of describing your own trouble, you ask whether the OTHER person can hear YOU, which is why it's phrased about them. The key grammar is voice: 들리다 is the intransitive/passive 'to be heard / be audible' (something reaches the ear on its own), so 잘 들리세요? literally asks 'does it come through to you well?' — the honorific -세요 raises the listener. English speakers must not confuse this with 듣다, the transitive 'to listen' that takes an object: asking 잘 듣고 있어요? means 'are you listening (paying attention)?', which sounds like you're scolding them, not checking reception — so the reception check is 들리세요?, never 듣다. A second look-alike trap is 들리다 (be audible) vs 들다 (to lift/hold, or 'cost/enter'): totally different verbs that only resemble each other on paper. Natural partners are 잘 (well) and 안 (not): 잘 들려요 / 잘 안 들려요 / 안 들려요. On video calls the same 들리세요? is the universal audio check.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘 듣고 있어요? to mean 'can you hear me.' That asks 'are you listening (paying attention)?' and sounds accusatory. The reception check is 잘 들리세요? with 들리다.
Confusing 들리다 (be audible) with 들다 (lift / cost / enter). Same-looking roots, unrelated meanings; the hearing verb is 들리다 → 들려요/들리세요.
Treating 들리다 as transitive with an object + 를. It's intransitive: the thing heard takes -가/-이 (제 목소리가 잘 들려요), not 제 목소리를 들려요.

entries.nuance: Explains that a person's line is occupied because they're already talking to someone else. 통화 중 = 'in the middle of a call,' where 통화(通話) is 'a connected conversation' (通 'connect' + 話 'speech') and 중(中) is the 한자 'middle/in the midst of,' so the whole thing is 'mid-call.' entries.nuance: 안녕히 가세요 is the goodbye you say to the person who is LEAVING while you remain. 안녕(安寧) is Sino-Korean for 'peace, well-being', 히 makes it adverbial ('peacefully'), and 가세요 is the polite command of 가다 'to go' — so the whole thing literally wishes them 'go in peace'. The decisive contrast is with its twin 안녕히 계세요 (계시다 'to stay'): the verb tells you who moves. The English-speaker pitfall is huge: English 'goodbye' is one word for both parties, so learners fire 안녕히 가세요 at the person they are leaving behind, which sounds like ordering your host out of their own home. Decide first: am I going, or are they? If they go, 가세요. Softer caring versions are 조심히 가세요 and 살펴 가세요 ('go carefully'); the steeliest formal register is 안녕히 가십시오, heard from staff toward customers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안녕히 가세요 when YOU are the one leaving — it tells the person staying to 'go', which makes no sense; if you leave, say 안녕히 계세요 instead.
Translating English 'bye' literally and using one phrase for everyone — Korean forces you to pick 가세요 (they leave) vs 계세요 (you leave) based on who is actually moving.
Writing 안녕이 가세요 — the adverb ending is 히, not 이: it is always 안녕히.

entries.nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the mirror image of 안녕히 가세요: you say it when YOU leave and the other person STAYS. The pivot is the verb — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/stay (of a person)', so 계세요 wishes the one remaining to 'stay well', exactly as 가세요 (가다 'go') wishes the one leaving to 'go well'. Same 안녕(安寧) 'peace' root in both. English speakers reliably swap the two because 'goodbye' carries no who-moves information; the fix is a one-second check — if your feet are the ones moving, it's 계세요. A common smoothing move is to add 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 가 볼게요 ('I'll go first') so leaving ahead of others doesn't seem abrupt. In a workplace, 안녕히 계세요 + 수고하세요 toward those still working is the natural exit line. Formal register: 안녕히 계십시오.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 안녕히 가세요 as you walk out the door — that tells the people staying to leave; the leaver always says 안녕히 계세요.
Saying 안녕히 있으세요 with plain 있다 — for a person you must use the honorific 계시다, so it is 안녕히 계세요, never 있으세요.
Just dropping 안녕히 계세요 and bolting in a group — add 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 가 보겠습니다 so leaving first reads as polite, not rude.

entries.nuance: 만나서 반가워요 = 만나서 ('because/upon meeting', from 만나다 + the -아서 link of cause) + 반가워요 (반갑다 'to be glad'). So it literally says 'I'm glad because I've met you'. Note 반갑다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before 어요 the ㅂ becomes 우, giving 반가워요 (not 반갑어요) — the same shift you see in 춥다→추워요, 돕다→도와요. The synonym line worth knowing is 만나다 vs 보다: 만나다 is a planned, face-to-face meeting (so it suits a first introduction), whereas 보다 is broader 'see'. Register-wise 반가워요 is warm and friendly; 반갑습니다 is the buttoned-up formal version for business. The English-speaker pitfall is reusing it like a casual 'good to see you' on later meetings — Koreans say 만나서 반가워요 essentially for the FIRST encounter; at later meetings they switch to 오랜만이에요 or 잘 지냈어요?. The natural reply is 저도 반가워요 ('me too').

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 반갑어요 — 반갑다 is ㅂ-irregular, so the form is 반가워요; the regular-looking 반갑어요 is wrong.
Re-using 만나서 반가워요 every time you see the same person — it is essentially a first-meeting greeting; for reunions use 오랜만이에요 instead.
Replying with a bare 네 to someone's 반가워요 — mirror it warmly with 저도 반가워요 so it doesn't feel one-sided.

entries.nuance: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the high-formality greeting for meeting someone for the very FIRST time, especially in business. 처음 means 'first time'; 뵙다 (also written 뵈다) is the HUMBLE verb for 'to meet/see (a superior)', the lowered counterpart of plain 만나다/보다, so you are figuratively 'lowering yourself to be seen by' the other person. The -겠- here is not future 'will' but a softening, intention-marking 겠 that adds courtesy ('I shall (now) meet you'). Contrast with 만나서 반가워요: that conveys your emotion ('glad'), while 처음 뵙겠습니다 conveys deference and formality — Koreans often say both, the humble greeting first, then 반갑습니다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like a casual 'hi, nice to meet you' and using it with friends or peers, where it sounds absurdly stiff and even sarcastic; reserve it for clients, executives, in-laws, and first formal introductions. It almost always pairs with 잘 부탁드립니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 처음 뵙겠습니다 with friends or peers — it is steep formal/humble language; among equals say 만나서 반가워요.
Mispronouncing/misspelling 뵙겠습니다 as 봽겠습니다 or 뵈겠습니다 — the standard set greeting is 뵙겠습니다.
Using it the second time you meet someone — 처음 means 'first time', so re-using it on a later meeting is contradictory; switch to 또 뵙겠습니다 / 다시 뵙겠습니다 or 오랜만입니다.

entries.nuance: 잘 먹겠습니다 is what you say JUST BEFORE eating, especially when someone has cooked for you or is treating you — functionally Korea's version of an at-the-table 'thank you for the food'. Structure: 잘 'well' + 먹다 'to eat' + the intention-marking -겠- ('I shall') + formal 습니다, so literally 'I shall eat well'. The crucial contrast is tense/aspect against its partner 잘 먹었습니다 (past, said AFTER finishing): -겠- looks forward, -었- looks back, and mixing them is the classic learner error. Casual register drops to 잘 먹을게요 or, among close friends, 잘 먹을게. A warmer variant aimed at the cook is 맛있게 먹겠습니다 ('I'll eat this deliciously'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting it to mean a literal promise about how much/how skillfully you'll eat — it's a fixed courtesy formula, not a statement about appetite, and you say it even for a tiny snack someone offers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘 먹겠습니다 after you've finished — the -겠- form is for BEFORE the meal; afterward switch to the past 잘 먹었습니다.
Skipping it entirely when someone treats or cooks for you — omitting the pre-meal 잘 먹겠습니다 can read as ungrateful in Korea.
Reading it as a literal vow ('I will eat well/a lot') and over-explaining — it's a set thank-you-for-the-food formula, so just say it and start eating.

entries.nuance: 잘 먹었습니다 is the AFTER-meal counterpart to 잘 먹겠습니다 — said as you finish, it thanks whoever cooked or paid, much like 'that was a wonderful meal'. The only structural change is tense: 먹다 + past -었- + 습니다 = 'I ate well', versus the pre-meal 먹겠습니다 with forward-looking -겠-. Note the vowel join: 먹 + 었 → 먹었습니다 (the ㄱ ㅓ stem takes 었 normally; pronounced 머거씀니다). Keeping the before/after pair straight (먹겠습니다 → 먹었습니다) is exactly the contrast learners stumble on. Casual register is 잘 먹었어요 or, with friends, 잘 먹었어. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as merely a factual report ('I have eaten') rather than a thank-you — so people forget to say it to the host, or say it to no one. It's customary to direct it to the cook/treater, and after being treated it pairs naturally with an offer like 다음엔 제가 살게요 ('I'll get the next one').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘 먹겠습니다 after the meal — that's the BEFORE form; once you've eaten it must be the past 잘 먹었습니다.
Treating it as a plain statement of fact and saying it to no one — it's a thank-you, so address it to whoever cooked or paid.
Stretching the stem into 먹었었습니다 — single past 먹었습니다 is correct; the double-past 먹었었 implies a discontinued state and sounds odd here.

entries.nuance: 오랜만이에요 is what you say when meeting someone after a long gap. It comes from 오래 'a long time' + 간만/만 'interval' contracted into 오랜만 (a span of time having passed), plus the polite copula 이에요 — literally 'it is (after) a long while'. Beware the spelling trap: it is 오랜만 (오래+ㄴ만), NOT 오랫만; many learners (and some natives) miswrite it. Register slides from casual 오랜만이야 → polite 오랜만이에요 → formal 오랜만입니다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, 'long time no see' is broken English, so don't try to map it word-for-word — 오랜만이에요 is a normal, grammatical copula sentence; second, it requires a genuinely long gap, so using it after a few days sounds sarcastic (Koreans even joke '오랜만이네?' when they just saw you yesterday). It naturally leads into 잘 지냈어요? ('have you been well?'), and a common echo reply is 그러게요, 오랜만이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 오랫만이에요 — the correct form is 오랜만이에요 (from 오래 + ㄴ + 만).
Using it after only a short separation — it implies a real lapse of time; after a couple of days it reads as sarcastic.
Saying just 오랜만 to someone you must speak politely to — drop the 이에요 only with close friends; otherwise keep 오랜만이에요 / 오랜만입니다.

entries.explanation: "How are you doing?" — that is 어떻게 지내요? (eotteoke jinaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 어떻게 지내요? ("how are you doing (these days)?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 어떻게 지내요? asks how someone has been LIVING/getting on lately — a span of life — not how they feel this exact second. 어떻게 = 'how', 지내다 = 'to get by / spend one's days', so it's closer to 'How have you been getting on?' than a snapshot 'How do you feel now?'. The synonym contrast: 어떻게 지내요? is open-ended ('in what way are you living?'), while 잘 지내요? is a yes/no-style 'Are you doing well?' that fishes for the reassuring 네, 잘 지내요. Register climbs with the honorific 지내시다 → 어떻게 지내세요? for seniors. It frequently follows 오랜만이에요 at reunions, and you can shift it to the past 어떻게 지냈어요? to mean 'how have you been (since we last met)'. The English-speaker pitfall is parsing 지내요 as 'go' (confusing it with 가요) and answering about a destination; 지내다 is about how life is going, not where you're headed — answer with 잘 지내요 / 그냥 그래요 ('so-so'), not a place.

structuredNuance.t: 어떻게 지내요? asks how someone has been LIVING/getting on lately — a span of life — not how they feel this exact second; it's closer to 'How have you been getting on?' than a snapshot 'How do you feel now?'. Register climbs with the honorific 지내시다 → 어떻게 지내세요? for seniors. It frequently follows 오랜만이에요 at reunions, and you can shift it to the past 어떻게 지냈어요? to mean 'how have you been (since we last met)'.
어떻게 지내요? is open-ended ('in what way are you living?'), while 잘 지내요? is a yes/no-style 'Are you doing well?' that fishes for the reassuring 네, 잘 지내요.
어떻게 = 'how', 지내다 = 'to get by / spend one's days'.

The pitfall is parsing 지내요 as 'go' (confusing it with 가요) and answering about a destination; 지내다 is about how life is going, not where you're headed — answer with 잘 지내요 / 그냥 그래요 ('so-so'), not a place.
