entries.nuance: 축하해요 congratulates someone on good news. 축하(祝賀) is Sino-Korean — 祝 'to wish/celebrate' + 賀 'to congratulate' — and it's a 하다-verb (축하 + 하다), so it conjugates 축하하다 → 축하해요, with the casual 축하해 and formal 축하합니다. The pattern is [occasion] + 축하해요: 졸업 축하해요, 합격 축하해요, 결혼 축하해요. A key register note: toward a senior, Koreans prefer the humble 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (드리다 'to give (humbly)') over plain 축하해요, because you are respectfully 'offering' the congratulation. The English-speaker pitfall is using it like the broad English 'congratulations' for any achievement-y moment including consolation — in Korean 축하해요 is strictly for genuinely happy events (births, weddings, jobs, awards). For sympathy or hardship you do NOT congratulate; you'd say something like 힘내세요 ('stay strong') or 고생했어요. Also don't confuse it with 화이팅 (cheering someone ON before an event); 축하해요 is for celebrating AFTER good news lands.

Mixing it up with 화이팅 — 화이팅 cheers someone on BEFORE a challenge; 축하해요 celebrates AFTER the good outcome.

entries.nuance: 생일 축하해요 = 생일(生日) 'birthday' (Sino-Korean: 生 'birth' + 日 'day') + 축하해요 'congratulations'. So Korean literally 'congratulates' a birthday rather than wishing it 'happy' — a small but useful mismatch from English. The register point is essential: 생일 is the everyday word, but elders get the HONORIFIC noun 생신 plus the humble verb 축하드리다, giving 생신 축하드려요/축하드립니다. Using plain 생일 축하해요 to your grandparents or a respected elder sounds under-polite, even disrespectful. Scale of register: 생일 축하해 (friend) → 생일 축하해요 (polite peer) → 생일 축하합니다 (formal) → 생신 축하드립니다 (elder). The English-speaker pitfall is leaving it at the bare verb level for everyone — English 'happy birthday' is one-size-fits-all, but Korean expects you to upgrade the NOUN (생일→생신) and the VERB (해요→드려요) together for elders. The famous birthday-song line is 생일 축하합니다.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 생일 instead of the honorific 생신 for elders — to grandparents or a respected senior, say 생신 축하드려요, not 생일 축하해요.
Pairing honorific 생신 with plain 축하해요 — match the levels: it's 생신 축하드려요, with the humble 드리다.
Expecting a 'happy' word in there — Korean uses 축하 ('congratulate') for birthdays, so there's no equivalent of 'happy' to translate.

entries.nuance: 수고하셨습니다 thanks someone for effort that is FINISHED. 수고 means 'trouble, effort, hard work', 하시— is the honorific stem of 하다 'to do', and the past -셨- marks completion, so it's 'you have done hard work'. The make-or-break contrast is tense: past 수고하셨습니다 (the job is over) vs present 수고하세요 (the person is still at it, said as you leave them to it) — pick by whether the work has ended. A warm near-synonym is 고생하셨습니다 (고생 'hardship'), which feels a touch more heartfelt about the toil endured. The big register caution for English speakers: 수고하셨습니다 is best from a senior/peer DOWN or sideways; saying it UPWARD to a clearly higher-ranking boss can sound presumptuous (as if you are evaluating their effort), so to a superior prefer 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 with care. The pitfall is using the wrong tense (telling someone whose work is done to 'keep working', or telling someone still working that they 'have finished'), and treating it as a casual 'thanks' you can drop on anyone of any rank.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 수고하셨습니다 to a clearly higher-ranking boss — directed upward it can sound like you're judging their effort; to a superior use 감사합니다 / 고생 많으셨습니다 carefully.
Mixing the tenses — 수고하셨습니다 is for finished work; if the person is still working, the present 수고하세요 is correct.
Using the plain banmal 수고했어 with someone you owe politeness to — that casual form is only for juniors or close peers; otherwise keep 수고하셨습니다 / 수고하셨어요.

entries.nuance: 잘 자요 = 잘 'well' + 자다 'to sleep' in polite command form, literally 'sleep well'. Here's the subtlety: 잘 자요 is friendly-polite, but it's the 해요체 of a fairly intimate phrase, so it lands best with peers, friends, and partners — it is NOT respectful enough for elders or superiors. For them you switch to a completely different, honorific verb: 주무시다 (the honorific of 자다), giving 안녕히 주무세요 ('please sleep peacefully'). This verb-swapping for respect (자다 → 주무시다, just like 먹다 → 드시다, 있다 → 계시다) is the heart of the lesson. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'good night' as one neutral phrase for everyone and saying 잘 자요 to a boss, in-law, or grandparent, which sounds far too familiar — almost like telling your CEO to 'sleep tight'. Decide by relationship: intimate/peer → 잘 자(요); elder/superior → 안녕히 주무세요. A warm add-on for either register is 좋은 꿈 꿔요 / 꾸세요 ('sweet dreams').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘 자요 to an elder or boss — it's too intimate; use the honorific 안녕히 주무세요 for people you respect.
Trying to make 자다 polite by adding endings (자세요) for an elder — respect requires the suppletive verb 주무시다, so it's 안녕히 주무세요, not 잘 자세요.
Using it as a general parting 'goodbye' in the daytime — 잘 자요 specifically wishes good SLEEP, so it only fits at bedtime/before sleep.

잘 자요 = 잘 'well' + 자다 'to sleep' in polite command form, literally 'sleep well'.

The pitfall is treating 'good night' as one neutral phrase for everyone and saying 잘 자요 to a boss, in-law, or grandparent, which sounds far too familiar — almost like telling your CEO to 'sleep tight'.

entries.nuance: 부탁 is Sino-Korean 付託 'to entrust/commit (a request) to someone', and 드리다 is the humble 'to give (upward to a superior)', so 부탁드려요 literally means 'I humbly hand you my request' — far more deferential than plain 부탁해요. Add 잘 ('well') and it becomes the all-purpose Korean phrase for 'please look after this/me kindly', said at first meetings, when joining a team, or when entrusting any task. It has no clean English equivalent: depending on context it covers 'nice to meet you', 'I look forward to working with you', and 'please take care of it'. The near-synonym 도와주세요 ('please help me') is a concrete request for assistance, while 잘 부탁드려요 is a softer, relationship-building bow that asks for general goodwill, not a specific action. English speakers misread it as a literal plea for help and look for what task to do; really it is social glue, so you simply receive it warmly. Never answer a polite 부탁드려요 with the casual 부탁해 back to a senior.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

부탁해 is casual 반말; upward you need the humble 드리다 form 부탁드려요/부탁드립니다, or it sounds presumptuous.

entries.nuance: 조심하세요 is built on Sino-Korean 操心 ('to manage/hold the heart-mind'), literally 'keep your mind on guard', and the 하다 verb takes the honorific imperative 하세요, so it means 'please be careful'. Korean splits two ideas English merges: 조심하다 (verb, 'to take care/be cautious') versus the adverb 조심히/조심해서 ('carefully') that modifies another verb — hence 조심하세요 'be careful' but 조심히 가세요 'go carefully'. It works both as a genuine safety warning and, very commonly, as a caring farewell, so it overlaps with 잘 가세요 but adds the nuance of 'mind yourself'. A signature pattern is NOUN + 조심하세요, where the noun names the danger: 발 조심 (your feet), 계단 조심 (the stairs), 감기 조심 (catching cold), 차 조심 (cars). English speakers wrongly tack on 조심 with the object particle as 발을 조심하세요 — natural Korean usually drops the particle here, just 발 조심하세요. Drop the honorific to 조심해 only with close friends or juniors.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 조심하세요 to mean 'go carefully' before a verb of motion.
As a standalone it means 'be careful', but to modify 가다 you need the adverb form: 조심히 가세요 / 조심해서 가세요, not 조심하세요 가세요.
Forcing the object particle in NOUN+조심: 계단을 조심하세요.
Fixed warnings drop the particle: 계단 조심하세요, 발 조심하세요. Adding 을/를 sounds stiff and textbook-like.
Saying 조심해 to a stranger or elder.
조심해 is bare 반말 and can sound like an order; to anyone you don't know well use the honorific 조심하세요.

entries.nuance: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know' (the opposite of 알다 'to know'), and 모르겠어요 adds -겠- before the polite 어요 ending. That -겠- is not future tense here; it softens the assertion into 'I'm not sure / I can't seem to tell', so 모르겠어요 sounds more tentative and humble than the flat 몰라요. The contrast matters: 몰라요 is a blunt fact ('I don't know'), even slightly curt or dismissive, while 모르겠어요 hedges politely and is what you'd say to a customer, teacher, or stranger. Adding 잘 in front (잘 모르겠어요) does NOT mean 'I know well' — counterintuitively it intensifies the not-knowing into 'I really have no idea', a common trap for English speakers who read 잘 as 'well'. It frequently embeds a question with -ㄴ지/-ㄹ지: 어디인지 모르겠어요 (I don't know where), 맞는지 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure if it's right). Because Korean rarely uses subject pronouns, you usually drop 저는 and just say 모르겠어요.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

잘 here intensifies the negative verb, so it means 'I really don't know', the opposite of what 잘 ('well') suggests in English.
Defaulting to 몰라요 with strangers or superiors.
몰라요 sounds blunt, even cold; the -겠- in 모르겠어요 adds politeness and humility, which is safer in service or formal settings.
Saying 안 알아요 for 'I don't know'.
Korean does not negate 알다 with 안; the dedicated antonym verb is 모르다. Use 몰라요 / 모르겠어요, never 안 알아요.

entries.nuance: 잠깐 means 'a brief moment, a short while', 만 is the particle 'only/just', and the 요 makes it polite — so 잠깐만요 is literally 'just a brief moment, please', i.e. 'hold on a sec'. entries.nuance: 천만에요 comes from 천만 (Sino-Korean 千萬 'ten million') + 에요, an idiom meaning roughly 'not in ten million (ways)' — i.e. 'don't even think of it', hence 'you're welcome / not at all'. It is the textbook reply to 감사합니다, but in real life it sounds a bit formal and even slightly old-fashioned, so younger Koreans more often deflect with 아니에요 ('no, no'), 별말씀을요, or a casual 뭘요. Compare the registers: 아니에요 is the everyday warm 'oh it was nothing', 별말씀을요 is humbly brushing off thanks or praise, and 천만에요 is the dictionary-perfect but stiffer 'you're welcome'. English speakers, mapping 'you're welcome' one-to-one, overuse 천만에요 and can sound textbook-ish; among friends a simple 응 or 아니야 fits better. Note 천만에요 only answers thanks, whereas 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments, so they aren't fully interchangeable. Keep the 요 ending; 천만에 alone is rarely said.

entries.nuance: 별말씀을요 breaks down as 별 ('special, out of the ordinary', Sino-Korean 別) + 말씀 (the humble/honorific word for 'words, what you say') + 을 (object particle) + 요, literally 'such special words (you say)!' — an idiom that humbly waves away thanks or praise, like English 'don't mention it' or 'you flatter me'. Its register is courteous and a touch humble, common among adults in polite exchanges; it's softer and more self-effacing than the brisk dictionary reply 천만에요. The key distinction from 천만에요 is range: 천만에요 only answers 감사합니다, but 별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you're too kind'), because you're literally protesting the 'special words' someone offered. The full form 별말씀을 다 하세요 ('you say all sorts of flattering things') leans even more into brushing off praise. English speakers stumble on the spelling and pronunciation — it's 말씀 (honorific) not 말 — and on the liaison, where 을요 links into [으료]. Don't reduce it to 별말 (that means 'a strange remark'), and keep 말씀, the respectful form.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Shortening it to 별말요 or 별말씀요 and dropping the object particle.
The set phrase keeps 말씀 plus 을: 별말씀을요. 별말alone means 'an odd remark', which changes the meaning entirely.
Assuming it only answers thanks like 천만에요.
별말씀을요 also deflects compliments ('you flatter me'). Using it after praise is correct and natural, which 천만에요 can't always cover.
Using plain 말 instead of the honorific 말씀.
The humility of the phrase depends on 말씀, the respectful word for someone's speech; 별말 sounds wrong and even slightly negative.

entries.nuance: 다음에 ('next time', 다음 'next' + 에 'at') + 또 ('again') + 오세요 (honorific imperative of 오다 'to come') = 'please come again next time' — the warm send-off shop and restaurant staff give customers. The pivotal verb is 오다 'to come', NOT 가다 'to go': from the staff's standpoint the customer returns toward them, so it must be 오세요; saying 가세요 ('go') would be a logical error. Note the difference from 다음에 봐요 ('see you next time'), which is a casual mutual goodbye between friends, whereas 다음에 또 오세요 flows one way, host inviting guest back. The little word 또 is doing the 'again' work; 다시 also means 'again' but leans toward 'redo/once more', while 또 fits 'come back another time'. The big pitfall for English speakers is using it the wrong direction: customers almost never say it back — you simply reply 네, 감사합니다 or 잘 먹었습니다. Only the one staying behind (the host) issues the invitation to return.

entries.nuance: 여기 있어요 = 여기 ('here', this place) + 있어요, the polite form of 있다 'to exist / to be (located)', so literally 'it is here' — used the moment you physically hand something over, like English 'here you go / here it is'. 있다 is the existence-and-location verb (the opposite of 없다 'to not exist'); don't confuse it with 이다 'to be (X)', so 'here it is' is 여기 있어요, never 여기 이에요. A crucial context split: the clipped 여기요 (just 'here' + 요) is the standard way to call a server or get attention in a restaurant ('excuse me, over here!'), so the same root can mean either 'here you go' or 'waiter!' depending on situation and whether you're holding something out. The fuller, more formal 여기 있습니다 is what polished service staff say. Near-synonym 여기 있어요 vs 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you'): the latter announces the giving, while 여기 있어요 presents the thing as already in hand. English speakers sometimes use 여기요 trying to say 'here you go' when handing an item — but bare 여기요 reads as 'excuse me, server', so add 있어요 when you mean 'here it is'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using bare 여기요 to mean 'here you go' when handing something over.
여기요 alone is the call for a server ('excuse me!'). To present an item, say the full 여기 있어요, or the listener hears 'waiter, over here'.
Saying 여기 이에요 instead of 여기 있어요.
Location/existence uses 있다 (있어요), not the identifying copula 이다 (이에요). 여기 이에요 is ungrammatical for 'it's here'.
Negating with 여기 안 있어요 for 'it's not here'.
있다 has its own antonym 없다; 'it's not here' is 여기 없어요, not 안 있어요.

entries.nuance: 얼마나 걸려요? combines 얼마나 ('how much / to what extent') with 걸리다 'to take (time), to be required', in the polite form 걸려요 — so it asks 'how much (time) does it take?'. The headword 걸리다 here means 'to take time'; the same verb also means 'to be caught/hung' or 'to catch (an illness)', so context disambiguates (시간이 걸리다 = takes time vs 감기에 걸리다 = catch a cold). The big trap for English speakers is mixing it up with 얼마예요? — that asks PRICE ('how much is it?'), while 얼마나 걸려요? asks DURATION; the extra 나 and the verb 걸리다 are what flip 'how much money' into 'how much time'. You sharpen the question with front modifiers: a destination with -까지 (집까지 'to home'), a means with -로 (지하철로 'by subway', 걸어서 'on foot'), or a start point with -에서/서 (여기서 'from here'). Korean puts the time word 시간이 optionally before 걸려요; you can drop it because 걸리다 already implies time. Answer with a duration like 30분쯤 걸려요 ('about 30 minutes').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 얼마예요? when you mean 'how long does it take?'
얼마예요? asks the price; duration needs the verb 걸리다 → 얼마나 걸려요? Mixing them gets you a cost, not a time.
Marking the destination with -에 instead of -까지.
For 'how long TO a place', the goal-of-extent particle is -까지: 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? -에 marks a static location, not the endpoint of travel time.
Saying 얼마나 시간 걸려요 with no particle on 시간.
If you state the time noun, mark it as subject: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? Or just drop 시간 entirely — 얼마나 걸려요? already means 'how long'.

entries.nuance: 이거 뭐예요? = 이거 (the casual spoken contraction of 이것 'this thing') + 뭐 (the colloquial form of 무엇 'what') + 예요 (polite copula) — the everyday 'what is this?' you say while pointing. Three contraction layers trip up learners: 이것 → 이거 in speech; 이것이 (with subject particle) → 이게; and 무엇이에요 → 뭐예요. So 이거 뭐예요? and 이게 뭐예요? are both fine, the second just adds the subject marker and sounds a touch more careful. The distance set is 이거 (this, near me) / 그거 (that, near you) / 저거 (that, away from both) — pick by where the object is. The headword 뭐 is for THINGS; the crucial pitfall is using it for PEOPLE — 'who is this?' must be 누구예요?, never 뭐예요?, which would sound rude about a person. Also keep the copula attached: 뭐예요 fuses 뭐 + 이에요; writing 뭐 이에요 separately is unnatural. For an object's purpose rather than identity, switch to 이거 뭐 하는 거예요? ('what does this do?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 이거 뭐예요? about a person.
뭐 (what) is for things only; asking 'who is this?' takes 누구 → 이분 누구세요? Using 뭐예요 for a person is grammatically wrong and sounds rude.
Writing 이것이에요 / 무엇이에요 in casual speech.
Spoken Korean contracts these to 이게 / 뭐예요. The full forms are correct but sound stiff and written; natives say 이거 뭐예요?
Mixing up the distance words 이거/그거/저거.
이거 = near me, 그거 = near you, 저거 = away from both. Pointing at a far object but saying 이거 confuses the listener about which thing you mean.

entries.shortExplanation: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 is a practical expression meaning "I will use the restroom".
entries.explanation: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 (hwajangsil jom sseulgeyo) = "I will use the restroom". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 ("I'll use the restroom"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: 화장실 좀 쓸게요 = 화장실 (Sino-Korean 化粧室, literally 'makeup/grooming room', the standard polite word for toilet) + 좀 (softener, a worn-down 조금 'a little') + 쓸게요, the -ㄹ게요 form of 쓰다 'to use'. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the key: it announces YOUR OWN intention/plan, as a courteous heads-up ('I'm going to use it, just letting you know'), not a request for permission. That separates it sharply from 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? ('may I use the restroom?'), which uses -아도 돼요 to actually ASK permission — say 쓸게요 in your own home or where it's obviously fine, but 써도 돼요? in someone's house or a shop where you need an OK. The little 좀 isn't 'a little' literally; it lubricates the sentence, making any request gentler. On vocabulary, 화장실 (the room) is the polite term, not the blunt 변소; and to ask its location it's 화장실 어디예요?. English speakers wrongly use the announcing 쓸게요 when they should be asking — if permission is in doubt, switch to 써도 돼요?. Also note 쓰다 'to use' is a separate verb from 쓰다 'to write', distinguished by context.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 쓸게요 when you actually need permission.
-ㄹ게요 announces your own plan, not a request. In someone's home or a shop, ask 화장실 좀 써도 돼요? with the permission ending -아도 돼요.
Treating 좀 as the literal 'a little'.
Here 좀 is a politeness softener that smooths the request, not a quantity. 화장실 좀 쓸게요 doesn't mean 'use the restroom a little'.
Calling the room 변소 or asking 화장실 있어요? to find it.
변소 is crude/dated; the neutral polite word is 화장실. To locate it, ask 화장실 어디예요?, not just 'is there a restroom?'

entries.nuance: 여보세요 is the dedicated telephone 'hello' and is almost never used face to face — saying it to someone in front of you sounds like a joke or a way to snap a daydreamer back to attention ('hello? anybody home?'). It comes from 여기 보세요 ('look here / over here'), literally a call for attention, which is why it also works mid-call to test a quiet line. The everyday in-person greeting is 안녕하세요, and the two are not interchangeable: 안녕하세요 means 'are you at peace', a wellbeing greeting, while 여보세요 just opens a voice channel. Register is neutral-polite (the 세요 ending), fine for strangers, customer service, and elders alike; the blunt 반말 version 여보 has drifted into meaning 'honey/darling' between spouses, so never shorten 여보세요 to 여보 with a stranger. The English-speaker trap is using it like 'hi' when you meet someone — keep it strictly for phones and for getting a distracted person's attention.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it only works on the phone or to grab a spaced-out person's attention; for meeting people say 안녕하세요.
Shortening it to 여보 to sound casual — 여보 alone means 'dear/honey' between a married couple, so to a stranger it's bizarre; keep the full 여보세요.

entries.nuance: 누구세요? is the polite way to ask a caller's identity, built from 누구 ('who') plus the honorific 이세요 — so literally it honors the unknown person while you find out who they are. The crucial contrast for learners is against 누구야? and 누구냐?: those are 반말/blunt and sound suspicious or hostile ('who the heck are you?'), fine only with close friends, never with a stranger on the line. For maximum politeness Koreans upgrade to 누구시죠? or 어디세요? (the latter literally 'where are you from?', i.e. which company/office), which is the norm in business calls. Note the particle trap: it stands alone, so don't bolt on 가/이 as in 누구가세요 — that's ungrammatical. Another pitfall is answering your own phone with 누구세요?; if you placed the call, you say who YOU are first (저는 ...예요), and 누구세요? is reserved for when you RECEIVE a call from someone unknown. Pair it naturally with a soft opener like 실례지만 or 죄송하지만 so it doesn't sound like an interrogation.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 누구야? or 누구냐? to a stranger — these are blunt 반말 and sound like a challenge; the honorific 누구세요? is required with anyone you don't know.
Adding a subject particle: 누구가세요/누구이세요 is wrong — it's simply 누구 + 세요, with no 가/이 between them.
Using 누구세요? on a call you yourself made — the caller introduces themselves first (저 민수예요); you only ask 누구세요? when answering an unknown caller.

entries.nuance: 통화 괜찮아요? literally asks 'is the phone-call okay?' — 통화 is Sino-Korean 通話 ('通 pass-through' + '話 talk'), i.e. a connected voice conversation, distinct from 전화 (電話 'electric-talk', the call/the phone as a device or the act of phoning). So you ask 통화 괜찮아요?, not 전화 괜찮아요?, because you're asking about the act of conversing, not the device. 괜찮아요 itself is the all-purpose 'it's fine / no problem', and here it means 'is it a convenient moment'. The near-synonym is 시간 괜찮아요? ('do you have time?'), which is broader and works for in-person meetings too, whereas 통화 괜찮아요? is specifically about taking THIS call right now. Register: the 요-ending is polite-casual and standard among colleagues and acquaintances; bump to 통화 괜찮으세요? for clients or elders. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요? — that asks about physical ability to speak and sounds odd; the idiomatic frame is the convenience check 통화 괜찮아요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 말할 수 있어요? for 'can you talk?' — that literally asks if you're capable of speaking; the natural phone phrase asks about convenience: 통화 괜찮아요?
Swapping in 전화 괜찮아요? — 전화 (電話) is the device/the call; the connected conversation is 통화 (通話), so the act of talking takes 통화.
Dropping the courtesy on a work call and just talking — Koreans almost always check 통화 괜찮으세요? first to respect the other person's time.

entries.nuance: 잘 안 들려요 is built on 들리다, the INTRANSITIVE/potential 'to be heard / be audible' — not 듣다 'to listen'. This is the key learner trap: 듣다 is what YOU actively do (저는 음악을 들어요 'I listen to music'), while 들리다 is what the sound DOES on its own ('it reaches the ear'). So a bad line is 안 들려요 ('[your voice] isn't getting through'), never 안 들어요 (which would mean 'I'm not listening', implying you're ignoring them — rude on a call!). The 려 comes from the 리 of 들리- meeting the 어요 ending: 들리+어요 → 들려요. Add 잘 ('well') and the negative 안 and you get 'doesn't come through well'. A close cousin is 안 들렸어요 (past, 'I didn't catch that') versus the present 안 들려요 ('I can't hear you [ongoing]'). Phrase it with 소리가 (the sound as subject) or 신호가 약하다 ('the signal is weak') for natural collocation. Register: the 요-form is polite and perfectly normal with anyone; just don't clip it to 안 들려 with strangers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 들어요 instead of 안 들려요 — 안 들어요 means 'I'm not listening' (you're ignoring them); the line being bad uses the passive/potential 들리다 → 안 들려요.
Marking yourself as subject: 저는 안 들려요 sounds off — it's the SOUND that fails, so use 소리가 잘 안 들려요 or just 잘 안 들려요.
Clipping to 안 들려 with someone you should be polite to — keep the 요 ending: 잘 안 들려요.

entries.nuance: 다시 걸게요 hinges on two things English speakers stumble over. First, the verb: Korean 'to make a phone call' is 전화를 걸다 — 걸다 literally 'to hang/hook', a relic of old hook-and-cradle phones — so you 'hook' a call, and 다시 걸다 = 'call again'. Don't use 부르다 ('to call out a name / summon'), which never means telephoning. Second, the ending -ㄹ게요 (걸+게요) is a SPEAKER'S PROMISE/INTENTION: it commits ME to the action and softly implies it's for your sake, unlike the plain future -ㄹ 거예요 ('I will [just a prediction]'). So 다시 걸게요 = 'I'll redial (you can count on me to)', warmer than 다시 걸 거예요. Crucially, -ㄹ게요 can only take a FIRST-PERSON subject — you can't say 그 사람이 다시 걸게요 about someone else. The natural opposite is 다시 걸어 주세요 ('please call me back'), which you say when THEY should redial. Pair with 이따 / 나중에 / 끊고 for timing. Register: polite-casual, fine for friends and coworkers; for a client use the deferential 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 부르다 for phoning (다시 불러요) — 부르다 is calling someone's name or summoning them; a phone call is 전화를 걸다, so 'call back' is 다시 걸게요.
Saying 다시 걸게요 when the OTHER person should redial — -ㄹ게요 promises that YOU will act; if they should call, it's 다시 걸어 주세요.
Confusing it with the flat prediction 다시 걸 거예요 — that just forecasts a fact; -ㄹ게요 makes it a personal commitment to the listener.

entries.nuance: 문자 보낼게요 = 'I'll send a text'. 문자 is Sino-Korean 文字 ('文 writing' + '字 character'), so literally 'written characters' — short for 문자 메시지 (SMS). The big learner contrast is 문자 vs 카톡 vs 메시지: 문자 is specifically a phone SMS, 카톡 (KakaoTalk) is the messenger app most Koreans actually use day to day, and 메시지 is the generic 'message'; younger people often say 카톡 보낼게요 in real life. Don't confuse 문자 with 전화 (a call) — 문자 is text, 전화 is voice; mixing them changes what you promise to do. The verb is 보내다 ('to send'), and note the channel particle: 문자로 보내다 = 'send BY text', where 로 marks the means. The ending -ㄹ게요 again makes it a personal promise to the listener (first-person only, warmer than the bare future). A subtle trap: 보내 줄게요 (with 주다) adds a nuance of 'I'll send it FOR you / as a favor', slightly more considerate than plain 보낼게요. Collocations: 주소/시간/사진/링크를 문자로 보내다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 문자 (a text message) with 전화 (a phone call) — promising 전화 보낼게요 is wrong; you send (보내다) a 문자 but you place (걸다) a 전화.
Using the wrong particle for the channel — it's 문자로 보내다 ('send by text'); 로 marks the means, so don't say 문자를 보내다 when you mean 'via text'.
Forgetting -ㄹ게요 is first-person — you can't say 그 사람이 문자 보낼게요; for others use 보낼 거예요 or 보낸대요.

entries.nuance: 메모 남겨 주세요 = 'please leave a message (for me to give them)'. 메모 is the loanword 'memo', here meaning a phone message/note; 남기다 is the TRANSITIVE 'to leave (something) behind, to make remain' — distinct from 떠나다 ('to leave / depart a place'). English 'leave a message' uses one word for both senses, so the trap is reaching for 떠나다: you'd never say 메시지를 떠나다 — a left-behind note is 남기다. The construction -아/어 주세요 ('please do X for me') makes it a polite request done as a favor; dropping 주세요 leaves the bare command 남겨 ('leave it!'), which sounds curt. Near-synonyms: 전할 말씀 있으세요? ('do you have something to relay?') is what a secretary asks, and 메시지 남겨 주세요 (with the English-derived 메시지) is interchangeable, slightly more modern. In office/voicemail register the whole phrase is polite-formal and very common. Collocations: 성함/연락처/용건을 남기다 ('leave your name/contact/business'). A finer point: 메모를 남기다 = leave a written note; 음성 메시지를 남기다 = leave a voice message.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reaching for 떠나다 because English says 'leave' — 떠나다 is leaving a PLACE; leaving a note/message behind is 남기다, so it's 메모 남겨 주세요.
Dropping 주세요 and saying just 메모 남겨 — that's a blunt command; the -어 주세요 frame makes it a polite request.
Calling the message 편지 — 편지 is a posted letter; a phone message is 메모 / 메시지.

entries.nuance: 끊지 마세요 = 'please don't hang up'. The verb 끊다 means 'to cut / sever' and is exactly how Korean conceptualizes ending a call (전화를 끊다 = 'cut the phone'), the natural opposite of 걸다 ('hook/place a call'). The grammar to master is the negative command -지 말다 → -지 마세요 ('please don't ~'): you attach -지 마세요 to the dictionary stem, so 끊다 → 끊지 마세요. The classic learner error is mixing this up with 안: 안 끊어요 just states 'I'm not hanging up', it does NOT tell the other person to stop — prohibitions need -지 마세요, not 안. Politeness ladder: 끊지 마 (반말, only with close friends), 끊지 마세요 (polite, default), 끊지 마십시오 (formal announcements). Note 끊다 also covers 'quit/cut off' more broadly — 담배를 끊다 ('quit smoking'), 연락을 끊다 ('cut off contact') — so context tells you it's the phone. Collocates with 잠깐만요 ('just a sec') and 바꿔 드릴게요 ('I'll transfer you'), the two things most often said right before it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 끊어요 to mean 'don't hang up' — that only describes your own action; a command not to do something needs -지 마세요, i.e. 끊지 마세요.
Using 끄다 instead of 끊다 — 끄다 is 'to turn off (a device/light)'; ending a call is 끊다, so 'don't hang up' is 끊지 마세요, not 끄지 마세요.
Clipping to 끊지 마 with someone you owe politeness — keep the 세요: 끊지 마세요.

structuredNuance.t: 끊지 마세요 = 'please don't hang up'. The verb 끊다 means 'to cut / sever' and is exactly how Korean conceptualizes ending a call (전화를 끊다 = 'cut the phone'), the natural opposite of 걸다 ('hook/place a call'). Note 끊다 also covers 'quit/cut off' more broadly — 담배를 끊다 ('quit smoking'), 연락을 끊다 ('cut off contact') — so context tells you it's the phone. Collocates with 잠깐만요 ('just a sec') and 바꿔 드릴게요 ('I'll transfer you'), the two things most often said right before it.

The grammar to master is the negative command -지 말다 → -지 마세요 ('please don't ~'): you attach -지 마세요 to the dictionary stem, so 끊다 → 끊지 마세요. Politeness ladder: 끊지 마 (반말, only with close friends), 끊지 마세요 (polite, default), 끊지 마십시오 (formal announcements).
The classic learner error is mixing this up with 안: 안 끊어요 just states 'I'm not hanging up', it does NOT tell the other person to stop — prohibitions need -지 마세요, not 안.

entries.nuance: 잠깐 기다리세요 = 'please wait a moment'. 잠깐 is an adverb meaning 'briefly, for a short while' — its near-twin 잠시 means the same but is a touch more formal/written (잠시만 기다려 주십시오 is the announcement-style version you hear at counters), while 잠깐 is the everyday spoken choice. Don't confuse 기다리다 ('wait') with 기대하다 ('to expect/look forward to') — similar opening syllable, totally different meaning. Also avoid the English calque 'hold on' as 잡으세요 (잡다 = physically grab); Korean 'hold the line' is simply 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요. Collocates with 잠깐만요 ('just a sec!'), the interjection Koreans throw out to freeze the moment.

entries.nuance: 연락해 주세요 = 'please contact me'. 연락 is Sino-Korean 連絡 ('連 connect/link' + '絡 entwine/tie'), literally 'making a link', so it covers ALL channels — call, text, email, messenger — and is broader than 전화하다 ('to phone specifically'). That breadth is the point: when you don't care HOW they reach you, 연락하다 is the word. The verb is a 하다-verb (연락 + 하다 → 연락해요), and 연락해 주세요 = 연락해 + 주세요 ('do the contacting for me'), a polite favor request. Watch the destination particle: 'contact ME' is 저한테/저에게 연락해 주세요, not 저를 — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게 (the 'to' marker), so 저를 연락하다 is wrong. Register: this 주세요 form is polite-standard for peers and most situations; to a client or superior, upgrade to the humble 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 or 연락 부탁드립니다. Note the very common clipped collocation 연락 주세요 (dropping 하), which natives say constantly and means the same. Don't confuse 연락 with 약속 ('a promised appointment') — 연락 is just reaching out, no commitment to meet.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 를: 저를 연락해 주세요 is wrong — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게, so it's 저한테 연락해 주세요.
Using 전화해 주세요 when you mean any channel — 전화하다 is specifically 'to phone'; 연락하다 covers call/text/email, so for general 'reach out' use 연락해 주세요.
Forgetting it's a 하다-verb when conjugating — the polite form is 연락해(요), not 연락하어요.

entries.nuance: 바꿔 주세요 on the phone means 'please switch the call over to ___ / put them on'. The verb 바꾸다 'to change, switch, swap' is the same word used for exchanging goods (옷을 바꾸다 'exchange clothes') — and THAT overlap is the trap: on a call, 바꿔 주세요 isn't asking to trade anything, it's asking the answerer to hand the receiver to someone else, i.e. swap who's speaking. So 김 선생님 바꿔 주세요 = 'change [the speaker] to Mr. Kim', not 'exchange Mr. Kim'. Form: 바꾸+어 주세요 → 바꿔 주세요 (the ㅜ+어 contracts to 워), with -어 주세요 making it a polite favor. The pattern is simply [person/extension] + 바꿔 주세요. A near-synonym in formal/business contexts is 연결해 주세요 ('please connect me'), which a switchboard operator expects; 바꿔 주세요 is what you say when a human picked up and you want a different person. Don't reach for the English calque 'put on' literally — there's no 놓다/올리다 here; the idiom is 바꾸다. For extra courtesy, 바꿔 주시겠어요? ('would you put them on?') is softer than the plain request.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 바꿔 주세요 as 'exchange' on a call — here 바꾸다 means switch WHO is on the line; [name] 바꿔 주세요 = 'please put that person on', no goods involved.
Calquing English 'put on' with 놓다/올리다 — there's no such verb here; the set phrase is [person] 바꿔 주세요.
Mis-contracting the verb: it's 바꿔 (from 바꾸+어), not 바꾸어 주세요 in speech, and never 바껴 주세요.

entries.nuance: 전화 잘못 걸었어요 = 'I called the wrong number'. The load-bearing word is 잘못, an ADVERB meaning 'mistakenly, wrongly' — and learners must not confuse it with the NOUN 잘못 ('a fault/wrongdoing', as in 제 잘못이에요 'it's my fault'). As an adverb it sits right before the verb: 잘못 걸다 ('dial wrongly'), 잘못 보다 ('misread'), 잘못 듣다 ('mishear'). Don't fuse it as 잘못걸다 — keep 잘못 as a separate word modifying the verb. The verb 걸다 here is the same 'place a call' (전화를 걸다); the past 걸었어요 comes from 걸+었어요. A frequent mix-up is 잘못 vs 못: 못 걸었어요 means 'I COULDN'T place the call' (inability), while 잘못 걸었어요 means 'I placed it WRONGLY' (wrong number) — totally different, so the spacing and word choice matter. Etiquette/register: Koreans almost always lead with 죄송해요/죄송합니다 and a quick 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') rather than just silently dropping; the 요-ending here is polite and appropriate to a stranger you've accidentally dialed. If you RECEIVE such a call, you tell them 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific, 'you've dialed wrong').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

structuredNuance.t: 전화 잘못 걸었어요 = 'I called the wrong number'. The verb 걸다 here is the same 'place a call' (전화를 걸다); the past 걸었어요 comes from 걸+었어요. Etiquette/register: Koreans almost always lead with 죄송해요/죄송합니다 and a quick 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') rather than just silently dropping; the 요-ending here is polite and appropriate to a stranger you've accidentally dialed. If you RECEIVE such a call, you tell them 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific, 'you've dialed wrong').

The load-bearing word is 잘못, an ADVERB meaning 'mistakenly, wrongly'. As an adverb it sits right before the verb: 잘못 걸다 ('dial wrongly'), 잘못 보다 ('misread'), 잘못 듣다 ('mishear'). Don't fuse it as 잘못걸다 — keep 잘못 as a separate word modifying the verb.

Learners must not confuse the adverb 잘못 with the NOUN 잘못 ('a fault/wrongdoing', as in 제 잘못이에요 'it's my fault'). A frequent mix-up is 잘못 vs 못: 못 걸었어요 means 'I COULDN'T place the call' (inability), while 잘못 걸었어요 means 'I placed it WRONGLY' (wrong number) — totally different, so the spacing and word choice matter.

entries.nuance: 힘내세요 is built from 힘 (strength) + 내다 (to put out/summon), so literally it is 'summon your strength' — you are urging someone to gather energy and push through a hard patch, not merely feeling sorry for them. Compare it with 괜찮아요 (it's okay), which only soothes; 힘내세요 actively pushes the person forward, so it fits before or during a struggle (an exam, illness, job loss), whereas pure sympathy like 안타깝네요 fits after a loss when there is nothing left to push toward. It collocates with 조금만 (just a little) and 같이 (together). Register matters: drop to 힘내 only with friends or juniors — saying 힘내 to your boss sounds presumptuous, so keep -세요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'cheer up' and expecting the same lightness; 힘내세요 carries real emotional weight and can feel too strong if someone is only mildly down, where a simple 파이팅! is lighter and more casual.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내 to a senior or boss
힘내 is 반말 and sounds like an order to an equal or junior; to anyone you respect it feels disrespectful. Use 힘내세요 instead.
Using 힘내세요 for mild, passing disappointment
It implies a genuine ordeal worth mustering strength for; for a small letdown it overdramatizes. A casual 파이팅! or 괜찮아요 fits better there.
Translating 'cheer up' as 기뻐하세요
기뻐하세요 commands someone to literally feel joy, which is unnatural and pushy. The set phrase for encouragement is 힘내세요.

entries.explanation: "Well done. / Good job." — that is 잘했어요 (jalhaesseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘했어요 ("you did well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 잘했어요 is 잘 (well) + 했어요 (the past of 하다, to do), so the past tense is the whole point: you praise something already finished, judging the result. Contrast it with 잘하네요, present tense, which admires an ongoing skill ('you're good at this') as you watch, and with 잘될 거예요 ('it'll go well'), which encourages before the fact — using 잘했어요 before someone starts is a logic error. Because 하다 is the most regular verb, the form is simply 하다 → 했어요; there is no irregularity to fear here. Watch the status angle: to a clear superior, bare 잘했어요 can sound like you are grading them from above, so toward a boss Koreans soften to 수고하셨어요 or 잘 보고 들었습니다 rather than praising their performance directly. The English-speaker pitfall is using 'good job' freely upward the way English does; in Korean, praise flows comfortably downward (to juniors, kids, peers) but feels presumptuous aimed up the ladder.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘했어요 before a task is finished
The past tense judges a completed result; said beforehand it's illogical. Encourage with 잘할 거예요 or 화이팅 instead.
Praising your boss with 잘했어요
Evaluating a superior's work sounds like you outrank them. Toward a senior, use 수고하셨습니다 or express thanks rather than a grade.
Confusing 잘했어요 with 잘하셨어요 for elders
To a respected adult, drop in the honorific -시-: 잘하셨어요. Plain 잘했어요 to an elder can feel a touch flat or familiar.

entries.nuance: 수고 is Sino-Korean 受苦 ('receive-suffering'), so 수고했어요 literally acknowledges that someone has taken on trouble and toil on your or the group's behalf — it thanks the effort itself, not the outcome. That separates it from 잘했어요, which judges how good the result was: a project can flop yet still earn a heartfelt 수고했어요 for the work poured in. It collocates with 많이/많았어요 (a lot) and 오늘도 (today again). The big register trap: many guides say 'never say 수고하셨어요 to a boss,' but in modern workplaces the honorific 수고하셨습니다/수고하셨어요 is widely accepted to seniors; what truly grates is bare 수고했어요 (반말-flavored) aimed upward, or worse 수고하세요 to a superior, which can read as 'keep slaving away.' The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for a single 'thanks for your hard work' and using the casual form everywhere — pick the level by who hears it, and lean on 수고하셨습니다 when in doubt about rank.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying bare 수고했어요 to a clear senior
Without -시- it carries a peer-to-junior tone that feels too familiar upward. Use 수고하셨습니다 or 수고하셨어요 for seniors.
Telling your boss 수고하세요 as you leave first
To a superior it can sound like 'you keep working away,' faintly cheeky. Better: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 / 먼저 가 보겠습니다.
Using 수고했어요 to praise the quality of a result
It thanks effort, not achievement; for a good result say 잘했어요 (down) or 고생하셨습니다. Mixing the two blurs your meaning.

examples.en: It's hot, so be careful.
examples.note: 반말 handing hot food to a friend; -니까 gives the reason

examples.romanization: giri mikkeureowoyo. bal josimhaseyo.
examples.en: The road is slippery. Watch your step.

entries.nuance: 조심 is Sino-Korean 操心 ('handle/manage the heart'), i.e. to keep your mind alert, so 조심하세요 tells someone to stay watchful and avoid harm. Distinguish two uses: as a literal warning it pairs with the danger named first — 발 조심 (watch your step), 감기 조심 (mind the cold), 차 조심 (watch for cars); but it also works as a caring farewell, where 조심히 가세요/들어가세요 is closer to English 'take care, get home safe' than a real alarm. Note 조심히 (adverb, 'carefully') modifies the verb of going, while 조심하세요 is the standalone command. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, forgetting to front the object, so 'be careful of colds' becomes vague — Koreans say 감기 조심하세요, not just 조심하세요; second, over-warning, since a brisk English 'be careful!' is light, but a bare 조심하세요 with no object can sound abrupt unless you add what to watch for or pair it with 가세요 as a goodbye.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping the object when there is a specific hazard
Bare 조심하세요 leaves the danger unnamed and sounds vague. Front it: 발 조심하세요, 감기 조심하세요, 차 조심하세요.
Saying 조심하다 with the wrong particle, e.g. 감기를 조심
Colloquially the noun attaches directly (감기 조심하세요); over-marking with 을/를 sounds stiff. Keep noun + 조심하세요.
Using 조심히 as if it meant 'be careful' on its own
조심히 is an adverb that needs a verb (조심히 가세요). The standalone command is 조심하세요.

drills.note: general warning about a hazard, polite
to someone heading out — a caring goodbye
noun + 조심: the thing to beware of comes first

structuredNuance.t: It tells someone to stay watchful and avoid harm. Two uses: as a literal warning it pairs with the danger named first — 발 조심 (watch your step), 감기 조심 (mind the cold), 차 조심 (watch for cars); but it also works as a caring farewell, where 조심히 가세요/들어가세요 is closer to English 'take care, get home safe' than a real alarm.
조심 is Sino-Korean 操心 ('handle/manage the heart'), i.e. to keep your mind alert.
Note 조심히 (adverb, 'carefully') modifies the verb of going, while 조심하세요 is the standalone command.

The pitfall is twofold: first, forgetting to front the object, so 'be careful of colds' becomes vague — Koreans say 감기 조심하세요, not just 조심하세요; second, over-warning, since a brisk English 'be careful!' is light, but a bare 조심하세요 with no object can sound abrupt unless you add what to watch for or pair it with 가세요 as a goodbye.

entries.shortExplanation: 행운을 빌어요 is a practical expression meaning "I wish you good luck.".
entries.explanation: "I wish you good luck." — that is 행운을 빌어요 (haenguneul bireoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 행운을 빌어요 ("I wish you luck"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: warm and polite, before a challenge
-ㅂ니다 for written notes or formal speech
-ㄹ게요 promises ongoing support
반말 to a close friend

examples.ko: 내일 시험이지? 행운을 빌어!
examples.romanization: naeil siheomiji? haenguneul bireo!
examples.en: Your exam's tomorrow, right? Good luck!
examples.note: 반말 cheering on a friend

examples.ko: 면접 잘 보세요. 행운을 빌어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeop jal boseyo. haenguneul bireoyo.
examples.en: Do well in the interview. I wish you luck.
examples.note: everyday encouragement before a one-off event

examples.ko: 새 가게 잘되길 바라요. 진심으로 행운을 빕니다.
examples.romanization: sae gage jaldoegil barayo. jinsimeuro haenguneul bimnida.
examples.en: I hope your new shop thrives. I sincerely wish you luck.
examples.note: real situation — a formal, heartfelt send-off with 진심으로

entries.nuance: 행운 is Sino-Korean 幸運 ('fortunate luck'), and 빌다 means to pray or beg, so 행운을 빌어요 is literally 'I pray for your good fortune' — a sincere hope that chance favors someone facing an exam, interview, audition, or contest. Note the object particle 을 (행운을), which English speakers often drop. Contrast it with 화이팅!/파이팅! (Fighting!), the breezy cheer Koreans actually shout most of the time: 화이팅 hypes up effort and spirit, while 행운을 빌어요 is gentler and points to luck and outcome, so it sounds warmer and a bit more formal. Beware: 빌다 also means 'to borrow' in other contexts (돈을 빌리다), but here the root is the prayer-빌다 — they are different verbs, so don't second-guess the meaning. The English-speaker pitfall is timing and weight: 'good luck' in English can even be sarcastic, but 행운을 빌어요 is unfailingly sincere and belongs strictly before the event — saying it afterward makes no sense; once results are out, switch to 축하해요 (congrats) or 아쉽네요 (too bad).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 행운을 빌어요 after the event is over
It hopes for a future outcome, so it only fits beforehand. After the fact use 축하해요 (good news) or 수고했어요/아쉽네요.
Dropping the particle: 행운 빌어요
The set phrase keeps the object marker — 행운을 빌어요. Omitting 을 sounds clipped and incomplete.
Confusing prayer-빌다 with borrow-빌리다
행운을 빌어요 uses 빌다 (to pray/wish). 빌리다 means to borrow and is unrelated; don't blend them.

entries.shortExplanation: 축하드려요 is a practical expression meaning "Congratulations.".
entries.explanation: 축하드려요 (chukhadeuryeoyo) = "Congratulations.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 축하드려요 ("congratulations (humble)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: raises the listener — for elders, bosses, formal joy
warm and equal, to a peer or friend
진심으로 = sincerely, for big milestones
생신 is the honorific of 생일

examples.ko: 합격 축하해! 한턱 쏴.
examples.romanization: hapgyeok chukahae! hanteok sswa.
examples.en: Congrats on passing! Treat me.
examples.note: 반말 ribbing a friend

examples.ko: 결혼 축하드려요. 두 분 행복하세요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhon chukadeuryeoyo. du bun haengbokaseyo.
examples.en: Congratulations on your wedding. Be happy, you two.
examples.note: everyday — at a wedding, raised with 두 분

examples.ko: 승진 축하드립니다, 부장님. 정말 잘되셨어요.
examples.romanization: seungjin chukadeurimnida, bujangnim. jeongmal jaldoesyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Congratulations on your promotion, sir. I'm so glad.
examples.note: real situation — to a superior, fully formal -ㅂ니다 + 부장님

entries.nuance: 축하 is Sino-Korean 祝賀 ('celebrate-congratulate'), and the form splits by humility: 축하해요 uses plain 하다, while 축하드려요 swaps in 드리다 ('to give, humbly'), so you are 'humbly offering' your congratulations and thereby elevating the listener — the natural choice for elders, bosses, in-laws, or weddings. Contrast 축하드려요 vs 축하해요 sharply: same warmth, different altitude — 축하해요 levels with a friend, 축하드려요 looks up. It collocates with 진심으로 (sincerely) and the celebrated event as a bare noun in front: 결혼 축하, 합격 축하, 생일 축하. Remember 생일 → 생신 and 생일 축하 → 생신 축하 when the celebrant is a senior. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'congratulations' as one flat word and defaulting to casual 축하해 with anyone — to a senior that is jarringly familiar; and note Korean fronts the occasion (합격 축하해요), unlike English 'congrats on passing,' so resist inserting extra particles between the event and 축하.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using casual 축하해 toward a senior or boss
반말 to someone you respect sounds disrespectful on a happy occasion. Use the humble 축하드려요/축하드립니다.
Saying 생일 축하드려요 to an elder
For a senior, 생일 becomes the honorific 생신: 생신 축하드려요. Plain 생일 to an elder is a touch impolite.
Inserting a particle: 합격을 축하해요
Colloquial Korean fronts the event directly — 합격 축하해요. Adding 을/를 here sounds stiff and textbook-like.

entries.english: It is cool. / You look great.
entries.shortExplanation: 멋있어요 is a practical expression meaning "It is cool. / You look great.".
entries.explanation: 멋있어요 (meosisseoyo) means "It is cool. / You look great.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 멋있어요 ("that's cool / impressive"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 멋있어요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.note: praising style, skill, or character
정말 strengthens the admiration
반말 to a friend
honorific -시- about an admired person

examples.ko: 우와, 그 재킷 멋있어!
examples.romanization: uwa, geu jaekin meosisseo!
examples.en: Whoa, that jacket's cool!
examples.note: 반말 complimenting a friend's clothes

examples.ko: 발표하시는 모습이 정말 멋있었어요.
examples.romanization: balpyohasineun moseubi jeongmal meosisseosseoyo.
examples.en: You looked really impressive presenting.
examples.note: everyday praise of someone's manner; 모습 = the way they appeared

examples.ko: 혼자 세계여행 하셨다니, 정말 멋있으세요.
examples.romanization: honja segyeyeohaeng hasyeotdani, jeongmal meosisseuseyo.
examples.en: You traveled the world alone? You're really amazing.
examples.note: real situation — admiring a person's life choice, honorific 멋있으세요

entries.nuance: 멋있어요 comes from 멋 (style, flair, class) + 있어요 (to have), literally 'to have flair,' so it praises whatever strikes you as stylish, impressive, or admirable — a look, a skill, a brave decision, even a person's whole vibe. Note it is an adjective built on the 있다 pattern, hence the past is 멋있었어요 and the honorific 멋있으세요. Contrast it with 예뻐요 (pretty) and 잘생겼어요 (good-looking): those judge surface appearance, while 멋있어요 admires coolness and impressiveness that can include character and competence, so a confident speech or a noble act can be 멋있다 but not 예쁘다. Casually you'll also hear the clipped 멋지다/멋져요. The big English-speaker pitfall is the near-homophone 맛있어요 ('tasty,' from 맛 = taste): 멋(eo) vs 맛(a) differ by one vowel, and swapping them turns 'you're cool' into 'you're delicious' — keep 멋 for style, 맛 for flavor.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 멋있어요 (cool) with 맛있어요 (tasty)
Only the vowel differs — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste). Say 멋있어요 to praise coolness; 맛있어요 is strictly for food.
Using 멋있어요 where you mean simply 'pretty'
멋있어요 admires style/impressiveness, not surface prettiness. For looks use 예뻐요 (pretty) or 잘생겼어요 (handsome).
Conjugating it like a 하다 verb, e.g. 멋있해요
It follows the 있다 adjective pattern: present 멋있어요, past 멋있었어요. There's no 하다 in it.

entries.shortExplanation: 귀여워요 is a practical expression meaning "It is cute.".
entries.explanation: "It is cute." — that is 귀여워요 (gwiyeowoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 귀여워요 ("that's cute"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

너무 = 'so/too,' the most common intensifier here
반말 to a friend

examples.ko: 어머, 너무 귀여워!
examples.romanization: eomeo, neomu gwiyeowo!
examples.en: Oh my, so cute!
examples.note: 반말 blurted on seeing a puppy; 어머 is a soft 'oh'

examples.ko: 아기가 웃는 게 정말 귀여워요.
examples.romanization: agiga unneun ge jeongmal gwiyeowoyo.
examples.en: The way the baby smiles is really cute.
examples.note: everyday — 게 nominalizes 'the way it smiles'

examples.ko: 고양이가 발로 세수해요. 진짜 귀엽다.
examples.romanization: goyangiga ballo sesuhaeyo. jinjja gwiyeopda.
examples.en: The cat washes its face with its paw. So cute.
examples.note: real situation — describing a charming action, plain-form 귀엽다 to yourself

entries.nuance: 귀여워요 reacts to something small, charming, and lovable — babies, pets, plushies, a child's antics. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the stem 귀엽- drops its ㅂ and adds 워 before vowel endings, giving 귀여워요 (not 귀엽어요) and past 귀여웠어요; this is the same pattern as 춥다 → 추워요 and 덥다 → 더워요, so learning it here transfers widely. Contrast 귀엽다 with 예쁘다 (pretty/beautiful): 예쁘다 admires refined beauty (a flower, a dress, an elegant woman), while 귀엽다 admires adorable, often youthful or tiny charm — calling a stately older person 귀엽다 can sound belittling, whereas 예쁘다 or 멋있다 flatters. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation, since the literal-looking 귀엽어요 is wrong, plus the status caution: 'cute' in English is harmless, but 귀여워요 aimed at a senior or someone you should respect can read as condescending, so reserve it for children, pets, peers, or sweethearts.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 귀엽어요 instead of 귀여워요
귀엽다 is ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ becomes 우/워 before a vowel ending → 귀여워요, past 귀여웠어요. 귀엽어요 is incorrect.
Calling a senior or boss 귀여워요
To someone you should respect it can sound patronizing. Reserve 귀엽다 for kids, pets, peers, or a partner.
Using 귀여워요 to mean elegant beauty
귀엽다 is adorable/charming, not refined-pretty. For graceful beauty use 예뻐요 or 아름다워요.

entries.nuance: 잘 지내요 pairs 잘 (well) with 지내다, a verb meaning 'to get along / pass one's days / live,' so it asks not about this very moment but about how life has been going lately — closer to 'how have you been keeping?' than a snapshot 'how do you feel right now?' Tone alone flips it: rising 잘 지내요? is the question, falling 잘 지내요. is the answer. Contrast it with 어떻게 지내요? (how are you getting on?), which is more open-ended and invites detail, whereas 잘 지내요? gently presumes things are fine and just seeks confirmation; also distinguish it from 기분이 어때요? ('how do you feel?'), which probes mood in the instant, not life in general. Because it spans a stretch of time, the past 잘 지냈어요? is common after a long absence. entries.explanation: "Long time no see." — that is 오랜만이에요 (oraenmanieyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오랜만이에요 ("long time no see"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 오랜만이에요 is 오랜만 ('a long while since,' itself from 오래 = long + 만 = the elapsed-interval marker) + 이에요 (to be), so it states 'it's been a long time' and works as a warm greeting the moment you reunite. The little 만 is the engine: it measures how much time has passed (일 년 만에 = after a whole year, 오랜만에 = after a long time), so anchor on it. Contrast 오랜만이에요 (the greeting, a complete sentence with 이에요) against the adverb 오랜만에 ('after a long time'), which modifies an action — 오랜만에 만나요 (we meet after a long time), 오랜만에 영화 봤어요 (I watched a movie for the first time in ages); mixing them up (saying 오랜만에 as a bare greeting) is a classic slip. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing 'long time no see' loosely for any short gap — in Korean it genuinely implies a real stretch apart (weeks or months), so greeting someone you saw yesterday with 오랜만이에요 sounds sarcastic or strange; for a short absence, just say 안녕하세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 오랜만이에요 for someone you saw very recently

Saying 오랜만에 as a standalone greeting
오랜만에 is an adverb ('after a long time') needing a verb — 오랜만에 만나요. The greeting form is 오랜만이에요.
Forgetting the interval-만, e.g. 오래만이에요
The correct word is 오랜만 (오래 + ㄴ + 만). Spelling it 오래만 drops the structure that means 'after a long interval.'

entries.nuance: 또 만나요 joins 또 (again) with 만나다 (to meet) in the 요-form, so it means 'let's meet again' — a hopeful goodbye implying you'd like to see the person another time. Crucially 만나다 means to meet up with a person (a scheduled or sought encounter), distinct from 보다 ('to see/look'); the casual goodbye 또 봐요 leans on the lighter 보다, while 또 만나요 sounds a touch more intentional, as if you value the relationship. Note 만나다 takes 을/를 or the comitative 와/과 (친구를 만나요 / 친구와 만나요), not 에서, for the person met. Contrast it with the time-buying 다음에 봐요 (see you next time, vaguer) and with 안녕히 가세요/계세요, the neutral 'goodbye' that carries no promise of reunion — 또 만나요 specifically projects a future meeting. The English-speaker pitfall is reflexively saying 'see you' to someone you'll likely never meet again the way English does; in Korean 또 만나요 sets up a genuine expectation of meeting, so for a one-off encounter with no plan to reconnect, the cleaner farewell is 안녕히 가세요.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 또 만나요 when you won't realistically meet again
It projects a genuine future meeting. For a one-time encounter with no plans, use 안녕히 가세요/안녕히 계세요 instead.
Using 보다 for arranging to meet a person, e.g. '친구를 봐요' meaning meet up
보다 is 'see/look'; to actively meet a person use 만나다 — 친구를 만나요. (또 봐요 as a casual 'bye' is fine, but for planning, 만나다.)
Marking the person with 에서: 친구에서 만나요
에서 marks a location, not the person met. Use 친구를 만나요 or 친구와 만나요; 에서 is for the place (카페에서 만나요).

Contrast it with the time-buying 다음에 봐요 (see you next time, vaguer) and with 안녕히 가세요/계세요, the neutral 'goodbye' that carries no promise of reunion — 또 만나요 specifically projects a future meeting.

The pitfall is reflexively saying 'see you' to someone you'll likely never meet again the way English does; in Korean 또 만나요 sets up a genuine expectation of meeting, so for a one-off encounter with no plan to reconnect, the cleaner farewell is 안녕히 가세요.

entries.nuance: 계좌 만들고 싶어요 is 계좌 (Sino-Korean 計座, 'account') + 만들다 ('to make') + -고 싶어요 ('want to'), the plain spoken way to tell a teller you want to open an account. Two words matter here: 계좌 is the technical 'account' (a number, used on forms and apps), while 통장 literally means the physical 'bankbook/passbook' but in daily speech doubles as 'account' — so 통장 만들고 싶어요 sounds just as natural and a bit more colloquial. The English-speaker trap is translating 'open' literally as 열다 ('to open a door/lid') and saying 계좌 열고 싶어요 — that is wrong; an account is 만들다 ('make') or 개설하다, never 열다. Default to 만들고 싶어요 with any teller; there is no 반말 version you'd use here since it's always a staff setting.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 계좌 열고 싶어요.
열다 ('to open') is for doors, lids, or shops — not bank accounts. You MAKE an account: 계좌 만들고 싶어요, or formally 계좌 개설하려고요.
Confusing 계좌 with 계산.
계좌 is a bank account; 계산 is 'calculation / paying a bill'. They sound close but 계산하고 싶어요 would mean 'I want to pay', not 'open an account'.
Using 통장 to mean the account number.
통장 is the physical passbook (and casually 'account'); the account NUMBER is 계좌번호. To give your number, say 계좌번호, not 통장.

entries.shortExplanation: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to check my balance".
entries.explanation: "I'd like to check my balance" — that is 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 (janae kwaginhago sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to check my balance"). examples.romanization: janae kwaginhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to check my balance.
examples.note: Said to a teller, or to yourself before using the ATM

examples.ko: 잔액 조회는 어디서 해요?
examples.romanization: janaek johoeneun eodiseo haeyo?
examples.en: Where do I check the balance?
examples.note: 조회 is the exact menu word you'll tap on the ATM screen

examples.romanization: ichehagi jeone janaekbuteo hwaginhalgeyo.

examples.note: 잔액부터 ('balance first') — 부터 means 'starting with'

entries.nuance: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 is 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining amount = balance') + 확인하다 ('to check/confirm') + -고 싶어요. There are two near-synonyms you must keep straight: 잔액 is the formal term printed on receipts, ATM menus, and statements, while 잔고 ('balance / what's left') is the warmer everyday word people use when chatting ('통장에 잔고가 없어' = 'my account's empty'). On machines and in apps the action is labeled 잔액 조회 ('balance inquiry'), where 조회 specifically means looking up information, so 조회 is the verb you tap, and 확인 is the broader 'check/confirm' you say aloud. The English-speaker trap is reaching for 균형 — the dictionary gives 균형 for 'balance', but 균형 means equilibrium/physical balance (as in keeping your balance), NEVER a bank balance. Saying 통장 균형 confuses Koreans completely. Also note the particle: it's 잔액을 확인하다 (object), so don't say 잔액에 확인하다. To a teller use the polite form; with a friend you'd casually ask 잔고 얼마야?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'balance' as 균형.
균형 is physical/abstract equilibrium ('keep your balance'). A bank balance is 잔액 (formal) or 잔고 (casual). 통장 균형 is meaningless to Koreans.
Saying 잔액에 확인하고 싶어요.
확인하다 takes the object particle 을/를: 잔액을 확인하고 싶어요. The particle 에 (location/time) is wrong here.
Mixing up 조회 and 충전.
조회 is 'inquiry/look up' (checking the balance); 충전 is 'top up/recharge' (adding money, e.g. to a transit card). Tap 조회 to SEE the balance, not 충전.

examples.romanization: hyeongeum jom ppobeuryeogoyo.
examples.en: I'm going to take out some cash.
examples.note: Said heading to the ATM, or to a teller for over-the-counter cash

examples.romanization: yeogi ATMeseo chulgeumdwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I withdraw at this ATM?

entries.nuance: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is 현금 ('cash', 現金) + 좀 (softener) + 뽑다 ('to pull/draw out') + -으려고요 ('I intend to'). Korean has three overlapping verbs for getting money out, and choosing right is the whole game: 뽑다 ('pull out') is the breezy spoken verb specifically for pulling cash from an ATM (돈 뽑다 = 'hit the ATM'); 찾다 — which elsewhere means 'find' — is the neutral standard 'withdraw' (돈을 찾다) used in any context, counter or machine; and 출금하다 (出金) is the formal Sino-Korean word you see on screens and forms. The opposite, depositing, is 입금하다 / 넣다 — keep 출금 (out) vs 입금 (in) firmly apart, since swapping them at a teller causes real mistakes. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'withdraw' as 철수하다 (which is 'withdraw troops/retreat!') or 인출 used as a bare verb; say 뽑다 or 찾다 in speech. Another trap: 찾다 here does NOT mean 'look for' — 돈 찾으러 가요 means 'going to withdraw money', not 'going to look for money'. With friends drop to 돈 좀 뽑을게.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'withdraw' as 철수하다 or 후퇴하다.
Those mean military/strategic withdrawal (retreat). For money it's 출금하다 / 돈을 찾다 / 돈을 뽑다.
Reading 돈 찾다 as 'look for money'.
In a banking context 찾다 means 'withdraw' (retrieve your money), not 'search'. 돈 찾으러 왔어요 = 'I came to withdraw money'.
Confusing 출금 and 입금.
출금 (出金) = money OUT (withdrawal); 입금 (入金) = money IN (deposit). Tell the teller 출금이요 to take cash out, 입금이요 to put money in.

examples.romanization: susuryo isseoyo?

examples.note: Asked before transferring or withdrawing at another bank's ATM

examples.ko: 다른 은행 ATM이라 수수료 붙어요?
examples.romanization: dareun eunhaeng ATMira susuryo buteoyo?

entries.nuance: 수수료 있어요? is 수수료 (手數料, 'handling fee/commission') + 있어요? ('is there?'). 수수료 is the all-purpose word for a transaction fee — ATM fees, transfer fees, wire fees, exchange margins — so it's the single most useful money word at a Korean bank. The natural verb pairing is 붙다 ('to stick/be attached'): Koreans say 수수료가 붙어요 ('a fee gets tacked on'), which sounds more idiomatic than the textbook 수수료를 내다 ('to pay a fee'); both are correct but 붙다 is what you'll hear about charges appearing automatically. To ask about getting out of a fee, use 면제 ('exemption'): 수수료 면제돼요?. entries.nuance: 비밀번호 (秘密番號, lit. 'secret number') is the one word covering PIN, password, and door code — Korean does NOT split 'PIN' from 'password' the way English does, so use 비밀번호 for your card PIN, your app login, and the restroom door code alike. With it you'll hear two verbs: 입력하다 ('to input', the formal screen word) and 누르다 ('to press', the spoken 'key it in') — 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 vs 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 are interchangeable, the latter just warmer. Note this phrase is usually said TO you by staff or the machine (the honorific 주세요 makes it a polite request to the customer); when YOU forgot it, you flip to 비밀번호 잊어버렸어요. Counting digits uses 자리 ('place/digit'): 네 자리 = four digits. The English-speaker trap is calling it 패스워드 (the loanword exists but sounds tech-only/IT) when 비밀번호 is the universal term, or saying 암호 — which means 'cipher/passcode' and feels more like a secret code or encryption than your everyday bank PIN. Also don't confuse 비밀번호 with 계좌번호 (account number) — one is secret, one you freely give out.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 비밀번호 with 계좌번호.
비밀번호 is your SECRET PIN/password (never share it); 계좌번호 is your account NUMBER (you give it out to receive money). Mixing them is a real security slip.
Using 암호 for a bank PIN.
암호 leans toward 'cipher/secret code/encryption'. Your everyday card PIN and app login are 비밀번호. Banks and ATMs all say 비밀번호.
Saying 비밀번호를 눌러요 to staff as a request.
As a polite request TO the customer it needs the favor form: 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 / 입력해 주세요. Bare 눌러요 sounds like a flat statement, not a courteous instruction.

entries.nuance: 여기 송금하고 싶어요 uses 송금 (送金, lit. 'send-money', i.e. 'remittance') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Three terms cluster here and the distinctions are practical: 송금 is the formal umbrella for sending money to someone (especially the word for overseas/wire transfers, 해외 송금); 계좌이체 (or just 이체) specifically means an account-to-account electronic transfer you do in an app or ATM; and 보내다 ('to send') is the plain verbal way to say it (돈 보내다). For a teller, 송금하고 싶어요 or 이체하고 싶어요 both work. The make-or-break point is particles for the destination: an account/bank/place takes 로/으로 ('to') — 이 계좌로 보내다 — while a PERSON takes 한테 / 에게 — 친구한테 송금하다. English speakers routinely overuse 에 here (이 계좌에 보내다 sounds off; native is 이 계좌로). Another trap is confusing 송금 (sending OUT) with 입금 (money coming IN to an account); if you want someone to pay YOU, you give them your 계좌번호 and they 입금/송금 to you. Don't translate 'transfer' as 옮기다 ('to move/relocate an object') — money transfer is 이체 / 송금, never 옮기다.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the destination account with 에 instead of 로.
Money goes TO an account with 로/으로: 이 계좌로 보내 주세요. 이 계좌에 보내다 sounds unnatural to natives.
Using 한테/에게 for an account number.
한테/에게 are for PEOPLE (친구한테 송금). An account or bank takes 로/으로 (이 계좌로). Match the particle to person vs. thing.
Translating 'transfer' as 옮기다.
옮기다 means physically moving/relocating something. A money transfer is 이체하다 or 송금하다. 돈을 옮기다 sounds like carrying cash around.

entries.nuance: 이체할게요 is 이체 (移替, 'transfer between accounts') + -할게요, the -ㄹ게요 ending announcing your own intended action politely. 이체 is the precise word for moving money account-to-account electronically; 계좌이체 spells it out fully ('account transfer') and is the standard label for 'pay by bank transfer' as a payment method — handy in Korea where many small transactions and rent are settled by 이체 rather than card. The everyday alternative is 보내다 ('send'), so 돈 보낼게요 and 이체할게요 mean the same in casual use, with 이체 sounding a touch more technical/correct. A crucial real-world pairing: when you've SENT money you say 이체했어요 (you transferred), but to confirm it ARRIVED in the recipient's account you ask about 입금 ('deposit in') — 입금됐어요? — because from their side it's an incoming deposit. The English-speaker trap is the register of -ㄹ게요 vs -겠어요: 이체할게요 is the natural conversational 'I'll transfer it', while 이체하겠습니다 is stiff/formal. Also, to send to someone senior, upgrade to the humble 이체해 드릴게요. Don't confuse 이체 with 환전 (currency exchange) — different operations entirely.

이체했어요 means YOU sent it. Whether it ARRIVED is 입금됐어요? (deposited on their end). The two sides have different verbs: 이체 (send) vs 입금 (receive).
Over-formalizing as 이체하겠습니다 in casual settings.
합쇼체 sounds stiff for an everyday transfer. The natural polite form is 이체할게요. Save 하겠습니다 for formal/business contexts.
Confusing 이체 with 환전.
이체 (移替) is account-to-account transfer; 환전 (換錢) is exchanging currency. Don't say 이체 when you mean to swap dollars for won.

structuredNuance.t: 이체 (移替, 'transfer between accounts') + -할게요, the -ㄹ게요 ending announcing your own intended action politely. 이체 is the precise word for moving money account-to-account electronically; 계좌이체 spells it out fully ('account transfer') and is the standard label for 'pay by bank transfer' as a payment method — handy in Korea where many small transactions and rent are settled by 이체 rather than card. A crucial real-world pairing: when you've SENT money you say 이체했어요 (you transferred), but to confirm it ARRIVED in the recipient's account you ask about 입금 ('deposit in') — 입금됐어요? — because from their side it's an incoming deposit. To send to someone senior, upgrade to the humble 이체해 드릴게요.

The everyday alternative is 보내다 ('send'), so 돈 보낼게요 and 이체할게요 mean the same in casual use, with 이체 sounding a touch more technical/correct. Don't confuse 이체 with 환전 (currency exchange) — different operations entirely.
이체 is 移替, 'transfer between accounts'.
The register of -ㄹ게요 vs -겠어요: 이체할게요 is the natural conversational 'I'll transfer it', while 이체하겠습니다 is stiff/formal.

entries.nuance: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요 is 계좌번호 ('account number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know', from 알리다 'to inform' + 주다 favor). This is the line you say constantly in Korea, where splitting bills and paying friends back by instant transfer is the norm — you ask for their 계좌번호 and 이체. Note 계좌번호 (the number, freely shared so people can pay you) is the OPPOSITE of 비밀번호 (your secret PIN, never shared); confusing them is a security mistake learners genuinely make. To request it, 알려 주세요 ('let me know') is the standard; 불러 주세요 ('read it out') is when they'll dictate and you type; casually friends say 계좌 찍어 줘 ('text me the account'). You'll often also need the 예금주 ('depositor / account holder') name, because banking apps make you confirm the recipient's name matches. The English-speaker trap is using 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'to teach', so 계좌번호 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson; the verb for 'let me know (info)' is 알려 주다. Default to 알려 주세요 with anyone; with close friends drop to 계좌번호 좀 알려 줘.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 가르쳐 주세요 to ask for the number.
가르치다 = 'to teach (a skill)'. For sharing information like a number, use 알리다: 계좌번호 알려 주세요. 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like requesting instruction.
Confusing 계좌번호 with 비밀번호.
계좌번호 (account number) is shared so people can pay you; 비밀번호 (PIN/password) is secret. Never give your 비밀번호 to receive money — only your 계좌번호.
Forgetting to give the 은행 (bank name).
A 계좌번호 alone isn't enough — the sender needs the BANK too (예: 국민은행 123-45-6789). Say the 은행 first, then the number.

entries.nuance: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is 입금 (入金, 'money in = deposit') + 되다 (passive 'be done') + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the exact word for money ARRIVING in an account — the receiving side of any transfer — and is the natural partner to 송금/이체 (the sending side): the sender 이체했어요 ('sent'), the receiver checks 입금됐어요? ('came in?'). A warmer, very common alternative is 들어오다 ('to come in'): 돈 들어왔어요? / 월급 들어왔어요? all mean 'did the money land?'. The grammar point English speakers stumble on is 입금되다 vs 입금하다: 입금되다 is passive/intransitive ('to be deposited / to come in', used when money simply arrives), while 입금하다 is the active 'to deposit (money into an account)' — so 'did it come in?' is 입금됐어요? (passive), but 'I'll deposit cash' is 입금할게요 (active). Mixing these is the classic error. The -는지 ('whether') turns it into an indirect question inside 확인해 주세요 — note it attaches to the verb stem (됐는지), not as a separate word. Casually you'd just ask a friend 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 입금되다 and 입금하다.
입금되다 = 'be deposited / come in' (passive, money arrives): 입금됐어요?. 입금하다 = 'to deposit' (active, you put money in): 입금할게요. Use the passive for 'did it arrive'.
Confusing 입금 (in) with 출금 (out).
입금 (入金) is money coming IN; 출금 (出金) is money going OUT. 입금됐어요? asks if a deposit arrived; for a withdrawal you'd say 출금.
Saying 입금했는지 확인해 주세요 to check arrival.
That asks whether someone DEPOSITED (active). To check if money CAME IN, use the passive: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'suspension/halt') + 시키다 ('to make happen') + 주세요. This is an urgent, high-stakes phrase, so getting it right matters. 정지(시키다) means to SUSPEND/freeze the card (it can sometimes be unfrozen); if the card is lost or stolen you'll more precisely 분실 신고하다 ('file a loss report'), which permanently blocks it, and then 재발급 ('reissue') a new one. The spoken urgent verb is 막다 ('to block/stop up') — 카드 막아 주세요 is what a panicked person actually blurts at the call center. The grammar trap is 정지하다 vs 정지시키다: 정지하다 can read as 'the card stops' (intransitive), while 정지시키다 ('cause it to stop') correctly expresses 'have it suspended' — for asking the bank to freeze YOUR card, 정지시켜 주세요 is cleaner. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'cancel' as 취소하다 — 취소하다 means cancelling a transaction/reservation/order, NOT killing a card; a card is 정지/해지(terminate)/분실 신고, never 취소. Also note 정지 (suspend) vs 해지 (terminate the account/card for good) are different: temporary freeze vs permanent close. This is always 존댓말 to staff; there's no casual version you'd realistically use.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 카드 취소해 주세요 to block a card.
취소하다 cancels a transaction/order/reservation, not a card. To block a card say 카드 정지시켜 주세요, or for a lost card 분실 신고하려고요.
Using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다.
정지하다 can sound like the card itself stops. To request the bank CAUSE it to be suspended, the causative 정지시키다 is clearer: 카드 정지시켜 주세요.
Confusing 정지 (suspend) with 해지 (terminate).
정지 is a (possibly temporary) freeze; 해지 permanently terminates the card/account. If you only lost it and want a new one, you 정지/분실 신고 + 재발급, not 해지.

entries.nuance: 카드가 안 됐어요 is 카드 + 가 (subject) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('to work/function') in past polite. 되다 is the workhorse verb for 'something functions/goes through', so 안 되다 ('doesn't work') covers a declined card, a frozen card, a dead chip — the catch-all you say first. To be specific at checkout, the precise noun is 결제 ('payment/settlement'): 결제가 안 돼요 ('the payment won't process'), and 결제 is the word on every card terminal. For an explicit 'declined', 거절되다 ('to be rejected') is clearer. A frequent real cause is 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded'), the literal on-screen error. The grammar trap is tense and the subject particle: it's 카드가 안 됐어요 (subject 가, past 됐), not 카드를 안 했어요 (which would mean 'I didn't do the card', nonsense). The English-speaker trap is translating 'work' as 일하다 ('to labor/have a job') — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and funny; a device/card 'working' is 되다, never 일하다. Also don't say 카드가 틀렸어요 ('the card is incorrect', like a wrong answer); a non-functioning card is 안 됐어요. Casual version: 카드 안 돼.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'work' as 일하다.
일하다 means 'to do labor/have a job'. A card/machine functioning is 되다: 카드가 안 됐어요. 카드가 일 안 해요 is incorrect.
Saying 카드를 안 했어요.
With 를 it means 'I didn't do the card'. The card is the SUBJECT of failing, so use 가: 카드가 안 됐어요.
Using 틀리다 for a declined card.
틀리다 = 'to be wrong/incorrect (an answer)'. A card that won't process is 안 되다 / 거절되다, not 틀리다. Say 카드가 안 됐어요.

entries.explanation: 환전하고 싶어요 (hwanjeonhago sipeoyo) = "I'd like to exchange money". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 환전하고 싶어요 ("I'd like to exchange currency"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
