entries.nuance: 환전하고 싶어요 is 환전 (換錢, lit. 'exchange-money') + 하다 + -고 싶어요, the standard request to swap one currency for another, done at a bank or a 환전소 (exchange booth). The essential partner word is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') — you'll ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? ('what's the rate?') and judge it with the collocation 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 ('the rate is good/bad'). To name currencies, use 로/으로 for the target: 달러로 환전하다 ('exchange INTO dollars'), 원화로 바꾸다. A plainer everyday synonym is 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') — 달러로 바꾸고 싶어요 is perfectly natural and a touch more colloquial than 환전하다. The English-speaker trap is mixing up 환전 (換錢, currency exchange) with 환불 (還拂, 'refund') — they look and sound similar but 환불 is getting your money back for a returned purchase; never say 환전 at a store return counter. Another trap: don't say 교환하다 ('to exchange/swap goods', like swapping a shirt for another size) for currency — 교환 is for trading items, 환전 is specifically for money. Also keep 환율 (rate) distinct from 수수료 (the exchange fee), which is separate and worth asking about. To staff use 존댓말; the form holds in casual speech too.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 환전 (exchange money) with 환불 (refund).
환전 (換錢) = swap currency; 환불 (還拂) = refund a purchase. At a store you ask 환불, at a bank 환전. They're not interchangeable.
Using 교환하다 for currency.
교환하다 is exchanging GOODS (swap a size/item). Currency is 환전하다 or 바꾸다. 돈을 교환하다 sounds like bartering objects, not changing money.
Marking the target currency with 에.
The currency you change INTO takes 로/으로: 달러로 환전하다. 달러에 환전하다 is wrong. Source uses 을/를: 원화를 달러로.

entries.nuance: 환율 어떻게 돼요? is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') + 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it come to be?'), the idiomatic Korean way to ask for a figure or status. The construction 어떻게 돼요? is hugely useful — Koreans use it to ask rates, prices, totals, even your name (이름이 어떻게 되세요?) — and it sounds more natural and polite than a blunt 얼마예요? for an abstract figure like a rate, though 환율 얼마예요? is also fine. A money-saving phrase to know is 환율 우대 ('preferential exchange rate'): banks give regulars or app users 우대 (優待, 'preferential treatment'), so asking 환율 우대 돼요? can get you a better deal. The English-speaker trap is the structure: learners try to calque 'what is the rate' as 환율이 뭐예요? — but 뭐예요? ('what is it?') asks for a definition/identity, not a numeric value, so it sounds like you're asking what 'exchange rate' means; use 어떻게 돼요? or 얼마예요? for the number. Another trap: don't confuse 환율 (rate) with 환전 (the act of exchanging) — 환율 is the number, 환전 is the transaction. Keep the polite 돼요?; with friends it'd casually be 환율 어떻게 돼?.

환율 우대 ('preferential rate') is a real discount banks offer. Asking 환율 우대 돼요? can save money; without the word you may pay the full rate.

entries.nuance: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 is 잔돈 ('small change/change') + -으로 ('into') + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + 주세요. 잔돈 covers both small-denomination bills and coins, and is also the word for the 'change' you get back after paying (거스름돈 is the more precise 'change returned', but 잔돈 is used loosely for it too). entries.nuance: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요 is 통장 ('bankbook/passbook') + 정리 (整理, 'tidying/sorting') + 좀 + 해 주세요. 통장 정리 is a specifically Korean banking ritual: feeding your physical passbook into a machine (통장정리기) or handing it to a teller to PRINT the latest transactions into it — 정리 here means 'putting the records in order', not its usual sense of 'cleaning up/throwing away'. Casually you'd say 통장 정리 좀 해 줘 to a teller you're friendly with, but 존댓말 is the norm.

entries.nuance: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 is 자동 (自動, 'automatic') + 이체 ('transfer') + 신청하다 ('to apply for/sign up') + -고 싶어요. 자동이체 is the recurring auto-debit you set up for rent (월세), utilities (공과금), phone (통신비), and subscriptions — essential for living in Korea, where most regular bills are pulled automatically from your account. 'hook it up and leave it'), using the -아/어 놓다 pattern that means 'do and leave in that state'. When money is auto-deducted, the vivid native verb is 빠져나가다 ('to slip out / be drawn out') — 돈이 빠져나가요 ('the money comes out'). To stop it, you 해지하다 ('terminate') the 자동이체. Another trap: 신청 ('apply for / request') vs 접수 ('receive/register an application') — you 신청 (apply), the bank 접수 (takes it in). Default 존댓말 with staff.

신청하다 = YOU apply/sign up. The bank's side of receiving it is 접수. Say 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 to request setup; the bank then 접수 (processes) it.

entries.nuance: 근처에 ATM 있어요? is 근처 ('vicinity/nearby') + 에 (location particle) + ATM + 있어요? ('is there?'). Koreans say the English initialism ATM (pronounced 에이티엠) constantly, but the native term is 현금인출기 (現金引出機, 'cash withdrawal machine') or the broader 자동화기기 ('automated machine', the bank's signage word for the all-in-one deposit/withdraw kiosks) — all three are understood. The location particle is the crunch point: a PLACE where something exists takes 에 (근처에 있어요?, '있다/없다' for existence), so 근처에 ATM 있어요? is right, while learners wrongly use 에서 here — 에서 marks where an ACTION happens (ATM에서 돈을 뽑다, 'withdraw AT the ATM'), not where a thing simply exists. Practically, ATMs sit in bank lobbies (24-hour 365코너), convenience stores (편의점), and subway stations; convenience-store and other-bank machines almost always charge a 수수료, and many bank ATMs stop free service or close after hours, so it's worth also asking 이 카드 여기서 돼요? ('does my card work here?'). The English-speaker trap, besides 에 vs 에서, is assuming all ATMs take all cards/foreign cards — ask 다른 은행 카드도 돼요? or look for a 'Global ATM' for overseas cards. Casual form: 근처에 ATM 있어?.

structuredNuance.t: 근처 ('vicinity/nearby') + 에 (location particle) + ATM + 있어요? ('is there?'). The location particle is the crunch point: a PLACE where something exists takes 에 (근처에 있어요?, '있다/없다' for existence), so 근처에 ATM 있어요? is right, while learners wrongly use 에서 here — 에서 marks where an ACTION happens (ATM에서 돈을 뽑다, 'withdraw AT the ATM'), not where a thing simply exists. Practically, ATMs sit in bank lobbies (24-hour 365코너), convenience stores (편의점), and subway stations; convenience-store and other-bank machines almost always charge a 수수료, and many bank ATMs stop free service or close after hours, so it's worth also asking 이 카드 여기서 돼요? ('does my card work here?'). Casual form: 근처에 ATM 있어?.

Koreans say the English initialism ATM (pronounced 에이티엠) constantly, but the native term is 현금인출기 (現金引出機, 'cash withdrawal machine') or the broader 자동화기기 ('automated machine', the bank's signage word for the all-in-one deposit/withdraw kiosks) — all three are understood.
현금인출기 is 現金引出機, 'cash withdrawal machine'.

entries.explanation: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 (iche hando jom ollyeo juseyo) = "Please raise my transfer limit". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 ("Please raise my transfer limit"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: 한도 초과 = the on-screen error blocking a big transfer

usagePhrases.romanization: chulgeum handodo gachi ollil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Can I raise the withdrawal limit too?
usagePhrases.note: 출금 한도 (withdrawal cap) is separate from the transfer cap

examples.ko: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요.
examples.romanization: iche hando jom ollyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Please raise my transfer limit.
examples.note: Said to a teller when you need to send a large amount

examples.ko: 1회 한도가 낮아서 송금이 안 돼요. 좀 올려 주세요.
examples.romanization: 1hoe handoga najaseo songgeumi an dwaeyo. jom ollyeo juseyo.
examples.en: The per-transfer cap is too low to send. Please raise it.
examples.note: 낮다 ('low') describes the cap; give it as the reason

examples.ko: 보안카드 없이는 한도를 못 올린다고요?
examples.romanization: boankadeu eopsineun handoreul mot ollindagoyo?

examples.note: 한도 increases often require 보안카드/OTP verification in Korea

entries.nuance: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 is 이체 ('transfer') + 한도 (限度, 'limit/ceiling') + 좀 + 올리다 ('to raise') + 주세요. 한도 is the cap on how much you can move, and Korea sets surprisingly low defaults — especially for new or foreigner accounts — split into 1회 한도 ('per-transaction limit') and 1일 한도 ('daily limit'), plus separate 출금 한도 (withdrawal) and 이체 한도 (transfer). New residents constantly hit these, so 한도 올려 주세요 ('please raise the limit') is a genuinely needed phrase, usually requiring identity re-verification, a 보안카드 (security card) or OTP. The natural verb pair is 올리다 ('raise') / 내리다 ('lower') for the cap, and the blocking error you'll see is 한도 초과 ('exceeded the limit'). The English-speaker trap is vocabulary: 한도 ('limit/quota/ceiling') is specifically a permitted maximum, not to be confused with 한계 ('limit' in the sense of a boundary of ability/endurance, e.g. 체력의 한계) — you say 이체 한도, never 이체 한계. Another is the verb: an account limit is 올리다/높이다 ('raise'), not 늘리다 in the sense of physically multiplying — though 한도를 늘리다 ('increase the limit') is also acceptable. Don't confuse 한도 (a cap) with 잔액 (your actual balance): you can have plenty of 잔액 but still be blocked by a low 한도. Always 존댓말 to staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 한계 instead of 한도 for an account cap.
한도 (限度) is a permitted maximum/quota (이체 한도). 한계 is a limit of ability/endurance (체력의 한계). For a transfer or withdrawal cap, always 한도.
Confusing 한도 (cap) with 잔액 (balance).
한도 is the MAX you're allowed to move; 잔액 is how much money you actually have. You can be blocked by a low 한도 even with a high 잔액. They're different problems.
Saying 한도 크게 해 주세요.
The idiomatic verb for a cap is 올리다/높이다 ('raise'): 한도 좀 올려 주세요. 크게 하다 ('make it big') sounds off for a numeric limit.

entries.explanation: 구경 좀 할게요 (gugyeong jom halgeyo) means "I'm just looking, thanks". Say it as one set phrase — for example 구경 좀 할게요 ("I'm just looking"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

Common variant; 둘러보다 = 'look around'
반말, only with a friend, not to staff

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to look on my own
usagePhrases.note: Gently signals you don't need to be followed

examples.ko: 구경 좀 할게요.
examples.romanization: gugyeong jom halgeyo.
examples.en: I'm just looking.
examples.note: Said the moment a clerk approaches and asks 뭐 찾으세요?

examples.ko: 네, 그냥 구경 좀 할게요. 필요하면 부를게요.
examples.romanization: ne, geunyang gugyeong jom halgeyo. piryohamyeon bureulgeyo.
examples.en: Yeah, just looking — I'll call you if I need help.
examples.note: 부를게요 ('I'll call you') politely sends them off

examples.note: Use when a clerk keeps hovering at your shoulder

entries.nuance: 구경 좀 할게요 is 구경 ('looking around, sightseeing') + 좀 (softener) + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 'I'm going to…' ending), so literally 'I'll do a little looking' — the polite, friendly way to tell an Olive Young or department-store beauty clerk you don't want help yet. In Korean cosmetics shops staff often greet you and shadow you, and this phrase, said with a small smile, releases the pressure without rudeness. The near-twin 그냥 둘러볼게요 ('I'll just browse') is interchangeable; 구경 leans slightly more 'window-shopping', 둘러보다 more 'walk around and look'. The English-speaker trap is translating 'just looking' as a flat 안 사요 ('I'm not buying') — that sounds cold and almost defensive, as if accusing them; 구경 좀 할게요 keeps it warm and leaves the door open. Another pitfall is dropping the 요 to a stranger (구경 좀 할게), which is 반말 and abrupt. Keep the -ㄹ게요 form because it frames it as your own gentle intention, not an order to them.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 사요 to mean 'just looking'.
안 사요 means 'I'm not buying' and sounds blunt or defensive to a clerk. The friendly, face-saving line is 구경 좀 할게요 — it doesn't shut them down, just postpones help.
Dropping 요 and saying 구경 좀 할게 to staff.
That's 반말 and sounds abrupt to a stranger. Keep the polite ending: 구경 좀 할게요.
Using 보다 alone as 좀 볼게요 expecting it to be clear.
좀 볼게요 ('I'll take a look') can sound like you want to look at one specific item the clerk is holding. For browsing the store, say 구경 좀 할게요 or 둘러볼게요.

Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: 손등 ('back of the hand') = where you swatch makeup

examples.ko: 이거 발라봐도 돼요?
examples.romanization: igeo ballabwado dwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I try this on?
examples.note: Pointing at a tester lipstick or cream

examples.ko: 립스틱 색 보려고요. 손등에 발라봐도 돼요?
examples.romanization: ripseutik saek boryeogoyo. sondeunge ballabwado dwaeyo?
examples.en: I want to see the lipstick color — can I swatch it on my hand?
examples.note: 손등 is the normal place to test color in Korea

examples.ko: 이 선크림 끈적이는지 발라봐도 돼요?
examples.romanization: i seonkeurim kkeunjeogineunji ballabwado dwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I try this sunscreen to see if it's sticky?
examples.note: 끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky') names what you're checking

entries.nuance: 이거 발라봐도 돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 발라보다 (바르다 'to apply/spread' + -아 보다 'try doing') + -도 돼요? ('is it okay to…?'), so 'is it okay if I try applying this?' — the go-to for testing a tester (테스터) cream, lotion, or lipstick. 바르다 is the specific verb for spreading skincare or makeup ON skin (cream, sunscreen, lip balm); it is NOT 칠하다 ('to paint/coat', for walls or nails-as-paint) — using 칠하다 for face cream sounds like you're painting yourself. The 손등 (back of the hand) is the culturally standard swatch spot, so naming it makes you sound like a regular. The English-speaker error is asking 'can I try this?' as 이거 해 봐도 돼요? — 해 보다 ('try doing') is too generic for putting product on skin; the precise verb is 발라보다. Another trap is the particle on the body part: you apply TO a surface with 에 (손등에 발라요), not 을/를. Default 존댓말; with a friend it drops to 발라봐도 돼?.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 칠하다 for applying cream or sunscreen.
칠하다 means 'to paint/coat' (walls, a fence). Skincare and makeup go on with 바르다. Say 발라봐도 돼요?, not 칠해 봐도 돼요?.
Saying 이거 해 봐도 돼요? to test a sample.
해 보다 ('try doing') is too vague for putting product on skin. The specific verb is 발라보다: 이거 발라봐도 돼요?
Marking the body part with 을/를: 손등을 발라봐도 돼요?
You apply product TO a surface, so the particle is 에: 손등에 발라봐도 돼요? (손등을 would mean you're applying the hand itself).

entries.nuance: 샘플 좀 주세요 is the loanword 샘플 ('sample') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). Sampling culture is huge in Korea — beauty staff routinely tuck free 샘플 (sachets) into your bag, especially after a purchase, so this is a normal, expected request, not begging. The warm insider version uses 챙기다 ('gather and pack thoughtfully for someone'): 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요 sounds friendlier than the plain 주세요. Note 샘플 (free trial sachet) is different from 테스터 (the open display tester you swatch in-store) and from 증정품/사은품 (a gift-with-purchase, often a full-size freebie) — asking for the wrong word gets you the wrong thing. The English-speaker error is over-explaining with 무료 ('free') as in 무료 샘플 주세요 — 샘플 already implies free, and adding 무료 sounds slightly grabby; just say 샘플 좀 주세요. Another pitfall: don't ask before buying as if entitled — Koreans usually buy first, then ask, and 좀 keeps it gracious.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 샘플 with 테스터.
샘플 is the free take-home sachet; 테스터 is the open in-store display you swatch but can't take. To take some home, ask for 샘플, not 테스터.
Adding 무료 as in 무료 샘플 주세요.
샘플 already implies it's free; tacking on 무료 ('free') sounds a bit grabby. Just say 샘플 좀 주세요.
Saying 샘플 줘 to staff.
줘 is 반말 and too casual for a clerk. Use 주세요 (or warmer 챙겨 주세요): 샘플 좀 주세요.

entries.nuance: 저 피부가 건성이에요 is 저 ('I', humble) + 피부 ('skin') + 가 (subject particle) + 건성 ('dry type', Sino-Korean 乾性) + 이에요 (polite copula). Korean names skin types with the -성 ('-type/-natured') suffix: 건성 (dry), 지성 (oily), 복합성 (combination), 민감성 (sensitive), 중성 (normal). These are the exact words beauty staff use when asking 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요?. The crucial point: 건성 is the SKIN-TYPE noun, while 건조하다 is the ADJECTIVE 'to be dry' for a condition right now (건조해요 = 'it feels dry'). So your constitutional type is 건성이에요, but if your skin feels parched today you'd say 피부가 건조해요 — mixing them (저 건조성이에요) is wrong; the type word is 건성, not 건조성. The English-speaker error is translating 'dry skin' literally as 마른 피부 — 마르다 means 'thin/skinny (body)' or 'dried out (laundry)', not skin type; never say 마른 피부 for 건성. Also keep 피부가 with the subject particle 가, not 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 마른 피부 for 'dry skin'.
마르다 means 'thin (body)' or 'dried (laundry)'. The skin-type word is 건성. Say 저 건성이에요 or 피부가 건성이에요, never 마른 피부.
Confusing the type noun 건성 with the adjective 건조하다.
건성 = your skin TYPE ('dry-type'); 건조하다 = a condition ('feels dry now'). Type: 건성이에요. Condition: 피부가 건조해요. Don't say 건조성.
Using 을/를 on 피부.
피부 is the subject here, so use 가: 피부가 건성이에요. 피부를 건성이에요 is ungrammatical.

entries.nuance: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? is 이거 ('this') + 무슨 ('what kind of') + 타입 (loanword 'type') + 이에요?, asking which skin type a product targets. The most efficient real-shop phrasing, though, uses the suffix -용 ('for the use of'): 건성용 ('for dry skin'), 지성용 ('for oily'), 민감성용 ('for sensitive') — so 이거 건성용이에요? ('is this the dry-skin one?') gets a yes/no instantly. The dividing line: 무슨 타입이에요? is open-ended ('what type?'), while -용이에요? pins down YOUR type. A subtle point: 무슨 vs. 어떤 — 무슨 asks 'what kind/which category', 어떤 asks 'what's it like / which one', and both work here, but 무슨 타입 is the set collocation. The English-speaker error is asking 'what is this for?' as 이거 뭐에 써요? — that asks the product's PURPOSE ('what do you use it for?', e.g. face vs. body), not which skin type; to ask about skin type, say 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?. Don't forget 이에요 fuses after 타입: 타입이에요, not 타입 이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 이거 뭐에 써요? to mean 'what skin type'.
That asks the product's purpose (face? body?), not skin type. For skin type, ask 이거 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?
Saying 건성을 위한 거예요? instead of 건성용.
건성을 위한 거 is grammatical but clunky. Koreans use the compact suffix -용: 이거 건성용이에요?

The fixed collocation is 무슨 타입. 어떤 타입 is understandable but less idiomatic for asking the category; default to 무슨 타입이에요?

entries.nuance: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? is 보습 ('moisture retention', Sino-Korean 保濕) + 잘 되는 ('that works well') + 거 ('thing') + 있어요? ('do you have?'). 보습 is THE beauty word for hydration/moisturizing; the product quality is 보습력 ('moisturizing power'), and the sensory result is 촉촉하다 ('dewy, moist'). The opposite sensation, 당기다 ('to feel tight/taut'), signals dryness ('당겨요' = 'my skin feels tight'). entries.nuance: 자외선 차단제 어디 있어요? is 자외선 ('ultraviolet rays', Sino-Korean 紫外線) + 차단제 ('blocking agent', 차단 'block' + 제 'agent') + 어디 있어요? Another trap: 자외선 차단 ('UV blocking', the function) vs. 자외선 차단제 ('the product') — drop the 제 and you've named the action, not the item, so to buy it keep 차단제 or just say 선크림. Default 존댓말 with 어디 있어요? for location.

자외선 차단 names the function ('UV blocking'), not the product. To buy the item, say 자외선 차단제 or, more naturally, 선크림 있어요?

entries.nuance: 이거 안 무거워요? is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 무겁다 ('to be heavy') in polite question form. In skincare, 무겁다 doesn't mean weight — it's the feel of a thick, occlusive product sitting on the skin; its opposites are 가볍다 ('light') and 산뜻하다 ('fresh, light, non-heavy'). The other big texture word is 끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky'), the thing people most dread in summer or with sunscreen. Koreans also discuss 발림성 ('spreadability/how it applies', from 발리다, the passive of 바르다) and 흡수 ('absorption', 잘 흡수돼요 = 'absorbs well'). The English-speaker error is translating 'heavy' literally as 무게 ('weight') and saying 무게 있어요? — that asks about physical heaviness, not texture; the adjective 무겁다 is the right feel word. Another trap: 'greasy' is 기름지다 / 번들거리다 ('to look oily/shiny'), not 무겁다, so distinguish a heavy feel (무겁다) from a greasy shine (번들거리다). The 안 …요? frame ('isn't it…?') is the natural way to voice a worry and invite reassurance. Default 존댓말.

Asking 무게 있어요? for a 'heavy' feel.
무게 means physical weight. The skincare feel is the adjective 무겁다: 이거 안 무거워요? (Does it feel heavy/thick on the skin?)

무겁다 is a thick, dense feel; greasy shine is 번들거리다 or 기름지다. If you mean shiny/oily, ask 번들거리지 않아요?

The natural verb forms are 끈적이다 → 끈적여요 or 끈적거리다 → 끈적거려요. 끈적해요 is non-standard; say 안 끈적여요?

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking for an in-store display tester

usagePhrases.en: Is there one I can try on?
usagePhrases.note: Descriptive version if 테스터 isn't understood
When you can't find the open display
For makeup; asks to view/swatch the shade

examples.romanization: teseuteo isseoyo?
examples.en: Is there a tester?
examples.note: Asked when a product is sealed and you want to try it

examples.romanization: i kusyeon teseuteo isseoyo? saek jom bogo sipeoseoyo.
examples.en: Is there a tester for this cushion? I want to check the shade.
examples.note: 색 보다 ('check the color') is the makeup reason

entries.nuance: 테스터 있어요? is the loanword 테스터 ('tester') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking for the open in-store display unit you can swatch. Crucially 테스터 (the try-in-store display) is NOT 샘플 (the free take-home sachet) and NOT 증정품/사은품 (a gift with purchase) — confusing these gets you the wrong answer. Korean beauty shops, especially Olive Young and brand stores, usually have 테스터 out, so this is a routine ask. The English-speaker error is saying 'sample' (샘플) when you mean a tester to swatch in-store — if you ask 샘플 있어요? while standing at a lipstick display, staff may think you want a freebie to take home, not to test the shade now. Another pitfall is over-formalizing as 시험용 제품 있습니까? ('do you have a trial-use product?'), which is stiff and unnatural — just say 테스터 있어요?. If the word itself fails, the descriptive fallback 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요? ('is there one I can try on?') always works. Default 존댓말; the 있어요? frame is the simplest existence question.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 샘플 있어요? when you want to swatch in-store.
샘플 is the take-home freebie. The in-store try unit is 테스터. To test a shade now, ask 테스터 있어요? or 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요?
Confusing 테스터 with 증정품/사은품.
테스터 = in-store try unit; 증정품/사은품 = a gift with purchase. They're different things; ask for 테스터 to test, not 증정품.
Over-formal 시험용 제품 있습니까?
That's stiff and bookish. The everyday word is the loanword 테스터: 테스터 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 테스터 있어요? is the loanword 테스터 ('tester') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking for the open in-store display unit you can swatch. Korean beauty shops, especially Olive Young and brand stores, usually have 테스터 out, so this is a routine ask. If the word itself fails, the descriptive fallback 발라볼 수 있는 거 있어요? ('is there one I can try on?') always works. Default 존댓말; the 있어요? frame is the simplest existence question.
Crucially 테스터 (the try-in-store display) is NOT 샘플 (the free take-home sachet) and NOT 증정품/사은품 (a gift with purchase) — confusing these gets you the wrong answer.

The English-speaker error is saying 'sample' (샘플) when you mean a tester to swatch in-store — if you ask 샘플 있어요? while standing at a lipstick display, staff may think you want a freebie to take home, not to test the shade now. Another pitfall is over-formalizing as 시험용 제품 있습니까? ('do you have a trial-use product?'), which is stiff and unnatural — just say 테스터 있어요?.

examples.en: Won't this break me out?

examples.ko: 저 피부 예민한데 이거 트러블 안 나요?
examples.romanization: jeo pibu yeminhande igeo teureobeul an nayo?
examples.en: My skin's sensitive — won't this break me out?
examples.note: 예민하다 ('sensitive/touchy') describes reactive skin

examples.ko: 새 제품 쓰면 잘 뒤집어져서요. 자극 없는 거 맞아요?

entries.nuance: 이거 트러블 안 나요? is 이거 ('this') + 트러블 (Konglish 'trouble' = a skin breakout/flare-up) + 안 나요? ('doesn't it come out / happen?'). 트러블 is the everyday beauty word for any skin breakout or flare — broader than 여드름 ('acne/pimples'), which means actual acne specifically. The verb is 나다 ('to break out/appear'): 트러블이 나다 = 'to break out', 여드름이 나다 = 'to get a pimple'. The other essential worry-word is 자극 ('irritation/stimulation'), so 자극 없어요? = 'is it non-irritating?' and 자극적이에요? = 'is it harsh?'. There's also the vivid slang 뒤집어지다 ('to flip over') for skin reacting badly. The English-speaker error is saying 'breakout' as 부서지다 ('to shatter/break apart') — a direct-translation disaster; the right verb is 나다 with 트러블/여드름. Another trap is the particle: things break out with 이/가 (트러블이 나요), but in the quick spoken question the particle is often dropped (트러블 안 나요?). Note 트러블 here has nothing to do with 'problem/trouble' in general — in beauty context it strictly means a skin breakout. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'break out' as 부서지다 or 깨지다.
Those mean 'shatter/break apart' for objects. Skin breaks out with 나다: 트러블이 나다 / 여드름이 나다. Ask 이거 트러블 안 나요?
Using 트러블 for general 'trouble/problem'.
In skincare 트러블 specifically means a skin breakout/flare. For a general problem use 문제. Here 트러블 = breakout only.
Saying 자극해요? to ask if it's irritating.
자극하다 means 'to stimulate/provoke (someone)'. For a harsh product ask 자극 있어요? / 자극적이에요?, or 자극 없어요? for non-irritating.

entries.shortExplanation: 화장 잘 안 지워져요 is a practical expression meaning "My makeup doesn't come off well".
entries.explanation: "My makeup doesn't come off well" — that is 화장 잘 안 지워져요 (hwajang jal an jiwojyeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 화장 잘 안 지워져요 ("My makeup doesn't come off well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.ko: 화장 잘 안 지워져요.
examples.romanization: hwajang jal an jiwojyeoyo.
examples.en: My makeup doesn't come off well.
examples.note: Telling staff the problem you want solved

examples.ko: 눈 화장이 잘 안 지워져요. 립앤아이 리무버 있어요?
examples.romanization: nun hwajangi jal an jiwojyeoyo. ribaenai rimubeo isseoyo?
examples.en: Eye makeup won't come off — do you have a lip & eye remover?
examples.note: 립앤아이 리무버 for stubborn eye/lip makeup

examples.ko: 선크림이 안 지워지는 느낌이라 클렌징오일 쓰려고요.
examples.romanization: seonkeurimi an jiwojineun neukkimira keullenjingoil sseuryeogoyo.
examples.en: My sunscreen feels like it won't wash off, so I'll use cleansing oil.
examples.note: 안 지워지는 느낌 ('feels like it won't come off')

entries.nuance: 화장 잘 안 지워져요 is 화장 ('makeup') + 잘 ('well') + 안 ('not') + 지워져요 — the passive of 지우다 ('to erase/remove'). The key verb pair is active 지우다 ('to remove makeup', 화장을 지우다) vs. passive 지워지다 ('to come off', 화장이 지워지다): you ACTIVELY remove with 지우다, but to say it doesn't come off you use the passive 안 지워져요. The whole act of cleansing off makeup is 클렌징; products include 클렌징오일 (oil, for heavy/waterproof), 클렌징워터 (micellar water), 클렌징폼 (foam), and 리무버 (point remover, esp. 립앤아이 리무버 for eyes/lips). The famous '이중 세안' (double cleansing) — oil first, then foam — is standard advice you'll hear. The English-speaker error is saying 'take off makeup' as 화장을 벗다 ('to take off', like clothes) — 벗다 is for clothing/shoes, never makeup; makeup is 지우다. Another is mixing the voices: don't say 화장이 안 지워요 (active verb with 이/가) — it must be passive 화장이 안 지워져요, or active 화장을 못 지워요. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 화장을 벗다 for removing makeup.
벗다 ('take off') is for clothes/shoes. Makeup is removed with 지우다: 화장을 지우다. Never 화장을 벗다.
Mixing active/passive: 화장이 안 지워요.
With the subject 화장이, you need the passive: 화장이 안 지워져요 ('it doesn't come off'). Active would be 화장을 못 지워요 ('I can't remove it').
Calling all cleansers 비누 (soap).
Makeup removers are 클렌징 products (클렌징오일/워터/폼) or 리무버, not 비누. For removal, ask about 클렌징 or 리무버, not 비누.

entries.explanation: 이거 향 있어요? (igeo hyang isseoyo?) = "Does this have a fragrance?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 향 있어요? ("Does this have a scent?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; checking if a product is scented
무향 ('no scent') for a quick yes/no
강하다 ('strong') to gauge intensity

usagePhrases.en: Do you have an unscented one?
usagePhrases.note: 향 안 나는 거 = 'the kind with no smell'

examples.romanization: igeo hyang isseoyo?
examples.en: Does this have a fragrance?
examples.note: Asked when you're sensitive to scents

examples.romanization: hyange jom mingamhaeseoyo. muhyangin geo isseoyo?
examples.en: I'm a bit sensitive to fragrance — do you have a fragrance-free one?
examples.note: 민감하다 + 무향 for scent-sensitive skin

examples.ko: 향 너무 강한 건 부담스러워요. 은은한 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: hyang neomu ganghan geon budamseureowoyo. euneunhan geo isseoyo?
examples.en: Strong scents are a bit much for me — anything subtle?
examples.note: 은은하다 ('faint, subtle') = a gentle scent

entries.nuance: 이거 향 있어요? is 이거 ('this') + 향 ('scent/fragrance', Sino-Korean 香) + 있어요? ('is there?'). 향 is the everyday word for a product's smell; 'fragrance-free' is 무향 (無香, 'no scent'), and the verb 'to smell/give off scent' is 향이 나다 (향 나요 = 'it's scented', 향 안 나요 = 'no scent'). Useful descriptors: 은은하다 ('faint, subtle'), 강하다 ('strong'), 인공적이다 ('artificial'). For people who react to fragrance, 향에 민감하다 ('sensitive to scent') explains the concern. The English-speaker error is translating 'smell' as 냄새 — but 냄새 is neutral-to-negative ('odor', often a bad smell), so asking 이거 냄새 나요? sounds like 'does this stink?', mildly insulting the product; for a pleasant or neutral product scent, use 향, not 냄새. Another trap: 무향 ('unscented') vs. 무향료 ('no added fragrance ingredient') — both exist on labels, but in conversation 무향 is what you say. Note 향 takes 있어요?/나요? but you wouldn't say 향을 있어요 — it's 향이 있어요 / 향 있어요. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 이거 냄새 나요? to mean 'is it scented?'.
냄새 leans negative ('odor/stink'). For a product's fragrance use 향: 이거 향 있어요? / 향 나요? 냄새 나요? implies it smells bad.
Saying 향 없어 instead of 무향.
To ask for a fragrance-free product, the clean term is 무향: 무향인 거 있어요? 향 없어 (반말) is also too casual for staff.
Using 향기 vs 향 wrongly in a question.
향기 ('a (nice) fragrance/aroma') is more poetic. For the plain functional question, 향 is standard: 향 있어요?, 향 강해요?

("What's the expiry date on this?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 이거 유통기한 언제까지예요? is 이거 ('this') + 유통기한 ('distribution/sell-by period', Sino-Korean 流通期限) + 언제까지 ('until when') + 예요?. Cosmetics in Korea carry dates, and there are two relevant terms: 유통기한 (the sell-by/best-before date, the everyday word) and 사용기한 ('use-by date'); newer products may instead print 개봉 후 사용기간 — the PAO (period-after-opening), e.g. '12M' meaning use within 12 months once opened. 임박 ('imminent') describes near-expiry stock, often why something is discounted (유통기한 임박 상품). The English-speaker error is asking 'expire' with the verb 만료되다 — that's for contracts/subscriptions, not food or cosmetics; products' dates are framed with 유통기한/사용기한 + 언제까지 or 지나다 ('to pass': 유통기한 지났어요 = 'it's expired'). Another trap: 언제까지예요 ('until when?') is the right frame for a deadline, not 언제예요 ('when is it?') which sounds like asking a single point in time. Keep 예요 fused after 언제까지. Default 존댓말; this is a smart thing to ask on discounted skincare.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 만료되다 for product expiry.
만료되다 is for contracts/memberships expiring. For cosmetics/food say 유통기한 / 사용기한, and 지나다 for 'expired': 유통기한 지났어요?
Asking 유통기한 언제예요? instead of 언제까지예요?
A deadline takes 까지 ('until'): 언제까지예요? 언제예요? asks for a single moment and sounds off for a 'good-until' date.
Confusing 유통기한 with 개봉 후 사용기간.
유통기한 = sell-by (unopened); 개봉 후 사용기간 (PAO, e.g. 12M) = how long after opening. For 'how long once I open it', ask 개봉 후에 얼마나 써요?

entries.english: My skin really broke out / freaked out
entries.shortExplanation: 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 is a practical expression meaning "My skin really broke out / freaked out".
entries.explanation: "My skin really broke out / freaked out" — that is 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 (pibuga neomu dwijibeojyeosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 ("My skin really broke out"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing a bad flare-up (slang 뒤집어지다)
More neutral; 트러블이 나다 + 심하게
여드름 for actual acne; 잔뜩 ('a whole lot')
예민해지다 = 'became sensitive/touchy'

examples.ko: 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요.
examples.romanization: pibuga neomu dwijibeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My skin really broke out.
examples.note: Telling staff or a derm what's happening

examples.ko: 새 제품 썼더니 피부가 다 뒤집어졌어요. 진정되는 거 있어요?
examples.romanization: sae jepum sseotdeoni pibuga da dwijibeojyeosseoyo. jinjeongdoeneun geo isseoyo?
examples.en: I used a new product and my skin freaked out — anything calming?
examples.note: 진정 ('calming/soothing') is what you then ask for

examples.ko: 환절기라 그런지 트러블이 심하게 나고 화끈거려요.
examples.romanization: hwanjeolgira geureonji teureobeuri simhage nago hwakkeungeoryeoyo.
examples.en: Maybe it's the changing season — I'm breaking out badly and it stings.
examples.note: 화끈거리다 ('to burn/sting') + 환절기 ('season change')

entries.nuance: 피부가 너무 뒤집어졌어요 is 피부 ('skin') + 가 + 너무 ('so/too') + 뒤집어졌어요 (past of 뒤집어지다, lit. 'to be flipped over') — vivid, very common slang for skin reacting badly, breaking out, going haywire. It's more dramatic and colloquial than the neutral 트러블이 났어요 ('I broke out') or the clinical 여드름이 났어요 ('I got acne'). When skin is in this state you ask for 진정 ('calming/soothing') products — 진정되는 거 ('something that calms'), since 진정 is the beauty word for soothing irritated skin. Related sensation verbs: 화끈거리다 ('to burn/sting'), 가렵다 ('to itch'), 붉어지다/빨개지다 ('to redden'). A common cause people cite is 환절기 ('the change of seasons'). The English-speaker error is taking 뒤집어지다 literally ('to turn upside down') and being baffled, or trying to say 'broke out' with the wrong verb — the natural options are 뒤집어지다 (slang), 트러블이 나다, 여드름이 나다. Another trap: this is informal/expressive, fine in a shop or with a friend in 존댓말 or 반말, but at a dermatology clinic you'd lean on the neutral 트러블이 났어요 or describe symptoms (붉어지고 가려워요). Particle: 피부가, not 피부를.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 뒤집어지다 literally as 'turn upside down'.
In skincare it's slang for skin reacting badly / breaking out. 피부가 뒤집어졌어요 = 'my skin freaked out', not anything physically flipping.
Asking for 진정시키는 거 wrongly as 진정 약.
For soothing skincare say 진정되는 거 / 진정 제품 ('calming product'). 진정 약 ('sedative') is medicine for nerves, not skin.
Using 너무 to mean simply 'very' in writing.
너무 means 'too/excessively' but colloquially also 'so'. It's fine in speech (너무 뒤집어졌어요); just know it carries an 'excessive' nuance, stronger than plain 아주.

entries.english: Can I get a refund on this?
entries.shortExplanation: 이거 환불돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refund on this?".
entries.explanation: 이거 환불돼요? (igeo hwanbuldwaeyo?) = "Can I get a refund on this?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 이거 환불돼요? ("Can I get a refund on this?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 이거 환불돼요? with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Can I get a refund on this?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking if a return is possible
교환 ('exchange') for swapping, not refunding

usagePhrases.en: I have the receipt — is a refund possible?
usagePhrases.note: 영수증 ('receipt') strengthens the request

usagePhrases.en: It doesn't suit my skin, so I'd like a refund
usagePhrases.note: 안 맞다 ('doesn't suit') = the common valid reason

examples.ko: 이거 환불돼요?
examples.romanization: igeo hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: Can I get a refund on this?
examples.note: Asked at the counter with the product and receipt

examples.ko: 한 번 발라봤는데 트러블이 나서요. 환불돼요?
examples.romanization: han beon ballabwanneunde teureobeuri naseoyo. hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: I tried it once and it broke me out — can I get a refund?
examples.note: Giving the breakout reason for a return

examples.ko: 개봉했는데도 환불 가능해요? 피부에 안 맞아서요.
examples.romanization: gaebonghaenneundedo hwanbul ganeunghaeyo? pibue an majaseoyo.
examples.en: Can I still get a refund even though I opened it? It doesn't suit my skin.
examples.note: 개봉했는데도 ('even though opened') addresses the usual catch

entries.nuance: 이거 환불돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불 ('refund', Sino-Korean 還拂) + 되다 ('to be possible') in polite question form: 'is a refund possible?'. The 되다 frames feasibility, the polite default for asking about store policy. Distinguish 환불 (refund — money back) from 교환 (exchange — swap for another item) and 반품 (return — sending/handing the goods back, the act): you ask 환불돼요? for money back, 교환돼요? to exchange. Cosmetics have a real wrinkle: 개봉 ('opening') often voids returns, so 개봉했는데도 환불돼요? ('refund even though opened?') is a key thing to ask, and the accepted reason is usually 피부에 안 맞아서 ('because it doesn't suit my skin') or 트러블이 나서 ('because it broke me out'). The English-speaker error is using the English 'refund' as a verb oddly, or saying 돈 돌려주세요 ('give my money back') bluntly — that's confrontational; 환불돼요? or 환불 가능해요? is the civil ask. Another trap: 환불하다 ('to refund') is what the store does; as the customer asking, the natural phrasing is the 돼요?/가능해요? feasibility question, then 환불하고 싶어요 ('I'd like a refund'). Keep 존댓말; bring the 영수증.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 돈 돌려주세요 to ask for a refund.
That's blunt ('give my money back'). The civil request is 환불돼요? / 환불 가능해요?, then 환불하고 싶어요 with a reason.
Confusing 환불 with 교환.
환불 = money back; 교환 = swap for another item. Ask 환불돼요? for a refund, 교환돼요? to exchange. They're different requests.
Assuming opened cosmetics are returnable.
개봉 (opening) often voids a return. Ask explicitly: 개봉했는데도 환불돼요?, and give a valid reason like 피부에 안 맞아서.

entries.english: Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?
entries.shortExplanation: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?".
entries.explanation: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? (pibugwaeseo badeun georang gachi sseodo dwaeyo?) means "Can I use this with what I got from the dermatologist?". entries.nuance: 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? is 피부과 ('dermatology (clinic)', Sino-Korean 皮膚科) + 에서 ('from/at') + 받은 거 ('the thing I got') + 랑 ('with') + 같이 ('together') + 써도 돼요? ('is it okay to use?'). This is the advanced, real-life question of layering store skincare with dermatologist-prescribed items. Key vocabulary: 피부과 (the derm clinic — note 과 '-department', as in 내과, 안과), 처방받다 ('to be prescribed'), 연고 ('ointment'), and active ingredients people worry about combining, e.g. 레티놀 (retinol), 비타민C (vitamin C), AHA/BHA. The layering 순서 ('order') matters: toner → essence → serum → cream → sunscreen. The English-speaker errors cluster around particles and words: (1) 'with' here is the casual 랑/이랑 or formal 와/과 — not 같이 alone, which means 'together' as an adverb, so you need 받은 거랑 같이; (2) 'dermatologist' the PERSON is 피부과 의사 / 피부과 선생님, while 피부과 alone is the CLINIC, so '피부과에서 받은' means 'got at the clinic', which is what you want; (3) 'use together' is 같이 쓰다, not 함께 사용 in casual speech (too formal). 써도 돼요? ('may I use…?') is the right permission/compatibility frame. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 랑/이랑 and saying 피부과 거 같이 써도 돼요?
'With X' needs the particle 랑/이랑 (casual) or 와/과 (formal): 피부과에서 받은 거랑 같이 써도 돼요? 같이 alone isn't enough to mark 'with what'.
Calling the clinic 피부과 의사 when you mean the place.
피부과 = the dermatology clinic/department; 피부과 의사/선생님 = the doctor (person). To say 'got it at the clinic', 피부과에서 받은 거 is right.
Using 함께 사용해도 됩니까? in a casual shop.
That's stiff and formal. In an everyday beauty shop say 같이 써도 돼요? It carries the same meaning, naturally.

entries.nuance: 제 피부톤에 맞는 쿠션 찾아 주세요 is 제 ('my', humble) + 피부톤 ('skin tone') + 에 맞는 ('that matches') + 쿠션 ('cushion (compact foundation)') + 찾아 주세요 ('please find for me'). Korean base makeup runs on a shade-number system every newcomer must learn: 21호 (light/fair), 23호 (medium), with half-steps like 21.5호, 13호 (very fair), 25호 (deeper) — staff will ask 몇 호 쓰세요? ('what number do you use?'). The undertone vocabulary is 쿨톤 (cool-toned) vs. 웜톤 (warm-toned), part of the huge 퍼스널 컬러 ('personal color') craze, and base type is 핑크 베이스 vs. 옐로 베이스. The verb 뜨다 ('to float') is the key idiom for a foundation that's too light/wrong-undertone and looks ashy or masky on the skin (피부에서 떠요). 커버력 = 'coverage'. The English-speaker error is saying 'shade' as 그림자 ('shadow') — a direct-translation disaster; the right word is 호 (the number) or 색상/톤. Another trap: 쿠션 in Korean beauty means the cushion-compact foundation, not a sofa cushion, and 파운데이션 (liquid foundation) is the other format. Don't translate 'match' as 매치하다 here; the natural phrase is 에 맞다 ('to fit/suit'). Default 존댓말; 찾아 주세요 politely hands the search to staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그림자 ('shadow') for a makeup 'shade'.
그림자 is a literal shadow. A foundation shade is a number 호 (21호, 23호) or 색상/톤. Ask 몇 호가 맞아요? not anything with 그림자.
Using Sino vs. native numbers wrongly with 호.
Shade numbers use Sino-Korean: 21호 = 이십일 호, 23호 = 이십삼 호. Say 이십일 호, not native 스물한. The counter 호 takes Sino numbers.
Translating 'it doesn't match / looks off' as 안 어울려요 only.
안 어울려요 ('doesn't suit') is general. For a foundation that sits wrong/looks ashy, the precise idiom is 떠요 ('it floats'): 피부에서 떠요.

entries.shortExplanation: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 is a practical expression meaning "My skin keeps flaking / peeling".
entries.explanation: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 (gakjiri jakku ireonayo) = "My skin keeps flaking / peeling". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 ("My skin keeps flaking"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; describing dry flaking (각질 일어나다)
각질 제거 ('dead-skin removal') = exfoliation
각질 정리 ('tidying dead skin') for a gentle ask
갈라지다 ('to crack/split') for severe dryness

examples.romanization: gakjiri jakku ireonayo.
examples.en: My skin keeps flaking.
examples.note: Telling staff your main dry-skin complaint

examples.en: When I do makeup, the flakes lift and it cakes — what should I do?
examples.note: 들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') is the makeup-over-flakes problem

examples.ko: 각질 제거하고 싶은데 너무 자극적이지 않은 거 있어요? 저 민감성이라서요.
examples.romanization: gakjil jegeohago sipeunde neomu jageukjeogiji aneun geo isseoyo? jeo mingamseongiraseoyo.
examples.en: I want to exfoliate but nothing too harsh — I have sensitive skin.
examples.note: Asking for gentle exfoliation given sensitivity

entries.nuance: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 is 각질 ('dead skin cells / flaky skin', Sino-Korean 角質) + 이 + 자꾸 ('repeatedly, keeps') + 일어나요 (from 일어나다, here 'to lift up/flake'). 각질 is THE word for dead-skin flakiness, and it pairs with specific verbs: 각질이 일어나다 ('skin flakes/peels up'), 각질 제거 ('exfoliation', lit. 'dead-skin removal'), 각질 정리 (a gentler 'tidying'). Exfoliating products include 필링 (peeling), 스크럽 (scrub), 각질 제거제 (exfoliant). The related makeup problem is 들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') — when foundation sits on top of flakes; don't confuse it with 떠다 ('to float', wrong shade). For severe dryness, 갈라지다 ('to crack/split') and 트다 ('to chap', e.g. 입술이 트다 'chapped lips'). The English-speaker error is saying 'peel' as 벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off', like sunburn skin sloughing) when they mean ongoing dry flaking — 벗겨지다 fits a sunburn or a peel mask result, but everyday dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Another trap: 'dead skin' isn't 죽은 피부 (literal 'dead skin', sounds morbid/medical) — the cosmetic word is 각질. Particle: 각질이 일어나다 (subject 이/가), and 자꾸 conveys the frustrating 'it keeps happening'. Default 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죽은 피부 for 'dead skin'.
죽은 피부 ('dead skin') sounds morbid/medical. The cosmetic term for flaky dead-skin cells is 각질: 각질이 일어나요, 각질 제거.
Using 벗겨지다 for everyday dry flaking.
벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off') fits sunburn sloughing or a peel-mask result. Ongoing dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Say 각질이 일어나요.
Confusing 들뜨다 (makeup cakes) with 뜨다 (wrong shade).
들뜨다 = foundation lifts/cakes over flakes; 뜨다 = a shade looks ashy/floats. For flaking-related caking, use 들떠요.

structuredNuance.t: 각질이 자꾸 일어나요 is 각질 ('dead skin cells / flaky skin', Sino-Korean 角質) + 이 + 자꾸 ('repeatedly, keeps') + 일어나요 (from 일어나다, here 'to lift up/flake'). 각질 is THE word for dead-skin flakiness, and it pairs with specific verbs: 각질이 일어나다 ('skin flakes/peels up'), 각질 제거 ('exfoliation', lit. 'dead-skin removal'), 각질 정리 (a gentler 'tidying'). Exfoliating products include 필링 (peeling), 스크럽 (scrub), 각질 제거제 (exfoliant). For severe dryness, 갈라지다 ('to crack/split') and 트다 ('to chap', e.g. 입술이 트다 'chapped lips'). Particle: 각질이 일어나다 (subject 이/가), and 자꾸 conveys the frustrating 'it keeps happening'. Default 존댓말.
The related makeup problem is 들뜨다 ('to lift/cake') — when foundation sits on top of flakes; don't confuse it with 떠다 ('to float', wrong shade).
각질 is Sino-Korean 角質 ('horny substance'), the cosmetic word for dead-skin flakiness.

The English-speaker error is saying 'peel' as 벗겨지다 ('to be peeled off', like sunburn skin sloughing) when they mean ongoing dry flaking — 벗겨지다 fits a sunburn or a peel mask result, but everyday dry flaking is 각질이 일어나다. Another trap: 'dead skin' isn't 죽은 피부 (literal 'dead skin', sounds morbid/medical) — the cosmetic word is 각질.

entries.nuance: Korean work emails almost always open with 안녕하세요 + your identity in the pattern [team/company] + [name] + [optional title] + 입니다. This is not optional fluff; jumping straight into the request feels abrupt and rude in Korean office culture. The verb 입니다 here means 'I am ~', and you state your OWN name plainly, never with honorific 님 attached to yourself (writing 김민수님입니다 about yourself is wrong — 님 honors others, not you). Note the title order differs from English: Koreans say 김민수 대리 (name THEN rank), not 대리 김민수. The nearest variant is 안녕하십니까, which is one notch more formal/official (used in announcements, to very senior people, or in 합쇼체 letters); everyday inter-office mail uses 안녕하세요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is translating 'My name is' as 제 이름은 ~예요, which sounds like a self-introduction in a textbook, not a professional email; the natural business form is simply [name]입니다. Also avoid 저는 ~입니다 with 저는 every time — Korean drops the 'I' once context is clear, so 김민수입니다 alone is cleaner than 저는 김민수입니다.

님 is an honorific for OTHERS. Referring to yourself you drop it: 김민수입니다. Using 님 on yourself sounds self-elevating and wrong.
Ordering title before name: 대리 김민수입니다.
Korean puts rank AFTER the name: 김민수 대리입니다. The English order 'Assistant Manager Kim' reversed sounds off.

entries.nuance: 참고 부탁드립니다 is 참고 ('reference/consultation', Sino-Korean 參考) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly request'), meaning 'please keep this in mind / for your reference'. It's a soft, information-sharing closer: you're not demanding an action, just asking the reader to be AWARE of something. The feeling is courteous and low-pressure. The crucial contrast is with 참조 (參照): in email, 참조 is the CC field ('참조: 박과장님') — it names who's copied — whereas 참고 means 'for your information/reference'. English speakers constantly confuse these because both translate loosely as 'reference'; if you write 참조 부탁드립니다 meaning 'please note this', it reads oddly like 'please CC this'. Another contrast: 참고하세요 (plain imperative 'refer to it') is fine to juniors/peers but can sound slightly directive to a superior; 참고 부탁드립니다 with 부탁드리다 is humbler and safer upward. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'FYI' as needing a verb of command; in Korean the humble-request frame 부탁드립니다 carries the politeness, so don't stack it with a blunt 하세요. Note 참고 is a 하다-noun, so to make it a verb you need 참고하다 — never 참고 주세요 (you can't 'give' a reference).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 참고 with 참조.
참조 is the email CC line ('참조: ~님'); 참고 means 'for your reference'. Writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note' sounds like 'please CC'. Use 참고 for FYI.
Saying 참고 주세요.
참고 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. The verb is 참고하다, so it's 참고해 주세요 or 참고 부탁드립니다, never 참고 주세요.
Using bare 참고하세요 to a senior.
The plain imperative can feel directive upward. To a superior, soften to 참고 부탁드립니다 or 참고하시기 바랍니다.

entries.nuance: 첨부했습니다 is 첨부 ('attachment', Sino-Korean 添附) + 하다 in formal past, 'I have attached'. It's the standard line for 'please find attached'. The everyday options are 첨부했습니다 (I attached), 첨부합니다 (I'm attaching), and the slightly warmer 첨부해 드립니다 / 첨부드립니다, where 드리다 ('to do for someone, humbly') signals you're doing the reader a service — common and polite in Korean business mail. The key contrast: 첨부 (添附) is electronically attaching a FILE, while 동봉 (同封) is physically enclosing something in a paper envelope — don't write 동봉했습니다 for an email PDF. A frequent English-speaker pitfall is over-literal 'please find attached' rendered as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요 ('please go look for the attached thing'), which sounds like the file is lost; you simply state 첨부했습니다. Another trap is the particle: it's 파일을 첨부했습니다 (object 을/를), not 파일에 첨부 — the file is the thing being attached. Also, 첨부 is a 하다-noun: the verb is 첨부하다, so you never say 첨부 주세요; to ask THEM to attach, it's 첨부해 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'please find attached' as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요.
찾다 ('to look for') makes it sound like the file is missing. Just state 첨부했습니다 or 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다.
Using 동봉 for an email file.
동봉 (同封) is enclosing something in a physical envelope. For an emailed file use 첨부 (添附): 파일을 첨부했습니다.
Saying 첨부 주세요 when asking someone to attach.
첨부 is a 하다-noun; it can't be 'given'. Use the verb: 첨부해 주세요 ('please attach it').

entries.nuance: 회신 부탁드립니다 is 회신 ('reply/response', Sino-Korean 回信) + 부탁드립니다, asking the reader to write back — the formal email staple for 'please respond'. 회신 is the crisp, businesslike word for a reply, slightly more formal than the everyday 답장 ('a letter/message back'); both are correct, but 회신 dominates in professional mail and 답장 feels a touch more personal. The contrast to watch: 회신 (a reply, the act of writing back) vs. 답변 (答辯, the ANSWER itself to a specific question). If you posed a concrete question and want that answer, 답변 부탁드립니다 fits; for a general 'please get back to me', use 회신. The English-speaker pitfall is over-literal 'reply to me' as 저에게 회신해 주세요 — the 저에게 ('to me') is usually unnecessary and sounds heavy; 회신 부탁드립니다 already implies 'to me'. Another trap is treating 'respond' as 반응 (反應, a physical/emotional reaction) — 반응 부탁드립니다 sounds like asking for a like/reaction, not an email reply. Note 회신 is a 하다-noun; the verb is 회신하다, so 회신해 주세요 or 회신 주시면, never 회신 주세요 without the verb being implied (회신 주다 is idiomatically tolerated, but 회신해 주세요 is cleanest).

회신 = a reply/getting back to you; 답변 = an answer to a specific question. If you asked something concrete, 답변 부탁드립니다; for general 'reply', 회신 부탁드립니다.

entries.nuance: 검토 부탁드립니다 is 검토 ('review/examination', Sino-Korean 檢討) + 부탁드립니다, asking the reader to read something critically and weigh in. Unlike the lighter 확인 ('just check/confirm'), 검토 implies real scrutiny — reading a proposal, catching problems, forming an opinion — so you send it to someone whose judgment you want, often a senior, and you're implicitly inviting feedback or approval. That's the key contrast English speakers blur: 확인 부탁드립니다 = 'please confirm/glance', 검토 부탁드립니다 = 'please examine and judge'. Asking a boss to merely 확인 a strategy doc undersells what you need; 검토 is right. The register is humble (부탁드리다), suitable upward. The English-speaker pitfall is the loanword 리뷰 (리뷰 부탁드립니다) — fine in casual startup slang but reads as Konglish in formal mail; use 검토. Another trap: don't confuse 검토 with 검사 (檢査, an INSPECTION/test, e.g. medical or quality checks) — 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like asking for a lab test, not a document review. Note 검토 is a 하다-noun: 검토하다, so 검토해 주세요 / 검토 부탁드립니다, never 검토 주세요.

entries.nuance: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 is 일정 ('schedule', Sino-Korean 日程) + 조율 ('tuning/coordination', Sino-Korean 調律, originally 'tuning an instrument') + 이 필요하다 ('is needed') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('seems/I think'). 조율 is the precise business word for negotiating and aligning times/terms among multiple people — richer than just 'scheduling'. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 ('it seems / I think') is doing important politeness work: Korean business culture prefers hedged, indirect phrasing, so 'we WILL need to coordinate' (필요합니다, flat) sounds blunt, while 'I think we'll need to' (필요할 것 같습니다) is softer and more collaborative. The contrast: 조율 (coordinating among parties, give-and-take) vs. 조정 (調整, adjusting/modifying a plan more unilaterally) — for 'let's find a time that works for everyone', 조율 is the natural fit. The English-speaker pitfall is over-literal 'schedule' as 스케줄 (스케줄 조정해요) — fine casually but 일정 is the professional term — and forcing 'coordinate' as 협력하다 ('to cooperate'), which is about teamwork in general, not aligning times. Also note the particle: 일정 조율'이' 필요하다 (subject 이/가 marks what is needed), not 일정 조율을 필요하다.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing flat 일정 조율이 필요합니다 to a client.
The bare assertion can feel blunt. Korean business prefers the hedged 필요할 것 같습니다 ('I think we'll need to'), which sounds more collaborative.
Using 협력 for 'coordinate the schedule'.
협력 ('cooperation') is about working together generally, not aligning times. For matching schedules, the word is 조율 (or 맞추다): 일정 조율.
Wrong particle: 일정 조율을 필요합니다.
필요하다 takes the subject marker 이/가 on what is needed: 일정 조율이 필요합니다, not 일정 조율을 필요합니다.

entries.nuance: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? is 언제 ('when') + 시간 ('time') + 괜찮으세요 (honorific 'is it okay/fine for you?'). It's the polite, natural way to ask someone's availability when arranging a meeting — literally 'when is your time okay?'. The honorific -으세요 on 괜찮다 directs the politeness to the listener, so this is safe upward and to clients. A close variant is 언제가 편하세요? ('when is convenient?'), using 편하다 — slightly warmer/considerate, stressing their comfort. The contrast: asking about THEIR availability (괜찮으세요/편하세요, honorific 'you') vs. stating YOUR availability (저는 ~ 괜찮아요/가능해요) — keep the honorific only on the other person's side. The English-speaker pitfall is the direct calque 'when are you available?' as 언제 가능해요? aimed at a senior without honorific — 언제 가능하세요? is fine, but the warmer 시간 괜찮으세요 / 편하세요 sounds more considerate in Korean. Another trap: don't say 언제 자유로워요? (literal 'when are you free?' using 자유롭다 = 'free as in liberty') — that's the wrong 'free'; Korean uses 시간 괜찮다 / 시간 되다 / 한가하다 for being available. Also 시간 되세요? ('does the time work for you?') is a very common equivalent worth knowing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 언제 자유로워요? for 'when are you free?'.
자유롭다 is 'free' as in liberty/freedom, not availability. Use 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? or 언제 시간 되세요?
Putting honorific on your own availability.
Honor the other person: 언제 괜찮으세요? For your own time, plain 저는 ~ 괜찮아요/가능합니다. Don't say 저는 괜찮으세요.
Dropping honorific to a senior: 언제 시간 괜찮아?
괜찮아 is 반말. To a boss or client use 괜찮으세요? or 편하세요?, never the casual 괜찮아.

entries.nuance: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 is 회의 ('meeting', Sino-Korean 會議) + 일정 ('schedule') + 을 잡다 ('to grab/set') + -고 싶습니다 ('I would like to'). The verb 잡다 ('to catch/grab') is the idiomatic word for 'fix/set' an appointment in Korean — 일정을 잡다, 약속을 잡다, 미팅을 잡다 — and English speakers rarely guess it. The -고 싶습니다 ('I'd like to') keeps it as a polite proposal rather than a command. The contrast: 회의 (a formal meeting, internal/decision-making) vs. 미팅 (the loanword, often an external or more casual business meet-up) — both common, but 회의 sounds more formal/internal and 미팅 a bit more flexible. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'set up / arrange' literally as 설치하다 ('to install') or 준비하다 ('to prepare') — 회의를 설치하다 is wrong (that's installing equipment), and while you can 회의를 준비하다 ('prepare a meeting'), to SCHEDULE one you 잡다. Another trap: the particle — 일정'을' 잡다 (object 을/를), not 일정에 잡다. Also note 싶습니다 marks YOUR desire, so don't attach it to the other person; to ask if THEY want to meet, you'd say 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 회의를 설치하고 싶습니다.
설치하다 is 'to install (equipment/software)'. To schedule a meeting, the verb is 잡다: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다.
Wrong particle: 일정에 잡고 싶습니다.
잡다 takes the object marker: 일정을 잡다. The particle is 을/를, not 에.
Attaching 싶다 to the other person.
-고 싶다 expresses YOUR desire. To ask if they'd like to meet, use 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?, not '~고 싶으세요' phrased about them awkwardly.

entries.nuance: 일정이 변경되었습니다 is 일정 ('schedule') + 이 ('subject') + 변경되다 ('to be changed', Sino-Korean 變更 + passive 되다) in formal past. The passive 변경되었습니다 ('has been changed') is deliberate: it states the change as a neutral fact without pointing fingers, which Korean business culture favors for delivering inconvenient news. If you say 일정을 변경했습니다 (active, 'I changed the schedule'), you take direct ownership — sometimes appropriate, but the passive softens. The contrast: 변경 (變更, changing/altering a plan, formal) vs. 바꾸다 (the plain native 'to change/swap', more casual) — in email you write 일정이 변경되었습니다, not the casual 일정 바꿨어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and voice: 일정'이' 변경되었습니다 needs the subject marker 이/가 with the passive, whereas the object marker 을/를 goes with the active 일정'을' 변경했습니다 — mixing them (일정을 변경되었습니다) is a classic grammar error. Another trap: don't translate 'change' as 바뀌었습니다 carelessly to a client for a schedule you yourself altered — 바뀌다 ('to get changed', also passive) is fine but feels a notch more colloquial than 변경되다. Pair changes with 양해 부탁드립니다 ('please understand') for courtesy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing voice/particle: 일정을 변경되었습니다.
Passive 변경되다 takes the subject marker: 일정'이' 변경되었습니다. The object marker 을/를 goes with active 일정'을' 변경했습니다.
Using casual 일정 바꿨어요 in formal mail.
바꾸다 is the plain/casual 'to change'. Professional email uses 변경: 일정이 변경되었습니다.
Announcing a change you caused with passive but no apology.
If you changed it and it inconveniences others, soften with 부득이하게 변경하게 되었습니다 and add 양해 부탁드립니다, rather than a cold passive alone.

entries.nuance: 보고드리겠습니다 is 보고 ('report', Sino-Korean 報告) + 드리다 (the HUMBLE form of 주다 'to give', used when the recipient is your senior) + -겠습니다 ('I will'). The 드리다 is the heart of it: it lowers YOU relative to the person you're reporting to, so 보고드리다 inherently means reporting UPWARD to a boss, client, or senior — you'd never 보고드리다 to a junior. The contrast: 보고드리다 (humble, upward) vs. plain 보고하다 (neutral 'to report', e.g. describing the act objectively or to peers) vs. 알리다 ('to inform/notify', more horizontal). If a superior tells YOU something, you don't 보고드리다 to them about it incorrectly framed — direction matters. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보고하다 flatly to a boss (보고합니다 / 보고할게요) — not wrong, but the humble 보고드립니다 / 보고드리겠습니다 is the expected register upward, and missing 드리다 can feel slightly under-polite in hierarchical Korean offices. Another trap: 보고 is a 하다/드리다-noun, so you say 보고드리다 / 보고하다, never 보고 드리다 split as if 'giving a report object' (it's written together, and you don't say 보고를 드리다 commonly — 보고드리다 is the set form). Also don't confuse 보고 (報告, report) with 보고 (the 보다 connective '보고', as in 보고 싶다 'want to see') — context and Sino-root differ.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using plain 보고합니다 to a senior.
To a boss/client the humble form 보고드립니다 / 보고드리겠습니다 (with 드리다) is expected. Plain 보고합니다 can feel under-polite upward.
Saying 보고드리겠습니다 to a junior.
드리다 lowers you toward a SENIOR. To a subordinate you wouldn't humble yourself; use 보고하다 or, depending on direction, just 알려 줄게요.
Confusing 보고 (報告) with 보고 (보다).
報告 = a report; 보고 in 보고 싶다 is the connective of 보다 ('see'). 보고드리겠습니다 means 'I'll report', not 'I want to see'.

entries.nuance: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 is 확인 ('check') + 후 ('after') + 다시 ('again') + 연락 ('contact', Sino-Korean 連絡) + 드리다 (humble 'give/do for a senior') + -겠습니다 ('I will'). entries.nuance: 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? is 확인 부탁드린 ('that I asked you to check', a relative clause) + 건 (contraction of 것은, 'the matter/thing') + 어떻게 ('how') + 되었을까요 ('I wonder how it turned out', the speculative -을까요 form). This is the diplomatic way to CHASE a pending request without sounding pushy — the soft -을까요 ('I wonder if…') and the indirect 어떻게 되었- ('how has it come along') let you nudge while saving the reader's face, which is essential in hierarchical Korean offices. The contrast: a blunt 왜 아직 확인 안 하셨어요? ('why haven't you checked yet?') is accusatory and damaging; 어떻게 되었을까요? frames it as innocent curiosity about status. Another contrast: 되었을까요 (speculative, gentle) vs. 됐어요? (flat 'is it done?', too direct upward). The English-speaker pitfall is the impatient calque 'any update?' as a bare 업데이트 있어요? — Konglish and curt; Korean wraps the nudge in indirectness. Another trap is omitting a face-saving softener (바쁘시겠지만 / 죄송하지만) before chasing a senior — going straight to the question can read as impatient. Note 건 = 것은 here ('the thing/matter'), not the counter 건 (件); both exist, so read by context.

Konglish and curt. Korean phrases a status nudge indirectly: 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? or 어떻게 되었을까요?
Skipping a softener before nudging a senior.
Going straight to the question can sound impatient. Lead with 바쁘시겠지만 or 죄송하지만 to cushion the follow-up.

entries.nuance: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 is 검토 ('review') + 후 ('after') + 의견 ('opinion/feedback', Sino-Korean 意見) + 주시면 ('if you would give') + 반영하겠습니다 ('I will reflect/incorporate', Sino-Korean 反映 'reflect'). The standout vocab is 반영하다 — literally 'to reflect (as in a mirror)', it's THE business verb for 'to incorporate feedback/changes into a document', and English speakers almost never produce it naturally. The -주시면 … 반영하겠습니다 frame ('if you give … I'll incorporate') is polite and collaborative, positioning you as receptive. The contrast: 반영하다 ('incorporate/apply feedback into the work') vs. 수정하다 (修正, 'to revise/correct' the document itself) vs. 적용하다 (適用, 'to apply' a rule/setting) — for taking someone's comments and working them in, 반영 is the precise choice. The English-speaker pitfall is the literal 'incorporate' as 포함하다 ('to include') — 의견을 포함하겠습니다 sounds like you'll attach their opinion verbatim, not actually act on it; the right verb is 반영하다. Another trap: 의견 ('considered opinion/feedback') vs. 생각 ('thought', more casual) — in business you ask for 의견, not 생각. Note 반영 is a 하다-noun: 반영하다, and 의견을 반영하다 (object 을/를) is the collocation.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 의견을 포함하겠습니다 for 'incorporate feedback'.
포함하다 is 'to include/contain'. To actually work feedback into the document, the verb is 반영하다: 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
Asking for 생각 instead of 의견.
생각 ('thought') is casual. In business you request 의견 ('considered opinion/feedback'): 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
Confusing 반영 with 수정.
반영하다 = incorporate (their feedback into the work); 수정하다 = revise/correct (the document). They pair — you 반영 the 의견 by 수정하는 것 — but use 반영 for 'apply the feedback'.

It is 검토 ('review') + 후 ('after') + 의견 ('opinion/feedback', Sino-Korean 意見) + 주시면 ('if you would give') + 반영하겠습니다 ('I will reflect/incorporate', Sino-Korean 反映 'reflect'). Note 반영 is a 하다-noun: 반영하다, and 의견을 반영하다 (object 을/를) is the collocation.
The pitfall is the literal 'incorporate' as 포함하다 ('to include') — 의견을 포함하겠습니다 sounds like you'll attach their opinion verbatim, not actually act on it; the right verb is 반영하다.

entries.nuance: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 is 바쁘신 (honorific 'busy', describing the reader) + 와중에 ('in the midst of', Sino-Korean 渦中 'whirlpool/turmoil') + 죄송하지만 ('I'm sorry, but'). It's a face-saving CUSHION you place before asking a senior or client for something — Korean business etiquette strongly favors acknowledging the other person's burden before adding to it, so opening a request this way is courteous and expected, not groveling. The honorific 바쁘'신' is essential (you honor THEIR busyness). Don't confuse 와중 with 도중 (途中, 'on the way/midway') — 와중 connotes commotion, 도중 just 'during/en route'. Another pitfall is over-apologizing by stacking too many (죄송하지만 미안하지만 실례지만 all at once); pick one. Also 죄송하지만 (more formal) outranks 미안하지만 (casual) for business — use 죄송하지만 upward.

entries.nuance: 양해 부탁드립니다 is 양해 ('understanding/forbearance', Sino-Korean 諒解) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly ask'), used to ask someone to be UNDERSTANDING about an inconvenience you've caused — a delay, a change, a limitation. It's the courteous companion to an apology: you say 죄송합니다 (sorry) then 양해 부탁드립니다 (please bear with us). The key contrast English speakers miss is 양해 vs. 이해 (理解): 이해 is 'comprehension' (grasping a concept or instructions), while 양해 is 'forbearance/tolerance' for an inconvenience — so 이해 부탁드립니다 wrongly asks 'please comprehend', as if they might not follow your meaning, when you really mean 'please tolerate this hiccup'. Use 양해 when something went sideways. Another contrast: 양해 부탁드립니다 (asking forbearance AFTER/ABOUT an inconvenience) vs. 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 (a cushion BEFORE making a request) — different jobs. The English-speaker pitfall is the literal 'thank you for your understanding' as 이해해 주셔서 감사합니다 — that's grammatical but means 'thanks for comprehending', subtly off; the set business phrase is 양해 부탁드립니다. Note 양해 is a 하다-noun: the verb is 양해하다, so 양해해 주세요 / 양해 부탁드립니다, never 양해 주세요.

이해 is 'comprehension' (grasping meaning). For tolerating an inconvenience, use 양해: 양해 부탁드립니다.
Saying 양해 주세요.
양해 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. Use the verb: 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다.

양해 asks forbearance for something. Pair it with a brief apology/reason — 늦어 죄송합니다, 양해 부탁드립니다 — or it sounds like asking a favor out of nowhere.

entries.nuance: 참조에 넣어 주세요 is 참조 ('reference/CC', Sino-Korean 參照) + 에 ('into') + 넣다 ('to put in') + 주세요 ('please'). In Korean email, 참조 (參照) is literally the CC field, and 참조에 넣다 ('put into CC') means to copy someone — the everyday office phrase for keeping a colleague in the loop. This is the critical contrast that trips English speakers: 참조 (參照, the CC line) vs. 참고 (參考, 'for your reference/FYI'). They look and sound nearly identical and both gloss as 'reference' in English, but 참조 = the CC recipients, while 참고 = 'please take note'. Saying 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — you don't 'put someone into FYI'. The other field words: 받는 사람 (To), 참조 (CC), 숨은 참조 (BCC). The English-speaker pitfall is using the loanword and writing 씨씨에 넣어 주세요 (CC as 씨씨) — understood in casual chat but not standard business Korean; use 참조. Another trap: the verb is 넣다 ('put in') with the particle 에 (참조'에' 넣다), not 참조를 넣다 in the sense of inserting a thing — you put the PERSON into the 참조 field. To say you copied someone, it's 참조로 넣었습니다 or 참조에 넣었습니다.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 참조 with 참고.
참조 (參照) is the CC line; 참고 (參考) is 'for your reference/FYI'. 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — to CC someone, say 참조에 넣어 주세요.
Writing 씨씨에 넣어 주세요.
씨씨 (CC) is casual/Konglish. Standard business Korean uses 참조: 참조에 넣어 주세요.
Wrong particle: 참조를 넣어 주세요 (meaning to CC a person).
You put the person INTO the CC field: 참조'에' 넣어 주세요. The location particle 에 marks where they go.

Another trap: the verb is 넣다 ('put in') with the particle 에 (참조'에' 넣다), not 참조를 넣다 — you put the PERSON into the 참조 field. To say you copied someone, it's 참조로 넣었습니다 or 참조에 넣었습니다.

entries.nuance: This is the customer's answer when staff ask hot or iced (따뜻한 거 / 아이스), or when you order unprompted. The choice particle -(으)로 attaches to the item you pick and means 'I'll go with the ~ one'; 걸로 is just 거 + 로 contracted, so 따뜻한 걸로 = 'the hot one, please' — much more natural than a full sentence. Register is plain polite -요, which covers every café and store; 반말 (따뜻한 거 줘) is only for friends, never for staff you don't know. The closest alternative is 핫으로 주세요 ('hot' as a loanword), which younger baristas accept, but 따뜻한 걸로 is the safe native choice and the dividing line is formality, not meaning. The classic English-speaker mistake is translating 'hot' as 뜨거운 — 뜨거운 means scalding/dangerously hot (a 뜨거운 냄비), whereas a warm drink is 따뜻한; ask for 뜨거운 거 and it sounds like you want to burn your tongue.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Dropping 로 and saying 따뜻한 거 주세요 — understandable but the 걸로 form ('the ~ one') is what signals you're choosing between options.
Using English 'hot one please' word order as 하나 따뜻한 주세요 — Korean puts the descriptor before the noun: 따뜻한 거 / 따뜻한 걸로.

entries.nuance: 아이스로 주세요 is how you order any cold drink in Korea — 아이스 is the English 'ice' borrowed as a fixed word, and Koreans say it far more than the native 차가운 거. The particle -로 marks the option you're selecting ('go with iced'). It pairs directly against 따뜻한 걸로, and the dividing line between 아이스로 and 차가운 걸로 is feel: 아이스로 is the everyday café default, while 차가운 걸로 sounds a touch formal or is used for bottled drinks in a store. Register is polite -요 for all staff; 반말 only with friends. The English-speaker trap is asking for 얼음 주세요 ('give me ice') thinking it means 'iced' — that literally requests a cup of ice cubes; the temperature choice is 아이스로, and 얼음 is only the ice itself (useful in 얼음 많이요 / 얼음 빼고요).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 얼음으로 주세요 to mean 'iced' — that asks for ice as the item; the cold-drink choice is 아이스로 주세요.
Pronouncing it 'ice' English-style and stopping — Korean needs the particle: 아이스로 (with -로) to mark it as your selection.
Mixing it as 아이스 차가운 걸로 — redundant; pick one, 아이스로 or 차가운 걸로, not both.

entries.nuance: This is a staff-to-customer line, so a learner mostly needs to recognize it and answer. 어떻게 드릴까요? literally 'how shall I give it to you?' is the polite service formula (드리다 is humble 'give', -ㄹ까요? offers/asks). You reply with a size + 거로/걸로: 작은 걸로요 / 큰 걸로요, or English sizes 톨/그란데/벤티 at chains. The near alternative the staff might use is 어떤 사이즈로 하시겠어요? — same meaning, a notch more formal. Politeness: staff always use 존댓말 to customers; you answer in plain polite -요. The English-speaker error is hearing 드릴까요 and freezing — don't translate it word-for-word; just catch 사이즈 and reply with the size. Another trap is answering 'medium' literally as 미디엄, which many Korean cafés don't use; they go 작은/큰 or 톨/그란데, so listen for the options they offer.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Freezing because 드릴까요 is unfamiliar — it's just polite 'shall I give you'; only the word 사이즈 matters, then answer with a size.
Answering with bare 작은 사이즈 and no particle — natural is 작은 걸로(요) or 작은 거로(요), marking your choice.
Saying 미디엄 expecting a medium — many cafés only have 작은/큰 or 톨/그란데/벤티; pick from what they list.

examples.romanization: "jeongnipae deurilkkayo?" "ne, jeongnipae juseyo."
examples.en: "Shall I add your points?" "Yes, please."
examples.note: Staff offer with 드릴까요; you confirm with 주세요

examples.ko: 적립해 주세요. 전화번호로요.
examples.romanization: jeongnipae juseyo. jeonhwabeonhoroyo.

examples.note: Real flow: ask to accrue, then read out your number

entries.nuance: 적립 (積立) means 'accumulating/saving up', and 적립해 주세요 asks the cashier to credit loyalty points or stamps to you — by phone number, an app barcode, or a membership card. It's customer-to-staff, plain polite -요; 반말 (적립해 줘) is for friends only. The nearest alternatives are 적립 부탁드려요 (more deferential) and just showing your barcode while saying 적립이요 (most casual but fine). The dividing line is purely politeness, not meaning. A frequent English-speaker mistake is using 포인트 모아 주세요 thinking 'collect points' — Koreans don't phrase it that way; the verb is 적립하다. Also note this differs from 사용 (using) points: to spend them you say 적립금으로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요, so don't mix earning (적립) with redeeming.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather points') — not the natural verb; use 적립하다: 적립해 주세요.
Confusing earning with spending — 적립 is earning; to redeem say 포인트로 결제할게요 / 포인트 쓸게요.
Forgetting to give the identifier — staff need your 전화번호, app barcode, or card; have it ready when you say 적립해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 적립해 주세요 asks the cashier to credit loyalty points or stamps to you — by phone number, an app barcode, or a membership card. It's customer-to-staff, plain polite -요; 반말 (적립해 줘) is for friends only.
The nearest alternatives are 적립 부탁드려요 (more deferential) and just showing your barcode while saying 적립이요 (most casual but fine). The dividing line is purely politeness, not meaning.
적립 (積立) means 'accumulating/saving up'.

A frequent English-speaker mistake is using 포인트 모아 주세요 thinking 'collect points' — Koreans don't phrase it that way; the verb is 적립하다. Also note this differs from 사용 (using) points: to spend them you say 적립금으로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요, so don't mix earning (적립) with redeeming.

entries.nuance: Since Korea restricts free plastic bags, the cashier almost always asks 봉투 드릴까요? (드리다 humble 'give' + offer -ㄹ까요?) or 봉투 필요하세요?, and bags usually cost a small fee. The English-speaker trap is answering 'okay' with 괜찮아요 meaning 'yes' — in Korean 괜찮아요 here means 'no thanks, I'm fine', so you'd end up refusing the bag you wanted; say 네, 주세요 to accept.

Answering 괜찮아요 to mean 'yes/sure' — here it declines the bag; to accept say 네, 주세요.

entries.nuance: 봉투 주세요 is the customer side: you ask for a bag the cashier didn't offer (or accept the offer by stating it). Plain polite -요 covers all stores; 반말 봉투 줘 is friends-only. The classic English-speaker error is requesting 가방 — 가방 is a backpack/handbag you wear, not a shopping bag; the disposable carry bag is 봉투/봉지. Another slip is over-using 주세요 abruptly without 네 when responding to an offer; if staff already asked 봉투 드릴까요?, answer 네, 주세요 rather than a flat 봉투 주세요.

examples.en: "Shall I heat it up?" "Yes, please."
examples.note: Staff offer with 드릴까요; you accept with 데워 주세요

examples.romanization: "dewo deurilkkayo?" "aniyo, geunyang juseyo."

entries.nuance: At 편의점 (convenience stores) and some cafés, staff offer 데워 드릴까요? for microwavable food — 도시락 lunchboxes, 삼각김밥 rice triangles, 컵라면-side items. 데우다 is 'to warm/heat up' (food specifically), so this is the right verb, not 끓이다 (boil) or 굽다 (grill). It's staff 존댓말; you accept with 데워 주세요 or decline with 그냥 주세요 / 괜찮아요. The near alternative is 따뜻하게 해 드릴까요? ('shall I make it warm?'), used loosely the same way; the dividing line is that 데우다 specifically means reheating in a microwave/heater. The English-speaker mistake is saying 뜨겁게 해 주세요 ('make it scalding') or using 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — you only want it reheated, so the verb is 데우다: 데워 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — that asks them to prepare a dish; reheating ready food is 데워 주세요.
Saying 끓여 주세요 ('boil it') for a lunchbox — 끓이다 is for liquids; microwaving solid food is 데우다.
Declining with a blunt 아니요 only — soften it like 아니요, 그냥 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요.

examples.note: 포장해 주세요 = 'pack it to go'; the real takeout answer

entries.nuance: This is the café's dine-in-or-takeout question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다, so 드시고 가세요? = 'will you eat (here) and go?'; 가져가세요? = 'will you take it away?'. It matters in Korea because dine-in drinks must use real cups/mugs by law while takeout uses disposables, and tax can differ. Staff use 존댓말; you answer with 먹고 갈게요 (stay) or 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요 (to go). The more formal phrasing is 매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요?. The English-speaker error is replying 'to go' as 고 (the English word) or saying 테이크아웃 — 테이크아웃 is understood but the natural answers are 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. Another trap: using 먹다 about yourself is fine, but when staff ask they use the honorific 드시다 — don't 'correct' it to 먹고 가세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering with English 'to go' or just 고 — say 포장이요 / 가져갈게요 / 포장해 주세요 instead.
Saying 드시고 갈게요 about yourself — use plain 먹고 갈게요; 드시다 is the honorific you reserve for others.
Assuming dine-in and takeout are identical — dine-in uses real mugs (and may be taxed/priced differently), so the answer actually changes your cup.
