structuredNuance.t: This is the café's dine-in-or-takeout question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다, so 드시고 가세요? = 'will you eat (here) and go?'; 가져가세요? = 'will you take it away?'. It matters in Korea because dine-in drinks must use real cups/mugs by law while takeout uses disposables, and tax can differ. Staff use 존댓말; you answer with 먹고 갈게요 (stay) or 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요 (to go).
The more formal phrasing is 매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요?.

The English-speaker error is replying 'to go' as 고 (the English word) or saying 테이크아웃 — 테이크아웃 is understood but the natural answers are 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. Another trap: using 먹다 about yourself is fine, but when staff ask they use the honorific 드시다 — don't 'correct' it to 먹고 가세요.

entries.nuance: 일회용 (一回用) means 'single-use', so 일회용 컵 is a disposable paper/plastic cup. You ask for this when you're dining in but want a to-go cup (Korean cafés default to real mugs/glasses for dine-in by law, so you must request disposable). Customer-to-staff plain polite -요; 반말 only with friends. The everyday alternative is 테이크아웃 컵 — interchangeable; some say 종이컵 if it's specifically paper. The English-speaker mistake is asking for a 'plastic cup' literally as 플라스틱 컵 (technically fine but stiff) or saying 일회용 잔 — 잔 is for glass/ceramic ware (와인 잔, 머그잔), while disposables take the counter 컵; keep 일회용 컵. Also don't confuse 일회용 (one-use) with 일회 ('one time/round') alone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 일회용 잔 — 잔 implies glass/ceramic ware; disposables are counted with 컵: 일회용 컵.
Assuming dine-in comes in a paper cup automatically — Korean cafés give real mugs for here; you must ask for 일회용 컵.
Using 플라스틱 컵 woodenly — understood but stiff; 일회용 컵 or 테이크아웃 컵 sounds natural.

examples.romanization: "teombeulleoe dama juseyo." "ne, harin deureogaseyo."
examples.en: "In my tumbler, please." "Sure, you get a discount."
examples.note: Bringing a tumbler usually earns a small discount in Korea

examples.ko: 이 텀블러 깨끗해요. 여기에 담아 주세요.
examples.romanization: i teombeulleo kkaekkeutaeyo. yeogie dama juseyo.
examples.en: This tumbler is clean. Please fill it here.
examples.note: Reassuring it's clean; 여기에 = 'in here', 에 marks the destination

examples.ko: 아이스 아메리카노 텀블러에 담아 주세요. 얼음 따로 주시고요.
examples.romanization: aiseu amerikano teombeulleoe dama juseyo. eoreum ttaro jusigoyo.
examples.en: An iced americano in my tumbler, please. And the ice separately.
examples.note: Real flow: drink + tumbler + a side request, all chained

entries.nuance: 텀블러 (tumbler) is a reusable personal cup; 텀블러에 담아 주세요 hands it over for the barista to fill, and 담다 ('to put/fill into') is the precise verb. Bringing one usually earns a 텀블러 할인 (discount), so it's worth knowing. Customer-to-staff plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only. The destination particle is -에 (텀블러에), marking where the drink goes — not -로. The nearest alternative is the looser 텀블러에 해 주세요. The English-speaker mistake is using -로 (텀블러로 주세요), which sounds like 'give me a tumbler (as the item)' rather than 'pour into my tumbler'; with a container you're filling, use -에. Another slip is 채워 주세요 ('fill it up') — fine for a refill, but for a fresh drink the natural verb is 담다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 텀블러로 주세요 — -로 reads as 'give me a tumbler'; to fill your cup use -에: 텀블러에 담아 주세요.
Using 넣어 주세요 ('insert it') — 넣다 is putting an object inside; pouring a drink into a cup is 담다.
Forgetting to mention the tumbler upfront — say 텀블러 가져왔어요 first, then 담아 주세요, so staff apply the discount.

entries.shortExplanation: 얼마예요? is a practical expression meaning "How much is it?".
entries.explanation: "How much is it?" — that is 얼마예요? (eolmayeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 얼마예요? ("How much is it?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.romanization: "eolmayeyo?" "4,500wonimnida."
examples.en: "How much?" "It's 4,500 won."

examples.romanization: i ppang eolmayeyo? gagyeokpyoga eopsneyo.
examples.en: How much is this bread? There's no price tag.
examples.note: -네요 notes a fresh observation (the missing tag)

examples.romanization: da haeseo eolmayeyo? kadeu dwaeyo?

examples.note: 다 해서 = 'all together'; a natural checkout combo

entries.nuance: 얼마예요? is the everyday 'how much?' and one of the first phrases any learner needs. 얼마 = 'how much/how many (price)', + 예요 the polite copula. Plain polite -요 fits every shop; 반말 얼마야? is for friends. A softer option is 얼마인가요?, and for a total you add 다 해서 얼마예요? ('how much altogether?'). The dividing line with 얼마인가요? is just register/indirectness, not meaning. The English-speaker trap is writing 얼마에요 — the copula after a vowel-final 얼마 is 예요, not 에요 (얼마예요 is correct). Another slip is 얼마 있어요? which means 'how much (money) do you have?', not 'how much does it cost'; the price question is 얼마예요?. Korean prices are in 원 and spoken in 만/천 units, so listen for 사천오백 = 4,500.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 얼마에요 — after the vowel-final 얼마 the copula is 예요: 얼마예요.
Saying 얼마 있어요? for a price — that asks how much money you have; the cost question is 얼마예요?.
Expecting digit-by-digit prices — Koreans say 만/천/백 units (사천오백원 = 4,500), so train your ear for those.

entries.explanation: 카드로 할게요 (kadeuro halgeyo) = "I'll pay by card". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 카드로 할게요. ("I'll pay by card."). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.romanization: "hyeongeumiseyo, kadeuseyo?" "kadeuro halgeyo."
examples.en: "Cash or card?" "By card."
examples.note: -로 marks the means; -ㄹ게요 declares your intent

examples.romanization: kadeuro halgeyo. ilsibulloyo.
examples.en: By card, please. In a single payment.
examples.note: 일시불 = 'lump-sum'; staff may ask 할부 (installments) vs 일시불

examples.romanization: kadeuro halgeyo. yeogi jjigeumyeon dwaeyo?

examples.note: 찍다 here = 'tap/insert' the card; asking where the reader is

entries.nuance: 카드로 할게요 tells the cashier you'll pay by card; -로 marks the method and -ㄹ게요 announces a decision affecting you ('I'll go with…'). Plain polite -요 for shops; formal -하겠습니다 in stiff settings; 반말 with friends. Staff may follow with 일시불이세요, 할부세요? (lump-sum or installments) — for a coffee just say 일시불로요. The near alternative is 카드로 계산할게요 / 카드 될까요? (asking if card is accepted); the line is that 할게요 commits, while 될까요? merely asks. The English-speaker mistake is 카드로 지불할게요 — 지불하다 is correct but bookish/stiff; spoken Korean uses 하다 or 계산하다. Another slip is the particle: it must be 카드'로' (by means of), not 카드를 or 카드에; -로 marks instrument.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Wrong particle 카드를/카드에 — payment method takes -로 (instrument): 카드로.
Freezing when asked 일시불이세요, 할부세요? — for small buys just answer 일시불로요 (one payment).

structuredNuance.t: 카드로 할게요 tells the cashier you'll pay by card; -로 marks the method and -ㄹ게요 announces a decision affecting you ('I'll go with…'). Plain polite -요 for shops; formal -하겠습니다 in stiff settings; 반말 with friends. Staff may follow with 일시불이세요, 할부세요? (lump-sum or installments) — for a coffee just say 일시불로요.
The near alternative is 카드로 계산할게요 / 카드 될까요? (asking if card is accepted); the line is that 할게요 commits, while 될까요? merely asks.

The English-speaker mistake is 카드로 지불할게요 — 지불하다 is correct but bookish/stiff; spoken Korean uses 하다 or 계산하다. Another slip is the particle: it must be 카드'로' (by means of), not 카드를 or 카드에; -로 marks instrument.

examples.en: "Shall I issue a cash receipt?" "Yes, please."
examples.note: Staff offer with 해 드릴까요; you confirm with 해 주세요

examples.ko: 현금으로 할게요. 현금영수증 해 주세요. 010-1234-5678이요.

examples.ko: 현금영수증 소득공제로 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: hyeongeumyeongsujeung sodeukgongjero hae juseyo.
examples.en: Register the cash receipt for income deduction, please.
examples.note: 소득공제 (personal) vs 지출증빙 (business) — say which type

entries.nuance: 현금영수증 (現金領收證) is a 'cash receipt' registered to your phone number or ID for year-end tax deduction — uniquely Korean, so learners must know to ask. 해 주세요 ('please do/issue it') is the everyday request; 발급해 주세요 is the formal verb. Plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only. Staff may ask 소득공제용이세요, 지출증빙용이세요? — personal income deduction vs business expense; for personal use say 소득공제로요. The near alternative is just 영수증 주세요, but that's the plain printed receipt — the dividing line is that 현금영수증 is the tax-registered one tied to your number, whereas 영수증 is the paper slip. The English-speaker mistake is asking only for 영수증 and missing the tax benefit, or giving a card when you said cash — 현금영수증 only applies to 현금 (cash) payment.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking for plain 영수증 expecting the tax benefit — that's just the printed slip; the tax-registered one is 현금영수증.
Requesting it on a card payment — 현금영수증 is for 현금 (cash) only; card already records itself.
Forgetting your phone number — the receipt registers to your 휴대폰 번호, so have it ready when you ask.

entries.shortExplanation: 빨대 어디 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Where are the straws?".
entries.explanation: "Where are the straws?" — that is 빨대 어디 있어요? (ppaldae eodi isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 빨대 어디 있어요? ("Where are the straws?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

반말; to a friend
Softer, more polite/indirect variant
Extension: just ask staff for one directly

examples.ko: "빨대 어디 있어요?" "저쪽 셀프바에 있어요."
examples.romanization: "ppaldae eodi isseoyo?" "jeojjok selpeubae isseoyo."
examples.en: "Where are the straws?" "Over at the self-serve bar."
examples.note: 셀프바 = self-serve station; 저쪽 = 'over there'

examples.ko: 빨대 어디 있어요? 안 보여서요.
examples.romanization: ppaldae eodi isseoyo? an boyeoseoyo.
examples.en: Where are the straws? I can't find them.
examples.note: 안 보여서요 = 'I don't see them', a soft reason for asking

examples.ko: 빨대랑 휴지 어디 있어요?
examples.romanization: ppaldaerang hyuji eodi isseoyo?
examples.en: Where are the straws and napkins?
examples.note: 랑 links two items; napkins (휴지/냅킨) are usually at the same bar

entries.nuance: Most Korean cafés have a 셀프바 (self-serve bar) for straws, lids, napkins, sugar, and water, so 빨대 어디 있어요? ('where are the straws?') is the practical question. 빨대 literally 'sucking stick' = straw. 어디 있어요? = 'where is it?'. Plain polite -요; 반말 with friends. If you'd rather have staff fetch one, say 빨대 좀 주세요 instead — the line is whether you locate it yourself (어디 있어요?) or have them hand it over (주세요). The English-speaker mistake is the location verb: it's 어디 있어요? (existence/location), not 어디예요? — 어디예요? asks 'where is (this place)?' and sounds odd about objects. Another slip is calling it a 스트로 (English 'straw'); the native 빨대 is the normal word. Note paper straws (종이 빨대) are now common.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 빨대 어디예요? — for object location use 있어요?: 빨대 어디 있어요?; 어디예요? asks where a place is.
Calling it 스트로 — the everyday word is 빨대 (스트로 sounds like a brand/loanword).
Expecting staff to bring it unasked — straws are usually self-serve at the 셀프바; either find it or say 빨대 좀 주세요.

entries.explanation: 자리 있어요? (jari isseoyo?) = "Are there any seats?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 자리 있어요? ("Are there seats available?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

반말; to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Are there seats, by any chance?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more polite/indirect variant

usagePhrases.en: Is there a table for two?
usagePhrases.note: Extension: state the party size with 명

examples.ko: "자리 있어요?" "네, 2층에 있어요."
examples.romanization: "jari isseoyo?" "ne, 2cheunge isseoyo."
examples.en: "Any seats?" "Yes, upstairs on the 2nd floor."
examples.note: Staff often direct you (2층 = 2nd floor) rather than seat you

examples.ko: 혹시 자리 있어요? 콘센트 있는 자리면 좋겠어요.
examples.romanization: hoksi jari isseoyo? konsenteu inneun jarimyeon jokesseoyo.
examples.en: Any seats, by chance? A spot with an outlet would be great.
examples.note: 혹시 softens the ask; 콘센트 자리 = a seat with a power outlet

examples.ko: 지금 자리 있어요? 두 명인데요.
examples.romanization: jigeum jari isseoyo? du myeongindeyo.
examples.en: Any seats right now? There are two of us.
examples.note: -인데요 tacks on context (party size) and invites a reply

entries.nuance: 자리 있어요? ('is there a seat/spot?') asks whether seating is free — at a busy café, a restaurant entrance, or to ask someone if a seat is taken. 자리 = 'seat/spot/place'. Plain polite -요; 반말 자리 있어? with friends; softer 자리 있나요?. Add 혹시 ('by any chance') to be gentle, or a party size (두 명 자리). The near alternative is 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?') — the dividing line is that 자리 있어요? asks about availability in general, while 앉아도 돼요? asks permission for one specific seat. The English-speaker mistake is the verb: availability is 있어요? (existence), not 자리예요?. Another slip is using 좌석 — correct but formal/written (좌석 번호, theater seats); in a café the natural word is 자리. Also don't confuse 자리 (seat) with 자리를 잡다 ('to grab/save a seat').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자리예요? for availability — use 있어요? (existence): 자리 있어요?.
Using 좌석 in a café — correct but formal/written; the everyday word is 자리.
Asking 자리 있어요? when you mean a specific empty seat — to ask permission for that seat say 여기 앉아도 돼요?.

entries.english: To go, please / Pack it up
entries.shortExplanation: 포장해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "To go, please / Pack it up".
entries.explanation: 포장해 주세요 (pojanghae juseyo) means "To go, please / Pack it up". Say it as one set phrase — for example 포장해 주세요. ("Please pack it to go."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Customer choosing takeout; 포장 = packing/wrapping
반말; friend context
Clipped one-word answer to 'for here or to go?'

usagePhrases.en: Can I get this to go?
usagePhrases.note: Extension: ask first whether takeout is possible

examples.ko: "드시고 가세요?" "아니요, 포장해 주세요."
examples.romanization: "deusigo gaseyo?" "aniyo, pojanghae juseyo."
examples.en: "Eating in?" "No, to go, please."
examples.note: The natural takeout answer to the dine-in question

examples.ko: 라떼 한 잔 포장해 주세요. 캐리어도 주시고요.
examples.romanization: ratte han jan pojanghae juseyo. kaerieodo jusigoyo.
examples.en: One latte to go, please. With a carrier too.
examples.note: 캐리어 = drink carrier; 주시고요 adds the second request

examples.ko: 남은 거 포장해 주세요. 집에서 먹을게요.
examples.romanization: nameun geo pojanghae juseyo. jibeseo meogeulgeyo.
examples.en: Please pack up the leftovers. I'll eat them at home.
examples.note: 남은 거 = 'the leftovers'; same verb works for restaurant doggy-bags

entries.nuance: 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it') is the all-purpose 'to go' request — for a fresh café drink, a bakery item, or restaurant leftovers. 포장 (包裝) literally 'wrapping/packaging'. Plain polite -요; clipped 포장이요 as a quick answer; 반말 포장해 줘 with friends. The near alternative is 가져갈게요 ('I'll take it away') — the dividing line is that 포장해 주세요 asks the staff to pack it, while 가져갈게요 just states you're leaving with it; both work for takeout. The English-speaker mistake is 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood, but 포장 is the natural native word, and 테이크아웃 컵 is more for the cup itself. Another slip is 싸 주세요 ('wrap it up'), which is fine and homey for leftovers but slightly informal for a café order; 포장해 주세요 is the clean default.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood but the natural word is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Confusing it with dine-in answers — 포장해 주세요 is takeout; to stay say 먹고 갈게요 / 여기서 먹을게요.
Using 포장 for gift-wrapping expectations — in a café it means 'pack to go'; for gift wrap you'd specify 선물 포장.

structuredNuance.t: 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it') is the all-purpose 'to go' request — for a fresh café drink, a bakery item, or restaurant leftovers. Plain polite -요; clipped 포장이요 as a quick answer; 반말 포장해 줘 with friends.

entries.nuance: 어디가 아프세요? is the doctor's or nurse's standard polite opening to a patient, built from 어디가 'where (subject)' + 아프다 'to hurt' + honorific 세요. entries.nuance: 열이 나요 is how you report a fever to a doctor, pharmacist, or anyone — literally 'heat comes out (열이 나다)'. Korean treats the fever as something that 'arises', so the natural verb is 나다, not 있다 or 하다; 열이 있어요 exists but sounds like 'there's some warmth', milder and more detached, while 열이 나요 is the everyday 'I'm running a fever'. The register shifts simply by ending: 열이 나 (반말) to a friend, 열이 나요 (존댓말) to a doctor, 열이 납니다 (격식) in formal speech. The big English-speaker error is 'I have a fever' → 열을 가지고 있어요 — a word-for-word calque with 가지다 'to possess' that no Korean says about symptoms; bodily states 'come' (나다) or 'exist' (있다), they are never 'had'. Also keep the particle 이: 열이 나요, not 열을 나요, because the fever is the subject of 나다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 열을 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a fever'.
This literally translates English 'have' with 가지다 (to possess) and is unnatural for symptoms. Korean uses 열이 나요 ('a fever arises').
Using 열을 나요 with the object particle.
나다 ('to come out/arise') is intransitive, so 열 is the subject: 열이 나요, with 이, not 열을.
Saying 뜨거워요 to mean 'I have a fever'.
뜨겁다 describes a hot object you touch (hot coffee). Your body temperature being up is 열이 나요; 뜨거워요 about yourself sounds like your skin is burning hot to the touch.

entries.nuance: 머리가 아파요 is the go-to way to report any head pain — body-part + 가/이 + 아파요. The particle on the body part is the subject marker 가, because 아프다 is descriptive: the head is what 'is hurting', so it's the subject, never 머리를. This same frame builds every symptom: 배가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 이가 아파요. Register shifts by ending only (머리가 아파 / 아파요 / 아픕니다). Note 머리 means both 'head' and 'hair', so context decides; for the pain sense, 아파요 makes it unambiguous. English speakers often reach for the noun 'headache' and try 두통이 있어요 — that is correct and slightly more clinical (두통 = 頭痛, 'head-pain'), but in everyday speech 머리가 아파요 is far more common and natural; save 두통약 ('headache medicine') for the pharmacy counter.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 머리를 아파요 with 를.
아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the body part is the subject and takes 가/이: 머리가 아파요, not 머리를 아파요.
Saying 나는 머리 아파요 dropping the particle in formal speech.
Casual speech can drop 가, but to a doctor keep it: 머리가 아파요 sounds complete and clear, while bare 머리 아파 is 반말-flavored.
Using 두통해요 as a verb.
두통 is a noun; you can't verb it with 하다. Say 두통이 있어요 or, more naturally, 머리가 아파요.

entries.nuance: 배가 아파요 covers stomachache, bellyache, and cramps — 배 is the whole belly/abdomen, not just the stomach organ. Same descriptive frame as all symptoms: subject particle 가, never 배를. A key cultural note: 배가 아프다 also has an idiomatic meaning, 'to be jealous/envious' (literally 'my belly hurts' = it gnaws at me that someone else got something good), so 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 is a proverb about envy — context makes the medical meaning clear at a clinic. To specify, Koreans add 윗배 (upper belly) or 아랫배 (lower belly). English speakers say 'stomach' and reach for 위(胃, the stomach organ), but 위가 아파요 sounds clinical and narrows it to the actual stomach; for a general bellyache always use 배가 아파요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 배를 아파요 with the object particle.
아프다 is descriptive, so 배 is the subject: 배가 아파요, not 배를.
Using 위가 아파요 for a general bellyache.
위 is specifically the stomach organ and sounds clinical. For ordinary belly/abdominal pain say 배가 아파요.
Reading every 배가 아파요 as physical pain.
It can idiomatically mean 'I'm jealous'. At a clinic it's literal, but among friends 배 아파 ~ may tease 'I'm so envious', so let context decide.

entries.nuance: 기침이 나요 reports a cough, again with 나다 ('to come out/arise') and the subject particle 이 — bodily phenomena 'arise' in Korean: 기침이 나다, 콧물이 나다, 열이 나다 all share this frame. entries.nuance: 콧물이 나요 means 'my nose is running' — 콧물 is literally 'nose-water' (코 + 물, with the linking ㅅ giving 콧물), and again it 'arises' with 나다 + subject particle 이. Notice the contrast pair the doctor will probe: 콧물이 나요 (runny, wet nose) versus 코가 막혔어요 (blocked, stuffy nose) — opposite problems, different phrases, so don't blur them. English speakers calque 'runny nose' as an adjective and get stuck; Korean treats the mucus itself as the subject that comes out, so the literal logic is 'nose-water comes out'. Keep the particle 이 (콧물이 나요, not 콧물을 나요). In casual speech the particle drops (콧물 나), but to a doctor the full 콧물이 나요 is cleaner. Pair-words to know: 재채기 (sneeze), 가래 (phlegm), 콧물 (snot/runny nose).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 콧물을 나요 with 를.
나다 is intransitive; 콧물 is its subject, so 콧물이 나요, never 콧물을 나요.

콧물이 나요 = a runny (wet) nose; 코가 막혔어요 = a blocked (stuffy) nose. They are opposite symptoms.

The compound 코 + 물 inserts a ㅅ받침: it is spelled 콧물 and pronounced [콘물]. 코물 is a spelling error.

examples.en: I get carsick the moment I'm in a car and feel like throwing up.
examples.note: Everyday cause; 멀미가 나다 = get motion sickness

examples.en: I'm dizzy and my stomach is churning, I really feel like I'll throw up.
examples.note: Fuller state; 울렁거리다 = (stomach) churn/heave

entries.nuance: 토할 것 같아요 = 토하다 'to vomit' + 을 것 같다 'it seems like / I feel like (it will happen)', so 'I feel like I'm about to throw up'. The 을 것 같다 frame is essential: it expresses an impending sensation, not a completed act, which is exactly what you want to warn a nurse before it happens. The blunter verb 토하다 is fine medically but graphic in polite small talk; gentler options are 속이 안 좋아요 ('my stomach's off'), 메스꺼워요/울렁거려요 ('I feel queasy') — the dividing line is intensity, with 토할 것 같아요 being the urgent one. English speakers misuse 같아요 as a hedge meaning 'I think' and attach it loosely; here it's bound to the 을 것 form (토할 것 같아요), so don't say 토해요 같아요. Also avoid the casual 게워요 with strangers — it's colloquial; 토하다 is the neutral verb.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 토해요 같아요 to mean 'I feel like throwing up'.
같다 must attach to the 을 것 form: 토할 것 같아요. You can't bolt 같아요 onto a finished verb.
Using 토할 것 같아요 only after you've already vomited.
The 을 것 같다 frame is for an impending feeling. If it already happened, say 토했어요.
Saying 던지다 because a dictionary glosses 'throw up' as 'throw'.
던지다 means physically throw an object. 'Throw up' (vomit) is 토하다 — a completely different verb.

entries.nuance: 어지러워요 means 'I feel dizzy/light-headed'. The base is the ㅂ-irregular adjective 어지럽다, which conjugates 어지럽다 → 어지러워요 (the ㅂ turns to 우/워), a spelling point learners stumble on. As a descriptive verb of state it stands alone — no body-part subject needed, unlike 머리가 아파요. The near-neighbor 현기증이 나요 ('I have vertigo', 현기증 = 眩氣症) is more clinical and names the symptom as a noun that 'arises' with 나다; the dividing line is everyday 어지러워요 vs. medical 현기증이 나요. English speakers regularize the ㅂ-irregular to 어지럽어요 — wrong; it must be 어지러워요. Another slip is reaching for 미쳐요 ('go crazy/spin') from 'my head is spinning'; that means losing your mind, not feeling faint. For light-headedness on standing, 어지러워요 is exactly right.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어지럽어요 by regularizing the verb.
어지럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the ㅂ becomes 워 before 어요, giving 어지러워요, not 어지럽어요.
Saying 머리가 어지러워요.
어지럽다 already describes your whole head/state, so a body-part subject is redundant. Just say 어지러워요.
Using 미쳐요 for 'my head is spinning'.
미치다 = go crazy/insane. Dizziness is 어지러워요 or 현기증이 나요; 미쳐요 has nothing to do with feeling faint.

entries.shortExplanation: 처방전 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please give me the prescription".
entries.explanation: "Please give me the prescription" — that is 처방전 주세요 (cheobangjeon juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 처방전 주세요 ("Please give me the prescription"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 처방전 주세요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.note: More formal, polite request with 시겠어요
Extension; 발급하다 = issue (a document)

examples.romanization: cheobangjeon juseyo. — yeogi itseumnida.
examples.en: The prescription, please. — Here you go.
examples.note: Bare request and the staff's reply at the desk

examples.ko: 약국에 가야 하니까 처방전 주세요.
examples.romanization: yakguge gaya hanikka cheobangjeon juseyo.
examples.en: I need to go to the pharmacy, so please give me the prescription.
examples.note: Everyday reason; the doctor's office issues it, the 약국 fills it

examples.ko: 전에 받은 처방전을 잃어버렸는데 다시 발급해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeone badeun cheobangjeoneul ireobeoryeonneunde dasi balgeupae juseyo.
examples.en: I lost the prescription I got before; please reissue it.
examples.note: Fuller situation; 잃어버리다 = lose, 발급 = issuance

entries.nuance: 처방전 주세요 asks for the prescription slip — 처방전 (處方箋, 'prescription document') + 주세요 'please give'. In Korea the system is split: the doctor (병원/의원) writes the 처방전, and you take it to a separate pharmacy (약국) to get the actual medicine — so you literally receive a paper (increasingly sent electronically) to hand over. Don't confuse 처방전 (the slip) with 처방 (the act of prescribing) or with 약 (the medicine itself). 주세요 is the standard polite 'give me'; to be softer use 주시겠어요? or 주실 수 있어요?. The English-speaker confusion is expecting the doctor to hand over pills directly, so they ask for 약 at the clinic — but at the 병원 you ask for the 처방전, and at the 약국 you ask them to fill it (약 지어 주세요). Saying 처방전 주세요 to the pharmacist is backwards; you GIVE the slip there.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 처방전 (the slip) with 약 (the medicine).
처방전 is the paper prescription from the doctor; 약 is the medicine from the pharmacy. Ask the clinic for 처방전, the pharmacy for 약.
Asking the pharmacist 처방전 주세요.
You HAND the 처방전 to the pharmacist, you don't receive it there. At the 약국 say 약 지어 주세요 or hand over the slip.
Saying 처방 주세요 instead of 처방전.
처방 is the act of prescribing; the physical slip is 처방전. Drop the 전 and it sounds incomplete.

examples.romanization: yak jom jieo juseyo. — cheobangjeon jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you fill this? — May I have the prescription?
examples.note: Bare request and the pharmacist's standard reply

examples.romanization: gamgiyak jom jieo juseyo. konmurirang gichimi simhaeyo.

examples.note: Everyday over-the-counter request describing symptoms

examples.en: It's for my child, so please make it up as powder medicine.
examples.note: Fuller request; 가루약 = powdered medicine, easier for kids

entries.nuance: 약 좀 지어 주세요 is what you say to a pharmacist: 약 'medicine' + 짓다 'to make/compose' + 주세요 'please (for me)'. The verb 짓다 is special — it's the same 'build/compose' used for 밥을 짓다 (cook rice) and 집을 짓다 (build a house); medicine is 'composed/made up', reflecting the traditional pharmacy that measures and combines doses. Note 짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular: 짓다 → 지어 (the ㅅ drops), so it's 지어 주세요, not 짓어 주세요. 좀 ('a bit') is the politeness softener that turns a bare order into a friendly request. The dividing line from 약 주세요 ('give me medicine') is that 지어 주세요 implies preparing/compounding from a prescription or for your symptoms, while 약 주세요 just means hand over a ready product. English speakers calque 'fill a prescription' with 채우다 ('to fill (a container)') — completely wrong here; the idiom is 약을 짓다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짓어 주세요 instead of 지어 주세요.
짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ drops before 어, giving 지어. So it's 약 지어 주세요.
Using 채우다 to translate 'fill a prescription'.
채우다 means fill a physical container. 'Make up medicine' is 약을 짓다 — 약 지어 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and saying just 약 지어.
Without 좀 and with 반말 it sounds like a brusque order. To a pharmacist use 약 좀 지어 주세요.

usagePhrases.note: Extension adding the dose; 한 알씩 = one tablet each

examples.romanization: haru se beon deuseyo. — ne, algetseumnida.
examples.en: Take it three times a day. — Okay, got it.
examples.note: Bare instruction and the patient's acknowledgment

examples.ko: 이 약은 하루 세 번, 식후에 드세요.
examples.romanization: i yageun haru se beon, sikue deuseyo.
examples.en: Take this three times a day, after meals.
examples.note: Everyday full instruction; 식후 = after eating

examples.ko: 증상이 없어져도 하루 세 번 끝까지 다 드세요.
examples.romanization: jeungsangi eopseojyeodo haru se beon kkeutkkaji da deuseyo.

entries.nuance: 하루 세 번 드세요 is the dosing instruction you'll hear constantly: 하루 'a day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 먹다 'to take/eat'. Crucial counting point — 번 ('times/occurrences') takes NATIVE Korean numbers in their counter form: 한 번, 두 번, 세 번, 네 번, so 'three times' is 세 번, never the Sino-Korean 삼 번. The verb to a patient is the honorific 드세요 (or clinical 복용하세요), while 먹어 is 반말 to a child. The English-speaker error is the number system: learners say 삼 번 by analogy with reading numbers aloud, but with the counter 번 you need native 세 번. Another slip is word order — Korean is 하루 세 번 ('day three times'), the opposite of English 'three times a day'; the time unit comes first. Pair it with 식후 (after meals) or 식전 (before meals) for the full instruction.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 삼 번 instead of 세 번 for 'three times'.
The counter 번 requires native Korean numerals: 한/두/세/네 번. 'Three times' is 세 번, not Sino-Korean 삼 번.
Putting it in English order: 세 번 하루.
Korean states the larger time unit first: 하루 세 번 ('a day, three times'), not 세 번 하루.
Using 먹으세요 vs 드세요 incorrectly to an elder patient.
To a patient the honorific 드세요 (or 복용하세요) is the norm; 먹어 is 반말 for a child. Plain 먹으세요 is acceptable but 드세요 is more polite.

structuredNuance.t: The dosing instruction you'll hear constantly: 하루 'a day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 먹다 'to take/eat'. Crucial counting point — 번 ('times/occurrences') takes NATIVE Korean numbers in their counter form: 한 번, 두 번, 세 번, 네 번, so 'three times' is 세 번, never the Sino-Korean 삼 번. The verb to a patient is the honorific 드세요 (or clinical 복용하세요), while 먹어 is 반말 to a child. Pair it with 식후 (after meals) or 식전 (before meals) for the full instruction.

The number-system error: learners say 삼 번 by analogy with reading numbers aloud, but with the counter 번 you need native 세 번. Another slip is word order — Korean is 하루 세 번 ('day three times'), the opposite of English 'three times a day'; the time unit comes first.

examples.romanization: siku samsip bune deuseyo. — ne.
examples.en: Take it 30 minutes after meals. — Okay.
examples.note: The bare instruction printed on most Korean medicine bags

examples.ko: 속 쓰릴 수 있으니까 꼭 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
examples.romanization: sok sseuril su isseunikka kkok siku samsip bune deuseyo.
examples.en: It can upset your stomach, so be sure to take it 30 minutes after eating.
examples.note: Everyday reasoning; 속 쓰리다 = have an acidy/burning stomach

examples.ko: 이건 식전, 저건 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. 헷갈리지 마세요.

examples.en: Take this before meals and that one 30 minutes after; don't mix them up.
examples.note: Fuller two-medicine instruction; 헷갈리다 = get confused/mixed up

entries.nuance: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 — literally '식후 (食後, after-meal) 삼십 분 (30 minutes) 에 (at) take' — is the timing line on almost every Korean prescription bag (약봉투). Note the number system flips here versus 번: time durations and Sino-Korean compounds use SINO numbers, so '30 minutes' is 삼십 분, and the particle 에 marks the point in time ('at 30 minutes after'). Learn the set: 식전 (before meals), 식후 (after meals), 식간 (between meals), 취침 전 (before bed). The contrast that matters is 식전 vs 식후 — taking a 식후 drug on an empty stomach can cause 속 쓰림 (stomach burning), so the distinction is medically real, not just vocabulary. English speakers mix the number systems (saying 세십 분 or using 분 with native numbers) and drop the time particle 에; keep it as 삼십 분에. Also don't translate 'after meals' as 식사 후에 only — 식후 is the compact written norm on labels.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using native numbers for the minutes (서른 분).
Clock/duration minutes use Sino-Korean numerals: 삼십 분, not native 서른 분.
Dropping the time particle 에: 식후 삼십 분 드세요.
The point in time needs 에: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. Without it the timing relation is unclear.
Confusing 식전 and 식후.
식전 = before meals, 식후 = after meals. They are opposites, and the wrong one can upset your stomach.

entries.shortExplanation: 진통제 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Do you have painkillers?".
entries.explanation: 진통제 있어요? (jintongje isseoyo?) = "Do you have painkillers?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 진통제 있어요? ("Do you have painkillers?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.ko: 진통제 있어요? — 네, 어떤 통증이세요?
examples.romanization: jintongje isseoyo? — ne, eotteon tongjeungiseyo?
examples.en: Do you have painkillers? — Yes, what kind of pain?
examples.note: Bare question and the pharmacist's natural probe

examples.ko: 생리통이 심한데 진통제 있어요?
examples.romanization: saengnitongi simhande jintongje isseoyo?
examples.en: My period cramps are bad — do you have painkillers?
examples.note: Everyday context; 생리통 = menstrual pain

examples.ko: 타이레놀 같은 진통제 있어요? 두통이 너무 심해서요.
examples.romanization: tairenol gateun jintongje isseoyo? dutongi neomu simhaeseoyo.
examples.en: Do you have a painkiller like Tylenol? My headache is really bad.
examples.note: Fuller request naming a brand; 같은 = like/such as

entries.nuance: 진통제 있어요? asks the pharmacist whether they stock painkillers — 진통제 (鎭痛劑, 'pain-suppress agent') + 있어요? 'is there?/do you have?'. 있어요? is the everyday polite way to ask about availability of any product, far more natural than a textbook 가지고 있어요?. Good vocabulary to pair: 두통약 (headache medicine), 소화제 (digestive aid), 해열제 (fever reducer), 소염제 (anti-inflammatory) — Korean names many drugs by the symptom + 제/약. The dividing line: 진통제 is the general painkiller category, while naming a brand (타이레놀) or a specific use (생리통약, period-pain medicine) narrows it. English speakers calque 'do you have' with 가지고 있어요?, which sounds like asking if the pharmacist personally carries one on them; for shop stock always use 있어요?. Also note painkillers like ibuprofen are sold over the counter (일반의약품) without a prescription, so this question is genuinely useful.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 진통제 가지고 있어요? for shop stock.
가지고 있다 = personally possess. To ask whether a store stocks something, use 있어요?: 진통제 있어요?
Saying 아픔약 for 'painkiller'.
There is no 아픔약. The word is 진통제, or by symptom e.g. 두통약 (headache medicine).
Confusing 진통제 with 해열제.
진통제 relieves pain; 해열제 reduces fever. They overlap in some products but ask for the right one.

entries.english: If it's really bad, go see a doctor
entries.shortExplanation: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 is a practical expression meaning "If it's really bad, go see a doctor".
entries.explanation: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 (mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo) means "If it's really bad, go see a doctor". Say it as one set phrase — for example 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 ("If it gets bad, go to the doctor"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.romanization: mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo. — ne, geureolgeyo.
examples.en: If it's bad, go see a doctor. — Okay, I will.
examples.note: Bare advice and the customer's agreement

examples.ko: 이 약 먹고도 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요.
examples.romanization: i yang meokgodo mani an joeumyeon byeongwon gaseyo.
examples.en: If you're still bad after this medicine, go to the doctor.
examples.note: Everyday pharmacist follow-up; 먹고도 = even after taking

examples.note: Fuller advice; 지켜보다 = keep an eye on, ~일 수도 있다 = might be

entries.nuance: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 is the kindly send-off a pharmacist gives: 많이 'a lot' + 안 좋으면 'if (it's) not good' (the conditional ~으면) + 병원 가세요 'go to the hospital/clinic'. Two cultural points. First, 병원 in Korea means any medical facility from a tiny neighborhood clinic (의원) up to a big hospital — 'go to 병원' just means 'see a doctor', not necessarily a hospital admission, which surprises English speakers. Second, 안 좋다 ('not good') is the gentle, idiomatic way to say a symptom is worsening; it's softer than 나빠지면 ('if it gets bad') and very natural. To be more polite, add the subject honorific: 많이 안 좋으시면 가 보세요, where 가 보세요 ('try going') is gentler than a flat 가세요. English speakers literally translate 'go to the hospital' and picture an ER; here it routinely means a regular clinic visit. Keep the conditional 으면 attached to 좋다 (안 좋으면), not a separate 만약 clause alone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing 병원 가세요 as 'go get hospitalized'.
병원 covers clinics too; it simply means 'see a doctor'. For admission you'd say 입원하다.
Saying 만약 안 좋다 병원 가세요 without the conditional ending.
'If' needs the ~으면 ending on the verb: 안 좋으면. 만약 is optional emphasis, not a replacement for 으면.
Using 나쁘면 instead of 안 좋으면 about how you feel.
For health, the idiomatic 'if you feel worse' is 안 좋으면. 나쁘다 about a person can sound like 'bad-natured'; 몸이 안 좋다 is the set phrase for feeling unwell.

entries.nuance: 몸살이 났어요 has no clean English equivalent: 몸살 is the run-down, achy-all-over, feverish-exhaustion state you get from overwork or a cold — body aches plus fatigue. It pairs with 나다 ('arise') in the past, 몸살이 났어요, meaning you've come down with it. Don't confuse 몸살 (body aches/exhaustion) with 감기 (a cold) — they often come together (감기몸살) but 몸살 specifically is the muscle-aching, drained feeling, while 감기 is the respiratory cold (runny nose, cough). The cause is typically overexertion (무리하다), so Koreans say 몸살 났어 after a hard week. English speakers have no word for this and try to describe it piecemeal ('I'm tired and my body hurts'); learning 몸살이 났어요 captures it in one phrase. Keep the subject particle 이 (몸살이 났어요) and the past tense for the resulting state, like 감기에 걸렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 몸살 as the same as 감기.
감기 is a respiratory cold; 몸살 is the body-ache/exhaustion state. They co-occur (감기몸살) but aren't identical.
Saying 몸살을 했어요 with 를 + 하다.
The collocation is 몸살이 나다: 몸살이 났어요. It 'arises', it isn't 'done'.
Using present 몸살이 나요 for a current case.
Like 감기에 걸렸어요, the past 몸살이 났어요 expresses the present state of having it. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.

entries.nuance: 주사 맞아야 해요? asks whether you need an injection — and the verb is the surprise: you 'receive/are hit by' a shot, 주사를 맞다, using 맞다 ('to be struck/get hit'), NOT 주사를 하다 or 주사를 받다. So 'get a shot' = 주사 맞다, 'get a vaccine' = 예방 주사 맞다. The ~아야 하다 frame means 'have to/must', so 맞아야 해요? = 'do I have to get (a shot)?'. In casual speech 해요 becomes 돼요 (맞아야 돼요?), both fine. The English-speaker error is almost universal here: calquing 'get/receive a shot' as 주사를 받다 (받다 = receive a thing handed to you) — wrong; injections are 맞다. Likewise 주사를 하다 ('do a shot') is what the nurse does to you, not what you say as the patient. 주사 itself (注射) covers both the injection and the needle. Pair it with 약만 먹으면 돼요? to ask for the pill alternative.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주사를 받아야 해요 with 받다.
받다 = receive a handed object. An injection uses 맞다 ('be struck'): 주사 맞아야 해요?
Saying 주사를 해야 해요 as the patient.
주사를 하다 is what the medical staff does (administers). As the one getting it, you say 주사를 맞다.
Confusing 맞다 'be hit' here with 맞다 'be correct'.
Same spelling, but 주사를 맞다 specifically means 'get an injection'. Context (주사) makes it the shot meaning.

examples.note: 놀랐죠 acknowledges the fright before checking on them

examples.en: You don't look well. Is something wrong? Are you all right?
examples.note: Pair with 무슨 일 있어요 to gently open the door

entries.nuance: 괜찮아요? is the all-purpose 'are you okay?' and it is the single most useful comfort line a newcomer can have — it works for someone who tripped, who got bad news, who looks sad, or who just had a fright. The verb 괜찮다 means 'to be fine / all right / acceptable', so as a question it checks on the person's state. Register matters a lot here: to a friend you say 괜찮아?, to an elder, a stranger, or a customer you must lift it to 괜찮으세요? with the honorific -으세요, and the flat 괜찮아요? sits politely in the middle. The near-miss learners make is confusing it with 괜찮아요 as a STATEMENT — the very same words said with falling intonation mean 'I'm fine / it's okay / no thank you', so tone (rising = question, falling = reassurance) does all the work. The classic English-speaker pitfall is over-translating 'Are you okay?' into something like 당신 괜찮습니까 — dropping 당신 ('you'), which sounds cold and textbook-ish in Korean; you almost never say 당신 to someone's face. Just say 괜찮아요? and let context supply the 'you'. Don't pair it with 너 to a stranger either; that's 반말 and rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 당신 괜찮아요? to someone's face.
당신 ('you') sounds distant or even confrontational when spoken directly. Korean drops the subject: just 괜찮아요? The 'you' is understood.
Using 괜찮아요? (rising) and 괜찮아요 (falling) interchangeably.
Rising intonation asks 'are you okay?'; falling intonation states 'I'm fine / it's all right'. Same words, opposite roles — control your tone.
Asking an elder 괜찮아? without the honorific.
괜찮아? is 반말 and too casual for an elder, customer, or stranger. Use 괜찮으세요? to show respect when checking on them.

entries.nuance: 힘내 is 힘 ('strength/energy') + 내다 ('to put out/summon'), literally 'put out your strength' — the everyday way to tell someone to keep going, stay strong, or cheer up when they're tired, stressed, or facing something hard. It is encouragement aimed at the FUTURE effort, not sympathy for what already happened, so you say it before an exam, during a rough patch, or to someone job-hunting. Register climbs cleanly: 힘내 (friend) → 힘내요 (peer) → 힘내세요 (elder/coworker/customer). The crucial contrast is with 힘들어 ('it's hard / I'm struggling', from the adjective 힘들다) — beginners constantly mix up 힘내 ('summon strength', a command to the other person) and 힘들어 ('it's tough', describing a state); they share 힘 but mean opposite things. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 힘내 at a FUNERAL or for a death — there 힘내세요 can sound tone-deaf, almost like 'snap out of it', because the person isn't facing a challenge to push through, they're grieving; for loss you use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요 instead. Also avoid the over-literal 'fighting!' substitution: 화이팅 is upbeat pep (sports, go-get-em), while 힘내 carries real warmth for someone hurting.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내세요 to someone who is grieving a death.
For a challenge ahead, 힘내 fits; for a death it can sound like 'cheer up', which is jarring. At a funeral say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요.
Confusing 힘내 with 힘들어.
힘내 = 'summon your strength' (encouragement to them); 힘들어 = 'it's hard / I'm struggling' (a state). Don't tell a tired friend 힘들어 when you mean 힘내.
Treating 화이팅 and 힘내 as identical.
화이팅 is energetic pep ('go go go!'); 힘내 carries gentle, caring support for someone who's down. To comfort a struggling friend, 힘내 lands warmer than 화이팅.

entries.nuance: 괜찮아질 거예요 is 괜찮다 ('to be okay') turned into the BECOMING form 괜찮아지다 ('to get/become okay') plus -ㄹ 거예요 (future, 'will'), so it literally promises 'it will become okay' — a gentle, forward-looking reassurance for someone anxious about an illness, a breakup, a work crisis, anything that time can heal. 괜찮다 has no 하/해 in it. The future is 괜찮을 거예요; the 'get better' form is 괜찮아질 거예요. Never insert 하.

examples.romanization: geokjeonghaji ma.
examples.en: Don't worry.

entries.nuance: 걱정하지 마 is 걱정하다 ('to worry') + -지 마 (the negative command 'don't'), so 'don't worry' — said to calm someone who's anxious, stressed, or fretting over a problem. The honorific path is 걱정하지 마 (friend) → 걱정하지 마요 (peer) → 걱정하지 마세요 (elder/boss/customer), and the deferential -지 마세요 is what you'll use most with anyone older or senior. A small but important softener is 너무 ('too much'): a bare 걱정하지 마세요 can sound like an order, whereas 너무 걱정하지 마세요 ('don't worry TOO much') feels kinder and more realistic. The contrast learners need is 걱정하지 마 ('don't worry', to the other person) vs. 걱정돼 ('I'm worried', describing your own feeling, from 걱정되다) — same root 걱정, opposite direction. The English-speaker pitfall is forming the negative command wrong: '-하지 않아' (걱정하지 않아 = 'I don't worry', a statement) is NOT a command; the imperative 'don't' is -지 마(요/세요). Another trap is over-using a flat 걱정 마! at an elder — drop the 하 only in very casual speech (걱정 마 is fine to a friend), but keep the full 걱정하지 마세요 for respect.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

걱정하지 마 tells the other person not to worry; 걱정돼 means 'I'm worried (about you/it)'. Don't say 걱정돼 when you mean to reassure them.
Using a curt 걱정 마! with an elder.
걱정 마 (dropping 하) is friendly-casual, fine for friends but too blunt for an elder or boss. Say 너무 걱정하지 마세요 to stay respectful and gentle.

entries.shortExplanation: 무슨 일 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is something wrong?".
entries.explanation: "Is something wrong?" — that is 무슨 일 있어요? (museun il isseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 무슨 일 있어요? ("Is something wrong? / What happened?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.en: Is something wrong?

examples.en: You look down. Is something wrong?
examples.note: 표정이 안 좋다 ('your expression is bad') invites them to open up

entries.nuance: 무슨 일 있어요? is 무슨 ('what kind of') + 일 ('matter/thing/event') + 있어요 ('is there'), literally 'is there some matter?' — the natural opener when you notice someone looks troubled and you want to gently ask what's going on. 일 here is the broad word for 'a happening/issue', not 'work', though it CAN mean work in other contexts — context disambiguates. Register: 있어? (friend) → 있어요? (neutral) → 있으세요? (honorific, where 있다 politely becomes 있으세요). The softener 혹시 ('perhaps, by any chance') is golden for this phrase: 혹시 무슨 일 있어요? feels caring rather than nosy. The contrast to know is 무슨 일이에요? ('what is it? / what's the matter?', asking the nature of a known issue) vs. 무슨 일 있어요? ('is something wrong?', checking whether there IS an issue) — close but the first assumes something's up, the second probes. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners say 무슨 일을 있어요 (object 을) — but 있다 ('to exist') takes the subject marker or none, never 을; it's 무슨 일(이) 있어요. Another trap is translating 'what's wrong WITH you' too literally and sounding accusatory — 무슨 일 있어요? is warm and open, so keep it that way; don't add 너 (you) to a stranger.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 무슨 일을 있어요?
있다 ('to exist') never takes the object marker 을. It's 무슨 일(이) 있어요? — subject marker or nothing, because the matter EXISTS, it isn't an object you act on.
Mixing up 무슨 일 있어요? and 무슨 일이에요?
무슨 일 있어요? checks IF something's wrong; 무슨 일이에요? asks WHAT a known matter is. Use 있어요? to gently probe when you're not sure anything happened.
Asking an elder 무슨 일 있어? without honorifics.
있어? is 반말. For an elder, customer, or boss, lift it to 무슨 일 있으세요?, where 있다 becomes the honorific 있으세요.

entries.explanation: 어떡해요 (eotteokaeyo) = "Oh no, what do we do". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 어떡해요 ("Oh no / what'll you do"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.en: Oh my, that's awful.
examples.note: 어머 + 어떡해요 is the instinctive reaction to sudden bad news

entries.nuance: 어떡해요 is a contraction of 어떻게 해요 ('how do (we/you) do?'), but as a set exclamation it has bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — a reflexive, warm reaction you blurt out when someone tells you something distressing (a loss, an accident, a piece of bad luck). It signals 'I feel for you, this is awful' rather than literally asking for a plan. Register: 어떡해 (friend) → 어떡해요 (polite); to an elder you'd more likely shift to 이를 어째요 or pair it with sympathy like 많이 놀라셨겠어요. The crucial spelling/meaning split is 어떡해 vs. 어떻게: 어떻게 ('how') is the question word used WITH another verb (어떻게 해요, 어떻게 가요), while 어떡해 is the standalone exclamation/contraction and can NOT take another verb after it — writing 어떡해 가요 is wrong; it's 어떻게 가요. This is one of the most-confused pairs for learners. The English-speaker pitfall is taking 어떡해요 literally as 'how should I do it?' and waiting for instructions, or answering it as a real question — in sympathy it's just 'oh no'. Another trap is overusing it for tiny inconveniences; it carries real concern, so save it for genuinely bad news, not a spilled coffee (there you'd say 아이고 or 어머).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 어떡해 when you mean 어떻게 ('how').
어떻게 is the question word and pairs with a verb (어떻게 해요). 어떡해 is the standalone exclamation ('oh no') and takes no following verb. 어떡해 가요 is wrong; say 어떻게 가요.

It carries genuine concern. For a tiny slip (spilled coffee) say 아이고 or 어머; reserve 어떡해요 for real bad news so it doesn't sound melodramatic.

structuredNuance.t: As a set exclamation 어떡해요 has bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — a reflexive, warm reaction you blurt out when someone tells you something distressing (a loss, an accident, a piece of bad luck). It signals 'I feel for you, this is awful' rather than literally asking for a plan.

The crucial spelling/meaning split is 어떡해 vs. 어떻게: 어떻게 ('how') is the question word used WITH another verb (어떻게 해요, 어떻게 가요), while 어떡해 is the standalone exclamation/contraction and can NOT take another verb after it — writing 어떡해 가요 is wrong; it's 어떻게 가요. This is one of the most-confused pairs for learners.
어떡해요 is a contraction of 어떻게 해요 ('how do (we/you) do?').
Register goes from friend to polite; to an elder you'd more likely shift to 이를 어째요 or pair it with sympathy like 많이 놀라셨겠어요.

The pitfall is taking 어떡해요 literally as 'how should I do it?' and waiting for instructions, or answering it as a real question — in sympathy it's just 'oh no'. usagePhrases.note: Honorific; to an elder, senior, or someone you respect

examples.ko: 오늘 고생했어요.
examples.romanization: oneul gosaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: You worked hard today.
examples.note: Said to a coworker at the end of a long day

examples.ko: 먼 길 오느라 고생하셨어요. 좀 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: meon gil oneura gosaenghasyeosseoyo. jom swiseyo.

examples.note: 오느라 ('in the course of coming') ties the effort to a specific act

examples.note: 겪으시느라 ('in going through it') turns it into sympathy for hardship

entries.nuance: 고생했어요 is 고생 ('hardship/toil', Sino-Korean 苦生) + 하다 in the past, literally 'you went through hardship' — a warm acknowledgment that someone put in real effort or endured something tough. It does double duty: it thanks a coworker for their work ('thanks for your effort, nice job') AND it sympathizes with someone who's had a rough time ('you've been through a lot'). Register is critical because of WHO toils: to a senior, elder, or anyone you respect you MUST honorify the verb to 고생하셨어요 (with -시-), since plain 고생했어요 to your boss sounds like you're patting them on the head. The deepest version is 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've toiled so much'). The contrast learners need is with 수고했어요 ('good work') — they overlap, but 수고하다 is the lighter 'good job / thanks for the work', often said downward to staff (a clerk, a delivery person), while 고생하다 implies harder, more draining toil and travels better upward; crucially, saying 수고하세요 to an elder or boss can feel slightly condescending, so 고생하셨어요 is safer for respect. The English-speaker pitfall is using it with no -시- toward a superior, and the 직역 trap of hearing 'hardship' and thinking it's negative — it's actually a compliment/thank-you. Don't say 고생했어 (반말) to your manager.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고생했어요 (no -시-) to your boss or an elder.
To a superior you must honorify: 고생하셨어요. Plain 고생했어요 to someone senior sounds like praising a junior — add -시- to show respect.
Using 수고하세요 to an elder or boss.
수고하다 is lighter and often directed downward (to staff). To a senior it can feel condescending; 고생하셨어요 or 고생 많으셨어요 conveys respect for their effort better.
Reading 고생 as purely negative and avoiding the phrase.
Though 고생 means 'hardship', 고생했어요 is a warm thank-you/compliment for someone's effort. Don't shy away from it; it's exactly what Koreans say to honor hard work.

entries.explanation: "Get some good rest" — that is 푹 쉬어요 (puk swieoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 푹 쉬어요 ("Rest up well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.romanization: oneureun puk swieoyo.
examples.en: Get some good rest today.
examples.note: Said to someone exhausted after a hard day

examples.ko: 감기 빨리 나으려면 푹 쉬어요.
examples.romanization: gamgi ppalli naeuryeomyeon puk swieoyo.
examples.en: Rest up well so your cold gets better fast.
examples.note: Tie the rest to recovery with 나으려면 ('to get better')

examples.romanization: mani himdeusyeosseul tende oneureun amu saenggang malgo puk swiseyo.
examples.en: It must have been so hard — today, don't think about anything, just rest well.
examples.note: 아무 생각 말고 ('without thinking of anything') deepens the care

entries.nuance: 푹 쉬어요 is the mimetic adverb 푹 ('deeply, soundly, thoroughly') + 쉬다 ('to rest'), so 'rest deeply/well' — a caring sign-off for someone who's worn out, stressed, sick, or grieving and just needs to recover. 푹 is the key flavor word: it's the same 푹 in 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly'), and it transforms a plain 'rest' into 'really rest, recharge fully'. Register: 푹 쉬어 (friend) → 푹 쉬어요 (peer) → 푹 쉬세요 (elder/boss). The natural cousin is 몸조리 잘하세요 ('take care of your body / recover well'), which is specifically for the SICK or postpartum/recovering, while 푹 쉬세요 is general fatigue or stress — pick 몸조리 when illness is the issue. The contrast to flag is 쉬다 ('to rest') vs. 쉬다 meaning other things in fixed phrases, but mainly learners confuse 푹 with 폭 — it's 푹 (soft 'u'), not 폭. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'take a rest' as 휴식을 취하세요, which is stiff, formal-written Korean (like a memo); spoken comfort is simply 푹 쉬세요. Another trap is forgetting that this works beautifully as a comforting closing after sympathy — after 고생하셨어요 you naturally add 오늘은 푹 쉬세요. Don't say it to someone in the middle of an urgent task; it's for when they can actually stop.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 휴식을 취하세요 to comfort someone.
That's stiff, written-style Korean (like an HR memo). In warm spoken comfort, say 푹 쉬세요 — natural and caring, not bureaucratic.
Writing 폭 쉬어요 instead of 푹 쉬어요.
The adverb is 푹 ('soundly, deeply'), not 폭. 폭 means something else (width/explosion sounds). For 'rest well' it's 푹 쉬어요.
Using 푹 쉬세요 for someone who's sick when 몸조리 fits better.
푹 쉬세요 is general fatigue/stress. For illness or recovery specifically, 몸조리 잘하세요 ('recover well, take care of your body') is the precise, caring phrase.

entries.shortExplanation: 얼른 나으세요 is a practical expression meaning "Get well soon".
entries.explanation: 얼른 나으세요 (eolleun naeuseyo) = "Get well soon". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 얼른 나으세요 ("Get well soon"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.romanization: eolleun naeuseyo.
examples.en: Get well soon.
examples.note: Said to a sick coworker, friend, or shopkeeper

examples.romanization: gamgi josimhasigo eolleun naeuseyo.
examples.en: Take care of that cold and get well soon.
examples.note: 조심하시고 ('take care, and') softens it into caring advice

examples.ko: 입원하셨다는 소식 들었어요. 쾌차하시길 바랍니다. 푹 쉬세요.
examples.romanization: ibwonhasyeotdaneun sosik deureosseoyo. kwaechahasigil baramnida. puk swiseyo.
examples.en: I heard you were hospitalized. Wishing you a swift recovery. Please rest well.
examples.note: Formal 쾌차하시길 바랍니다 fits serious illness or a message

entries.nuance: 얼른 나으세요 is 얼른 ('quickly, soon') + 낫다 ('to get well/heal') in the honorific imperative 나으세요, so 'please get well soon' — the standard thing you say to anyone who's sick, from a friend with a cold to a coworker who's been hospitalized. The verb 낫다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before a vowel, so 낫다 → 나아요 / 나으세요 / 나았어요, which trips up nearly every learner. The big homophone trap is that 낫다 ('to heal') and 낮다 ('to be low') and 낳다 ('to give birth') all sound similar — 나으세요 is from 낫다 (heal); 낳으세요 would bizarrely mean 'please give birth'. Register: 빨리 나아 (friend) → 얼른/빨리 나으세요 (honorific) → 쾌차하시길 바랍니다 (formal-written, from Sino-Korean 快差 'swift recovery'), which you'd use in a card or to a senior. The contrast with 푹 쉬세요 ('rest well') is scope: 나으세요 specifically wishes RECOVERY from illness, while 푹 쉬세요 is just rest (fatigue, stress) — they pair beautifully (얼른 나으세요, 푹 쉬세요). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the ㅅ-irregular, is the 직역 'get well' as 잘 되세요 (which means 'may you succeed/prosper', not heal) or 좋아지세요 (awkward) — the idiomatic verb for healing is 낫다. Don't use 나으세요 for emotional pain or a death; it's for physical illness/injury.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating 낫다 as 낫으세요 or 낫아요.
낫다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before a vowel. Correct forms are 나으세요, 나아요, 나았어요 — not 낫으세요, 낫아요.
Saying 낳으세요 instead of 나으세요.
낳다 means 'to give birth'; 낫다 means 'to heal'. 낳으세요 tells someone to give birth! For 'get well', it's 나으세요 (from 낫다).
Translating 'get well' as 잘 되세요.
잘 되세요 means 'may things go well / may you succeed', not recover from illness. The verb for healing is 낫다: 얼른 나으세요.

entries.nuance: 너무 무리하지 마세요 is 너무 ('too much') + 무리하다 ('to overdo/strain oneself', from Sino-Korean 無理 'unreasonable, beyond one's limits') + -지 마세요 ('please don't'), so 'please don't push yourself beyond your limits' — the caring thing you say to someone overworking, pushing through sickness, or carrying too much. 무리하다 specifically means straining past what's reasonable for your body or situation, which is why it pairs so naturally with 몸 ('body') and rest. Register: 무리하지 마 (friend) → 무리하지 마요 (peer) → 무리하지 마세요 (elder/boss). The contrast learners need is with 힘내세요 ('stay strong, push harder') — they're almost OPPOSITE in spirit: 힘내세요 urges MORE effort, while 무리하지 마세요 urges LESS, telling them to ease off; using 힘내세요 on someone already overexerting can backfire, whereas 무리하지 마세요 shows you see they're depleted. The English-speaker pitfall is the noun 무리 ('a group/herd') being a homonym — don't let that confuse you; the verb 무리하다 is 'to strain'. Another trap is the 직역 'don't push yourself' as 너 자신을 밀지 마 (literally 'don't push your self'), which is nonsense in Korean — 무리하다 already carries the whole idea. Keep 너무 in front; bare 무리하지 마세요 is fine but 너무 makes it gentler and realistic.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내세요 to someone who's already overworking.
힘내세요 pushes for MORE effort; an exhausted person needs the opposite. Say 너무 무리하지 마세요 ('don't overdo it') to tell them to ease off.
Translating 'don't push yourself' as 너 자신을 밀지 마세요.
밀다 is physical 'to push (an object)'. The idea of overexerting is carried by 무리하다. Correct: 너무 무리하지 마세요.

They're homonyms. 무리 can mean 'a herd/crowd', but 무리하다 means 'to strain beyond one's limits'. Context (the verb form) makes it 'overdo it' here.

examples.note: 들으니까 ('now that I've heard') ties the ache to their news

entries.nuance: 마음이 아프다 is 마음 ('heart/mind/feelings') + 이 (subject) + 아프다 ('to hurt'), literally 'the heart hurts' — the way Korean expresses emotional pain, heartbreak, or deep sympathy when you hear something sad. Note 마음 is the EMOTIONAL heart (feelings, mind), NOT the physical organ 심장 — saying 심장이 아파요 means you have literal chest pain and need a doctor, a classic and important learner mix-up. You use 마음이 아파요 about YOUR OWN ache (at their loss, their struggle), and you turn it toward them as 마음이 아프시겠어요 ('your heart must ache', honorific -시-) to sympathize. Register: 아파 (friend) → 아파요 (peer) → 아프시겠어요 (toward an elder's feelings). The contrast to know is 속상하다 ('to be upset/distressed', a more everyday 'I'm bummed/it bothers me') vs. 마음이 아프다 ('heartbroken', heavier, for genuine sorrow) — don't use 속상해요 for a death; it's too light. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the 심장/마음 trap, is the particle: it's 마음이 아프다 (subject 이), and learners wrongly say 마음을 아파요 (object 을) — 아프다 is an adjective describing a state, so the heart is the SUBJECT that hurts, never an object. Also 가슴이 아프다 ('the chest/breast aches') is a near-synonym for heartbreak and equally natural.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 심장이 아파요 to mean 'heartbroken'.
심장 is the physical heart organ — 심장이 아파요 means literal chest pain (see a doctor!). Emotional heartbreak is 마음이 아파요 or 가슴이 아파요.
Saying 마음을 아파요 with the object marker.
아프다 is an adjective; the heart is what hurts, so it's the subject: 마음이 아파요. You can't take 마음 as an object with 을.
Using 속상해요 for a serious loss like a death.
속상하다 is everyday 'upset/bummed' — too light for grief. For real sorrow or a death, 마음이 아파요 (heartbroken) carries the proper weight.

examples.ko: 저런, 속상하시겠어요.

examples.en: Oh no, you must be so upset.
examples.note: 저런 ('oh dear') is the perfect lead-in to sympathy

examples.romanization: aesseo junbihaenneunde an dwaetdani, jeongmal soksanghagesseoyo.

examples.note: 당하셨으니 ('having suffered that') validates the hurt

entries.nuance: 속상하시겠어요 is 속상하다 ('to be upset/distressed/heartsore') + the GUESSING/empathy suffix -겠- ('must be') + honorific -시- + polite -어요, so 'you must be upset' — the workhorse phrase for putting yourself in someone's shoes when they've been let down, hurt, frustrated, or saddened by an everyday misfortune (a failed plan, a betrayal, a sick pet, a bad grade). 속상하다 breaks down as 속 ('insides/inner self') + 상하다 ('to be spoiled/damaged'), a vivid 'my insides are spoiled' = 'I'm eaten up with distress'. The magic ingredient is -겠어요, which projects the feeling onto THEM ('that must feel...'), the single most natural Korean way to empathize; learners who only say 속상해요 are saying THEY are upset, not acknowledging the other person. Register: 속상하겠다 (friend) → 속상하겠어요 (peer) → 속상하시겠어요 (honorific). The contrast is with 마음이 아프시겠어요 ('your heart must ache') — 속상하다 is everyday upset/frustration, lighter and broader, while 마음이 아프다 is deeper sorrow; for a death use the heartache one, for a ruined trip use 속상하시겠어요. The English-speaker pitfall is omitting -겠- and saying 속상해요 to comfort someone (that's about your own feeling), and the register slip of dropping -시- with an elder. Lead with 저런 or 아이고 for natural warmth.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 속상해요 to empathize with someone else.
속상해요 means 'I'M upset'. To acknowledge THEIR feeling, use the guessing -겠-: 속상하시겠어요 ('you must be upset'). That's how Korean shows empathy.
Dropping -시- with an elder: 속상하겠어요.
To an elder or someone you respect, include the honorific: 속상하시겠어요. The -시- shows you're respecting whose feelings you're imagining.
Using 속상하다 for a death or deep grief.
속상하다 is everyday distress/frustration — too light for grief. For profound sorrow or loss, 마음이 아프시겠어요 carries the right weight.

examples.romanization: mani pyeonchaneusidagoyo? eolmana himdeuseyo.
examples.en: I heard you're quite ill — how hard this must be for you.
examples.note: 편찮으시다 (honorific 'be ill') sets up sincere sympathy

entries.nuance: 얼마나 힘드세요 is 얼마나 ('how much') + 힘들다 ('to be hard/difficult/draining') + honorific -으세요, used as an EXCLAMATION of sympathy rather than a real question: 'how hard this must be for you!' — the warm, grown-up way to acknowledge that someone is going through something genuinely heavy (illness, caregiving, loss, a crisis). The 얼마나 ... -세요 frame is a Korean sympathy idiom; it isn't asking for a number, it's expressing 'I can only imagine how much you're suffering'. Register: 얼마나 힘들어 (friend) → 얼마나 힘들어요 (peer) → 얼마나 힘드세요 / 힘드셨어요 (honorific, present/past). The contrast with 힘내세요 is essential: 힘내세요 ('stay strong') pushes them forward, while 얼마나 힘드세요 first SITS with their pain and validates it — and for someone deep in hardship, leading with validation lands far better than a quick 'cheer up'; mature comfort often goes 얼마나 힘드세요 first, then 힘내세요. The English-speaker pitfall is taking it literally as a question and pausing for an answer (it's rhetorical), and mis-conjugating 힘들다 (ㄹ-irregular: 힘들 + -세요 → 힘드세요, the ㄹ drops) — learners wrongly say 힘들으세요. Also note 힘들다 (hard/tiring) vs. 힘세다 ('to be physically strong') — don't confuse them.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 얼마나 힘드세요 as a literal question.
It's a rhetorical exclamation of sympathy ('how hard this must be!'), not a request for information. Don't wait for them to quantify it — it's empathy, not an inquiry.
Saying 힘들으세요 instead of 힘드세요.
힘들다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before -세요, giving 힘드세요. 힘들으세요 is incorrect.
Jumping straight to 힘내세요 with someone deep in grief or hardship.
Validating first lands better. Lead with 얼마나 힘드세요 (acknowledging their pain), then optionally 힘내세요 — not the reverse.

entries.explanation: "It's such a shame / heartbreaking" — that is 안타깝다 (antakkapda). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 안타깝네요 ("What a shame / how unfortunate"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.en: Oh no, that's truly heartbreaking.
examples.note: 저런 + 안타깝네요 is a natural reaction to bad news

examples.romanization: geureoke yeolsimhi haenneunde tteoreojyeotdani neomu antakkawoyo.

examples.note: Name the effort (열심히 했는데) to make the regret heartfelt

examples.note: 듣는 제가 다 ('even I, hearing it') shows the news moves you

entries.nuance: 안타깝다 is an adjective meaning 'to be regrettable / pitiful / heartbreaking', the feeling you get when something sad or unfortunate happens that you wish were otherwise but often can't change — a young person's misfortune, a near-miss failure, someone's suffering, bad luck. It carries a tinge of helpless sympathy ('what a shame, I wish it weren't so'). You typically use the reactive forms 안타깝네요 / 안타까워요 / 안타깝습니다 to comment ON a situation or someone's plight. The key contrast is with 불쌍하다 ('pitiful/pathetic') — 불쌍하다 looks DOWN with pity ('poor thing', can sound condescending if said to the person's face), while 안타깝다 expresses sympathetic regret about the situation and is far safer and kinder to say about an adult's hardship; calling someone 불쌍해요 to their face can offend, but 안타까워요 about their circumstance is gracious. The other near-neighbor is 아쉽다 ('disappointing/too bad', for minor letdowns like a sold-out item) — much lighter than 안타깝다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 불쌍하다 where 안타깝다 is meant (sounding pitying), and mis-conjugating the ㅂ-irregular: 안타깝다 → 안타까워요 / 안타까운 (the ㅂ becomes 워/운), not 안타깝아요. Also it's a feeling-adjective, so you don't say 안타깝해요 with a stray 하.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 불쌍해요 to someone's face about their hardship.
불쌍하다 ('pitiful') looks down with pity and can offend an adult. To express sympathetic regret about their situation, use 안타까워요 — kinder and not condescending.
Conjugating it as 안타깝아요.
안타깝다 is a ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 워, giving 안타까워요 (and 안타까운 for the modifier). Never 안타깝아요.
Using 아쉽다 for a serious misfortune.
아쉽다 is light 'too bad / disappointing' (a sold-out dish, a rained-out picnic). For genuine, heavier misfortune, 안타깝다 carries the real weight of sympathy.

entries.explanation: 기운 내요 (giun naeyo) = "Cheer up / Lift your spirits". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 기운 내요 ("Cheer up / Perk up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.romanization: giun naeyo. masinneun geo meogeureo gayo.
examples.en: Cheer up. Let's go eat something tasty.
examples.note: Offer a concrete pick-me-up after the encouragement

examples.ko: 그렇게 축 처져 있지 말고 기운 좀 내요.
examples.romanization: geureoke chuk cheojyeo itji malgo giun jom naeyo.
examples.en: Don't be so down in the dumps — come on, cheer up a little.
examples.note: 축 처져 있다 ('drooping/dejected') names the mood

examples.note: Acknowledge first (속상하시겠지만), then lift them

entries.nuance: 기운 내요 is 기운 ('energy/spirits/vitality', from 氣運) + 내다 ('to summon/put out'), literally 'summon your spirits' — a gentle 'cheer up, perk up' for someone who looks deflated, sad, or low-energy. It's a close sibling of 힘내요 ('stay strong'), and they're often interchangeable, but there's a nuance: 힘내요 leans toward summoning STRENGTH to push through a challenge (an exam, a tough task), while 기운 내요 leans toward lifting one's MOOD/spirits when feeling down or drained — so for someone who's emotionally low rather than facing a hurdle, 기운 내요 fits a touch better. Register: 기운 내 (friend) → 기운 내요 (peer) → 기운 내세요 (honorific). The contrast learners should note is that, like 힘내요, this is for someone who needs lifting toward the future, NOT for fresh grief at a funeral — telling the bereaved 기운 내세요 can feel premature. The English-speaker pitfall is the spacing/form: it's 기운(을) 내다 ('put out energy'), two words, not a single verb; learners sometimes invent 기운하다, which doesn't exist. Another trap is confusing 기운 ('spirits/energy') with 기분 ('mood/feeling') — you 기운(을) 내다 (summon energy) but you 기분(이) 좋다/나쁘다 (feel good/bad); you can't 기분 내다 to mean cheer up (기분 내다 actually means 'to splurge / treat oneself for fun', a totally different idiom).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 기분 내요 to mean 'cheer up'.
기분 내다 actually means 'to splurge / live it up'. 'Cheer up' is 기운 내요 (summon your spirits). Don't swap 기운 (energy) and 기분 (mood).
Inventing the verb 기운하다.
There's no 기운하다. It's 기운(을) 내다 — the noun 기운 plus the verb 내다. Say 기운 내요, 기운 내세요.
Telling the recently bereaved 기운 내세요.
For fresh grief, 'cheer up' can feel premature or dismissive. Offer 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요 first; save 기운 내세요 for later, lighter lows.

entries.shortExplanation: 내가 있잖아 is a practical expression meaning "You've got me / I'm here for you".
entries.explanation: 내가 있잖아 (naega itjana) means "You've got me / I'm here for you". Say it as one set phrase — for example 내가 있잖아 ("You've got me, you know"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 반말; reassuring a close friend you're there
Polite; to a peer or someone you respect a bit

usagePhrases.en: I'll be right here beside you
usagePhrases.note: A promise to stay present (반말)
Reassurance that they have support

examples.ko: 걱정 마. 내가 있잖아.
examples.romanization: geokjeong ma. naega itjana.
examples.en: Don't worry. You've got me.
examples.note: Follow 걱정 마 with the reassurance that you're there

examples.ko: 무슨 일 있으면 언제든 말해. 내가 있잖아.
examples.romanization: museun il isseumyeon eonjedeun malhae. naega itjana.
examples.en: If anything's wrong, tell me anytime. You've got me.
examples.note: 언제든 말해 ('tell me anytime') makes the support open-ended

examples.en: Don't suffer alone when things are hard. You've got me.
examples.note: 끙끙대다 ('to agonize alone') sets up the offer of support

entries.nuance: 내가 있잖아 is 내가 ('I') + 있다 ('to be/exist') + -잖아 (the sentence ender 'you know / remember / after all'), literally 'I'm here, you know' — a tender reassurance that the person isn't alone, that you've got their back. The whole emotional payload is in -잖아: it gently reminds the listener of something they should take comfort in ('don't forget — I'm right here'), so it's warmer and more intimate than a plain 내가 있어 ('I'm here'). Register: 내가 있잖아 (반말, to a close friend) → 제가 있잖아요 (polite, where 내가 humbly becomes 제가 and you add 요). This is genuinely close, affectionate language, so you'd use it with friends, family, or a partner — NOT typically with a boss or stranger, where it would be oddly intimate. The contrast to know is with the bare 내가 있어 ('I exist / I'm here') — without -잖아 it's flatter and can even sound like answering a roll call; the -잖아 is what makes it comfort. The English-speaker pitfall is the I-particle: humble/polite speech uses 제가, not 내가, so to anyone you respect it's 제가 있잖아요 (saying 내가 있잖아요 mixes 반말 pronoun with 요 awkwardly). Another trap is misreading -잖아 as argumentative ('but I'm here!') — in this caring context it's soft and warm, carried by gentle intonation, not a retort.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 내가 있잖아요 to someone you respect.
내가 is the casual 'I'; polite speech uses the humble 제가. To a peer or senior it's 제가 있잖아요 — don't mix casual 내가 with the polite 요.
Dropping -잖아 and saying just 내가 있어.
Bare 내가 있어 ('I'm here') is flat, almost like a roll-call answer. The ender -잖아 ('you know') makes it a warm, comforting reminder: 내가 있잖아.
Using 내가 있잖아 with a boss or stranger.
This is intimate, affectionate reassurance for friends/family/partners. To a boss or stranger it sounds oddly close. For them, keep comfort more formal (예: 제가 도와드릴게요).

structuredNuance.t: 내가 있잖아 literally means 'I'm here, you know' — a tender reassurance that the person isn't alone, that you've got their back. The whole emotional payload is in -잖아: it gently reminds the listener of something they should take comfort in ('don't forget — I'm right here'). This is genuinely close, affectionate language, so you'd use it with friends, family, or a partner — NOT typically with a boss or stranger, where it would be oddly intimate.
The contrast to know is with the bare 내가 있어 ('I exist / I'm here') — without -잖아 it's flatter and can even sound like answering a roll call; the -잖아 is what makes it comfort.
It is 내가 ('I') + 있다 ('to be/exist') + -잖아 (the sentence ender 'you know / remember / after all').
Register goes from 내가 있잖아 (반말, to a close friend) to 제가 있잖아요 (polite, where 내가 humbly becomes 제가 and you add 요).

The pitfall is the I-particle: humble/polite speech uses 제가, not 내가, so to anyone you respect it's 제가 있잖아요 (saying 내가 있잖아요 mixes 반말 pronoun with 요 awkwardly). Another trap is misreading -잖아 as argumentative ('but I'm here!') — in this caring context it's soft and warm, carried by gentle intonation, not a retort.

entries.explanation: "I don't know if this is any comfort, but..." — that is 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 (wiroga doelji moreugetjiman). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 ("I don't know if this helps, but...").
