entries.nuance: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 is 위로 ('comfort/consolation', Sino-Korean 慰勞) + 가 (subject) + 되다 ('to become') + -ㄹ지 모르겠다 ('I'm not sure whether') + -지만 ('but'), literally 'I don't know whether this will become comfort, but...' — a humble, gracious preface you put BEFORE offering words of comfort to someone in real pain. It signals modesty: 'I know words may not fix this, but let me try.' This is more advanced, adult register, exactly what you'd say to a grieving coworker, a friend who lost a job, or anyone facing something heavy — it shows emotional tact. The verb 위로하다 ('to console') and noun 위로 ('comfort') are the core vocabulary of this whole situation; 위로가 되다 means 'to BE a comfort / to be comforting'. The contrast to note is with bluntly dispensing advice or a cheery 힘내세요 — leading with 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 cushions whatever follows and respects that the person is hurting, whereas charging in with advice can feel insensitive. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'comfort' as a verb on the listener — e.g. 당신을 위로하고 싶어요 ('I want to console YOU') is grammatical but sounds clinical and a bit presumptuous; the natural move is the humble 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 + your actual comforting words. Another trap is the structure -ㄹ지 모르겠다: learners drop the 지 or say 될지 몰라서; the set polite form is 될지 모르겠지만.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 당신을 위로하고 싶어요 to a grieving person.
It's grammatical but sounds clinical and presumptuous ('I want to console you'). The natural, humble move is 위로가 될지 모르겠지만... followed by your actual words of comfort.
Mangling the structure as 될지 몰라서 or 되는지 모르겠지만.
The set polite preface is 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 (-ㄹ지 모르겠지만 = 'I'm not sure whether..., but'). Keep the 지 and the 지만.
Leading with 힘내세요 or advice at deep grief.
Charging in can feel insensitive. Cushion it: open with 위로가 될지 모르겠지만 (or 뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지) to show tact before saying anything else.

entries.english: My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)
entries.shortExplanation: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is a practical expression meaning "My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)".
entries.explanation: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida) = "My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 ("My deepest condolences"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.ko: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.

examples.en: My deepest condolences.

examples.ko: 부친상 소식 들었습니다. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
examples.romanization: buchinsang sosik deureotseumnida. samga goinui myeongbogeul bimnida.
examples.en: I heard the news of your father's passing. My deepest condolences.
examples.note: 부친상 ('father's funeral') names the loss before the condolence

examples.ko: 갑작스러운 비보에 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.

examples.en: At such sudden, sorrowful news I'm at a loss for words. My deepest condolences.
examples.note: 비보 ('tragic news') + 말씀이 없다 sets a solemn, respectful tone

entries.nuance: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is the fixed, formal condolence formula: 삼가 ('respectfully, humbly') + 고인 ('the deceased', 故人) + 의 (possessive) + 명복 ('the bliss of the afterlife', 冥福) + 을 + 빕니다 ('I pray', from 빌다), literally 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's peace in the afterlife' — Korea's standard equivalent of 'my deepest condolences / rest in peace'. This is THE thing to say or write at a funeral (장례식), in a condolence text, or on a wreath ribbon. It is high, formal register by nature (it's a ritual phrase), so you keep -ㅂ니다 and do NOT casualize it. Crucially, you say this ABOUT the deceased and to/around the bereaved; the huge English-speaker pitfall is saying comfort meant for the LIVING here — e.g. 힘내세요 ('stay strong') or 괜찮아질 거예요 ('it'll be okay') can sound jarringly light at a wake, so 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (and to the family, 얼마나 상심이 크세요 'how great your grief must be', or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 'I'm lost for words') is the correct tone. Another pitfall: the phrase honors the deceased, so don't misapply it to someone merely sick or struggling — it's specifically for death. Also note the origin of 명복 is Buddhist, but the phrase is used universally regardless of religion (for a devout Christian family some prefer 삼가 조의를 표합니다 'I offer condolences', which is religion-neutral). Pronounce/parse it as one unit; don't drop 삼가.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 힘내세요 or 괜찮아질 거예요 at a funeral.
Those are for the living facing a challenge and sound too light at a wake. The proper condolence is 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다; to the family, 얼마나 상심이 크세요 or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
Using it for someone who is merely sick or struggling.
고인 means 'the deceased' and 명복 is afterlife peace — this phrase is ONLY for a death. For someone ill, say 얼른 쾌차하세요 / 몸조리 잘하세요 instead.
Casualizing it (e.g. 고인의 명복을 빌어 / 빌어요).
It's a formal ritual phrase; keep the formal 빕니다. Dropping to 반말 or even 빌어요 sounds wrong at a solemn occasion. Say the full 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 영수증 여기 있어요 is a practical expression meaning "Here's the receipt".
entries.explanation: 영수증 여기 있어요 (yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo) means "Here's the receipt". Say it as one set phrase — for example 영수증 여기 있어요 ("Here's the receipt"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; handing over your receipt at the counter
반말, to a friend helping you return something
Formal 합쇼체, stiffer or to a manager
Saying you have it before you hand it over

examples.romanization: yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: Here's the receipt.
examples.note: Said as you place the receipt on the counter

examples.ko: 환불하려고요. 영수증 여기 있어요.
examples.romanization: hwanbulharyeogoyo. yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: I'd like a refund. Here's the receipt.
examples.note: State your purpose first, then offer the proof

examples.romanization: eoje san geonde, yeongsujeung yeogi isseoyo.

examples.note: 어제 산 거 ('the thing bought yesterday') sets up the return

entries.nuance: 영수증 여기 있어요 is 영수증 ('receipt', Sino-Korean 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it is here / here it is'), the line you say while handing your receipt to staff for a return or exchange. 여기 있어요 is the natural Korean for 'here you go / here it is' when presenting an object — it literally says 'it exists here', and the offering meaning is understood from the gesture. Keep the receipt, because almost every Korean store requires 영수증 for a refund or exchange; without it you may only get store credit or be refused. The dividing line from 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you') is formality and warmth: 영수증 드릴게요 actively announces you're giving it and is a touch more deferential, while 여기 있어요 simply presents it — both are fine, 여기 있어요 is the everyday default. The English-speaker trap is translating 'here you go' word-for-word as 여기 가요 ('here I go / I'm going here'), which is nonsense in this context; the set phrase is 여기 있어요. Another pitfall is confusing 영수증 (receipt, proof of payment) with 계산서 (the bill/itemized statement) — for a return you need the 영수증.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기 가요 for 'here you go'.
여기 가요 means 'I'm going here / here I go', not 'here it is'. To present an object, say 여기 있어요 — the existence verb 있다, not the motion verb 가다.
Confusing 영수증 with 계산서.
영수증 is the receipt (proof you paid); 계산서 is the bill/itemized statement before paying. For a refund or exchange the staff want the 영수증.
Attempting a return with no receipt and expecting a full refund.
Most Korean stores require 영수증 for a cash refund; without it you may get only 교환 (exchange) or store credit. Keep and present it: 영수증 여기 있어요.

entries.nuance: 환불해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me', from 해 주다, the favor verb). The 해 주다 is what turns it into a courteous request for the staff's help rather than a flat command; without it (환불하세요) you'd be ordering them to refund, which sounds bossy. This is the line you use AFTER confirming a refund is possible with 환불돼요?. Note 환불 is a 하다-noun, so it needs the verb 하다: the joined form is 환불해 주세요, and you cannot say 환불 주세요 ('please give a refund') because you can't directly 'give' a refund the way you give an object. To sound extra polite — useful when staff are reluctant — soften to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요. The English-speaker error is the missing favor verb (환불하세요, too blunt) or the ungrammatical 환불 주세요. Another pitfall is register mismatch: 환불 부탁드립니다 in a casual market stall can sound oddly formal, while bare 환불 in a department store sounds rude — default to 환불해 주세요 and adjust. Also, mention your payment method (카드로 / 현금으로), since card purchases are refunded to the card by law, not in cash.

Saying 환불하세요 to the staff.
Bare 환불하세요 is an imperative ('you, refund!') and sounds commanding. The polite favor form is 환불해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Saying 환불 주세요 without 하다.
환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given' directly. It needs 하다 + the favor 주다: 환불해 주세요, not 환불 주세요.
Demanding cash back for a card purchase.
By card you're refunded to the same card, not in cash (카드 결제는 카드로 환불). Say 카드로 결제했어요, 환불해 주세요, and expect the card to be credited.

entries.nuance: 교환하고 싶어요 is 교환 ('exchange', Sino-Korean 交換) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'), 'I want to exchange (this)'. Unlike ordering food — where 'I want to' (먹고 싶어요) sounds too desire-focused — for returns and exchanges 교환하고 싶어요 is perfectly natural and polite, because you're stating your purpose to staff who'll then guide you. The dividing line from 교환돼요? is that 교환돼요? checks IF an exchange is possible, while 교환하고 싶어요 declares that you WANT one; many people open with 교환하고 싶은데요… (with the soft -ㄴ데요 ender) to invite the staff to respond. Crucially, distinguish 교환 (swap for another item, same or different) from 환불 (money back) and 반품 (sending the goods back) — 교환 means you walk out with a replacement, not a refund. The English-speaker error is confusing 교환 with 변경 ('change/alter', used for reservations, plans, settings) — you 교환 a product but 변경 a booking. Another pitfall: when you want a specific replacement, mark it with -로/-으로 ('into/for'): 큰 사이즈로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환 — forgetting the -로 makes the target unclear.

To name what you're swapping for, use -로: 큰 걸로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. Without it (큰 거 교환) the target item is unclear.

교환 gets you a different item, not cash. If you want your money, say 환불해 주세요, not 교환하고 싶어요.

entries.nuance: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is 다른 ('different/other') + 걸로 (걸 = 거 'thing' + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please change it for me'). 바꾸다 is the native verb 'to change/swap', warmer and more everyday than the Sino-Korean 교환하다 — both work, but 바꿔 주세요 is what people most naturally say at a counter. The -로 on 다른 걸로 is essential: it marks the target you're swapping INTO ('for a different one'); drop it and 다른 거 바꿔 주세요 sounds incomplete. The dividing line from 환불해 주세요 is outcome: 바꿔 주세요 gets you a replacement item, 환불해 주세요 gets you your money — don't say 바꿔 주세요 if you actually want a refund. The English-speaker error is treating 바꾸다 like English 'change' and using it for money/reservations incorrectly, or saying 다른 거 주세요 ('give me a different one') without the exchange framing — that sounds like you're starting a fresh purchase, not swapping the one you have. Another pitfall: specify what's wrong or what you want (다른 색으로, 큰 사이즈로, 새 걸로) so staff know whether it's a defect swap or a preference swap.

That sounds like asking for a different item as a new request, not swapping the one you hold. For an exchange, use 바꿔 주세요: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.

바꾸다 swaps one item for another; it doesn't return money. If you want a refund, say 환불해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 이거 불량인데요 is 이거 ('this') + 불량 ('defect/defective', Sino-Korean 不良) + 인데요 (the copula 이다 + the soft ender -ㄴ데요). 불량 means the product is faulty from the maker — a manufacturing defect — and 불량품 is the noun 'a defective item'. The -ㄴ데요 ender is the politeness engine: it raises the problem as 'here's the situation…' and invites the staff to respond, so it's far gentler than a flat 이거 불량이에요, which can sound like an accusation. The dividing line from 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) is nuance: 불량 implies it doesn't work right / is faulty in function, while 하자 is a flaw or blemish (a scratch, a crack, a defect in condition); for electronics that won't turn on, 불량 fits; for a visible blemish, 하자 있어요 is more precise. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'broken' and saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new faulty item — 고장 means it broke down (often from use/over time), whereas a product that was faulty out of the box is 불량. Another pitfall: 불량 is also slang for a 'delinquent' person (불량 학생), so context matters, but with a product it clearly means defective.

The bare statement can sound accusatory. The soft ender raises it gently: 이거 불량인데요? lets staff respond without feeling blamed.
Confusing 불량 (faulty function) with 하자 (blemish/flaw).
불량 = doesn't work right; 하자 = a flaw like a scratch or crack. For a non-working item say 불량, for a visible blemish say 하자 있어요.

entries.nuance: 여기 하자 있어요 is 여기 ('here') + 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) + 있어요 ('there is'). 하자 is the precise word for a defect in condition — a scratch, crack, tear, stain, or other blemish — as opposed to 불량, which leans toward a functional fault (it doesn't work). Pointing with 여기 ('here') as you say it makes the complaint concrete and helps staff see exactly what you mean. For an everyday surface mark, the native 흠집 ('scratch/nick') is even more specific: 여기 흠집 났어요. The dividing line: 하자 있어요 is calm and somewhat formal (it's the word used in warranties and refund policies), 흠집 났어요 is plainer and very visual, while 불량이에요 says the thing is faulty in function. The English-speaker error is using the verb 'have' literally and saying 이거 하자를 가지고 있어요 ('this possesses a flaw') — Korean expresses 'there's a flaw' with the existence verb 있다, not 가지다; say 하자 있어요. Another pitfall is the particle: it's 하자 있어요 (or 하자가 있어요), never 하자를 있어요 — 있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Pair it with a reason word (터지다 'burst', 깨지다 'cracked', 찢어지다 'torn') to be unambiguous.

있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Say 하자 있어요 or 하자가 있어요, never 하자를 있어요.
Using 하자 for something that simply doesn't work.
하자 is a blemish/flaw in condition. If the item won't function at all, that's 불량 or 고장 — say 작동이 안 돼요 or 불량이에요.

entries.nuance: 이거 고장 났어요 is 이거 ('this') + 고장 ('breakdown/malfunction', Sino-Korean 故障) + 났어요 (past of 나다, here 'to occur/arise'). The fixed collocation is 고장이 나다 — literally 'a breakdown occurs' — so 'it's broken' comes out as 고장 났어요, NOT 고장됐어요 or 부러졌어요. This is for machines, devices, and appliances that stop working (a phone, fridge, washing machine). The dividing line from 불량 is timing/cause: 고장 means it broke down, usually after some use, while 불량 means it was faulty from the factory; if your week-old phone dies you can say either depending on emphasis, but a never-worked item out of the box leans 불량. Don't confuse 고장 (a machine malfunctioning) with 부러지다 ('to snap', for rigid things like bones, pencils, branches) or 깨지다 ('to shatter', for glass/ceramics) — a cracked screen is 깨졌어요, a dead circuit is 고장 났어요. The English-speaker error is the wrong verb pairing: saying 고장했어요 (treating 고장 as a 하다-verb) is wrong; it pairs with 나다, so 고장 났어요. Another pitfall is using 고장 for non-mechanical 'broken' — a torn bag isn't 고장, it's 찢어졌어요; a broken zipper is 지퍼가 고장 났어요 or 지퍼가 안 돼요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요.
고장 pairs with the verb 나다: the correct form is 고장 났어요 ('a breakdown occurred'). 고장하다/고장되다 are not standard.
Using 고장 for non-machines.
고장 is for devices/machinery. A snapped pencil is 부러졌어요, shattered glass is 깨졌어요, a torn bag is 찢어졌어요 — not 고장 났어요.
Confusing 고장 (broke down) with 불량 (faulty from the start).
If it worked then failed, 고장 났어요; if it never worked out of the box, 불량이에요. Pick based on whether it ever functioned.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 ('this') + 고장 ('breakdown/malfunction', Sino-Korean 故障) + 났어요 (past of 나다, here 'to occur/arise'). This is for machines, devices, and appliances that stop working (a phone, fridge, washing machine).

The fixed collocation is 고장이 나다 — literally 'a breakdown occurs' — so 'it's broken' comes out as 고장 났어요, NOT 고장됐어요 or 부러졌어요. It pairs with 나다, so 고장 났어요 — saying 고장했어요 (treating 고장 as a 하다-verb) is wrong.

The dividing line from 불량 is timing/cause: 고장 means it broke down, usually after some use, while 불량 means it was faulty from the factory; if your week-old phone dies you can say either depending on emphasis, but a never-worked item out of the box leans 불량. Don't confuse 고장 (a machine malfunctioning) with 부러지다 ('to snap', for rigid things like bones, pencils, branches) or 깨지다 ('to shatter', for glass/ceramics) — a cracked screen is 깨졌어요, a dead circuit is 고장 났어요.
Another pitfall is using 고장 for non-mechanical 'broken' — a torn bag isn't 고장, it's 찢어졌어요; a broken zipper is 지퍼가 고장 났어요 or 지퍼가 안 돼요.

entries.nuance: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? is 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불하다 ('to refund') + -아야 되다 ('have to / must'), so 'within how many days do I have to get the refund (done)?'. The core grammar is -아/어야 되다 ('must, have to'), the everyday way to express obligation or a deadline; 안에 ('within') sets the time frame. This is a smart question to ask at the moment of buying, because Korean stores commonly allow returns only within 7 or 14 days (7일/14일 이내). Two traps for English speakers. First, 며칠 ('how many days', a question word) vs. 몇 일 — the correct spelling is 며칠, not 몇 일, even though it feels like it should be 몇 ('how many') + 일 ('day'); 몇 일 is a common native misspelling and definitely wrong for learners to imitate. Second, 안에 means 'within (a time/space)', not 'inside a thing' in the physical sense here; don't confuse it with 안 ('not'). The dividing line from 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? ('how long is the refund period?') is angle: 며칠 안에 …해야 돼요? frames it as your obligation/deadline, while 환불 기간 asks for the policy length as a fact — both get the same info. Note 안에 takes the time noun directly (일주일 안에, 14일 안에), and the obligation ending is 돼요 (from 되다), not 해요.

entries.nuance: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 is 이거 ('this') + 반품 ('returning goods', Sino-Korean 返品) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is specifically the act of SENDING THE PRODUCT BACK — the physical/logistical return — which then triggers a 환불 (refund) or sometimes 교환 (exchange). This word dominates online and app shopping, where you 반품 신청 (file a return request) and ship the item back. The three-way distinction is the heart of this set: 반품 = give the goods back; 환불 = get your money back; 교환 = swap for another item. They're related but not interchangeable — 반품하고 싶어요 says 'I want to return the item', and the refund/exchange is the consequence you sort out next. The English-speaker error is using 'return' for everything and saying 환불하고 싶어요 when you really mean the act of sending it back, or vice versa; if a courier needs to pick it up, it's 반품, and you'll discuss 택배비 (shipping fee) — who pays often depends on whether it's 단순 변심 ('simple change of mind', you pay) or 불량 ('defect', the seller pays). Another pitfall: don't confuse 반품 with 반납 ('returning something borrowed', like a library book or rental) — you 반품 a purchase but 반납 a rental. For in-store, 반품 also works, but people often just say 환불해 주세요 directly.

반품 is for goods you bought; 반납 is for things you borrowed or rented (books, equipment). Don't say 반납하고 싶어요 for a store purchase.

For 단순 변심 ('change of mind') the buyer usually pays return shipping; for 불량 ('defect') the seller does. Ask 택배비는 누가 내요? when you say 반품하고 싶어요.

entries.nuance: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? is 영수증 ('receipt') + 없이 ('without', the adverb from 없다) + -도 ('even/also') + 환불돼요? ('is a refund possible?'). The key piece is 없이도 — 없이 means 'without', and the -도 adds 'even', so the whole thing asks 'is a refund possible EVEN without the receipt?'. This is a high-value question because Korean stores usually require 영수증, but a card purchase leaves a 카드 내역 (card record) that can sometimes substitute. The dividing line from 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요? is framing: 없이도 …돼요? hopefully asks 'can it still be done?', while 없으면 …안 돼요? pessimistically asks 'is it impossible without one?' — both are polite, but 없이도 sounds more constructive. The English-speaker error is forming 'without' with a negative verb clause like 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? ('refund without bringing the receipt?'), which is clumsy; the clean adverb is 없이. Another pitfall is dropping the -도 and saying 영수증 없이 환불돼요?, which is fine but loses the 'even' nuance that politely acknowledges you know the receipt is normally needed. If you paid by card, add 카드로 샀어요 — it strengthens your case.

entries.nuance: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 is 그냥 ('just/simply') + 환불받다 ('to receive a refund', 환불 + 받다) + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). The 그냥 is doing important social work: it gently signals 'just / never mind the alternatives', which is how you decline a pushy exchange offer without sounding harsh — Korean staff often steer you toward 교환 (exchange) or store credit, and 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 politely insists on money back. Note 환불받다 (receive a refund) is from the customer's side, while 환불하다/환불해 주다 is from the staff's side (issue a refund); as the customer wanting your money, both 환불받고 싶어요 and 환불해 주세요 work, but 받다 emphasizes that YOU get it back. The dividing line from a bare 환불해 주세요 is the softener: adding 그냥 frames it as 'I'd simply prefer…', which de-escalates. The English-speaker error is omitting 그냥 and repeating a flat 환불해 주세요 when pushed, which can feel confrontational; 그냥 keeps it gentle but firm. Another pitfall is mixing up the giver/receiver verbs — saying 환불해 주고 싶어요 ('I want to give a refund') reverses the roles. To be unambiguous against an exchange, you can stack 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 ('not an exchange, just a refund').

환불해 주다 is to GIVE a refund (the staff's action). As the customer receiving money, say 환불받고 싶어요.

Without 그냥, repeating 환불해 주세요 can sound blunt under pressure. 그냥 softens it to 'I'd simply prefer a refund' while staying firm.

entries.nuance: 안 쓴 거예요 is 안 ('not') + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'to use') + 거예요 ('it is the thing that…'), literally 'it's a not-used thing' → 'it's unused'. The 쓰다 here means 'to use' (쓰다 also means 'to write' and 'to wear (glasses/hat)' and 'to be bitter' — context disambiguates). This phrase matters because Korean return policies hinge on condition: 미개봉 (unopened), 미사용 (unused), 택 그대로 (tag intact) all strengthen your claim. The dividing line: 안 쓴 거예요 ('unused') is the everyday spoken version of the formal 미사용 (未使用) printed on policies; 포장 안 뜯었어요 ('didn't open the packaging') and 택 안 뗐어요 ('didn't remove the tag') are even more concrete and persuasive. The English-speaker error is the perfect-tense translation trap: saying 안 사용했어요 is fine ('I didn't use it'), but to describe the ITEM as unused, natives often use the adnominal 안 쓴 거예요. Another pitfall is confusing 쓰다 'use' with 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 would mean 'it's something I didn't buy', the opposite of helpful. Also, 쓰다 is irregular only in some forms; the past adnominal is simply 쓴, so 안 쓴 거예요 — not 안 쓰은 거예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 쓰은 거예요.
The past adnominal of 쓰다 is 쓴, not 쓰은. Say 안 쓴 거예요.
Confusing 쓰다 'use' with 사다 'buy'.
안 쓴 거 = unused; 안 산 거 = not bought. To say the item is unused, it's 안 쓴 거예요, not 안 산 거예요.
Thinking 'unused' alone guarantees a return.
Stores also check 택 (tag), 포장 (packaging), and time limits. Reinforce with 택도 안 뗐어요 / 포장도 안 뜯었어요 alongside 안 쓴 거예요.

entries.nuance: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 산 (past adnominal of 사다 'to buy') + 지 (the bound noun marking elapsed time SINCE an action) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much has become' → 'not long has passed'). The construction -ㄴ 지 …되다 is the standard way to say 'it's been [time] since I did X': 산 지 일주일 됐어요 ('it's been a week since I bought it'). Here 얼마 안 됐어요 means 'not long has passed', i.e. 'I bought it recently' — a key thing to establish because refund/exchange eligibility depends on how recent the purchase is. The English-speaker error is a spacing/grammar trap: this 지 (elapsed time) is written with a SPACE (산 지), unlike the connective -는지 ('whether'); confusing them changes the meaning. Another classic error is using the wrong tense — it must be the past adnominal 산 (not 사는 지), because the buying already happened. Also don't say 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 — the verb is 되다 ('to become', for time passing), not 하다, so it's 안 됐어요. The dividing line from 어제 샀어요 ('I bought it yesterday') is precision: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is a vaguer 'recently', while naming the day (어제 산 거예요) is more concrete and convincing.

entries.nuance: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 is 받다 ('to receive/get') + -았을 때 ('at the time when [past]') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 (contraction of 이러했어요, 'was like this'). So it means 'it was already like this from the moment I received it' — the line you use when staff suspect YOU caused the damage and you need to insist it arrived faulty. 이랬어요 is the spoken past of 이렇다 ('to be like this'); pointing at the defect as you say it makes it land. This matters in disputes over 불량 (defect) and 하자 (flaw): proving the fault is pre-existing (not 사용자 과실, 'user's fault') is what secures a free exchange or refund. The dividing line from 처음부터 이랬어요 ('it was like this from the start') is nuance: 받았을 때부터 pins it to the exact moment of receipt (strong for online orders/deliveries), while 처음부터 is a looser 'from the beginning'. The English-speaker error is tense and structure: saying 받을 때 이래요 (present) misses that both the receiving and the state are past — you need 받았을 때 (past 'when') + 이랬어요 (past state). Another pitfall is over-literal blame-shifting like 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault'), which is fine but more confrontational; 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 makes the same point by stating facts. Offering 사진 (photos) of the unboxing greatly strengthens it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 받을 때 이래요 (present tense).
Both the receiving and the condition are in the past: 받았을 때 ('when I received it') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). Present tense misses that it was already faulty.
Trying to say 이랬어요 as 이렇었어요.
이렇다 contracts in the past to 이랬어요 (from 이러했어요), not 이렇었어요. Use 이랬어요.
Leading with 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault').
That's confrontational. Stating the fact — 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 — makes the same point more calmly and is harder to argue with, especially with 사진 (photos).

entries.nuance: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 처리 ('processing/handling', Sino-Korean 處理) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Adding 처리 ('process/handle') makes it about completing the administrative action — running the card cancellation, logging the return — which is the natural register at a service desk where the refund is a procedure, not a casual handover. The 좀 cushions the request. The dividing line from a plain 환불해 주세요 is stage: 환불해 주세요 is the general 'please refund me' (good at any point), while 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요 specifically asks them to EXECUTE the refund now — you use it once the reason is accepted and you just need them to push it through. 처리 is a versatile word for handling tasks (교환 처리, 취소 처리, A/S 처리), so this pattern transfers. The English-speaker error is treating 처리 as optional decoration and either over-formalizing in a tiny shop (where bare 환불해 주세요 is warmer) or, conversely, sounding too casual at a corporate counter (where 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 fits). Another pitfall is the particle: it's 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요 — 처리 is the object of 하다 — not 환불 처리가 해 주세요. Mention the method (카드 취소 / 현금) so they process it correctly.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불 처리가 해 주세요.
처리 is the object of 하다, so it takes 를 (often dropped), not 가: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요.
Over-formalizing in a tiny shop.
At a small market stall, 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 can sound stiff. A warm 환불해 주세요 fits better; save 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 for service desks and counters.
Not stating the refund method.
Refunds go back by the original method (카드 결제 → 카드 취소). Say 카드 취소로 / 현금으로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 so it's done correctly.

entries.nuance: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불이 안 되다 ('a refund isn't possible') + -다고요? (a quotative ending that echoes back what was just said, with rising intonation). The -다고요? is the heart of it: it repeats the other person's statement to confirm or gently challenge it — 'you're saying…?' — and is the polite, non-aggressive way to push back when a store refuses a refund. It buys you a beat and often makes staff re-explain or soften. The dividing line from a blunt 왜 안 돼요? ('why not?') is tone: 안 된다고요? mirrors their words and sounds like incredulous confirmation rather than a demand, which keeps the exchange civil while signaling you're not satisfied. To go fully polite, use 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? ('do you mean…?', with honorific 말씀). The English-speaker error is the intonation/structure trap: dropping the quotative and saying 환불 안 돼요? again just re-asks the yes/no question, losing the 'wait, you're telling me…' force; the -다고요? is what conveys pushback. Another pitfall is using -다고 without the final 요 to staff (이거 환불 안 된다고?), which slips into 반말 and can sound rude. Keep the 요. Note the particle 이 in 환불이 안 돼요 (subject), not 환불을.

entries.nuance: 잘했어요 is the everyday 'well done' you say AFTER someone has finished or achieved something — it judges a completed action, built from 잘 'well' + 했다, the past of 하다 'to do'. Crucially it flows DOWNWARD or sideways: a senior to a junior, a parent to a child, friends to each other. The decisive line is against 잘하시네요, which praises ongoing SKILL ('you're good at this') in the present, while 잘했어요 praises a finished result. The English-speaker pitfall is firing 잘했어요 UP at a boss or teacher: praising a superior's performance sounds presumptuous, like you are grading them. To an elder you respect, fold in 시 as 잘하셨어요, but even then heap-praising a senior's work is best softened into thanks (수고하셨어요) rather than evaluation. Register-shift is simply 잘했어 (banmal) ↔ 잘했어요 (polite) ↔ 잘하셨어요 (honorific).

entries.nuance: 잘하시네요 is the present-tense 'you're good at this' you say WHILE watching or tasting someone's skill — 잘하다 'to do well' + honorific -시- + the noticing ending -네요 ('oh, I notice'). entries.nuance: 멋있어요 means 'cool / stylish / impressive' and stretches from a sharp outfit and a slick car to an admirable ACTION or character ('that was a cool thing to do'). Note the split learners miss: 멋있다/멋지다 lean toward cool, dashing, impressive (often men, or anyone's cool deed), while 예쁘다 means pretty/cute (people, objects) — they are not interchangeable. The decisive line is 멋있다 (cool, impressive) vs 예쁘다 (pretty, lovely): a tuxedo and a brave act are 멋있다, a flower and a baby are 예뻐요. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing 'cool' as filler — Korean 멋있다 is a real compliment with weight, so dropping it constantly dilutes it; and many forget the honorific 멋있으세요 when admiring an elder's character. 멋있다 and 멋지다 are near-twins; 멋지다 sounds a touch more exclamatory ('how splendid'). Register: 멋있어 (banmal) ↔ 멋있어요 (polite) ↔ 멋있으세요 (honorific).

Saying 멋있어 to an elder you respect — use the honorific 멋있으세요 when praising a senior's looks or character.
Spelling it 맛있어요 (delicious) by mistake — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste); one vowel flips 'cool' into 'tasty'.

The dividing line is against 귀엽다 'cute' and 멋있다 'cool': 예쁘다 = pretty/lovely, 귀엽다 = cutely endearing (puppies, a giggling toddler), 멋있다 = cool/impressive — calling a strong handsome man 예뻐요 can sound off, where 멋있어요 fits. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation (saying 예쁘어요) and over-aiming it at strangers: complimenting a stranger's looks can feel forward in Korean, so 예뻐요 is warmest toward friends, items, or kids. To an older woman, soften with the honorific 예쁘세요. Register: 예뻐 (banmal) ↔ 예뻐요 (polite) ↔ 예쁘세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

Conjugating it 예쁘어요 — 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular, so 으 drops before 어요: the correct form is 예뻐요.
Calling a cool, manly guy 예뻐요 — it implies pretty/feminine; use 멋있어요 for cool or handsome men.

entries.nuance: 대단하세요 expresses genuine AWE at someone's achievement, effort, or ability — 대단하다 'to be remarkable/great' + honorific -세요. It is heartfelt admiration for something hard ('I couldn't do that'), so it naturally points UP at people you respect, which is why the -세요 honorific form is the default. The dividing line is against 잘하시네요: 잘하시네요 praises a SKILL ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses being IMPRESSED by the whole accomplishment or person ('that's incredible'). The English-speaker pitfall is the bare 대단해 toward an elder — fine between friends, but to a senior it sounds flippant, so you need 대단하세요 or formal 대단하십니다. A subtler trap: 대단하다 can turn sarcastic with a flat tone ('oh, great...'), so deliver it warmly. Register: 대단해 (banmal) ↔ 대단해요 (polite) ↔ 대단하세요 / 대단하십니다 (honorific/formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 대단해 to an elder or boss — the bare banmal can sound flippant; admire a senior with 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다.
Using 대단하세요 for a minor everyday compliment — it carries real awe, so reserve it for genuinely impressive feats, not 'nice shoes'.
Delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, wonderful'); say it with clear warmth so it lands as praise.

entries.nuance: 화이팅 (from English 'fighting') is Korea's all-purpose cheer of encouragement — 'go for it, you've got this, good luck' — fired before exams, interviews, games, or any effort, often with a raised fist. By itself it is casual and friendly; toward someone you respect, attach a verb as 화이팅 하세요 ('please do your best'). The dividing line is against 잘될 거예요: 화이팅 pumps up ENERGY for the effort ahead ('push!'), while 잘될 거예요 reassures about the OUTCOME ('it'll turn out fine'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: it means encouragement, NOT literal combat, so never read it as 'let's fight'; and the bare 화이팅 to a much older person or in a formal setting feels too light — use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다. Spelling note: 파이팅 is the National-Institute-correct spelling, but 화이팅 is what most people actually write. There is no honorific form of the noun itself — politeness rides on the attached verb.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight / I'll fight you' — it is borrowed to mean encouragement ('go for it'), never literal fighting.
Shouting bare 화이팅 at a senior in a formal setting — soften it to 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다.
Assuming 파이팅 is wrong — it is actually the standardized spelling; both are accepted, with 화이팅 more common in casual writing.

entries.explanation: 힘내세요 (himnaeseyo) means "Cheer up / Stay strong / Hang in there.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 힘내세요 ("stay strong / hang in there"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.note: real situation: gentle encouragement in grief, paired with empathy

entries.nuance: 힘내세요 literally 'put out strength' (힘 'strength' + 내다 'to bring out' + -세요) is the warm 'cheer up / hang in there / stay strong' you give someone who is tired, sad, or going through a hard time. It is encouragement during ONGOING hardship, which is the dividing line from 화이팅 (a pre-event pump-up) and 잘될 거예요 (reassurance about the result). The English-speaker pitfall is register and tone: bare 힘내 is banmal for friends, while a struggling senior or colleague needs 힘내세요. A deeper trap is using it in heavy grief — at a funeral, 힘내세요 can feel like pressure to 'snap out of it', so for serious loss Koreans prefer 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 얼마나 힘드세요 (acknowledging the pain) before any 힘내세요. Don't pair it with a literal 'fight' image. Register-shift: 힘내 (banmal) ↔ 힘내세요 (polite) ↔ 힘내십시오 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying bare 힘내 to an elder, boss, or grieving senior — use 힘내세요; the banmal can sound dismissive of their hardship.
Using 힘내세요 as the main thing said at a funeral — it can pressure the bereaved; lead with 얼마나 힘드세요 or 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
Confusing it with 화이팅 — 힘내세요 comforts someone already struggling, while 화이팅 cheers on an effort that hasn't started yet.

entries.nuance: 축하해요 (祝賀, 축하 'congratulation' + 해요) is the all-purpose 'congratulations' for any happy milestone — passing, a wedding, a promotion, a birthday. The key politeness move is the humble verb: to an elder, a boss, or in formal settings you swap 하다 for 드리다 → 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 ('I offer my congratulations'), which is more respectful than plain 축하해요. The dividing line is 축하해요 (neutral polite, peers) vs 축하드립니다 (humble formal, upward). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and word order: learners say 축하해요 그 일 or attach 을/를, but the natural pattern names the occasion FIRST, e.g. 합격 축하해요, 생일 축하해요 — the thing being celebrated comes before 축하해요, with no object particle needed in speech. Also avoid bare 축하해 to a senior. Register: 축하해 (banmal) ↔ 축하해요 (polite) ↔ 축하드립니다 (humble/formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

entries.explanation: "It'll work out / Things will be fine." — that is 잘될 거예요 (jaldoel geoyeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘될 거예요 ("it'll work out fine"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 잘될 거예요 ('it will go well', 잘되다 'to turn out well' + future -ㄹ 거예요) reassures someone about a FUTURE OUTCOME they are anxious about — a test result, a job, a recovery. The dividing line is clear: 잘될 거예요 calms worry about how things will TURN OUT, while 힘내세요 gives strength for the present struggle and 화이팅 pumps energy for the effort itself; the smoothest comfort stacks them ('너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요'). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb and spelling: it is 잘되다 (one word, intransitive 'turn out well'), so 잘될 거예요 — not 잘할 거예요, which means 'I/you WILL do well' (an action by a doer), a different meaning. Also the future ending is 거예요 (not 꺼에요/거에요). To an elder, raise it with -시- as 잘되실 거예요. Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) ↔ 잘될 거예요 (polite) ↔ 잘되실 거예요 (honorific).

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘할 거예요 to comfort someone — that means 'will perform well' (active doer); the reassurance about how things turn out is 잘될 거예요 (intransitive).
Spelling the ending 잘될 꺼에요 / 거에요 — the standard future form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.
Using bare 잘될 거야 to an elder — add the honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요.

examples.note: real situation: professional reassurance with a commitment

entries.nuance: 너무 걱정 마세요 ('don't worry too much', 너무 'too' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't') tells an anxious person to ease off their worry, usually paired with a reason or 잘될 거예요. 마세요 is the contracted polite prohibitive of 말다; the full form 걱정하지 마세요 is identical in meaning and a touch softer/more careful. The dividing line is against 잘될 거예요: 걱정 마세요 addresses the WORRY directly ('stop fretting'), while 잘될 거예요 addresses the OUTCOME ('it'll be fine') — they pair beautifully. The English-speaker pitfall is the negative command itself: learners build it from 안 ('안 걱정하세요' is wrong) instead of the prohibitive 말다; and they say bare 걱정 마 to an elder. Keep 너무 — without it, 걱정 마세요 alone is fine but a bit blunt; 너무 softens it to 'don't worry SO much'. Register: 걱정 마 (banmal) ↔ 걱정 마세요 (polite) ↔ 걱정 마십시오 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Forming the negative as 안 걱정하세요 — a prohibition uses 말다: 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요, never 안 + verb here.
Saying bare 걱정 마 to an elder or boss — use 걱정 마세요 or 걱정 마십시오.
Confusing 걱정 마세요 (address the worry) with 잘될 거예요 (address the outcome) — natural comfort uses both together.

entries.explanation: 자랑스러워요 (jarangseureowoyo) means "I'm proud (of you).". Say it as one set phrase — for example 자랑스러워요 ("I'm proud of you"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.ko: A: 저 1등 했어요 / B: 우와, 자랑스러워요!
examples.romanization: A: jeo 1deung haesseoyo / B: uwa, jarangseureowoyo!
examples.en: A: I came in first / B: Wow, I'm so proud!
examples.note: the bare expression of pride at someone's success

examples.ko: 졸업한 딸에게 "우리 딸, 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
examples.romanization: joreopan ttarege "uri ttal, jeongmal jarangseureowo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my graduating daughter I said, 'I'm so proud of you, my girl.'
examples.note: everyday: a parent's pride in banmal toward a child

examples.ko: 후배가 큰 상 받았을 때 "네가 우리 팀의 자랑이야. 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
examples.romanization: hubaega keun sang badasseul ttae "nega uri timui jarangiya. jeongmal jarangseureowo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: When the junior won a big award I said, 'You're our team's pride. I'm truly proud.'
examples.note: real situation: pairs with 자랑이야 'you're our pride'

entries.nuance: 자랑스러워요 ('to be proud', from 자랑 'pride/boast' + -스럽다 'to feel like') expresses pride in someone's achievement or in someone you care about. The crucial cultural rule is DIRECTION: you express pride DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a senior to a junior, friends to each other. Telling a teacher, boss, or elder 자랑스러워요 sounds odd, even presumptuous, as if you were positioned above them; toward a respected senior, Koreans instead say 존경스러워요 ('I admire/respect you') or 대단하세요. That is the dividing line: 자랑스럽다 (pride, looking down/across) vs 존경스럽다 (respect, looking up). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this — English 'I'm proud of you' is said freely to anyone, so learners aim 자랑스러워요 at their Korean teacher and it lands wrong. Note the -ㅂ irregular: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요. Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) ↔ 자랑스러워요 (polite) ↔ 자랑스럽습니다 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 자랑스러워요 to a teacher, boss, or elder — pride implies a higher position; toward a senior use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요.
Conjugating it 자랑스럽어요 — 자랑스럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스러워요.
Confusing 자랑스럽다 (proud of someone) with 자랑하다 (to boast/show off) — 자랑하지 마 means 'don't brag', a different sense of 자랑.

entries.shortExplanation: 보기 좋아요 is a practical expression meaning "That looks nice / It's good to see.".
entries.explanation: "That looks nice / It's good to see." — that is 보기 좋아요 (bogi joayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 보기 좋아요 ("it looks nice / good to see"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: it looks nice / good to see
usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
honorific -으시-, to an elder
-네요 adds a warm, noticing tone

examples.ko: A: (커플 사진을 보여주며) / B: 와, 보기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: A: (keopeul sajineul boyeojumyeo) / B: wa, bogi joayo.
examples.en: A: (showing a couple photo) / B: Aw, you look great together.
examples.note: the bare warm comment on a pleasant sight

examples.ko: 살 빠진 친구한테 "얼굴 좋아 보인다, 보기 좋아" 했어요.
examples.romanization: sal ppajin chinguhante "eolgul joa boinda, bogi joa" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my friend who lost weight I said, 'You look well — looks good.'
examples.note: everyday: complimenting someone's healthier look

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만난 두 분이 사이좋게 지내셔서 "두 분 보기 좋으세요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraenmane mannan du buni saijoke jinaesyeoseo "du bun bogi joeuseyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: Seeing the two get along well I said, 'It's lovely to see you two together.'
examples.note: real situation: honorific 보기 좋으세요 toward elders, approving warmly

entries.nuance: 보기 좋아요 (보다 'to see' + -기 nominalizer + 좋다 'good' = 'good to look at') is the warm 'that looks nice / it's nice to see' you say about a pleasing sight — a happy couple, someone looking healthy, a tidy room, people getting along. It often carries APPROVAL of a wholesome scene, not just visual prettiness, which is the dividing line from 예뻐요 (pretty appearance) and 멋있어요 (cool/impressive): 보기 좋다 = 'this is a good thing to see / heartwarming'. The English-speaker pitfall is the structure — learners try 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기, but the fixed form is 보기 좋다 (nominalized 보기 + 좋다). Also it sits next to the look-like form 좋아 보여요 ('looks good/well'), which describes condition; don't confuse 보기 좋다 ('nice to see') with 좋아 보이다 ('appears good'). To an elder, use the honorific 보기 좋으세요/좋으시네요. Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) ↔ 보기 좋아요 (polite) ↔ 보기 좋으세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다: 보기 좋아요.
Mixing it up with 좋아 보여요 — 보기 좋아요 = 'nice to see', while 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good/well' (condition); related but not identical.
Using bare 보기 좋아 toward an elder you're complimenting — use the honorific 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋으시네요.

entries.shortExplanation: 부러워요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm jealous / I envy you (in a good way).".
entries.explanation: 부러워요 (bureowoyo) = "I'm jealous / I envy you (in a good way).". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 부러워요 ("I envy you / lucky you"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 부러워요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend
격식 -습니다, polite admiration
exclamatory -다, said with feeling

examples.ko: A: 저 다음 주에 하와이 가요 / B: 와, 부러워요!
examples.romanization: A: jeo daeum jue hawai gayo / B: wa, bureowoyo!
examples.en: A: I'm going to Hawaii next week / B: Wow, I'm so jealous!
examples.note: the bare good-natured envy as a reaction to good news

examples.ko: 친구가 새 집 샀다고 해서 "우와, 진짜 부럽다" 했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga sae jip satdago haeseo "uwa, jinjja bureopda" haesseoyo.
examples.en: Since my friend bought a new house I said, 'Wow, I'm so jealous.'
examples.note: everyday: a warm compliment dressed as envy, in banmal

examples.ko: 동안인 선배한테 "피부가 너무 좋으세요. 부러워요" 했어요.
examples.romanization: donganin seonbaehante "pibuga neomu joeuseyo. bureowoyo" haesseoyo.
examples.en: To my youthful-looking senior I said, 'Your skin is so good. I'm jealous.'
examples.note: real situation: envy used as a friendly compliment about looks

entries.nuance: 부러워요 ('I'm envious', from 부럽다 'to be enviable') is, in Korean, a FRIENDLY compliment far more often than a complaint — said brightly, it means 'lucky you, I wish that were me' and warmly congratulates someone's good fortune (a trip, a new house, nice skin). The dividing line is against 질투하다 (jealousy that resents) and 샘나다 (petty envy): 부럽다 is the harmless, admiring kind, so it functions as praise, while 질투 implies real ill feeling. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation and tone: 부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular → 부러워요 (not 부럽어요); and learners worry it sounds negative like English 'jealous', but with a smile it is a beloved compliment, so don't avoid it. Saying it flatly, though, can tip into sounding genuinely resentful, so deliver it lightly. Register: 부러워 (banmal) ↔ 부러워요 (polite) ↔ 부럽습니다 (formal).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating it 부럽어요 — 부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the correct form is 부러워요.
Avoiding it because 'jealous' sounds negative — said with a smile, 부러워요 is a warm compliment ('lucky you'), not a complaint.
Using 질투해요 to mean friendly envy — 질투 is resentful jealousy; the admiring kind is 부러워요.

structuredNuance.t: 부러워요 ('I'm envious') is, in Korean, a FRIENDLY compliment far more often than a complaint — said brightly, it means 'lucky you, I wish that were me' and warmly congratulates someone's good fortune (a trip, a new house, nice skin).
The dividing line is against 질투하다 (jealousy that resents) and 샘나다 (petty envy): 부럽다 is the harmless, admiring kind, so it functions as praise, while 질투 implies real ill feeling.

부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular, giving 부러워요 (not 부럽어요). Register: 부러워 (banmal) to 부러워요 (polite) to 부럽습니다 (formal).

The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation and tone: learners worry it sounds negative like English 'jealous', but with a smile it is a beloved compliment, so don't avoid it. Saying it flatly, though, can tip into sounding genuinely resentful, so deliver it lightly.

entries.nuance: 응원할게요 (應援, 응원 'support/cheering' + -ㄹ게요 'I will (for you)') is a personal pledge — 'I'll cheer you on, I'm in your corner' — promising ongoing support for someone's effort or challenge. It is warmer and more committed than 화이팅: 화이팅 is a quick shout in the moment, while 응원할게요 promises that YOU will keep backing them. The -ㄹ게요 ending is itself a speaker's promise, so it always implies 'I, for your sake, will…'. The English-speaker pitfall is the ending: learners write 응원할께요 (wrong spelling — standard is 할게요) or use plain future 응원할 거예요 ('I will cheer', a flat prediction) instead of the promissory 할게요 that conveys personal commitment to the listener. To a senior or in formal settings, raise it to 응원하겠습니다. Register: 응원할게 (banmal) ↔ 응원할게요 (polite) ↔ 응원하겠습니다 (formal).

Treating it as identical to 화이팅 — 화이팅 is an in-the-moment shout, while 응원할게요 pledges ongoing, personal support.

entries.explanation: "It suits you / It looks good on you." — that is 잘 어울려요 (jal eoullyeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잘 어울려요 ("it suits you well"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 잘 어울려요 (잘 'well' + 어울리다 'to match/go together') is the everyday 'it suits you / it looks good on you' for clothes, glasses, a haircut, makeup, or a color — and the single most natural thing to say when someone shows off a new look. The dividing line from 예뻐요/멋있어요 is key: 예뻐요 judges the THING itself as pretty, while 잘 어울려요 says it MATCHES the person well — so it flatters the wearer, not just the item, which is why Koreans reach for it constantly. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: the particle is 와/과 or colloquial 랑/하고 for 'goes WITH' (그 색이 너랑 잘 어울려, not 너를), and 어울리다 is intransitive, so you never say 어울려요 + object; second, learners drop 잘 and say bare 어울려요, but the warm compliment almost always keeps 잘 ('suits you WELL') — bare 어울리다 alone sounds like a neutral 'matches'. For two people who look good together you can also say 두 사람 잘 어울려요 ('you two make a good couple'). Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) ↔ 잘 어울려요 (polite) ↔ 잘 어울리세요 (honorific).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing 'goes with' you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요.
Dropping 잘 and saying bare 어울려요 — the compliment keeps 잘 ('suits you well'); without it, it sounds like a flat 'it matches'.
Saying 예뻐요 when you mean it flatters the person — 예뻐요 praises the item itself, while 잘 어울려요 says it suits the wearer.
Using bare 잘 어울려 to an elder — raise it to the honorific 잘 어울리세요 when complimenting a senior's outfit or hair.

examples.en: Do you have a boyfriend?

entries.nuance: 남자친구 있어요? is 남자친구 ('boyfriend') + 있다 ('to exist/have'), the everyday way to find out whether someone is romantically taken. Notice Korean uses 있다 ('exist'), NOT 가지다 ('possess') — you never say 남자친구를 가지고 있어요?, which sounds like you own a person; relationships, family and possessions you 'have' all take 있다. The clipped forms 남친/여친 are very common in casual speech and texting, but in a first polite conversation use the full 남자친구/여자친구. A gentler near-synonym is 만나는 사람 있어요? ('are you seeing someone?'), which avoids the committed label and feels less blunt when you barely know the person, or when you're hinting at your own interest. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: many add 를 (남자친구를 있어요?), but 있다 takes the subject particle 이/가 or none at all in speech — never the object 을/를. Also, asking a near-stranger this with no 혹시 or reason can feel intrusive, so soften it. To an older person, raise it to 있으세요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 남자친구를 있어요? with the object particle.
있다 ('to have/exist') is not a transitive verb; it takes 이/가 or nothing, not 을/를. Say 남자친구 있어요? (or 남자친구가 있어요?).
Translating 'have a boyfriend' as 남자친구를 가지고 있어요?
가지다 ('to possess') is for objects; using it for a person sounds like ownership. Korean 'has' people and relationships with 있다: 남자친구 있어요?
Confusing 남자친구 with 남자 사람 친구.
남자친구 by default means a romantic boyfriend. A male friend (just a friend) is 남사친 (남자 사람 친구). Saying 남자친구 about a buddy implies you're dating.

entries.nuance: 첫눈에 반하다 is 첫눈에 ('at first sight', 첫 'first' + 눈 'eye/look' + 에 'at') + 반하다 ('to fall for / be smitten'), the set phrase for instant infatuation — love at first sight. The core verb 반하다 means to be captivated by someone, and crucially its target takes 에게/한테 ('to/by'), NOT 을/를: 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for YOU'), so the English-speaker's instinct to say 너를 반했어 is wrong. Note 반하다 is almost always used in the PAST (반했어요 'I've fallen for you') because it describes a state you've already entered — saying present 반해요 sounds incomplete. The contrast: 반하다 (smitten, captivated — can be sudden, surface/charm-level) vs. 사랑하다 ('to love', deep and serious) vs. 좋아하다 ('to like'); 반하다 is the spark/crush, not yet deep love, so don't substitute 사랑하다 for the giddy first-attraction feeling. 첫눈에 반하다 and 한눈에 반하다 are interchangeable ('first sight' vs. 'one look'). Pitfall: don't confuse 반하다 ('be smitten') with the unrelated 반하다 homophones or with 반갑다 ('glad to meet') — totally different. Register: 첫눈에 반했어요 (polite) is a lovely confession line; 반했어 in 반말 with someone close.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 반했어.
반하다 takes 에게/한테 ('to/by'): 너한테 반했어 ('I fell for you'). The one you're smitten by is not a direct object.
Using present 반해요 for the feeling.
반하다 describes a state already entered, so it's normally past: 반했어요 ('I've fallen for you'). Present 반해요 sounds unfinished.
Swapping in 사랑해요 for instant attraction.
사랑하다 is deep, serious love. The sudden crush/smitten feeling is 반하다. 'I fell for you at first sight' is 첫눈에 반했어요, not 첫눈에 사랑했어요.

entries.nuance: 썸 타다 is 썸 (from English 'something') + 타다 (lit. 'to ride'), the wildly common slang for the ambiguous pre-dating stage — flirting, texting, clear mutual interest, but no one has confessed or made it official yet. There's no clean English equivalent; 'talking to someone' or 'a situationship' is closest. The verb is fixed as 타다 ('ride'), the same 타다 you use for buses — never 하다 (썸 하다 is wrong) — so memorize 썸(을) 타다 as a unit. The crucial contrast is 썸 타다 vs. 사귀다 ('to officially date'): 썸 is BEFORE you're a couple, 사귀다 is AFTER you've agreed to be one, usually following a 고백 (confession). Saying 우리 사귀어? when you mean 썸 jumps the gun. This is pure 반말/casual register — you'd never say 썸 in a formal setting or to your boss. English-speaker pitfall: don't literally translate 'something' as 뭔가 — the slang noun is the loanword 썸, and the whole idiom is 썸(을) 타다. Younger Koreans say it constantly; older generations may not use it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 썸 하다 instead of 썸 타다.
The fixed verb is 타다 ('to ride'): 썸을 타다. 썸 하다 is not how Koreans say it. Memorize the collocation 썸 타다.
Using 썸 타다 for an official couple.
썸 is the stage BEFORE dating. Once you've confessed and agreed, you're 사귀다 ('dating'). Calling a committed couple 썸 implies it's still unofficial.
Translating 'something' word-for-word as 뭔가 타다.
The slang comes from English 'something' but is borrowed as the noun 썸. It's 썸 타다, not 뭔가 타다 or any literal rendering.

entries.nuance: 사귀다 means 'to date / be in a committed relationship', and 우리 사귈래요? is the ritual question that turns 썸 into an official couple. The ending -ㄹ래요? asks the listener's willingness ('do you want to / will you?'), which is exactly the soft, inviting tone you want here — not a command. The huge contrast is 사귀다 (committed, official) vs. 만나다 ('to meet/see'): 만나다 can be casual dating or even just meeting up, while 사귀다 is the boyfriend/girlfriend label, so confessing with 사귀다 is the moment a couple is 'official'. Right after a yes, couples say 오늘부터 1일 ('day one starts today') and count anniversaries from there. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the spelling/conjugation — 사귀다 → 사귀어요 (NOT 사겨요, a common typo); (2) particle — it's 저랑/너랑 사귀다 ('date WITH me') using 랑/와, never 을 (you don't 'date someone' as a direct object the English way). Register note: -ㄹ래요 is friendly-polite; with someone you've been 존댓말 with, this is perfect; drop to 사귈래? only when you're already informal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing/saying 사겨요 instead of 사귀어요.
사귀다 keeps the 위: present polite is 사귀어요. 사겨요 is a frequent misspelling. Conjugate it as 사귀어요, 사귀었어요.
Using 만나다 to mean 'be my official partner'.
만나다 ('to meet/see') is vaguer and can mean casual dating or just meeting up. To ask for a committed relationship, use 사귀다: 우리 사귈래요?
Attaching 을/를: 너를 사귈래?
사귀다 takes the comitative 랑/와 ('with'), not the object 을/를. Say 나랑 사귈래? ('go out WITH me?'), not 너를 사귈래?

entries.nuance: 고백하다 is 고백 ('confession', Sino-Korean 告白) + 하다, and in a dating context it specifically means telling someone you have romantic feelings — the pivotal event that usually precedes 사귀다. Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 고백하다 to mean 'admit I did something wrong'.

고백하다 = YOU confess to them; 고백받다 = THEY confess to you. 'I got confessed to' is 고백받았어요, not 고백했어요.

usagePhrases.note: The direct invite itself, friendly-polite

examples.ko: 저 데이트 신청하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeo deiteu sincheonghago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to ask you out.
examples.note: A sincere, slightly nervous way to open

examples.ko: 우리 이번 주말에 데이트할래요?
examples.romanization: uri ibeon jumare deiteuhallaeyo?
examples.en: Want to go on a date this weekend?
examples.note: 데이트하다 + -ㄹ래요 for the actual invitation

examples.ko: 오늘 완전 데이트 코스네요.
examples.romanization: oneul wanjeon deiteu koseuneyo.
examples.en: This is totally a date course today.
examples.note: 데이트 코스 ('date itinerary') — half-joking that the day feels like a date

entries.nuance: 데이트 is the loanword 'date', and the two key verbs are 데이트하다 ('to go on a date') and 데이트 신청하다 ('to ask someone out', lit. 'apply for a date', 신청 = Sino-Korean 申請 'application'). 신청하다 is the same verb you use to sign up for a class or apply for something, so 데이트 신청 frames asking-out as 'putting in a request' — natural and a bit endearing in Korean. Contrast 데이트하다 (the act of dating/going out that day) with 사귀다 (being in a committed relationship): you can 데이트 with someone you're not officially dating yet, so 데이트 ≠ being a couple. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 데이트 as a verb on its own with 하다 dropped, and don't say 데이트를 물어보다 ('ask about a date') for 'ask out' — the set phrase is 데이트 신청하다. Also, Koreans rarely announce 'it's a date' bluntly to a near-stranger; they often start indirectly with 주말에 시간 있어요? ('free this weekend?'). The word 데이트 itself is casual but register-flexible; keep the sentence ending polite (-요) with someone you don't know well.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 데이트를 물어보고 싶어요 for 'I want to ask you out'.
물어보다 means 'ask a question'. To ask someone ON a date, the set phrase is 데이트 신청하다: 데이트 신청하고 싶어요.
Treating the loanword 데이트 as a verb on its own.
데이트 is a noun; the verb needs 하다: 데이트하다. 'Let's go on a date' is 데이트하자/데이트할래요 — you can't conjugate the noun directly (no 데이트자 / 데이트요 to mean 'let's date').
Assuming 데이트 means you're officially a couple.
데이트 is the activity of going out; you can date casually before being official. The committed-couple status is 사귀다, a separate step.

entries.shortExplanation: 연락해요 is a practical expression meaning "Let's keep in touch / Text me".
entries.explanation: 연락해요 (yeollakaeyo) means "Let's keep in touch / Text me". Say it as one set phrase — for example 연락해요 ("Let's stay in touch"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; said when parting, hoping to talk again
반말, to a friend or someone you're close with
Promising YOU will reach out

usagePhrases.en: Please contact me / give me a call
usagePhrases.note: Asking THEM to reach out; 주다 puts the action on them

examples.ko: 조심히 들어가고 연락해요.
examples.romanization: josimhi deureogago yeollakaeyo.
examples.en: Get home safe and text me.
examples.note: 조심히 들어가다 ('get home safely') + 연락해요, a warm sign-off

examples.ko: 나중에 연락할게요.
examples.romanization: najunge yeollakalgeyo.
examples.en: I'll get in touch later.
examples.note: 연락할게요 promises your own future contact

examples.ko: 왜 연락 안 했어? 기다렸잖아.
examples.romanization: wae yeollak an haesseo? gidaryeotjana.
examples.en: Why didn't you text? I was waiting.
examples.note: 연락 안 하다 ('not contact'); a mild gentle complaint

entries.nuance: 연락하다 is 연락 ('contact/communication', Sino-Korean 連絡) + 하다, the all-purpose verb for reaching out — calling, texting, messaging. In dating it's loaded: '연락 잘 하는 사람' (someone who texts back well) is prized, and 연락이 뜸하다 ('contact grows sparse') is an early breakup warning sign. The critical contrast is direction via the verb: 연락할게(요) = 'I'll contact YOU' (-ㄹ게 promises your own action), while 연락해(요) = 'you contact me / let's be in touch' (imperative/suggestion), and 연락 줘(요)/연락 주세요 = 'give me contact' = asking them to reach out. Mixing these up sends the wrong message. The particle pitfall: the person you contact takes 에게/한테 ('to'), e.g. 나한테 연락해 ('contact me'), never 나를 연락해. Also 연락하다 is the verb, so you can't say 연락하 주세요 — it's 연락 주세요 (noun + 주다) or 연락해 주세요 (verb + favor 주다). Register: 연락해요 is friendly-polite and great for someone new; 연락해 is for friends. English-speaker trap: literally translating 'keep in touch' as 손 잡고 있어요 (lit. 'hold hands') — the idiom is 연락하다, no body part involved.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 연락할게 when you mean 'you text me'.
연락할게(요) promises YOUR own action ('I'll reach out'). To ask them to contact you, say 연락해(요) or 연락 줘(요)/연락 주세요.
Marking the person with 을/를: 너를 연락해.
The contact target takes 한테/에게 ('to'): 나한테 연락해 ('contact me'). 연락하다 doesn't take a direct-object person.
Translating 'keep in touch' literally with unrelated idioms.
There's no body-part idiom; the verb is simply 연락하다. 'Let's keep in touch' = 연락해요 / 연락하고 지내요.

entries.explanation: "I miss you" — that is 보고 싶어요 (bogo sipeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 보고 싶어요 ("I miss you / I want to see you"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: I miss you / I want to see you
usagePhrases.note: Polite; tender, said to someone you care about
반말, to a partner or close friend
Past — 'I've been missing you', great on reunion
많이 ('a lot') adds warmth and weight

examples.ko: 오늘 하루 종일 보고 싶었어요.
examples.romanization: oneul haru jongil bogo sipeosseoyo.
examples.en: I missed you all day today.
examples.note: 하루 종일 ('all day long') intensifies the longing

examples.ko: 빨리 보고 싶어.
examples.romanization: ppalli bogo sipeo.
examples.en: I want to see you soon.
examples.note: 빨리 ('quickly/soon') — eager to meet a partner

examples.ko: 멀리 있으니까 더 보고 싶네요.
examples.romanization: meolli isseunikka deo bogo simneyo.
examples.en: Being far apart makes me miss you even more.
examples.note: Long-distance context; 더 ('even more') + soft -네요

entries.nuance: 보고 싶다 is literally 보다 ('to see') + -고 싶다 ('want to'), so it means BOTH 'I want to see you' and 'I miss you' — Korean fuses the two ideas, because missing someone IS wanting to see them. It's the standard romantic 'I miss you', warmer than any clinical word. The key contrast: don't use 그리워하다 / 그립다 ('to long for, to miss') for a person you'll see soon — 그립다 is heavier, often for something distant, lost, or nostalgic (a hometown, late grandmother, the past), so saying 당신이 그리워요 to a partner you'll meet tomorrow sounds overly dramatic; everyday 'miss you' is 보고 싶어요. entries.nuance: 자기 (lit. 'oneself', Sino-Korean 自己) is repurposed as a romantic pet name — 자기야 (with the vocative 야) is the standard 'babe/honey' that couples call each other instead of names. entries.nuance: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아? is the playful 'who do you like more, me or ___?' that a partner asks to fish for reassurance — equal parts cute and lightly jealous (애교 + 질투). It plugs into a fixed pattern: X가 좋아? Y가 좋아?, where Y is the 'rival' (friends, games, work, an ex). The verb is 좋다 ('to be good/likable'), an ADJECTIVE, so the thing liked takes the subject marker 이/가 — 내가 좋아? literally 'is I good (to you)?' = 'do you like me?'. This is the single biggest trap: English speakers use 좋아하다 ('to like', a verb) and the object 를, producing 나를 좋아해? — which is grammatical and means 'do you like me?', but the idiomatic comparison frame uses 좋다 + 가: 내가 좋아? 친구가 좋아?. Also don't confuse 좋다 (a feeling/preference: 'I like it') with 좋아하다 (the active verb): both mean 'like', but the 'me or them' game uses 좋다. Register here is 반말 — it's an intimate, teasing thing; the polite 내가 더 좋아요? softens it but it's still couple-talk, never something for strangers or work.

Marking 'me' with 를: 내를 좋아?
좋다 is an adjective; what's liked takes 이/가, and 'I' becomes 내가. So it's 내가 좋아?, never 내를.
Saying it in 존댓말 to a non-partner.
This is intimate, teasing couple-talk. Asking a coworker or stranger 내가 좋아, 친구가 좋아? is bizarre. Keep it for someone you're dating.

entries.explanation: "I'm jealous" — that is 질투 나요 (jiltu nayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 질투 나요 ("I'm jealous"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

Telling someone to stop being jealous

entries.nuance: 질투 나다 is 질투 ('jealousy', Sino-Korean 嫉妬) + 나다 ('to arise/come out'), so it frames jealousy as a feeling that WELLS UP in you — 'jealousy arises' = 'I feel jealous'. The verb 나다 ('to occur') is the same one in 화나다 ('get angry'), 짜증 나다 ('get annoyed'): emotions 'come out'. The key contrast is 질투 나다 vs. 질투하다: 질투 나다 ('jealousy arises') describes the feeling welling up in you (you experience it), while 질투하다 ('to be jealous / act jealous') describes the behavior or accusing someone of it — so 'I feel jealous' is naturally 질투 나(요), and 질투하지 마 ('don't be jealous') uses the active verb to tell someone to quit it. There's also 부럽다 ('to envy', wanting what someone has, with NO romantic sting) — don't mix it up: if your friend got a new phone, that's 부럽다 (envy), not 질투 (romantic jealousy). English speakers blur 'jealous' and 'envious', but Korean keeps 질투 (romantic/possessive) apart from 부럽다 (covetous envy). Particle/usage trap: it's 질투(가) 나다 with the feeling as subject — don't force a 'I jealous YOU' structure. Register: 질투 나요 is fine and even endearing with a partner; in dating it's usually said semi-playfully, not as a serious accusation.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 부럽다 when you mean romantic jealousy.
부럽다 is envy (wanting what someone has, no romance). Feeling jealous about a partner is 질투 나다. 'I'm jealous (of who you're with)' = 질투 나, not 부러워.
Saying 질투해요 to describe your own feeling.
질투하다 leans toward the behavior/accusation ('to act jealous'). To say you FEEL jealous, the natural phrase is 질투 나요 (the feeling arises).
Forcing an English structure like 너를 질투해 for 'I'm jealous of you'.
질투(가) 나다 takes the feeling as subject: 질투 나. To say you got jealous over a situation, name the trigger + 질투 났어, e.g. 다른 사람이랑 있어서 질투 났어 ('I got jealous because you were with someone else').

Korean keeps 질투 (romantic/possessive) apart from 부럽다 (covetous envy).
질투 is Sino-Korean 嫉妬 ('jealousy').

English speakers blur 'jealous' and 'envious', but Korean splits them (질투 vs. 부럽다). Particle/usage trap: it's 질투(가) 나다 with the feeling as subject — don't force a 'I jealous YOU' structure like 너를 질투해.

entries.nuance: 바람피우다 is the idiom for cheating / having an affair, literally 바람 ('wind') + 피우다 ('to give off, kick up') — 'to kick up wind', i.e. to stray. It is the standard word for romantic infidelity. Two related forms confuse learners: 바람피우다 (the active 'to cheat', what the cheater DOES) vs. 바람나다 (lit. 'wind arises', meaning an affair has happened / someone has been swept into one) — you say 바람피우지 마 ('don't cheat', commanding behavior) but 바람났대 ('I heard they had an affair', describing the event). The English-speaker pitfall is the literal trap: 바람 means 'wind', so beginners panic, but the fixed idiom has nothing to do with weather — never translate it piece by piece. Also don't reach for 속이다 ('to deceive/lie to') for cheating; 속이다 is general lying, while romantic infidelity specifically is 바람피우다. commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 바람 literally as 'wind' and getting lost.
바람피우다 is a fixed idiom for cheating; 바람 here is not weather. Learn the whole phrase as 'to cheat', don't decode it word-by-word.

바람피우다 = the active 'to cheat' (what one does); 바람나다 = 'an affair occurred / got swept into one' (the event). Command form is 바람피우지 마.

entries.nuance: 어울리다 means 'to match / suit / go well together', and 우리 잘 어울려요 is the warm way to say a couple fits — looks good together, has chemistry. It's also the everyday verb for clothes suiting a person (이 색 잘 어울려요 'this color suits you'), so it spans both 'we're a good couple' and 'that looks good on you'. The key contrast is 어울리다 vs. 사귀다: 어울리다 is about COMPATIBILITY/fit (we match), while 사귀다 is the relationship STATUS (we're dating) — saying 우리 잘 어울려 doesn't mean you're official, just that you'd fit. For destiny-level praise, Koreans escalate to 천생연분 ('heaven-made match') or 잘 맞다 ('we click / are compatible', more about personality fit). English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 어울리다 is intransitive and uses 와/랑 or just a plural subject — 'we suit each other' is 우리(는) 잘 어울려요, and 'X suits you' is 너한테 잘 어울려 (target takes 한테/에게), never 너를 어울려. (2) Don't confuse it with 맞다 ('to be correct/to fit') used alone — 잘 맞다 ('click', compatible) overlaps but 어울리다 leans visual/'go together', 맞다 leans personality/fit. Register: 우리 잘 어울려요 is friendly-polite and a lovely thing to say early on.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the person with 를: 너를 잘 어울려.
어울리다 is intransitive; the one something suits takes 한테/에게: 너한테 잘 어울려 ('it suits you'). For a couple, just use a plural subject: 우리 잘 어울려.
Thinking 잘 어울려 means 'we're officially dating'.
어울리다 = compatible / go well together (fit), not relationship status. To say you're a couple, that's 사귀다. You can suit each other without being official.
Confusing 어울리다 with 어울다/어우르다.
The verb is 어울리다 ('to match/suit'). 'It suits you' = 잘 어울려요. Don't mangle the stem; conjugate 어울리다 → 어울려요.

entries.nuance: 밀당 is a slangy contraction of 밀고 당기기 ('pushing and pulling'), the dating game of playing hot-and-cold — acting interested then aloof to keep someone hooked. 밀당하다 ('to do push-pull') = to play hard to get / play games. It comes from 밀다 ('push') + 당기다 ('pull'). This is informal, very current slang, common among younger Koreans; you would not use it in formal speech. The contrast to draw: 밀당 (strategic push-pull, a tactic) vs. 튕기다 ('to play coy / pretend reluctance', literally 'to bounce', often refusing/holding back at first to seem less eager) — they overlap, but 밀당 is the ongoing back-and-forth strategy, while 튕기다 is more 'feigning reluctance' at a single moment (acting reluctant or hard-to-get when first asked, to seem less eager). English-speaker pitfall: there's no literal route to this — don't try 'play hard to get' word-by-word (게임 하다 means literally playing a videogame, not romance games); the idiom is 밀당하다. Also it's a 하다-noun, so it's 밀당하다 / 밀당하지 마, never 밀당 주세요. Register: pure casual/반말; the polite 밀당하지 마세요 exists but the whole concept lives in informal couple/friend talk.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'play games' as 게임 하다.
게임 하다 means playing a (video)game. The dating push-pull is 밀당하다. 'Stop playing games (with my feelings)' = 밀당하지 마, not 게임 하지 마.
Using 밀당 in formal or professional settings.
밀당 is casual slang for romance/relationships. It sounds out of place in formal speech or non-dating contexts. Keep it to friends and partners.
Confusing 밀당 (ongoing strategy) with 튕기다 (feigning reluctance once).
밀당하다 is the continuous hot-and-cold game; 튕기다 is acting coy/refusing at a moment to seem less eager. Related but not identical — pick by whether it's a one-time coyness or a pattern.

entries.nuance: 권태기 (Sino-Korean 倦怠期, lit. 'weariness period') is the relationship 'slump' — the stage in a long-term couple when the excitement fades and things feel routine, like the English 'we've lost the spark' or 'the honeymoon's over'. It's collocated with 오다 ('to come'): 권태기가 오다 ('the slump comes/arrives'), as if it's a phase that visits you — a very Korean way to frame emotional states as arriving (cf. 사춘기가 오다 'puberty hits'). The contrast: 권태기 (boredom/staleness in an ongoing relationship) is NOT a breakup — couples talk about 권태기 극복 ('overcoming the slump'); whereas 헤어지다 is actually splitting up. So 권태기 왔어 ≠ 'we broke up'; it means the relationship feels stale. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the verb — it's 권태기가 오다 (it 'comes'), not 권태기를 하다 or 가지다; learners wrongly try to 'have' it as an object. (2) It implies a fairly established relationship — you wouldn't say 권태기 about a week-old fling. structuredNuance.t: 권태기 (lit. 'weariness period') is the relationship 'slump' — the stage in a long-term couple when the excitement fades and things feel routine, like the English 'we've lost the spark' or 'the honeymoon's over'. It's collocated with 오다 ('to come'): 권태기가 오다 ('the slump comes/arrives'), as if it's a phase that visits you — a very Korean way to frame emotional states as arriving (cf. 사춘기가 오다 'puberty hits'). Register: normal everyday vocabulary, fine in polite or casual; 권태기가 왔어요 works confiding to anyone, 권태기 왔어 with friends.

권태기 (boredom/staleness in an ongoing relationship) is NOT a breakup — couples talk about 권태기 극복 ('overcoming the slump'); whereas 헤어지다 is actually splitting up. So 권태기 왔어 ≠ 'we broke up'; it means the relationship feels stale.
권태기 is Sino-Korean 倦怠期, literally 'weariness period'.

entries.nuance: 헤어지다 means 'to break up / part', and 우리 헤어져요 is the direct breakup line. Crucially, 헤어지다 is intransitive and reciprocal — it means 'to part (from each other)', so the partner is marked with 와/랑/하고 ('with'), NOT 을/를: 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요 ('I broke up WITH my boyfriend'). The single most common English-speaker error is 남자친구를 헤어졌어요 with the object particle — wrong; you part WITH someone, you don't 'break up someone'. Note 헤어지다 also just means 'to part ways' in a neutral sense (after meeting, 여기서 헤어져요 'let's part here / say bye here'), but in dating context it's the romantic breakup. Softer alternatives Koreans use to avoid the harsh word: 그만 만나다 ('stop seeing each other') and 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어 — gentler than the blunt 헤어지자. Don't confuse 헤어지다 with 차다/차이다: 차다 ('to dump'), 차이다 ('to get dumped') describe WHO did the dumping (one-sided), while 헤어지다 is the mutual 'we parted'. Register: 우리 헤어져요 (polite) / 헤어지자 (반말 'let's'); even softened, this is a heavy line. The past 헤어졌어요 is what you tell friends.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the partner with 을/를: 남자친구를 헤어졌어요.
헤어지다 is reciprocal ('part WITH'): the partner takes 랑/와/하고. Say 남자친구랑 헤어졌어요. You don't break someone up as a direct object.
Confusing 헤어지다 with 차다/차이다.
헤어지다 = mutually parted. 차다 = 'to dump (someone)'; 차이다 = 'to get dumped'. 'I got dumped' is 차였어요, not 헤어졌어요 (which is neutral 'we broke up').
Using only the blunt 헤어져 when you want to soften it.
헤어지자 is direct. To be gentler, Koreans say 우리 그만 만나자 / 그만 만나는 게 좋겠어 ('let's stop seeing each other'), which lands softer.

entries.nuance: 재회하다 (Sino-Korean 再會 're-meet' + 하다) means 'to reunite / get back together', the formal-ish word for rekindling with an ex. In everyday speech, though, Koreans more often say the plainer 다시 만나다 ('meet again / get back together') — 재회 sounds a touch literary or like a 'reunion' headline, so 전 남친이랑 다시 만나요 ('I'm seeing my ex again') is the casual norm, while 재회하고 싶어요 is more earnest/formal. The contrast to nail: 다시 만나다 in this context = romantically reuniting, but 다시 만나다 can ALSO just mean 'meet again' (see each other again sometime) — context decides, so with an ex it reads as reuniting. Don't confuse 재회 ('reunite, get back together') with 화해 ('to make up / reconcile after a fight') — you 화해 after an argument (still together), but you 재회 after you'd actually broken up. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the partner takes 랑/와 ('with'), not 를 — 전 여자친구랑 재회했어요. (2) 재회 is a 하다-noun, so 재회하다 / 재회하고 싶다, never 재회 주세요. (3) Beginners overuse the formal 재회 in casual chat where 다시 만나다 sounds far more natural. Register: 재회하고 싶어요 leans formal/earnest; 다시 만나고 싶어 is the intimate 반말 you'd actually whisper to an ex.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking the ex with 을/를: 전 남자친구를 재회했어요.
재회/만나다 take 랑/와 ('with'): 전 남자친구랑 재회했어요. The reunion partner is not a direct object.
Confusing 재회 (get back together) with 화해 (reconcile after a fight).
화해하다 = make up while still together after an argument. 재회하다 = reunite after an actual breakup. Use 재회 only if you'd split up.
Overusing formal 재회 in casual conversation.
재회 sounds literary. In everyday speech Koreans say 다시 만나다: 전 남친이랑 다시 만나기로 했어 ('decided to get back with my ex'). Save 재회하다 for earnest/formal moments.
