entries.nuance: 취하다 ('to get drunk/intoxicated') is the core verb; 안 취했어요 = 'I'm not drunk', literally 'I didn't get drunk' — and here's the tense trap: Korean uses the PAST 취했어요 to describe the CURRENT state of being drunk (the getting-drunk already happened, so you're now in that state) — this is the same change-of-state pattern as 잘생겼어요 ('is good-looking') or 닮았어요 ('resembles'), where the past form names a present condition, so for 'I am drunk' you say 취했어요, NOT the present 취해요. Thus 'I'm not drunk' is 안 취했어요, not 안 취해요. Degrees: 살짝/조금 취하다 (tipsy), 많이 취하다 (very drunk), 만취하다 (dead/blackout drunk, 滿醉 'full-drunk'), 꽐라(되다) (slang for wasted). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond tense, is the 직역 of 'drunk' as an adjective — Korean treats it as the verb 취하다 in past form, so don't try 나는 drunk-하다. Also 취하다 has a homonym meaning 'to take/adopt (a measure/attitude)' (조치를 취하다), but the drinking sense is unmistakable in context. Culturally, insisting 안 취했어요 is a common (and often unconvincing) protest at 회식; if you genuinely want to stop, it's smarter to admit 조금 취한 것 같아요 and pivot to water, since claiming you're fine can invite another pour. Companion: 술기운(이) 오르다 ('the alcohol is hitting me').

Korean uses past 취했어요 for the current drunk state. 'I'm not drunk' = 안 취했어요, not 안 취해요.
Treating 'drunk' as an English-style adjective.
There's no adjective 'drunk' to attach; use the verb 취하다 in past form: 취했어요 / 안 취했어요.

Same spelling, but with 술 it means intoxicated. 조치를 취하다 ('take action') is the other sense — context disambiguates.

entries.nuance: 숙취 (宿醉, 'leftover/lodged drunkenness') is the HANGOVER itself — the headache, nausea and fog the morning after. 숙취가 심하다 = 'the hangover is severe'; 숙취가 있다 = 'to have a hangover'. The essential contrast for learners is 숙취 (the condition you suffer) vs. 해장 (the act of eating to relieve it) — they're two halves of the same morning, and conflating them is the most common mix-up: you HAVE 숙취 and you DO 해장 to cure it. Also distinguish 숙취 (next-day aftermath) from 취하다 (being drunk during the drinking) — 취했어요 is tonight, 숙취 is tomorrow. The particle pattern: 숙취 is a noun taking 가/이 with descriptive predicates — 숙취가 심하다, 숙취가 있다 — so don't try to verb it as 숙취하다 (not a word). The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'I'm hungover': there's no adjective in Korean, so you can't say 나 hungover-해요; you must use the NOUN 숙취 with 있다/심하다, e.g. 숙취가 있어요 / 숙취가 심해요. Culturally relevant companions: 과음 ('excessive drinking'), 술병(이) 나다 ('to get sick from drinking'), 해장 ('hangover cure-meal'), and 숙취해소제 / 숙취해소음료 (the hangover-relief pills and drinks Koreans buy at convenience stores before or after drinking — worth knowing for any 회식 survivor).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

취했어요 = drunk now, during drinking. 숙취 = the aftermath the next day. 'I have a hangover' = 숙취가 있어요/심해요, not 취했어요.
Trying to say 숙취하다 as a verb.

structuredNuance.t: 숙취 is the HANGOVER itself — the headache, nausea and fog the morning after. 숙취가 심하다 = 'the hangover is severe'; 숙취가 있다 = 'to have a hangover'. The particle pattern: 숙취 is a noun taking 가/이 with descriptive predicates — 숙취가 심하다, 숙취가 있다 — so don't try to verb it as 숙취하다 (not a word). Culturally relevant companions: 과음 ('excessive drinking'), 술병(이) 나다 ('to get sick from drinking'), 해장 ('hangover cure-meal'), and 숙취해소제 / 숙취해소음료 (the hangover-relief pills and drinks Koreans buy at convenience stores before or after drinking — worth knowing for any 회식 survivor).

The essential contrast for learners is 숙취 (the condition you suffer) vs. 해장 (the act of eating to relieve it) — they're two halves of the same morning, and conflating them is the most common mix-up: you HAVE 숙취 and you DO 해장 to cure it. Also distinguish 숙취 (next-day aftermath) from 취하다 (being drunk during the drinking) — 취했어요 is tonight, 숙취 is tomorrow.
숙취 is Sino-Korean 宿醉, 'leftover/lodged drunkenness'.
The pitfall is the 직역 of 'I'm hungover': there's no adjective in Korean, so you can't say 나 hungover-해요; you must use the NOUN 숙취 with 있다/심하다, e.g. 숙취가 있어요 / 숙취가 심해요.

entries.nuance: 해장 (解酲, 'relieving the after-effects of drink') is the Korean ritual of eating — usually a hot, brothy soup — to recover from a hangover or the morning-after queasiness. 해장하다 = 'to cure a hangover (by eating)'; 해장국 is the soup itself (e.g. 선지해장국, 콩나물국밥, 북엇국). 해장하러 가요 uses -(으)러 가다 ('go in order to ~'), the purpose construction, so it means 'go for the purpose of 해장'. The synonym 속(을) 풀다 literally 'loosen/soothe the stomach' is interchangeable in feeling. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: there's NO single English word for 해장, so don't 직역 it as just 'hangover' (that's 숙취, the hangover STATE) — 해장 is the ACT of eating to cure it, and conflating 숙취 (the condition) with 해장 (the remedy meal) is a common mix-up. Second, the -(으)러 가다 grammar: learners drop it or use -고 가다; the correct 'go to do X' is -(으)러 가다 (해장하러 가다). Culturally this is a bonding ritual — coworkers who drank together the night before often 해장 together the next morning, and even 해장술 ('a little hair-of-the-dog drink') exists, though that's its own debated custom. Knowing 해장 signals you understand the full drinking cycle, not just the night itself.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 해장 (the cure-meal) with 숙취 (the hangover).
숙취 is the hangover condition; 해장 is the act of eating to relieve it. 'I have a hangover' = 숙취 있어요; 'let's get hangover food' = 해장하러 가요.
Using -고 가다 instead of -(으)러 가다 for purpose.
To say 'go in order to 해장', use -(으)러 가다: 해장하러 가요. 해장하고 가요 would mean 'do 해장 and then go', a different meaning.
Calling any post-drinking meal 해장 even without a hangover.
해장 specifically targets relieving drink after-effects. A normal next-day meal isn't necessarily 해장; the point is soothing the stomach/숙취.

entries.nuance: 주차 어디에 해요? is 주차 ('parking', Sino-Korean 駐車) + 어디에 ('at where') + 해요 (polite 'do'), literally 'where do I do parking?' — the everyday way to ask where to leave your car. The particle to memorize is 에 (location-of-action 'at'), NOT 에서: many learners say 주차 어디에서 해요?, but with 주차하다 the destination/spot takes 에 because you END UP parked there, like 도착하다 (arrive AT). A softer, very common variant is 어디에 하면 돼요? ('where is it OK to park?'). Note the contrast with the verb 대다 ('to pull a car in') which staff often use back to you — 뒤에 대세요 ('park in the back') — so recognize 대다 even though you'll say 하다. The English-speaker trap is translating 'park' as a place and saying 주차 어디 있어요? — that asks where the PARKING LOT is located (use 주차장 어디예요? for that), whereas 어디에 해요? asks where YOU should perform the act of parking. To staff always keep 요; drop to 어디에 해? only with a friend. Don't confuse 주차 (parking) with 주유 (refueling) — they look similar but 주유 is for gas.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주차 어디에서 해요? with 에서.
주차하다 marks the spot you end at with 에, not the action-location 에서. Say 주차 어디에 해요? (or 어디에 하면 돼요?). 에서 makes it sound like you're asking where the activity of parking happens in general.
Using 주차 어디 있어요? to ask where to park.
That asks where the parking LOT exists. To ask where YOU should park your car, say 주차 어디에 해요?; to find the lot, say 주차장 어디예요?
Mixing up 주차 and 주유.
주차 is parking a car; 주유 is putting in fuel. 주유 어디에 해요? would be asking where to pump gas. Keep 주차 for parking.

entries.nuance: 주차장 있어요? is 주차장 ('parking lot', 주차 + 場 'place') + 있어요 ('is there'), the basic feasibility check you do before driving somewhere — by phone or at the door. 있다 is the existence verb, so this literally asks 'does a parking lot exist (here)?'. The near-synonym 주차 가능해요? ('is parking possible?', 가능 = 可能) is more formal and shows up on signs and websites; in casual speech 주차장 있어요? is warmer. Crucially, in Korea 'is there parking' is NOT the same as 'is it free' — many lots exist but charge, so follow up with 무료예요? ('is it free?') or 얼마예요? The English-speaker trap is forcing the subject particle and saying 주차장이 있어요? in quick speech — natives usually drop 이 here (주차장 있어요?). Another trap: don't say 주차 있어요? without 장 — 주차 ('parking' the act) + 있어요 sounds incomplete; you want the place noun 주차장. With staff keep 요; 주차장 있어? is only for friends. Also distinguish 주차장 (a lot) from 주차 자리 / 자리 ('a parking SPACE'), which you ask about when the lot is full: 자리 있어요?

Many Korean lots exist but charge by time. After 주차장 있어요?, confirm cost with 무료예요? ('is it free?') or 주차비 얼마예요?

주차장 = 주차 + 場 ('place'); 가능 in the variant is 可能.

entries.nuance: 가득이요 is 가득 ('full, to the brim') + 이요 (polite ender), an elliptical 'full, please' — the classic thing you say at a 주유소 (gas station) when you want a full tank. It's short because the verb (채우다/넣다 'to fill/put in') is understood; fuller forms are 가득 채워 주세요 or 가득 넣어 주세요, both 100% natural and clearer if the attendant doesn't catch the short version. The big contrast is full-tank vs. fixed-amount: instead of 가득이요 you can order by money — 삼만 원어치요 ('30,000 won's worth') or 오만 원어치요 — where -어치 means 'worth of'; English speakers often forget you can buy gas by won amount, which is extremely common in Korea. Also, you MUST name the fuel type to be safe: 휘발유 (gasoline), 경유 (diesel), or 고급 (premium) — putting 경유 in a gasoline car is a real disaster, so say the type, then 가득이요. At self-service pumps (셀프 주유소) you won't say this at all; it's for attended stations.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying just 가득 with no ending to an attendant.
Bare 가득 can sound abrupt. Add the polite 이요 (가득이요) or use a full verb: 가득 채워 주세요 / 가득 넣어 주세요.
Forgetting to state the fuel type.
가득이요 alone doesn't say gasoline or diesel. Lead with 휘발유 가득이요 or 경유 가득이요 — putting diesel in a petrol car causes serious damage.

'30,000 won's worth' is 삼만 원어치요, not 삼만 원요 alone. The suffix -어치 ('worth of') is what turns the money into a fuel quantity.

entries.nuance: 기름 넣어야 돼요 is 기름 ('oil/fuel', the everyday word for gasoline) + 넣다 ('to put in') + -어야 되다 ('have to'), literally 'I have to put fuel in' — the casual, most common way Koreans say 'I need to get gas.' 기름 literally means 'oil' but in a car context everyone understands it as gas/fuel; the formal counterpart is 주유하다 (주유 = 注油 'pour fuel'), which you see on signs (주유소 = gas station). The verb to lock in is 넣다 ('put in'), because you put fuel INTO the tank — learners wrongly say 기름 사야 돼요 ('I have to BUY gas'), which isn't how Koreans frame it; you 넣다 (put in) gas, you don't talk about buying it. -어야 돼요 vs. -어야 해요: both mean 'have to'; 돼요 is the more conversational spoken choice. The English-speaker trap is also calling fuel 가스 (gas), but 가스 in Korean means cooking/LPG GAS, not gasoline — so 가스 넣어야 돼요 sounds like you're filling a gas cylinder. Use 기름 for car fuel. To a friend drop to 기름 넣어야 돼.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 기름 사야 돼요 ('I have to buy gas').
Koreans frame refueling as 넣다 ('put in'), not 사다 ('buy'). Say 기름 넣어야 돼요. 사야 돼요 sounds like buying oil as a product off a shelf.
Calling gasoline 가스.
가스 means cooking/LPG gas in Korean. Car fuel is 기름 (or 휘발유/경유). 가스 넣어야 돼요 sounds like refilling a gas canister.
Using the wrong particle: 기름에 넣어야 돼요.
기름 is the thing you put in (object), so it takes 을/를 or no particle: 기름(을) 넣어야 돼요. 기름에 would mean 'put something INTO the oil'.

entries.explanation: "Is it self-service?" — that is 셀프예요? (selpeuyeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 셀프예요? ("Is it self-service?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 셀프예요? is the loanword 셀프 ('self', from 'self-service') + 예요 (polite copula), 'is it self-service?'. Korean gas stations split into 셀프 주유소 (you pump your own, cheaper) and full-service stations where a 직원 (attendant) does it; 셀프 stations are now very common and usually noticeably cheaper, so this is a real money question. Note 셀프 is used as a standalone noun/adjective in Korean far more than English 'self' — 셀프 세차 (self car-wash), 셀프 계산 (self-checkout) — so 셀프예요? fully means 'is it self-service?' on its own. The contrast to know is 직접 넣다 ('to pump it yourself', 직접 = 'in person/directly') for what you do at a 셀프 station. The English-speaker trap is over-explaining with 'do I have to do it myself?' as 제가 직접 해야 돼요? — that works but 셀프예요? is the crisp local phrasing. Another trap: the copula contracts to 예요 after a vowel (셀프 + 예요), so it's 셀프예요, not 셀프이에요. At a self station you'll then deal with a screen: pick 휘발유/경유, amount, and pay — often prepay by card.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 셀프이에요? after the vowel.
셀프 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 예요: 셀프예요? 셀프이에요 is the wrong form for a vowel-final noun.
Thinking 셀프 needs an English-style full phrase.
In Korean 셀프 stands alone as 'self-service'. You don't need 셀프 서비스예요?; 셀프예요? is complete and natural.
Confusing 셀프 (self-serve) with 무인 (unmanned).
셀프 means you pump it yourself, usually with staff around to help. 무인 ('unmanned') means no staff at all. They overlap but aren't identical; ask 셀프예요? for the pump-it-yourself question.

entries.explanation: 신호 바뀌었어요 (sinho bakkwieosseoyo) = "The light changed". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 신호 바뀌었어요 ("The light changed"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

반말, to a friend driving
Naming the color directly (초록불 = green light)
The stop version — 빨간불 = red light

examples.romanization: sinho bakkwieosseoyo, gado dwaeyo.
examples.en: The light changed, you can go.
examples.note: Tell the driver it's green and safe to move

examples.romanization: ape sinho ppalganburieyo, meomchwoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: Red light ahead, you need to stop.
examples.note: 멈추다 ('to stop') paired with a red signal

examples.romanization: sinho bakkwieosseoyo! dwieseo ppangppanggeoryeoyo.
examples.en: The light changed! They're honking behind us.

entries.nuance: 신호 바뀌었어요 is 신호 ('signal/traffic light', Sino-Korean 信號) + 바뀌다 ('to change/switch') in polite past, 'the light (has) changed' — what a passenger says to nudge a driver, or what you note about a signal. 신호 by itself means the traffic signal in driving context (full form 신호등 = the signal LIGHT/lamp), so 신호 바뀌었어요 ('the signal changed') is completely natural. Colors: 초록불/파란불 (green — Koreans often say 파란불 'blue light' for green!), 빨간불 (red), 노란불 (yellow). That 파란불-for-green quirk surprises English speakers, so don't 'correct' it. The verb 바뀌다 is intransitive ('it changes by itself'), distinct from transitive 바꾸다 ('to change something') — a top learner error is saying 신호 바꿨어요, which means 'I/someone changed the signal' (impossible). Use 바뀌었어요 (it changed). Also distinguish 신호 ('traffic signal') from 신호위반 ('running a red', 위반 = violation). With a friend driving, drop to 신호 바뀌었어. The English-speaker trap is mixing 신호 up with 사인 (a sign/signature) — for a road SIGN it's 표지판, not 신호.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 신호 바꿨어요 instead of 바뀌었어요.
바꾸다 is transitive ('to change something'); 바뀌다 is intransitive ('it changes'). A light changes on its own, so 신호 바뀌었어요. 바꿨어요 wrongly says someone changed it.
Assuming 파란불 is literally a blue light.
Koreans commonly call the green go-signal 파란불 ('blue light'). It means GREEN. Don't try to correct it to 초록불 as if it's an error — both are normal.

entries.nuance: 안전벨트 매세요 is 안전벨트 ('seatbelt', 안전 'safety' 安全 + 벨트 'belt') + 매다 ('to fasten/tie') in polite imperative, 'please fasten your seatbelt.' The verb is 매다 ('to tie/fasten') — NOT 하다 or 끼다 — so a top error is 안전벨트 하세요 or 끼세요; you 매다 (fasten) a belt, the same verb used for tying a necktie (넥타이 매다). In Korea ALL passengers including the back seat must buckle up by law, with a 벌금/과태료 (fine) for not doing so, so this is a normal, expected instruction, not nagging. The opposite action is 풀다 ('to unfasten/undo'): 벨트 푸세요 ('undo your belt') when arriving. 안전벨트 is often shortened to just 벨트 in a car ('벨트 매세요'). The English-speaker trap is the verb choice and also saying 'wear a seatbelt' as 입다 ('to wear clothes') — you don't 입다 a belt; you 매다 it. Register: 매세요 to an adult passenger; 매 to a kid or close friend; the softer favor form 매 주세요 sounds extra gentle. Also don't confuse 매다 ('fasten') with 메다 ('to carry on the shoulder', like a backpack 가방 메다) — same pronunciation, different verb.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안전벨트 하세요 or 끼세요.
A seatbelt is fastened with 매다: 안전벨트 매세요. 하다 is too generic and 끼다 ('to insert/wear glasses') is the wrong verb for a belt.
Using 입다 ('to wear') for a seatbelt.
입다 is for clothing. A belt is tied/fastened: 매다. So it's 안전벨트 매세요, never 안전벨트 입으세요.
Confusing 매다 (fasten) with 메다 (carry on shoulder).
They sound the same but 매다 = fasten a belt/tie, 메다 = sling a bag over your shoulder. For a seatbelt use 매다: 벨트 매세요.

examples.ko: 여기 세워 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi sewo juseyo.
examples.en: Please stop here.
examples.note: Standard line to a taxi driver at your destination

examples.ko: 저 횡단보도 앞에서 세워 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeo hoengdanbodo apeseo sewo juseyo.
examples.en: Please pull over before that crosswalk.
examples.note: 횡단보도 ('crosswalk') as a landmark; cars can't stop ON it

examples.ko: 여기 잠깐 세워 주세요. 금방 올게요.
examples.romanization: yeogi jamkkan sewo juseyo. geumbang olgeyo.
examples.en: Pull over here a sec, I'll be right back.
examples.note: 잠깐 ('for a moment') + 금방 올게요 ('back soon') for a quick stop

entries.nuance: 여기 세워 주세요 is 여기 ('here') + 세우다 ('to make stop / bring to a halt') + 주세요 ('please, as a favor'), 'please stop (the car) here' — the essential taxi/passenger line. The verb is the causative 세우다 ('to make X stand/stop'), distinct from intransitive 서다 ('to stop, of oneself'): YOU ask the driver to 세우다 the car, because the driver causes it to stop. Saying 여기 서 주세요 (intransitive) is a classic learner error meaning roughly 'please you yourself stand here.' The particle on the place is usually none or 에서 for 'pull over AT that point' (저 앞에서 세워 주세요). The passenger-side twin is 여기서 내릴게요 ('I'll get off here', 내리다 = 'to get out/off'), which announces your own action rather than instructing the driver — both are natural, slightly different framing. The English-speaker trap is using 멈추다 ('to halt/cease') instead — 멈추다 is more about motion stopping abruptly and isn't how you tell a taxi to drop you; 세우다 ('pull over and park momentarily') is right. Also don't say 정지해 주세요 (정지 = 'stop', the word on traffic signs) — that's stiff and signage-like for a taxi. To a friend, 여기 세워 줘.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 여기 서 주세요 with intransitive 서다.
서다 ('to stand/stop oneself') would tell the driver to personally stand. You want the causative 세우다 ('make the car stop'): 여기 세워 주세요.
Using 멈춰 주세요 to mean 'pull over'.
멈추다 is 'to halt/cease' and sounds abrupt. To have a taxi drop you, say 여기 세워 주세요; 멈추다 is more for stopping motion or a machine.
Saying 정지해 주세요.
정지 is the formal 'STOP' on signs and signals. As a request to a driver it's stiff and odd. Use the everyday 세워 주세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 길이 막혀요 is a practical expression meaning "The traffic is bad / the road is jammed".
entries.explanation: 길이 막혀요 (giri makyeoyo) = "The traffic is bad / the road is jammed". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 길이 막혀요 ("There's a traffic jam"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

차가 막히다 ('cars are jammed') with surprised -네요
The opposite — 뚫리다 ('to be clear/flowing')

examples.ko: 지금 길이 막혀요.
examples.romanization: jigeum giri makyeoyo.
examples.en: The roads are jammed right now.
examples.note: Explaining why you're late or slow

examples.ko: 퇴근 시간이라 길이 많이 막혀요.
examples.romanization: toegeun siganira giri mani makyeoyo.
examples.en: It's rush hour so traffic is really heavy.
examples.note: 퇴근 시간 ('commute-home time') = rush hour, the usual cause

examples.ko: 사고 났나 봐요, 길이 너무 막혀요.
examples.romanization: sago nanna bwayo, giri neomu makyeoyo.
examples.en: Looks like there was an accident — traffic's terrible.
examples.note: 사고 나다 ('an accident happens') as a guessed reason with -나 봐요

entries.nuance: 길이 막혀요 is 길 ('road/way') + 이 (subject) + 막히다 ('to be blocked/clogged') in polite present, 'the road is jammed.' 막히다 is the intransitive/passive of 막다 ('to block') — the road IS blocked by traffic — so the road or the cars are the subject: 길이 막히다 or 차가 막히다, both standard. A top learner error is using transitive 막다 and saying 길을 막아요 ('I block the road'), which means YOU are blocking it. The natural opposite is 뚫리다 ('to be unclogged/flowing'): 길이 뚫렸어요 ('the road's clear'). The English-speaker trap is calquing 'there is traffic' as 트래픽이 있어요 or 교통이 많아요 — 교통 (交通) means 'transportation/traffic' as a system, not a jam, so 교통이 많아요 sounds odd; Koreans say the road/cars are 막히다. For the noun 'traffic jam' itself there's 교통 체증 or the casual 차 막힘, but the verb 막히다 is what you'll actually say. Tenses: 막혀요 (it's jammed now), 막혔어요 (it got jammed / was jammed), 막힐 거예요 (it'll be jammed). To a friend, 길 막혀. Don't confuse 막히다 ('be jammed') with 막다 ('to block, to defend').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 길을 막아요 ('I block the road').
막다 is transitive ('to block something'); the road being jammed is intransitive 막히다. Say 길이 막혀요. 길을 막아요 means you are physically blocking it.
Saying 교통이 많아요 for heavy traffic.
교통 means 'transportation/traffic' as a system, not a jam. 'Traffic is heavy' is 길이/차가 막혀요. 교통이 많아요 sounds unnatural.
Using 막혀요 for a clogged drain only.
막히다 covers both a jammed road and a blocked pipe/nose. In a driving context 길이 막혀요 clearly means a traffic jam — context, not a different verb, distinguishes them.

entries.nuance: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 is 내비 (clipped from 내비게이션 'navigation', i.e. car GPS) + 좀 (softener) + 찍다 ('to punch in / tap / mark') + 주세요 ('please, as a favor'), 'please punch the destination into the GPS.' The killer vocabulary is 찍다: its core sense is 'to stamp/press,' and Koreans use it for entering something on a screen — 주소를 찍다 ('punch in the address'), 점을 찍다 ('mark a point'). This is NOT obvious to English speakers, who reach for 입력하다 ('to input', correct but stiff/technical) or invent 내비 해 주세요 (vague). 내비 is the everyday clipped form; the full 내비게이션 is fine but longer, and the brand-name 'GPS' isn't used as a verb in Korean. Useful partner words: 켜다 ('turn on') the nav, and 내비대로 ('according to the nav') for following it. The English-speaker trap is also the particle — the address goes 내비에 ('into the nav', location), and the thing punched in takes 을/를 or nothing: 내비에 주소(를) 찍어 주세요. Register: 찍어 주세요 to anyone polite; 찍어 줘 to a friend. Don't confuse 찍다 ('punch in / photograph') senses — context (a screen vs. a camera) tells you which; here it's entering the destination.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 내비 입력해 주세요 in casual speech.
입력하다 ('to input') is technically correct but sounds stiff/technical. Everyday Korean uses 찍다: 내비 좀 찍어 주세요.
Wrong particle: 내비를 찍어 주세요 for the destination.
You punch the destination/address INTO the nav: 내비에 (주소를) 찍어 주세요. 내비를 찍다 sounds like you're tapping the device itself, not entering a place.
Inventing 내비 해 주세요.
내비 ('navigation') isn't used with 하다 as a verb here. To set it, use 찍다 ('punch in') or 켜다 ('turn on'): 내비 좀 찍어 주세요 / 내비 켜 주세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 막차 끊겼어요 is a practical expression meaning "The last bus/train is gone".
entries.explanation: "The last bus/train is gone" — that is 막차 끊겼어요 (makcha kkeunkyeosseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 막차 끊겼어요 ("The last bus/train's gone"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 막차 끊겼어요 is 막차 ('the last bus/train of the day', 막 'final' + 車 'vehicle') + 끊기다 ('to be cut off / stop running') in polite past, 'the last ride has stopped.' The idiom is 끊기다 — the passive of 끊다 ('to cut') — used for service ending: 막차가 끊기다 literally 'the last vehicle gets cut off,' i.e., it's no longer running. This is very useful living in Korea, where subways (지하철) stop around midnight and you scramble for the 막차 or a taxi. Contrast 막차 (last departure) with 첫차 ('the first bus/train', 첫 'first'). To ask the time it's 막차 몇 시예요?; to say you missed it, 막차 놓쳤어요 (놓치다 = 'to miss/let slip'). The English-speaker trap is calquing 'the last bus left' with 떠나다 ('to depart') as 막차 떠났어요 — understandable but the idiomatic, lived-in phrase is 끊기다 ('service is cut'), because it's about the line STOPPING, not one bus leaving. Another trap is 막 vs. 마지막: both can mean 'last,' but the fixed compound is 막차 (not 마지막차) for the night's final ride. To a friend, 막차 끊겼어. Don't confuse 끊기다 ('be cut off, of a phone call or service') with 끊다 ('to hang up / quit / cut').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 막차 떠났어요 for 'last train's gone'.
Koreans idiomatically use 끊기다 ('service is cut off') for transit ending: 막차 끊겼어요. 떠났어요 ('it departed') is understandable but not the lived-in phrase.
Saying 마지막차 instead of 막차.
The fixed word for the night's final bus/train is 막차 (and 첫차 for the first). 마지막 차 is understandable but 막차 is the natural compound.
Using 끊다 instead of 끊기다.
끊다 is transitive ('to cut/hang up/quit'). The last train STOPPING on its own is passive 끊기다: 막차 끊겼어요. 막차 끊었어요 would mean someone cut it off.

entries.nuance: 면허 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 면허 ('license', 免許; full 운전면허 = driver's license) + 따다 ('to obtain/win', the verb for GETTING a license/certificate) + -ㄴ 지 ('since [doing]') + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much [time] has passed'), i.e. 'it hasn't been long since I got my license.' Two idioms to nail: (1) 면허를 따다 — you 따다 ('pluck/win') a license, NOT 받다 ('receive') or 가지다 ('have'); 면허 받았어요 sounds wrong because 따다 captures passing the test. (2) -은 지 + 얼마 안 됐다 is the set frame for 'I recently started/did X' — note this 지 is the time-elapsed 지 (always spaced, attached to a past-style -ㄴ/은 form), totally different from the ending -ㄹ지 ('whether'). A culturally key partner phrase is 초보운전 ('beginner driver'), the label new drivers put on their car so others give them room. The English-speaker trap is the time construction (using 동안 'during' instead of -은 지) and saying 면허 가져요 ('I have a license') when they mean they recently passed. Tense: it's frozen as 딴 지 ... 안 됐어요 (past 됐). To a friend, ...얼마 안 됐어. Don't confuse 면허 ('license/permit') with 자격증 (a skills certificate) — driving specifically is 운전면허.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 면허 받았어요 instead of 면허 땄어요.
A license is obtained with 따다 ('to win/get', as in passing a test): 면허(를) 땄어요. 받다 ('receive') sounds like it was simply handed to you.
Using 동안 instead of -은 지 for elapsed time.
'It's been (not long) since I got it' uses -은 지 ... 됐어요: 딴 지 얼마 안 됐어요. 동안 ('during') is for an ongoing duration, not time-since-an-event.
Confusing the time 지 with the ending -ㄹ지.
딴 지 ('since getting it') is the spaced time-noun 지 after a past form. -ㄹ지 ('whether') is a verb ending, e.g. 갈지 (whether to go). They look alike but do different jobs.

entries.nuance: 주차비 얼마예요? is 주차비 ('parking fee', 주차 + 費 'cost/fee') + 얼마예요 ('how much is it?'), the basic cost question for a paid lot. The suffix -비 (費) attaches to many fees you'll meet driving: 주차비 (parking), 주유비 / 기름값 (fuel cost), 통행료 (toll — note this one uses 료, not 비), so recognizing -비 ('cost of') is high-leverage. A slightly more formal variant is 주차 요금 어떻게 돼요? (요금 = 'charge/rate'); 얼마예요? is the warm everyday choice. Practically, ask about 할인/무료 (discount/free): customers often get 무료 (free) for a few hours or 할인 (validation) with a receipt, so the smart follow-up is 식당 이용하면 할인돼요? ('discount if I eat here?'). The English-speaker trap is using 가격 ('price', for goods) for a service fee — a parking CHARGE is 주차비/요금, not 주차 가격; 가격 sounds like the price tag of an object. Another trap: 비 here is the fee suffix, unrelated to 비 ('rain'). For per-time rates, frame it as 30분에 얼마예요? (에 = 'per'). With a friend, 주차비 얼마야? Don't confuse 주차비 ('parking fee') with 주차장 ('parking lot') — one is the cost, the other the place.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주차 가격 얼마예요?
가격 is the price of goods. A service charge like parking is 주차비 or 주차 요금. 주차 가격 sounds like the 'price' of parking as a product.

Many Korean lots are free or discounted for customers. After 주차비 얼마예요?, ask 무료예요? or 할인돼요? to check for 무료 (free) hours or a customer 할인 (discount).

entries.nuance: 여기 주차하면 안 돼요? is 여기 ('here') + 주차하다 ('to park') + -면 안 돼요 ('it's not OK if...'), literally 'is it not OK if I park here?' — a polite check on whether parking is forbidden. Two opposite patterns to keep straight: -아/어도 돼요? = 'may I? / is it OK to?' (asking PERMISSION), and -(으)면 안 돼요 = 'it's not allowed / you mustn't' (a PROHIBITION). So 주차해도 돼요? asks 'can I park?', while 주차하면 안 돼요 states/asks 'you can't park / can't I park?'. Mixing these up is the single biggest -돼요 error for learners. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'is it allowed' as 허락돼요? (허락 = formal 'permission/consent') — too formal for parking; use the -도 돼요/-면 안 돼요 frames. Don't confuse 안 돼요 ('not allowed', from 되다) with 안 해요 ('don't do').

허락 ('formal permission/consent') is too heavy for parking. Use the everyday 주차해도 돼요? ('is it OK to park?') instead.

From 되다, the correct form is 돼요 (되어요 → 돼요). 되요 is a common misspelling. So it's 주차하면 안 돼요.

entries.nuance: 여기서 좌회전해요? is 여기서 ('here', 여기 + 서 from 에서 'at') + 좌회전하다 ('to turn left', 좌 'left' 左 + 회전 'rotation/turn' 回轉) + 해요? (polite question), 'do I turn left here?'. The four directions you must know while driving are Sino-Korean compounds: 좌회전 (left turn), 우회전 (right turn), 직진 (going straight, 直進), and 유턴 (U-turn, the English loan). These are exactly the words the 내비 (GPS) speaks and the road signs show, so memorize them as a set. The particle is 에서 (contracted to 서 in speech) because the turn is an action happening AT a location: 여기서 ('at here'). A top learner error is using 에 instead — 여기에 좌회전해요 is wrong because the turn is an activity at that spot, not a destination you arrive at. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'turn left' with the plain verb 돌다 ('to turn/spin') as 왼쪽으로 돌아요? — understandable in casual talk but 좌회전하다 is the precise driving term matching signs and nav. A culturally key word is 비보호 (좌회전) — an 'unprotected left turn' you make only when oncoming traffic is clear or on a green arrow; foreigners get tickets misjudging these. To a friend, 여기서 좌회전해? Don't mix up 좌 (left) and 우 (right) — a one-syllable slip that sends you the wrong way.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에 instead of 에서/서 for the turn location.
A turn is an action performed AT a place, so use 에서 (spoken 서): 여기서 좌회전해요? 여기에 좌회전 is wrong — 에 marks a destination, not where an action happens.
Saying 왼쪽으로 돌아요? for a driving turn.
돌다 ('to spin/turn around') is loose. The exact driving verb is 좌회전하다, matching road signs and your nav: 여기서 좌회전해요?
Confusing 좌회전 (left) with 우회전 (right).
좌 = left (左), 우 = right (右). Swapping them reverses your route. Lock in 좌회전/우회전/직진/유턴 as the four driving directions.

entries.nuance: 하이패스로 가세요 is 하이패스 ('Hi-Pass', Korea's electronic toll-collection system) + 로 ('via/by way of', the means/route particle) + 가세요 ('please go'), 'go through the Hi-Pass lane.' This is essential for highway (고속도로) driving: 하이패스 is the prepaid transponder (단말기 'unit' + a 카드) that lets you pass tollgates without stopping, while drivers without it use a 일반 차로 ('regular lane') to pay 통행료 ('toll', 通行料 — note 료, not 비) by cash or card. The particle 로/으로 here marks the route/means ('via Hi-Pass'), a very useful pattern: 이쪽으로 가세요 ('go this way'), 카드로 내다 ('pay by card'). A top learner error is using 에 or 에서 instead of 로 — 하이패스로 가다 means 'go BY WAY OF Hi-Pass', which is what you want. The English-speaker trap is treating 'Hi-Pass' as just a card; in Korean 하이패스 names the whole lane/system, so 하이패스로 가세요 ('take the Hi-Pass route') is natural. Also distinguish 통행료 (highway toll) from 주차비 (parking fee) and 주유비 (fuel cost) — all driving costs but different words. Practically, if your 하이패스 카드 is out of money it beeps and the gate may not open, so locals top it up; if you have no unit, you MUST take the 일반 차로. To a friend, 하이패스로 가. Don't confuse 차로 ('traffic lane') with 차료 (not a word) or 통행료.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에/에서 instead of 로 for the lane.
To go VIA the Hi-Pass lane you mark the route with 로/으로: 하이패스로 가세요. 하이패스에 가세요 sounds like going TO a place called Hi-Pass, not passing through that lane.
Thinking 하이패스 is only a card.
In Korean 하이패스 names the whole electronic-toll lane/system, not just the card. So 하이패스로 가세요 ('take the Hi-Pass lane') is the natural instruction.
Confusing 통행료 (toll) with 주차비/주유비.
통행료 (uses 료) is the highway toll; 주차비 is parking, 주유비/기름값 is fuel. At a tollgate you 통행료(를) 내다 ('pay the toll'), not 주차비.

entries.shortExplanation: 도와주세요! is a practical expression meaning "Help me, please!".
entries.explanation: 도와주세요! (dowajuseyo!) means "Help me, please!". Say it as one set phrase — for example 도와주세요! ("Please help me!"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: Standard polite call for help to anyone, strangers included
반말, shouted to a close friend or family member
Softer, more formal request when there's no immediate danger
누가 (someone) added when calling out to a crowd

examples.romanization: dowajuseyo! dowajuseyo!
examples.en: Help! Help me!
examples.note: Shouted twice — the bare cry that draws attention fast

examples.en: I can't lift this bag. Please help me.
examples.note: Everyday non-emergency use; 좀 softens it to 'a little'

entries.nuance: 도와주세요 is the all-purpose cry for help, built from 돕다 (to help) + 주세요 (please give/do for me), so it literally asks someone to 'do the helping for me'. In a true emergency you shout it bare and loud; for ordinary favors you cushion it with 좀 ('a little') or upgrade to 도와주시겠어요? to sound polite rather than panicked. The 반말 form 도와줘 is only for a close friend or younger family, never a stranger. The nearest alternative, 살려 주세요 ('save my life'), is reserved for life-or-death danger — use 도와주세요 for everything from a heavy suitcase to a medical scare. English speakers often say just 'help' as 도움 (the noun) or drop the 주세요 and bark 도와, which sounds like an order; keep 주세요 to stay both clear and polite.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 도움 to mean 'Help!'
도움 is the noun 'help/aid', not a cry. To call for help you need the verb plus 주세요: 도와주세요.
Shouting 도와 to a stranger.
Bare 도와 is a blunt 반말 command that sounds rude under stress. Add 주세요 (도와주세요) for anyone you don't know.
Building it as 도와 주세요 with the wrong stem, e.g. 돕아주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 도와주세요 is the all-purpose cry for help. In a true emergency you shout it bare and loud; for ordinary favors you cushion it with 좀 ('a little') or upgrade to 도와주시겠어요? to sound polite rather than panicked. The 반말 form 도와줘 is only for a close friend or younger family, never a stranger.
The nearest alternative, 살려 주세요 ('save my life'), is reserved for life-or-death danger. Use 도와주세요 for everything from a heavy suitcase to a medical scare.
Built from 돕다 (to help) + 주세요 (please give/do for me), so it literally asks someone to 'do the helping for me'.
English speakers often say just 'help' as 도움 (the noun) or drop the 주세요 and bark 도와, which sounds like an order. Keep 주세요 to stay both clear and polite.

entries.nuance: 살려 주세요 comes from 살리다 (to save a life, the causative of 살다 'to live') + 주세요, so it literally begs 'please keep me alive' — far stronger than 도와주세요. You use it only when your life is genuinely at risk: drowning, an attacker, a fire. The dividing line from 도와주세요 is mortal danger: a heavy bag gets 도와주세요, a person grabbing you gets 살려 주세요. The stem is 살리- → 살려, and the ending is 주세요 (not 주새요). Correct: 살려 주세요.

entries.nuance: 불이야! is the fixed Korean equivalent of yelling 'Fire!' — 불 (fire) + the exclamatory 이야, a 반말-rooted alarm everyone shouts no matter who's listening, because there's no time to be polite. entries.explanation: 길을 잃었어요 (gireul ireosseoyo) means "I'm lost.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 길을 잃었어요 ("I'm lost (lit. I lost the road)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말, said to a passerby or staff when you can't find your way
반말 to a friend or on the phone with family
-어버리다 stresses it fully happened — more helpless

usagePhrases.en: It's my first time here, so I don't really know the way
usagePhrases.note: Softer, explains why you're lost

examples.ko: 저… 길을 잃었어요.
examples.romanization: jeo… gireul ireosseoyo.
examples.en: Um… I'm lost.
examples.note: Bare admission; 저… buys a beat to flag a stranger politely

examples.ko: 친구 집을 찾고 있는데 길을 잃었어요.
examples.romanization: chingu jibeul chatgo inneunde gireul ireosseoyo.
examples.en: I'm looking for my friend's house but I got lost.
examples.note: Everyday context with 찾고 있는데 ('I'm looking for, but…')

examples.ko: 지하철역에서 나왔는데 길을 잃었어요. 이 주소 어떻게 가요?
examples.romanization: jihacheoryeogeseo nawanneunde gireul ireosseoyo. i juso eotteoke gayo?
examples.en: I came out of the subway station and got lost. How do I get to this address?
examples.note: Real situation handing over an address to ask directions

entries.nuance: 길을 잃었어요 literally says 'I lost the road' — 길 (road/way) + 을 (object marker) + 잃다 (to lose) in the past tense, which is exactly how Korean expresses being lost. Note the particle: it is 길을 잃다 with the object marker 을, not 길에 or 길이. To a stranger you use the 존댓말 잃었어요; to a friend, 잃었어. Adding -어버리다 (길을 잃어버렸어요) makes it sound more hopelessly done. The nearest alternative is simply asking 여기가 어디예요? ('where is this?'), but that only asks your location, whereas 길을 잃었어요 explains your whole predicament and invites help. English speakers say 나는 잃어버렸어요 ('I lost [something]') with no object, which leaves the listener wondering what you lost; you must keep 길을.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나는 잃어버렸어요 with no object.
잃어버리다 needs an object. To mean 'I'm lost', say what was lost — the way: 길을 잃었어요.
Using the wrong particle: 길이 잃었어요 or 길에 잃었어요.
잃다 takes the object marker. It must be 길을 잃었어요.
Saying 길을 잊었어요.
잊다 is 'to forget'; 잃다 is 'to lose'. Being lost is 길을 잃었어요, not 잊었어요.

examples.en: I lost my wallet.

entries.nuance: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 = 지갑 (wallet) + 을 + 잃어버리다, where -어버리다 adds the nuance that the loss is total and you feel the regret, which is why Koreans almost always say 잃어버리다 rather than bare 잃다 for personal belongings. English speakers calque 'I lost' as plain 잃었어요 (sounds clipped) or forget 지갑 takes 을, saying 지갑이 — but the thing lost is the object, so it must be 지갑을.

잃어버리다 implies you misplaced it. If stolen, say 지갑을 도둑맞았어요 or 도난당했어요.

지갑 is a wallet/purse; 가방 is a bag. Name the right item: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.

entries.nuance: 경찰을 불러 주세요 = 경찰 (police) + 을 + 부르다 (to call/summon) + 주세요. Korea's police line is 112 (fire/ambulance is 119) — mixing them up is the classic foreigner error. English speakers also say 경찰에게 전화 (to phone the police), which is fine but less natural in a shout than 경찰 좀 불러 주세요.

The verb is 부르다 → 불러, not 불어 (which is 불다 'to blow'). Correct: 경찰을 불러 주세요.

entries.nuance: 한국어를 잘 못해요 = 한국어 (the Korean language) + 를 + 잘 (well) + 못하다 (to be unable to do well). The key is 잘 못해요 ('can't do well') vs. 안 해요 ('don't do it') — you're saying you lack ability, not that you refuse; and 못해요 is written as one idea even though 못 (cannot) negates 하다. 한국어 is the neutral/formal word; 한국말 is more colloquial. The dividing line from 한국어 못해요 (without 잘) is degree: with 잘 it softens to 'not very good', without it sounds like 'I can't speak Korean at all'. The polite follow-up is 천천히 말씀해 주세요. English speakers say 한국어를 안 해요 ('I don't do Korean', sounds unwilling) or 한국어가 못해요 with the wrong particle — the language is the object, so 한국어를.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 한국어를 안 해요.
안 하다 = 'choose not to do'. To say you lack ability, use 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Using the subject particle: 한국어가 잘 못해요.
The language is the object of 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.

Here 못 means 'cannot' (잘 못해요 = can't do well). 잘못하다 as one word means 'to do wrong / make a mistake' — a different meaning.

entries.nuance: 영어 하시는 분 계세요? = 영어 (English) + 하시는 (honorific 'who does/speaks') + 분 (the honorific word for 'person') + 계세요 (honorific 'is there?'). The dividing line from 영어 할 줄 아세요? is target: 계세요? scans a group ('is there someone…?'), while 할 줄 아세요? asks one specific person directly. The softener 혹시 ('by any chance') makes either gentler. English speakers say 영어 말해요? (calquing 'speak') or use plain 사람 있어요? to an elder/official, which is under-polite; to a room, the honorific 하시는 분 계세요? is the natural, courteous form.

Saying 영어 말해요? for 'speak English'.
Korean uses 하다 for languages: 영어 하시는 분, or 영어 할 줄 아세요? for one person.
Using 있으세요? wrongly here.
For 'is there a person', the honorific existence verb is 계세요 (people exist with 계시다): 영어 하시는 분 계세요?

entries.nuance: 사고가 났어요 = 사고 (accident) + 가 (subject marker) + 나다 ('to break out/occur') in the past. Korean says accidents and fires 'occur' with 나다, and the thing that occurs takes 가/이: 사고가 나다, 불이 나다. The dividing line: 사고 is any accident; 교통사고 specifies a traffic/car accident — give the specific word when phoning 119 so they send the right unit. The nearest report phrase is 사고를 당했어요 ('I had/suffered an accident'), which centers the victim, vs. 사고가 났어요, which simply states it happened. English speakers calque 'I made an accident' as 사고를 만들었어요 (wrong — accidents aren't 'made'), or use the object 사고를 with 나다; with 나다 the accident is the subject, so 사고가 났어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 사고를 만들었어요 for 'there was an accident'.
Accidents 'occur' with 나다, not 'are made'. Say 사고가 났어요.
Using 사고를 났어요.
With 나다 the accident is the subject: 사고가 났어요. (Use 사고를 당했어요 if you want 'I had an accident'.)
Saying just 사고 to a dispatcher.
Specify what kind for the right response: 교통사고가 났어요 for a car crash.

entries.nuance: 아파요 is the polite form of 아프다, which covers both 'to be in pain' and 'to be sick/ill' — one word does both jobs in Korean. The body part that hurts takes the subject marker 가/이: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요. The dividing line from 다쳤어요 is cause: 아프다 = pain or illness from any source (a cold, a stomachache); 다치다 = an injury from an accident (a fall, a cut). Note the irregular conjugation: 아프 + 아요 contracts to 아파요 (the ㅡ drops). English speakers say 나는 아파요 fine, but then mark the body part with 을/를 (배를 아파요) — in Korean the body part is the subject of 아프다, so 배가 아파요. They also overuse 병 ('disease') to say 'I'm sick'; everyday 'I'm sick/unwell' is just 아파요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

The hurting part is the subject of 아프다: 배가 아파요.
Writing 아프요 instead of 아파요.
아프다 is a ㅡ-irregular: 아프 + 아요 → 아파요.
Using 아파요 for an accident injury.
For a wound from a fall or cut, use 다쳤어요; 아파요 is general pain/illness.

entries.nuance: 부러워요 comes from the adjective 부럽다 ('to be envious'), and it is the GOOD, warm kind of envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Koreans say it constantly as a friendly compliment when you hear someone's nice news: a trip, a new phone, a close commute. It is NOT bitter or hostile. The phrase to keep far away from it is 질투 / 질투하다 ('jealousy'), which is the dark, possessive jealousy of a romantic rival or someone who resents your success — calling a friend's good news 질투나요 sounds creepy or resentful, so use 부러워요 for the everyday 'I envy you.' Register: 부러워요 is polite, 부러워 is 반말, and Koreans love the bare exclamation 부럽다 muttered out loud even to elders as a soft 'ahh, lucky.' The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the direction: you do NOT say 당신을 부러워요 ('I envy YOU' with an object) — the natural pattern marks what is envied with 이/가, so the bag you covet is 가방이 부러워요 ('I envy [your] bag'), the person/their situation is 네가 부러워, or, most often, you just say 부러워요 about the whole thing. A real trap is mixing up 부럽다 ('envious') with the look-alike 부끄럽다 ('shy/embarrassed') — they share 부 but mean opposite-feeling things; 'I'm jealous' is 부러워요, not 부끄러워요. To name what you envy, use 이/가: 네 휴가가 부러워.

질투 is dark, possessive jealousy (a love rival, resentment). Friendly 'lucky you' envy is 부러워요. 질투나요 to a friend's vacation sounds hostile.

부럽다 takes the envied thing/situation with 이/가, not a person with 을/를. Say 네가 부러워 ('I envy you/your situation') or just 부러워.

Don't use 에. The envied thing takes 이/가: 차가 부러워요, or simply 부러워요 about the whole thing.

entries.nuance: 짜증나요 is from 짜증(이) 나다 ('irritation arises'), the everyday word for the prickly, fed-up feeling when small things go wrong — the bus is late, the wifi drops, someone nags. It is honest and extremely common, but it is BLUNT and a little crude, so the safe zone is venting about a SITUATION to a friend or muttering to yourself; saying 짜증나요 straight to a person's face (especially a senior, a coworker, or staff) is rude and confrontational, like snapping 'you're pissing me off.' For a more controlled, polite 'that's a bit much,' Koreans soften with 좀 짜증나네요 or step up to the gentler-sounding 불편해요 ('it's uncomfortable/inconvenient') when complaining officially. The phrase people confuse it with is 화나요 ('I'm angry'): 화나다 is real, bigger anger, while 짜증나다 is petty irritation/annoyance — using 화나요 for a late bus overstates it, and using 짜증나요 about a serious betrayal understates it. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: it is the intransitive 짜증(이) 나다 ('irritation comes up'), so you say 짜증나요 (it arises in you), NOT 짜증해요 (not a word) and NOT 나를 짜증나요. If something/someone makes you annoyed, mark the cause with 때문에: 너 때문에 짜증나 ('I'm annoyed because of you') — still 반말-only and pointed.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짜증나요 directly to staff or a senior.
It's blunt and confrontational, like 'you're annoying me.' For a polite complaint use 좀 불편해요 or describe the problem; save 짜증나 for friends/yourself.
Saying 짜증해요.
There is no verb 짜증하다. It's 짜증(이) 나다 — the irritation 'arises': 짜증나요. The 나다 part is essential.
Using 화나요 for minor annoyances.
화나다 is genuine anger; for a late bus or slow wifi it's overkill. The right word for petty irritation is 짜증나요.

entries.nuance: 설레요 comes from 설레다 ('to flutter, to feel one's heart race with sweet anticipation'). This is the warm, hopeful, butterflies-in-the-stomach excitement — before a trip, a date, a reunion, the first snow. It is gentle and romantic-leaning, and Koreans use it a lot in everyday life and all over song lyrics and dramas. The word to contrast it with is 떨리다 ('to tremble / be nervous'): 떨리다 is the JITTERY nerves before an exam or a speech (can be bad nerves), while 설레다 is the PLEASANT flutter you welcome — they overlap (a first date is both), but if you say 설레요 before a scary job interview it sounds odd, because 설레다 implies you're looking forward to it. Another near-word is 기대돼요 ('I'm looking forward to it'), which is cooler and more mental — 설레다 is the physical heart-flutter. Register: 설레요 polite, 설레 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation and spelling: the stem is 설레-, so it's 설레요 / 설렜어요 — NOT 설레여요 (a common wrong form) and NOT 설래요 (frequent misspelling). Also it's intransitive: 마음이 설레요 ('my heart flutters'), you don't 'do' 설레 to an object.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing or saying 설레여요 / 설래요.
The stem is 설레-, so present is 설레요 and past is 설렜어요. 설레여요 and 설래요 are common but wrong; keep it 설레요.
Using 설레요 before something you dread (exam, scary interview).
설레다 implies happy anticipation. For nervous jitters use 떨려요 ('I'm nervous'). Mixing is fine only when you're genuinely excited too.
Treating it as 'excited' in the loud/hyped sense.
설레다 is a soft inner flutter, not pumped-up hype. For 'pumped/thrilled' loudness, 신나요 fits better; 설레다 is gentle anticipation.

entries.nuance: 민망해요 (from 민망하다) is the squirmy, awkward embarrassment you feel after a small social misstep — you fell in public, you got caught, you received too much praise, an awkward silence dragged on. It's the 'oh no, this is so awkward, I want to shrink' feeling, and it's light/social, not deep shame. The big contrast is with 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: 부끄럽다 is shy/bashful (a blushing, modest shyness — also used for moral shame in writing), while 창피하다 is stronger, more 'humiliated / lost face' (you really screwed up publicly). Roughly: 민망하다 = awkward/uncomfortable embarrassment, 부끄럽다 = shy/blushing, 창피하다 = mortified/humiliated. Many learners pick one and overuse it; matching the strength matters. Register: 민망해요 polite, 민망해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 부끄러워요 for every kind of 'embarrassed' — but a fall in public or an awkward moment is more 민망해요 or 창피해요 than the shy 부끄러워요. Also it's an adjective describing your state: 민망해요 ('I feel awkward'), so don't say 민망당했어요 or attach an object — and don't confuse 민망하다 with the unrelated 미안하다 ('to be sorry'), which sound alike to beginners.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 민망하다 with 미안하다.
They sound similar but 미안하다 = 'sorry (apology)', 민망하다 = 'awkward/embarrassed'. 'I feel awkward' is 민망해요, not 미안해요.
Using 부끄러워요 for an awkward public slip-up.
부끄럽다 leans 'shy/bashful.' A public fall or cringe moment is better 민망해요 (awkward) or 창피해요 (mortified). Pick the strength that fits.
Overshooting with 창피해요 for a tiny awkwardness.
창피하다 is strong 'humiliated/lost face.' For a small, harmless awkward moment, 민망해요 is the right, lighter word.

entries.nuance: 뿌듯해요 (from 뿌듯하다) is the warm, full, satisfied pride you feel inside after you (or someone you love) accomplished something — you finished a hard task, your kid did well, your effort paid off. The image is your chest swelling with quiet, happy fullness. It is INWARD and humble-feeling, which is why Koreans use it freely about themselves without sounding arrogant. The key contrast is with 자랑스럽다 ('to be proud (of)'): 자랑스럽다 is more outward/declarative pride you express ABOUT someone or something (아들이 자랑스러워요 'I'm proud of my son'), often spoken to or about others, while 뿌듯하다 describes the felt inner glow of satisfaction, usually about your own effort or a heartwarming moment. Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 ('I'm proud of myself') can sound boastful, but 뿌듯해요 sounds modest and relatable. Register: 뿌듯해요 polite, 뿌듯해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is using 자랑스럽다 for the personal warm-fuzzy feeling and accidentally sounding boastful, or trying to attach an object to 뿌듯하다 — it's an adjective for YOUR state (뿌듯해요), so you don't say 너를 뿌듯해요. Mark the cause with -아서/-니까: 끝내서 뿌듯해요 ('I feel fulfilled because I finished'). Don't confuse it with 만족하다 ('to be satisfied'), which is cooler and more evaluative.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 for personal satisfaction.
자랑스럽다 is outward, declarative pride and can sound boastful about yourself. The humble inner glow is 뿌듯해요.
Attaching an object: 시험을 뿌듯해요.
뿌듯하다 describes your state, not a target. Mark the cause: 시험 끝나서 뿌듯해요 ('I feel fulfilled because the exam's over').
Swapping in 만족해요 for the warm feeling.
만족하다 is cool, evaluative 'satisfied (it met the standard).' The warm, chest-swelling pride is 뿌듯해요. They're not interchangeable.

entries.nuance: 답답해요 (from 답답하다) is a uniquely Korean feeling word covering a whole family of 'closed-in' sensations: physically stuffy/cramped (a tiny room, tight clothes, a stuffy chest), AND emotionally stifled/frustrated when you can't get through — communication isn't working, a slow person won't understand, you're stuck and powerless. The thread is 'blocked, can't breathe/can't get out.' This is different from 짜증나다 ('irritated') and 화나다 ('angry'): 짜증나다 is prickly annoyance at small things, 화나다 is outward anger, but 답답하다 is the INWARD, helpless, suffocating frustration of being stuck — often with no one to blame, just a blocked situation. There's no single English word, which is exactly why learners miss it: English speakers say 화나요 ('angry') when a Korean would say 답답해요 ('stifled/stuck'). A stronger sibling idiom is 속(이) 터지다 ('my insides burst') for extreme 답답함. Register: 답답해요 polite, 답답해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) defaulting to 화나요/짜증나요 for this stuck feeling, and (2) the particle: the cause takes -아서/-때문에 (말이 안 통해서 답답해요), and the thing that's stifling can be the subject (가슴이 답답해요 'my chest feels tight'). Don't translate it as just 'frustrated (angry)' — it's the boxed-in, can't-get-through frustration.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 화나요 for the stuck, can't-get-through feeling.
화나다 is outward anger at someone. The helpless, boxed-in 'I can't make this work/get through' feeling is 답답해요. They're different emotions.
Forcing one English word and missing the physical sense.
답답하다 also means physically stuffy/cramped (room, chest, clothes): 가슴이 답답해요 ('my chest feels tight'). It's not only emotional.
Saying 답답나요 like 짜증나요.
답답하다 is an adjective: 답답해요, not 답답나요. Only 짜증 takes 나다. Keep 답답해요.

entries.nuance: 서운해요 (from 서운하다) is one of the most important feeling words in Korean relationships and has NO clean English equivalent. It is the soft, wistful hurt/disappointment you feel when someone CLOSE — a friend, family, partner — does less than you hoped: they forgot to call, left you out, didn't notice your effort, or are leaving sooner than you'd like. It's gentle and tinged with affection: you say it BECAUSE you care, not to attack. The contrast to nail down is 섭섭하다 (a near-synonym, almost interchangeable, maybe a touch more 'sad to part') versus 화나다 ('angry') and 실망하다 ('disappointed (in someone's character/standards)'). Crucially, 서운하다 is NOT anger and NOT cold disappointment — say 화났어요 and you've declared a fight; say 실망했어요 and you've judged their character harshly; say 서운했어요 and you've gently shown that their distance hurt because you're close. This is the phrase that repairs relationships. The English-speaker pitfall is huge: there's no English word, so learners reach for 'I was hurt/disappointed' and pick 상처받았어요 (too strong — 'I was wounded') or 실망했어요 (too judgmental) when the warm, fixable feeling is 서운해요. Also it's an adjective for your state (서운해요 / 서운했어요); mark the cause with -아서/-니까/-아서 (연락 안 해서 서운했어요). You can also say 서운하게 ('in a hurtful way'). Register: 서운해요 polite, 서운해 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 화났어요 when you mean 서운했어요.
화나다 is anger and signals conflict. 서운하다 is gentle, affectionate hurt that someone close let you down. To repair rather than fight, say 서운했어요.
Reaching for 상처받았어요 ('I was wounded').
That's too strong for a small letdown — it implies deep damage. For 'you kind of hurt my feelings,' the soft word is 서운했어요.
Translating it as cold 'disappointed' with 실망했어요.
실망하다 judges someone's character/standards harshly. 서운하다 is warm and relational ('I wish you'd cared more'). Don't swap them; the tone is opposite.

entries.nuance: 후련해요 (from 후련하다) is the clean, lightened, cleared-out RELIEF you feel right after a heavy burden lifts — exams end, you finally say what was bottled up, a long worry resolves, you have a good cry. The image is your chest/insides (속) opening up and breathing freely; it's the natural opposite of 답답하다 ('stifled'). Often paired with 속이: 속이 후련해요 ('what a load off'). The word to distinguish it from is 시원하다, which overlaps a lot ('refreshing/relieving') but literally means 'cool/refreshing' and covers cold drinks, cool weather, and even oddly a hot bath or spicy soup that 'hits the spot' — 후련하다 is specifically the EMOTIONAL/psychological unburdening, while 시원하다 is broader and more physical. entries.explanation: "Man, I'm seriously jealous (mutter)" — that is 부럽다 진짜 (bureopda jinjja). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 부럽다 진짜 ("Ugh, so jealous, for real"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.note: The drawn-out mutter of genuine, warm envy

entries.nuance: 부럽다 진짜 is the spoken, exclamatory form of 부럽다 ('to be envious') — Koreans constantly drop the polite ending and just exhale 부럽다 (often with 진짜 'for real' or 아 'ahh') as a warm, wistful 'lucky you / I wish that were me.' It is the SAME friendly envy as 부러워요 but in its most natural muttered shape; you can say the bare 부럽다 even around elders as a soft reaction without it being rude, because exclamatory adjective-다 functions like thinking out loud rather than 반말 directed AT someone. To say it politely straight to the person, use 부럽네요. The contrast to keep in mind is the dark 질투(나다) ('possessive jealousy') — 부럽다 is never hostile. There's also a famous playful phrase 부러우면 지는 거다 ('if you're envious, you've already lost'), used to tease yourself for being jealous. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, learners over-formalize and never use the natural 부럽다 exclamation, so they sound stiff; second, they confuse the plain-form exclamation 부럽다 (fine to mutter aloud) with using 반말 verbs/commands at an elder (not fine). Also, mark what you envy with 이/가 if you name it (네가 부럽다), and don't attach 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking the bare 부럽다 is rude to elders.
Exclamatory adjective-다 is like thinking aloud, not 반말 aimed at someone. Muttering 부럽다 near an elder is fine; to address them say 부럽네요.
Always saying 부러워요 and never the natural 부럽다.
Koreans constantly exclaim 부럽다 / 부럽다 진짜. Only using the textbook 부러워요 sounds stiff. Learn the muttered form too.
Adding 을/를 to what you envy.
It's 네가 부럽다 / 그게 부럽다 with 이/가, not 너를 부럽다. The envied thing/situation takes the subject marker.

entries.shortExplanation: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please don't make this so frustrating / annoying".

entries.nuance: This entry teaches the CAUSATIVE — 짜증 나게 하다 ('to make (someone) annoyed/irritated'), built from 짜증(이) 나다 plus -게 하다 ('make it so that...'). It's how you point at the SOURCE of irritation instead of just venting your own state. Be warned: it's confrontational. 짜증 나게 하지 마(세요) ('stop annoying me') and 사람 짜증 나게 하네 ('you're getting on my nerves') are things you say to people you're close to or genuinely irritated with — NOT to staff, seniors, or in polite company, where you'd instead say 좀 그만해 주세요 ('please stop') or describe the problem calmly. The phrase to distinguish is 신경 쓰이다 / 신경 쓰게 하다 ('to bother / weigh on the mind'), which is milder and more about distraction/worry, whereas 짜증 나게 하다 is openly 'you're pissing me off.' The English-speaker pitfall is structural: learners try 너 나를 짜증해 (wrong on two counts) — remember it's 짜증(이) 나다 (intransitive), and to make someone feel it you need the causative -게 하다: 짜증 나게 하다. So 'you're annoying me' is 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해, NOT 너 짜증나. Also note 사람 here doesn't mean a specific person 'human'; idiomatically 사람 짜증 나게 하다 = 'you're irritating me.' Default to softer phrasing unless you really mean to push back.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 너 짜증나 to mean 'you're annoying me'.
너 짜증나 means 'YOU feel annoyed.' To say someone annoys YOU, use the causative: 너 (나를) 짜증 나게 해. Direction matters.
Using it with staff or seniors.
짜증 나게 하다 is blunt and confrontational. With staff/seniors say 좀 그만해 주세요 or calmly state the issue. Reserve this for close, genuinely-fed-up moments.
Writing 짜증나게해 as one chunk wrongly.
It's 짜증(이) 나다 + -게 하다 → 짜증 나게 하다. Spacing/structure: the 나다 + 게 하다 causative is what carries 'make someone annoyed.'

entries.shortExplanation: 마음이 설레요 is a practical expression meaning "My heart is fluttering".
entries.explanation: 마음이 설레요 (maeumi seolleyo) means "My heart is fluttering". Say it as one set phrase — for example 마음이 설레요 ("My heart is fluttering"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.en: Whenever I see them, my heart flutters.
examples.note: Romantic flutter; -만 보면 = 'every time I just see...'

examples.en: The concert's tomorrow, so my heart's already pounding and fluttering.
examples.note: Pairs 두근거리다 (pounding) with 설레다 (fluttering)

examples.note: 설레는 마음으로 as a warm sign-off in a message

entries.nuance: 마음이 설레요 makes explicit what 설레다 implies — that it's the HEART (마음, the heart/mind) that flutters. This teaches the natural subject pattern: in Korean, body/heart words often take 이/가 as the grammatical subject of a feeling (마음이 설레요, 가슴이 두근거려요, 가슴이 답답해요), which is very different from English 'I feel...'. Learning this pattern fixes a whole class of errors. The flutter words to keep straight: 설레다 = sweet anticipatory flutter (you welcome it); 두근거리다 / 두근두근하다 = the heart physically POUNDING (can be excitement OR fear/nerves); 떨리다 = trembling/nervous (often bad nerves). For a happy crush, 마음이 설레요 and 가슴이 두근거려요 overlap nicely. The lovely set phrase 설레는 마음으로 ('with a fluttering/eager heart') is common in messages and cards. Register: 설레요 polite. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) saying 나는 설레요 and forgetting that Korean prefers 마음이/가슴이 as subject for these heart-feelings, and (2) the perennial 설레여요/설래요 misspelling — keep it 설레요 / 설렜어요. Don't use 두근거려요 alone if you mean specifically sweet anticipation, since pounding can also be fear; 설레요 disambiguates it as the happy kind.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나는 설레요 and skipping the heart subject.
Korean heart-feelings often take 마음이/가슴이 as subject: 마음이 설레요. It's a different structure from English 'I feel...'. Learn the body-as-subject pattern.
Using 두근거려요 assuming it's always happy.
두근거리다 is the heart POUNDING — could be excitement or fear. For specifically sweet anticipation, 설레요 makes the happy meaning clear.

structuredNuance.t: 마음이 설레요 makes explicit what 설레다 implies — that it's the HEART (마음, the heart/mind) that flutters. This teaches the natural subject pattern: in Korean, body/heart words often take 이/가 as the grammatical subject of a feeling (마음이 설레요, 가슴이 두근거려요, 가슴이 답답해요), very different from English 'I feel...'. Learning this pattern fixes a whole class of errors. The lovely set phrase 설레는 마음으로 ('with a fluttering/eager heart') is common in messages and cards.

The flutter words to keep straight: 설레다 = sweet anticipatory flutter (you welcome it); 두근거리다 / 두근두근하다 = the heart physically POUNDING (can be excitement OR fear/nerves); 떨리다 = trembling/nervous (often bad nerves). For a happy crush, 마음이 설레요 and 가슴이 두근거려요 overlap nicely. Don't use 두근거려요 alone if you mean specifically sweet anticipation, since pounding can also be fear; 설레요 disambiguates it as the happy kind.
Register: 설레요 polite. Korean prefers 마음이/가슴이 as the subject for these heart-feelings: 마음이 설레요. Keep it 설레요 / 설렜어요.
The pitfall is twofold: (1) saying 나는 설레요 and forgetting that Korean prefers 마음이/가슴이 as subject for these heart-feelings, and (2) the perennial 설레여요/설래요 misspelling — keep it 설레요 / 설렜어요.

entries.explanation: "Somehow my heart's fluttering" — that is 왠지 설레네요 (waenji seolleneyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 왠지 설레네요 ("Somehow I feel giddy"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; 왠지 ('for some reason') + soft 네요

examples.ko: 첫눈이 와서 그런가, 왠지 설레네요.
examples.romanization: cheonnuni waseo geureonga, waenji seolleneyo.
examples.en: Maybe because the first snow fell — somehow I feel giddy.
examples.note: 왠지 + 네요 muses about a vague happy flutter

examples.ko: 내일부터 새 직장이라 괜히 설레요.

entries.nuance: 왠지 설레네요 layers two very natural Korean pieces onto 설레다: 왠지 ('somehow, for some reason I can't name') and the soft sentence-ending -네요 (mild realization/observation, shared with the listener). The result is the cozy, atmospheric 'ooh, somehow this gives me butterflies' you say about first snow, a song, a season changing, a small good omen. Mastering 왠지 / 괜히 / 뭔가 here is the real lesson — they're filler-feelings Koreans sprinkle constantly: 왠지 ('for some reason'), 괜히 ('for no good reason,' often self-deprecating), 뭔가 ('something/somehow'). And -네요 vs. -요: 설레요 just states it; 설레네요 adds 'oh, I notice I'm fluttering' and invites the listener to feel it too — warmer and more conversational. The big English-speaker pitfall is spelling/sound-alikes: 왠지 ('somehow') is correct, but it's constantly confused with 웬일 ('what's up / what brings this'), and people miswrite 왠지 as 웬지 — remember only 왠지 (= 왜인지, 'why-ever') is right for 'somehow,' while 웬 is for 웬일/웬만하면. Also keep 설레네요 (not 설레네 with no 요 to a non-intimate), and avoid the 설래/설레여 misspelling again. Don't translate 왠지 as a literal 'why' — it's a vibe word, 'somehow.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 웬지 instead of 왠지.
'Somehow' is 왠지 (from 왜인지). 웬지 is wrong; 웬 belongs to 웬일/웬만하면. For the giddy-for-some-reason feeling: 왠지 설레네요.
Translating 왠지 as literal 'why'.
왠지 is a vibe word meaning 'somehow/for some reason I can't pin down,' not a question 'why.' It softens the statement, it doesn't ask anything.
Dropping 요 from 설레네 with non-intimates.
-네 alone is 반말. Politely it's 설레네요. The -네요 adds 'oh, I notice...' warmth while staying polite.

entries.shortExplanation: 속상해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)".
entries.explanation: 속상해요 (soksanghaeyo) = "I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 속상해요 ("I'm upset / it pains me"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; heartsore upset over something that went wrong
반말, to a friend or family
-아 죽겠어요 maxes the heartache
Empathy version (honorific) to comfort someone

examples.ko: 아끼던 컵이 깨져서 속상해요.
examples.romanization: akkideon keobi kkaejyeoseo soksanghaeyo.
examples.en: My favorite cup broke, so I'm upset.
examples.note: Heartsore over a small loss; 아끼던 = 'that I treasured'

examples.ko: 애가 아픈데 해 줄 게 없어서 너무 속상해요.
examples.romanization: aega apeunde hae jul ge eopseoseo neomu soksanghaeyo.
examples.en: My child is sick and there's nothing I can do — it breaks my heart.
examples.note: 속상하다 for distressed, helpless heartache about a loved one

examples.ko: 시험 망쳐서 속상하지? 괜찮아, 다음에 잘하면 돼.
examples.romanization: siheom mangchyeoseo soksanghaji? gwaenchana, daeume jalhamyeon dwae.
examples.en: You're upset you bombed the test, right? It's okay, do well next time.
examples.note: Comforting someone; -지? checks their feeling gently

entries.nuance: 속상해요 (from 속상하다, literally 속 'insides' + 상하다 'to be spoiled/hurt') is the heartsore, distressed UPSET you feel when something goes wrong and it pains your insides — you broke something dear, your kid is hurting, your effort failed, someone you love is in trouble. It's warmer and more tender than anger: it's the 'aw, this makes my heart sink' feeling, often with a note of helplessness. Distinguish it from neighbors: 화나요 ('angry') is outward and aimed at someone; 짜증나요 ('annoyed') is petty irritation; 서운해요 ('hurt/let down') is specifically about someone close disappointing you; but 속상하다 is broad heart-pain over a bad situation or loss, not necessarily anyone's fault. It's also gentler/more sympathetic than 슬프다 ('sad,' bigger grief) — 속상하다 is everyday heartache. A huge use is COMFORTING others: 많이 속상하시겠어요 ('you must be so upset') is how you empathize. Register: 속상해요 polite, 속상해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 화나요 for 'upset' — but English 'upset' is usually 속상해요 (heartsore), not 화나요 (angry); choosing 화나요 wrongly signals you're mad at someone. Also it's an adjective for your state (속상해요); mark the cause with -아서/-니까 (깨져서 속상해요). Don't confuse 속상하다 with 속(이) 상하다's literal cousin 배탈 ('upset stomach') — emotional upset is 속상하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'upset' as 화나요.
English 'upset' is usually heartsore distress = 속상해요, not anger. 화나요 means you're mad at someone, which changes the message. Default to 속상해요.
Using 속상해요 for an upset STOMACH.
Emotional upset is 속상하다. A bad stomach is 배탈(이) 나다 / 속이 안 좋다. Don't say 속상해요 when you mean indigestion.
Attaching an object: 그 일을 속상해요.
속상하다 describes your state. Mark the cause: 그 일 때문에 속상해요 ('I'm upset because of that').

What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.en: It's so vexing / it gets my goat
usagePhrases.note: Polite-casual; that teased, can't-have-it frustration
반말, to a friend
약(을) 올리다 = to taunt; the causative you'll hear a lot
Idiom: 'my stomach hurts' = resentful envy of others' luck

examples.ko: 나만 안 됐다고? 아, 약 올라.
examples.romanization: naman an dwaetdago? a, yak olla.
examples.en: Only I didn't get it? Ugh, that's so vexing.
examples.note: The teased, 'why-not-me' frustration; 나만 = 'only me'

examples.ko: 동생이 자꾸 자랑해서 약 올라요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi jakku jaranghaeseo yak ollayo.
examples.en: My sibling keeps bragging, so it's getting on my nerves.
examples.note: 약 오르다 from someone flaunting/taunting

examples.romanization: geuman yak ollyeoyo! nado gatgo sipdan marieyo.

examples.note: Causative 약 올리다 + -단 말이에요 ('I'm telling you')

entries.nuance: 약 올라요 (from 약(이) 오르다, literally 'the 약/sap rises') is a vivid colloquial feeling: the prickly, vexed, 'argh, why not me / stop rubbing it in' frustration — a blend of envy and being teased/provoked. You feel 약 오르다 when others have what you can't, when someone flaunts or taunts you, when you're SO close but miss out. It's playful-to-genuinely-annoyed depending on tone, and very common among friends and siblings. The crucial pair is the causative 약(을) 올리다 ('to taunt, to rub it in, to get a rise out of someone'): 약 올리지 마 ('don't tease me') is everyday speech. Distinguish from plain 부럽다 (warm, clean envy 'lucky you') and 짜증나다 (general irritation): 약 오르다 specifically has that taunted/provoked, sour-grapes edge. A related idiom is 배(가) 아프다 ('my stomach hurts' = I'm resentfully envious of someone's good fortune), from the proverb 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 ('when your cousin buys land, your stomach aches'). Register: 약 올라요 is casual/colloquial — fine with friends, but in formal settings you'd say 부럽다 or describe it neutrally. The English-speaker pitfall: (1) mixing up 약 오르다 (I feel vexed) with 약 올리다 (to taunt someone) — 너 약 올라 wrongly says 'you feel vexed' when you mean 너 나 약 올리지 마 ('don't taunt me'); (2) reading 약 literally as 'medicine' (here it's an idiom, the rising sap/bile); (3) overusing it in polite/formal company where it sounds too slangy.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 약 오르다 (feel vexed) with 약 올리다 (taunt).
약 올라요 = 'I feel vexed/taunted.' To tell someone to stop teasing: 약 올리지 마(세요). Mixing the two reverses who's doing what.
Reading 약 as 'medicine'.
Here 약 is idiomatic (the rising sap/bile), not 약 'medicine.' 약 올라요 means 'I'm vexed,' nothing to do with drugs.
Using 약 올라요 in formal/polite settings.
It's colloquial and a bit slangy. With seniors or in formal talk, use 부럽다 or neutrally describe the situation. Save 약 올라 for friends.

Distinguish from plain 부럽다 (warm, clean envy 'lucky you') and 짜증나다 (general irritation): 약 오르다 specifically has that taunted/provoked, sour-grapes edge. A related idiom is 배(가) 아프다 ('my stomach hurts' = I'm resentfully envious of someone's good fortune), from the proverb 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 ('when your cousin buys land, your stomach aches').
약 올라요 is from 약(이) 오르다, literally 'the 약/sap rises' — here 약 is idiomatic (the rising sap/bile), not 약 'medicine.'
Register: 약 올라요 is casual/colloquial — fine with friends, but in formal settings you'd say 부럽다 or describe it neutrally.

The pitfall: (1) mixing up 약 오르다 (I feel vexed) with 약 올리다 (to taunt someone) — 너 약 올라 wrongly says 'you feel vexed' when you mean 너 나 약 올리지 마 ('don't taunt me'); (2) reading 약 literally as 'medicine'; (3) overusing it in polite/formal company where it sounds too slangy.

entries.nuance: This entry teaches how to TELL someone they're hurting you — the relational repair move built on 서운하다. 서운하게 그러지 마세요 (lit. 'don't act in a way that makes me 서운') and 서운하게 왜 그래 ('why are you being so [cold/distant]?') are how Koreans gently push back when someone close is being cold, distant, or neglectful — WITHOUT escalating to a fight. The tone is intimate and a little vulnerable; you're saying 'you're hurting me because I care.' This only works with people you're close to (family, close friends, a partner); to a stranger or in formal settings it would be out of place. The near-synonym 섭섭하다 is fully interchangeable here (섭섭하게 왜 그러세요). Crucially, contrast this with the angry/blaming alternatives: 왜 이렇게 차갑게 굴어요? leans colder/accusatory, and 화내지 마 assumes anger — but the 서운하게 그러지 마 frame keeps it tender and reparative. The grammar lesson is the adverbial -게 + 그러다/그래 pattern: 서운하게 그러다 = 'to act in a 서운-causing way,' a super common construction (속상하게 하지 마, 섭섭하게 하지 마). The English-speaker pitfall is (1) not having this move at all — English speakers either bottle it up or escalate to 'I'm angry,' missing the gentle 서운 repair; (2) misusing -게: it attaches to the adjective stem (서운하게), and 그러지 마(세요) = 'don't do/act (that way)'; (3) confusing 그러다 ('to act/do so') with 그렇다 ('to be so'). Default register here is the intimate-polite 마세요 or 반말 왜 그래 — never formal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Escalating to 화내지 마 / 왜 화났어 instead.
Those assume anger and can start a fight. 서운하게 그러지 마 keeps it tender — 'you're hurting me because I care' — which repairs rather than escalates.
Using it with strangers or in formal settings.
This is an intimate, vulnerable move for close relationships only. To a stranger/senior it's out of place; you'd state concerns neutrally instead.
Confusing 그러지 마 (don't act so) with 그렇지 마.
그러다 = 'to act/do so' → 그러지 마(세요) ('don't be like that'). 그렇다 = 'to be so' and doesn't take 마. Keep 서운하게 그러지 마세요.

entries.nuance: 이제야 좀 후련하네요 layers the time-nuance 이제야 ('only now, finally, at long last') and reflective -네요 onto 후련하다, producing the satisfying 'phew, AT LAST a weight is off me' you say when something you'd carried for a long time finally resolves. The real lessons here are (1) 이제야 vs. 이제: 이제 just means 'now,' but 이제야 adds 'only now / not until now,' implying it took too long — a small word that carries real feeling; and (2) the deep, idiomatic register of relief. For big, long-awaited release Koreans use vivid idioms: 속이 다 후련하다 ('my insides are completely cleared'), 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려가다 (lit. 'a ten-year-old case of indigestion finally goes down' = enormous pent-up relief), and 한(이) 풀리다 ('a deep grudge/regret is resolved'). Contrast 후련하다 with 시원하다 again (시원하다 is broader 'cool/refreshing'; 후련하다 is the emotional unburdening). Register: 후련하네요 polite; the -네요 ('oh, I notice') makes it sound like genuine, just-felt realization rather than a flat report. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) using flat 이제 and missing the 'finally/at last' weight that 이제야 adds; (2) defaulting to a generic 다행이에요 ('thank goodness') for this felt, bodily 'load off my chest' — they're different; (3) the -야 attaches to time/nouns to mean 'only then/only that' (이제야, 그제서야, 너야), so don't confuse it with the vocative 야 ('hey'). Match the size of relief to the phrase: small relief 후련해요, huge long-pent relief 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 이제 instead of 이제야 for 'finally'.
이제 = 'now'; 이제야 = 'only now / at long last,' carrying the 'it took too long' feeling. For the 'finally!' relief, use 이제야.
Substituting 다행이에요 for the 'load off my chest' feeling.
다행이에요 = 'thank goodness it turned out OK' (about the situation). The felt bodily unburdening is 후련하네요. Different kinds of relief.
Reading the -야 in 이제야 as 'hey'.
Here -야 attaches to a time word meaning 'only then/at last' (이제야 = 'only now'). It's not the vocative 야 ('hey, you'). Don't mix them up.
