entries.english: It's on my mind / it keeps bothering me
entries.shortExplanation: 신경 쓰여요 is a practical expression meaning "It's on my mind / it keeps bothering me".
entries.explanation: 신경 쓰여요 (singyeong sseuyeoyo) means "It's on my mind / it keeps bothering me". Say it as one set phrase — for example 신경 쓰여요 ("It keeps bothering me / I can't stop thinking about it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 신경 쓰여요 (from 신경(이) 쓰이다, lit. '나의 nerves get used/spent on it') is the everyday word for something that NAGS at your mind — you can't stop thinking about a comment, a staring stranger distracts you, a small unresolved thing pulls at your attention. It's mid-strength: more than nothing, less than full-blown 걱정 ('worry'). The crucial pair is the active vs. passive: 신경(을) 쓰다 = 'to pay attention to / care about / put effort into' (제가 신경 쓸게요 'I'll take care of it'), while 신경(이) 쓰이다 = the passive 'it bothers/preoccupies me (without my choosing).' Learners constantly mix these: 신경 써요 means 'I (actively) pay attention,' but 신경 쓰여요 means 'it nags at me.' The other essential phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't bother/worry about it'), an extremely common kindness. Distinguish from 걱정되다 ('I'm worried,' future-oriented anxiety about an outcome) and 거슬리다 ('it grates/irritates,' more negative/annoyed) — 신경 쓰이다 is the neutral 'it's on my mind/distracting me.' Register: 신경 쓰여요 polite, 신경 쓰여 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) confusing 쓰다 (active, 'spend nerves on = care/mind') with 쓰이다 (passive, 'be minded = it bothers me'); (2) literally translating 'bother' as 귀찮다 — but 귀찮다 is 'can't be bothered / it's a hassle (too lazy),' a different feeling; (3) marking it wrong — the thing that bothers you takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요, not 그 말을 신경 쓰여요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 신경 써요 with 신경 쓰여요.
신경 써요 = 'I (actively) pay attention/care.' 신경 쓰여요 = 'it (passively) bothers me.' Different voice, different meaning. For 'it nags at me,' use 신경 쓰여요.
Translating 'it bothers me' as 귀찮아요.
귀찮다 = 'it's a hassle / I can't be bothered (lazy).' For 'it preoccupies/nags at me,' the word is 신경 쓰여요. They're different feelings.
Marking the cause with 을/를: 그 말을 신경 쓰여요.
With the passive 쓰이다, the thing takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요. (Only the active 신경(을) 쓰다 takes 을/를.)

structuredNuance.t: 신경 쓰여요 is the everyday word for something that NAGS at your mind — you can't stop thinking about a comment, a staring stranger distracts you, a small unresolved thing pulls at your attention. It's mid-strength: more than nothing, less than full-blown 걱정 ('worry'). The other essential phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't bother/worry about it'), an extremely common kindness.

Distinguish from 걱정되다 ('I'm worried,' future-oriented anxiety about an outcome) and 거슬리다 ('it grates/irritates,' more negative/annoyed) — 신경 쓰이다 is the neutral 'it's on my mind/distracting me.' Also don't translate 'bother' as 귀찮다 — that's 'can't be bothered / it's a hassle (too lazy),' a different feeling.
신경 쓰여요 is from 신경(이) 쓰이다, lit. 'my nerves get used/spent on it' (신경 = nerves).

Register: 신경 쓰여요 polite, 신경 쓰여 반말. The crucial pair is active vs. passive: 신경(을) 쓰다 = 'to pay attention to / care about / put effort into' (제가 신경 쓸게요 'I'll take care of it'), while 신경(이) 쓰이다 = the passive 'it bothers/preoccupies me without my choosing.' The thing that bothers you takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요.

The pitfall is (1) confusing 쓰다 (active, 'care/mind') with 쓰이다 (passive, 'it bothers me') — 신경 써요 means 'I actively pay attention,' but 신경 쓰여요 means 'it nags at me'; (2) translating 'bother' as 귀찮다; (3) marking it wrong — say 그 말이 신경 쓰여요, not 그 말을 신경 쓰여요.

entries.nuance: 부담스러워요 (from 부담스럽다, built on 부담 '負擔, a burden/load') is a socially essential Korean feeling with no neat English word: the uneasy 'this is too much for me' you feel under pressure, heavy expectation, intense attention, or someone's over-generosity. A too-expensive gift, a compliment that's over the top, everyone staring, a favor so big you'll feel indebted — all 부담스럽다. The thread is 'I feel weighed down / put on the spot, and I'd rather you dial it back.' It's polite and relational, often used to gently DECLINE or to soften: 부담스러우면 안 하셔도 돼요 ('if it's too much, you don't have to'). The key partner phrases are 부담(을) 주다 ('to pressure/burden someone') and 부담(을) 갖다 ('to feel pressured'), so 부담 갖지 마세요 ('don't feel pressured / no pressure') is a constant kindness, and 부담 주려는 건 아닌데 ('I don't mean to pressure you, but...') softens a request. Distinguish from 어렵다 (here 'someone feels intimidating/hard to be around,' e.g. a strict boss) and 무겁다 (literally 'heavy') — 부담스럽다 is specifically the felt social weight of expectation/obligation. Register: 부담스러워요 polite, 부담스러워 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) having no word for it and instead bluntly refusing ('no, too expensive'), where a Korean softens with 부담스러워요 to decline graciously; (2) the -스럽다 adjective form — it's 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (irregular ㅂ), not 부담해요 or 부담있어요; (3) mixing up 부담 주다 ('to burden someone') with 부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened') — 'you're pressuring me' is 부담스러워요 / 부담 주지 마세요, while 'I don't want to burden you' is 부담 드리고 싶지 않아요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Bluntly refusing instead of softening with 부담스러워요.
To decline a big gift/favor graciously, Koreans say 좀 부담스러워요 ('it's a bit much for me'). A flat 'no, too expensive' is harsher; 부담스럽다 keeps it polite and relational.
Saying 부담해요 or 부담있어요.
The adjective is 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (ㅂ-irregular). There's no 부담하다 for this feeling, and 부담있어요 isn't natural. Use 부담스러워요.
Confusing 부담 주다 with 부담스럽다.
부담 주다 = 'to pressure/burden someone (else)'; 부담스럽다 = 'I feel pressured/burdened.' 'You're pressuring me' = 부담스러워요 / 부담 주지 마세요, not 부담스러워 주세요.

entries.nuance: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose 존댓말 greeting you use with strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers — basically any adult you are not close with. It comes from 안녕(安寧) 'peace/well-being' + 하세요, so it literally asks 'are you at peace?', but Koreans hear it simply as 'hello' and it works morning, noon, and night (there is no separate 'good morning/afternoon'). Drop to 반말 안녕 only with close friends, kids, or clear juniors; step up to 안녕하십니까 for formal or service settings. The classic English-speaker mistake is splitting greetings by time of day or adding a literal 'how are you?' every time — in Korean 안녕하세요 alone is the complete, polite hello, and over-asking 어떻게 지내세요? to a stranger sounds oddly probing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안녕 to a teacher, boss, or older stranger — that is 반말 and sounds rude/childish; use 안녕하세요 with anyone you owe respect.
Searching for a 'good morning / good evening' equivalent — Korean uses one 안녕하세요 all day; time-of-day greetings are not standard.
Writing or saying 안녕하새요 — the verb ending is 세요 (하 + 세요), never 새요.

entries.nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the goodbye YOU say when you are the one leaving and the other person stays — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/stay', so you are wishing them 'stay in peace'. Its mirror twin is 안녕히 가세요 (가다 'to go'), said TO the person who is leaving; the moving party decides which verb you pick. Use 반말 잘 있어 with a close friend who stays, and 안녕히 계십시오 in stiff formal settings. The number-one English-speaker error is treating 'goodbye' as one fixed phrase: learners say 안녕히 가세요 as they themselves walk out the door, which literally tells their host to leave their own home. Always ask: am I leaving (계세요) or are they (가세요)?

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 안녕히 가세요 when YOU are leaving — that tells the person staying to 'go'; if you exit and they remain, say 안녕히 계세요.
Saying 안녕히 계세요 to BOTH people in a two-way parting — only the person leaving says it; the stayer replies with 안녕히 가세요.
Spelling it 안녕히 게세요 — the verb is 계시다, so it is 계세요, not 게세요.

entries.nuance: 안녕히 가세요 is the goodbye you say to the person who is LEAVING while you remain — 가다 'to go' + the polite command, so you wish them 'go in peace'. With close friends or juniors switch to 반말 잘 가; in service settings staff use 안녕히 가십시오. The big English-speaker trap is that 'goodbye' is one word in English, so learners fire 안녕히 가세요 at the host they are leaving — telling the host to leave their own house. Decide who actually walks away: if it's them, 가세요; if it's you, 계세요. A friendlier touch is 조심히 가세요 / 조심히 들어가세요 ('go safely / get home safe').

Saying 안녕히 가세요 when YOU are the one leaving — it orders the person staying to 'go'; if you leave, use 안녕히 계세요.

entries.nuance: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the formal, respectful phrase for a FIRST meeting — 처음 'first time' + 뵙겠습니다, where 뵙다 is the humble-honorific form of 보다 'to see/meet', so it literally means 'I will be seeing you for the first time'. The typical English-speaker mistake is reaching for plain 보다 (처음 보겠습니다), which sounds blunt or even rude, or translating 'nice to meet you' as 만나서 반갑습니다 in a stiff formal setting where 처음 뵙겠습니다 is expected first.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 처음 보겠습니다 with plain 보다 — it drops the required humility; the honorific 뵙다 → 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the only natural form here.

entries.nuance: 오랜만이에요 means 'it's been a long time' and is the warm greeting you open with when reuniting with someone you haven't seen in a while — 오랜만 is a contraction of 오래간만 'after a long interval'. Using 오랜만이에요 with someone you saw yesterday — it implies a genuinely long gap; for a short break just say 안녕하세요.

entries.nuance: 어떻게 지내세요? asks 'how are you getting on (these days)?' about someone's present life — 지내다 'to live/get by' + honorific 시, present tense, so unlike 잘 지냈어요? For a brand-new person, lead with 안녕하세요, not 어떻게 지내세요?.

entries.nuance: 또 봬요 means 'let's see each other again' — 또 'again' + 봬요, the contraction of 뵈어요 from honorific 뵈다 'to see (someone respected)'. It's a warm, optimistic parting implying you expect to meet again, softer than a plain goodbye. Ladder: 또 봐 (반말) → 또 봬요 (polite) → 또 뵙겠습니다 (formal, to seniors/clients). The spelling is the notorious trap even for natives: it's 봬요 (뵈+어요 → 봬요), NOT 뵈요 — a test is whether 'see' works in the slot: if 해 fits, write 봬; if 하 fits, write 뵈. English speakers also overuse a literal '나중에 봐요' from 'see you later'; 또 봬요 / 다음에 봬요 sound more natural as set partings. Don't confuse 봬요 (see you) with 봐요 (look at it).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 또 뵈요 — the correct contraction is 봬요 (뵈어요 → 봬요); 뵈요 is a spelling error.
Confusing 봬요 (see/meet, honorific) with 봐요 (look at, plain 보다) — for parting it's 또 봬요.
Using 또 봬요 with a senior where formality is expected — upgrade to the honorific 또 뵙겠습니다.

What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 들어가세요 literally means 'please go in(side)', i.e. get home/indoors, and is a warm Korean parting that wishes the other person a safe trip home — often softened to 조심히 들어가세요 ('go in carefully'). It also doubles as a standard way to END A PHONE CALL ('okay, take care now'). Ladder: 들어가 (반말) → 들어가세요 (polite) → 들어가십시오 (formal). The English-speaker confusion is taking it literally: at a doorway it can sound like 'go inside', but as a farewell it just means 'take care / get home safe', and on the phone it is NOT telling you to walk indoors — it's 'bye, look after yourself'. It overlaps with 안녕히 가세요 but feels more caring/intimate, used with people you have some warmth toward rather than pure strangers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading 들어가세요 on the phone as literally 'go inside' — at the end of a call it just means 'take care / bye'.
Saying 들어가세요 to someone who is NOT heading home/inside — it wishes a safe trip home; otherwise use 안녕히 가세요.
Using 반말 들어가 with a senior — for respect say 들어가세요 (or 들어가십시오).

entries.nuance: 밥 먹었어요? literally 'did you eat (rice/a meal)?' is one of Korea's most characteristic greetings — historically food was scarce, so asking whether someone had eaten became a way of showing care, and today it functions much like English 'how are you?' rather than a real question about food. It is NOT an invitation to eat; the expected reply is a quick 네, 먹었어요 / 아직요, then bounce it back. Register ladder: 밥 먹었어? (반말) → 밥 먹었어요? (polite) → 식사하셨어요? (honorific, swapping 밥→식사 and adding 시) → 진지 드셨어요? (to the elderly, with honorific nouns 진지/드시다). The English-speaker mistake is taking it literally and either thinking they're being invited to a meal, or earnestly listing what they ate — Koreans just want the brief ritual reply. Use the 식사하셨어요? / 진지 드셨어요? upgrades for anyone you owe respect; plain 밥 먹었어요? among peers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Taking 밥 먹었어요? literally as a dinner invitation — it's a caring greeting like 'how are you?'; just answer 네, 먹었어요 and ask back.
Using 밥 먹었어? (반말) with a senior — upgrade to 식사하셨어요?, or 진지 드셨어요? for an elderly person.
Answering by describing your whole meal — the ritual reply is short (네, 먹었어요 / 아직 안 먹었어요), then return the question.

entries.explanation: "I'd like to sign up for the gym" — that is 헬스장 등록하려고요 (helseujang deungnokaryeogoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 헬스장 등록하려고요 ("I'd like to register for the gym"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 헬스장 등록하려고요 is 헬스장 ('gym' — Korean uses the loanword 헬스 'health' for weight-training gyms, plus 장 'place') + 등록하다 ('to register', Sino-Korean 登錄) + -려고요, an ending that announces your intention ('I'm intending to…') as a soft opener. Note the big false-friend trap: 헬스 in Korean does NOT mean 'health' the way English speakers expect — 헬스장 / 헬스클럽 specifically means a weight/fitness gym, and 헬스 알아보다 means 'to look into joining a gym', not 'to check on health'. The -려고요 ending is gentler than a flat 등록할게요 ('I'll register') because it frames the visit as 'I'm here intending to sign up', inviting the staff to walk you through plans before you commit. The dividing line from 등록했어요 (past, 'I registered') is tense — many learners blur intention and completion. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 가입하다 ('to join/subscribe', used for clubs, memberships, insurance) and producing 헬스장 가입하려고요 — understandable, but for a gym the natural verb is 등록하다; 가입 sounds more like joining an organization or signing a contract. Also don't say 헬스 하려고요 if you mean signing up — that means 'I'm going to work out'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 헬스 means 'health'.
헬스 in Korean is a loanword meaning a weight-training gym (헬스장). 'Health' as a concept is 건강. So 헬스 하다 = 'to work out at the gym', not 'to do health'.
Saying 헬스장 가입하려고요.
가입하다 is for joining clubs/memberships/insurance. For a gym the idiomatic verb is 등록하다: 헬스장 등록하려고요.
Using past 등록했어요 when you mean to sign up now.
등록했어요 means 'I (already) registered'. To state you want to join now, use the intention form: 등록하려고요.

entries.nuance: 한 달에 얼마예요? is 한 달 ('one month') + 에 (the particle marking rate/per) + 얼마 ('how much') + 예요, literally 'per one month, how much is it?'. The load-bearing piece is the particle 에, which here means 'per' — 한 달에 = 'per month', 한 명에 = 'per person', 하나에 = 'each'. English speakers very often drop it or replace it, saying 한 달 얼마예요 (understandable but missing the 'per' feel) or wrongly 한 달로 얼마예요. For gyms, Koreans frequently use 끊다 ('to cut/buy a pass') for multi-month memberships — 3개월 끊다 = 'to buy a 3-month pass' — and 회비 ('dues', Sino-Korean 會費) for the recurring fee, so 한 달 회비 is crisper than the generic 가격. The dividing line from 얼마예요? alone is scope: bare 얼마예요 asks the price of a single thing in front of you, while 한 달에 얼마예요 specifically asks the monthly rate. The English-speaker pitfall is calculating with 'cost' verbs and saying 한 달에 비용이 들어요? ('does it cost per month?'), which sounds like a yes/no feasibility question rather than asking the amount — just ask 얼마예요. Numbers for the answer come in 원 (won), and 만 원 ('ten-thousand won') is the everyday unit.

entries.nuance: 운동복 갈아입을 데 있어요? is 운동복 ('workout clothes' = 운동 'exercise' + 복 'clothing') + 갈아입다 ('to change clothes') in the future-modifier form 갈아입을 + 데 ('place') + 있어요 ('is there?'). The key verb is 갈아입다 — a compound of 갈다 ('to swap') + 입다 ('to wear') meaning specifically 'change one's clothes'; learners wrongly say 옷을 바꾸다 ('to exchange/swap clothes for different ones', like at a store) when they mean changing into what they brought. Also note 데 here is a bound noun meaning 'place/spot', interchangeable with 곳 but more colloquial; 갈아입을 데 = 'a spot to change'. The direct noun is 탈의실 ('changing room', Sino-Korean), which is crisper if you just want the room. The dividing line: 갈아입을 데 있어요 asks whether a changing spot exists at all, while 탈의실 어디예요 assumes there is one and asks WHERE. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'changing room' → 바꾸는 방, which is meaningless in Korean; use 탈의실 or 갈아입는 곳. Another trap: 운동복 is the clothes themselves, while 운동화 ('athletic shoes') is footwear — don't confuse 복 (clothing) with 화 (shoes).

바꾸다 means 'to exchange/swap for something different'. Changing into your gym clothes is 갈아입다: 운동복으로 갈아입다.
Translating 'changing room' literally as 바꾸는 방.
That's not a real Korean phrase. The room is 탈의실, or describe it as 갈아입는 곳.

운동복 is workout clothing; 운동화 is athletic shoes. 복 = clothes, 화 = footwear. Don't mix them up at the desk.

entries.nuance: 오늘은 유산소만 할 거예요 is 오늘 ('today') + 은 (topic/contrast particle) + 유산소 ('aerobic/cardio', Sino-Korean 有酸素, lit. 'with oxygen') + 만 ('only') + 할 거예요 ('will do'). The two particles do real work: 은 here is contrastive ('today, as opposed to other days'), and 만 means 'only/just'. 유산소 (운동) is the standard gym word for cardio — treadmill, cycle, running — and its opposite is 무산소 (無酸素) or, more commonly in gym talk, 근력 운동 / 웨이트 ('weight/strength training'). The dividing line: 유산소 = cardio for endurance/fat-burn, while 웨이트/근력 = lifting for muscle; saying 유산소 when you mean lifting confuses a trainer. The English-speaker pitfall is the loanword reflex — saying 카디오, which Koreans don't really use; the native gym term is 유산소. Another particle trap: putting 만 in the wrong slot, e.g. 오늘만 유산소 할 거예요 means 'only today (and never again) I'll do cardio', a totally different meaning from 오늘은 유산소만 ('today I'll do only cardio'). Keep 만 attached to 유산소 to limit the activity, not the day.

오늘만 = 'only today (uniquely)'. To mean 'today I'll do only cardio', attach 만 to the activity: 오늘은 유산소만 할 거예요.

유산소 is cardio; lifting is 근력 운동 or 웨이트. Telling a trainer 유산소 할게요 when you want to lift will send you to the treadmill.

entries.nuance: 스트레칭 먼저 하고 할게요 is 스트레칭 ('stretching', loanword) + 먼저 ('first') + 하고 ('do, and then…') + 할게요 ('I'll do'). The grammar hinge is -고, the connective meaning 'and then' in sequence: A 하고 B = 'do A, then B'. A very natural Korean alternative to 스트레칭 is the idiom 몸을 풀다 — literally 'to loosen/untie the body', meaning to warm up; Koreans say 몸 좀 풀고 ('after loosening up') constantly. The dividing line: 스트레칭 is the specific stretching motion, while 몸을 풀다 / 준비운동 covers the whole warm-up including light cardio — use 몸 풀다 for the general idea. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'warm up' as 따뜻하게 하다 ('to make warm'), which is nonsense in this context; warming up the body is 몸을 풀다 or 준비운동(을) 하다. Another trap: the second 할게요 ('I'll do [it]') refers back to the main workout — learners sometimes leave the sentence dangling without the follow-on verb, so it's clearer to name it: 스트레칭 먼저 하고 운동 시작할게요. Also note -ㄹ게요 here signals YOUR own plan as a courteous heads-up, which is exactly the right register with a trainer.

그리고 ('and') links separate sentences; within one flow use the connective -고: 스트레칭 하고 할게요, not 스트레칭 해요 그리고…

entries.nuance: 이 기구 어떻게 쓰는 거예요? is 이 ('this') + 기구 ('apparatus/equipment', Sino-Korean 器具) + 어떻게 ('how') + 쓰는 거예요 ('is the way of using'). The natural gym word for a weight/exercise machine is 기구 or 운동 기구; 머신 (the loanword 'machine') is heard among hardcore lifters but 기구 is the safe everyday term. The grammar to notice is -는 거예요, the '-는 것이에요' pattern that turns 'use' into 'the act/way of using' and makes the question sound like a genuine 'how is this done?' rather than a blunt command. English speakers often produce the flat 어떻게 써요? ('how do you use it?'), which is fine but a touch more abrupt; the -는 거예요 framing is softer and very common when you want someone to explain. The verb is 쓰다 ('to use') — careful, 쓰다 also means 'to write' and 'to be bitter', so context carries it. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'use this machine' → 이 기계를 사용하다 with the stiff Sino verb 사용하다 in casual speech — 사용하다 is fine in writing, but spoken Korean prefers 쓰다. Another trap: 기구 vs 기계 — 기계 is a 'machine' in the industrial sense (engines, factory machines), while gym equipment is 기구; calling a leg-press a 기계 sounds slightly off.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling gym equipment 기계.
기계 is an industrial/mechanical machine. Exercise equipment is 기구 or 운동 기구: 이 기구 어떻게 써요?
Over-using 사용하다 in speech.
사용하다 is bookish. Spoken Korean uses 쓰다: 이거 어떻게 쓰는 거예요?, not 어떻게 사용해요? in a casual gym chat.
Dropping 이/이거 so it's unclear what you mean.
Without pointing, 어떻게 쓰는 거예요 is ambiguous. Gesture and say 이 기구 / 이거 to specify the machine.

entries.nuance: PT 받아 보고 싶은데요 is PT (an English initialism for 'personal training' that Koreans say as 피티, fully read 퍼스널 트레이닝) + 받다 ('to receive') + -아 보다 ('to try doing') + -고 싶다 ('want to') + -는데요 (soft, inviting ender). Two crucial points: first, the verb for taking a lesson/training/treatment is 받다 ('to receive'), NOT 하다 — you 받다 PT just as you 받다 마사지 (a massage) or 받다 수업 (a class); English speakers wrongly say PT 하다, which sounds like YOU are the one providing the training. Second, -아 보다 adds 'give it a try', so 받아 보다 = 'try receiving (it)', which softens the commitment — perfect when you're testing the waters. The trailing -는데요 again signals 'I'm thinking…, what do you say?', inviting the staff to respond. The dividing line: PT 받다 = take personal training; PT 하다 would (wrongly) imply coaching others. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond 하다, is over-formalizing with 개인 트레이닝을 받고 싶습니다 — correct but stiff; in a gym 피티 받아 보고 싶은데요 is the natural register. Also distinguish 상담 ('consultation', a sit-down chat) from 체험 ('a trial session you actually do').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying PT 하고 싶어요.
하다 makes it sound like you'll be the trainer. You receive training: PT 받고 싶어요 / 받아 보고 싶어요.
Using 가르치다 to mean 'be taught'.
가르치다 is 'to teach (someone)'. To be taught/trained, use 배우다 ('learn') or 받다 (for PT/lessons): PT 받다, 수업 받다.
Confusing 상담 and 체험.
상담 is a consultation (talking about it); 체험 is a trial session (actually doing it). Ask 상담 받을 수 있어요? to chat, 체험 가능해요? to try.

entries.nuance: 운동한 지 얼마나 되셨어요? is 운동하다 ('to exercise') in the past-modifier 운동한 + 지 (a bound noun marking elapsed time SINCE an action) + 얼마나 ('how much/long') + 되셨어요 (honorific 되다 'to become', + -시- honorific + past). The make-or-break grammar is the 지 of duration: V-(으)ㄴ 지 + 되다 = 'it has become [time] since V-ing'. Learners constantly confuse this 지 with the connective -지 of 운동하지 않다 ('don't exercise') — totally different; the duration 지 is a noun, spaced separately (한 지), and always pairs with 되다/지나다. The honorific 되셨어요 (with -시-) is right when asking someone you respect — a trainer, an older member; drop to 됐어요 with a peer. The dividing line from 얼마나 운동했어요? ('how much did you exercise?') is meaning: 운동한 지 얼마나 되셨어요 asks the TIME ELAPSED since you started the habit, while 얼마나 운동했어요 asks the AMOUNT/length of a workout. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'since' as 부터 — 운동부터… is wrong here; elapsed-time 'since' is the 지 + 되다 construction. entries.nuance: 근육통이 너무 심해요 is 근육통 ('muscle pain' = 근육 'muscle' + 통 '-ache', Sino-Korean 筋肉痛) + 이 (subject particle) + 너무 ('too/really') + 심하다 ('to be severe') conjugated 심해요. Pedagogically the most useful thing here is the everyday idiom Koreans actually use for post-exercise soreness: 알이 배기다 — literally 'eggs/knots form (in the muscle)', meaning DOMS, that stiff next-day ache. 근육통 is the clinical word (you'd see it on medicine), while 알 배기다 is what friends say: 다리에 알 배겼어 ('my legs are sore'). The dividing line: 근육통 = the medical noun for muscle ache; 알 배기다 = the colloquial 'I'm sore from working out'. Note the subject particle 이 attaches to 근육통 because the soreness is the subject of 심하다. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'sore' as 아프다 ('to hurt/be sick') used too broadly — 아프다 covers general pain or illness, but for the specific gym-soreness Koreans prefer 근육통이 있다 / 알이 배기다 / 쑤시다. Another trap: 너무 in standard grammar means 'too (excessively)', but colloquially it's used like 'really/very' — 너무 심해요 reads as 'it's really bad', which is fine and natural in speech.

아프다 is general 'hurt/be ill'. For workout soreness be specific: 근육통이 있어요, 알이 배겼어요, or 쑤셔요.

The noun for muscle ache is 근육통. 근육 아파요 sounds incomplete; say 근육통이 심해요 or 근육이 쑤셔요.
Translating 'sore' as 부드럽다 because of a dictionary.
부드럽다 means 'soft/tender (texture)', not painful. 'Sore' here is 쑤시다 / 결리다 / 근육통, never 부드럽다.

entries.nuance: 오늘 무슨 운동해요? is 오늘 ('today') + 무슨 ('what kind of') + 운동 ('exercise') + 해요 ('do'). The word to nail is 무슨 vs 어떤 vs 뭐: 무슨 운동 asks 'what (kind of) exercise' expecting a category answer (가슴/등/하체 — chest/back/legs); 어떤 운동 leans toward 'what sort/which' among known options; bare 뭐 운동 is ungrammatical (뭐 can't directly modify a noun like this). Gym culture in Korea is split-routine heavy, so the answer is usually a body part: 부위 ('body part') is the operative noun, and people say 오늘 어디 (부위) 해요? Common parts: 가슴 (chest), 등 (back), 어깨 (shoulders), 하체 (lower body/legs), 팔 (arms), 복근 (abs). The dividing line: 무슨 운동 asks the activity, 어디 (부위) asks the body region — both natural. The English-speaker pitfall is addressing the trainer wrong: a personal trainer is your 트레이너 or, address-wise, 쌤/선생님 — NOT 코치 (used more for sports team coaches) and never by bare name. Another trap: 운동하다 is one word/verb, so don't insert a particle as 운동을 해요 in this quick question — 운동해요 flows better, though 운동을 해요 isn't wrong.

뭐 can't directly modify a noun. Use 무슨: 무슨 운동해요?, not 뭐 운동해요.
Calling a gym trainer 코치.
코치 fits sports-team coaches. A gym PT is your 트레이너; address them as 쌤 or 선생님.
Asking 어디 운동해요 to mean which body part.
어디 운동해요 sounds like 'where do you exercise (which gym)'. For body part say 어디 부위 해요 or name it: 오늘 하체 해요?

examples.en: I'm on a diet these days.

entries.nuance: 요즘 다이어트 중이에요 is 요즘 ('these days') + 다이어트 (loanword 'diet') + 중 ('in the middle of', Sino-Korean 中) + 이에요. The crucial false-friend: in Korean 다이어트 almost always means 'losing weight / a weight-loss regimen', NOT merely 'the food you eat' as English 'diet' can. So 다이어트 중이에요 = 'I'm in weight-loss mode', and 다이어트 하다 = 'to be on a diet (to slim down)'. If you mean the composition of meals (a controlled eating plan, what a clinician calls your diet), that's 식단 ('meal plan'), e.g. 식단 관리하다. The grammar piece is N + 중이다 ('to be in the middle of N'), a handy 'currently doing' frame: 운동 중, 회의 중, 다이어트 중. The plain-Korean equivalent of dieting is 살(을) 빼다 ('to take off flesh/weight'); its opposite is 살이 찌다 ('to gain weight'). The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'I'm on a diet' → 다이어트 위에 있어요 ('I'm on top of a diet'), which is meaningless — Korean uses 중이다, not the spatial 'on'. Another trap: 다이어트 하다 implies trying to LOSE weight; if you actually need to GAIN, you wouldn't say 다이어트 — you'd say 살 찌우다 ('to put on weight').

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'on a diet' as 다이어트 위에 있어요.
위에 있다 means 'physically on top of'. 'On a diet (currently)' is 다이어트 중이에요.
Using 다이어트 to mean your meal composition.
다이어트 means weight-loss in Korean. For 'my diet/meal plan' (what you eat) use 식단: 식단 관리해요.
Saying 다이어트 to mean gaining weight.
다이어트 implies slimming down. To gain (e.g. muscle/weight) say 살(을) 찌우다 or 벌크업, not 다이어트.

structuredNuance.t: 요즘 ('these days') + 다이어트 (loanword 'diet') + 중 ('in the middle of') + 이에요. The grammar piece is N + 중이다 ('to be in the middle of N'), a handy 'currently doing' frame: 운동 중, 회의 중, 다이어트 중. So 다이어트 중이에요 = 'I'm in weight-loss mode', and 다이어트 하다 = 'to be on a diet (to slim down)'. The plain-Korean equivalent of dieting is 살(을) 빼다 ('to take off flesh/weight'); its opposite is 살이 찌다 ('to gain weight').

If you mean the composition of meals (a controlled eating plan, what a clinician calls your diet), that's 식단 ('meal plan'), e.g. 식단 관리하다. Also 다이어트 하다 implies trying to LOSE weight; if you actually need to GAIN, you wouldn't say 다이어트 — you'd say 살 찌우다 ('to put on weight').
중 ('in the middle of') is Sino-Korean 中.

The crucial false-friend: in Korean 다이어트 almost always means 'losing weight / a weight-loss regimen', NOT merely 'the food you eat' as English 'diet' can. And the 직역 'I'm on a diet' → 다이어트 위에 있어요 ('I'm on top of a diet') is meaningless — Korean uses 중이다, not the spatial 'on'.

entries.nuance: 락커 키 어디서 받아요? is 락커 (loanword 'locker') + 키 (loanword 'key') + 어디서 ('from where') + 받아요 ('do I receive'). Vocabulary first: a gym locker is commonly called 락커 (also spelled 라커) or, in pure Korean, 사물함 ('personal-belongings box'); both are fine, 사물함 a touch more standard/formal. The verb is again 받다 ('to receive') for getting the key handed to you. The grammar nugget is 어디서 — the contraction of 어디(에)서, the particle 서 marking the LOCATION OF AN ACTION ('at/from where do you DO this?'). Learners often wrongly use 어디 (location of existence, for 있다) and say 락커 키 어디 받아요 — you need 어디서 because 받다 is an action: 어디서 받아요. The dividing line: 어디예요 (where IS it) vs 어디서 해요/받아요 (where do you DO/get it). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the particle, is the 직역 'locker key' word order being fine, but assuming a physical key — many Korean gym lockers use a 비밀번호 (door code) or a wristband, so it's smart to ask 키예요, 비밀번호예요? Also note 보증금 ('deposit') may apply, returned when you leave.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 어디 instead of 어디서 with 받다.
받다 is an action verb, so it needs the action-location 어디서: 키 어디서 받아요? 어디 받아요 is incomplete.
Assuming every locker has a physical key.
Korean gym lockers often use a 비밀번호 (code) or band. Ask 키예요, 비밀번호예요? rather than just 키.
Saying 가방함 or 옷함 for a locker.
Those aren't words. A locker is 사물함 (or the loanword 락커). Use 사물함 어디 있어요?

entries.nuance: 샤워실은 어디예요? is 샤워실 ('shower room' = 샤워 loanword + 실 'room', Sino-Korean 室) + 은 (topic particle) + 어디 ('where') + 예요. The teaching point is the topic particle 은 vs the subject particle 이/가 in a 'where is X' question. With 은/는 (샤워실은 어디예요) you gently TOPICALIZE — 'as for the showers, where are they?' — which is natural when you've been talking about the gym and now single one thing out. With 이/가 (샤워실이 어디예요) you neutrally ask the location. Both are correct; 은 adds a faint 'and the showers?' contrast that fits a string of questions (탈의실은…? 샤워실은…?). The dividing line is subtle but real: overusing 이/가 for every where-question sounds list-like, while 은/는 connects your questions conversationally. Note the suffix 실 ('room') builds many gym words: 탈의실 (changing room), 샤워실 (shower room), 휴게실 (lounge). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the particle entirely (샤워실 어디예요) — acceptable in fast speech but flatter; and the 직역 'shower' alone (샤워) means the act of showering, while the ROOM is 샤워실. Don't say 샤워 어디예요 for the room.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 샤워 어디예요 for the shower room.
샤워 is the act of showering. The room is 샤워실: 샤워실은 어디예요?
Always using 이/가 for where-questions.
이/가 is neutral; 은/는 topicalizes and links questions naturally. In a series, 샤워실은 어디예요 flows better than another 이가.
Confusing 실 (room) suffix words.
실 builds 탈의실/샤워실/휴게실. Mixing them up (asking 휴게실 when you want showers) sends you to the lounge, not the showers.

entries.nuance: 자세 좀 봐 주세요 is 자세 ('posture/form', Sino-Korean 姿勢) + 좀 (politeness softener) + 봐 주세요 (보다 'to look' + 주다 favor + 주세요), i.e. 'please look at (it) for me'. 자세 is exactly the gym word for 'form' — squat form, deadlift form — so 자세를 보다 ('to check form') and 자세가 좋다/나쁘다 ('good/bad form') are the natural collocations; learners reaching for 'form' as 폼 (the loanword) will be half-understood (폼 exists in slang like 폼 난다 'looks cool') but 자세 is correct for technique. The 좀 here is the softener (not 'a little'), and 봐 주세요 with the favor verb 주다 makes it a request for the trainer's help rather than a command to merely look. The dividing line: 자세 봐 주세요 ('check my form for me') vs the bare 자세 보세요 ('you, look at the posture') — the latter sounds like ordering them around; keep 주세요 with the favor 주다. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'check' as 체크하다 (자세 체크해 주세요) — understandable but the idiomatic verb is 보다 ('look at'); and confusing 자세 ('posture') with 자세히 ('in detail', an adverb) — 자세히 봐 주세요 means 'please look closely/in detail', a different nuance from 자세(를) 봐 주세요 ('check my form').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 폼 for exercise form.
폼 is slang for 'looking cool/stylish'. Exercise technique is 자세: 자세 좀 봐 주세요.
Saying 자세 보세요 without 주다.
보세요 commands them to look. The polite favor request is 봐 주세요 ('look for me'): 자세 좀 봐 주세요.
Confusing 자세 with 자세히.
자세 = posture (noun); 자세히 = in detail (adverb). 자세히 봐 주세요 = 'look closely', not 'check my form'. For form, say 자세(를) 봐 주세요.

entries.nuance: 오늘은 무리했나 봐요 is 오늘 ('today') + 은 (contrast topic) + 무리하다 ('to overdo / push beyond one's limit', Sino-Korean 無理 'unreasonable' + 하다) + -았/었나 봐요 ('I guess/seems that…'). Two rich pieces: first, 무리하다 is THE word for overexerting — pushing past what your body can handle — and its standard caution is 무리하지 마세요 ('don't overdo it'), which trainers, doctors, and friends say constantly; English speakers reach for the 직역 'too much exercise' → 너무 많이 운동했어요 ('I exercised too much'), which is fine but flatter than the idiomatic 무리했어요. Second, -나 보다 is the inferential 'it seems / I guess', used when you conclude something from evidence (the soreness tells you): 무리했나 봐요 = 'seems I overdid it'. The opposite advice is 살살 하다 ('to go gently/easy'); 살살 is a great mimetic adverb meaning 'softly, gradually'. The dividing line: 무리하다 (overexert beyond limits) vs 많이 하다 (just do a lot — neutral). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the 직역, is misreading 무리 — it's NOT 'a group/herd' (무리 also means 'a crowd', a homonym); in 무리하다 it's the 無理 'pushing the unreasonable'. Also -나 봐요 attaches to the past stem here (했나 봐요) because you're inferring about a completed action.

That's literally 'exercised a lot' — neutral. The idiomatic 'overexerted/pushed too hard' is 무리했어요.
Reading 무리 as 'a group'.
무리 is a homonym: 'a crowd/herd' AND, in 무리하다, '(doing) the unreasonable = overexerting'. Here it means overdoing it, not a group.
Using -ㄴ 것 같다 where -나 보다 fits better.
Both express guessing, but -나 보다 stresses inference from evidence. Given the soreness, 무리했나 봐요 sounds natural; 무리한 것 같아요 also works but is more 'I feel'.

entries.nuance: 이거 몇 세트 해요? is 이거 ('this') + 몇 ('how many') + 세트 (loanword 'set') + 해요 ('do'). Gym counting in Korea splits into two loanword units: 세트 ('set') and, for the individual repetitions, 개 ('count/piece') — so '3 sets of 15 reps' is 세 세트에 열다섯 개씩 (개 is the everyday counter people use for reps, more than the technical 회). The make-or-break point is the NUMBER SYSTEM: counters like 세트, 개, 회 take NATIVE Korean numbers (한, 두, 세, 네, 다섯…), so it's 세 세트 ('three sets'), 열 개 ('ten reps') — NOT Sino-Korean 삼 세트 / 십 개, the single most common English-speaker error with counters. The little word 씩 means 'each/per' and distributes the count: 열 개씩 = 'ten each (per set)'. The dividing line: 세트 = a set; 개 (or 회) = a single rep within it; mixing them ('몇 개 해요' when you mean sets) confuses the trainer. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond Sino numbers, is the 직역 of 'rep' — there's no need for a fancy word; Koreans just say 개 (or 회). Also 몇 ('how many') here triggers a counter, so don't drop it: 몇 세트, not just 세트 해요 (which would mean 'do you do sets?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using Sino-Korean numbers with 세트/개.
Counters take native numbers: 세 세트, 열 개 — not 삼 세트, 십 개. So 'three sets' is 세 세트, never 삼 세트.
Confusing 세트 and 개/회 for reps.
세트 is a set; an individual rep is 개 (or 회). Asking 몇 개 해요 asks reps, 몇 세트 해요 asks sets. Use the right one for what you mean.
Dropping 씩 when distributing reps.
씩 means 'each/per'. '10 reps each set' is 한 세트에 열 개씩. Without 씩 it sounds like a single total, not per-set.

entries.nuance: 회원권 잠깐 정지할 수 있어요? is 회원권 ('membership (pass)' = 회원 'member' + 권 'ticket/right', Sino-Korean 會員券) + 잠깐 ('for a moment/briefly') + 정지하다 ('to suspend/halt', 停止) + -ㄹ 수 있어요 ('can I…?'). Two practical things: first, the right noun for the membership itself is 회원권 (the pass/right), distinct from 등록 (the ACT of registering) — you 정지 the 회원권, you don't 정지 the 등록. Second, gyms universally also use the loanword 홀딩 ('holding') for freezing a membership — 홀딩 돼요? ('can I hold it?') is what regulars actually say, often more than 정지. The grammar 잠깐 ('briefly') flags it's temporary, important because a permanent stop would be 해지/탈퇴 ('cancellation/withdrawal') — a totally different action; freezing keeps the membership but pauses the clock, and the days usually get added to the end (기간이 밀리다 / 늘어나다). The dividing line: 정지/홀딩 = temporary pause (you'll return); 해지/환불 = ending it for good. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'freeze' as 얼리다 ('to freeze (into ice)') — 회원권을 얼리다 is nonsense in Korean; the term is 정지하다 or 홀딩하다. Another trap is 정지 ('suspend') vs 중지 ('stop/discontinue') — both exist, but for a membership pause 정지(홀딩) is standard. Also keep 회원권 as the object: 회원권(을) 정지하다.

정지/홀딩 temporarily pauses the membership; 해지/탈퇴 ends it. If you only want a pause, say 정지/홀딩, not 환불 or 해지.

등록 is the act of registering; the thing you pause is the membership 회원권. Say 회원권(을) 정지하다 or 홀딩하다.

entries.english: Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)
entries.shortExplanation: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 is a practical expression meaning "Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)".
entries.explanation: "Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)" — that is 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bong mani badeuseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 새해 복 많이 받으세요 ("Happy New Year (please receive many blessings)"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 새해 복 많이 받으세요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.en: Happy New Year (please receive many blessings)
usagePhrases.note: Polite default; say to elders, bosses, anyone you respect at New Year
반말, to close friends and younger people
합쇼체; very formal, to a CEO, in a speech, or a written card
Shortened; also used at 추석 and other holidays, not just New Year

examples.ko: 새해 복 많이 받으세요!
examples.romanization: saehae bong mani badeuseyo!
examples.en: Happy New Year!
examples.note: The all-purpose New Year greeting to almost anyone older or respected

examples.ko: 할머니, 새해 복 많이 받으세요. 건강하세요.
examples.romanization: halmeoni, saehae bong mani badeuseyo. geonganghaseyo.
examples.en: Grandma, Happy New Year. Stay healthy.
examples.note: Add 건강하세요 ('stay healthy') to an elder — the most-wished thing for grandparents

examples.ko: 올해도 잘 부탁드립니다. 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
examples.romanization: olhaedo jal butakdeurimnida. saehae bong mani badeuseyo.
examples.en: I look forward to working with you this year too. Happy New Year.
examples.note: A polite work/colleague version pairing the greeting with 잘 부탁드립니다

entries.nuance: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 literally means 'in the new year, please RECEIVE much 복 (blessing/fortune)' — 복 is a Sino-Korean word (福) for luck and good fortune, and the verb is 받다 ('to receive'), so you are wishing that blessings come TO the person. This is the single most important holiday phrase in Korea and you say it at 설날 (Lunar New Year) to basically everyone: elders, bosses, neighbors, shop owners. The default register is the 세요 form (honorific), which is safe for anyone older or not close; with friends and kids you drop to 새해 복 많이 받아. The huge English-speaker pitfall is the verb: learners say 새해 복 많이 주세요 ('please GIVE me blessings') by mistake — 주다 ('give') flips it into asking for blessings for yourself, which sounds absurd; it must be 받으세요 ('receive'). A second trap is the 직역 'Happy New Year' instinct to translate the English word 'happy' (행복) — Korean does not say 행복한 새해; the fixed idiom is the 복 받으세요 formula. Note it's also fine to shorten to 복 많이 받으세요 at 추석 and other holidays. When greeting an elder you usually combine it with a 세배 (deep bow); the words alone are the everyday version.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 새해 복 많이 주세요.
주다 means 'give', so this asks the listener to give YOU fortune — backwards and comical. The blessing flows toward the listener, so use 받다: 새해 복 많이 받으세요.
Translating literally as 행복한 새해 (보내세요).
Korean doesn't use 행복한 ('happy') for the New Year greeting; the set idiom is the 복 받으세요 formula. 행복한 새해 sounds like translated English.
Using 받아 with your boss or an elder.
받아 is 반말 and too casual for someone you should respect. Keep the honorific 받으세요; only drop to 받아 with friends and younger people.

entries.shortExplanation: 세배 드릴게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll do the New Year bow for you".
entries.explanation: 세배 드릴게요 (sebae deurilgeyo) = "I'll do the New Year bow for you". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 세배 드릴게요 ("I'll bow to you (New Year bow)"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: 세배 (歲拜) is the deep, kneeling New Year bow younger people give to elders on 설날, and 드리다 is the humble verb for 'to give (to a superior)' — so 세배 드릴게요 is literally 'I'll give you a New Year bow', the polite way to announce you're about to bow. The verb choice is everything here: you 드리다 (humbly give) a 세배 UP to an elder, and the elder 받다 (receives) it, often replying with a blessing (덕담) and 세뱃돈 (New Year money). The big English-speaker pitfall is using the plain verb 주다 instead of the humble 드리다 — 세배 줄게요 is wrong because 주다 isn't humble enough toward an elder; with anyone you bow to, it must be 드리다. A second trap is the particle: you bow 할머니께 (honorific 'to', not 할머니한테 which is casual). Don't confuse 세배 (the New Year bow) with 절 (a bow in general, including the bows at a funeral or to ancestors) — all 세배 are 절, but you only call it 세배 at New Year. Also note the bow itself has a correct form (men and women fold hands differently); if unsure, just watch and copy the family — the words 세배 드릴게요 plus a sincere bow are what matter.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 세배 줄게요 to an elder.
주다 isn't humble enough when the recipient is someone you respect. The humble give-verb is 드리다: 세배 드릴게요.
Using 한테 instead of 께: 할머니한테 세배.
한테 is casual 'to'; for an elder use the honorific 께: 할머니께 세배 드려요. 한테 sounds disrespectful in this ritual context.
Calling every bow 세배.
세배 is specifically the New Year bow to elders. The bows to ancestors (차례) or at a funeral are just 절, not 세배. Reserve 세배 for 설날.

entries.nuance: 떡국 is the rice-cake soup Koreans eat on 설날 morning, and there's a deep cultural belief that eating a bowl of 떡국 makes you a year older — so 떡국 드셨어요? ('did you have tteokguk?') is really a warm idiomatic way of saying 'did you celebrate the New Year / are you a year older now?'. The follow-up joke is 한 살 더 먹었네요 ('you ate one more year of age') — note Korean uses the verb 먹다 ('eat') for gaining age (나이를 먹다). The English-speaker pitfall is taking it literally and answering only about food, missing the New-Year-greeting subtext; the natural move is to smile and play along. examples.note: 미리 ('in advance') is added when you say it a day or two before the holiday

examples.ko: 고향 잘 다녀오시고, 명절 잘 보내세요.
examples.romanization: gohyang jal danyeoosigo, myeongjeol jal bonaeseyo.
examples.en: Travel safely to your hometown, and have a good holiday.

entries.nuance: 명절 is the word for a traditional Korean holiday — specifically the big two, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (Chuseok/harvest festival) — and 잘 보내세요 means 'spend (it) well', from 보내다 ('to spend/pass time'). So 명절 잘 보내세요 is the standard 'have a good holiday' you say to coworkers, neighbors, and shopkeepers in the days BEFORE the holiday. The key contrast is 명절 vs 연휴: 명절 names the cultural holiday (with its rituals), while 연휴 just means the consecutive days off — say 연휴 잘 보내세요 when you mean 'enjoy the long weekend' generically (works for any holiday block). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: learners reach for 가지세요 ('have/possess') as a 직역 of English 'have a good holiday', but Korean uses 보내다 ('spend/pass'); 명절 가지세요 is wrong. A second pitfall is timing — 잘 보내세요 (future, 'spend it well') is said BEFORE/at the start of the holiday; afterward you'd ask 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?', past). Adding 미리 ('in advance') is common because people scatter to their hometowns right before the holiday.

명절 is the cultural holiday (설날/추석); 연휴 is just the string of days off. For a generic long weekend say 연휴 잘 보내세요; for the traditional holiday, 명절.

보내세요 (future) wishes a good holiday ahead. After it's done, switch to past: 명절 잘 보내셨어요? ('did you have a good holiday?').

entries.nuance: 차례 (茶禮) is the ancestral memorial rite families perform on the morning of 설날 and 추석 — food is set on a table for the ancestors and the family bows. The crucial collocation is the verb: you 지내다 a rite, never 하다. 지내다 here means 'to observe/hold (a ceremony)', so it's 차례(를) 지내다, 제사(를) 지내다, 결혼식 is 올리다, etc. — using 차례 해요 marks you instantly as a learner. The key contrast is 차례 vs 제사: 차례 is the simpler rite tied to the two big HOLIDAYS (done in the morning, no late-night timing), while 제사 is the memorial held on the ANNIVERSARY of a specific ancestor's death (traditionally at night). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the verb, is assuming every family does it — increasingly families skip or simplify (간소화) charye, and many Christian families don't perform it at all (they may do a 추도 예배, a memorial worship, instead), so it's polite to ask rather than assume. Don't confuse 차례 with 차레/차이 — and note it's unrelated to 차 ('tea'/'car') despite the 차 syllable. Pair words you'll hear: 성묘 (visiting graves) and 벌초 (clearing weeds from the grave before Chuseok).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 차례 해요 instead of 차례 지내요.
Rituals take the verb 지내다, not 하다. It's 차례(를) 지내다, 제사(를) 지내다. 차례 해요 sounds wrong to natives.
Confusing 차례 with 제사.
차례 is the rite on the holidays (설날/추석), held in the morning. 제사 is the rite on an ancestor's death anniversary, traditionally at night. They're not interchangeable.
Assuming everyone holds 차례.
Many families simplify or skip it, and Christian families often hold a 추도 예배 instead. Ask 차례 지내세요? rather than assuming.

examples.note: 송편 (half-moon rice cakes) is the signature Chuseok food

entries.nuance: 송편 are the small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut that Koreans make for 추석 (Chuseok). The verb is the lovely specific 빚다 — used for things you shape with your hands from dough or clay: you 빚다 송편, 빚다 만두 (dumplings), even 빚다 (brew) traditional liquor. You do NOT 만들다 ('make') them in the careful family-ritual sense; 송편 빚어요 captures the hand-shaping. 빚다 is a regular consonant-stem verb (빚다 → 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는), but learners often mangle the stem-final ㅈ and produce wrong forms. The cultural point: making 송편 together the night before Chuseok is a bonding activity across generations, hence the famous line 송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는다 ('shape pretty songpyeon and you'll bear a pretty daughter'). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 만들다 for everything ('make') — while 송편 만들어요 is understood, 빚다 is the idiomatic, warmer verb a native uses for this. A second pitfall is mixing up 송편 (Chuseok) with 떡국 (Seollal/New Year) — each holiday has its signature food. Note 빚다 also means 'to brew' and 'to cause/incur' (빚을 빚다 puns aside, 빚 also means 'debt' — different word, same sound).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 송편 만들어요 in the ritual context.
Native speakers use the hand-shaping verb 빚다 for songpyeon and dumplings: 송편 빚어요. 만들다 ('make') is understood but less idiomatic here.
Mangling the conjugation (빚다 → 빚다요/빚는다요).
빚다 conjugates 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는. Attach endings to the 빚 stem (빚-어요), not the dictionary form; 빚어요 is the polite present.
Mixing up holiday foods: 송편 at New Year.
송편 is the 추석 (Chuseok) food; 떡국 is the 설날 (New Year) food. Pair the right rice cake with the right holiday.

structuredNuance.t: 송편 are the small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut that Koreans make for 추석 (Chuseok). Making 송편 together the night before Chuseok is a bonding activity across generations, hence the famous line 송편 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는다 ('shape pretty songpyeon and you'll bear a pretty daughter').

Don't mix up 송편 (Chuseok) with 떡국 (Seollal/New Year) — each holiday has its signature food. Also note 빚다 itself means 'to brew' and 'to cause/incur', and 빚 means 'debt' — a different word with the same sound.

The verb is the lovely specific 빚다 — used for things you shape with your hands from dough or clay: you 빚다 송편, 빚다 만두 (dumplings), even 빚다 (brew) traditional liquor. 빚다 is a regular consonant-stem verb (빚다 → 빚어요, 빚으면, 빚는), but learners often mangle the stem-final ㅈ and produce wrong forms.

The pitfall is defaulting to 만들다 for everything ('make') — you do NOT 만들다 them in the careful family-ritual sense; 송편 빚어요 captures the hand-shaping. While 송편 만들어요 is understood, 빚다 is the idiomatic, warmer verb a native uses for this.

entries.nuance: 한복 (韓服) is traditional Korean dress, worn for 설날, 추석, weddings, and 돌잔치 (first-birthday parties). Culturally, wearing hanbok on holidays used to be near-universal but is now optional — many families wear regular clothes, and renting (빌리다) a hanbok for photos at palaces is popular, so don't assume everyone owns or wears one. Don't confuse 한복 (Korean dress) with 한식 (Korean food) — similar shape, different word.

entries.nuance: On holidays money flows two ways, and Korean forces you to pick the verb by DIRECTION of respect. 용돈 is 'spending money/pocket money'; 세뱃돈 is specifically the cash children receive after giving their 세배 (New Year bow). When YOU give money UP to a parent or elder, you must use the humble 드리다: 부모님께 용돈 드려요. When you give DOWN to a child or junior, you use plain 주다: 조카한테 세뱃돈 줘요. Swapping these is the #1 English-speaker pitfall — 부모님한테 용돈 줘요 sounds disrespectful (wrong verb AND wrong particle: 한테 is casual, elders take 께). A second contrast: 용돈 (general allowance, any time) vs 세뱃돈 (only at New Year, tied to the bow) — don't call a holiday gift to your parents 세뱃돈 (adults bowing to parents still give 용돈, and parents don't get 세뱃돈). Culturally, adult children giving parents 용돈 at holidays is a strong expectation and a sign of filial care; the verb 챙기다 ('to see to / not forget') is often used warmly (용돈 챙겨 드렸어요). New money is traditionally given in a clean envelope, fresh bills preferred.

드리다 is humble (giving UP). To a child you give DOWN, so use plain 주다: 조카한테 세뱃돈 줬어요. 드리다 to a kid is wrong.

entries.nuance: 축의금 (祝儀金) is the cash gift you put in an envelope for a wedding — in Korea you almost never bring a wrapped present, you give MONEY at a reception desk. The idiomatic verb is 하다 ('to do', here 'to put in / contribute an amount'): 축의금 얼마 해요? literally 'how much do you do as wedding money?'. You can also say 내다 ('to pay/submit') — 축의금 내다 — but 하다 is the most natural for asking the going rate. The amount is socially calibrated: ~5만 원 for an acquaintance, ~10만 원 for a normal friend/colleague, more if you're close or eat at the reception (a real rule: 밥값 ('the meal cost') is factored in). The English-speaker pitfall is bringing a gift instead of cash, or using odd amounts — Koreans give 'auspicious' figures (3, 5, 7, 10만; avoid 4 because 四 sounds like 死 'death', and even/round non-traditional numbers feel off). The biggest verb trap: do NOT confuse 축의금 (wedding/congratulations) with 부의금/조의금 (funeral/condolence) — giving the wrong envelope wording at the wrong event is a serious gaffe. The general umbrella term is 부조(금). At the desk you sign a guestbook (방명록) and hand over a white envelope (the wedding one can be decorative; funeral envelopes are plain white).

Bringing a wrapped gift instead of cash.
Korean weddings expect 축의금 (money in an envelope) at the reception desk, not presents. A physical gift can be awkward; give cash.
Giving an amount with 4 in it (4만, 14만).
4 (四) sounds like 死 ('death') and is avoided for celebrations. Stick to auspicious figures like 3, 5, 7, or 10만 원.

축의금 is congratulatory money (weddings, happy events); 부의금/조의금 is condolence money (funerals). The envelopes and wording differ — never mix them up.

entries.nuance: 결혼 축하해요 ('congratulations on your marriage') is the core wedding congratulation. 축하하다 (祝賀) is 'to congratulate', and the politeness ladder matters at a formal event like a wedding: 축하해 (반말, friends) → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (humble, to elders, the couple's parents, or in a speech). The humble 드리다 form is genuinely common at weddings because you're often congratulating people older than you (the parents at the door). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners say 결혼을 축하해요 with 을 inserted, but the natural set phrase drops it — 결혼 축하해요 (noun + 축하하다 directly). Another trap is the 직역 instinct: 'congratulations on your wedding' tempts 결혼식 축하해요 ('congrats on the wedding CEREMONY'), but Koreans congratulate the 결혼 (the marriage/getting married), not the event. entries.nuance: This is an idiom you must not take literally. 잔치국수 (banquet noodles) were traditionally served at wedding feasts, so '국수 먹다' ('to eat noodles') became slang for 'to attend someone's wedding', and 국수 먹여 주다 ('to feed (us) noodles') means 'to get married'. So 국수 언제 먹여 줘요? literally 'when will you feed us noodles?' actually means 'when are you two getting married?' — a teasing, affectionate thing said to a long-term dating couple. The English-speaker pitfall is total: a 직역 leaves you baffled by why anyone is asking about noodles, and worse, you might answer about actual food. Recognize it as a set marriage joke. Register-wise it's inherently casual/teasing, so even the 요 form is playful; with close friends it's 반말 (국수 언제 먹여 줄 거야?). The causative chain matters: 먹다 ('eat') → 먹이다/먹여 주다 ('feed someone') — the couple FEEDS the noodles (i.e., hosts the wedding), the friends EAT them. A second nuance: this can feel like social pressure to marry, so it's used among people close enough to joke; don't say it to acquaintances or anyone sensitive about being single. Compare 잔치 ('feast/celebration') — a 돌잔치 is a first-birthday feast, same 잔치 root.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Taking it literally as an offer of food.
국수 먹여 주다 is idiom for 'get married' (from wedding banquet noodles). Don't answer about real noodles — it means 'when's the wedding?'
Saying it to acquaintances or the marriage-sensitive.
It's a tease that implies 'hurry up and marry'. Use only with people close enough to joke; to others it can feel like pressure.
Mangling the causative: 국수 언제 먹어 줘요?
The couple FEEDS the noodles, so it's the causative 먹여 주다 ('feed someone'), not 먹어 ('eat'). 먹여 줘요? = 'when will you feed (treat) us?'

entries.nuance: This is THE funeral phrase, and it is almost entirely fixed — memorize it whole. Breaking it down: 삼가 ('respectfully/humbly'), 고인 (故人, 'the deceased'), 명복 (冥福, 'happiness/blessing in the afterlife'), 빌다 ('to pray/wish') → 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's blessing in the next life'. You say it (and write it on the white condolence envelope and on funeral wreaths) at a 장례식/빈소. The single most important rule for English speakers: NEVER say 축하해요 ('congratulations') or anything cheerful, and never say a 직역 of English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다 (that's apologizing for a fault) or 미안해요 — Korean condolence is this 명복을 빕니다 formula, or to the family directly 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 ('I don't know what to say'). A second pitfall: 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is for the DECEASED; you don't say it TO the grieving person as a greeting — to the bereaved you offer the softer 얼마나 힘드세요 / 힘내세요. Note 명복 only fits this context (afterlife blessing), and the whole phrase is solemn and formal — there's no 반말 version. At the funeral you bow twice to the portrait, then once to the family (the 절 there is NOT called 세배). Don't smile; tone is everything.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죄송합니다 or 미안해요 as 'I'm sorry (for your loss)'.
Those mean 'I apologize (for a fault)'. Korean condolence isn't an apology — say 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다, or to the family 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
Saying 축하해요 or anything upbeat by reflex.
축하하다 ('congratulate') is for happy events; at a funeral it's deeply offensive. Keep to the solemn 명복을 빕니다 formula.
Directing 명복을 빕니다 at the living as a hello.
That phrase prays for the DECEASED. To comfort the grieving person, say 얼마나 힘드세요 or 힘내세요; reserve 명복을 빕니다 for the deceased.

entries.nuance: 조의금 (弔意金) / 부의금 (賻儀金) is the cash given at a funeral, the somber counterpart to wedding 축의금. The verbs: you 내다 ('submit/pay') or 하다 it (조의금 하다, 부조 하다), and if you can't stay you 전하다 ('convey') it. The make-or-break point for English speakers is the ENVELOPE and wording: funeral money goes in a PLAIN WHITE envelope (흰 봉투) with sober wording like 부의 (賻儀) or 근조 (謹弔) written on it — using a decorative/colored envelope or congratulatory wording (祝) at a funeral is a grave offense. So the cardinal mistake is reusing a wedding 축의금 mindset (verbs are similar, but tone, envelope, and wording are opposite). 조의 vs 부의 vs 근조: all relate to mourning gifts — 조의(금)/부의(금) name the money; 근조 is the wreath/banner wording ('humbly mourning'). Amounts mirror weddings (~5–10만 원), with the same avoidance of 4. Logistically, you sign the 부의록 (condolence guestbook), hand the white envelope, then go in to bow. The English-speaker pitfall also includes over-talking — at a funeral, handing the envelope is often done quietly; you don't need a cheerful speech, and you definitely don't say 축하 anything. Pair phrase: at the desk staff may simply nod; the words 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 carry the sentiment.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using a colored/decorative envelope or 祝 wording.
Funeral money requires a PLAIN WHITE envelope with sober wording (부의/근조). Festive envelopes or 祝('congratulate') are a serious gaffe — that's for weddings.
Calling it 축의금.
축의금 is congratulatory (weddings). Funeral money is 조의금/부의금. The words AND the envelopes are opposite; don't transfer the wedding term.
Giving an amount containing 4.
As with weddings, avoid 4 (四 ~ 死 'death'), which is doubly inappropriate at a funeral. Use figures like 5, 7, or 10만 원.

structuredNuance.t: 조의금 (弔意金) / 부의금 (賻儀金) is the cash given at a funeral, the somber counterpart to wedding 축의금. The make-or-break point is the ENVELOPE and wording: funeral money goes in a PLAIN WHITE envelope (흰 봉투) with sober wording like 부의 (賻儀) or 근조 (謹弔) written on it — using a decorative/colored envelope or congratulatory wording (祝) at a funeral is a grave offense. Amounts mirror weddings (~5–10만 원), with the same avoidance of 4. Logistically, you sign the 부의록 (condolence guestbook), hand the white envelope, then go in to bow. At the desk staff may simply nod; the words 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 carry the sentiment.
조의 vs 부의 vs 근조: all relate to mourning gifts — 조의(금)/부의(금) name the money; 근조 is the wreath/banner wording ('humbly mourning').
The verbs: you 내다 ('submit/pay') or 하다 it (조의금 하다, 부조 하다), and if you can't stay you 전하다 ('convey') it.

The cardinal mistake is reusing a wedding 축의금 mindset (verbs are similar, but tone, envelope, and wording are opposite). The pitfall also includes over-talking — at a funeral, handing the envelope is often done quietly; you don't need a cheerful speech, and you definitely don't say 축하 anything.

entries.nuance: While 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is addressed about the DECEASED, 상심이 크시겠어요 is what you say TO the grieving family member — and that distinction is exactly the thing English speakers get wrong. 상심 (傷心) is 'heartbreak/grief', 크다 ('to be great') in the honorific guess form 크시겠어요 ('must be great for you') → 'your grief must be immense.' The -겠- here is the empathetic 'must be' (inferring the other person's feeling), and the honorific -시- shows respect to the mourner; both are essential, so a flat 상심이 크겠어요 (no -시-) sounds cold. The cardinal pitfall is, again, translating English 'I'm sorry' as 죄송합니다/미안해요 — that's apology for wrongdoing, not condolence. Korean comfort is indirect and often unfinished: trailing off (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요..., 'I don't know what to say...') is genuinely the most natural, respectful move; a complete, articulate sentence can feel less heartfelt than a sympathetic silence. Another trap is being too cheerful or solution-y ('they're in a better place') — Korean funeral register is restrained sorrow, low voice, eyes down. Pair it with 힘내세요 ('stay strong') only AFTER acknowledging the grief; leading with 힘내세요 alone can feel dismissive. 상심하다 also exists ('to be heartbroken'), but to the mourner the empathetic 상심이 크시겠어요 is the set comfort.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 죄송합니다/미안해요 to mean 'sorry for your loss'.
Those apologize for a fault. To comfort the bereaved, say 상심이 크시겠어요 or 얼마나 힘드세요 — empathy, not apology.

To the grieving family you need -시-: 상심이 크시겠어요. Without it the sympathy sounds detached and under-respectful.
Trying to say something upbeat or 'fix it'.
Korean condolence is restrained and indirect. Trailing off (뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없네요...) is more appropriate than a cheerful or solution-oriented remark.

entries.nuance: 돌잔치 is the celebration of a baby's first birthday (돌 = first birthday + 잔치 = feast/party), a major family event in Korea — historically because surviving the first year was significant. 초대하다 (招待) is 'to invite', and 초대할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 intention form) is the host warmly saying 'I'll invite you / consider yourself invited.' The highlight ritual is the 돌잡이, where the baby picks an object (money, pencil, thread, etc.) said to foretell their future. Gift-wise, the traditional present is a 돌 반지 (a small gold ring) or money in an envelope (similar 축의금 logic, white-vs-decorative not as strict since it's joyful). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the EVENT verb — a 잔치 can take 하다 (돌잔치 하다, 'hold a party'), which feels inconsistent with rituals like 차례 지내다, but for celebratory 잔치/파티 you DO use 하다; don't say 돌잔치 지내다. (2) Don't confuse 돌 ('first birthday'/'stone'/'turn') homonyms — here it's the birthday. (3) Register: 초대하다 ('invite') is the right verb; learners sometimes say 부르다 ('to call'), but 부르다 for guests sounds blunt — 초대하다 is the courteous choice. A polite host commonly says you needn't bring the gold ring (금값 is high), so 돌 반지 안 가져오셔도 돼요 is a real, gracious line. Compare 환갑잔치/칠순잔치 (60th/70th birthday feasts), same 잔치 root, for elders.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

지내다 is for ancestral rites (차례/제사). A celebratory party takes 하다: 돌잔치 해요. Save 지내다 for memorial rituals.
Using 부르다 instead of 초대하다 for guests.
부르다 ('call') sounds blunt for inviting people to an event. The courteous verb is 초대하다: 돌잔치에 초대할게요.

Hosts politely wave off the 돌 반지, but guests typically still give money or a small gold gift. The disclaimer is courtesy, not a literal 'bring nothing'.

entries.shortExplanation: 벌써 일 년이네요 is a practical expression meaning "It's already been a year (said at a first birthday/memorial)".
entries.explanation: "It's already been a year (said at a first birthday/memorial)" — that is 벌써 일 년이네요 (beolsseo il nyeonineyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 벌써 일 년이네요 ("It's already been a year"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 벌써 일 년이네요 ('it's already been a year') is a warm, reflective remark perfect for a 돌잔치 (first birthday) — and, in a somber key, for a one-year memorial. 벌써 means 'already (sooner than expected)', 일 년 is 'one year', and -네요 is the soft exclamatory ending for noticing/realizing something on the spot ('oh, it's already a year, isn't it'). That -네요 is the heart of it: it conveys mild surprise and shared feeling, which is exactly the register for cooing over how fast a baby's first year flew. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 벌써 vs 이미 — both translate 'already', but 벌써 carries the emotional 'wow, so soon!' nuance ideal here, while 이미 is flatter and factual ('already done'), so 이미 일 년이네요 loses the warmth. (2) The number: 일 년 (one year) uses Sino-Korean 일, and the counter 년 is read with Sino numbers — learners sometimes say 한 년 (native number), which is wrong; it's 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년. (3) Tone-matching: at a happy 돌잔치 this is delighted; at a memorial the same words turn wistful — read the room. A natural companion line praising the parents is 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard raising the child'). Compare 엊그제 같다 ('feels like just the other day'), a frequent partner phrase.

The counter 년 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년. 한 년 (native number) is incorrect. One year is 일 년.
Dropping -네요 for flat 일 년이에요.
-네요 adds the on-the-spot 'oh, it's already a year!' feeling that fits the moment. Plain 일 년이에요 just states a fact and sounds cold.

structuredNuance.t: 벌써 일 년이네요 ('it's already been a year') is a warm, reflective remark perfect for a 돌잔치 (first birthday) — and, in a somber key, for a one-year memorial. -네요 is the soft exclamatory ending for noticing/realizing something on the spot ('oh, it's already a year, isn't it'); it conveys mild surprise and shared feeling, which is exactly the register for cooing over how fast a baby's first year flew. Tone-matching matters: at a happy 돌잔치 this is delighted; at a memorial the same words turn wistful — read the room. A natural companion line praising the parents is 키우느라 고생 많으셨어요 ('you've worked hard raising the child'). Compare 엊그제 같다 ('feels like just the other day'), a frequent partner phrase.
벌써 vs 이미 — both translate 'already', but 벌써 carries the emotional 'wow, so soon!' nuance ideal here, while 이미 is flatter and factual ('already done'), so 이미 일 년이네요 loses the warmth.
The number is a trap: 일 년 (one year) uses Sino-Korean 일, and the counter 년 is read with Sino numbers — learners sometimes say 한 년 (native number), which is wrong; it's 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년.

entries.shortExplanation: 성묘 가요 is a practical expression meaning "We go to visit the ancestors' graves".
entries.explanation: 성묘 가요 (seongmyo gayo) = "We go to visit the ancestors' graves". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 성묘 가요 ("We go grave-visiting"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.ko: 추석에 가족들이랑 성묘 가요.
examples.romanization: chuseoge gajokdeurirang seongmyo gayo.
examples.en: On Chuseok we go grave-visiting with the family.
examples.note: 성묘 is a core Chuseok/Seollal activity alongside 차례

examples.ko: 성묘 가서 할아버지 산소에 절했어요.
examples.romanization: seongmyo gaseo harabeoji sansoe jeolhaesseoyo.
examples.en: We went and bowed at Grandfather's grave.
examples.note: 산소 ('grave', honorific) + 절하다 ('to bow') — the actions at the grave

examples.ko: 요즘은 벌초 대행 서비스 부르는 집도 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun beolcho daehaeng seobiseu bureuneun jipdo manayo.
examples.en: These days many families hire a grave-weeding service.
examples.note: 벌초 대행 ('weeding-by-proxy') — a real modern convenience

entries.nuance: 성묘 (省墓) is visiting and tending an ancestor's grave, a key part of both 추석 and 설날 — families travel to the gravesite, clean it, set out a little food/drink, and bow (절하다). The verb is simply 가다 ('go') for the trip (성묘(를) 가요), and to report it's done you use the very useful 갔다 오다 ('go and come back'): 성묘 갔다 왔어요. A related word is 벌초 (伐草), specifically cutting the weeds/grass on the grave mound, traditionally done shortly before Chuseok — so 성묘 (the visit) and 벌초 (the weeding) are different: you might go 성묘 to pay respects, or 벌초 to maintain the grave, and many busy families now hire a 벌초 대행 service. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) vocabulary register — at the grave you refer to it as 산소 (honorific for an ancestor's grave) or 묘, not the blunt 무덤 ('a grave' in general), which can feel cold for your own ancestor. (2) The bow there is 절, NOT 세배 (세배 is only the living New Year bow to elders). (3) Don't 직역 'visit' as 방문하다 — 방문하다 is for visiting a person/place socially; for graves the set verb is just 성묘 가다. Note Korean burial is increasingly cremation (화장) with 납골당 (charnel houses), so 성묘 may mean visiting a 납골당 rather than a hillside mound.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling your ancestor's grave 무덤.
무덤 is a generic/blunt 'grave'. For your own ancestor use the respectful 산소 or 묘: 할아버지 산소에 성묘 가요.
Saying 세배 for the bow at the grave.
세배 is only the living New Year bow to elders. The bow at a grave (or any ritual bow) is just 절: 산소에서 절했어요.
Using 방문하다 for visiting the grave.
방문하다 is for social visits to people/places. The fixed expression is 성묘 가다 ('go grave-visiting'); 산소를 방문하다 sounds off.

entries.english: I go down to my hometown for the holiday
entries.shortExplanation: 명절에 고향 내려가요 is a practical expression meaning "I go down to my hometown for the holiday".
entries.explanation: 명절에 고향 내려가요 (myeongjeore gohyang naeryeogayo) means "I go down to my hometown for the holiday". Say it as one set phrase — for example 명절에 고향 내려가요 ("I go down to my hometown for the holiday"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.en: Busan is my hometown, so I go down every holiday.
examples.note: 고향이라(서) ('because it's my hometown') sets up why you travel

examples.romanization: seolnare gohyang naeryeoganeunde cha makyeoseo daseot sigan geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Going home for Seollal, traffic made it a 5-hour drive.
examples.note: 차 막히다 ('traffic jams') — the universal holiday-travel complaint

examples.romanization: ibeonen gohyang an naeryeogago geunyang jibeseo swiryeogoyo.
examples.en: This time I'm not going home, just resting at home.
examples.note: A natural way to say you're skipping the trip this year

entries.nuance: During 설날 and 추석 most Koreans travel to their family hometown, and the set verb is 내려가다 ('to go down') — because Seoul is thought of as 'up' and the provinces 'down', you 내려가다 to your 고향 ('hometown') and 올라오다 ('come up') back to the city. So 명절에 고향 내려가요 is 'I go down home for the holiday', even if your hometown is geographically east or west; the up/down is about Seoul-centric perception, not the compass — that's the key thing English speakers miss (they 직역 'go to my hometown' as 고향에 가요, which is fine but 내려가다 is the idiomatic, lived-in choice). The whole holiday exodus is 귀성 (歸省), and the brutal traffic on the way is 귀성길 ('the road home'), 귀성 전쟁 ('the going-home war') — knowing these makes you sound local. The particle point: it's 고향에 내려가다 (destination 에) but in fast speech 에 is often dropped (고향 내려가요), which is natural. A second nuance: 내려가다 vs 내려오다 depends on YOUR position — from Seoul you 내려가다 (go down there), but someone already in the hometown says a Seoulite 내려온다 (comes down here). Don't confuse 고향 ('hometown/where you're from') with 집 ('house/home') — you go 고향 to see parents and do 차례, then 올라와요 (come back up). If you're staying in the city, just say 고향 안 내려가요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고향에 올라가요 to mean going home to the provinces.
From Seoul you go DOWN to the provinces: 내려가요. 올라가요 ('go up') is for heading toward Seoul. The up/down is Seoul-centric, not compass-based.
Mixing 내려가다 and 내려오다.
Use 내려가다 ('go down there') when you're in Seoul heading to the hometown. 내려오다 ('come down here') is from the hometown's viewpoint. Direction depends on where you are.
Translating 'hometown' as 집.
집 is your house/home; 고향 is the region you're from / your parents' place. For the holiday journey it's 고향 내려가요, not 집에 내려가요.

entries.english: Your parcel's here / A delivery came
entries.shortExplanation: 택배 왔어요 is a practical expression meaning "Your parcel's here / A delivery came".
entries.explanation: "Your parcel's here / A delivery came" — that is 택배 왔어요 (taekbae wasseoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 택배 왔어요. ("Your parcel's here."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 택배 왔어요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말 — courier or family member announcing a delivery
반말 — to a friend, roommate, or younger family member
격식 — an app/SMS notification or a building intercom announcement

usagePhrases.en: There's a delivery — can you come get it?
usagePhrases.note: Courier at the door checking if you can receive it now

examples.ko:
택배 왔어요.
네, 감사합니다.
examples.romanization: taekbae wasseoyo. ne, gamsahamnida.
examples.en: Your parcel's here. — Yes, thank you.
examples.note: The bare announcement and the natural one-word reply

examples.ko: 어, 택배 왔나 봐. 누가 좀 받아 줘.
examples.romanization: eo, taekbae wanna bwa. nuga jom bada jwo.
examples.en: Oh, looks like a delivery came. Someone grab it.
examples.note: 왔나 봐 = 'looks like it came', guessing from the doorbell

examples.ko: 택배 왔는데 지금 집에 아무도 없어서요. 경비실에 맡겨 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: taekbae wanneunde jigeum jibe amudo eopseoseoyo. gyeongbisire matgyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: A parcel came but nobody's home right now. Could you leave it at the security office?
examples.note: Real situation: redirecting a delivery you can't receive

entries.nuance: This is the everyday phrase for 'a package arrived', said by a courier (택배 기사님) at your door, by a family member who heard the bell, or by an app push. 택배 means a courier/parcel-delivery service, so 택배 왔어요 literally is 'the delivery came'. To a stranger-courier you keep 존댓말 (왔어요); inside the family it drops to 반말 (왔어), and an automated notice uses the stiff 도착했습니다. The nearest alternative is 배송 왔어요, but 배송 is the abstract 'shipping' process word (used by stores: 배송 시작/배송 완료) while 택배 is the physical parcel and the human who brings it — say 택배 for the box at your door. English speakers often try to translate 'the delivery guy is here' word-for-word as 배달원이 있어요, which sounds robotic; Koreans just say 택배 왔어요 or call the person 택배 기사님. Also note 배달 (with ㄹ) means hot food delivery (pizza, chicken), not parcels — don't mix 택배 and 배달.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 배달 왔어요 for a parcel — 배달 is food delivery (치킨, 피자); a courier box is 택배, so the bell-ring announcement is 택배 왔어요.
Calling the courier 택배맨 or 배달원 to their face — the polite term is 택배 기사님 (driver-sir); 기사님 shows respect.
Using 배송 for the box itself (배송 왔어요 sounds off) — 배송 is the shipping process; the arrived parcel is 택배.

The nearest alternative is 배송 왔어요, but 배송 is the abstract 'shipping' process word (used by stores: 배송 시작/배송 완료) while 택배 is the physical parcel and the human who brings it — say 택배 for the box at your door. Also note 배달 (with ㄹ) means hot food delivery (pizza, chicken), not parcels — don't mix 택배 and 배달.
English speakers often try to translate 'the delivery guy is here' word-for-word as 배달원이 있어요, which sounds robotic; Koreans just say 택배 왔어요 or call the person 택배 기사님.

entries.nuance: This is the contactless-delivery line you say to a courier or type into the app's 요청사항 (request) box. 놔 주세요 is the contracted spoken form of 놓아 주세요 ('please place it'); both are correct — 놔 주세요 in speech, 놓아 주세요 in careful writing. The near-synonym is 두고 가세요 ('leave it and go'), which adds the nuance that they don't need to wait for you; 놔 주세요 just specifies the spot. English speakers often build 'leave it at the front door' literally as 앞문에 두세요, but 앞문 means the physical 'front door (leaf)' of a building, whereas 문 앞 means 'in front of the door' — the location you want is 문 앞에 (door + 앞 'front-space' + 에 'at'). Getting the order wrong (앞문 vs 문 앞) is the classic slip.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 앞문에 놔 주세요 — 앞문 = the front door panel itself; the spot 'in front of the door' is 문 앞에. Particle/word-order matters.
Using 놓으세요 as a bare command — to a service person, soften with 주세요 (놔 주세요) so it's a request, not an order.
Writing 나 주세요 for 놔 주세요 — it's 놓다 → 놔, with ㅎ; spelling it 나 changes the verb entirely.
