entries.nuance: You say this to flag noise — to a neighbor at the door, to staff in a public place, or as a written complaint. With a stranger keep 존댓말 (시끄러워요); to a friend it's 시끄러워; a formal report swaps to the noun 소음 + 심하다 ('the noise is severe'). The dividing line with the near-synonym 조용히 해 주세요 ('please be quiet') is direction: 시끄러워요 describes the problem (it IS loud), while 조용히 해 주세요 requests the fix — Koreans usually soften by stating the problem first, then the request. The English-speaker trap is treating 시끄럽다 like a verb you 'do'; it's an adjective (descriptive verb), so you never say 시끄러워 해요. Also, leading straight with a blunt 시끄러워요! to a neighbor sounds aggressive — open with 안녕하세요, 아래층인데요 ('I'm from downstairs') so it lands as a neighborly heads-up, not an attack.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 시끄럽다 as an action verb (시끄러워 해요) — it's a descriptive adjective; just say 시끄러워요.
Confusing 시끄럽다 (noisy) with 조용하다 (quiet) — to ask for silence you flip to 조용히 해 주세요, not 시끄럽게 하지 마요 only.
Opening a neighbor complaint with a bare 시끄러워요! — without 안녕하세요/아래층인데요 it sounds like a fight; identify yourself first.

entries.nuance: This is the request form of a noise complaint, said to a neighbor, a loud stranger, or in a quiet venue. 조용히 = 'quietly', 해 주세요 = 'please do (for me)', and the little 좀 ('a little / please') is what makes it polite rather than a command — dropping 좀 makes it noticeably sharper. Register climbs 조용히 좀 해 → 조용히 좀 해 주세요 → 조용히 해 주시겠어요?; the last (a yes/no question) is the gentlest. Versus 시끄러워요, which merely describes the noise, this one asks for the fix, so Koreans often pair them: 너무 시끄러워요. 조용히 좀 해 주세요. The English-speaker mistake is the bare imperative 조용히 해 ('be quiet') to a stranger — in English 'please be quiet' sounds fine, but Korean without 좀 and 주세요 sounds like scolding a child; always cushion it with 좀 … 주세요 for anyone you don't know.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 좀 and 주세요 (just 조용히 해) with strangers — it becomes a curt order; the polite form needs 좀 … 해 주세요.
Saying 조용해 주세요 — 조용하다 is an adjective; the request uses the adverb 조용히 + 해 주세요, i.e. 'do (it) quietly'.
Over-literal 'please be silent' as 침묵해 주세요 — 침묵 is heavy/literary ('silence, reticence'); everyday Korean is 조용히 해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 고장 나다 is the go-to phrase for a machine or appliance that stopped working — elevators, boilers, washing machines, intercoms, your phone. It pairs with the subject + 가/이 (보일러가 고장 났어요). To a landlord or office it's 존댓말 (났어요); among family 났어; a written notice uses 고장이 났습니다. The key dividing line: 고장 나다 is for things with a mechanism, while 망가지다 means 'got wrecked/ruined' and covers physical breakage of any object (a toy, a zipper, a relationship) — a glass that shatters is 깨졌어요, not 고장 났어요. The English-speaker trap is mapping 'broken' onto 부러졌어요 ('snapped in two', like a bone or stick) for an appliance — a TV that won't turn on is 고장 났어요, never 부러졌어요. Also note it's intransitive: the thing 고장 나다 ('breaks'); you don't 'break' it with this verb — to say you broke something, that's 고장 냈어요 (causative) or 망가뜨렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 부러졌어요 ('snapped') for an appliance — that's for sticks/bones; a non-working machine is 고장 났어요.
Saying 깨졌어요 for a machine — 깨지다 = shatter (glass, screen); a malfunctioning device is 고장 났어요.
Mixing up 고장 났어요 (it broke, by itself) with 고장 냈어요 (I broke it) — the second blames you; use 났어요 to just report the fault.

entries.nuance: This requests a repair from a landlord, building office, or service center. 수리 is the Sino-Korean noun 'repair' and pairs with 하다, so 수리(를) 해 주세요 = 'please do the repair'; the casual everyday equivalent is the pure-Korean verb 고치다 (고쳐 주세요). The register split is also a word split: in 존댓말 to officials, 수리해 주세요 / 수리 부탁드려요 sounds proper; in 반말 to a friend you'd say 고쳐 줘, almost never 수리해 줘. The dividing line with 고치다: both mean 'fix', but 수리 implies a professional/paid repair of a machine or building, while 고치다 is broader and can also mean 'correct/mend' (fix a habit, mend clothes). English speakers often reach for 'repair' as 리페어 or try 만들어 주세요 ('make it') — 만들다 is 'create from scratch', wrong for fixing; use 수리해 주세요 or 고쳐 주세요. Adding 좀 keeps the request soft and natural.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Saying 수리해 줘 to a friend — 수리 sounds officialese in 반말; friends say 고쳐 줘.
Dropping 주세요 (just 수리해) when asking staff — it becomes an order; soften to 수리 좀 해 주세요 / 부탁드려요.

entries.nuance: In a Korean apartment (아파트) or officetel, the 관리실 (management/superintendent's office) handles building problems — elevators, water, heating, parking, deliveries — so this is the line a neighbor gives you when something breaks. 관리실에 takes 에 ('to a place'); -해 보세요 = 'try doing', which makes it a gentle suggestion rather than a command. To a stranger it's 존댓말 (보세요); to a friend 봐; formally you'd say 관리실로 문의하세요. The nearest term is 경비실 (the security/guard booth at the gate): 경비실 watches the entrance and receives parcels, while 관리실 deals with maintenance and bills — for a broken boiler you want 관리실, not 경비실. English speakers often call it the 'office' and say 사무실, but 사무실 is a generic business office; a residential building's maintenance desk is specifically 관리실, and the staffer is 관리소장님 or 경비 아저씨.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling it 사무실 — that's a generic office; an apartment's maintenance desk is 관리실.
Confusing 관리실 (maintenance/admin) with 경비실 (security gate) — boiler/water issues go to 관리실; parcels and entry to 경비실.
Using 에서 instead of 에 (관리실에서 전화해 보세요) — 에서 marks where an action happens; 'call TO the office' takes 관리실에.

entries.nuance: This reports a water outage to your building office or landlord. 물이 안 나와요 = 'water + subject + doesn't come out' — 나오다 ('come out') is the verb for water/gas/electricity flowing from a tap or outlet, and 안 negates it. To officials use 존댓말 (나와요); to family 나와; an official outage notice says 단수(가) 됐습니다. The distinction to learn: plain 물 covers all water, but 온수 = hot water and 냉수/찬물 = cold — if only the hot is out (a boiler issue) say 온수가 안 나와요, which points to a different fix than a full 단수 (supply cut). The English-speaker trap is translating 'the water doesn't work' as 물이 안 돼요 — 되다 ('work/function') suits machines, but water 'comes out', so it's 나와요. Saying 물이 없어요 is also wrong here: 없어요 = 'there isn't any (in stock)', fine for a water bottle, but a dead tap is 물이 안 나와요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 물이 안 돼요 — 되다 is for devices; water flowing from a tap uses 나오다, so 물이 안 나와요.
Using 물이 없어요 for a dead tap — 없다 = 'there's none (in supply/stock)'; a non-flowing faucet is 안 나와요.
Saying just 물이 안 나와요 when only hot water is out — specify 온수가 안 나와요 so they check the boiler, not the mains.

entries.nuance: 분리수거 (separate-collection, i.e. sorted recycling) is a daily ritual in Korean apartments, with separate bins for 플라스틱, 캔, 유리, 종이, 비닐, and strict collection days — so newcomers genuinely need this question. 분리수거(를) 어떻게 해요? = 'how do I do the sorting?'; the verb is 하다, and you 버리다 ('throw out / put out') each item. To a neighbor it's 존댓말 (해요); to a friend 해; formally -하면 됩니까. The related word 음식물 쓰레기 (food waste) is collected separately again — don't fold it into 분리수거 in your head. The English-speaker trap is calling it 'recycling' as 재활용 only: 재활용 is the abstract concept 'recycling/reuse', whereas the household act of sorting-and-putting-out is 분리수거 — ask 분리수거 어떻게 해요, not 재활용 어떻게 해요. Also 비닐 (plastic film/bags) and 플라스틱 (rigid plastic) go in different piles; lumping them is the usual newcomer error.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

Asking 재활용 어떻게 해요? — 재활용 is the concept 'recycling'; the household sorting act is 분리수거.
Putting 음식물 쓰레기 in with 분리수거 — food waste is a separate collection; keep it out of the recycling bins.
Confusing 비닐 (soft film/bags) with 플라스틱 (rigid) — they're separate categories; lumping them gets your bag rejected.

entries.nuance: 음식물 쓰레기 ('food-stuff garbage') is the compostable food-waste stream that Korean homes must separate from 일반 쓰레기 (general trash) and from 분리수거 recyclables — usually into a dedicated bin or a paid 음식물 봉투. You put it out with 버리다 or, formally, 배출하다. Saying what something is uses 이에요/예요; the chore request is 버려 줄래/주세요. The dividing line with 일반 쓰레기 is sharp and trips everyone: only soft, decomposable food counts — 달걀 껍데기 (eggshells), 뼈 (bones), 조개껍데기 (clam shells), tea bags, and onion skins are NOT 음식물 and must go to general trash. The English-speaker trap is thinking 'food waste = anything from the kitchen'; in Korea the test is 'could an animal eat it / will it rot', so hard shells and bones are excluded. Another slip is calling it 음식 쓰레기 — the correct compound is 음식물 쓰레기 (with 물).

entries.nuance: 층간 소음 (literally 'between-floors noise') is a hugely common and emotionally charged issue in Korean apartment living — footsteps, dragged chairs, kids running — and it's the fixed term everyone uses, so a newcomer should know it as a set phrase, not build it word by word. 층 = floor, 간 = 'between', 소음 = noise. A cultural note baked into the language: Koreans strongly advise handling it 관리실을 통해서 ('through the office') rather than confronting the neighbor directly, because direct 층간 소음 confrontations are notorious for escalating.

entries.nuance: This is the practical report you make to the 관리실 or warn neighbors with when the lift is out — a real concern in tall Korean apartments. 엘리베이터 (loanword; some older people say 승강기) takes 가/이, and the breakdown verb is 고장 나다. To the office it's 존댓말 (났어요); to a friend 났어; a posted sign reads 고장 나서 점검 중입니다. A useful contrast: 고장 났어요 = 'it's broken (out of service)', while 멈췄어요 / 갇혔어요 = 'it stopped' / 'someone's trapped', which signals an emergency needing an immediate call. The English-speaker trap is the word itself — saying 'lift' as 리프트 (which in Korean means a ski lift or a jack), or trying 'elevator is down' literally as 엘리베이터가 내려갔어요 (which just means 'the elevator went down a floor'). 'Out of order' is 고장 났어요 / 운행 중지, not 내려갔어요. Many learners also forget the subject particle and say 엘리베이터 고장, which is sign-language shorthand, not a full spoken sentence.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 엘리베이터가 내려갔어요 to mean 'out of order' — that means it descended a floor; broken is 고장 났어요.
Calling it 리프트 — in Korean 리프트 is a ski lift/jack; the building lift is 엘리베이터 (or 승강기).
Confusing 고장 났어요 (broken/out of service) with 멈췄어요/갇혔어요 (stopped/trapped) — the latter is an emergency; call 관리실 at once.

entries.nuance: Korean homes and units overwhelmingly use keypad door locks (도어록), so 비밀번호가 뭐예요? ('what's the passcode?') is essential for a guest, tenant, or visitor — for the front door (현관), the building entrance (공동현관), or the Wi-Fi (와이파이). 비밀번호 = 'secret number/password'; the polite ask is 뭐예요?, and the gentler 어떻게 되나요? sounds more refined. To a host/landlord it's 존댓말; to a friend 비밀번호 뭐야. The near-synonym 암호 ('cipher/passcode') exists but feels technical or spy-ish; for everyday locks and Wi-Fi, Koreans say 비밀번호 (often shortened 비번 in casual speech). The English-speaker trap is reaching for 패스워드 — understood, but native and natural is 비밀번호. Another trap is the digits: Koreans read door codes with 공 for 0 (공일공일 = 0101) and may say 별표 (the * key) or 우물 정자/샵 (#), so listen for those, not 'zero'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 패스워드 — it's understood but the natural word is 비밀번호 (casual 비번).
Reading 0 as 제로 in a code — Koreans say 공 (공일이삼 = 0123); using 제로 sounds off for door/phone codes.
Asking 비밀번호가 어디예요? — 어디 = 'where'; to ask the value use 뭐예요? or 어떻게 되나요?.

entries.nuance: This is the warm invitation a host gives at the door — to a neighbor returning something, a delivery person, or a guest you want to usher in out of the cold or rain. 잠깐 = 'for a moment/briefly', 들어오세요 = 'please come in' (들어오다, 'enter, come in', from the listener-toward-speaker direction). To most people it's 존댓말 (들어오세요); to a close friend 들어와; the politest is 잠시 들어오시겠어요? (a question is softer). The verb pair to keep straight is 들어오다 ('come in', toward the speaker, what a host says) vs 들어가다 ('go in', away from the speaker) — a host at home always says 들어오세요, never 들어가세요 (which would mean 'go in, away from me'). The English-speaker trap is exactly that direction error, plus translating 'come in' as the bare 와요 ('come') without 들어-, which loses the 'into the space' meaning. Note Korean homes are shoes-off, so the invitation implies stepping up past the 현관; a guest may answer 신발 벗어야 돼요? ('should I take my shoes off?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 들어가세요 as a host — that's 'go in (away from me)'; inviting someone toward you is 들어오세요.
Using bare 와요 for 'come in' — 와요 is just 'come'; 'come inside' needs 들어오다 → 들어오세요.
Forgetting the shoes-off norm — after 들어오세요, expect to remove shoes at the 현관; barging in with shoes on is a real faux pas.

structuredNuance.t: This is the warm invitation a host gives at the door — to a neighbor returning something, a delivery person, or a guest you want to usher in out of the cold or rain. 잠깐 = 'for a moment/briefly', 들어오세요 = 'please come in' (들어오다, 'enter, come in', from the listener-toward-speaker direction). To most people it's 존댓말 (들어오세요); to a close friend 들어와; the politest is 잠시 들어오시겠어요? (a question is softer). Note Korean homes are shoes-off, so the invitation implies stepping up past the 현관; a guest may answer 신발 벗어야 돼요? ('should I take my shoes off?').

The verb pair to keep straight is 들어오다 ('come in', toward the speaker, what a host says) vs 들어가다 ('go in', away from the speaker) — a host at home always says 들어오세요, never 들어가세요 (which would mean 'go in, away from me').
The English-speaker trap is exactly that direction error, plus translating 'come in' as the bare 와요 ('come') without 들어-, which loses the 'into the space' meaning.

entries.nuance: Removing shoes indoors is a firm rule in every Korean home, so a host says this routinely and a newcomer must both understand it and obey it. 신발 = shoes, 벗다 = take off (clothing/shoes), and -고 links it to 들어오세요 ('take off AND come in'). To a guest it's 존댓말 (벗고 들어오세요); to a friend 벗고 들어와. The verb to nail is 벗다 ('take off') vs its opposite 신다 ('put on', for footwear specifically) — you 신발을 벗다 to remove and 신발을 신다 to wear; note shoes/socks use 신다, not 입다 (which is for clothing on the torso). The English-speaker trap is using 입다/벗다 wrong for footwear ('take off shoes' as 신발을 입다 is impossible) and stepping up onto the raised floor (마루/거실) with shoes still on — the line between the 현관 (lowered entry) and the floor is exactly where shoes must come off. Forgetting and walking in shod is one of the most noticeable foreigner mistakes in Korea.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 신발을 입다/벗으세요 mismatched — footwear uses 신다 (put on) / 벗다 (take off), never 입다.
Stepping onto the 거실/마루 with shoes on — shoes come off at the 현관; the raised floor is shoes-free.
Translating 'take off' as 빼다 (신발 빼세요) — 빼다 is 'pull out/remove (an object)'; for shoes/clothes it's 벗다.

entries.nuance: This is the phrase you say through a closed door or the 인터폰 (intercom) when someone rings — distinct in feel from answering the phone, though the words overlap. 누구세요? = 'who are you?' with the honorific 세요, polite enough for any stranger. To family it drops to 누구야?; a gentler, more formal alternative is 어떻게 오셨어요? ('what brings you?'), which asks purpose instead of bluntly demanding identity and is what you'd use for a guest you half-expect. The dividing line: 누구세요? is direct ('who?') and fine for an unknown buzz; 어떻게 오셨어요? is softer and better once you're opening the door to someone who looks legitimate. The English-speaker trap is answering a knock with 여보세요? — that's strictly the telephone 'hello' and sounds odd at a door; at the door it's 누구세요?. Another slip is 당신 누구예요?: 당신 ('you') sounds confrontational or even like a challenge to a stranger, so drop it — the subject-less 누구세요? is the natural, safe form.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering the door with 여보세요? — that's the phone 'hello'; at a door or intercom say 누구세요?.
Adding 당신 (당신 누구예요?) — 당신 to a stranger sounds confrontational; the bare 누구세요? is correct.
Using 누구예요? flat — at the door the honorific 누구세요? is safer/politer to an unknown adult than plain 누구예요?.

entries.nuance: Greeting the neighbors as a new arrival is a real social step in Korea, and 이사 왔어요 ('I have moved in / come by moving') is the core line — said at the door to 옆집 (next door), 윗집/아랫집 (upstairs/downstairs), or the 경비/관리실. 이사(를) 오다 = 'to move in (toward here)'; note the directional verb 오다 ('come') because you've arrived where you now are — 이사 갔어요 (with 가다, 'go') means you moved OUT/away, the opposite. To neighbors it's 존댓말 (왔어요); to a peer 이사 왔어; formally 이사 오게 되었습니다. It's almost always followed by the set phrase 잘 부탁드립니다 ('please treat me well / let's get along'), which has no literal English equivalent — leaving it off feels abrupt. The English-speaker trap is exactly the 오다/가다 direction error (saying 이사 갔어요 to a new neighbor implies you're leaving), plus translating 'move' as 움직이다 ('move physically/budge'), which is wrong: relocating houses is 이사하다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이사 갔어요 to a new neighbor — 가다 = 'go (away)', meaning you moved OUT; arriving here is 이사 왔어요 (오다).
Using 움직였어요 for 'I moved' — 움직이다 is physical motion/budging; changing residence is 이사하다.
Ending at 이사 왔어요 with nothing more — Koreans expect the follow-up 잘 부탁드립니다; omitting it sounds curt.

entries.nuance: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어요 is the core opening line at 출입국 (Immigration) or a service center: 외국인등록증 ('Alien Registration Card', the ARC every foreigner staying over 90 days must get) + 발급받다 ('to be issued / receive issuance') + -으러 왔어요 ('came in order to'). entries.nuance: 체류 기간 연장 is the official term for extending your authorized stay: 체류 ('staying/residence', Sino-Korean 滯留) + 기간 ('period') + 연장 ('extension', 延長). On forms and signs you'll see 체류기간 연장허가 ('permission to extend period of stay'), so 체류 기간 연장 is the phrase that matches the bureaucracy. In everyday speech many foreigners and even staff say 비자 연장 ('visa extension'), and that's understood — but technically you extend your 체류 기간 (the stay tied to your status), and the 비자 (the entry sticker) is a slightly different thing; for talking to officials, 체류 기간 연장 is the precise term. The dividing line: use -하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to') to state the goal politely, or -하러/하려고 왔어요 ('I came in order to') to frame it as why you're here — both are natural; officials respond to either. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'renew': learners reach for 갱신, but 갱신 (renewal) is mostly for re-issuing an expiring card/ARC, while 연장 (extension) is for adding more time to your stay — picking the wrong one confuses the clerk about which service you want. Register is plain 존댓말, perfect for a counter. Don't drop 기간 awkwardly mid-sentence; 체류 연장 (without 기간) is the accepted short form, but 체류만 연장 sounds incomplete.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

연장 adds time to your stay; 갱신 re-issues an expiring document. To stay longer, say 체류 기간 연장; to replace an expiring ARC, say 갱신.
Saying 체류를 늘리고 싶어요.
늘리다 ('to increase/lengthen') is too literal/physical here. The fixed bureaucratic verb is 연장하다: 체류 기간 연장하고 싶어요.
Treating 비자 and 체류 기간 as identical to an official.
Casually 비자 연장 is fine, but precisely you extend 체류 기간 (your stay). For accuracy with staff, say 체류 기간 연장.

entries.nuance: 비자 종류가 뭐예요? is 비자 ('visa') + 종류 ('type/kind', 種類) + 가 뭐예요 ('what is'), used to ask or confirm which visa category (D-2 student, E-2 teaching, E-7 work, F-6 marriage, etc.) is in play. Knowing your 종류 matters because every service — 연장, 변경, 신고 — depends on it. The key register split is who asks: a clerk will ask you honorifically, 비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요? (어떻게 되세요 is the polite 'how is it / may I ask'), and you answer plainly with the code, 'E-7이요'. If YOU ask, the neutral 비자 종류가 뭐예요? or casual 무슨 비자예요? is right — but never answer a clerk's honorific question by bouncing 어떻게 되세요 back at yourself. The near-synonym 비자 상태 ('visa status') sounds like English 'status' but in Korean offices the operative word is 종류 (category) or 체류자격 ('status of stay', the formal term on documents); if you want to sound official, 체류자격이 어떻게 되세요? is what appears on forms. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'what is my visa status' as 제 비자 상태가 뭐예요?, which Koreans parse as 'is my visa okay/valid?' rather than 'which category'; to ask the category, say 종류 or 체류자격. Particle note: it's 종류'가' 뭐예요 (subject 가), not 종류'를'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering a clerk's 어떻게 되세요? with 어떻게 돼요 about yourself.
어떻게 되세요 is honorific, aimed AT you. You answer plainly: just state the code, 'F-6이요', not by re-asking 어떻게 돼요.
Saying 비자 상태가 뭐예요 to mean 'which category'.
상태 ('state/condition') sounds like asking if it's valid. For the category, say 비자 종류가 뭐예요 or the formal 체류자격.
Using 를 instead of 가: 비자 종류를 뭐예요.
'What is X' takes the subject particle: 비자 종류가 뭐예요. 를 marks an object and is ungrammatical with 뭐예요.

entries.nuance: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요? is 신청서 ('application form', 申請書) + 어떻게 ('how') + 작성하다 ('to fill out / draw up', 作成), the line that gets a clerk to walk you through the paperwork. 작성하다 is the proper, slightly formal verb for completing a form or document; in casual speech you'd say 쓰다 ('write') or 적다 ('jot/note'), and 어떻게 써요? is perfectly natural and a bit warmer. The dividing line: 작성하다 is for filling out a whole document (form, report), while 적다/쓰다 fit a single field — so 'how do I fill out the form' is 작성, but 'what do I write in this box' is 여기 뭐 적어요?. The near-synonym 기입하다 ('to enter/inscribe') also means filling in fields and shows up on official instructions, but it sounds bookish to say aloud; stick with 작성/적다 when speaking. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'fill out' as 채우다 ('to fill (a container)') — 신청서를 채워요 sounds like physically stuffing the form full, not completing it; the right verb is 작성하다. Register stays plain 존댓말. Particle-wise you can drop the object marker in speech (신청서 작성해요 rather than 신청서를), which is natural and common. Pair it with 영어로 작성해도 돼요? to check if you may write in English, a very common real concern.

entries.nuance: 어디에서 접수해요? is 어디에서 ('at where') + 접수하다 ('to submit / receive intake', 接受). 접수 is the bureaucratic word for the intake of documents — handing in your application so it's officially received and processed. It cuts both ways: as the applicant you 접수하다 (submit), and the office 접수받다/접수하다 (receives) it; the counter where this happens is the 접수처 or 접수 창구. The subtle point English speakers miss is that 접수 is NOT just 'submit a paper' — it means lodging it into the system so it's logged, so 'I submitted my application and got a receipt number' is all 접수. The near-synonym 제출하다 ('to submit/turn in', 提出) overlaps but leans toward handing over a specific document (a report, a certificate), while 접수 emphasizes the office accepting and registering your case — at immigration, 접수 is the word on the signs and tickets. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'submit' always as 제출, then being confused by 접수 on every sign; learn 접수 as the front-desk intake verb. Particle trap: location of an action takes -에서 (어디에서 접수해요), not -에 (which marks a static location or destination) — 어디에 접수해요 sounds slightly off. Register is plain 존댓말, ideal for staff. The passive 접수되다 ('to be accepted/received') is handy to ask 이거 접수돼요? ('will this be accepted?').

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using -에 instead of -에서 for the action: 어디에 접수해요.
An action's location takes -에서: 어디에서 접수해요? -에 marks a destination/static spot, which sounds off with the verb 접수하다.
Assuming 접수 just means handing over one paper.
접수 is the office formally receiving and logging your case. It covers submitting, getting a number, and being entered into the system — broader than 제출.
Mixing up 접수 (intake) and 영수증 (receipt).
접수 is submitting/intake; 영수증 is a payment receipt. After 접수 you may get a 접수증 (acknowledgment slip), not an 영수증. Keep them separate.

entries.nuance: 방문 예약하고 왔어요 is 방문 ('visit', 訪問) + 예약하다 ('to reserve/book', 豫約) + -하고 왔어요 ('did it and came'), the line that tells staff you hold an online appointment — essential because Korean immigration offices (출입국) now largely run on mandatory reservations through 하이코리아 (HiKorea), and walking in without one often means being turned away or waiting forever. The -하고 왔어요 structure ('I did X and came') is the natural way to report a completed precondition: you booked, then showed up. The key vocabulary point is 예약 ('reservation/booking', for a future slot — restaurants, hospitals, offices) — don't confuse it with 약속 ('a promise / a personal appointment to meet someone'); saying 약속하고 왔어요 would mean 'I made a personal promise and came', which baffles a clerk. That 예약 vs 약속 mix-up is a classic English-speaker trap because English 'appointment' covers both a booked slot and a meeting. The 직역 pitfall: 'I have a reservation' rendered as 예약을 가지고 있어요 ('I possess a reservation') is unnatural — Korean says 예약했어요 ('I reserved') or 예약하고 왔어요. Register is plain 존댓말, right for the counter. Note the contrast 예약 (booking ahead) vs 접수 (intake on arrival): you 예약 to secure the slot, then 접수 your documents once there — two different steps. If you have no booking, the useful question is 예약 안 하고 왔는데 접수돼요? ('I came without a reservation — can I still be processed?'). Particle: 2시'로' 예약 ('booked FOR 2 o'clock') uses -로 to mark the chosen time slot.

약속 is a personal promise/meeting. A booked office slot is 예약: 방문 예약하고 왔어요 / 예약했어요.

Korean doesn't 'possess' a reservation. Say 예약했어요 ('I reserved') or 예약하고 왔어요 ('I booked and came').
Confusing 예약 (book ahead) with 접수 (intake on arrival).
예약 secures a future slot; 접수 is submitting your case once you're there. Booking the visit is 예약, handing in papers is 접수.

entries.nuance: 번호표 뽑고 기다리시면 돼요 is what the staff or a sign tells YOU: 번호표 ('number ticket', 番號票) + 뽑다 ('to pull/draw out', i.e. take from a dispenser) + 기다리다 ('wait') + -시면 돼요 (honorific 'you may / it's fine if you'). The verb for taking a queue ticket is specifically 뽑다 ('pull out'), the same verb as drawing a card or pulling a weed — Korean conceives of yanking the slip from the machine. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'take a ticket' as 가지다/가져가다 ('possess/carry'), giving 번호표 가져가세요, which sounds like 'take the ticket away with you'; the idiomatic verb is 뽑다. Register is the big lesson here: -시면 돼요 carries the honorific -시- because the STAFF are politely addressing you the customer — when YOU repeat the action about yourself, you drop the -시-: 번호표 뽑고 기다릴게요 ('I'll take a number and wait'), never 뽑으시고 about your own action. A common slip is echoing the honorific back onto yourself. entries.nuance: 여기 서명하면 돼요? is 여기 ('here') + 서명하다 ('to sign', 署名) + -면 돼요? ('is it okay if I…?'), the line for confirming where your signature goes. Two words mean 'sign': the formal/native-feeling 서명 (signature) and the loanword 사인 (from English 'sign'); both are used constantly, with 사인 more casual and 서명 what appears on official documents — but beware that 사인 also means 'autograph (of a celebrity)', so context carries it. The bigger cultural point is 도장/인감 ('seal, name stamp'): Korea traditionally uses a carved name seal instead of a handwritten signature for official acts, so a clerk may ask 도장 있으세요? ('do you have a seal?'), and you can reply 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? ('I don't have a seal — may I sign?'). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming a signature is always accepted and not knowing the word 도장; also the 직역 of 'sign' as the verb 사인하다 is fine, but in a formal sentence 서명하다 reads better. The -면 돼요? structure is the key polite confirm pattern: '-면 돼요?' = 'is it fine if I (do)?'; learners often over-translate 'should I sign here' as 서명해야 돼요? ('must I sign?'), which asks about obligation rather than confirming the spot — for 'is THIS where I sign', use 여기 서명하면 돼요?. Register is plain 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

Saying 서명해야 돼요? when you mean 'is this where I sign?'.
-해야 돼요 asks about obligation ('must I sign?'). To confirm the spot, use -하면 돼요: 여기 서명하면 돼요?
Not knowing 도장 and insisting only on a signature.
Korean offices often expect a 도장 (name seal). If asked 도장 있으세요?, you can say 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? to offer a signature instead.
Using 사인 in a strictly formal document context.
사인 is casual and also means 'autograph'. On official paperwork the cleaner word is 서명: 여기 서명하면 돼요?

entries.nuance: 여권 사본 필요해요? is 여권 ('passport', 旅券) + 사본 ('copy/duplicate', 寫本) + 필요해요 ('is needed'), asking whether a photocopy is required. The crucial pair is 사본 ('a copy') vs 원본 ('the original', 原本): immigration often wants both your passport 원본 (to verify) and a 사본 (to keep on file), so knowing both words prevents a wasted trip. The verb for making/issuing an official copy or certificate is 떼다 (literally 'to detach') — 사본 떼다 ('make a copy'), 등본 떼다 ('get a certified extract') — which baffles English speakers because its dictionary sense is 'peel off'; just learn 떼다 = 'obtain an official paper'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'copy' as 카피, which Koreans rarely use for documents (카피 sounds like advertising copy); the document word is 사본. Another trap is the verb 'need': learners say 필요로 해요 (over-literal 'have need of'), but natural Korean is simply 필요해요 ('is needed') — note 필요하다 takes the thing as the SUBJECT (여권 사본'이' 필요해요), not the object, so 여권 사본을 필요해요 is a particle error. Register plain 존댓말. Pair with 원본도 필요해요? to cover the most common follow-up about originals.

필요하다 makes the needed thing the SUBJECT: 여권 사본이 필요해요. Marking it with object 을/를 is ungrammatical.

카피 reads as 'advertising copy' in Korean. A photocopy/duplicate of a document is 사본: 여권 사본 필요해요?

To get an official copy you 떼다 it: 사본 떼다, 등본 떼다. Saying 사본 만들다 is understandable but 떼다 is the natural office verb.

entries.nuance: 이 서류 다 준비했어요 is 이 ('this/these') + 서류 ('documents/paperwork', 書類) + 다 ('all') + 준비하다 ('to prepare', 準備) in past tense, the line that says you've brought everything required. 서류 is the all-purpose word for official papers (forms, certificates, copies) and is treated as a mass noun, so 서류 covers one paper or a whole stack — you don't pluralize it. The verb 준비했어요 (past of 준비하다) is exactly right for 'I have prepared/got ready'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'documents' as 다큐먼트 or even 문서 in the wrong place: 문서 ('a document/text file') is more about a written document or computer file, while the bundle of papers you bring to a government office is 서류 — say 서류 at immigration. Another trap is 다 ('all') placement: 다 goes right before the verb (다 준비했어요), not before the noun as English 'all the documents' might tempt you (it's not 다 서류). The follow-up 서류 더 필요한 거 있어요? ('is there any more document needed?') is invaluable — note 더 ('more') + 필요한 거 ('thing that's needed'). Register plain 존댓말. A natural softener when handing them over is the -는데 lead-in: 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요 ('I've prepared everything, so please check'), pairing your statement with a polite request to verify.

문서 leans toward a written document or file. The packet of official papers is 서류: 이 서류 다 준비했어요.
Placing 다 before the noun: 다 서류 준비했어요.
다 ('all') normally sits right before the verb: 서류 다 준비했어요. Fronting it onto the noun sounds off.
Saying 준비해요 (present) for 'I have prepared'.
Completed preparation is past tense: 준비했어요. 준비해요 sounds like a general/habitual 'I prepare', not 'I've got it ready'.

structuredNuance.t: 이 ('this/these') + 서류 ('documents/paperwork', 書類) + 다 ('all') + 준비하다 ('to prepare', 準備) in past tense, the line that says you've brought everything required. 서류 is the all-purpose word for official papers (forms, certificates, copies) and is treated as a mass noun, so it covers one paper or a whole stack — you don't pluralize it. The verb 준비했어요 (past of 준비하다) is exactly right for 'I have prepared/got ready'. Register plain 존댓말. A natural softener when handing them over is the -는데 lead-in: 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요 ('I've prepared everything, so please check'). The follow-up 서류 더 필요한 거 있어요? ('is there any more document needed?') is invaluable — note 더 ('more') + 필요한 거 ('thing that's needed').
문서 ('a document/text file') is more about a written document or computer file, while the bundle of papers you bring to a government office is 서류 — say 서류 at immigration.

The 직역 of 'documents' as 다큐먼트 or 문서 in the wrong place (문서 leans toward a written document or file, not the office packet). Another trap is 다 ('all') placement: 다 goes right before the verb (다 준비했어요), not before the noun as English 'all the documents' might tempt you (it's not 다 서류).

entries.nuance: 주소 변경 신고하러 왔어요 is 주소 ('address', 住所) + 변경 ('change', 變更) + 신고하다 ('to report/declare to authorities', 申告) + -하러 왔어요 ('came in order to'). 신고하다 is the load-bearing verb: it means an official, legally-required REPORT to the government — you 신고 a change of address, a birth, a lost ARC, taxes. It is NOT casual 'telling someone'; the everyday 'tell/say' is 말하다, and confusing them (e.g. 주소 바뀐 거 말하러 왔어요, 'I came to tell you my address changed') sounds like you're just chatting, not filing. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 직역 of 'report' or 'let you know' as 알려주다/말하다 when the legal act is 신고하다. For foreigners specifically, an address change is filed as 체류지 변경신고 ('change of residence report') at immigration or via 전입신고 ('move-in report') at the 구청/주민센터 — 전입신고 is the precise term for registering that you've moved INTO a new place, so if a clerk says 전입신고, that's the move-in registration. The near-contrast: 변경 ('change') is the general word, while 전입 ('moving in') is specific to relocating residence. Register plain 존댓말. Note the deadline culture — address changes must be reported within 14 days (14일 이내), so staff may stress 기간 ('the deadline'); knowing 신고 is mandatory and time-bound is part of the meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 말하러 왔어요 instead of 신고하러 왔어요.
말하다 is casual 'to tell'. An official report to the government is 신고하다: 주소 변경 신고하러 왔어요.
Confusing 신고 (report/declare) with 신청 (apply/request).
신고 declares a fact (address change, loss); 신청 requests a service (extension, issuance). A move is a 신고, not a 신청.
Using 변경 when 전입신고 is the specific term.
Registering that you moved INTO a new home is 전입신고. 주소 변경 is fine generally, but if staff say 전입신고, that's the exact move-in report.

entries.nuance: 수수료 얼마예요? is 수수료 ('handling/service fee', 手數料) + 얼마예요 ('how much is it'), the standard way to ask the processing fee for an immigration service (extension, ARC issuance, etc.). 수수료 specifically means the administrative fee charged for a service or transaction — distinct from 요금 ('a charge/fare', like a bus 요금 or utility 요금) and 비용 ('cost/expense', a general word). At a government office the operative word on the fee schedule is 수수료, sometimes 행정 수수료 ('administrative fee'); using 가격 ('price', for goods you buy) or 값 ('the cost of an item') here sounds wrong because you're not buying a product, you're paying a service charge. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'fee' as 피 (the loanword) or defaulting to 가격 — neither fits a government fee; say 수수료. A practical wrinkle: some immigration fees are still paid with 수입인지 ('revenue stamps') that you buy and affix, or via a kiosk, so 수수료 어떻게 내요? ('how do I pay the fee?') and 카드로 내도 돼요? ('can I pay by card?') are essential follow-ups, since cash-only or stamp-only situations exist. 얼마예요 keeps the copula fused (얼마+예요); don't split it as 얼마 이에요. Register plain 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 가격 or 값 for the government fee.
가격/값 are for buying goods. A service/processing charge at an office is 수수료: 수수료 얼마예요?
Saying 피 (the English loan 'fee').
피 isn't used for this. The Korean word is 수수료. Asking 피 얼마예요 won't be understood as 'fee'.
Splitting the copula: 수수료 얼마 이에요.
얼마 + 예요 fuses to 얼마예요. 얼마 이에요 is unnatural; say 수수료 얼마예요?

entries.nuance: 처리 기간 얼마나 걸려요? is 처리 ('processing/handling', 處理) + 기간 ('period') + 얼마나 ('how much/long') + 걸리다 ('to take (time)'). 처리하다 is the verb for an office processing/handling your case, so 처리 기간 is the official 'processing period' you see on notices. The verb 걸리다 is the natural way to express 'time is taken' — and the big particle lesson is that 걸리다 is intransitive: time is the SUBJECT, so it's 며칠 걸려요? / 얼마나 걸려요? with no object marker on you; English speakers wrongly add themselves as subject ('how long do I take') and produce 제가 얼마나 걸려요?, which is nonsense — the TIME takes, not you. The near-synonym for 'how long': 얼마나 걸려요? (duration) vs 언제 나와요? ('when does it come out', asking the date the result/card is ready) vs 언제 받을 수 있어요? ('when can I receive it') — all common, slightly different angles. The English-speaker pitfall is also 직역 of 'process' as 프로세스 or using 진행 ('progress/proceeding') for the duration; 진행 is about an ongoing action, while the time it takes is 처리 기간/걸리는 시간. Register plain 존댓말. A useful real follow-up is 문자로 알려 주세요? ('will you let me know by text?'), since many offices send a 문자 (SMS) or have you check status online.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제가 얼마나 걸려요? ('how long do I take?').
걸리다 makes TIME the subject, not you: 얼마나 걸려요? / 며칠 걸려요? Putting 제가 as subject is ungrammatical here.
Using 진행 for the duration.
진행 means an action is in progress, not the length of time. For how long it takes, say 처리 기간 얼마나 걸려요? or 며칠 걸려요?
Adding an object marker to the time: 며칠을 걸려요.
걸리다 is intransitive; the duration isn't an object. Say 며칠 걸려요? without 을/를.

Note also 진행 ('progress/proceeding') is about an ongoing action, while the time it takes is 처리 기간/걸리는 시간.

English speakers wrongly add themselves as subject ('how long do I take') and produce 제가 얼마나 걸려요?, which is nonsense — the TIME takes, not you. Also the 직역 of 'process' as 프로세스, or using 진행 for the duration.

entries.nuance: 이거 다시 와야 돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 다시 ('again') + 오다 ('to come') + -아야 돼요? ('do I have to…?'), asking whether you must make a second trip — a constant worry when paperwork might be incomplete. The grammar core is -아야 되다/하다 ('must/have to'): -와야 돼요 is the 'have to come' obligation form, and learners must get the irregular conjugation (오다 + 아야 → 와야), not the mistaken 오아야. The dividing line between 다시 and 또: both mean 'again', but 다시 leans 'do it over/once more (properly)' while 또 carries a slight 'yet again' nuance, sometimes mild exasperation — for a neutral 'come back', 다시 와야 돼요 is safest, though 또 와야 돼요 is extremely common and fine. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'come back' as 돌아오다 ('return to where you started'), which sounds like going home, not revisiting the office — for 'return to the counter another day', use 다시 오다, not 돌아오다. Another pitfall: rendering 'do I need to' as 필요해요 (필요하다 is for needing a thing) instead of the obligation -아야 돼요 (for needing to DO something); 'do I need to come' is 와야 돼요, never 오는 거 필요해요. Register plain 존댓말. Pair with 다음에 뭐 가져와야 돼요? to find out what to bring if you must return.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

오다 is irregular: 오 + 아야 → 와야. The correct obligation form is 다시 와야 돼요?, not 오아야 돼요.
Using 돌아와야 돼요 for revisiting the office.
돌아오다 means returning to your origin (like home). To come to the office again, use 다시 오다: 이거 다시 와야 돼요?
Saying 오는 거 필요해요 for 'do I need to come'.
필요하다 is for needing a thing. Needing to DO something uses -아야 돼요: 와야 돼요? not 오는 거 필요해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 외국인등록증 잃어버렸어요 is a practical expression meaning "I lost my Alien Registration Card".
entries.explanation: 외국인등록증 잃어버렸어요 (oegugindeungnokjeung ireobeoryeosseoyo) means "I lost my Alien Registration Card". Say it as one set phrase — for example 외국인등록증 잃어버렸어요 ("I lost my ARC"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 외국인등록증 잃어버렸어요 is 외국인등록증 + 잃어버리다 ('to lose (and it's gone)') in past tense, the line for reporting a lost ARC. The verb is 잃어버리다, built from 잃다 ('to lose') + -어버리다 (an auxiliary adding 'completely / to my regret'), which is why it carries that sense of irreversible loss — exactly right for a lost card. The English-speaker pitfall is confusing two 'lose' verbs: 잃어버리다 ('lose a possession') vs 잊어버리다 ('forget') — they look and sound almost identical, but 외국인등록증 잊어버렸어요 would mean 'I FORGOT my ARC (from memory)', which is absurd; for losing the physical card it must be 잃어버렸어요. This is one of the most notorious learner mix-ups. After reporting, the service you need is 재발급 ('reissue', 再發給) — note 재발급 (re-issue, after loss/damage) vs plain 발급 (first issuance) vs 갱신 (renewal of an expiring one); a lost card is 재발급. The formal counter term is 분실 신고 ('loss report', 紛失) — you 분실 신고하다 to declare the loss officially, similar to reporting it lost so it can't be misused. Register plain 존댓말. Particle note: you can drop the object marker in speech (외국인등록증 잃어버렸어요), which is natural; the full 외국인등록증을 잃어버렸어요 is also correct and slightly more emphatic.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 외국인등록증 잊어버렸어요.
잊어버리다 means 'to forget (from memory)'. Losing the physical card is 잃어버리다: 외국인등록증 잃어버렸어요.
Asking for 발급 when you mean a reissue.
발급 is first issuance. Replacing a lost card is 재발급: 재발급받으러 왔어요 / 재발급 수수료 얼마예요?
Using 없어졌어요 ('it disappeared') to report it to staff.
없어졌어요 is vague ('it's gone'). To report a loss clearly, say 잃어버렸어요 or the formal 분실했어요 / 분실 신고하러 왔어요.

entries.english: Is there someone who can interpret?
entries.shortExplanation: 통역 가능한 분 계세요? is a practical expression meaning "Is there someone who can interpret?".
entries.explanation: "Is there someone who can interpret?" — that is 통역 가능한 분 계세요? (tongyeok ganeunghan bun gyeseyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 통역 가능한 분 계세요? ("Is there someone who can interpret?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

Asking about a formal interpreter service/line

examples.note: 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the request

examples.note: 잘 못해서 ('because I'm not good at it') explains the need

entries.nuance: 통역 가능한 분 계세요? is 통역 ('interpretation (spoken)', 通譯) + 가능한 ('possible/able', 可能) + 분 (honorific 'person') + 계세요 (honorific 'is there/exists'), the polite way to ask whether an interpreter is available — immigration offices and many 구청 do offer interpreters or a phone interpretation line. The honorifics here are pointed: 분 is the respectful counter for a person (vs plain 사람), and 계세요 is the honorific existence verb (vs plain 있어요) used because you're referring respectfully to the staff/person — so 통역 가능한 분 계세요? sounds appropriately courteous. The crucial vocabulary contrast is 통역 ('interpretation', spoken, real-time) vs 번역 ('translation', written text): asking 번역 가능한 분 계세요? would oddly request someone to translate a DOCUMENT, not to interpret your conversation — for live help, it's 통역. This is a classic English-speaker trap, since English 'translate' blurs both. The 직역 pitfall: 'someone who can speak English' often comes out as 영어 할 수 있는 사람 있어요?, which is grammatical but flatter; the warmer, more natural 영어 되는 분 계세요? (되다 = 'to work/be doable', 분 + 계세요 honorific) is what people actually say. Register: keep the honorific 분/계세요 for staff. A vital fallback when no interpreter exists is 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요? ('could you speak slowly?') — 말씀하다 is the honorific 'to speak' and 주시겠어요 the most polite request form.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 번역 가능한 분 계세요? for a live interpreter.
번역 is WRITTEN translation. For spoken, real-time help say 통역: 통역 가능한 분 계세요?
Using plain 있어요/사람 instead of 계세요/분 for the person.
Referring to staff politely uses honorifics: 분 ('person') + 계세요 ('is there'). 통역 가능한 분 계세요? is more courteous than 통역 되는 사람 있어요?
Over-literal 영어 말할 수 있는 사람을 원해요 ('I want a person who can speak English').
원하다 ('to want') sounds demanding for a service request. Ask naturally: 영어 되는 분 계세요? or 통역 가능한 분 계세요?

('could you speak slowly?') — 말씀하다 is the honorific 'to speak' and 주시겠어요 the most polite request form.

entries.nuance: 재입국 허가 받아야 돼요? is 재입국 ('re-entry', 再入國) + 허가 ('permit/permission', 許可) + 받다 ('to receive') + -아야 돼요? ('do I have to…?'), the essential question before leaving Korea temporarily so your residence status survives the trip. 재입국 허가 (re-entry permit) is the formal term; many statuses are now exempt for short trips, which is exactly why you ask whether you 받아야 돼요 ('have to get one'). The verb pairing is the lesson again: you 허가를 받다 ('receive a permit'), while the government 허가를 내주다/허가하다 ('grants/issues' it) — so it's 허가 받아야 돼요 (you receive), never 허가 해야 돼요 (which sounds like YOU grant the permit). The English-speaker pitfall: the 직역 of 'permit' as 퍼밋 or as 허락; 허락 ('permission/consent') is the everyday word for personal permission (parents 허락, a boss's 허락), whereas the official governmental authorization is 허가 — at immigration it's 허가. The dividing line in plain speech: 재입국 허가 받아야 돼요? (formal) vs 출국했다가 다시 들어와도 돼요? ('can I leave and re-enter?', 들어오다 = 'come in') — both work, the first matching the bureaucratic term. Useful is the 안 ~아도 돼요 frame for exemptions: 재입국 허가 안 받아도 돼요? ('is it okay NOT to get one?'). Register plain 존댓말. Note 출국 ('leaving the country') vs 입국 ('entering') vs 재입국 ('re-entering') as a clean trio worth learning together.

허락 is personal permission (from a parent, boss). Government authorization is 허가: 재입국 허가.
Confusing 입국 (enter), 출국 (leave), and 재입국 (re-enter).
입국 is entering, 출국 is leaving, 재입국 is entering AGAIN after leaving. For coming back after a trip, the term is 재입국.

entries.nuance: 지원하다 here is Sino-Korean 志願 ('aspire + wish', i.e. to volunteer/apply) and is THE verb for applying to a job, school, or program — you put yourself forward as a candidate. The make-or-break grammar point for English speakers is the particle: the target you apply TO takes 에 (a place can also take 에, 에게 rarely), NOT the object particle 을/를. So it is 회사에 지원하다 ('apply TO a company'), never 회사를 지원하다 — and that wrong particle is doubly dangerous because there is a homophone 지원(支援)하다 'to support/sponsor', which IS transitive, so 회사를 지원하다 lands as 'I sponsor the company' (this 支援 is the 지원 in 정부 지원 'government aid'). Two different Hanja, same sound: 志願 = apply, 支援 = support. Native speakers rely on context, but the particle is your safety rail. Do not confuse 지원하다 with 신청하다 ('to sign up / request', used for things like courses, refunds, cards): you 지원 for a competitive position where you might be rejected, but 신청 for a service you simply request. Register-wise 지원했어요 is the safe spoken default; the cover letter wants 지원하겠습니다 or 지원하게 되어. A frequent 직역 trap is calling a job application an 'application' and reaching for 어플리케이션 (which Koreans hear as a phone app); the document is 지원서, the act is 지원하다.

Using 신청하다 to apply for a competitive job.
신청하다 is 'to request/sign up' (a course, a card, a refund). For a job where you compete and can be rejected, use 지원하다.
Calling the application an 어플 / 어플리케이션.
That means a smartphone app in Korean. The application document is 지원서; the action is 지원하다.

structuredNuance.t: 지원하다 is THE verb for applying to a job, school, or program — you put yourself forward as a candidate. 지원했어요 is the safe spoken default; a cover letter wants 지원하겠습니다 or 지원하게 되어.

Sino-Korean 志願 ('aspire + wish', i.e. to volunteer/apply). Beware the homophone 지원(支援)하다 'to support/sponsor', which is transitive (this 支援 is the 지원 in 정부 지원 'government aid'). Two different Hanja, same sound: 志願 = apply, 支援 = support.
Don't confuse 지원하다 with 신청하다 ('to sign up / request', used for courses, refunds, cards): you 지원 for a competitive position where you might be rejected, but 신청 for a service you simply request.

The make-or-break point is the particle: the target you apply TO takes 에, NOT the object particle 을/를. So 회사에 지원하다, never 회사를 지원하다 — which, because of the homophone 支援, lands as 'I sponsor the company'. The particle is your safety rail. Also, a job application document is 지원서, not 어플리케이션 (which Koreans hear as a phone app); the act is 지원하다.

entries.nuance: 면접 (Sino-Korean 面接, 'face + meet') is the job interview, and the verb that pairs with it from YOUR side as the candidate is 보다 — literally 'to see/take', the same 보다 you use for 시험 보다 ('take an exam'). This collocation is the single biggest pitfall for English speakers, who calque 'do an interview' into 면접 하다 — but 면접하다 sounds like the COMPANY is conducting/administering the interview, i.e. the interviewer's side, so a candidate saying 저 면접 해요 sounds off. Say 면접 봐요. The matching pair is 시험 보다 / 시험 치다 ('take a test'), so think of an interview as a test you 'take'. From the employer's angle they 면접을 진행하다 ('conduct the interview') or 면접관 ('interviewer') 이 면접을 보다 can also occur, but as a learner-candidate, lock in 면접 보다. Register: 면접 봐요 is the polite everyday form; in 반말 it's 면접 봐. Don't confuse 면접 (the interview event) with 인터뷰 — the loanword 인터뷰 leans toward a media/press interview, while a JOB interview is 면접. Also note 면접관 = interviewer (the 관 means 'official/officer'), and 지원자/면접자 = the candidate.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

Saying 면접 해요 for taking an interview.
면접하다 sounds like the company is conducting it. The candidate 'takes' the interview: 면접 봐요 (like 시험 보다).
Using 인터뷰 for a job interview.
인터뷰 suggests a press/media interview. A hiring interview is 면접. Say 면접 보다.
Marking it 면접에 봐요.
면접 takes the object particle (often dropped in speech): 면접을 봐요 or just 면접 봐요, not 면접에 봐요.

entries.nuance: 이력서 (Sino-Korean 履歷書, 'career-record document') is your résumé/CV — the form listing your education and work history. The verb you want is 내다 ('to hand in/submit') or 보내다 ('to send'), e.g. 이력서를 내다 / 보내다; you WRITE or fill it out with 쓰다 or 적다. The big content note for English speakers: a Korean 이력서 traditionally pairs with a separate 자기소개서 ('self-introduction document', the cover-letter-style essay, often shortened to 자소서), and many applications expect BOTH. Don't merge them — the 이력서 is the fact sheet (dates, titles), the 자기소개서 is the narrative ('why me'). A second culture point: traditional Korean 이력서 often included a photo, birth date, and personal details that Western résumés omit, though many modern/foreign companies have dropped the photo. The pitfall is calling it a 'CV' and saying 씨브이 — Koreans say 이력서; 씨비 is not used in everyday hiring talk. Also avoid the false friend 레쥬메; it's understood by some but 이력서 is the real word. Don't confuse 이력서 with 경력 ('career/experience' itself) — 이력서 is the document, 경력 is the substance it records.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 씨브이 or 레쥬메 for a résumé.
Everyday Korean hiring uses 이력서. The English loans are not standard; say 이력서를 내다 / 보내다.
Assuming the 이력서 includes your self-introduction.
The narrative 'about me' is a separate 자기소개서 (자소서). The 이력서 is just facts; many applications require both.
Using 만들다 as 이력서를 만들다 only.
만들다 ('make') is okay for creating the file, but to submit it use 내다/보내다, and to fill it in use 쓰다/적다.

entries.nuance: 자기소개 (Sino-Korean 自己紹介, 'self-introduction') is the opening ritual of nearly every Korean interview, and 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 is what the INTERVIEWER says to you — so you'll mostly HEAR this and need to respond, not say it yourself. The verb is 소개하다 ('to introduce'); note 자기소개하다 can be one word, or you split it as 자기소개(를) 해 주세요. The 좀 here is the politeness softener (not 'a little bit of'), and 해 주세요 frames it as a courteous request. English speakers make two errors. First, they answer by literally translating 'My name is...' and stop — but a Korean 자기소개 is expected to be a short pitch: name, background, the role you're applying for, a strength, and 잘 부탁드립니다 to close; just stating your name feels incomplete. Second, when they themselves want to introduce someone else, they reuse 자기소개 — but 자기소개 is reflexive ('introduce ONESELF'); to introduce another person it's just 소개하다 (제 친구를 소개할게요). Register: the interviewer's polite forms are 해 주세요 / 부탁드립니다 / 해 보세요; your reply stays in 존댓말 (-습니다 or -요). Don't say 자기소개를 만들다 ('make a self-intro') — you 하다 (do/give) it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering with only your name.
A Korean 자기소개 is a mini-pitch: name + background + the role + a strength + 잘 부탁드립니다. Stopping at 저는 ...입니다 feels unfinished.
Reusing 자기소개 to introduce another person.
자기소개 is reflexive ('introduce oneself'). For someone else, use 소개하다: 제 동료를 소개하겠습니다.
Saying 자기소개를 만들어 주세요.
You don't 'make' a self-intro on the spot; you 'do/give' it: 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 / 자기소개해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 잘 부탁드립니다 is one of the most important and untranslatable Korean phrases: 잘 ('well') + 부탁 ('a request/favor') + 드리다 (humble 'to give', so 'I humbly make a request'). It has no clean English equivalent — depending on context it means 'please treat me well', 'I look forward to working with you', 'please consider my application favorably', or 'thanks in advance for your help'. In an interview it closes your 자기소개 and your final remarks, signaling humility and goodwill. The humble verb 드리다 (not the plain 하다) is what makes it interview-appropriate; 잘 부탁해요 is the softer peer version and 잘 부탁드리겠습니다 is the most deferential. The English-speaker error is twofold: first, trying to translate it literally and producing something like '저를 잘 다뤄 주세요' ('please handle me well') — which sounds bizarre; you must use the set phrase. Second, omitting it entirely because English interviews don't have a parallel — but skipping 잘 부탁드립니다 makes a Korean self-introduction feel abrupt and a little arrogant. Note it can also mean 'please do this for me' in office life (이거 잘 부탁드립니다 = 'please take good care of this task'), so context decides whether it's a greeting or a request. Always pair it with a slight bow in person.

That means 'please handle me well' and sounds strange. It's a fixed expression; just say 잘 부탁드립니다.

Korean interviews expect this humble closer. Without it your 자기소개 sounds abrupt; end with 잘 부탁드립니다.
Using plain 잘 부탁해 to an interviewer.
잘 부탁해 is 반말. To an interviewer use the humble 드리다 form: 잘 부탁드립니다 (or 잘 부탁드리겠습니다).

entries.nuance: 지원 동기 (Sino-Korean 志願動機; 지원 志願 'apply' + 동기 動機 'motive') is the reason you applied, and 'What's your 지원 동기?' is the single most predictable interview question in Korea. You will HEAR it constantly, so prepare to answer in 존댓말. Two phrasings matter: the textbook 지원 동기가 뭐예요? and the smoother, very common 지원 동기가 어떻게 되세요? — the latter uses 어떻게 되세요, a polite formula for asking someone's info (also used for name, age, contact), and sounds more natural and courteous than the blunt 뭐예요 in a formal setting. English speakers stumble in two ways. First, they confuse 동기 ('motive') with its homonym 동기 (同期, 'someone who entered the same year', a cohort-mate) — same sound, totally different word; context disambiguates, but be aware. Second, when answering, learners give a self-centered reason ('good salary', 'it's near my house') — Korean interview culture expects you to frame motivation around fit with the company and role (회사의 비전, 직무 적합성), so a purely personal-benefit answer reads as immature. The matching answer frame is ...때문에 지원했습니다 or ...에 기여하고 싶어 지원했습니다 ('I applied because I want to contribute to...'). Don't translate 'motivation' as 모티베이션; the word is 동기.

동기 (動機) is 'motivation'; the homonym 동기 (同期) means a same-year colleague/classmate. Context decides — in 지원 동기 it's always 'motive'.
Answering with purely personal benefits.
Saying '월급이 높아서' or '집이 가까워서' sounds immature. Frame your 지원 동기 around fit with the company/role: ...에 기여하고 싶어서 지원했습니다.

지원 동기가 뭐예요 is fine but blunt. The polished interviewer/answer register prefers 어떻게 되세요 / ...때문에 지원했습니다.

entries.nuance: 경력 (Sino-Korean 經歷, 'things one has gone through') means professional work experience / career history — the years and roles you've held. 경력이 어떻게 되세요? again uses the polite info-asking formula 어떻게 되세요, making it the courteous interview standard. The crucial distinction for English speakers is 경력 vs. 경험. 경력 specifically means formal, usually paid, career experience that 'counts' (jobs, professional roles, measured in years), while 경험 (經驗) is any experience broadly (an internship, a project, travel, life experience). So a new grad correctly says 경력은 없지만 경험은 있어요 ('no career experience, but I have experience'). This maps onto the hiring split between 신입 (新入, 'new entry / entry-level') and 경력직 (經歷職, 'experienced hire') — job posts are labeled 신입 채용 vs 경력 채용, and calling yourself the wrong one is a real mistake. A second pitfall: 경력 is the experience itself, while 이력 (履歷) is the documented record of it (your 이력서 lists your 이력/경력). Don't say 경험이 어떻게 되세요 in a hiring context when you mean years on the job — ask 경력. And the verb is 있다/없다 (경력이 있다), or for counting years, 경력이 3년 됐어요 ('my career reached 3 years').

No career yet = 신입 (entry-level). 경력직 means an experienced hire. Say 저는 신입이에요 / 경력은 없어요.
Confusing 경력 with 이력.
경력 is the experience itself; 이력 is the written record of it (in your 이력서). Ask 경력이 어떻게 되세요, not 이력이 어떻게 되세요.

examples.romanization: boninui gangjeomi mworago saenggakaseyo?
examples.en: What do you consider your strength?
examples.note: 본인 + 라고 생각하세요 = textbook interviewer phrasing

examples.ko: 제 강점은 꼼꼼함이에요.
examples.romanization: je gangjeomeun kkomkkomhamieyo.
examples.en: My strength is being meticulous.
examples.note: 제 강점은 X(이)에요 = clean answer frame; 꼼꼼함 = 'meticulousness'

examples.ko: 제 강점은 어떤 일이든 끝까지 책임지고 해낸다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je gangjeomeun eotteon irideun kkeutkkaji chaegimjigo haenaendaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My strength is that I take responsibility and see any task through to the end.
examples.note: ...다는 거예요 lets you state a strength as a whole behavior

entries.nuance: 강점 (Sino-Korean 強點, 'strong point') is your strength, the positive half of the inevitable interview pair 강점/약점 (strengths/weaknesses). The answer frame is 제 강점은 ___이에요/입니다. A subtlety English speakers miss: 강점 vs. 장점. 장점 (長點, 'good point') is the broad everyday word for any merit (of a person, product, or plan), while 강점 leans toward a competitive/professional strength you bring — interviewers often specifically ask 강점, and answering with 장점 is fine but slightly more casual/general. (Their opposites differ too: 강점↔약점, 장점↔단점.) The classic pitfall is the 직역 of 'strength' as 힘 ('physical force/power') — 제 힘은... would mean 'my physical strength is...', comically wrong; never use 힘 for a character strength. Another trap is humility miscalibration: Korean interview culture rewards confident-but-not-arrogant phrasing, so state your 강점 plainly (제 강점은 ...입니다) rather than over-hedging with 별로 없는데요 ('I don't really have one'), which reads as a non-answer. When you describe the strength as a behavior rather than a single noun, use the nominalizer: 끝까지 해내는 거 ('the fact that I see things through'). Register stays 존댓말 throughout; 본인 is how the interviewer refers to 'you'.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'strength' as 힘.
힘 is physical force. A character/professional strength is 강점 (or 장점). Say 제 강점은..., never 제 힘은...
Answering 강점이 별로 없어요.
Excessive humility reads as a non-answer. State it plainly: 제 강점은 ...입니다. Confidence (not arrogance) is expected.
Mixing the opposites: pairing 강점 with 단점.

structuredNuance.t: 강점 is your strength, the positive half of the inevitable interview pair 강점/약점 (strengths/weaknesses). The answer frame is 제 강점은 ___이에요/입니다. When you describe the strength as a behavior rather than a single noun, use the nominalizer: 끝까지 해내는 거 ('the fact that I see things through'). Register stays 존댓말 throughout; 본인 is how the interviewer refers to 'you'.
강점 is Sino-Korean 強點, 'strong point'.

A subtlety: 강점 vs 장점. 장점 (長點, 'good point') is the broad everyday word for any merit (of a person, product, or plan), while 강점 leans toward a competitive/professional strength you bring — interviewers often specifically ask 강점, and answering with 장점 is fine but slightly more casual/general. Their opposites differ too: 강점↔약점, 장점↔단점.

The classic pitfall is the 직역 of 'strength' as 힘 ('physical force/power') — 제 힘은... would mean 'my physical strength is...', comically wrong; never use 힘 for a character strength. Another trap is humility miscalibration: Korean interview culture rewards confident-but-not-arrogant phrasing, so state your 강점 plainly (제 강점은 ...입니다) rather than over-hedging with 별로 없는데요 ('I don't really have one'), which reads as a non-answer.

entries.nuance: 약점 (Sino-Korean 弱點, 'weak point') is your weakness, the flip side of 강점. The expected answer is not just naming a flaw but pairing it with how you're improving — 제 약점은 ___인데, 고치려고/보완하려고 노력하고 있어요 ('my weakness is X, but I'm trying to fix/supplement it'). Like the strengths pair, watch 약점 vs 단점: 단점 (短點, 'short point') is the everyday word for any flaw, 약점 is the more interview-flavored 'weak point/vulnerability', and opposites are 약점↔강점, 단점↔장점. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the 직역 of 'weakness' as 약함 ('weakness' as an abstract noun) or 힘이 없다 ('to lack strength/be physically weak') — wrong register entirely; the noun is 약점. (2) Cultural over-honesty: English coaching says 'give a real weakness', but in Korea a brutally honest fatal flaw ('저는 게을러요' = 'I'm lazy') can sink you — the norm is a manageable weakness plus a clear improvement effort. (3) Register: keep it 존댓말; when stating the weakness as a behavior use the nominalizer 거 (못 하는 거 = 'the not-being-able-to-do'). Note also 보완하다 ('to supplement/shore up') is the polished verb interviewers love to hear over the plainer 고치다 ('fix').

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'weakness' as 약함 or 힘이 없어요.
Those mean abstract/physical weakness. The interview noun is 약점: 제 약점은 ...이에요.

저는 게을러요 ('I'm lazy') with nothing more reads badly in Korea. Give a manageable weakness + 고치려고/보완하려고 노력하고 있어요.

약점 pairs with 강점; 단점 pairs with 장점. Don't list '강점과 단점' — say 강점과 약점 or 장점과 단점.

entries.nuance: 성격의 장단점 means 'the strong and weak points of one's personality (성격)', and 장단점 is the fused noun 장점(strengths) + 단점(weaknesses) — Korean loves these compressed pairs (장단점, 찬반, 손익). Interviewers very often ask the combined question 성격의 장단점, so you answer BOTH halves: 제 성격의 장점은 ___이고, 단점은 ___이에요. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) Misreading the compound — 장단점 is ONE word meaning 'pros and cons', not two separate things to pick between; you must address both. (2) The genitive 의: 성격의 장단점 ('personality's pros/cons'), where 의 (often pronounced '에') links them — learners drop it or overuse it; in speech 성격 장단점 without 의 is also natural. (3) The smooth 'both at once' phrasing 장점이자 단점 (using -이자 'being both A and B simultaneously') is a high-value structure interviewers reward, letting you reframe one trait as double-edged — but learners rarely know -이자 and instead clumsily repeat the trait. (4) Register: keep 존댓말, and note the interviewer's polite question can shorten to 성격의 장단점은요? with the topic-marking -은요. Don't confuse 성격 ('personality/temperament') with 성질 — 성질 can imply a bad temper ('성질부리다' = throw a tantrum), so describe yourself with 성격, never 성질.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 장단점 as 'choose pros OR cons'.
장단점 is one compound = 'pros and cons'. The question wants BOTH: 장점은 ...이고, 단점은 ...이에요.
Describing yourself with 성질 instead of 성격.
성질 often implies a bad temper (성질부리다 = throw a fit). Your character is 성격: 제 성격은...
Repeating the trait instead of using -이자.
To say one trait is both, use -이자: 꼼꼼한 게 장점이자 단점이에요, rather than awkwardly stating it twice.

entries.nuance: 연봉 (Sino-Korean 年俸, 'yearly stipend') is ANNUAL salary, and Korea quotes pay annually by default — a job post saying 연봉 4,000 means 40 million won PER YEAR, not per month. This is a major trap for English speakers, who may hear a number and think monthly: distinguish 연봉 (yearly) from 월급 (月給, monthly wage). Asking about pay is delicate; the polite formula 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? / 어떻게 되세요? (again the courteous info-asking 어떻게 되다) softens it far better than the blunt 얼마예요? ('how much?'), which can sound money-first in a formal interview. From the employer's side you'll be asked your 희망 연봉 ('desired annual salary') — and the pitfall is answering with a monthly figure or an unrealistic number; you state a yearly range, often adding 협의 가능합니다 ('negotiable'). Cultural note: bringing up salary TOO early or too aggressively reads poorly in Korea; many candidates wait until the employer raises it or until a later round. Also know the cluster: 복지 (benefits/welfare), 인센티브, 성과급 ('performance pay'), 4대 보험 (the four major insurances), and 세전/세후 (pre-/post-tax) — 연봉 figures are usually 세전 ('before tax'). Don't translate 'salary' as 샐러리; the words are 연봉/월급.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Hearing a 연봉 figure as monthly.
연봉 is ANNUAL. 연봉 3,600 means 36 million won per year (≈ 300/month). Monthly pay is 월급.
Asking 얼마예요? bluntly in a formal interview.
Money questions need cushioning. Use 연봉이 어떻게 되나요? or 협의 가능한가요?, and ideally let the employer raise it first.
Stating your 희망 연봉 as a monthly number.
Desired salary is quoted yearly: 희망 연봉은 4,000만 원 정도입니다. Giving a monthly figure confuses the negotiation.

structuredNuance.t: 연봉 is ANNUAL salary, and Korea quotes pay annually by default — a job post saying 연봉 4,000 means 40 million won PER YEAR, not per month. 연봉 is Sino-Korean 年俸, 'yearly stipend'.

entries.nuance: 언제부터 출근 가능하세요? means 'from when are you able to come to work?' — 출근 (Sino-Korean 出勤, 'go to work/report for duty') + 가능하다 ('to be possible'). Hearing this question is usually a GOOD sign; it implies they're picturing you on the team. entries.nuance: 궁금한 점 있으세요? ('do you have anything you're curious about?') is the interviewer's standard closing line — 궁금하다 ('to be curious') + 점 ('point/thing') + 있으세요 (honorific 'do you have'). The hidden rule English speakers miss is cultural, not grammatical: answering '아니요, 없어요' ('no, none') is a soft red flag in Korean interviews — it signals low interest. You're expected to have a prepared 역질문 (reverse question) about the role, team, or growth. So treat this as a prompt to engage, and when YOU ask, use the humble verb 여쭤보다 ('to ask, humbly') rather than the plain 묻다/물어보다: 하나 여쭤봐도 될까요? sounds far more polished to an interviewer than 하나 물어봐도 돼요?. entries.nuance: 합격하다 (Sino-Korean 合格, 'meet the standard') means to pass / be accepted — for an exam, a school, or a job. 합격했어요 is how you announce you got in. The everyday casual synonym is 붙다 (literally 'to stick/adhere', as if you stuck to the position), and its opposite 떨어지다 ('to fall', i.e. to fail/be rejected) — this 붙다/떨어지다 pair is extremely common in speech (서류 붙었어 / 면접 떨어졌어). English speakers trip on several things: (1) 합격하다 is intransitive — you don't 'pass' the test as a direct object the way English does; you say 시험에 합격하다 (with 에) or 시험을 붙다, and 'I passed it' is 합격했어요, NOT 시험을 합격했어요 with 을 in formal grammar (though spoken Korean bends this). (2) Keep 합격 (you meet the bar / are accepted) apart from 채용 (採用, 'hiring/recruitment', the employer's act of taking you on) — you 합격, the company 채용한다 — and from 통과 (通過, 'get through', the everyday verb for clearing one stage, e.g. 서류 통과); 합격 is the formal verdict, 통과 is the casual 'made it past'. (3) The 직역 trap: 'I won the job' → there's no 이기다 ('win') here; you 합격했어요. (4) Register: 합격했어요 (polite) is safe; 붙었어요 is fine with friends/peers but a touch casual for announcing to a senior, where 합격했습니다 fits. Note also the stages: 서류 합격 (passed the résumé screen) → 면접 → 최종 합격 (final acceptance).

합격하다 is intransitive; the standard pattern is 시험에 합격하다. Spoken Korean sometimes uses 을, but the safe form is 시험에 합격했어요 or simply 합격했어요.

There's no 'winning' here. Getting the job is 합격하다 / 붙다: 합격했어요, not 일을 이겼어요.
Using 합격 for the company's action.
You 합격 (pass); the company 채용한다 (hires) or 뽑는다 (picks). Don't say 회사가 저를 합격했어요 — say 회사가 저를 뽑았어요 / 채용했어요.

Traps: (1) 합격하다 is intransitive — you don't 'pass' the test as a direct object the way English does; say 시험에 합격하다 (with 에), and 'I passed it' is 합격했어요, NOT 시험을 합격했어요 in formal grammar (though spoken Korean bends this). (2) The 직역 trap: 'I won the job' → there's no 이기다 ('win') here; you 합격했어요.

entries.nuance: 불합격 (불 不 'not' + 합격) is the formal 'fail/rejection', the direct opposite of 합격. But in real speech Koreans far more often say 떨어졌어요 ('I fell' = I got rejected) than the clinical 불합격했어요 — 떨어지다 is the everyday counterpart to 붙다 ('to pass'). For softening bad news, 안 됐어요 ('it didn't work out') or 아쉽게 안 됐어요 is gentle and face-saving. English speakers stumble on: (1) Reaching for 실패하다 ('to fail') — but 실패하다 implies a broad failure of a venture/plan, and using it for a single rejection (면접에 실패했어요) sounds heavier and odd; the right verbs are 떨어지다 / 불합격하다. (2) The 직역 of 'they rejected me' with 거절하다 — 거절하다 means to decline an OFFER or request (you 거절 a confession, an invitation), so a company turning you down is 떨어뜨리다 / 불합격시키다, and from your side you 떨어졌어요; saying 회사가 저를 거절했어요 misframes it. (3) Particle/voice: 떨어지다 is intransitive ('I fell/was dropped'), so it's 면접에서 떨어졌어요 (with 에서), describing the place you fell at, not 면접을 떨어졌어요. Register: 불합격했어요 is neutral-formal; 떨어졌어요 is the natural spoken form among peers; with a senior who asked, a composed 아쉽게 안 됐습니다 is graceful.

실패하다 = a broad failure of a plan/venture. For one job rejection use 떨어지다 / 불합격하다: 면접에서 떨어졌어요.

떨어지다 is intransitive. Use 에서 for where you were dropped: 면접에서 떨어졌어요, not 면접을 떨어졌어요.

entries.nuance: 입사하다 (Sino-Korean 入社, 'enter the company') means to join a company / begin employment there — the formal counterpart to the casual 'start a job'. Its opposite is 퇴사하다 (退社, 'to leave/resign from a company'), and the pair 입사/퇴사 is everyday office vocabulary. The crucial grammar point for English speakers is, once again, the particle: the company you join takes 에, not 을/를 — 회사에 입사하다 ('enter INTO the company'), never 회사를 입사하다. (The 에 makes sense because 입사 already contains 'enter', so you enter INTO it.) Distinctions to keep straight: 입사 is joining a COMPANY specifically; joining a school is 입학 (入學), joining the military is 입대 (入隊) — don't generalize 입사 to all of them. Also separate 입사 (the act of joining) from 출근 (出勤, coming to work on a given day): your first day you 입사 AND 출근, but daily commuting to work is only 출근. The 직역 trap: 'I got the job' translates as 취직했어요/취업했어요 ('became employed', the broad state of landing employment), while 입사했어요 zooms in on joining that PARTICULAR company — both true, slightly different focus. Register: 입사했어요 polite; the humble 입사하게 됐어요 ('it came about that I'm joining') sounds gracious and modest, which Koreans favor when sharing good news. Useful collateral: 정규직 (permanent), 계약직 (contract), 수습 기간 (probation period), 신입 사원 (new employee).

Using 입사 for school or the army.
입사 is for a company. School = 입학, military = 입대. Match the 입- word to the institution.
Confusing 입사 (joining) with 출근 (commuting to work).
입사 is starting at the company (a one-time event); 출근 is going to work each day. Don't say 매일 입사해요 — that's 매일 출근해요.

examples.en: First I have to get past the document screening.

entries.nuance: 서류 전형 is the document-screening round: 서류 ('documents', i.e. your 이력서 + 자기소개서) + 전형 (銓衡, 'screening/selection stage'). It's the FIRST gate in a typical Korean hiring process — 서류 전형 → 인적성/필기 (aptitude or written test) → 면접 (interview) → 최종 합격 — so newcomers meet this term immediately on job boards. The verb pairings are the learner trap. To PASS this stage you say 서류 전형에 합격하다 or, very commonly, 서류 통과하다 ('pass through the documents') / 서류 붙다; to FAIL it, 서류에서 떨어지다. English speakers mishandle 전형 in two ways: (1) they treat 전형 as if it meant the documents themselves, but 전형 is the SCREENING PROCESS — 서류 전형 = 'the screening done via documents', so you don't 'submit a 전형', you 지원하다 and then pass/fail the 전형. (2) They confuse 전형 with 서류 alone; 서류 are the papers, 전형 is the evaluation round. Particle care: you pass IN/AT a stage with 에 (전형에 합격) and get dropped FROM it with 에서 (전형에서 떨어지다). Register: these are neutral words used in both 존댓말 and casual speech; 통과했어요 (polite) vs 통과했어 (반말). Don't say 서류 전형을 이겼어요 ('won the screening') — there's no winning; you 통과/합격. Also note the related 공채 (公採, open mass recruitment, common at big Korean firms) vs 수시 채용 (rolling/as-needed hiring).

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Treating 전형 as the documents themselves.
전형 is the screening PROCESS; 서류 are the documents. You don't submit a 전형 — you 지원하다, then pass the 서류 전형: 서류 전형에 합격했어요.
Saying 서류 전형을 합격했어요 with 을.
합격하다 is intransitive and takes 에: 서류 전형에 합격했어요. To use an object particle, switch verbs: 서류 전형을 통과했어요 (통과하다 can take 을).
Marking the failure with 에 not 에서.
You're dropped FROM a stage: 서류에서 떨어졌어요 (에서), not 서류에 떨어졌어요. Pass uses 에 (합격), fail uses 에서 (떨어지다).

entries.explanation: 이상입니다 (isangimnida) means "That concludes my answer / That's all". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이상입니다 ("That concludes it / That's all"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.en: That's the end of my introduction. That concludes it.

examples.en: With that I'll conclude my self-introduction. Thank you.

examples.ko: 답변은 이상입니다. 추가로 궁금한 점 있으실까요?
examples.romanization: dapbyeoneun isangimnida. chugaro gunggeumhan jeom isseusilkkayo?
examples.en: That's my full answer. Is there anything else you'd like to know?
examples.note: 답변은 이상입니다 = 'that completes my response'

entries.nuance: 이상입니다 literally is 이상 (以上, 'the above / that much') + 입니다 ('it is'), i.e. 'that is the extent of it' — the crisp, formal way to signal you've FINISHED speaking, used to cap a 자기소개, an interview answer, or a presentation. It tells the listener 'I'm done, your turn', which matters in interviews because trailing off ambiguously leaves the interviewer unsure whether to jump in. English speakers underuse this because English has no exact single-word equivalent (you'd just stop talking), and the result is awkward dead air; learning to land on 이상입니다 or 여기까지입니다 makes you sound composed and structured. Two pitfalls: (1) the homonym confusion — 이상 also shows up in 이상하다 ('to be weird/abnormal') and as 'more than' (3개 이상 = 'three or more'); but as a standalone closing 이상입니다 it purely means 'that's all'. Don't let 이상하다 ('to be strange') bleed into it. (2) The 직역 trap: translating 'that's all' as 그게 다예요 is fine in casual speech but too light for a formal interview close; 이상입니다 carries the right businesslike register. For an even more formal sign-off (end of a longer talk) use 이상으로 마치겠습니다 ('with that, I will conclude'). Register: 이상입니다 is formal-polite and exactly right for interviews; the casual equivalent among peers would be 이게 다야 (반말). Always follow it with 감사합니다 and a slight bow.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Letting it bleed into 이상하다 ('to be strange').
Standalone 이상입니다 means 'that's all/that concludes it'. It is unrelated to 이상하다 ('weird'). Don't avoid it for fear of sounding 'strange'.

그게 다예요 is fine casually but too light for an interview. The composed close is 이상입니다 (or 이상으로 마치겠습니다).
Trailing off with no closing signal.
Silence leaves the interviewer unsure you're finished. Mark the end clearly: 이상입니다. 감사합니다.

entries.explanation: "Please change the diaper" — that is 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 (gijeogwi jom gara juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 ("Please change the diaper"). examples.ko: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요.
examples.romanization: gijeogwi jom gara juseyo.
examples.en: Please change the diaper.
examples.note: Handing the baby (or a fresh diaper) to the teacher at drop-off

examples.ko: 애기 기저귀 찼는데 좀 갈아 주세요.
examples.romanization: aegi gijeogwi channeunde jom gara juseyo.
examples.en: The baby's diaper is wet — please change it.
examples.note: 찼다 ('it's wet/full') tells them why; 애기 is the cozy spoken form of 아기

examples.ko: 등원할 때 기저귀 여유분 가방에 넣어 뒀어요. 필요하면 갈아 주세요.
examples.romanization: deungwonhal ttae gijeogwi yeoyubun gabange neoeo dwosseoyo. piryohamyeon gara juseyo.
