usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; you reposted/forwarded content
반말, to a friend
Asking people to spread your post

usagePhrases.en: I shared it to my story
usagePhrases.note: Reposting to your story with destination -에

examples.ko: 이 글 좋아서 공유했어요.
examples.romanization: i geul joaseo gongyuhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I liked this post so I shared it.
examples.note: -아서 ('because') links the reason to the share

examples.ko: 친구한테 링크 공유했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguhante ringkeu gongyuhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I shared the link with a friend.
examples.note: 공유 takes -한테 ('to a person') for who you sent it to

examples.romanization: mani gongyuhae juseyo, neolli allyeoya haeyo.

examples.note: 널리 알리다 ('spread far') is why you ask for shares

entries.nuance: 공유(하다) (Sino-Korean 共有, 'to share/hold in common') is the verb for reposting or forwarding content so others can see it — the 'Share' button on Instagram, KakaoTalk, YouTube, Naver. 'I shared the post' = 글 공유했어요; to ask others to spread it, 공유 좀 해 주세요. The destination/recipient particles matter: -에 for a place you repost TO (스토리에 공유했어요, 'shared to my story'), -한테/에게 for a PERSON you send it to (친구한테 공유했어요, 'shared with a friend'). The contrast learners need: 공유하다 (share/spread to many, the SNS button) vs 보내다 ('to send' one-to-one privately) vs 퍼가다 ('to take/grab and repost', the older blog-era word for copying content to your own page). For modern SNS, 공유하다 is the default; 퍼가다 sounds dated or implies lifting someone's content. Don't confuse 공유 with 좋아요 (like) — sharing actively redistributes, liking just reacts. Register: -했어요/-아 주세요 polite; friends get 공유했어. The English-speaker pitfall is the original meaning trap: 공유 also means 'to share/co-own' in real life (방을 공유하다 = 'share a room', 정보를 공유하다 = 'share information'), so learners sometimes over-apply it; on SNS it specifically means reposting/forwarding, which is fine, but don't use it for 'sharing food' (that's 나눠 먹다). Another trap: the recipient particle — saying 친구를 공유했어요 with object -를 sounds like you shared the FRIEND; use -한테 for the person you sent it to.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 친구를 공유했어요 to mean 'I shared it with a friend'.
Object -를 makes it sound like you shared the friend. Use -한테/에게 for the recipient: 친구한테 공유했어요.
Using 공유하다 for sharing food.
공유하다 is for content/information/co-owning. Sharing food is 나눠 먹다 ('divide and eat'). 'Let's share' (food) = 나눠 먹어요.
Confusing 공유 (share/repost) with 좋아요 (like).
공유 actively redistributes a post; 좋아요 just reacts to it. 'I shared it' = 공유했어요, not 좋아요 눌렀어요.

examples.romanization: gyesok gwichanke haeseo chadanhaesseoyo.
examples.en: They kept bothering me so I blocked them.

examples.ko: 스팸 번호라서 바로 차단했어요.

entries.nuance: 차단(하다) (Sino-Korean 遮斷, 'to cut off/block') is the verb for blocking someone — on SNS, KakaoTalk, or your phone — so they can't contact you or see you. 'I blocked them' = 차단했어요; to undo it, 차단 풀다 ('release the block', 차단 풀었어요). The active/passive split is crucial: 차단하다 = YOU block someone, 차단당하다/차단되다 = you GET blocked (it happened to you) — 차단당했어요 means 'I was blocked', the opposite victimhood. Korean adds emotional color with 차단해 버렸어요 (-아 버리다 = 'just did it decisively, good riddance'). The contrast learners need: 차단 (block, total cut-off — they vanish from your world) vs 언팔 (unfollow, you just stop seeing them but no wall) vs 신고 (report, flag to the platform). These are escalating: unfollow < block < report. Don't confuse 차단 with 삭제 ('delete', e.g. delete a friend/contact) — blocking walls them off, deleting just removes the entry. Register: -했어요 polite; friends get 차단했어. The English-speaker pitfall is the active/passive direction (saying 차단했어요 when you were the one blocked — should be 차단당했어요), and over-using the loanword '블록' — Koreans say the native 차단, not 블록하다. Another trap: don't confuse 차단 ('block', a hard cut-off) with 숨기기/뮤트 ('hide/mute') — muting just stops their posts showing in your feed while they can still see and message you, whereas 차단 severs everything; saying 차단했어요 when you only muted overstates what you did.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 차단했어요 when YOU got blocked.
차단하다 = you did the blocking. If it happened to you, use the passive 차단당하다: 차단당했어요 ('I was blocked').
Using 블록하다 instead of 차단하다.
The native, standard word is 차단. 블록 sounds like raw English. Say 차단했어요.
Confusing 차단 (block) with 언팔 (unfollow).
언팔 just stops you seeing them; 차단 cuts them off entirely (they can't see or reach you). To fully cut contact, say 차단했어요.

entries.nuance: 제 생각에는 is the standard polite way to flag 'this is just my view' before you state an opinion, used learner-to-anyone in conversation, meetings, or class. 제 is the humble 'my' (저+의), and the particle 에는 frames it as 'as for in my thinking'. To go casual with a friend, swap to 내 생각에는; for a more weighed, formal feel use 제 생각으로는. The nearest alternative is 제가 보기에는 ('the way I see it'), but 제 생각에는 is about your reasoning/opinion while 제가 보기에는 leans on what you observe — name that line: thinking vs seeing. The classic English-speaker mistake is calquing 'in my opinion' as 제 의견에는, which sounds stiff and is rarely said; spoken Korean overwhelmingly uses 제 생각에는. Another is dropping the particle and saying 제 생각 괜찮아요, which is ungrammatical — keep 에는.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제 의견에는 as a literal translation of 'in my opinion' — it sounds bookish; natural speech uses 제 생각에는.
Using 제 생각에는 with a friend — it's polite register; with friends drop to 내 생각에는.
Omitting the particle (제 생각 좋아요) — you need 제 생각에는 / 제 생각엔; the bare noun can't open the clause this way.

entries.nuance: 제가 보기에는 means 'judging from what I see/observe', used when you give an assessment based on appearances or your read of a situation — learner to anyone, polite. It's built on 보다 'to see' + 기 (nominalizer) + 에는, literally 'as for in my seeing'. Casual form is 내가 보기에는; the contracted 제가 보기엔 is very common in speech. The nearest neighbor is 제 생각에는 — the dividing line is evidence vs opinion: 제가 보기에는 implies 'from observable signs', while 제 생각에는 is your inner reasoning. English speakers often force 제 의견으로는 or translate 'I see' too literally; also they may say 제가 봤을 때 (past, 'when I looked') when they mean the general present judgment 제가 보기에는. Keep it present and nominalized.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing it with 제가 봤을 때 ('when I saw it', a specific past moment) — for a general read use the present 제가 보기에는.
Saying 제 보기에는 without 가 — the subject marker is needed: 제가 보기에는.
Using it for pure feelings ('I feel sad') — 보기에는 is for judgments/assessments, not emotions; for feelings use 제 생각에는 or just state the feeling.

entries.explanation: "That's right / You're right." — that is 맞아요 (majayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 맞아요 ("that's right"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 맞아요 (from 맞다 'to be correct/to fit') confirms that what the other person said is true, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech; it's the everyday 'right / exactly'. Casual is 맞아 and formal is 맞습니다 (service staff, presentations). The nearest alternative is 그래요 / 그렇죠 — the line is: 맞아요 judges a statement as factually correct, while 그래요/그렇죠 expresses general agreement or 'yeah, that's how it is'. The biggest English-speaker trap is treating 맞아요 like 'okay/sure' for requests — for 'okay, I'll do it' you need 알겠어요 / 좋아요, not 맞아요. Another pitfall: answering a negative question. To Korean '안 더워요?' ('Isn't it hot?'), 맞아요 is confusing; Koreans answer the literal proposition, so be careful. Note 맞다 is intransitive here, so never say 맞아요 하다 — 맞아요 stands alone.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 맞아요 to mean 'okay, I'll do that' — for agreeing to a request say 알겠어요 or 좋아요; 맞아요 only confirms correctness.
Writing 맞어요 — the conjugation of 맞다 is 맞아요 (ㅏ stem), not 맞어요.
Saying 맞아요를 해요 or adding 하다 — 맞다 already is the verb; 맞아요 is a complete reply.

entries.nuance: 그렇죠 (from 그렇다 'to be so' + the 죠 ending) expresses warm, shared agreement — 'right, that's how it is' — used learner-to-anyone in polite conversation. The 죠 (contraction of 지요) seeks mutual confirmation, so 그렇죠 often feels like nodding along with someone. Casual is 그렇지; formal is 그렇습니다. The nearest alternative is 맞아요 — the dividing line: 맞아요 confirms a statement is factually correct, while 그렇죠 signals empathetic 'yeah, exactly' and is great for small talk and building rapport. With a rising tone 그렇죠? invites the other person to agree with YOU. English speakers often overuse 맞아요 where 그렇죠 sounds warmer, and they sometimes write 그렇죠 as two thoughts; also beware spelling — it's 그렇죠, not 그러죠 (the ㅎ stays).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

entries.nuance: 글쎄요 is the go-to hedge for 'hmm, I'm not sure / let me think', used learner-to-anyone in polite speech when you don't want to commit, don't know, or are gently declining. Casual is 글쎄. Crucially it's not just 'I don't know' — it signals hesitation or reservation, so Koreans use it to soften a 'no' or to avoid a direct answer without seeming rude. English speakers wrongly treat 글쎄요 as a casual 'whatever' or use it where a clear answer is expected (a boss asking a direct work question), which can read as evasive. It is polite but vague — use it when vagueness is acceptable.

entries.nuance: 잘 모르겠어요 is the natural, polite 'I'm not sure / I don't really know', used learner-to-anyone. The nearest alternative is 글쎄요 — the line: 잘 모르겠어요 honestly reports lack of knowledge, while 글쎄요 is noncommittal hedging. The big mistake is using bare 몰라요 in answer to someone (especially a request), which sounds curt; soften to 잘 모르겠어요. Also don't translate 'I don't know him' with 모르겠어요 — for not knowing a person use 몰라요 (잘 몰라요).

entries.nuance: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 ('that seems a bit not-right') is how Koreans disagree or disapprove POLITELY without a blunt 'no', used learner-to-anyone. The machinery is key: 아니다 'to not be (so)' + -ㄴ 것 같다 'seems' softens it to opinion, and 좀 ('a bit') cushions the blow — together they let you object while saving face. Casual is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아; formal 그건 좀 아닌 것 같습니다. The nearest alternative is 저는 반대예요 ('I'm against it') — the dividing line: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is gentle, indirect, situational disapproval, while 저는 반대예요 is a clear, on-the-record objection (meetings, votes). The classic English-speaker mistake is bald directness — saying 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') or 안 돼요 to disagree, which feels harsh and confrontational in Korean. Keep 좀 and 것 같아요 to stay polite. Also note it's 아닌 (from 아니다), not 안 인.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Disagreeing with 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') — too blunt/confrontational; soften to 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
Dropping 좀 and 것 같아요 (그건 아니에요) — that's much harsher; the hedges are what make it polite.
Writing 안인 것 같아요 — the correct form from 아니다 is 아닌 것 같아요.

entries.nuance: 그렇긴 한데 is the 'yes, but...' move — you concede the other person has a point, then pivot to your reservation, used learner-to-anyone. The grammar: 그렇다 + -긴 하다 (the -기는 하다 'it IS so, granted' concession pattern) + -ㄴ데 ('but/and'). So it literally grants 'it is indeed so, but'. This same form is used in 반말 and 존댓말 (the politeness lives in what follows); the formal version is 그렇긴 합니다만. The nearest alternative is 그럴 수도 있죠 ('that could be so') — the line: 그렇긴 한데 actively concedes then disagrees, while 그럴 수도 있죠 merely allows the possibility without committing. English speakers often jump straight to 하지만/그러나 ('but/however') with no concession, which sounds abrupt and argumentative; 그렇긴 한데 cushions disagreement by agreeing first. Mistake to avoid: writing 그렇긴 한대 (wrong ending) instead of 한데.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Jumping to 하지만 with no concession — 그렇긴 한데 softens by conceding first; bare 하지만 sounds blunt.
Spelling the ending 한대 — the connective is -ㄴ데, so it's 그렇긴 한데.
Confusing 긴 (concession, =기는) with future — 그렇긴 한데 means 'it is so, granted, but', not anything future.

entries.explanation: 별로예요 (byeolloyeyo) means "It's not great / I don't really like it.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 별로예요 ("it's not that good"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 별로예요 is the everyday way to say something is 'not that great / meh', a softly negative opinion used learner-to-anyone. 별로 originally means 'particularly' and pairs with negatives, but in speech 별로예요 stands alone as 'it's nothing special'. Casual is 별로야; the hedged 별로인 것 같아요 is gentler; past is 별로였어요 (after you've tried it). The nearest alternative is 그저 그래요 ('so-so') — the line: 별로예요 leans clearly negative ('I don't like it'), while 그저 그래요 is neutral 'meh, average'. The top English-speaker mistakes: (1) spelling — it's 별로예요, never 별로에요 (after a noun-like 별로 the copula is 예요); (2) overusing 별로 as a strong 'bad' — it's mild, so for genuinely bad use 안 좋아요/별로 안 좋아요; (3) saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 must go with a negative, so it's 별로 안 좋아요 or just 별로예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 별로에요 — the correct copula spelling here is 별로예요.
Saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 needs a negative; use 별로 안 좋아요 or 별로예요.
Treating 별로예요 as strongly 'bad' — it's mild ('not great'); for strong dislike use 너무 별로예요 or 안 좋아요.

entries.nuance: 그런 것 같아요 ('it seems to be so') is the soft, hedged 'I think so', used learner-to-anyone constantly — Koreans love -ㄴ/는 것 같다 because it states opinions tentatively and politely instead of asserting flatly. Casual is 그런 것 같아; formal 그런 것 같습니다. The nearest alternatives are the confident 맞아요/그렇죠 — the dividing line: 그런 것 같아요 hedges ('seems so, I'm not 100% sure'), while 맞아요/그렇죠 confirm with confidence. This hedging is a politeness device: even when fairly sure, Koreans soften with 것 같아요 to avoid sounding pushy. The English-speaker mistake is over-asserting — saying 그래요 or 맞아요 where 그런 것 같아요 would sound more modest and natural — or, conversely, misusing 것 같다 about their OWN clear feelings (saying 좋은 것 같아요 'it seems good' when you simply like it; that's actually common and fine, but for strong personal certainty 좋아요 is more direct). Also: it's 그런 것, two words, not 그런것.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Over-asserting with 맞아요/그래요 when unsure — 그런 것 같아요 is the natural hedge for 'I think so'.
Writing 그런것 같아요 — 것 is a bound noun and is spaced: 그런 것 같아요.
Confusing 그런 것 같다 (seems so) with 그렇다 (is so) — the 것 같다 version is tentative on purpose.

entries.nuance: 그럴 수도 있죠 ('that could be so, right') concedes that something is possible without fully committing to it, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech. The build: 그렇다 → 그럴 (prospective) + 수도 있다 ('it's possible, even') + 죠 (seeking shared acknowledgment). It's a diplomatic, open-minded reaction — 'fair enough, that's possible'. Casual is 그럴 수도 있지; formal 그럴 수도 있습니다. The nearest alternative is 그렇긴 한데 — the dividing line: 그럴 수도 있죠 grants a possibility neutrally (no pushback implied), while 그렇긴 한데 concedes specifically in order to then disagree. English speakers tend to translate 'maybe' as 아마 and miss this concession nuance, or overuse 가능해요 ('it's possible/feasible'), which is more about feasibility than 'I'll grant you that'. Keep the 수도 있다 frame; spacing is 그럴 수도 있죠 (수 is spaced).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 가능해요 to mean 'that could be (in conversation)' — 가능하다 is about feasibility; for granting a point use 그럴 수도 있죠.
Writing 그럴수도 있죠 — 수 is a bound noun and is spaced: 그럴 수도 있죠.
Forcing 아마 ('maybe/probably') in its place — 아마 estimates likelihood; 그럴 수도 있죠 concedes a possibility someone raised.

entries.shortExplanation: 저는 반대예요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm against it / I disagree.".
entries.explanation: 저는 반대예요 (jeoneun bandaeyeyo) means "I'm against it / I disagree.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 저는 반대예요 ("I'm against it"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

반말; to a friend
격식; meetings, votes

examples.ko: 저는 반대예요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun bandaeyeyo.
examples.en: I'm against it.
examples.note: stating clear opposition to a proposal

examples.ko: 미안하지만 저는 반대예요. 위험할 것 같아서요.
examples.romanization: mianhajiman jeoneun bandaeyeyo. wiheomhal geot gataseoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, but I'm against it. I think it could be risky.
examples.note: polite opposition with a reason

examples.ko: 다들 찬성하시는 것 같은데, 저는 솔직히 반대예요.

examples.en: Everyone seems to be in favor, but honestly I'm against it.
examples.note: voicing a minority objection in a group

entries.nuance: 저는 반대예요 ('I'm against it') is the clear, on-the-record way to disagree with a proposal or position, used learner-to-anyone but typical in meetings, planning, or votes. 반대[反對] = 'opposition'; 찬성[贊成] = 'approval/being for' is its antonym. Casual is 나는 반대야; formal 저는 반대합니다. The nearest alternative is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 — the dividing line: 저는 반대예요 is explicit, committed opposition (you're stating a stance), while 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is gentle, indirect disapproval that avoids a hard 'no'. Because direct opposition can feel strong in Korean, soften with 미안하지만 ('sorry, but') or add a reason (-아서/어서). The particle is 에: you oppose something with 그 의견에 반대예요, not 그 의견을 반대예요. English speakers calque 'I disagree' as 저는 동의 안 해요 (understandable but flatter) or use the wrong particle 을/를 — keep 에.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그 의견을 반대예요 — 반대(하다) takes 에: 그 의견에 반대예요.
Opposing bluntly with no cushion — add 미안하지만 or a reason (-아서요) so it doesn't sound combative.
Confusing 반대 with 반대로 — 반대로 means 'on the contrary/in reverse'; for 'I'm against it' it's 저는 반대예요.

entries.shortExplanation: 좋은 생각이에요 is a practical expression meaning "That's a good idea.".
entries.explanation: "That's a good idea." — that is 좋은 생각이에요 (joeun saenggagieyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 좋은 생각이에요 ("that's a good idea"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: polite; approving someone's suggestion
반말; to a friend
격식; toward a senior, deferential
extension reacting with mild surprise/approval

examples.ko: 좋은 생각이에요!
examples.romanization: joeun saenggagieyo!
examples.en: That's a good idea!
examples.note: endorsing a suggestion enthusiastically

examples.ko: 같이 점심 먹을까요? — 좋은 생각이에요.
examples.romanization: gachi jeomsim meogeulkkayo? — joeun saenggagieyo.
examples.en: Shall we have lunch together? — Good idea.
examples.note: accepting a suggestion warmly

examples.ko: 회의를 오전으로 옮기자고요? 좋은 생각이에요. 그게 더 효율적일 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: hoeuireul ojeoneuro olmgijagoyo? joeun saenggagieyo. geuge deo hyoyuljeogil geot gatayo.
examples.en: Move the meeting to the morning? Good idea. I think that'd be more efficient.
examples.note: endorsing and backing it with a reason

entries.nuance: 좋은 생각이에요 ('that's a good thought') endorses someone's suggestion or idea, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech — a friendly, positive reaction. 좋은 (from 좋다 'good') + 생각 'thought/idea' + 이에요. Casual is 좋은 생각이야; with -네요 (좋은 생각이네요) it adds a touch of fresh realization. The nearest alternative is 좋아요 ('sounds good / okay') — the dividing line: 좋은 생각이에요 specifically praises the IDEA as clever/sensible, while 좋아요 just signals general assent ('sure, fine'). For accepting a plan, both work, but 좋은 생각이에요 is warmer about the suggestion itself. English speakers sometimes say 좋은 아이디어예요 (using the loanword 아이디어), which is fine and common, but 좋은 생각이에요 is the more native default. Watch the copula spelling: after the consonant-ending 생각, it's 생각이에요, not 생각에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 좋은 생각에요 — after 생각 (ends in a consonant) the copula is 이에요: 좋은 생각이에요.
Saying 좋는 생각 — 좋다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 좋은, not 좋는.
Reducing it to bare 좋아요 when you mean to praise the idea — 좋아요 is general assent; 좋은 생각이에요 compliments the idea itself.

entries.english: What I mean is... / My point is...
entries.shortExplanation: 제 말은 is a practical expression meaning "What I mean is... / My point is...".
entries.explanation: 제 말은 (je mareun) = "What I mean is... / My point is...". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 제 말은 ("what I mean is"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 제 말은 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.

usagePhrases.note: polite; clarifying or restating your point
반말; to a friend
격식; raising your humility a notch

usagePhrases.en: what I mean is, it's not that
usagePhrases.note: extension correcting a misunderstanding

examples.ko: 아니, 제 말은...
examples.romanization: ani, je mareun...
examples.en: No, what I mean is...
examples.note: restarting to clarify after being misread

examples.ko: 제 말은, 지금 당장 하자는 게 아니에요.
examples.romanization: je mareun, jigeum dangjang hajaneun ge anieyo.
examples.en: What I mean is, I'm not saying we should do it right now.
examples.note: clarifying to prevent a misunderstanding

examples.ko: 제 말은 그게 아니라, 순서를 좀 바꾸면 어떨까 하는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je mareun geuge anira, sunseoreul jom bakkumyeon eotteolkka haneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My point isn't that — it's that maybe we could change the order a bit.
examples.note: correcting and then restating the real suggestion

entries.nuance: 제 말은 ('as for my words/what I'm saying') is how you clarify, restate, or rescue your point when you've been misunderstood, used learner-to-anyone in polite speech. 제 = humble 'my', 말 = 'words/speech', 은 = topic particle. Casual is 내 말은; the humble-formal 제 말씀은 raises deference. It very often precedes 그게 아니라 ('it's not that') to correct a misreading: 제 말은 그게 아니라.... The nearest alternative is 그러니까 ('so / what I'm saying is') — the dividing line: 그러니까 reframes/continues your reasoning, while 제 말은 explicitly re-centers on YOUR intended meaning, usually after a misunderstanding. English speakers calque 'I mean' as 제가 의미하는 건, which is unnatural; spoken Korean uses 제 말은. Also, don't confuse 말 with 말씀 in the wrong direction: 말씀 is humble/honorific and 제 말씀은 elevates your own speech politely toward a senior.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calquing 'I mean' as 제가 의미하는 건 — unnatural; say 제 말은.
Using 내 말은 with someone you must be polite to — switch to 제 말은 (or 제 말씀은).
Dropping the topic particle (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은: 제 말은 그게 아니라.

entries.english: I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)
entries.shortExplanation: 강아지 키워요 is a practical expression meaning "I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)".
entries.explanation: 강아지 키워요 (gangaji kiwoyo) means "I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)". Say it as one set phrase — for example 강아지 키워요 ("I have a dog"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 강아지 키워요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; the everyday way to say you own/raise a pet
반말, with friends
Progressive; stresses you currently have one
Swap 강아지 → 고양이 for a cat

examples.ko: 저 강아지 키워요.
examples.romanization: jeo gangaji kiwoyo.
examples.en: I have a dog.
examples.note: 키우다 ('to raise') is the verb for owning any pet, not 있다 alone

examples.ko: 집에서 고양이 두 마리 키워요.
examples.romanization: jibeseo goyangi du mari kiwoyo.
examples.en: I have two cats at home.
examples.note: Count pets with 마리: 한 마리, 두 마리

examples.ko: 강아지 키운 지 3년 됐어요.
examples.romanization: gangaji kiun ji 3nyeon dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I've had my dog for 3 years.
examples.note: -(으)ㄴ 지 ... 됐어요 = 'it's been ... since I started'

entries.nuance: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up', and it is THE verb Koreans use for having a pet — you 'raise' a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant. Saying 강아지 키워요 sounds completely natural and warm; it implies you care for the animal, not just that one exists nearby. This is polite-neutral 존댓말, fine with anyone; drop to 강아지 키워 with friends. The big English-speaker trap is translating 'I have a dog' as 강아지 있어요 — that is grammatical but means 'a dog exists / there is a dog (here)', so it sounds like you're reporting a dog is present, not that you own one as a pet; for ownership-as-caretaking, Koreans say 키워요. A second trap: don't use 가지다 ('to possess') as 강아지 가지고 있어요 — that frames a living animal like an object you hold, which feels cold and odd. Also note 강아지 technically means 'puppy' but in speech Koreans call any dog, even an old one, 강아지 affectionately; the neutral word for 'dog' is 개, but 개 can sound blunt, so 강아지 is the friendly default. Count animals with the counter 마리 and native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

Saying 강아지 있어요 to mean 'I have a dog'.

structuredNuance.t: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up', and it is THE verb Koreans use for having a pet — you 'raise' a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant. entries.nuance: 산책 is 'a (leisurely) walk / stroll' (Sino-Korean 散策), and 산책 가다 = 'go for a walk' is the daily ritual every Korean dog owner knows. There's a crucial split English speakers miss: 산책하다 / 산책 가다 means YOU go for a walk, while 산책시키다 (causative -시키다) means you WALK THE DOG — you make the animal take its walk. So to your dog you cheerfully say 산책 가자 ('let's go for a walk', joining it), but to another person you'd report 강아지 산책시켜요 ('I walk the dog'). Mixing these up — saying 강아지를 산책해요 — is wrong, because 산책하다 is intransitive (you can't 'walk' the dog with it); you need the causative 산책시키다 to put the dog as the object. Note 산책 is for relaxed walking; if you mean brisk exercise-walking, that's 걷기 운동, and hiking a mountain is 등산 — don't call a mountain hike 산책. The set phrase 산책 가자 is also a sweet way to invite a friend out, but with a person use polite 산책 가요 unless they're close.

entries.nuance: 사료 is the specific word for animal feed / pet kibble (Sino-Korean 飼料) — you do NOT call it 밥 or 음식 when you mean commercial pet food, though owners affectionately say 밥 먹자 ('let's eat') to the pet. The verb pair here trips up English speakers: 먹다 = '(the pet) eats', but 먹이다 = '(I) feed / make eat' (causative). So 'I feed the dog kibble' is 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요, while 'the dog eats kibble' is 강아지가 사료를 먹어요. Using 먹다 where you mean 'feed' (e.g. 강아지 사료 먹어요 when you mean YOU feed it) blurs who's doing what. The particle on the pet is 한테 (or formal 에게) — the dog is the recipient: 강아지한테 먹여요; saying 강아지를 먹여요 alone can sound like you're 'feeding ON the dog'. This phrase is polite-neutral, perfect for chatting with another owner, a 펫숍 (pet shop) clerk, or a vet. Note 어떤 거 ('what kind / which one') invites a category answer (brand, wet vs. dry), whereas 뭐 ('what') is more open; both are natural. Don't confuse 사료 (dry/commercial feed) with 간식 ('treats/snacks') — asking about 사료 is about the staple diet.

entries.nuance: 물그릇 = 'water bowl' (물 'water' + 그릇 'bowl/dish'), and 밥그릇 = 'food bowl' — these compound words are how owners refer to pet dishes. The verb choices matter: 채우다 = 'to fill (up)', 갈다 = 'to change/replace' (swap old water for fresh), and 비우다 = 'to empty'. Koreans distinguish 물 채워 줘 ('fill it up', add water) from 물 갈아 줘 ('change the water', dump and replace) — for hygiene you usually 갈아 주다 daily, so don't just say 채우다 if you mean fresh water. The -아/어 줄게 ending ('I'll do it for you') and -아/어 줘 ('do it for me') express doing the action as a favor, which is the warm register owners naturally use toward pets (in 반말). The English-speaker trap is reaching for generic 만들다 or 넣다 — 'put water in' is fine as 물 넣어 줘, but the idiomatic care-verbs are 채우다/갈다. Also note 그릇 is the bowl; don't confuse it with 접시 ('flat plate'), which isn't used for a pet's water. Since you're speaking to or about your pet, 반말 with -줄게/-줘 is natural; to a person helping you, say 물 좀 채워 주세요.

채우다 just adds water to what's there. To replace stale water with clean, say 물 갈아 줘 ('change the water').

접시 is a flat plate. A pet's bowl is 그릇: 물그릇, 밥그릇.

Honorifics like 드리다 are for elevating people. To a pet, 반말 is normal: 물그릇 채워 줄게.

entries.explanation: "I have to pick up the poop" — that is 응가 치워야 돼요 (eungga chiwoya dwaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 응가 치워야 돼요 ("I have to pick up the poop"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite-neutral; 응가 = cute word for poop
반말; 똥 is blunter than 응가

usagePhrases.en: Did you grab a poop bag?
usagePhrases.note: 배변봉투 = poop/waste bag
오줌 (을) 싸다 = to pee; 쌌어 = peed

examples.ko: 산책할 때 응가 꼭 치워야 돼요.
examples.romanization: sanchaekal ttae eungga kkok chiwoya dwaeyo.
examples.en: You must pick up poop when walking.
examples.note: 꼭 = 'definitely/without fail' — it's a rule and courtesy

examples.ko: 배변봉투로 똥 치우고 왔어.
examples.romanization: baebyeonbongturo ttong chiugo wasseo.
examples.en: I picked up the poop with a bag and came back.
examples.note: 배변봉투로 = 'using a waste bag' (instrument 로)

examples.ko: 우리 강아지 아직 화장실 못 가려요.
examples.romanization: uri gangaji aji kwajangsil mot garyeoyo.
examples.en: My dog isn't potty-trained yet.
examples.note: 화장실 가리다 = to be house-trained / control toileting

entries.nuance: 치우다 = 'to clear away / clean up / pick up', the exact verb for scooping pet waste — not 청소하다 ('to clean a room/surface'), which is too broad for picking up a single poop. For the waste itself, 응가 is a soft, slightly babyish word ('poop / number two') that owners and parents use; 똥 is the plain, blunter 'poop / crap' (fine in 반말 but earthy); the clinical term is 대변. A 배변봉투 ('defecation bag') is the poop bag you must carry on walks — picking up after your dog is both etiquette and, in many places, the law. The English-speaker trap is saying 응가 잡다 — 잡다 means 'to grab/catch (a moving thing)', wrong here; you 치우다 ('clear away') waste. Another trap: don't say 응가 만들다. For peeing, 오줌 (을) 싸다 or politely 소변 보다; 'potty-trained' is 화장실(을) 가리다 (lit. 'to distinguish the bathroom'). This phrase is polite-neutral; with friends you'd say 똥 치워야 돼. Because 응가/똥 are casual, in a vet or formal context use 대변/소변.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 응가 잡다 to mean 'pick up the poop'.
잡다 = grab/catch (something moving). For cleaning up waste use 치우다: 응가 치워야 돼요.
Using 청소하다 for scooping a single poop.
청소하다 = clean (a whole area). For picking up pet waste, the verb is 치우다.
Saying 똥 in a formal vet conversation.
똥 is blunt/casual. In a clinic, use 대변 (feces) and 소변 (urine): 대변 색이 이상해요.

entries.english: Does it need to get vaccinated?
entries.shortExplanation: 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Does it need to get vaccinated?".
entries.explanation: 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? (yebangjeopjong majaya dwaeyo?) = "Does it need to get vaccinated?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? ("Does it need a vaccination?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the vet
Reporting it's done (접종하다)
접종 = the shot; short form

usagePhrases.en: I got it the rabies shot
usagePhrases.note: 주사 맞히다 = have (it) get a shot

examples.ko: 강아지 예방접종 언제 맞아야 돼요?
examples.romanization: gangaji yebangjeopjong eonje majaya dwaeyo?
examples.en: When should my dog get vaccinated?
examples.note: 맞다 (passive 'receive a shot') — the pet 'gets' the shot

examples.ko: 이번에 광견병 예방접종 맞혔어요.
examples.romanization: ibeone gwanggyeonbyeong yebangjeopjong matyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I had it get the rabies vaccine this time.
examples.note: 맞히다 (causative) = I make it receive the shot

examples.ko: 접종 기록 카드 가지고 오세요.
examples.romanization: jeopjong girok kadeu gajigo oseyo.
examples.en: Bring the vaccination record card.
examples.note: 접종 기록 = vaccination record (kept by the clinic)

entries.nuance: 예방접종 = 'preventive vaccination' (예방 'prevention' + 접종 'inoculation'), the umbrella word for pet shots; 광견병 = 'rabies', a key annual one. The verb is the classic learner minefield: 주사/접종을 맞다 = '(the patient) receives a shot' (it's the way Korean says 'get a shot', not literally 'be hit'), while 맞히다 (causative) = '(I) have/make it receive a shot'. So your dog 주사를 맞아요 ('gets the shot'), and you 주사를 맞혔어요 ('had it get the shot'). English speakers wrongly use the active 'do' verb and say 주사를 해요 or import 'inject' as 주사하다 about themselves — for receiving, it's 맞다. Saying 주사를 때려요 (맞다's other meaning is 'be struck', so learners over-correct to 'hit') is wrong. This is polite-neutral, exactly right for the 동물병원 (animal hospital/vet). Note 동물병원 literally 'animal hospital' is the standard word for a vet clinic — there's no separate word like 'vet's office'; the vet themselves is 수의사(선생님). Keep the 접종 기록 (vaccine record); clinics ask for it. The -아야 돼요? frame ('must / should?') politely asks about requirement.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주사를 해요 / 주사하다 for getting a shot.
To receive an injection, Korean uses 맞다: 주사를 맞아요. 주사하다 isn't how you say 'get a shot'.
Confusing 맞다 (the pet gets it) with 맞히다 (you have it get it).
강아지가 주사를 맞아요 = the dog gets the shot. (제가) 강아지한테 주사를 맞혔어요 = I had it vaccinated. Pick by who's doing what.
Calling the vet clinic 병원 only.
병원 alone implies a human hospital. The vet is 동물병원: 동물병원 가야 돼요.

entries.shortExplanation: 동물병원 예약했어요 is a practical expression meaning "I made a vet appointment".
entries.explanation: 동물병원 예약했어요 (dongmulbyeongwon yeyakaesseoyo) means "I made a vet appointment". Say it as one set phrase — for example 동물병원 예약했어요 ("I made a vet appointment"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; reporting it's booked

usagePhrases.en: I'd like to book the clinic
usagePhrases.note: Saying it to the clinic / on the phone
진료 받다 = receive a medical exam
접수 = reception/check-in at a clinic

examples.ko: 내일 동물병원 예약했어요.
examples.romanization: naeil dongmulbyeongwon yeyakaesseoyo.
examples.en: I made a vet appointment for tomorrow.
examples.note: 예약하다 = to reserve/book (an appointment)

examples.ko: 강아지 진료 예약하려고 전화했어요.
examples.romanization: gangaji jillyo yeyakaryeogo jeonhwahaesseoyo.
examples.en: I called to book my dog's exam.
examples.note: 진료 = medical consultation/exam at a clinic

examples.ko: 접수처에서 이름이랑 증상 말씀하세요.
examples.romanization: jeopsucheoeseo ireumirang jeungsang malsseumhaseyo.
examples.en: Tell them the name and symptoms at reception.
examples.note: 접수처 = the reception desk; 증상 = symptoms

entries.nuance: 예약하다 = 'to reserve / book' (an appointment, table, ticket), and 동물병원 예약 is how you book a vet visit. Don't confuse the steps Korean clinics use: 예약 = the booking made in advance, 접수 = checking in / registering when you arrive, and 진료 = the actual exam/consultation. So you 예약하다 by phone, 접수하다 at the desk, then 진료(를) 받다 ('receive an exam'). English speakers often collapse these and say only 'appointment', but using 접수 on arrival and 진료 for the exam makes you sound fluent. Note 진료 받다 uses 받다 ('to receive') — you receive the exam; saying 진료해요 about yourself is wrong, since 진료하다 is what the DOCTOR does. This phrase is polite-neutral. A frequent trap: 'reservation' as 예약 is right, but don't say 약속 — 약속 is a 'promise / social plans (with a person)', not a booked appointment with a business. For symptoms tell the desk the 증상 (symptoms). The clinic may say 보호자분 ('guardian', i.e. you the owner) — Koreans call pet owners 보호자, literally 'protector/guardian', in medical settings.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 약속 for a clinic appointment.
약속 is a promise / plans with a person. A booked business appointment is 예약: 동물병원 예약했어요.
Saying 진료해요 to mean 'I'm getting an exam'.
진료하다 is what the doctor does (examines). The patient side is 진료(를) 받다: 진료 받으러 왔어요.
Skipping 접수 and going straight to the vet.
Korean clinics have you 접수 (check in) at the desk first. Say 접수 먼저 할게요 on arrival, then wait to be called.

entries.english: Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?
entries.shortExplanation: 어디가 아파요? is a practical expression meaning "Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?".
entries.explanation: "Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?" — that is 어디가 아파요? (eodiga apayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 어디가 아파요? ("Where does it hurt?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 어디가 아파요? with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: What the vet asks; you describe the symptom
안 먹어요 = refuses food (a key symptom)
토하다 = to throw up; 계속 = continuously
다리를 절다 = to limp

examples.ko: 우리 강아지가 어제부터 밥을 안 먹어요.
examples.romanization: uri gangajiga eojebuteo babeul an meogeoyo.
examples.en: My dog hasn't eaten since yesterday.
examples.note: 어제부터 = 'since yesterday' — give onset time

examples.ko: 고양이가 자꾸 토하고 기운이 없어요.
examples.romanization: goyangiga jakku tohago giuni eopseoyo.
examples.en: The cat keeps throwing up and has no energy.
examples.note: 기운이 없다 = to be lethargic / have no energy

examples.ko: 여기를 만지면 아파하는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: yeogireul manjimyeon apahaneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: It seems to hurt when I touch here.
examples.note: 아파하다 = to show pain (about an animal/other); -것 같다 = 'seems'

entries.nuance: 아프다 = 'to be sick / hurt / in pain', and 어디가 아파요? ('where does it hurt / what's wrong?') is what the 수의사 asks — you'll mainly ANSWER by describing symptoms. A subtle but important point: 아프다 describes YOUR OWN felt pain, but for an animal (or another person whose pain you observe), Korean uses 아파하다 ('to act like it's in pain / show pain') — so 강아지가 아파해요 ('the dog seems to be in pain'), not 강아지가 아파요 in careful speech, though casually owners do say 아파요 too. Key symptom verbs: 토하다 (vomit), 설사하다 (have diarrhea), 절다 (limp), 기운이 없다 (be lethargic), 안 먹다 (won't eat). English speakers often say only 'sick' and stop — but Korean vets expect the onset (언제부터, 'since when') and the concrete symptom. Don't translate 'feel sick' as 아픈 느낌 — just say 아파요 or name the symptom. Also 토하다 (vomit) is not 뱉다 ('to spit out') — a dog 토해요 when it throws up. This frame is polite-neutral. Give the time with -부터 ('from/since'): 어제부터, 아침부터.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying only '아파요' without naming the symptom.
Vets need specifics. Add the symptom and onset: 어제부터 밥을 안 먹고 토해요.
Using 아프다 vs. 아파하다 loosely for the pet.

structuredNuance.t: 아프다 = 'to be sick / hurt / in pain', and 어디가 아파요? ('where does it hurt / what's wrong?') is what the 수의사 asks — you'll mainly ANSWER by describing symptoms. Key symptom verbs: 토하다 (vomit), 설사하다 (have diarrhea), 절다 (limp), 기운이 없다 (be lethargic), 안 먹다 (won't eat). This frame is polite-neutral. Give the time with -부터 ('from/since'): 어제부터, 아침부터.

A subtle but important point: 아프다 describes YOUR OWN felt pain, but for an animal (or another person whose pain you observe), Korean uses 아파하다 ('to act like it's in pain / show pain') — so 강아지가 아파해요 ('the dog seems to be in pain'), not 강아지가 아파요 in careful speech, though casually owners do say 아파요 too. Also 토하다 (vomit) is not 뱉다 ('to spit out') — a dog 토해요 when it throws up.

English speakers often say only 'sick' and stop — but Korean vets expect the onset (언제부터, 'since when') and the concrete symptom. Don't translate 'feel sick' as 아픈 느낌 — just say 아파요 or name the symptom.

entries.nuance: 중성화 = 'neutering / spaying' (中性化, lit. 'making neuter'), and 중성화 수술 = the operation; conveniently this single word covers BOTH males and females, so you don't need separate English-style words for 'neuter' vs. 'spay' — just 중성화. 고치다 = repair a broken thing. For the procedure say 중성화 수술 했어요, not 고쳤어요.

중성화 covers spaying females too. You don't switch words by sex — 암컷도 중성화 한다 ('females are also neutered').

usagePhrases.note: Polite; ask BEFORE petting a stranger's dog
Asking permission to touch
Reassuring answer; 안 물어요
순하다 = mild-tempered

examples.ko: 강아지 만져도 돼요? 안 물어요?
examples.romanization: gangaji manjyeodo dwaeyo? an mureoyo?
examples.en: Can I pet the dog? Does it bite?
examples.note: Always ask both before approaching a strange dog

examples.ko: 저희 강아지는 안 물어요, 순해요.
examples.romanization: jeohui gangajineun an mureoyo, sunhaeyo.
examples.en: My dog doesn't bite, it's gentle.
examples.note: 순하다 = good-natured; reassures the asker

examples.ko: 낯선 사람 보면 좀 짖어요.
examples.romanization: natseon saram bomyeon jom jijeoyo.
examples.en: It barks a bit at strangers.
examples.note: 짖다 = to bark (≠ 물다 'to bite')

entries.nuance: 물다 = 'to bite', and 물어요? ('does it bite?') plus 만져도 돼요? ('may I pet it?') are the two phrases you say BEFORE touching anyone's dog — essential etiquette. -아도 돼요? = 'is it okay if I...? / may I...?', the standard permission frame; 만지다 = 'to touch/pet'. The English-speaker trap is confusing the animal-sound verbs: 물다 = bite, but 짖다 = 'to bark' and 으르렁거리다 = 'to growl' — a dog that 짖어요 (barks) isn't necessarily going to 물다 (bite). Don't say 물기 해요 or import 'bite' oddly; the plain verb 물다 conjugates 물어요. Also note 물다 sounds like 묻다 ('to ask' / 'to bury' / 'to get stained') — keep them apart: 물어요 from 물다 = 'bites', but 물어요 from 묻다 can mean 'asks'; context (a dog) makes it clear, but learners sometimes mis-hear. Petting culture: many Koreans will let you pet their dog if you ask, but always ask 만져도 돼요? first — reaching out silently is considered rude and can startle the dog.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

물어요? = does it bite? 짖어요 = it barks. A barking dog isn't necessarily biting — use the right verb.
Petting a stranger's dog without asking.
Always ask first: 만져도 돼요? 물어요? Reaching out silently can startle the dog and annoy the owner.
Mixing 물다 (bite) and 묻다 (ask).
Both can surface as 물어요, but from different verbs. With a dog, 물어요? = 'does it bite?' Keep the base verbs straight.

entries.shortExplanation: 목줄 해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please put it on a leash".
entries.explanation: "Please put it on a leash" — that is 목줄 해 주세요 (mokjul hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 목줄 해 주세요 ("Please leash it"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request; 목줄 = leash/collar lead
채우다 = to fasten (a leash/collar)
입마개 = muzzle (required for some breeds)
짧게 잡다 = hold (the lead) short

examples.ko: 여기서는 목줄 꼭 해 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogiseoneun mokjul kko kae juseyo.
examples.en: Please keep it leashed here.
examples.note: 꼭 = without fail; leashing in public is the law

examples.ko: 대형견은 입마개도 해야 돼요.
examples.romanization: daehyeonggyeoneun immagaedo haeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: Large dogs must also wear a muzzle.
examples.note: 대형견 = large-breed dog; 입마개 = muzzle

examples.ko: 엘리베이터에서는 안아 주시거나 목줄 짧게요.
examples.romanization: ellibeiteoeseoneun ana jusigeona mokjul jjalbgeyo.
examples.en: In the elevator, hold it or keep the leash short.
examples.note: 안다 = to hold in arms; 짧게(요) = keep it short

entries.nuance: 목줄 = 'leash / collar-lead' (목 'neck' + 줄 'cord/line'), the standard word; 가슴줄 / 하네스 = a 'harness' (chest lead). 목줄 (을) 하다 or 채우다 = 'to put on / fasten a leash'. In Korea, leashing your dog in public is legally required, and certain large or 'dangerous' breeds must also wear an 입마개 ('muzzle', 입 'mouth' + 마개 'plug/stopper') — so 목줄 해 주세요 and 입마개 해야 돼요 are phrases you may hear or need. The verb 채우다 here means 'to fasten/buckle' (same verb as filling a bowl, but with a leash it's 'fasten') — 목줄 채우다 = clip the leash on. The English-speaker trap is calling a leash 끈 (a generic 'string/strap') — understandable but 목줄 is the specific term. Don't use 묶다 ('to tie up') for normal leashing — 묶다 implies tethering the dog to a post; routine leash-walking is 목줄 하다/잡다 ('hold the lead'). This phrase as 해 주세요 is a polite request to another owner; 안다 ('to hold in one's arms') is what you do with a small dog in tight spaces like elevators. Korean apartment etiquette: in elevators many owners 안아요 (carry) or keep the 목줄 짧게 (short) out of courtesy.

끈 is a generic strap/string. The specific word is 목줄 (leash) or 하네스/가슴줄 (harness).

묶다 = tie up (to a post). Routine leashing is 목줄 하다 / 잡다. Say 목줄 해 주세요, not 묶어 주세요, for normal walks.

Some large breeds legally need a muzzle: 입마개. Don't invent 입 가리개; the standard word is 입마개.

entries.nuance: Korean pet owners overwhelmingly treat pets as family, so they call them 애기/아기 ('baby'), 우리 막내 ('our youngest'), or 우리 가족 ('our family') — 우리 애기예요 ('this is my baby') is genuine, everyday speech, not baby-talk you'd be embarrassed by. Note the all-important 우리 ('our/my'): Koreans say 우리 강아지, 우리 고양이 ('our dog/cat') rather than 제 강아지, treating the pet as shared family — using 제 (my, humble-possessive) for a beloved pet can sound oddly distancing. Owners also refer to a pet's sex as 남자아이 / 여자아이 ('boy / girl') rather than the blunt animal terms 수컷 ('male') / 암컷 ('female'), which are used in clinical/breeding contexts; calling your cute pet 수컷 in casual chat sounds like a livestock report. Ages take native numbers + 살: 세 살. The endearing -이 suffix attaches to names ending in a consonant (콩 → 콩이, 별 → 별이). The English-speaker trap is over-formal 제 애완동물 ('my pet animal') — 애완동물 is a correct dictionary word but feels stiff and a bit dated; the warmer modern term is 반려동물 ('companion animal'), and in affectionate speech people just say 우리 애기/강아지. This register is casual-affectionate; with strangers you still keep 존댓말 endings (예요).

수컷/암컷 (male/female) are clinical/livestock terms. Owners say 남자아이/여자아이 for a pet's sex in friendly conversation.
Using 애완동물 thinking it's the warm word.
애완동물 is correct but stiff/dated. The modern, kinder term is 반려동물; affectionately, just 우리 애기/강아지.

entries.shortExplanation: 털이 너무 많이 빠져요 is a practical expression meaning "It sheds so much (the fur falls out a lot)".
entries.explanation: "It sheds so much (the fur falls out a lot)" — that is 털이 너무 많이 빠져요 (teori neomu mani ppajyeoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 털이 많이 빠져요 ("It sheds a lot"). examples.romanization: yojeum teori neomu mani ppajyeoyo.
examples.en: It's shedding a ton lately.
examples.note: 빠지다 (intransitive) = (fur) falls out, comes off

examples.romanization: teolgari cheoren maeil bitjilhae juneun ge joayo.
examples.en: In shedding season, brush it daily.
examples.note: 철 = season; 빗질하다 = brush the coat

examples.note: 미용 맡기다 = entrust (the pet) for grooming

entries.nuance: 털 = 'fur / hair (of an animal)', and 빠지다 = 'to fall out / come off' (intransitive) — so 털이 빠져요 = 'the fur sheds / falls out'. The grammar trap for English speakers is voice: shedding is described with the intransitive 빠지다 ('fur falls out by itself'), with 털 as the SUBJECT (털이 빠져요), NOT 'the dog sheds fur' transitively. Don't say 강아지가 털을 빠져요 — wrong, because 빠지다 isn't transitive; either 강아지 털이 빠져요 or 강아지가 털이 많이 빠져요 (double-subject, very natural). 털갈이 = the seasonal 'coat change / molt' (털 + 갈이 'changing'), and 털갈이 철 ('shedding season') is when it's worst. Grooming words: 빗질(하다) = brushing, 미용 = the professional grooming/haircut (you 맡기다 'entrust' your pet to a 애견미용실 'dog grooming salon'), 목욕(시키다) = bathing (causative — you bathe the pet). The English-speaker trap is using 머리카락 ('head hair, human') for animal fur — animals have 털, only humans have 머리카락. Also don't say 떨어지다 ('to drop/fall') for shedding — 빠지다 is the verb for hair/fur coming out. This phrase is polite-neutral, common small-talk among owners and with groomers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 강아지가 털을 빠져요 (transitive).
빠지다 is intransitive — the fur is the subject. Say 강아지 털이 빠져요 or 강아지가 털이 빠져요.
Using 머리카락 for animal fur.
머리카락 is human head hair. Animal fur/hair is 털: 털이 많이 빠져요.
Saying 털이 떨어져요 for shedding.
떨어지다 = drop/fall (off a surface). Hair/fur coming out is 빠지다: 털이 빠져요.

entries.explanation: 동물등록 해야 돼요 (dongmuldeungno kaeya dwaeyo) = "I have to register my pet (microchip/registration)". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 동물등록 해야 돼요 ("I have to register my pet"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: I have to register my pet
usagePhrases.note: Polite; 동물등록 = the legal pet registration

usagePhrases.en: Did you get the microchip done?
usagePhrases.note: 내장칩 = implanted microchip option
동물등록증 = the registration certificate/tag

usagePhrases.note: 인식표 = external ID tag (the other option)

examples.ko: 강아지는 법적으로 동물등록 해야 돼요.
examples.romanization: gangajineun beopjeogeuro dongmuldeungno kaeya dwaeyo.
examples.en: Dogs must be registered by law.
examples.note: 법적으로 = 'legally'; dog registration is mandatory in Korea

examples.romanization: dongmulbyeongwoneseo naejangchibeuro dongmuldeungno kaesseoyo.
examples.en: I registered with a microchip at the vet.
examples.note: 내장칩으로 = 'by/with the microchip' (method 으로)

examples.ko: 등록 안 하면 과태료 나올 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: deungnok an hamyeon gwataeryo naol su isseoyo.

examples.note: 과태료 = an administrative fine; 나오다 = to be issued

entries.nuance: 동물등록 = 'animal registration' (動物登錄), the legally required registration of your dog with the local government — a real obligation newcomers often don't know about, with a 과태료 ('fine') for skipping it. You register via two methods: 내장칩 ('internal/implanted microchip', injected at the 동물병원) or an 외장형 인식표 ('external ID tag'); the microchip is most common. You receive a 동물등록증 ('registration certificate'). The verb is 등록(을) 하다 = 'to register'; 동물등록 했어요 = 'I registered (the pet)'. The English-speaker trap is using 가입하다 ('to sign up / join', for memberships, insurance, services) for registration — 가입 is for subscribing to something you join, whereas official record-registration is 등록; so it's 동물등록 했어요, never 동물 가입했어요. Another trap: 칩 (chip) alone is understood, but the set term is 내장칩 (internal chip) vs. 인식표 (tag). This phrase is polite-neutral, exactly what you'd say to a vet or another owner. Note 과태료 (administrative fine) differs from 벌금 (a criminal/court fine) — pet-registration penalties are 과태료. Currently only dogs are legally required to register; cat registration is voluntary in most areas.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 동물 가입했어요 for registering a pet.
가입하다 is for joining/subscribing (memberships, insurance). Official registration is 등록하다: 동물등록 했어요.
Thinking registration is optional for dogs.
Dog 동물등록 is legally required in Korea, with a 과태료 (fine) for non-compliance. Do it at the 동물병원 (microchip) or a 동사무소.
Saying 벌금 for the non-registration penalty.
벌금 is a criminal/court fine. An administrative penalty like this is 과태료: 과태료 나올 수 있어요.

structuredNuance.t: 동물등록 = 'animal registration', the legally required registration of your dog with the local government — a real obligation newcomers often don't know about, with a 과태료 ('fine') for skipping it. You register via two methods: 내장칩 ('internal/implanted microchip', injected at the 동물병원) or an 외장형 인식표 ('external ID tag'); the microchip is most common. You receive a 동물등록증 ('registration certificate'). The verb is 등록(을) 하다 = 'to register'; 동물등록 했어요 = 'I registered (the pet)'. This phrase is polite-neutral, exactly what you'd say to a vet or another owner. Currently only dogs are legally required to register; cat registration is voluntary in most areas.
칩 (chip) alone is understood, but the set term is 내장칩 (internal chip) vs. 인식표 (tag). Also note 과태료 (administrative fine) differs from 벌금 (a criminal/court fine) — pet-registration penalties are 과태료.
동물등록 is 動物登錄, 'animal registration'.

The English-speaker trap is using 가입하다 ('to sign up / join', for memberships, insurance, services) for registration — 가입 is for subscribing to something you join, whereas official record-registration is 등록; so it's 동물등록 했어요, never 동물 가입했어요.

entries.nuance: 진료비 = 'consultation / treatment fee' (診療費), the vet bill; -비 is the Sino-Korean suffix for 'fee/cost' (교통비 transport, 식비 food, 병원비 hospital). The natural verb for a bill is 나오다 ('to come out / be issued') — 얼마 나왔어요? = 'how much did it come out to?' — which English speakers rarely guess; they tend to say 얼마였어요? ('how much was it?'), understandable but less idiomatic for a calculated total. Korean vet care is largely NOT covered by national health insurance (that's only for humans), so bills can be high and surprising; 펫보험 ('pet insurance') exists but you must 들다/가입하다 ('take it out / sign up') in advance. Another trap: don't confuse 진료비 (the exam/treatment fee) with 약값 ('medicine cost') — they may be itemized separately. Currency reminder: amounts use Sino-Korean numbers + 원 (만 원 = 10,000 won), and Koreans count in 만 (ten-thousands), so 십만 원 = 100,000 won. This phrase is polite-neutral, fine with staff at checkout or with another owner comparing costs.

Understandable, but for a calculated bill Koreans say 얼마 나왔어요? ('how much did it come out to'). Use 나오다 for bills.

건강보험 covers humans only; vet care isn't covered, so it's pricey. For coverage you need private 펫보험, taken out in advance.

entries.nuance: 반려동물 = 'companion animal', the modern, respectful umbrella term for pets (반려 'companion' + 동물 'animal'), now standard on signs and in media — much warmer than the older 애완동물 ('pet animal', lit. 'plaything animal'). 출입 = 'entry / coming and going' (出入), so 출입 돼요? = 'is entry allowed?'; 동반 = 'accompanying', so 반려동물 동반 가능 = 'pets may accompany (you)' = pet-friendly, the exact phrase on café/store signs. The English-speaker trap is asking 'allowed' with 허락 ('permission/consent') as 허락돼요? — 허락 is for personal permission between people; for public access the natural phrase is 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?. Many indoor places require a 이동장 / 케이지 ('carrier') or that small dogs be carried; cafés may be 노키즈/펫 프렌들리. This phrase is polite-neutral. Note: 동반 sounds formal/sign-like; in speech 강아지 데리고 가도 돼요? is the everyday spoken version.

Soft way to say a pet died
What you say to a grieving owner
펫로스 = pet loss (the grief)

examples.ko: 우리 강아지가 어제 무지개다리 건넜어요.
examples.romanization: uri gangajiga eoje mujigaedari geonneosseoyo.
examples.en: My dog crossed the rainbow bridge yesterday.
examples.note: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 = the pet euphemism for dying

examples.ko: 많이 힘드시겠어요, 위로의 말 전해요.
examples.romanization: mani himdeusigesseoyo, wiroui mal jeonhaeyo.
examples.en: You must be hurting — my condolences.
examples.note: 위로의 말 = words of comfort (to the bereaved owner)

examples.ko: 반려동물 장례식장도 있어요.
examples.romanization: ballyeodongmul jangnyesikjangdo isseoyo.
examples.en: There are pet funeral homes too.
examples.note: 장례식장 = funeral hall; pet funerals exist in Korea

entries.nuance: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 = 'to cross the rainbow bridge', the same tender euphemism English uses, and the most common gentle way Koreans speak of a pet's death; 하늘나라(에) 가다 ('go to heaven/the sky country') is another soft option. You generally AVOID the blunt 죽었어요 ('it died') when comforting a grieving owner — that's factually correct but cold; the euphemisms show respect for how deeply Koreans grieve pets (펫로스 증후군 = 'pet loss syndrome' is a recognized concept). To express condolences to the owner, 많이 힘드시겠어요 ('you must be having a hard time') or 위로의 말 전해요 ('I offer words of comfort') are warm and appropriate; the formal funeral phrase 삼가 고인의 명복을 빌어요 (traditionally for people) is increasingly used for pets too. The English-speaker trap is translating 'put to sleep / euthanize' carelessly — that's 안락사 (安樂死), a heavy clinical word; don't blurt it in casual sympathy. Another: don't say 잃어버렸어요 ('I lost it') to mean the pet died — 잃어버리다 means you misplaced/lost track of it (it ran away), a different, confusing meaning. This register is gentle 존댓말. Korea now has 반려동물 장례식장 ('pet funeral homes') and cremation services, so these aren't just figures of speech.

It's correct but cold. Use the gentle 무지개다리 건넜어요 or 하늘나라 갔어요 when comforting someone.

잃어버리다 = lost track of / misplaced (it ran away). For death, say 무지개다리 건넜어요, not 잃어버렸어요.

안락사 (euthanasia) is a heavy clinical term. Don't introduce it lightly; offer comfort: 많이 힘드시겠어요.

structuredNuance.t: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 = 'to cross the rainbow bridge', the same tender euphemism English uses, and the most common gentle way Koreans speak of a pet's death; 하늘나라(에) 가다 ('go to heaven/the sky country') is another soft option. You generally AVOID the blunt 죽었어요 ('it died') when comforting a grieving owner — that's factually correct but cold; the euphemisms show respect for how deeply Koreans grieve pets (펫로스 증후군 = 'pet loss syndrome' is a recognized concept). The classic English-speaker error is using 여보세요 like 'hi' when meeting people — keep it strictly for phones.

entries.nuance: 누구세요? politely asks a caller's identity — 누구 ('who') plus honorific 이세요 — so it honors the unknown person while you find out who they are. The key contrast is against 누구야? and 누구냐?, which are 반말/blunt and sound suspicious or hostile ('who the heck are you?'), fine only with close friends. For business politeness Koreans upgrade to 누구시죠? or 어디세요? (literally 'where are you from?', i.e. which company), the norm on work calls; the dividing line is that 어디세요? asks for the affiliation, not the personal name. Watch the particle trap: it stands alone, so never add 가/이 (누구가세요 is wrong). Another pitfall is answering with 누구세요? on a call you placed — the caller introduces themselves first (저 ...인데요); 누구세요? is for when you RECEIVE a call from someone unknown.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 누구야?/누구냐? to a stranger — these are blunt 반말 and sound like a challenge; the honorific 누구세요? is required with anyone you don't know.
Adding a subject particle: 누구가세요/누구이세요 is wrong — it is simply 누구 + 세요.
Using 누구세요? on a call you yourself made — the caller introduces themselves first; you only ask 누구세요? when answering an unknown caller.

entries.nuance: 잠시만요 means 'just a moment' and is the all-purpose 'hold on' on the phone, at a counter, or to slip past someone in a crowd. On a call it tells the other person you are stepping away briefly without ending the conversation. 잠시 is slightly more formal than the everyday 잠깐, but 잠시만요/잠깐만요 are interchangeable in practice; the 반말 form is 잠깐만 (or 잠시만), dropping the polite 요. The dividing line with 기다려 주세요 ('please wait') is length and tone: 잠시만요 is a quick, almost reflexive 'sec', while 기다려 주세요 is a fuller, more explicit request. The English-speaker error is reaching for a literal 'wait' as 기다리세요, which sounds like a command ('you, wait!'); the natural, softening idiom is 잠시만요, and the polite request form adds 주시겠어요?.

Saying 잠깐만 to a customer or elder — it is 반말; use 잠시만요 or the fuller 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
Spelling/spacing it as 잠시 만요 — it is one chunk, 잠시만요, with 만요 attached.

entries.nuance: 잘 안 들려요 reports that the other person's voice is faint — 들리다 is the intransitive 'to be heard/audible', so the sound is the subject, not you. This is the right verb: 듣다 ('to listen') would wrongly imply you are choosing not to listen, while 들리다 means the audio itself isn't coming through. Keep the order 잘 안 들려요 ('well-not-audible'); 안 잘 들려요 is ungrammatical. To go gentler/more formal, use 잘 안 들리는데요; the 반말 is 잘 안 들려. The nearest alternative is 소리가 작아요 ('the volume is low'), but that blames the volume specifically, whereas 잘 안 들려요 covers any reason — static, dropout, noise. The English-speaker trap is 당신을 못 들어요 ('I can't hear you'), which uses 듣다 with a person object and sounds like a personal refusal; native phrasing makes the sound, not the person, the subject.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 못 들어요 with the person as object — use 들리다 (안 들려요), because the sound is what isn't getting through.
Word order 안 잘 들려요 — the adverb order is fixed as 잘 안 들려요.
Confusing it with 못 알아들어요 ('I can't understand') — that is about comprehension; for a bad line use 잘 안 들려요.

entries.nuance: 전화가 끊겼어요 says the call ended unintentionally — 끊기다 is the passive/intransitive of 끊다 ('to cut'), so the call 'got cut off' on its own. Choosing the wrong voice flips the meaning from an accident to a deliberate hang-up — potentially rude. To soften or sound more formal, 통화가 끊어졌어요 works; the 반말 is 전화 끊겼어. The nearest neighbor 전화 끊을게요 is unrelated in meaning ('I'll hang up now'), a polite sign-off, so don't confuse 끊다 (deliberate) with 끊기다 (accidental). The English-speaker trap is using 끊었어요 for an accidental drop, which sounds like you cut them off yourself.

Mixing particles: 전화를 끊겼어요 — the passive 끊기다 takes the subject marker 가 (전화가 끊겼어요).
Confusing it with 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') — that announces ending the call on purpose, not a dropout.

entries.nuance: 다시 전화할게요 is a promise that YOU will phone again — the -ㄹ게요 ending specifically marks the speaker's own intention/commitment, which is why it fits a personal promise and would be wrong for asking someone else to act. 다시 means 'again', so the whole thing is 'I'll call again.' To raise politeness toward a boss or client, swap 전화하다 for the humble 전화드리다 → 다시 전화드릴게요/전화드리겠습니다; the 반말 is 다시 전화할게. The nearest alternative 다시 걸게요 uses 걸다 (the dialing verb) and is equally natural; the difference is negligible. The English-speaker trap is 'call you back' producing 당신을 다시 불러요 — 부르다 means 'to call out to / summon' a person physically, not to telephone; the phone verb is 전화하다/전화 걸다, and you do not insert 당신을.

Adding 당신을 — 전화하다 doesn't take a person as object that way; just say 다시 전화할게요.

structuredNuance.t: 다시 전화할게요 is a promise that YOU will phone again — the -ㄹ게요 ending specifically marks the speaker's own intention/commitment, which is why it fits a personal promise and would be wrong for asking someone else to act. 다시 means 'again', so the whole thing is 'I'll call again.'
The nearest alternative 다시 걸게요 uses 걸다 (the dialing verb) and is equally natural; the difference is negligible.
To raise politeness toward a boss or client, swap 전화하다 for the humble 전화드리다 → 다시 전화드릴게요/전화드리겠습니다; the 반말 is 다시 전화할게.

entries.nuance: 메시지 남겨 주세요 asks a caller to leave word — 남기다 ('to leave behind') plus the polite-request 주세요. The verb is specifically 남기다 for leaving a message/note behind, not 두다 ('to put/place') or 놓다; 메시지를 두세요 sounds odd. To go more formal for business, extend to 남겨 주시면 전달해 드리겠습니다; the casual 반말 is 메시지 남겨. The nearest alternative 메모 남겨 주세요 uses 메모 ('a memo/note') and is common at a desk when you'll jot it on paper, whereas 메시지 leans toward voicemail or a relayed verbal message — the line is paper-note (메모) versus voice/relayed message (메시지). The English-speaker trap is calquing 'leave a message' as 메시지를 떠나세요 — 떠나다 means 'to depart/leave a place', never 'to leave an item or note'; for leaving something behind you must use 남기다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 떠나다 for 'leave a message' — 떠나다 is to depart a place; leaving a note/message takes 남기다 (메시지 남겨 주세요).
Saying 메시지를 두세요/놓으세요 — 두다/놓다 are 'put/place' objects; the idiom is 남기다.
Dropping 주세요 and barking 남겨 — without 주세요 it sounds like an order; keep 남겨 주세요 or 남겨 주시겠어요?.

entries.nuance: 약속 잡을까요? proposes pinning down a meeting — the verb for arranging/fixing an appointment is 잡다 (literally 'to grab/catch'), so 약속을 잡다 is the set phrase for 'to make plans.' The -ㄹ까요? ending makes it a soft 'shall we?' suggestion that invites the other's agreement, ideal for proposals. Note 약속 here means a personal arrangement to meet; for a formal business meeting Koreans may say 미팅을 잡다 or 일정을 잡다. To go casual it's 약속 잡을까?; to go formal, 약속을 잡으시죠. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'make a promise/appointment' as 약속을 만들까요? — 만들다 ('to make/create') is wrong here; appointments are 'caught/grabbed' with 잡다. Also beware that 약속 also means 'a promise', so context and the verb 잡다 are what mark it as scheduling.

Confusing 약속 with only 'promise' — with 잡다 it means scheduling a meet-up; the verb signals the meaning.
Using a flat statement 약속 잡아요 when proposing — the inviting form is the -ㄹ까요? question, 약속 잡을까요?.

entries.nuance: 좀 늦을 것 같아요 softly warns that you'll arrive late — the -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems/I think') frame turns a blunt 늦어요 into a hedged, polite prediction, which is exactly the cushioning Korean expects when delivering bad news like lateness. 좀 ('a bit') further softens it. The verb is 늦다 ('to be late'); for a thing being delayed (a train) Koreans use 연착되다/지연되다, but for a person it's 늦다. To go formal, 늦을 것 같습니다; the 반말 is 늦을 것 같아. The nearest alternative 늦겠어요 also predicts lateness but feels more certain/abrupt, while -ㄹ 것 같아요 stays tentative and apologetic — the dividing line is hedged versus assertive. The English-speaker trap is the flat 늦어요 ('I'm late'), which sounds like a curt fact with no apology; native speakers wrap it in 죄송한데 ... -ㄹ 것 같아요.

entries.nuance: 약속을 미뤄도 될까요? asks permission to postpone — 미루다 ('to put off / postpone') plus the permission frame -아도 될까요? ('would it be okay if...'). The -아도 될까요? makes it a request for the other's consent rather than a unilateral announcement, which is the polite move when you're the one inconveniencing them. 미루다 specifically means pushing to a later time; cancelling outright is 취소하다, so the dividing line is postpone-and-rebook (미루다) versus call-off (취소하다) — using 취소 when you actually want to reschedule can alarm the other person. To go formal, 미뤄도 괜찮으실까요?; the 반말 is 미뤄도 돼?. The English-speaker trap is the bare command 약속을 미뤄요 ('postpone the appointment'), which orders the other person around; soften to the permission question, and add 죄송한데 to acknowledge the imposition.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Commanding 약속을 미뤄요 — that orders them; ask permission with 미뤄도 될까요?.
Confusing 미루다 with 늦추다 alone — both can mean delay, but for rescheduling plans 약속을 미루다 is the set collocation.

entries.nuance: 연락드릴게요 promises you'll make contact — 연락하다 ('to contact') in the humble form 연락드리다, where 드리다 ('to give, humbly') lowers the speaker to elevate the listener, so it's the courteous choice for bosses, clients, and elders. The -ㄹ게요 again marks YOUR own intention. 연락 covers any channel — call, text, message — so it's broader than 전화할게요 (specifically a phone call); the dividing line is medium-neutral (연락) versus phone-only (전화). To go casual, drop the humble: 연락할게 (반말) or 연락할게요 (plain polite); to go formal, 연락드리겠습니다. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'I'll contact you' as 당신에게 연락할게요 with 당신 — 당신 is rarely used to a real second person and can sound confrontational or oddly intimate; Korean simply omits it. Another trap is 연락이 될게요, mixing in the intransitive 되다 incorrectly.

Using plain 연락할게요 to a client or boss — prefer the humble 연락드릴게요 to show respect.
Saying 연락이 될게요 — the speaker's intention uses active 연락하다/연락드리다 + -ㄹ게요, not 되다.

entries.nuance: 이따 전화드릴게요 promises to call later today — 이따(가) means 'in a little while / later (the same day)', so it's near-term, unlike 나중에 ('sometime later', open-ended). entries.nuance: 전화번호 좀 알려 주세요 politely asks for a phone number — 알리다 ('to let someone know / inform') plus 주세요, with 좀 ('a little') softening the request into 'if you would.' The verb is 알려 주다 ('let me know'), not 가르치다 ('to teach'): 가르치다 is for teaching skills/subjects, so 번호를 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like you want a lesson. For a more formal, business feel, swap 전화번호 for 연락처 ('contact details', which can include phone or email). The 반말 is 알려 줘. The nearest alternative 전화번호가 어떻게 되세요? ('what is your number?') is also very polite and idiomatic — note it uses 어떻게 되세요?, the honorific way to ask for personal info, not 뭐예요?. The English-speaker trap is dropping 좀 and 주세요 and saying 전화번호 알려, which is abrupt; the softeners are what make it courteous.

Dropping 좀/주세요 (전화번호 알려) — it sounds abrupt; keep 좀 알려 주세요 to stay polite.

entries.nuance: 유심 is the Korean pronunciation of 'USIM' (the chip), and it's the everyday word — Koreans almost never say 'SIM card' in English; they say 유심. The pattern 사러 왔어요 is verb-stem + -(으)러 ('in order to') + 왔어요 ('came'), literally 'I came in order to buy', which is exactly how you state your purpose on entering a shop. Default to 존댓말 with staff; the 반말 유심 사러 왔어 is only for a friend. A key contrast: 사러 왔어요 announces WHY you're here, while 유심 하나 주세요 ('one SIM, please') is the direct order — open with the first, then move to the second once they confirm stock. The big English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 유심 카드 살 수 있어요? ('can I buy a SIM card?'), which is understandable but sounds like you're checking your own ability or permission; the natural opener is the purpose statement 사러 왔어요. Also don't attach the object particle and say 유심을 사러 — in speech the 을 is usually dropped. Note 유심 (the chip) is different from 개통 (activating service); buying the chip and activating the line are two steps.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 유심 카드 (sim-card) as two English words.
Koreans say just 유심. Adding '카드' is redundant and sounds learner-ish. Use 유심 하나 주세요 or 유심 사러 왔어요.
Asking 유심 살 수 있어요? to open.
That literally checks your ability/permission to buy. To state your purpose on entering, say 유심 사러 왔어요; to order, 유심 하나 주세요.
Confusing 유심 with 개통.
유심 is the physical chip; 개통 is activating the phone line. Buying a 유심 doesn't automatically mean 개통 — you may still need to ask them to 개통해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 개통 (Sino-Korean 開通, 'opening through') means activating a phone line so it can actually make calls and use data — the moment your number goes live. The pattern is again -(으)러 왔어요 ('came in order to'), so 개통하러 왔어요 = 'I came to activate.' Say this in 존댓말 to staff. The crucial contrast is 개통 vs. 가입: 가입 ('signing up/joining', 加入) is enrolling in a carrier/plan as a subscriber, while 개통 is the technical act of turning the line on — when you start fresh you often do both, but if you ask only for 개통 with no plan chosen, staff will ask about 요금제 (the plan) and 약정 (contract) first. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 폰 켜러 왔어요 ('I came to turn the phone ON'), but 켜다 means powering the device on, not activating service — use 개통. Another is over-translating 'set up' as 셋업/설정, which sounds like configuring settings, not registering a line. Keep 개통 for the line going live. Foreigners should be ready with 외국인 등록증 (ARC) or 여권 since 개통 legally requires ID.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 폰 켜러 왔어요 to mean activate service.
켜다 is to power the device ON (the screen). Activating the line/number is 개통: say 개통하러 왔어요.
Using 셋업하러 / 설정하러 왔어요.
셋업/설정 sound like configuring phone settings, not registering a line. The right word for going live is 개통.
Confusing 개통 with 가입.
가입 is becoming a subscriber (joining a plan/carrier); 개통 is the line being switched on. Mention 요금제 if you also need to pick a plan, since 개통 alone doesn't choose one.

entries.nuance: 요금제 (요금 'fee/charge' + 제 'system', 料金制) is the monthly PLAN — the bundle of data, calls, and texts at a set price. 추천해 주세요 is 추천하다 ('recommend', 推薦) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'), the favor form that politely asks staff to choose for you. Default 존댓말. A precise contrast: 요금제 is the recurring plan, while 약정 is the CONTRACT term (how long you're locked in) and 기기값/단말기 is the phone's price — newcomers blur these, but staff treat them as three separate questions. Another near-synonym issue: don't say 플랜 추천해 주세요 using the English 'plan' — Koreans say 요금제; 플랜 sounds off in this context. The English-speaker pitfall is the favor-verb trap: saying bare 요금제 추천하세요 is an imperative ('you, recommend!') that sounds bossy, and 요금제 추천 주세요 is ungrammatical because you can't 'give' a recommendation — it must be 추천 + 해 + 주세요. To get a concrete answer, pair it with your usage: 데이터 많이 써요 ('I use lots of data') or 통화 많이 해요 ('I call a lot') so they can match 요금제 to you.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 플랜 추천해 주세요.
The English 'plan' (플랜) is unnatural here. The word for a phone plan is 요금제: 요금제 추천해 주세요.
Saying 요금제 추천하세요 to staff.
Bare 추천하세요 is a command ('recommend!') and sounds bossy. Use the favor form 추천해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Confusing 요금제 with 약정.
요금제 is the monthly plan (data/calls); 약정 is the contract length you commit to. They're separate — asking about a plan doesn't settle how long you're locked in.

structuredNuance.t: 요금제 is the monthly PLAN — the bundle of data, calls, and texts at a set price. 추천해 주세요 is 추천하다 ('recommend') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'), the favor form that politely asks staff to choose for you. Default 존댓말. To get a concrete answer, pair it with your usage: 데이터 많이 써요 ('I use lots of data') or 통화 많이 해요 ('I call a lot') so they can match 요금제 to you.

entries.nuance: 데이터 (loanword 'data') 무제한 (無制限, 'no limit') is the unlimited-data option, and 무제한으로 해 주세요 uses -(으)로 ('as/into') + 해 주세요 ('please make it') — 'please set it up AS unlimited.' A real-world contrast every newcomer needs: 완전 무제한 ('fully unlimited', no throttling) vs. plans that are 무제한 only up to a daily cap and then 속도 제한 (speed-throttled) — so 무제한 alone doesn't guarantee full speed; ask 완전 무제한이에요? Don't confuse 무제한 ('unlimited') with 추가 ('extra/add-on'); if you only want a top-up of data, that's 데이터 추가, a different request.

entries.nuance: 약정 (約定, 'agreement/commitment') is the CONTRACT term — the period (often 24개월) you promise to stay, usually in exchange for a phone discount. 약정 없이 ('without a contract') + 쓸 수 있어요? ('can I use it?') asks to go commitment-free. Default 존댓말. The exact word for the no-contract option is 무약정 (無約定), so 무약정으로 하고 싶어요 ('I want to go contract-free') is the cleanest way to request it. A critical contrast newcomers miss: 약정 (the commitment period) is NOT the same as 요금제 (the monthly plan) — you can change plans, but breaking an 약정 early triggers a 위약금 (early-termination penalty). The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 계약 없이 — 계약 ('contract') is the general legal word and sounds odd for a phone plan; the industry term is 약정 / 무약정. Another is asking 약정 안 해도 돼요? ('do I not have to commit?'), which works but the crisper phrasing is 약정 없이 쓸 수 있어요? or 무약정 돼요? Be aware: going 무약정 often means no device discount, so the phone may cost more upfront — that's why people ask 약정 없이 쓰면 더 비싸요?

Contracts usually subsidize the phone. 무약정 ('no contract') often means no device discount, so ask 약정 없이 쓰면 더 비싸요?

entries.nuance: 데이터 얼마예요? is 데이터 + 얼마 ('how much') + 예요, asking the size of a plan's data allowance. Note 얼마 normally asks PRICE, so here it's slightly ambiguous; the sharper, unambiguous version is 데이터 몇 기가예요? ('how many gigabytes?') using 기가 (GB), which staff immediately understand as the data amount. Default 존댓말. The contrast to nail: 데이터 몇 기가예요? asks the AMOUNT of data, while 얼마예요? on its own (no 데이터) asks the PRICE of the plan — say the full 데이터 얼마예요? or use 기가 to avoid being misheard as asking the cost. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 데이터 얼마나 많아요? ('how plentiful is the data?'), which sounds like commenting on quantity rather than asking the spec — Koreans ask 몇 기가예요?. Also useful: when the cap matters, ask what happens after — 다 쓰면 ('once it's all used') 속도 느려져요? (does it throttle) or 추가 요금 있어요? (is there an overage charge). Counting GB uses Sino-Korean numbers with 기가: 십 기가 (10GB), not 열 기가.

entries.nuance: Here 와이파이 ('Wi-Fi') colloquially stands for home internet/the router, and 설치하다 ('to install', 設置) + -고 싶어요 ('want to') states your wish to get it put in. Default 존댓말 with a call-center agent or shop. An important distinction: technically you're ordering 인터넷 (the broadband line), and the 와이파이 (the wireless signal from the 공유기/router) comes with it — Koreans loosely say 와이파이 설치 anyway, but the formal term staff use is 인터넷 설치. The native-feeling casual verb is 깔다 ('to lay down/install'): 와이파이 깔다 is very common in speech, while 설치하다 is the neutral/formal choice. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 와이파이 사고 싶어요 ('I want to BUY Wi-Fi') — you don't buy Wi-Fi, you have it installed (설치) or apply for service (신청), so use 설치하다 or 신청하다, not 사다. Another is confusing this home-internet 와이파이 with public hotspot Wi-Fi; for installation always anchor it with 집에 ('at home') or 인터넷. To actually book it, the next step is 설치 신청 ('apply for installation') and arranging a 기사님 (technician) visit.

와이파이 alone can mean a public hotspot. For home service anchor it: 집에 와이파이 설치하고 싶어요, or say 인터넷 설치.
