Both mean 'install'. 설치하다 is neutral/formal, 깔다 is casual spoken ('와이파이 깔다'). Same request, different register.

entries.nuance: 기사님 is the respectful term for a service/installation technician (기사 'engineer/driver' + 님 honorific) — you ALWAYS add 님 and use honorific verbs for them in Korea, so it's 기사님 오세요? ('does the technician come?' with subject-honorific 오시-), not plain 와요?. Default 존댓말. The honorific here is the load-bearing point: because the 기사님 is the one doing the action and you're speaking respectfully about them, you elevate the verb — 오세요/오시- not 와요. The contrast: 기사님 언제 오세요? asks WHEN the person arrives, while 설치 언제 돼요?/가능해요? asks when the installation itself is available — both useful, but the first schedules the human, the second the service. The English-speaker pitfall is the register-mismatch trap of saying 기사 언제 와요? — dropping 님 and using plain 와요 sounds curt/rude about a worker you should honor; keep 기사님 ... 오세요. Another 직역 trap is calling them '테크니션' or '엔지니어' — the everyday word is 기사님 (also used for taxi/delivery drivers). Practical note: you usually must be home for the visit, so confirm 집에 있어야 돼요? and whether they'll 연락 주세요 (call ahead).

Saying 기사 언제 와요? (no 님, plain verb).
It's rude to a service worker. Add the honorific: 기사님 언제 오세요? — 님 plus the subject-honorific 오시-.
Calling them 테크니션 / 엔지니어.
The natural Korean is 기사님. It covers installers, repair techs, and even drivers — use it, not the English loanwords.
Using 가다 instead of 오다 from your view.
From you (waiting at home), the technician 'comes' to you: 오세요. 가다 ('go') would be from the company's side, not yours.

entries.nuance: 기존 (旣存, 'existing/current') 번호 ('number') + 그대로 ('as-is, unchanged') + 쓸 수 있어요? ('can I use?') asks to keep your phone number when changing carriers or plans. 그대로 ('exactly as it is') is the key word that means 'no change.' Default 존댓말. The industry term for this is 번호 이동 ('number movement', i.e. porting/MNP) — so 번호 이동하고 싶어요 explicitly requests a port. The contrast to know: 번호 이동 is moving your EXISTING number to a NEW carrier (keep number, switch company), versus 기기 변경 ('device change', staying with the same carrier but new phone) and 신규 가입 ('new signup', brand-new number) — staff will ask which of the three you want, and confusing them changes everything. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 같은 번호 ('same number') — understandable, but the idiomatic 'keep it as-is' is 번호 그대로, and the formal action is 번호 이동. Another is asking 번호 유지할 수 있어요? — 유지 ('maintain') works but 그대로 쓸 수 있어요? is more natural in speech. Porting usually keeps your number live with no gap, but confirm there's no 공백 (downtime).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying just 같은 번호 쓸 수 있어요?
It's understandable, but the natural phrase is 번호 그대로 쓸 수 있어요?, and the formal action is 번호 이동 (porting).
Confusing 번호 이동 with 신규 가입.
번호 이동 keeps your existing number while switching carriers; 신규 가입 gives you a brand-new number. Specify which you want.
Mixing up 번호 이동 and 기기 변경.
번호 이동 = change carrier, keep number. 기기 변경 = same carrier, new phone. They are different processes — say the right one.

entries.nuance: 데이터 다 썼어요 is 데이터 + 다 ('all') + 썼어요 (past of 쓰다 'to use') — 'I used it all up.' This is the everyday way to say you're out of data, whether explaining to staff or a friend. Default 존댓말 with the carrier; 반말 데이터 다 썼어 with friends. A natural synonym is 데이터 다 떨어졌어요 (떨어지다 'to run out/be depleted'), which frames it as the data running out on its own rather than you using it — both are idiomatic. The contrast for the FIX: once out, you either 데이터 충전 ('top up/recharge', for prepaid) or 데이터 추가 ('add an extra data pack', often a paid add-on) — 충전 suggests refilling a prepaid balance, 추가 suggests buying more on top. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 데이터 끝났어요 ('the data finished/ended') — 끝나다 is for events ending (a movie, class), not for a resource being depleted; use 다 썼어요 or 다 떨어졌어요. Another is 데이터 없어요 ('there's no data'), which sounds like you never had any rather than having exhausted it. To get back online, follow with 충전 어떻게 해요? or 데이터 추가하고 싶어요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 데이터 끝났어요.
끝나다 is for events ending (a class, a show), not a resource being depleted. Say 데이터 다 썼어요 or 데이터 다 떨어졌어요.
Saying 데이터 없어요 when you mean you used it up.
없어요 ('there is none') sounds like you never had data. To say you exhausted it, use 다 썼어요.
Confusing 충전 and 추가.
충전 = top up / refill a (prepaid) balance; 추가 = buy an additional data pack on top. Use the one matching your plan type.

entries.nuance: 와이파이 ('Wi-Fi') 비밀번호 (祕密番號, 'secret number' = password) 뭐예요? ('what is it?') is the go-to at any café, guesthouse, or friend's place. Crucially, Koreans very commonly shorten 비밀번호 to 비번 in casual speech — 와이파이 비번 뭐예요? is extremely natural and not rude, just informal. Default 존댓말 (뭐예요); 반말 is 뭐야. The contrast: 비밀번호 ('password') is what you type to connect, while 와이파이 이름 / 와이파이 이름이 뭐예요? asks the network's NAME (SSID) — you may need both. Also 비밀번호 (the password) is different from 본인 인증 번호 or 인증 번호 (a one-time verification code) — don't mix them. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 패스워드 — while understood, the native word is 비밀번호/비번; 패스워드 sounds foreign here. Another is asking 와이파이 코드 ('Wi-Fi code'), which isn't idiomatic; it's 비밀번호. A practical note: in cafés the password is often printed on your 영수증 (receipt) or posted on the wall, so a natural follow-up is 영수증에 있어요? ('is it on the receipt?'). Korean passwords are frequently just 8 digits, often the shop's phone number.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 패스워드 or 와이파이 코드.
The native word is 비밀번호 (or casual 비번). 패스워드 sounds foreign and 코드 isn't used for Wi-Fi: 와이파이 비밀번호 뭐예요?
Confusing 비밀번호 with 인증 번호.
비밀번호 is the Wi-Fi password; 인증 번호 is a one-time verification code (for signups). They're different — don't ask for the wrong one.
Mixing up the network name and password.
와이파이 이름 (SSID) is which network to join; 비밀번호 is what unlocks it. If several networks show, ask both: 이름이 뭐예요? and 비밀번호 뭐예요?

entries.nuance: 인터넷이 안 돼요 is 인터넷 + 이 (subject particle) + 안 돼요 (negative of 되다 'to work/function') — 'the internet doesn't work.' 되다 is THE verb for things functioning, so 안 돼요 = 'not working,' the standard way to report any service failure. Default 존댓말 to support. The contrast among complaints: 안 돼요 (completely down/won't connect) vs. 끊겨요 (끊기다, 'keeps cutting out' — intermittent) vs. 느려요 ('slow but working') — picking the right one tells the technician what's wrong. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle trap: many say 인터넷을 안 돼요 with the object 을, but 되다 ('to work') is intransitive and takes the SUBJECT particle 이/가 — it must be 인터넷이 안 돼요. Another 직역 trap is 인터넷이 일 안 해요 ('the internet doesn't do work', personifying it) — wrong; machines/services 'don't work' as 안 돼요, not 일 안 해요. Also avoid 인터넷이 깨졌어요 ('the internet is broken/shattered') — 깨지다 is for physical breakage. Useful troubleshooting vocab: 공유기 (router), 모뎀 (modem), 다시 켜다/재부팅 (reboot). When you can't connect at all, 안 돼요; when it drops in and out, 끊겨요.

안 돼요 means fully down. If it cuts in and out, say 끊겨요 (끊기다); if just slow, 느려요. The right word guides the fix.

entries.nuance: 추가 (追加, 'addition') 요금 (料金, 'fee/charge') = an extra/added charge, and 있어요? ('is there?') checks whether anything beyond the headline price applies. This is essential armor against surprise costs in phone/internet contracts. Default 존댓말. Common hidden items to name specifically: 설치비 (installation fee), 부가세 (VAT, usually added unless 포함 'included'), 위약금 (early-termination penalty), and 가입비 (signup fee). The contrast: 추가 요금 있어요? asks broadly 'any extra?', while 다 포함이에요? / 포함된 가격이에요? ('is it all included?') approaches from the other side, confirming the quoted price is final — asking both ways protects you. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 숨은 요금 ('hidden fee', a literal calque) — understandable but not how Koreans phrase it; the natural questions are 추가 요금 있어요? or 다른 비용 있어요? ('are there other costs?'). Another is confusing 요금 ('a recurring fee/charge') with 가격 ('price of an item') — for monthly service it's 요금, for a phone's sticker price it's 가격/기기값. When the answer is yes, follow up with 얼마예요? ('how much?').

요금 is a recurring service charge/fee; 가격 is an item's price. For monthly plans and installs, use 요금/비; for the phone's sticker, 기기값.
Assuming the quoted price includes VAT.
부가세 (VAT) is often added on top. Confirm with 부가세 포함이에요? ('is VAT included?') or ask 추가 요금 있어요?

entries.nuance: 약정 (約定, 'commitment') 기간 (期間, 'period') + 얼마나 ('how much') + 남았어요? (past of 남다 'to remain') = 'how much of the contract period is left?' This matters because switching carriers, upgrading, or canceling early all hinge on your remaining 약정. Default 존댓말. The verb 남다 ('to be left over') is intransitive and pairs with 이/가, so it's 기간이 남았어요, not 기간을. The contrast: 얼마나 남았어요? asks the remaining DURATION, while 언제까지예요? / 언제 끝나요? asks the END DATE — both useful, one gives a span, the other a date. (when will it end) — watch the tense. If the term is nearly up, people often wait it out to avoid the 위약금.

entries.nuance: 해지 (解止, 'termination/cancellation') is the precise word for canceling a contract or subscription — phone line, internet, anything ongoing. 해지하고 싶은데요 uses -고 싶다 ('want to') + the soft ender -는데요, which gently opens the topic and invites the agent to respond, the polite way to start a cancellation. Default 존댓말. The contrast newcomers must get right: 해지 (cancel an ongoing contract/service) vs. 환불 (還拂, refund of money paid) vs. 취소 (取消, cancel a one-off order/reservation before it's fulfilled) — you 해지 a phone plan, you 환불 a product, you 취소 a booking; using 취소 for your phone contract sounds wrong. Also 해지 (you ending it) differs from 정지 (一時停止, temporarily suspending the line, e.g. while traveling) — if you might come back, ask about 일시 정지 instead. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 끝내고 싶어요 ('I want to end it') or 취소하고 싶어요 — 끝내다 is vague and 취소 is for orders/reservations; the contract word is 해지. Critically, 해지 before your 약정 ends triggers a 위약금 (penalty), so the essential follow-up is 위약금 얼마예요? Some carriers also require you to 해지 in person or verify identity, so be ready.

끝내다 ('to finish') is vague for a contract. Use the specific term 해지하다 for canceling a phone/internet plan.
Forgetting 해지 may cost a 위약금.
Canceling before the 약정 ends usually incurs a 위약금 (penalty). Always ask 해지하면 위약금 얼마예요? If you'll return, consider 일시 정지 (suspend) instead.

structuredNuance.t: 해지 is the precise word for canceling a contract or subscription — phone line, internet, anything ongoing. 해지하고 싶은데요 uses -고 싶다 ('want to') + the soft ender -는데요, which gently opens the topic and invites the agent to respond, the polite way to start a cancellation. Default 존댓말. Critically, 해지 before your 약정 ends triggers a 위약금 (penalty), so the essential follow-up is 위약금 얼마예요? Some carriers also require you to 해지 in person or verify identity, so be ready.

The contrast newcomers must get right: 해지 (cancel an ongoing contract/service) vs. 환불 (refund of money paid) vs. 취소 (cancel a one-off order/reservation before it's fulfilled) — you 해지 a phone plan, you 환불 a product, you 취소 a booking; using 취소 for your phone contract sounds wrong. Also 해지 (you ending it) differs from 정지 (temporarily suspending the line, e.g. while traveling) — if you might come back, ask about 일시 정지 instead.
해지 is 解止, 'termination/cancellation'; 환불 is 還拂; 취소 is 取消; 정지 is 一時停止 (suspension).
The 직역 trap of saying 끝내고 싶어요 ('I want to end it') or 취소하고 싶어요 — 끝내다 is vague and 취소 is for orders/reservations; the contract word is 해지.

entries.nuance: 한 달에 얼마예요? is 한 달 ('one month') + 에 (the particle 'per/in') + 얼마예요? ('how much is it?') — the core question for the monthly cost of any plan. The particle 에 here means 'per' (한 달에 = 'per month'), which is the natural way Koreans express a recurring rate. Default 존댓말. A very common, slightly more vivid variant is 한 달에 얼마 나와요? using 나오다 ('to come out') — Koreans love 나오다 for bills/amounts that 'come out' on the statement, so 얼마 나와요? asks the real billed figure including taxes and add-ons, whereas 얼마예요? asks the listed price. The contrast: 한 달에 얼마예요? targets the RECURRING monthly charge, while a bare 얼마예요? could be misread as the one-time phone price (기기값) — anchor it with 한 달에 to be clear you mean per month. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle trap of saying 한 달 얼마예요? dropping 에 — it's understood but the natural 'per month' needs 에: 한 달에. Another 직역 trap is 매달 얼마 비용이에요? ('every month how much cost is it?'), which is clunky; just say 한 달에 얼마예요? Crucially, ask whether the figure includes 기기값 (the phone installment) and 부가세 (VAT), since the plan price and the total bill often differ.

That's clunky and unidiomatic. Koreans ask 한 달에 얼마예요? or 한 달에 얼마 나와요? (the amount that 'comes out' on the bill).

entries.nuance: 가입 (加入, 'joining/enrollment') 할 때 ('when [you] sign up') + 뭐 ('what') + 필요해요? ('is needed?') asks what to bring to become a subscriber — the practical prep question before any phone/internet signup. Default 존댓말. 가입 is specifically becoming a member/subscriber (vs. 개통, turning the line on, and 신청, applying for a service) — here you're asking about the enrollment paperwork. The likely answer for a newcomer involves 신분증 (ID): a Korean uses 신분증/민증 (ID card), but a foreigner needs 외국인 등록증 (ARC) or 여권 (passport), plus often a 통장 (bankbook) or 카드 for 자동이체 (auto-pay). The contrast: 뭐 필요해요? asks broadly 'what's needed', while 필요한 서류 있어요? narrows it to DOCUMENTS (서류) specifically — use the second when you only care about paperwork. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap of saying 사인업할 때 ('when sign-up') with the English word — use the native 가입; 사인업 isn't Korean. Another is asking 뭐 가져와요? ('what do I bring?') which is okay but 뭐 필요해요? ('what's needed?') is smoother and more standard. Note 필요하다 ('to be necessary') is an adjective taking 이/가 on its subject (서류가 필요해요), so don't force an object 을 — and the question form just fronts 뭐.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 사인업할 때 with the English 'sign up'.
사인업 isn't Korean. Use 가입 (enroll/join): 가입할 때 뭐 필요해요?
Confusing 가입 with 개통.
가입 is becoming a subscriber (the paperwork); 개통 is the line being switched on. Asking what's needed to 가입 is about ID and documents.
Using object 을 with 필요하다: 서류를 필요해요.
필요하다 ('to be needed') is an adjective; its subject takes 이/가, not 을. Correct: 서류가 필요해요 / 뭐가 필요해요?

entries.shortExplanation: 택배 보내려고요 is a practical expression meaning "I'd like to send a parcel".
entries.explanation: "I'd like to send a parcel" — that is 택배 보내려고요 (taekbae bonaeryeogoyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 택배 보내려고요 ("I'd like to send a parcel"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.en: I'd like to send a parcel.

examples.note: 택배로 ('by parcel') marks the method, then ask the price

entries.nuance: 택배 보내려고요 is 택배 ('courier parcel', Sino-Korean 宅配, lit. 'home-delivery') + 보내다 ('to send') in the -려고요 form, which states YOUR intention: 'I intend to send a parcel.' That -려고(요) ending is the natural, soft way to announce why you've walked up to a counter — it signals a plan and gently invites the staff to help, rather than barking an order. 택배 specifically means a courier package delivered to a door (by 우체국택배, CJ대한통운, etc.), as opposed to 우편/편지 (ordinary mail/letters) — so use 택배 for boxes and goods, not for a simple letter. The near-synonym verb 부치다 ('to post/send off') is interchangeable here (택배 부치려고요) and sounds a touch more classic-post-office; 보내다 is the everyday default. The English-speaker pitfall is over-translating 'I want to send' as 보내고 싶어요 ('I desire to send'), which sounds like confessing a wish rather than doing a transaction; Koreans announce the action with -려고요. Another trap is saying 택배 하려고요 ('I want to do parcel') — 하다 doesn't fit; the verb is 보내다 or 부치다. Default to 보내려고요 with staff; with a friend drop to 보내려고.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 택배 보내고 싶어요 to the counter staff.
That means 'I want/desire to send a parcel' and sounds like stating an emotion. For a counter transaction, announce your intention: 택배 보내려고요.
Saying 택배 하려고요.
택배 is a noun; you don't 'do' it with 하다. The verb is 보내다 or 부치다: 택배 보내려고요 / 택배 부치려고요.
Using 택배 for a plain letter.
택배 is a courier parcel (a box/goods to the door). A letter goes by 우편/편지 — say 편지 보내려고요 or 우편으로 보내려고요 for that.

택배 is Sino-Korean 宅配, literally 'home-delivery'.

entries.nuance: 이거 등기로 보내 주세요 is 이거 ('this') + 등기 ('registered mail', Sino-Korean 登記, lit. 'registration') + -로 ('by/via', the method particle) + 보내 주세요 ('please send for me'). 등기(우편) is mail that is logged, tracked, and requires the recipient's signature on delivery — you use it for contracts, official documents, anything you must prove arrived. Don't confuse 등기 (registered MAIL) with 등기부등본 (a property-registration certificate) — same 등기 root, totally different errand. The English-speaker pitfall is calling it 'certified mail' and trying to coin 인증우편, which isn't the term; the real word is 등기. Also, learners often forget the favor verb and say 등기로 보내요, which describes rather than requests — keep 보내 주세요 to actually ask the clerk to do it. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 등기로 보내 줘.

entries.nuance: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요 is 송장 ('waybill/invoice slip', Sino-Korean 送狀, the shipping label on a parcel) + 번호 ('number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'). The 송장 is the slip stuck on the box; its 송장 번호 (also called 운송장 번호 or 택배 번호) is what you punch into a tracking site to follow the parcel. The verb you pair with it is 조회하다 ('to look up/track'), and on screen Koreans say the info 뜨다/뜨다 ('comes up'). A key distinction: 송장 ('shipping waybill') is NOT 영수증 ('the receipt') — the 송장 number tracks the parcel, the 영수증 proves you paid; asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong slip. Note 송장 also means a commercial 'invoice' in trade contexts, but at a parcel counter it's the shipping label. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'tracking number' literally as 추적 번호 — understandable, and 추적 ('tracking') exists, but the everyday term Koreans actually use is 송장 번호 / 운송장 번호. Another slip is using 가르치다 ('to teach') instead of 알려 주다 ('to inform'): 송장 번호 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson; 알려 주세요 is 'let me know.' Default 존댓말; with a friend, 알려 줘.

송장 is the shipping waybill used to track the parcel; 영수증 is the payment receipt. Ask for 송장 번호 to track, 영수증 to prove you paid.

가르치다 means 'to teach (a skill)'. To ask someone to tell you a number, use 알려 주다: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요.

entries.nuance: 착불로 보내 주세요 is 착불 ('payment on arrival', Sino-Korean 着拂, lit. 'pay-on-arrival') + -로 ('by', method particle) + 보내 주세요 ('please send'). 착불 means the RECIPIENT pays the shipping fee when the parcel is handed to them — extremely common in Korea for online resale (중고거래), returns, and favors. Its exact opposite is 선불 ('prepay', 先拂), where the SENDER pays at the counter now. The clerk will often ask 선불이에요, 착불이에요?, and this is your answer — so getting the pair straight is essential: 착불 = receiver pays later, 선불 = sender pays now. The method particle -로 is required (착불로); 착불을 would wrongly make it the object. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 착불 to 'C.O.D.' and assuming it means the receiver pays for the GOODS — no, in Korean parcels 착불 almost always refers only to the SHIPPING FEE, not the product price. Another trap is courteously deciding 착불 for someone without telling them — socially you should confirm the recipient agreed, since they'll be charged at their door. Don't confuse 착불 with 반품 ('return of goods'); they often co-occur (returns are frequently sent 착불) but mean different things. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 착불로 보내 줘.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 착불 and 선불.
착불 = the recipient pays on delivery; 선불 = the sender pays now at the counter. If YOU want to pay up front, say 선불로 보내 주세요, not 착불로.
Thinking 착불 means the receiver pays for the product.
In parcels, 착불 refers to the SHIPPING FEE, not the item's price. The goods are settled separately; 착불 only decides who pays delivery.
Dropping -로: 착불 보내 주세요 / 착불을 보내 주세요.
착불 is a method, so it takes -로: 착불로 보내 주세요. 착불을 wrongly treats 'C.O.D.' as the thing being sent.

Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 ("It's fragile, so please handle it carefully"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

entries.nuance: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 is 깨지는 거 (깨지다 'to break/shatter' + 거 'thing' = 'a breakable thing') + -라서 ('because it is') + 조심히 ('carefully') + 다뤄 주세요 (다루다 'to handle' + 주세요 = 'please handle for me'). It warns staff or a mover that the contents are fragile. The verb pairing matters: 깨지다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it breaks/shatters on its own'), which is why you describe the object as 깨지는 거 — learners wrongly reach for 깨다 ('to break something deliberately'), but you're not smashing it, so 깨지다 is correct. The post-office set term is 파손 주의 ('caution: breakage', the printed Fragile label), so a very natural request is 파손 주의로 보내 주세요 or asking for the 파손 주의 스티커. Contrast 조심히 다뤄 주세요 ('handle carefully', a general plea) with 파손 주의로 해 주세요 (asking for the official fragile-handling/label) — the second is the concrete service. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'be careful' → 조심하세요, which tells the PERSON to be careful (almost like a warning to watch themselves) rather than asking them to handle the BOX gently; 조심히 다뤄 주세요 keeps the focus on the parcel. Also avoid 부서지다 confusion: 부서지다 is for things crumbling/falling apart (furniture), while glass and ceramics 깨지다. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 조심히 다뤄 줘.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 깨다 instead of 깨지다.
깨다 means 'to break something on purpose'; the contents break by themselves, so use intransitive 깨지다: 깨지는 거라서…. 깨는 거 would imply you smash it.
Saying just 조심하세요 to mean 'handle it carefully'.
조심하세요 tells the person 'be careful (for yourself)'. To ask them to handle the parcel gently, say 조심히 다뤄 주세요 or 파손 주의로 보내 주세요.
Mixing up 깨지다 and 부서지다.
깨지다 is for glass/ceramics shattering; 부서지다 is for things crumbling apart (like furniture). For dishes or bottles, 깨지는 거예요 is the right word.

examples.ko: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요?

examples.en: Can I buy a box?

entries.nuance: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? is 박스 (loanword 'box') + 하나 ('one') + 살 수 있어요? (살다→사다 'to buy' + -ㄹ 수 있다 'can/be able' = 'can I buy?'). Post offices and convenience stores sell 우체국 택배 박스 in numbered sizes (1호, 2호, 3호…), so this is a practical first step when you show up with loose items. The natural shop alternative is 박스 파나요? ('do you sell boxes?') or 박스 있어요? ('do you have boxes?') — Koreans very often ask availability with 있어요/파나요 rather than the literal 'can I buy.' A subtle distinction: 박스 (box) is the loanword everyone uses for a shipping carton, while 상자 is the native word — both are fine, but 박스 is more colloquial for parcels. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'can I buy' becoming an ability question with the wrong frame, e.g. 제가 박스를 살 수 있나요? — grammatical but a bit heavy; the light, natural ask is 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? or simply 박스 있어요?. Another trap: asking for 종이 ('paper') when you mean a 'cardboard box' — say 박스 or 종이 박스. Sizes are counted with 호 (1호, 2호); the bigger the number, the bigger the box. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 박스 하나 살 수 있어?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 종이 있어요? when you want a box.
종이 is 'paper'. A shipping box is 박스 (or 상자/종이 박스). Say 박스 있어요? or 박스 하나 살 수 있어요?
Over-heavy 제가 박스를 구매할 수 있습니까?
구매하다 ('to purchase') is stiff/formal for a counter. The natural everyday ask is 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? or 박스 있어요?
Assuming there's one box size.
Post-office boxes come in numbered sizes (1호, 2호…); bigger number = bigger box. Ask 제일 작은 거 / 제일 큰 거 to specify which size.

entries.english: Do I write the recipient's address here?
entries.shortExplanation: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Do I write the recipient's address here?".
entries.explanation: "Do I write the recipient's address here?" — that is 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? (banneun saram jusoneun yeogi jeogeumyeon dwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? ("Do I write the recipient's address here?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 받는 사람 주소는 여기 적으면 돼요? is 받는 사람 (받다 'to receive' + -는 + 사람 'person' = 'the receiving person/recipient') + 주소 ('address') + 는 (topic) + 여기 ('here') + 적으면 (적다 'to write down' + -(으)면 'if') + 돼요? (되다 'to be okay/acceptable' = 'is it okay if…?'). The frame -(으)면 돼요? ('is it okay if I…?') is the polite way to confirm a procedure you're about to do — perfect for checking where to write on a parcel slip. The two parties on every Korean parcel form are 받는 사람 ('recipient', the one who receives) and 보내는 사람 ('sender', the one who sends); these participial labels (받는/보내는, 'one who receives/sends') are exactly what's printed on the slip, so memorize the pair. The verb 적다 ('to write down/note') is the right one for filling in a form — distinct from 쓰다, which also means 'to write' but is broader (and notoriously also 'to use' and 'to be bitter'); both 적다 and 쓰다 work for forms, but 적다 specifically connotes jotting into a field. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 confusion of 'receiver/sender' — learners invent 수신자/발신자 (which are correct but formal/技术적, used for mail headers and telecoms), when the everyday parcel words are 받는 사람/보내는 사람. Another trap is 돼요? vs 되요? — the correct spelling is 돼요 (되 + 어요 → 돼요), a constant native error too. Also note 적다 the verb ('write') is a homograph of 적다 the adjective ('to be few') — context disambiguates. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 여기 적으면 돼?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 수신자/발신자 at the parcel counter.
수신자/발신자 ('addressee/sender') are formal telecom/mail-header terms. On a parcel slip the everyday words are 받는 사람 (recipient) and 보내는 사람 (sender).
Writing 되요 instead of 돼요.
되 + 어요 contracts to 돼요. 되요 is a spelling error. The question 'is it okay if I write here?' is 여기 적으면 돼요?
Reaching only for 쓰다 to mean 'fill in'.
쓰다 works but is broad (also 'use', 'bitter'). For noting something into a form field, 적다 is the precise verb: 주소 적으면 돼요?

structuredNuance.t: 받는 사람 ('the receiving person/recipient') + 주소 ('address') + 는 (topic) + 여기 ('here') + 적으면 (적다 'to write down' + -(으)면 'if') + 돼요? (되다 'to be okay' = 'is it okay if…?'). The frame -(으)면 돼요? ('is it okay if I…?') is the polite way to confirm a procedure you're about to do — perfect for checking where to write on a parcel slip. The two parties on every Korean parcel form are 받는 사람 ('recipient') and 보내는 사람 ('sender'); these participial labels (받는/보내는) are exactly what's printed on the slip, so memorize the pair. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 여기 적으면 돼?.

The verb 적다 ('to write down/note') is the right one for filling in a form — distinct from 쓰다, which also means 'to write' but is broader (and notoriously also 'to use' and 'to be bitter'); both 적다 and 쓰다 work for forms, but 적다 specifically connotes jotting into a field. Also note 적다 the verb ('write') is a homograph of 적다 the adjective ('to be few') — context disambiguates.

The 직역 confusion of 'receiver/sender' — learners invent 수신자/발신자 (which are correct but formal, used for mail headers and telecoms), when the everyday parcel words are 받는 사람/보내는 사람. Another trap is 돼요? vs 되요? — the correct spelling is 돼요 (되 + 어요 → 돼요), a constant native error too.

entries.nuance: 언제쯤 도착해요? is 언제 ('when') + -쯤 ('approximately/around') + 도착하다 ('to arrive', Sino-Korean 到着) in polite form. The -쯤 is the polite, realistic softener — it acknowledges you want an estimate, not a guarantee, which is exactly how you ask staff about delivery timing without sounding demanding. The key verb-direction point: 도착하다 ('to arrive') describes the PARCEL reaching its destination, so the subject is the package, not you — don't say 제가 도착해요 (that means YOU arrive). A natural alternative framing is duration: 며칠 걸려요? ('how many days does it take?'), using 걸리다 ('to take time'). Contrast 언제쯤 도착해요? (asks for an arrival date/time) with 며칠 걸려요? (asks for length of time) — pick by whether you want a calendar point or a count of days. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'when does it come?' → 언제 와요?, which is fine for something coming TO YOU but odd when you've just SENT something away; for outbound parcels, 도착하다 ('arrive at the destination') is cleaner. Another slip is forgetting -쯤 and asking the blunt 언제 도착해요?, which demands an exact time staff often can't promise. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 언제쯤 도착해?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제가 도착해요 to mean 'when will it arrive'.
도착하다's subject is the parcel, not you. 제가 도착해요 means 'I arrive'. For the package, say (택배가) 언제쯤 도착해요?
Dropping -쯤 and demanding 언제 도착해요?
Without -쯤 it asks for an exact time, which staff can't always promise. 언제쯤 도착해요? politely signals you want an estimate.
Using 걸리다 for a date: 언제 걸려요?
걸리다 measures duration, so it pairs with 며칠/얼마나: 며칠 걸려요? For a date use 도착하다: 언제쯤 도착해요?

entries.nuance: 택배 받으러 왔어요 is 택배 ('parcel') + 받으러 (받다 'to receive' + -(으)러 'in order to') + 왔어요 ('I came'). The -(으)러 왔어요 frame literally means 'I came in order to receive,' the standard way to state your PURPOSE on arriving somewhere. There are three near-synonyms with different registers: 받다 ('to receive', everyday and warm), 찾다 ('to claim/retrieve', also very common for picking up something held for you), and 수령하다 ('to take receipt', Sino-Korean 受領, formal/official — what signs and staff use). For a friendly pickup, 받으러/찾으러 왔어요 is natural; 수령하러 왔어요 sounds官方/bureaucratic, good for matching official phrasing. The crucial grammar point is the connective -(으)러 (purpose, 'in order to'), which English speakers confuse with -(으)려고 ('intending to'): -(으)러 must attach to a movement verb like 오다/가다, so 받으러 왔어요 is right, but 받으려고 왔어요 (also possible) shifts nuance toward 'I came because I intend to receive.' The pitfall is the 직역 'I came for my parcel' → 택배를 위해 왔어요 (위해 = 'for the sake of'), which sounds abstract; use the purpose-of-motion -(으)러. Also don't confuse 받다 ('receive') with 받히다/받치다 (unrelated). Default 존댓말; with a friend, 택배 받으러 왔어.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 택배를 위해 왔어요.
위해 ('for the sake of') is abstract and unnatural for an errand. Use purpose-of-motion -(으)러: 택배 받으러 왔어요 / 찾으러 왔어요.
Attaching -(으)러 to a non-motion verb.
-(으)러 needs 오다/가다. 받으러 왔어요 (came to receive) is correct; you can't say 받으러 했어요. With 하다, use a different frame.
Using 수령하러 왔어요 with a casual clerk.
수령 is formal/bureaucratic. For an ordinary pickup, 받으러 왔어요 or 찾으러 왔어요 sounds friendlier and more natural.

entries.nuance: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요 is 이거 ('this') + 반송하다 ('to return/send back', Sino-Korean 返送) + -고 싶다 ('want to') + -은데요 (soft, conversation-opening ender). 반송 specifically means sending a parcel BACK to its origin/sender — because of a wrong address, a refused delivery, or a return. The trailing -은데요 is the politeness engine: it raises your request gently and invites the clerk to guide you, rather than issuing a flat command. Distinguish 반송 ('return to SENDER', the mail going back where it came) from 반품 ('product return/refund', the consumer act of returning goods to a shop for a refund) — they overlap (a 반품 is often shipped as a 반송) but aren't synonyms: 반품 is about the transaction/refund, 반송 is about the physical redirection back. Another related term is 수취 거부 ('refusal of receipt'), where you decline the parcel at your door and it returns automatically — useful when you never want to accept it. The English-speaker pitfall is using 돌려주다 ('to give back to a person') for mailing something back — 돌려주다 fits handing an item back face-to-face, not posting a parcel to its origin; for that, 반송하다 is the term. Also note -고 싶은데요 ('I'd like to, so…') is softer and more natural to staff than the bare 반송할래요. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 반송하고 싶어.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 반송 with 반품.
반송 = sending a parcel back to its sender/origin; 반품 = returning purchased goods for a refund. For a refund request to a shop, you'd talk about 반품; to physically send the box back, 반송.
Using 돌려주다 to mean 'return by mail'.
돌려주다 is handing something back to a person directly. To post a parcel back to where it came from, use 반송하다: 이거 반송하고 싶은데요.
Saying flat 반송할래요 to staff.
-(으)ㄹ래요 can sound a bit willful. Softer and more natural is 반송하고 싶은데요 or 반송 처리 좀 해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 내용물이 뭐예요? — 옷이에요 pairs the clerk's question 내용물 ('contents', Sino-Korean 內容物) + 이 (subject) + 뭐예요? ('what is it?') with your answer 옷 ('clothes') + 이에요 ('it is'). Staff routinely ask what's inside before accepting a parcel — for safety and to flag prohibited or fragile items — so you'll usually be ANSWERING this. The subject particle 이 attaches because 내용물 ends in a consonant (내용물이); the copula then agrees with your answer's final sound: a consonant-final noun takes 이에요 (옷이에요, 책이에요, 가방이에요, 신발이에요), while a vowel-final noun takes 예요 (우유예요 'it's milk', 커피예요 'it's coffee'). That 이에요/예요 split is the classic learner trap. A natural casual version of the question is 안에 뭐 들어 있어요? ('what's inside?'), using 들어 있다 ('to be contained'). The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'what is it?' → 이게 뭐예요?, which asks about the OBJECT itself rather than its CONTENTS — fine pointing at a thing, but when staff mean 'what's IN the box,' the precise word is 내용물. commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 이에요 and 예요 in the answer.
Consonant-final nouns take 이에요 (옷이에요, 책이에요); vowel-final nouns take 예요 (우유예요, 커피예요). Match the noun's last sound — 신발 ends in ㄹ, so it's 신발이에요, not 신발예요.

내용물 means 'the contents (inside)'. The question asks what's IN the parcel, so answer with the item (옷이에요), not 'it's a box'.

At a counter a plain 옷이에요 is natural. The bookish 의류입니다 ('it is apparel') sounds like a customs form, not speech.

entries.nuance: 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요 is 제일 ('most', the everyday superlative) + 싼 (싸다 'to be cheap', adnominal) + 걸로 (것 'thing' + -로 'with/by' = 'with the ___ one') + 보내 주세요 ('please send'). The whole frame '제일 ___ㄴ 걸로 (해/보내) 주세요' is the all-purpose way to pick the most-X option at any counter, swapping the adjective: 싼 (cheap), 빠른 (fast), 안전한 (safe). The 걸로 (것+로) is doing the work of 'go with / choose' an option — a structure English speakers underuse, defaulting instead to the heavier 제일 싼 방법으로. The key word-choice point: 싸다 means 'cheap (low price)' and is correct here, whereas 저렴하다 is its softer, more polite twin ('inexpensive/economical'), so 제일 저렴한 걸로 sounds a touch more refined; avoid 값이 낮다 (too literal). The English-speaker pitfall is confusing 싸다 ('to be cheap') with 비싸다 ('to be expensive') — they differ by one syllable, and asking for 제일 비싼 걸로 ('the most expensive') is the opposite of your intent. Another is the 직역 'the cheapest one' → 가장 값싼 것, grammatical but stiff; spoken Korean prefers 제일 싼 걸로. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 제일 싼 걸로 보내 줘.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 싸다 and 비싸다.
싸다 = cheap, 비싸다 = expensive. They sound similar but are opposites; 제일 싼 걸로 = the cheapest, 제일 비싼 걸로 = the most expensive.

Understandable but heavy. The natural counter phrase uses 걸로 (것+로): 제일 싼 걸로 (보내) 주세요 = 'go with the cheapest one'.
Over-literal 가장 값싼 것을 보내 주세요.
값싸다 / 가장 ... 것을 is bookish. In speech use 제일 싼 걸로 보내 주세요, or politely 제일 저렴한 걸로.

entries.nuance: 국제 배송도 돼요? is 국제 ('international', Sino-Korean 國際) + 배송 ('delivery/shipping', 配送) + 도 ('also/too') + 돼요? (되다 'to be possible' → 'is it possible?'). 되다 frames it as a feasibility/availability question — 'is international shipping (also) doable here?' — which is exactly how you check a service exists before committing. The particle 도 ('too') subtly implies 'on top of domestic,' a natural way to ask whether they ALSO handle overseas. For sending abroad, Koreans name concrete services: EMS (익스프레스 국제특송, fast & trackable), 국제우편/국제소포 (regular international post), and 항공/선편 ('air/sea' shipping). Distinguish 배송 ('the delivery/shipping process', what carriers do) from 배달 ('delivery to a door', often food/local) — for cross-border parcels the word is 배송 or 국제우편, not 배달. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'can you ship internationally' becoming an ability question about the staff (당신이 보낼 수 있어요?), which sounds like doubting their competence; the idiomatic frame is the impersonal 국제 배송 돼요? ('is it possible?'). Another slip is confusing 국제 ('international') with 국내 ('domestic', 國內) — one syllable apart, opposite meanings; 국내 배송 is local shipping. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 국제 배송도 돼?.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

국제 배송 = overseas shipping; 국내 배송 = domestic. They differ by one syllable but mean opposite directions.
Using 배달 for cross-border shipping.
배달 is door delivery (often food/local). For sending a parcel abroad, the word is 배송 / 국제우편: 국제 배송도 돼요?
Framing it as 당신이 보낼 수 있어요?
That questions the staff's ability and sounds rude. Use the impersonal feasibility frame: 국제 배송 돼요? / 해외로 보낼 수 있어요?

entries.nuance: 무게 좀 달아 주세요 is 무게 ('weight') + 좀 (softener) + 달아 주세요 (달다 'to weigh/measure on a scale' + 주세요 = 'please weigh for me'). The English-speaker pitfall is the homophone-ish confusion of 달다: it also means 'to be sweet' (맛이 달다) and 'to hang/attach' (간판을 달다), so context carries the 'weigh' sense; pair it with 무게 to be unambiguous. entries.nuance: 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해요? is 오늘 ('today') + 보내면 (보내다 + -(으)면 'if/when') + 모레 ('the day after tomorrow') + 도착해요? ('does it arrive?'). The conditional -(으)면 ('if I send…') is the engine: it sets up a hypothetical send-day and asks the resulting arrival, the precise way to confirm a deadline. Korea has a tidy set of day words you MUST keep straight: 어제 (yesterday), 오늘 (today), 내일 (tomorrow), 모레 (the day after tomorrow), 글피 (two days after tomorrow) — learners constantly mix 모레 with 내일. The verb 도착하다's subject is the parcel (it arrives), not you. Contrast asking from the SEND side (보내면 ... 도착해요?, 'if I send, does it arrive?') vs the RECEIVE side (받을 수 있어요?, 'can they receive it?') — same timeline, different viewpoint; choose based on whether you're tracking your action or the recipient's. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'if' as 만약/만일 alone or a clunky 만약에 내가 보내다면 — Korean folds 'if' into the verb with -(으)면 (보내면), no separate word needed. Another slip is rendering 'the day after tomorrow' as 다음다음 날, when the single word 모레 is what people say. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 오늘 보내면 모레 도착해?.

내일 = tomorrow; 모레 = the day after tomorrow. They're different days; confirm which you mean: 모레 도착해요? vs 내일 도착해요?

Korean expresses 'if' with the verb ending -(으)면: 오늘 보내면…. You don't need 만약/만일, and 보내다면 is the wrong form (use 보내면).
Saying 다음다음 날 for 'day after tomorrow'.
The natural single word is 모레. 다음다음 날 is clunky; for two days after tomorrow there's even 글피.

entries.nuance: 주소가 바뀌었는데 변경할 수 있어요? is 주소 ('address', Sino-Korean 住所) + 가 (subject) + 바뀌었는데 (바뀌다 'to change/be changed' + -었- past + -는데 soft connective) + 변경하다 ('to change/modify', 變更) + -ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can I?'). The -는데 links your situation ('the address has changed, so…') to the request, softening it. A crucial verb-pair distinction: 바뀌다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it changed/got changed', happened on its own) — right for stating that the address is now different — while 바꾸다 is TRANSITIVE ('to change something') and 변경하다 is its formal twin used for official records; so you describe the situation with 바뀌었다 and request the action with 변경하다 (or 바꾸다). For records the noun-verb 변경 ('a change/modification') and 수정 ('a correction', for fixing an error) are both apt: use 변경 for an updated address, 수정 for fixing a typo. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'change' collapsing the intransitive/transitive split — saying 주소를 바뀌었어요 (wrong: object marker on an intransitive verb) instead of 주소가 바뀌었어요. Another is over-asking with 'is it possible' when the parcel already shipped — note timing words 출발/배송 중 ('departed/in transit'), since changes are easier 출발 전 ('before departure'). Default 존댓말; with a friend, 변경할 수 있어?.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 주소를 바뀌었어요.
바뀌다 is intransitive, so the address takes 가, not 를: 주소가 바뀌었어요. To actively change it, use the transitive 바꾸다/변경하다: 주소를 변경하다.
Confusing 바뀌다 and 바꾸다.
바뀌다 = 'it changed (on its own)'; 바꾸다 = 'to change something'. State the situation with 바뀌었다, request the action with 바꾸다/변경하다.
Using 변경 when you mean fixing a typo.
변경 = updating to a new value; 수정 = correcting a mistake. For a wrong-written address, 수정 가능해요? is more precise.

Another is over-asking with 'is it possible' when the parcel already shipped — note timing words 출발/배송 중 ('departed/in transit'), since changes are easier 출발 전 ('before departure').

entries.nuance: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요 is 박스 ('box') + 안 ('not') + 터지게 (터지다 'to burst/split open' + -게 'so that') + 단단히 ('firmly/sturdily') + 포장해 주세요 (포장하다 'to pack/wrap', Sino-Korean 包裝 + 주세요). The -게 of 터지게 means 'so that/in such a way' and, with 안, expresses purpose-of-prevention: 'so that it does NOT burst.' This 안 ...-게 (해 주세요) frame is the natural way to request an outcome you want to AVOID. 단단히 ('firmly, solidly') is the adverb of choice for secure packing (from 단단하다 'to be hard/firm'); a near-synonym is 꼼꼼히 ('thoroughly/meticulously'), which stresses care/detail rather than tightness — use 단단히 for strength, 꼼꼼히 for thoroughness. The verb 터지다 is intransitive ('it bursts open by itself'), correct for a box giving way; don't use 깨지다 (that's for fragile contents shattering) — the BOX 터지다, the GLASS inside 깨지다. entries.nuance: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? is 택배 ('parcel') + 가 (subject) + 안 왔는데 (안 'not' + 오다 'come', past 왔다 + -는데 soft connective) + 어떻게 ('how') + 된 거예요? (되다 'to become/turn out' + -ㄴ 거예요 = 'what has it become / what's the situation?'). The set phrase 어떻게 된 거예요? literally 'how did it become?' is the standard way to ask 'what's going on / what happened?' about a problem — firm but not rude, leaning on the impersonal 되다 ('turn out') rather than blaming a person. The -는데 again links your situation ('it hasn't come, so…') to the question, softening the complaint. Useful companion vocabulary: 배송 조회 ('tracking lookup'), 배송 완료 ('delivery complete' status), 분실 ('loss/missing', 紛失), 지연 ('delay', 遲延). A key contrast: 어떻게 된 거예요? asks for an explanation of the situation, whereas 어떡해요? (어떻게 해요?) means 'what do I do / what now?' — don't swap them; the first seeks info, the second seeks a remedy. The English-speaker pitfall is the angry-sounding 직역 'why didn't it come?' → 왜 안 왔어요?, which can read as accusatory toward the listener; the neutral 어떻게 된 거예요? (or adding 혹시, 'by any chance') keeps it civil while still pressing for answers. Also note 오다's subject is the parcel (택배가 안 왔다), not you. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 어떻게 된 거야?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 어떻게 된 거예요? with 어떡해요?
어떻게 된 거예요? = 'what's the situation/what happened?' (asks for info); 어떡해요? = 'what should I do?' (asks for a remedy). Use the first to query a missing parcel.
Blunt 왜 안 왔어요? as the opener.
왜 ('why') can sound accusatory toward the listener. The neutral, civil query is 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?, optionally softened with 혹시.
Saying 제가 안 왔어요.
오다's subject here is the parcel: 택배가 안 왔어요 ('the parcel didn't come'). 제가 안 왔어요 would mean 'I didn't come'.

entries.nuance: 정말요? (polite) / 정말? (casual) is the everyday 'really?' you say to confirm you heard correctly, with light surprise or interest — not strong disbelief. The English-speaker pitfall is intonation — Korean 'really?' MUST rise sharply at the end to read as a question; said flat, 정말요 turns into 'truly' as a statement and confuses the listener. Also, don't pile on 정말 진짜요? thinking it's stronger; pick one.

entries.nuance: 진짜요? (polite) / 진짜? (casual) is the more emotional, colloquial cousin of 정말요? — it leaks more genuine surprise and excitement. It comes from 진짜 'real, genuine' (the 진 is the 한자 眞 'true') plus -요, so 진짜? alone is banmal and 진짜요? is the polite version. The dividing line versus 정말요? is tone and setting: 진짜? feels warmer, more spontaneous, and slightly more casual, so among friends it is the default, while in a stiff formal or business context 정말요? is safer because 진짜요? can sound a touch too relaxed. The English-speaker pitfall is register over-confidence: 진짜요? is polite-ish but still informal-flavored, so to a CEO, a much older stranger, or in a ceremony, the cleaner choice is 정말요? or 그래요?. Also, like all these, intonation must rise — flat 진짜 means 'genuinely / for real (emphasis),' not the question.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 진짜요? in a very formal or ceremonial setting — it stays casual in flavor; with a CEO or in a formal context use 정말요? or 그래요?.
Saying flat 진짜 expecting it to mean 'really?' — without rising pitch it's the emphasis adverb 'for real / genuinely,' a statement, not a question.
Confusing 진짜 (real, the opposite of fake) with 정말 in writing — as a reaction they overlap, but 진짜 is more colloquial and 정말 more neutral; don't assume they're interchangeable in every sentence.

entries.nuance: 대박 literally means 'a big hit / jackpot,' and as a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme — amazingly good, but also shocking or unbelievably bad. It is slang and firmly casual: 대박 alone is banmal among friends, and to add even a little politeness you say 대박이에요, though even that stays informal in flavor. The line against 헐 is direction: 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('whoa, what?!'), while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's huge,' though both can overlap. Because it is young, casual slang, the English-speaker pitfall is using it with a boss, an elder, or in any formal setting — it sounds flippant and too street; there you'd say 정말 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요 instead. Another pitfall is assuming it's only positive; Koreans say 대박 at a car crash too, meaning 'unbelievable.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 대박 with a boss, professor, or elder — it's casual slang and sounds disrespectful in formal settings; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요.
Assuming 대박 is only for good news — it reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad events; tone and context decide the meaning.
Adding -요 as 대박요 — that's not natural; the polite form is 대박이에요, since 대박 is a noun that needs the 이에요 copula.

entries.nuance: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the sound you make when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you, hugely common in texting and casual speech. It has no polite form because it's a raw exclamation; it lives entirely in banmal/casual territory among friends and peers. The dividing line versus 대박 is feeling: 헐 carries surprise often tinged with 'oh no' / dismay, while 대박 leans 'wow, that's huge' — that's why 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry) is natural but 대박 어떡해 is odd. The English-speaker pitfall is using it in any professional or respectful setting — to an elder or boss 헐 sounds childish and rude; there you'd react with 어머 (more neutral surprise) or a full 정말요? 그런 일이. Also don't write it as 헉 expecting the same thing — 헉 is a sharp gasp of fright, slightly different from the disbelieving 헐.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 헐 with a boss, elder, or in a formal email — it's casual youth slang and sounds immature/rude; use 어머 or 정말요? instead.
Trying to make a polite version like 헐요 — it doesn't exist; 헐 is a raw interjection that stays casual, so switch words for politeness.
Mixing up 헐 and 헉 — 헐 is disbelief/dismay ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a startled gasp of fright; they aren't interchangeable.

entries.nuance: 와 멋있다 is the spontaneous 'wow, that's cool / awesome' you exclaim at something or someone impressive — 와 is the gasp 'wow' and 멋있다 means 'is cool/stylish/admirable.' The plain 멋있다 is the casual exclamatory form (used even to oneself), 멋있어요 is polite, and to praise an elder or senior you add honorific -으시- → 멋있으시다/멋있으세요. The dividing line versus 예쁘다 ('pretty') and 대단하다 ('remarkable, impressive') is what you admire: 멋있다 is cool/stylish/admirable (a person's skill, a view, an attitude), 예쁘다 is cute/pretty (looks, small things), 대단하다 stresses achievement/effort. The English-speaker pitfall is the exclamatory -다 ending: learners think 멋있다 is dictionary form so they avoid saying it, but 멋있다! as a live reaction is completely natural and idiomatic. Another pitfall is praising a senior with plain 멋있어 — drop the honorific and it sounds over-familiar.

Using 멋있다 for something cute or pretty — that's 예쁘다; 멋있다 is for cool/stylish/admirable things, a different flavor of praise.
Avoiding 멋있다! as a reaction because -다 looks like dictionary form — the bare -다 exclamation is natural spoken Korean for live admiration.

entries.nuance: 잘됐다 means 'it turned out well / that's great' — the warm reaction when something works out for someone (or yourself). Another pitfall is mistaking it for sarcasm: said flat or with an eye-roll 잘됐다 can mean 'serves you right,' so keep your tone clearly warm.

entries.nuance: 다행이다 is the 'thank goodness, what a relief' you breathe out when a feared bad outcome was avoided — built from the noun 다행 'good fortune/luck (that it wasn't worse)' + 이다. The dividing line versus 잘됐다 is the emotional starting point: 다행이다 implies you were WORRIED and disaster was dodged, while 잘됐다 is plain happiness at good news with no prior dread — a clean bill of health you feared → 다행이다, a promotion you hoped for → 잘됐다. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'lucky' as 운이 좋다: 운이 좋다 is 'fortunate (won something, got a break),' but the relief that 'it could have been bad but wasn't' is specifically 다행이다. Another pitfall is forgetting the copula and saying 다행 alone — it needs 이다/이에요 to be a complete reaction.

Using 운이 좋다 ('lucky') for relief — 운이 좋다 means fortunate/got a break, but 'phew, it wasn't bad' is 다행이다, a different feeling.
Swapping in 잘됐다 — 잘됐다 is happiness at good news, while 다행이다 specifically means a feared bad outcome was avoided; the worry is the key difference.

entries.nuance: 어떡해(요) is the distressed 'oh no, what do I do?!' you blurt when a problem hits and you feel stuck — often it's an exclamation of dismay, not a literal request for instructions. It's the contracted spoken form of 어떻게 해 'how (shall I) do': casual 어떡해, polite 어떡해요. The critical dividing line is spelling: 어떡해 is the contraction you SAY ('what do I do'), while 어떻게 is the adverb 'how' that modifies a verb (어떻게 가요? 'how do I go?') — Koreans themselves mix these up in writing, but they are not interchangeable. The English-speaker pitfall is writing 어떻해 (a non-word) or using 어떻게 where the exclamation 어떡해 belongs. Another pitfall is register: 어떡해 is banmal, so to a boss or elder keep 어떡해요, or to genuinely ask for help say 어떻게 하면 좋을까요? Said softly to someone else's misfortune, 어떡해 also means sympathetic 'oh no, poor you.'
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 어떻해 — this is not a word; the exclamation is 어떡해 (contraction of 어떻게 해), and the adverb is 어떻게.
Using 어떻게 where you mean the dismay 'oh no' — 어떻게 is 'how' (어떻게 해요? = how do I do it), while the panicked exclamation is 어떡해(요).
Saying plain 어떡해 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; use 어떡해요, or to ask for actual help say 어떻게 하면 좋을까요?.

entries.nuance: 아쉽다 is the mild, wistful 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise' — soft regret that something nice didn't happen or is ending, NOT deep sadness. Casual 아쉽다/아쉬워, polite 아쉬워요, in-the-moment 아쉽네(요). entries.nuance: 짜증 나 means 'it's irritating / getting on my nerves' — the prickly frustration of small things piling up (errors, delays, noise). 짜증 is the noun 'irritation/peevishness' and 나(다) is 'arises,' so literally 'irritation arises.' Casual 짜증 나, exclamatory 짜증 난다; the polite 짜증 나요 exists but stays informal and a bit blunt, so you rarely say it to a boss. The dividing line versus 화나다 is degree and color: 짜증 나다 is low-grade peevish annoyance/frustration ('ugh, this again'), while 화나다 is real anger directed at someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and spacing: it's 짜증(이) 나다 — 짜증 is the thing that 'comes up,' so don't say 짜증해 (no such verb) or 짜증을 해; if you must mark it, it's 짜증이 나다 or the verb 짜증 내다 ('to act irritated'). Another pitfall is register: even 짜증 나요 sounds too raw to an elder; there, soften to 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요.

entries.nuance: 신난다 is bright, bubbling excitement — 'yay, this is fun, I can't wait!' — the happy buzz before or during something enjoyable. From 신(이) 나다 'spirit/excitement arises': plain 신나, exclamatory 신난다, polite 신나요. The dividing line versus 기대돼요 ('I'm looking forward to it') and 재미있다 ('it's fun/interesting') is the feeling: 신나다 is active, energetic excitement/joy (you're bouncing), 기대되다 is calm anticipation, 재미있다 describes how fun an activity IS. Anticipating a trip with energy → 신난다; quietly looking forward → 기대돼요; describing the trip afterward as fun → 재미있었어. The English-speaker pitfall is using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means worked-up/agitated (even aroused or angry) and sounds off for innocent fun; happy excitement is 신나다. Another pitfall is register: 신난다 is breezy and casual, fine with friends, but to express enthusiasm to a superior you'd say 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.

Forming it as 신하다 or 신해 — there's no such verb; it's 신(이) 나다, so the forms are 신나 / 신난다 / 신나요.

entries.nuance: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' → 'that makes no sense / no way / that's ridiculous,' a strong reaction of disbelief or protest at something absurd, shocking, or unfair. Casual 말도 안 돼, polite 말도 안 돼요. The dividing line versus 진짜? / 정말요? is strength: 진짜? is a light 'really?' that's open to it being true, while 말도 안 돼 flatly rejects it as impossible/outrageous — much stronger. It also differs from 대박 (which is 'wow, huge'); 말도 안 돼 is 'that can't be right.' The English-speaker pitfall is the spacing and negation: it's 말도 안 돼 (안 + 되다 → 안 돼), four parts, and 돼 is spelled 돼 (되+어), never 되; writing 말도 안 되 (no final ㅓ) is a common error. Another pitfall is register/strength — said to a superior 말도 안 돼요 can sound confrontational, so to politely push back you might soften to 그럴 리가요 ('surely not') or 이해가 안 되네요.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing 말도 안 되 — the form is 말도 안 돼 (되+어 = 돼); as a sentence-final reaction it must end in 돼, not 되.
Using 말도 안 돼(요) for mild surprise — it's strong rejection ('impossible/ridiculous'); for open-minded 'really?' use 진짜? / 정말요?.
Dropping 말도 안 돼요 on a superior in a dispute — it can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

entries.nuance: 그러게(요) means 'right? / I feel the same' — you AGREE with something the other person just said, often with a faint helpless or regretful tinge ('yeah, I know, what can you do'). Casual 그러게, polite 그러게요, emphatic 그러게 말이에요 'exactly, you said it.' The crucial dividing line is against 그렇구나/그렇군요: 그러게(요) responds to a SHARED feeling or opinion you already had ('I know, right'), while 그렇구나 reacts to NEW information you just learned ('oh, I see, I didn't know that'). So to '오늘 진짜 덥다' you say 그러게요 (I feel it too), but to '나 사실 부산 출신이야' you say 그렇구나 (news to you) — swap them and you sound off. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그러게요 for new facts, which implies you already knew and can seem dismissive. Another pitfall is hearing it as disagreement; it is agreement. To a superior, 그러게요 is fine but 맞아요 / 그러네요 can feel a touch more attentive.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew; for news you just learned use 그렇군요 / 그렇구나.
Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; keep the polite 그러게요 (or 그러게 말이에요) with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Reading 그러게요 as disagreement or doubt — it actually means 'right, I feel the same,' a soft, often resigned agreement.

entries.nuance: 어머 is a quick, soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — far more neutral and polite-safe than slangy 헐 or 대박, so it works in many settings and across ages. Stronger is 어머나; surprise plus worry is 어머 어떡해. It is a reflexive interjection, so it doesn't take -요, but because it's gentle and non-slang you can use it in front of elders and in semi-formal moments where 헐 would sound rude. The dividing line versus 헐 is register and tone: 헐 is casual youth slang skewing toward shock/dismay, while 어머 is softer, more refined surprise that anyone can use politely. Note the usage skew: 어머/어머나 is used by everyone but especially associated with women's speech; men also reach for 어 / 어이쿠 / 헐 more. The English-speaker pitfall is using only 헐 in every surprised moment, which sounds too slangy with older people — 어머 is the safe, graceful default. Another is over-using it flatly; it carries real emotional color, so it should sound like a genuine gasp.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment, including with elders — 헐 is slang and can sound rude; 어머 is the neutral, polite-safe gasp.
Adding -요 as 어머요 — it's a reflexive interjection and doesn't take -요; for politeness, follow it with a full polite sentence.
Treating 어머 as meaningless filler — it carries genuine surprise/emotion, so saying it flatly with no feeling sounds odd; it should sound like a real gasp.

The dividing line versus 헐 is register and tone: 헐 is casual youth slang skewing toward shock/dismay, while 어머 is softer, more refined surprise that anyone can use politely.

Using only 헐 in every surprised moment, which sounds too slangy with older people — 어머 is the safe, graceful default. Another is over-using it flatly; it carries real emotional color, so it should sound like a genuine gasp.

entries.nuance: 집 보러 왔는데요 is 집 ('house/home') + 보러 (the -러 'in order to' form of 보다 'to see') + 왔- (past of 오다 'come') + -는데요, the soft ender that opens a topic and waits for the agent to respond. So literally 'I came in order to see places, and…' — the universal first line when you walk into a 부동산. Here 보다 does NOT mean 'watch'; for housing it specifically means 'view/inspect a property', the way English says 'look at a place'. The dividing line from 집 구하러 왔는데요 ('I came to find/secure a place') is stage: 보러 is for the act of viewing today, while 구하러 frames the whole search for housing — both are natural, but 보러 is what you say when you're ready to actually walk through rooms. The English-speaker trap is dropping -는데요 and saying a flat 집 보러 왔어요, which is fine but blunter; the -는데요 invites the agent to take over ('what's your budget? this way…'). Another trap is using 찾다 ('to look for/search') as 집 찾으러 왔어요 — understandable, but for the agent-office context Koreans say 보러 (to view) or 구하러 (to secure), not 찾으러. Default to 존댓말 with any agent; 반말 here would be jarringly rude to a stranger doing business.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 집 봐 주세요 to mean 'show me a place'.
봐 주세요 means 'please look at it (for me)' — as if asking the agent to inspect something on your behalf. To say you've come to view places, say 집 보러 왔는데요; to be shown one, 집 좀 보여 주세요.
Dropping -는데요 and stating a flat 집 보러 왔어요.
It's correct but abrupt as an opener. The soft ender 집 보러 왔는데요 hands the conversation to the agent and sounds like a real customer easing in.
Using 찾으러 instead of 보러/구하러.
찾다 is 'to search for' a lost or hidden thing. For house-hunting at an office, Koreans say 보러 왔어요 (to view) or 집 구하러 왔어요 (to secure a place), not 찾으러 왔어요.

entries.nuance: 월세 (月貰, 'monthly rent') and 전세 (傳貰, 'jeonse') are the two pillars of Korean renting, and you'll say this line constantly. 월세 means you pay a deposit (보증금) plus rent every month, like renting in most countries. 전세 is uniquely Korean: you hand the landlord one enormous lump sum (often 50–80% of the home's value) for the whole lease, pay ZERO monthly rent, and get the entire sum back when you move out — the landlord profits by investing your money. There's also 반전세 ('half-jeonse'): a large-ish deposit AND a smaller monthly rent, the middle ground. The dividing line learners blur is 보증금 vs. 전세금: in 월세 the deposit is a smallish security 보증금; in 전세 the lump sum IS the rent mechanism (전세금/전셋돈), not a 'deposit' in the Western sense. The English-speaker trap is calling 전세 a 'deposit' and expecting to also pay monthly — with true 전세 there is no monthly rent at all. Another trap is the particle/copula: it's 월세'예'요 after a vowel but you'll hear learners say 월세'이'에요 — the contracted 예요 is natural here. Always 존댓말 with an agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 전세 means 'deposit' on top of monthly rent.
With 전세 you pay a huge lump sum and NO monthly rent, getting it all back at move-out. If there's monthly rent plus a deposit, that's 월세 (or 반전세), not 전세.
Confusing 보증금 with 전세금.
보증금 is the (usually smaller) security deposit in a 월세 contract; 전세금 is the whole lease sum in 전세. They aren't the same number or the same idea — ask 보증금 얼마예요? for 월세, 전세금 얼마예요? for 전세.
Saying 월세이에요 instead of 월세예요.
After the vowel-ending 월세, the copula contracts to 예요: 월세예요, 전세예요. 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form.

entries.nuance: 보증금 (保證金, 'security deposit') is the up-front money the landlord holds against unpaid rent or damage, returned when you leave. In Korean renting, 보증금 and 월세 trade off on a sliding scale: a higher deposit usually buys a lower monthly rent and vice versa, so asking 보증금 얼마예요? is really asking where this unit sits on that scale. Amounts are spoken in 만원 (10,000-won) units, so '천' means 천만 원 (10 million) and '오십' means 오십만 원 (500k) — you almost never say the full digits. The very natural agent-friendly variant is 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does the deposit come out?'), softer than the bare 얼마예요?. The dividing line from 전세금 (the whole 전세 lump) is which contract you're in — don't ask 전세금 얼마예요? about a 월세 place. The English-speaker trap is the particle: with 얼마예요? you say 보증금 얼마예요? (no 이/가 needed in casual speech), but with 어떻게 돼요? you add 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. Another trap is treating 보증금 like a Western 'first-and-last month' — it's a single lump tied to the rent scheme, and it can be large (often 10–20× the monthly rent). Stay in 존댓말; this is a money negotiation with a professional.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Reading '천' as 1,000 won instead of 천만 원.
Housing amounts are in 만원 units. 천 means 천만 원 (10 million); 오십 means 오십만 원 (500k). Hearing '보증금 천' as a literal 1,000 won will mis-set your whole budget.
Saying 보증금이 얼마예요 vs 보증금이 어떻게 돼요 with the wrong particle.
With 얼마예요? Koreans usually drop the particle (보증금 얼마예요?). With 어떻게 돼요? keep 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. Mixing them sounds off.
Treating 보증금 like Western first-and-last-month rent.
보증금 is one lump tied to the rent scheme, often many times the monthly rent, and it slides against 월세. It is not 'two months' rent up front'; ask the actual figure and the trade-off.

entries.nuance: 관리비 (管理費, 'maintenance/management fee') is the monthly building charge ON TOP of your rent — covering things like cleaning of common areas, the elevator, security, hallway lighting, sometimes water (수도세), internet, or even heating, depending on the building. It can be a few 만원 in a small 원룸 or much more in an apartment complex, so 관리비는 따로예요? ('is it separate?') is an essential cost question. The dividing line is 따로 ('separate, on top') vs. 포함 (包含, 'included'): 관리비는 따로예요? asks if it's an extra charge, while 관리비 포함이에요? asks if it's already in the rent — they expect opposite yes/no answers, so don't muddle them. Crucially, always follow up with 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? because a 'cheap' rent can hide a fat 관리비, and what it bundles varies wildly. The English-speaker trap is assuming 관리비 is like a Western 'HOA fee' for owners only — no, renters pay it monthly too. Another trap is the topic particle: 관리비는 따로예요? uses 는 to set up the contrast ('as for the maintenance fee…'); dropping it is okay casually but the 는 sounds natural here. Use 존댓말 with the agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Ignoring 관리비 because the rent looks cheap.
A low 월세 can hide a high 관리비. Always ask 관리비 얼마예요? and 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? — the real monthly cost is 월세 + 관리비.
Mixing up 따로 and 포함.
관리비는 따로예요? asks if it's a separate extra charge; 관리비 포함이에요? asks if it's already included in rent. They expect opposite answers — pick the one you mean.
Assuming renters don't pay 관리비.
Unlike a Western owners-only HOA fee, Korean renters pay 관리비 every month on top of rent. Budget for 월세 + 관리비 + utilities, not rent alone.

entries.shortExplanation: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "What's included (appliances/furniture)?".
entries.explanation: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? (opsyeoneun mwoga isseoyo?) means "What's included (appliances/furniture)?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? ("What options (appliances) are included?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.en: What's included here?

entries.nuance: 옵션 here is the loanword 'option' used in a Korean-specific real-estate sense: the appliances and furniture that come WITH the rental — fridge (냉장고), washer (세탁기), air conditioner (에어컨), stove/induction (인덕션/가스레인지), bed (침대), desk, wardrobe, etc. 풀옵션 ('full option') means it's basically move-in ready with everything; a 'no-option' place is bare. This matters enormously because furnishing a Korean apartment yourself is costly, so 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? is one of the most practical viewing questions. The dividing line from 관리비 is category: 옵션 is the stuff INSIDE the unit, 관리비 is the monthly building charge — don't conflate 'what's included' across the two. The English-speaker trap is using 옵션 in its general English sense ('choices/alternatives') and confusing the agent — in housing it specifically means built-in appliances/furniture. Another trap is the particle: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? sets 옵션 as the topic with 은, then asks 뭐가 있어요 ('what exists') — note it's 뭐'가' (subject) inside, a spot where learners wrongly say 뭐를. Confirm item by item, because '풀옵션' can still be missing the one thing you need (e.g. no 침대). Stay in 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 옵션 in its general English sense ('choices').
In Korean real estate 옵션 means the included appliances/furniture, not 'alternatives'. 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? asks what the unit comes with, not what your choices are.
Trusting '풀옵션' without checking specifics.
풀옵션 varies by listing and may still lack the item you need (e.g. no bed). Confirm piece by piece: 세탁기 있어요? 침대도 있어요?
Saying 옵션은 뭐를 있어요.
있다 ('to exist') takes a subject, not an object: 옵션은 뭐'가' 있어요? The object particle 를 is wrong with 있다.

entries.shortExplanation: 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요? is a practical expression meaning "When can I move in?".
entries.explanation: "When can I move in?" — that is 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요? (i jip eonje ipju ganeunghaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 언제 입주 가능해요? ("When is move-in possible?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking the available move-in date

More formal, naming 입주 가능일 ('available date')

usagePhrases.en: Can I move in right away?
usagePhrases.note: Asking if immediate move-in (즉시입주) is possible

examples.ko: 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요?
examples.romanization: i jip eonje ipju ganeunghaeyo?
examples.en: When can I move into this place?
examples.note: Pinning down availability on a unit you like

examples.ko: 다음 달 초에 입주하고 싶은데 가능해요?
examples.romanization: daeum dal choe ipjuhago sipeunde ganeunghaeyo?
examples.en: I'd like to move in early next month — is that possible?
examples.note: State your target with 입주하고 싶다, then ask 가능해요

examples.ko: 지금 사람이 살고 있어서 다음 달에나 입주 가능해요.
examples.romanization: jigeum sarami salgo isseoseo daeum darena ipju ganeunghaeyo.
examples.en: Someone's living here now, so move-in's only possible next month.
examples.note: 다음 달에나 ('not until next month') explains the wait

entries.nuance: 입주 (入住, 'moving in / taking up residence') is the formal word for occupying a home, and 입주 가능해요? asks when the unit is free for you to move in. This is critical timing in Korea because leases, deposits, and the previous tenant's move-out all have to line up, and a place you love might not be 입주 가능 until weeks later. 즉시입주 ('immediate move-in') is a common listing tag; 바로 입주 돼요? asks for that. The dividing line from the casual 들어가다 ('to go in', also used for moving in) is register: 입주하다 is the proper real-estate verb on contracts and with agents, while 언제 들어갈 수 있어요? is the everyday spoken version — both fine, but 입주 sounds more 'official.' The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'move in' as 움직이다 ('to move/budge physically') or 이사 오다 in the wrong frame — 이사하다/이사 오다 is 'to relocate (the whole act)', while 입주 is specifically taking up the new residence; for the date a place becomes available, say 입주 가능해요?. Another trap is 가능하다's conjugation: it's 가능해요 (가능 + 하다), and learners sometimes say 가능있어요, which is wrong. Use 존댓말 with the agent.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'move in' as 움직이다.
움직이다 means to physically move/budge. Moving into a home is 입주하다 (formal) or 들어가다 (casual). Ask 언제 입주 가능해요? or 언제 들어갈 수 있어요?
Saying 입주 가능있어요.
가능하다 is a 하다-adjective: 가능해요, not 가능있어요. Correct: 언제 입주 가능해요? or 입주 가능한가요?
Confusing 입주 with 이사.
입주 is taking up the new residence (and its available date); 이사 is the act of relocating/moving your stuff. For when the place is free, ask 입주 가능해요?; for the moving day itself, 이사 언제 해요?

entries.shortExplanation: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? is a practical expression meaning "How long is it from the station?".
entries.explanation: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? (yeogeseo eolmana geollyeoyo?) = "How long is it from the station?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? ("How long does it take from the station?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: How long does it take from the station?
usagePhrases.note: Polite; asking walking distance to the subway
반말, with a friend

usagePhrases.en: How many minutes on foot from the station?
usagePhrases.note: Specifies 걸어서 ('on foot') for an exact walk time

usagePhrases.en: Is this near a station (prime location)?
usagePhrases.note: 역세권 = the desirable 'within walking distance of a station' zone

examples.ko: 여기 역에서 얼마나 걸려요?
examples.romanization: yeogi yeogeseo eolmana geollyeoyo?
examples.en: How long is it from the station here?
examples.note: Standard location question at a viewing

examples.ko: 지하철역에서 걸어서 한 십 분 정도 걸려요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoryeogeseo georeoseo han sip bun jeongdo geollyeoyo.
examples.en: It's about a 10-minute walk from the subway station.
examples.note: 걸어서 한 십 분 정도 = 'about a 10-min walk'; 한 softens it

examples.ko: 역세권이라 좀 비싸도 출퇴근은 편해요.
examples.romanization: yeoksegwonira jom bissado chultoegeuneun pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: It's near the station, so it's pricey but the commute's easy.
examples.note: 역세권 justifies higher rent with 출퇴근 ('commute') convenience

entries.nuance: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? is 역 ('station') + 에서 ('from') + 얼마나 ('how much') + 걸리다 ('to take [time]'), asking how long it takes to reach the place from the subway station — the make-or-break question for commuters in Korea, where proximity to a 지하철역 hugely affects both convenience and price. The buzzword is 역세권 (驛勢圈), literally the 'station-influence zone' = within easy walking distance of a station, a major selling point that pushes rent up. Crucially, 걸리다 here means 'to take (time/effort)', a totally different verb from 걷다 ('to walk') and from 걸다 ('to hang/dial') — they look alike but mean different things, a classic confusion. Add 걸어서 ('on foot') to force a walking answer, since an agent might otherwise quote driving time. The English-speaker trap is the particle: it's 역'에서' (from the station, 에서 marks the source); learners wrongly say 역'에' 얼마나 걸려요, but 에 marks a destination, not a starting point. structuredNuance.t: 역 ('station') + 에서 ('from') + 얼마나 ('how much') + 걸리다 ('to take [time]'), asking how long it takes to reach the place from the subway station — the make-or-break question for commuters in Korea, where proximity to a 지하철역 hugely affects both convenience and price. The buzzword is 역세권 (驛勢圈), literally the 'station-influence zone' = within easy walking distance of a station, a major selling point that pushes rent up.

entries.nuance: 햇빛 잘 들어요? is 햇빛 ('sunlight') + 잘 ('well') + 들다 ('to enter/come in') + 요, literally 'does sunlight come in well?' — asking whether the unit gets good natural light, which strongly affects mood, mold, heating bills, and resale in Korea. The verb 들다 here means 'to enter/be admitted' (light coming in), one of 들다's many senses, NOT 'to hold' or 'to lift' — so 햇빛이 들다 is a fixed collocation 'light comes in.' The pro term is 채광 (採光, 'lighting/sun exposure'); 채광 좋아요? asks the same thing more technically. Direction language is key: 남향 (south-facing) is the gold standard for sun, while 북향 (north-facing) gets little; 반지하 (semi-basement) and low floors often mean dark units, so this question can reveal a hidden downside. The English-speaker trap is the verb choice — 직역-ing with 가지다 ('to have') as 햇빛 가져요? is meaningless; the natural collocation is 햇빛이 들다. Another is the particle: casually you can say 햇빛 잘 들어요? (no particle), but the fuller form is 햇빛이 잘 들어요? with 이 as subject — never 햇빛을, since 들다 (to come in) is intransitive here. Stay in 존댓말 at viewings; ask the same about 곰팡이 ('mold'): 곰팡이 안 생겨요? to probe damp.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 햇빛 가져요? or 햇빛 있어요? for 'gets sunlight'.
The natural collocation is 햇빛이 들다 ('light comes in'). Ask 햇빛 잘 들어요?. 가지다 ('to have') and a bare 있다 don't fit how Korean talks about sun exposure.
Using the object particle: 햇빛을 잘 들어요.
들다 ('to come in') is intransitive here, so 햇빛 is the subject: 햇빛이 잘 들어요?. The object marker 을 is wrong.
Ignoring 남향/북향 and 반지하.
Direction and floor decide the light. 남향 (south-facing) is sunny; 북향 and 반지하 (semi-basement) are often dark. If sun matters, confirm 남향이에요? and avoid surprises.

entries.explanation: "Could you lower the rent a bit?" — that is 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 (wolse jom kkakka juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 ("Please lower the rent a bit"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please lower the rent a bit
usagePhrases.note: Polite; the standard rent-negotiation line

usagePhrases.romanization: wolse jogeumman kkakka jusimyeon an dwaeyo?
usagePhrases.en: Couldn't you take just a little off the rent?
usagePhrases.note: Softer, more pleading 'wouldn't it be okay if…'

examples.romanization: wolse jom kkakka juseyo. oman wonmanyo.
examples.en: Please lower the rent a bit — just 50,000 off.
examples.note: Name a concrete cut (오만 원) to make the ask real

examples.ko: 계약 바로 할 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주시면 안 돼요?
examples.romanization: gyeyak baro hal tenikka wolse jom kkakka jusimyeon an dwaeyo?
examples.en: I'll sign right away, so couldn't you lower the rent a little?
examples.note: Offer to commit (계약 바로) as leverage to negotiate

examples.ko: 보증금 더 낼 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주세요.
examples.romanization: bojeunggeum deo nael tenikka wolse jom kkakka juseyo.
examples.en: I'll pay more deposit, so please lower the monthly rent.
examples.note: The 보증금↑ → 월세↓ trade stated as a bargaining chip

entries.nuance: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is 월세 ('monthly rent') + 좀 (politeness softener) + 깎다 ('to cut/shave down a price') + 아 주세요 ('please do for me'), the bread-and-butter line for haggling rent down. 깎다 is THE verb for knocking money off a price (also used at markets: 좀 깎아 주세요), so it's exactly right here. Negotiation is normal in Korean renting, especially on 월세 and 관리비, and landlords expect some back-and-forth. The 좀 is not 'a little' in amount — it's the softener that turns a demand into a polite request; you then state the actual amount separately (오만 원만요 = 'just 50k'). The dividing line from 보증금 깎아 주세요 is which lever you pull: you can ask to cut the deposit OR the monthly rent, and often you TRADE them (raise deposit to drop rent). The English-speaker trap is using 내리다 ('to lower/bring down') as 월세 내려 주세요 — understandable, but for prices Koreans say 깎다 ('shave off'); 내리다 sounds like physically lowering something. Another trap is 직역-ing 'give me a discount' as 디스카운트 주세요 (unnatural) or 할인해 주세요 (할인 fits stores/sales, not rent haggling). Always 존댓말 with the landlord/agent — bargaining hard but politely is expected; 반말 would torpedo the deal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 월세 내려 주세요 for 'lower the rent'.
내리다 is to physically lower/bring down. For shaving money off a price, Koreans use 깎다: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요. 내리다 sounds like lowering an object.
Using 할인해 주세요 to haggle rent.
할인 (discount) fits stores and sales, not rent negotiation. For bargaining down rent, say 깎아 주세요. 할인해 주세요 sounds like asking a shop for a coupon.
Dropping 좀 and demanding 월세 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without the softener 좀 it sounds pushy. 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is polite; pair it with leverage (보증금 더 낼게요 / 계약 바로 할게요) to negotiate gracefully.
