entries.shortExplanation: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I look around a bit more?".
entries.explanation: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? (yeogi jom deo bol su isseoyo?) = "Can I look around a bit more?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? ("Can I look around a bit more?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Softer, asks to view at your own pace

examples.en: Can I look around a bit more? I'd like to see the bathroom too.
examples.note: Give a reason (화장실도 보고 싶다) to extend the viewing

examples.en: Could I take my time checking the water pressure and appliances?
examples.note: Name what to inspect (수압 'water pressure', 옵션)

entries.nuance: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is 여기 ('here') + 좀 ('a bit', softener) + 더 ('more') + 볼 수 있어요 ('can I see?'), asking the agent for more time to inspect a unit — open closets, check the bathroom, test 수압 ('water pressure'), look for 곰팡이 ('mold'). Korean viewings can feel rushed because agents juggle many clients, so this phrase buys you the time to look properly. The dividing line from 다른 집도 보여 주세요 ('show me other places') is scope: 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? extends THIS viewing, while 보여 주세요 requests ADDITIONAL units — use the right one. Note 보다 ('to see/inspect') vs. 보여 주다 ('to show'): you 보다 the place yourself, the agent 보여 준다 (shows) it to you, so don't say 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you just want to keep looking on your own. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'look around' as 둘러보다 in a way that's fine but stiffer — 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is the natural spoken ask; 둘러봐도 돼요? also works. Another trap is over-using 봐도 돼요? ('may I look?') as if you need permission for everything; 볼 수 있어요? ('can I look more?') is softer and assumes cooperation. structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 좀 ('a bit', softener) + 더 ('more') + 볼 수 있어요 ('can I see?'), asking the agent for more time to inspect a unit — open closets, check the bathroom, test 수압 ('water pressure'), look for 곰팡이 ('mold'). entries.nuance: 이 집으로 할게요 is 이 집 ('this house') + -으로 ('with/by', marking a choice) + 하다 ('to do/go with') + -ㄹ게요 (announcing your own decision). The -으로 + 하다 pattern means 'I'll go WITH this one' — the same structure as ordering food (이걸로 할게요), here applied to choosing a home among options. The -ㄹ게요 ending is exactly right: it courteously declares YOUR decision ('I'll take it'). The dividing line from 이 집 계약할게요 ('I'll sign for this place') is finality: 이 집으로 할게요 announces your CHOICE, while 계약하다 commits to the legal CONTRACT — saying 할게요 first, then arranging 계약, is the natural sequence. The English-speaker trap is dropping -으로 and saying 이 집 할게요 — understandable but it loses the 'choosing among options' nuance that -으로 carries; the clean form is 이 집으로 할게요. Another trap is 직역-ing 'I'll take it' as 가질게요 ('I'll have/possess it') or 잡을게요 — you don't 'take/grab' a rental that way; for selecting it you 하다 it (이 집으로 할게요), and to lock it you 계약하다. Also note 마음에 들다 ('to like') uses the particle 에: 이 집이 마음에 들어요, a fixed expression learners often mangle as 마음을 들어요. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent as you close.

entries.nuance: 계약 (契約, 'contract') is the legal rental agreement, and 계약은 어떻게 해요? asks the agent to explain HOW the signing works — what you bring, what you pay, and when. The verb is 계약하다 ('to sign a contract'). Key money words cluster here: 계약금 (the down payment you pay on signing to lock the deal, often ~10% of the deposit), and 잔금 ('the balance', paid later, usually at 입주). The dividing line from 보증금 is timing/role: 계약금 secures the contract NOW and is part of the total, while 보증금 is the full security deposit; you typically pay 계약금 at signing and the rest (잔금) at move-in. The English-speaker trap is the topic particle and copula: 계약은 어떻게 해요? uses 은 to topicalize ('as for the contract…'); a bare 계약 어떻게 해요? is okay casually but 은 is natural. Another trap is 직역-ing 'sign a contract' as 사인하다 ('to sign [autograph]') — while 사인 is used colloquially, the proper verb is 계약하다, and you'll see 도장 ('seal/stamp') used too, since Koreans often stamp rather than sign. Critically, ask about 전입신고 ('move-in registration') and 확정일자 ('fixed date stamp') — official steps that legally protect your deposit; a newcomer who skips them can lose protection. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent throughout.

entries.nuance: 수압은 괜찮아요? is 수압 (水壓, 'water pressure') + 은 (topic) + 괜찮아요? ('is it okay?'), one of those practical questions that separates a savvy renter from a regretful one — weak pressure or no hot water is misery you only discover after moving in. Pair it with 온수 잘 나와요? ('does hot water come out well?') and probe 난방 ('heating') and 곰팡이 ('mold') for a full inspection. The verb 나오다 ('to come out') is the natural collocation for water/heat flowing: 물이 잘 나와요, 온수가 잘 나와요. The dividing line from 난방 (heating) is system: 수압/온수 is about water flow, 난방 is about warmth — Korean homes often use 온돌 (under-floor heating), and you'll want to ask if it's 가스 (gas) or 도시가스, which affects bills. The English-speaker trap is the particle on 나오다: water is the SUBJECT coming out, so 물'이' 잘 나와요? (이/가), never 물을 — 나오다 is intransitive. Another trap is 직역-ing 'water pressure' awkwardly or asking 'is the water strong?' as 물이 세요? — 물이 세다 ('the water is strong/forceful') is actually used colloquially, but 수압 괜찮아요? / 수압 세요? is cleaner. Bills depend on it. Ask 난방 어떻게 해요? — 도시가스 (city gas) vs. other systems changes your winter costs a lot. 온돌 (floor heating) is common but cost varies by source.

structuredNuance.t: 수압 (水壓, 'water pressure') + 은 (topic) + 괜찮아요? ('is it okay?'), one of those practical questions that separates a savvy renter from a regretful one — weak pressure or no hot water is misery you only discover after moving in. Pair it with 온수 잘 나와요? ('does hot water come out well?') and probe 난방 ('heating') and 곰팡이 ('mold') for a full inspection. The verb 나오다 ('to come out') is the natural collocation for water/heat flowing: 물이 잘 나와요, 온수가 잘 나와요. Top floors (꼭대기 층) and old buildings often have weak 수압, so this question can surface a real defect.

The dividing line from 난방 (heating) is system: 수압/온수 is about water flow, 난방 is about warmth — Korean homes often use 온돌 (under-floor heating), and you'll want to ask if it's 가스 (gas) or 도시가스, which affects bills.
수압 is 水壓, literally 'water pressure' — the pressure of water in the pipes.

The English-speaker trap is the particle on 나오다: water is the SUBJECT coming out, so 물'이' 잘 나와요? (이/가), never 물을 — 나오다 is intransitive. Another trap is 직역-ing 'water pressure' awkwardly or asking 'is the water strong?' as 물이 세요? — 물이 세다 ('the water is strong/forceful') is actually used colloquially, but 수압 괜찮아요? / 수압 세요? is cleaner. Stay in 존댓말 at the viewing.

entries.nuance: 계약 기간은 얼마예요? is 계약 ('contract') + 기간 (期間, 'period/term') + 은 (topic) + 얼마예요? ('how much/how long?'), asking the length of the lease — essential because it locks how long you're committed and when rent can be raised. The Korean default is often 2년 (two years), especially for 전세, though 월세 can be 1년; and tenant-protection law gives renters a right to request one renewal, so the practical stay can be longer. The verb 계약하다 ('to contract') pairs with a term: 이 년 계약하다 ('sign for two years'). The dividing line from 재계약 (再契約, 'renewal/re-signing') is timing: 계약 기간 is the original term, 재계약 is extending it at 만기 (滿期, 'expiry') — ask both so you know your options. The English-speaker trap is using 얼마 ('how much') and worrying it only means money — here 얼마예요? naturally covers duration too ('how long?'), so 계약 기간은 얼마예요? is correct; you could also say 계약 기간이 어떻게 돼요?. Another trap is the counter for years: native vs. Sino — for years you use Sino-Korean (일 년, 이 년), NOT native (한 년 is wrong); learners often misapply native numbers here. Also note 만기 ('term expiry') vs. 만료 — both exist, but 계약 만기 is the everyday phrase for a lease running out. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent, and ask early, since term length affects your whole plan.

Saying 한 년, 두 년 for years.
Years take Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년 — never 한 년/두 년. So 'a two-year lease' is 이 년 계약, not 두 년 계약.

entries.nuance: 여기 좀 시끄러워요? is 여기 ('here') + 좀 (softener, 'kind of') + 시끄럽다 ('to be noisy') + 요, asking whether the place is loud — a quietly crucial question, because thin walls and 층간소음 (層間騷音, 'noise between floors') are a famous source of stress and even disputes in Korean apartments. 시끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 시끄럽다 → 시끄러워요 (the ㅂ turns to 워), a conjugation learners stumble on. The pro terms are 방음 (防音, 'soundproofing') and 층간소음, and 방음 잘 돼요? ('is it well soundproofed?') asks about the building's insulation directly. The dividing line: 시끄럽다 describes the experienced noise ('it's loud'), while 방음 is the structural defense against it ('soundproofing') — ask both, since a quiet day-viewing can hide noisy nights. The English-speaker trap is the irregular conjugation (saying 시끄럽어요 instead of 시끄러워요), and 직역-ing 'noisy' fine but forgetting the softener 좀, which keeps the question from sounding like a complaint. Another trap is 소리 ('sound') vs. 소음 ('noise'): 소음 is unwanted noise (층간소음, 소음 심해요?), while 소리 is neutral sound (차 소리, 옆집 소리) — use 소음 for the nuisance sense. entries.nuance: 혹시 융자 있어요? is 혹시 ('by any chance', a softener for delicate questions) + 융자 (融資, 'a loan/financing') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking whether the property carries debt — a make-or-break question, because if a landlord has borrowed heavily against the home and later defaults, a tenant's 보증금 can be wiped out in foreclosure. This is one of the most important phrases for protecting your money in Korea. The technical term is 근저당 (根抵當, 'maximum-amount mortgage/lien'), shown on the 등기부등본 (登記簿謄本, 'certified copy of the property register'), which you have every right to request and read before signing. The dividing line: 융자/대출 is the loan itself, 근저당 is its registered claim on the property, and 등기부등본 is the document proving both — ask to see the 등기부등본 to verify. The English-speaker trap is not knowing to ask at all (the concept of 보증금 being at risk via the landlord's debt is unfamiliar), and 혹시 is essential to ask without sounding accusatory. Another trap is 융자 vs. 대출 (貸出): both mean a loan, nearly interchangeable, but 융자 is the common word in this property context; 빚 ('debt') sounds bluntly personal. Also note 깡통전세 ('empty-can jeonse') and 전세사기 ('jeonse fraud') — terms for scams where the deposit exceeds the home's safe value; this question is your first line of defense. structuredNuance.t: 혹시 ('by any chance', a softener for delicate questions) + 융자 (融資, 'a loan/financing') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking whether the property carries debt — a make-or-break question, because if a landlord has borrowed heavily against the home and later defaults, a tenant's 보증금 can be wiped out in foreclosure. This is one of the most important phrases for protecting your money in Korea. Also note 깡통전세 ('empty-can jeonse') and 전세사기 ('jeonse fraud') — terms for scams where the deposit exceeds the home's safe value; this question is your first line of defense. 융자 is 融資 ('financing/loan'). The technical term is 근저당 (根抵當, 'maximum-amount mortgage/lien'), shown on the 등기부등본 (登記簿謄本, 'certified copy of the property register'), which you have every right to request and read before signing.

entries.shortExplanation: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I talk to the landlord directly?".
entries.explanation: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요? (jipjuinirang jikjeop yaegihal su isseoyo?) means "Can I talk to the landlord directly?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요? ("Can I speak with the landlord directly?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요? is 집주인 ('house owner/landlord') + 이랑 ('with') + 직접 ('directly/in person') + 얘기하다 ('to talk') + ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can I?'), asking to deal with the actual owner rather than only the agent — important for clarifying repairs, rules, and whether the person signing is truly the owner (a fraud safeguard). 집주인 is the everyday word; the honorific is 집주인분 / 임대인 (賃貸人, the formal 'lessor' on contracts), versus you the 임차인 (賃借人, 'lessee'). The dividing line from the agent is role: the 부동산 (agent/공인중개사, licensed broker) brokers the deal and earns a 복비/중개수수료 (brokerage fee), while the 집주인 owns the place — for binding promises (repairs, move-in date), you want the owner's word. The English-speaker trap is the particle 이랑 vs. 하고/와: all mean 'with', but 이랑 is the casual-natural choice in speech (집주인이랑); 와/과 is more formal/written. Another trap is 직역-ing 'directly' as 똑바로 ('straight/upright') — 직접 ('in person, firsthand') is the right word for dealing with someone directly; 똑바로 means physically straight. Also verify the signer is the registered owner on the 등기부등본 — a key anti-fraud step. Use 존댓말, and refer to the owner with honorifics (집주인분, -세요) even when they're not present.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

똑바로 means 'straight/upright' (physically). To deal with someone in person/firsthand, use 직접: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요?

와/과 is formal/written. In conversation Koreans say 집주인이랑 or 집주인하고. Save 와/과 for documents.

The 부동산 (공인중개사) is a broker who earns a fee (복비); the 집주인 (임대인) owns the place. For binding promises, talk to the owner — and confirm they're the one on the 등기부등본.

examples.note: Ask the commission as part of total move-in cost

entries.nuance: 복비는 얼마예요? is 복비 (the colloquial word for the real-estate agent's commission, a contraction of 복덕방 비(費) — 복덕방(福德房) being the old-fashioned word for a realtor's office) + 은 (topic) + 얼마예요? ('how much?'). The formal term is 중개수수료 (仲介手數料, 'brokerage fee') or 중개보수, and rates are legally capped on a sliding 요율표 (rate table) based on the deposit/rent and property type — so the fee isn't arbitrary, and you can ask the agent to show the rate. Crucially, BOTH the landlord and the tenant each pay their own 복비 to the agent (각자 부담), a fact that surprises newcomers expecting only one side to pay. The dividing line from 보증금/월세 is who gets the money: 복비 goes to the 부동산 (agent), not the landlord, and it's a ONE-time cost at contract, not monthly. ('can I get a cash receipt?') for your records, and confirm the agent is a licensed 공인중개사 (certified broker) — unlicensed brokering is a fraud red flag. The fee is negotiable only within the legal cap. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent.

The agent's commission is a real one-time fee at signing, separate from deposit and rent. Ask 복비는 얼마예요? early so the total cost doesn't surprise you.
Thinking only the landlord pays the agent.
Both sides each pay their own 복비 (각자 부담). As the tenant you owe your own brokerage fee to the 부동산, not just the landlord's.

복비 is capped by a legal 요율표 based on the deposit/rent. It's set within limits, not freely haggled. Ask the agent to show the rate, and request a 현금영수증.

entries.english: Please help me / Help me out a bit
entries.shortExplanation: 좀 도와주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please help me / Help me out a bit".
entries.explanation: 좀 도와주세요 (jom dowajuseyo) = "Please help me / Help me out a bit". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 좀 도와주세요 ("Please help me a bit"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
entries.learnerPriority: Memorize 좀 도와주세요 with one situation and one follow-up phrase. Do not translate it word by word while speaking.
entries.contextHint: Use this expression in basic everyday communication. Check the examples to see whether it fits staff, strangers, teachers, friends, or emergencies.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; the everyday polite way to ask anyone (clerk, stranger, coworker) for help
반말; to a friend, sibling, or someone younger you're close to
softer/more formal; asking a stranger or in a service setting, sounds more considerate

usagePhrases.en: Can you help me with this?
usagePhrases.note: natural extension; points at a specific task so they know what you mean

examples.ko: 저기요, 좀 도와주세요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, jom dowajuseyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, please help me.
examples.note: '저기요' first gets a stranger's attention before the request

examples.ko: 짐이 너무 무거워서요, 좀 도와주세요.
examples.romanization: jimi neomu mugeowoseoyo, jom dowajuseyo.
examples.en: The luggage is too heavy, so please help me.
examples.note: giving the reason first makes the request feel reasonable, not pushy

examples.ko: 죄송한데 길을 잃어서요, 좀 도와주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande gireul ireoseoyo, jom dowajusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, I'm lost — could you help me?
examples.note: '죄송한데' + reason is how Koreans politely open a help request to a stranger

entries.nuance: This is the all-purpose 'help me' you say to almost anyone — a shop clerk, a passerby, a coworker. The little word 좀 ('a bit') is not really about quantity; it softens the request and is almost mandatory, because '도와주세요' alone can sound blunt or like an emergency. To go more casual drop to 도와줘 with friends; to go softer or more formal use 도와주시겠어요? or 도와주실 수 있어요?. The nearest alternative is 도움이 필요해요 ('I need help'), which states your situation rather than directly asking the person to act — use 도와주세요 when you want this specific person to help now. The classic English-speaker mistake is omitting 좀 and barking '도와주세요', or translating 'help me' as a command; always pad it with 좀 and ideally a reason.

structuredNuance.t: This is the all-purpose 'help me' you say to almost anyone — a shop clerk, a passerby, a coworker. The little word 좀 ('a bit') is not really about quantity; it softens the request and is almost mandatory, because '도와주세요' alone can sound blunt or like an emergency.
The nearest alternative is 도움이 필요해요 ('I need help'), which states your situation rather than directly asking the person to act — use 도와주세요 when you want this specific person to help now.
To go more casual drop to 도와줘 with friends; to go softer or more formal use 도와주시겠어요? or 도와주실 수 있어요?.
The classic English-speaker mistake is omitting 좀 and barking '도와주세요', or translating 'help me' as a command; always pad it with 좀 and ideally a reason.

examples.en: Um, I have a favor to ask.

examples.ko: 바쁘시겠지만 부탁이 있는데요, 혹시 시간 괜찮으세요?
examples.romanization: bappeusigetjiman butagi inneundeyo, hoksi sigan gwaenchaneuseyo?
examples.en: I know you're busy, but I have a favor — do you have a moment?

examples.en: I have a favor — I'm moving next week, could you help out?
examples.note: opener first, then the actual request, is the natural two-step order

entries.nuance: This is the polite 'warning shot' you fire before asking a real favor, giving the listener a second to brace and not feel ambushed. The -는데요 ending deliberately trails off ('I have a favor, but…'), which is softer than stating the favor outright. With friends drop to 부탁이 있는데; to a boss or stranger raise it to 부탁 좀 드려도 될까요? (드리다 is the humble form of 주다). The nearest alternative is jumping straight to 혹시…해 주실 수 있어요? ('could you possibly…'), which works for small asks; use 부탁이 있는데요 for bigger favors where you want to prepare the ground. English speakers often skip this opener and dive into the request, which feels abrupt to Koreans, or they mistranslate 'favor' as a direct demand — lead with 부탁이 있는데요 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Skipping the opener and stating the favor cold.
Koreans soften big asks by flagging them first. Say '부탁이 있는데요' then the request, rather than launching straight in.
Saying '부탁이 있어요' flatly to a superior.
The flat -어요 sounds like an announcement. The trailing '있는데요' or formal '부탁 좀 드려도 될까요?' is gentler and more appropriate upward.
Using 부탁 for a tiny ask like passing salt.
부탁 implies a real favor that costs the other person something. For trivial things just say '소금 좀 주세요' — reserve 부탁이 있는데요 for genuine favors.

entries.shortExplanation: 잠깐만요 is a practical expression meaning "Just a second / Hold on".
entries.explanation: "Just a second / Hold on" — that is 잠깐만요 (jamkkanmanyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 잠깐만요 ("Just a moment / Hold on"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

반말; to a friend — 'wait a sec'
slightly more formal/polished; common in service and phone settings

examples.ko: 잠깐만요, 금방 올게요.
examples.romanization: jamkkanmanyo, geumbang olgeyo.
examples.en: Hold on, I'll be right back.
examples.note: buys you a few seconds before you step away

examples.ko: 잠깐만요, 지나갈게요.
examples.romanization: jamkkanmanyo, jinagalgeyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, I'll squeeze through.
examples.note: in a packed subway/elevator, '잠깐만요' = 'let me get past'

examples.ko: 잠깐만요, 지금 계산 도와드릴게요.
examples.romanization: jamkkanmanyo, jigeum gyesan dowadeurilgeyo.
examples.en: One moment, I'll help you check out now.
examples.note: a cashier uses it to ask a customer to wait briefly

entries.nuance: 잠깐만요 does double duty: 'wait a second' and 'excuse me, coming through' in a crowd — context tells which. It's neutral-polite, fine for strangers and service. With friends it's 잠깐만; in polished/phone service 잠시만요 sounds a touch more refined. The nearest alternative for getting past someone is 실례합니다 ('excuse me'), which is more formal and apologetic; 잠깐만요 is quicker and more casual for everyday squeezing-by. The big English-speaker error is using 잠깐만요 to mean 'excuse me, may I ask you something' — for getting attention you want 저기요 or 실례지만, not 잠깐만요. Also note it stops an action ('hold on'), so don't use it to apologize.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 잠깐만요 to get a stranger's attention to ask a question.
잠깐만요 means 'wait' or 'let me pass', not 'excuse me, I have a question'. To flag someone down use '저기요' or '실례지만'.
Saying 잠깐만 to a boss or customer.
Bare 잠깐만 is 반말 and sounds curt upward. Use '잠깐만요' or the smoother '잠시만요' in any polite setting.
Confusing 잠깐만요 with '미안해요'.
It tells someone to wait; it is not an apology. If you bump someone, say '죄송합니다', not '잠깐만요'.

반말; to a friend or family member

entries.nuance: You say this when your hands are full and you want someone to hold or carry something briefly. The ending -ㄹ래요 literally asks 'are you willing to…', which feels warm and gives them room to agree, so it's gentler than a flat 들어 주세요. Drop to 들어 줄래? with friends; raise to 들어 주시겠어요? for strangers. Note the verb: 들다 = lift/hold in the hand, while 들고 있다 = keep holding it — say 들고 있어 주세요 if you need them to hold it for a while, not just take it once. English speakers often reach for the verb 잡다 ('grab/grip') here, but 잡다 is for gripping (a handle, a hand), not holding an object for someone; use 들다. Also don't say 캐리 or translate 'carry' as 나르다, which means hauling/transporting loads.

It's grammatically fine but feels like an order. -ㄹ래요 or -주시겠어요? asks their willingness and sounds more courteous.
Translating 'carry this' as '이것 나르세요'.
나르다 means transport/haul (loads, repeatedly). For 'hold this for me right now' the verb is 들다.

entries.nuance: This is the tourist-and-everyday phrase for asking a stranger to photograph you or your group. Open with 저기요 (to get attention) and add 좀; the -ㄹ래요 ending is friendly and easy to refuse, which is why it's preferred over a flat 찍어 주세요. entries.nuance: -아/어도 돼요? is THE permission pattern: '(if I) do X, is it okay?' So 들어가도 돼요? = 'is it okay if I enter?'. It's neutral-polite for any door — office, classroom, someone's room. Drop to 들어가도 돼? with friends; soften to 들어가도 될까요? upward or when you're unsure of a yes. entries.nuance: Same permission pattern (-아도 돼요?) applied to taking a seat — you ask the person nearby, not the empty chair. entries.nuance: This requests a slice of someone's time for a (often serious or private) conversation. -ㄹ 수 있을까요? ('would it be possible…') is tentative and polite, perfect for not imposing. With friends use 할 수 있어?; with a boss switch to the honorific frame 말씀 좀 나눌 수 있을까요?, where 말씀 is the respectful word for 'words/speech' and 나누다 ('to share') is the dignified verb for conversing. The nearest casual alternative is 얘기 좀 해 ('let's talk', 반말) or 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time?'); the dividing line is formality and how much you're imposing. English speakers tend to literally translate 'can we talk' as '우리 말할 수 있어요?' using 말하다, which sounds stiff and odd — Koreans say 얘기(하다) for casual talking and 말씀 나누다 when formal, rarely bare 말하다 for 'have a chat'. Also 잠깐/잠시 ('briefly') reassures them it's short.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '우리 말할 수 있어요?' for 'can we talk?'.
말하다 is 'to speak/say' and sounds stiff for a chat. Use '얘기 좀 할 수 있을까요?' (or formal '말씀 좀 나눌 수 있을까요?').
Using bare 얘기하자 to a superior.
That's casual 반말. Upward, raise the register: '잠시 말씀 좀 나눌 수 있을까요?'
Dropping 잠깐/잠시.
Without it the ask sounds open-ended and bigger. Adding '잠깐' signals it'll be quick, making people more willing.

English speakers tend to literally translate 'can we talk' as '우리 말할 수 있어요?' using 말하다, which sounds stiff and odd — Koreans say 얘기(하다) for casual talking and 말씀 나누다 when formal, rarely bare 말하다 for 'have a chat'.

entries.nuance: The go-to pattern for borrowing small things. Key verb split: 빌리다 = borrow (you receive), 빌려주다 = lend (they give) — so '제가 빌릴 수 있을까요?' (I borrow) and '빌려주실 수 있어요?' (you lend) are two sides of the same request; both are natural, just different subjects. Polite default is -ㄹ 수 있을까요? or -아도 될까요?; with friends use -빌릴 수 있어?. The classic English-speaker mistake is mixing up 빌리다 and 빌려주다 — saying '빌려줄 수 있을까요?' when you mean YOU want to borrow makes you the lender by accident; if the subject is you, it must be 빌리다. Another trap is the English habit of 'borrow me a pen' — there's no such thing; either you 빌리다 or they 빌려주다. Add 좀 to soften, as always.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '펜 좀 빌려줄 수 있을까요?' when YOU want to borrow.
빌려주다 = lend (they give). If the subject is you, use 빌리다: '펜 좀 빌릴 수 있을까요?' (Use 빌려주다 only as '빌려주실 수 있어요?' = you lend me.)

대여하다 is formal/commercial ('rent/lease', e.g. equipment). For borrowing a pen from a person, it's 빌리다.

'펜 빌릴 수 있을까요?' is understandable but bare. Native speakers add 좀: '펜 좀 빌릴 수 있을까요?'

entries.shortExplanation: 자리 좀 바꿔도 될까요? is a practical expression meaning "Would it be okay to switch seats?".
entries.explanation: 자리 좀 바꿔도 될까요? (jari jom bakkwodo doelkkayo?) = "Would it be okay to switch seats?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 자리 좀 바꿔도 될까요? ("Could we switch seats?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.en: Could you switch seats with me, please?
usagePhrases.note: more deferential; asks them to do you the favor of swapping

usagePhrases.romanization: hoksi jeorang jari jom bakkwo jusil su isseoyo?
usagePhrases.en: Could you possibly swap seats with me?
usagePhrases.note: natural extension; '저랑' makes clear it's a swap with you

examples.ko: 자리 좀 바꿔도 될까요?
examples.romanization: jari jom bakkwodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: Could we switch seats?
examples.note: asking the neighbor when you'd rather sit elsewhere

examples.ko: 일행이랑 같이 앉고 싶어서요, 자리 좀 바꿔도 될까요?
examples.romanization: ilhaengirang gachi anjgo sipeoseoyo, jari jom bakkwodo doelkkayo?
examples.en: I'd like to sit with my companion — could we switch seats?
examples.note: the reason (sitting together) is the usual, well-received justification

examples.ko: 창가 자리시죠? 제가 멀미를 해서요, 혹시 자리 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: changga jarisijyo? jega meolmireul haeseoyo, hoksi jari jom bakkwo jusil su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: You've got the window seat, right? I get motion sick — could we possibly swap?
examples.note: polite, reason-first; 멀미 (motion sickness) is a sympathetic excuse

entries.nuance: Used to ask a stranger or friend to swap seats — on a train, plane, or in a theater. 바꾸다 = change/swap; with -아도 될까요? it asks permission, while 바꿔 주실 수 있을까요? (with 주다) frames it as a favor THEY do for you, which is even more polite for a stranger. Casual is 바꿔도 돼?. Because you're imposing on a stranger's comfort, always give a reason (sitting with family, motion sickness) and use 혹시 ('by any chance') to soften. The nearest alternative 자리 좀 옮겨도 될까요? uses 옮기다 (move/relocate) and means 'may I move (myself) to another seat' — a different action from swapping, so don't confuse them: 바꾸다 = trade places, 옮기다 = relocate yourself. English speakers sometimes say '자리 좀 바꿀 수 있어요?' (ability) instead of permission/favor, or forget 저랑/주다 so it's unclear it's a mutual swap.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 바꾸다 (swap) with 옮기다 (move yourself).
'자리 바꾸다' = trade seats with someone; '자리 옮기다' = relocate to a different seat. Use 바꾸다 when you want them to swap with you.
Asking with bare ability: '자리 바꿀 수 있어요?'.
That asks if it's physically possible. For a polite request use '자리 좀 바꿔도 될까요?' or the favor form '바꿔 주실 수 있을까요?'
Not giving a reason or 혹시.
Swapping inconveniences a stranger. Soften with '혹시' and a reason ('일행이랑 같이 앉고 싶어서요') so they're willing.

examples.romanization: joesonghande cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo.
examples.en: Sorry, please speak slowly.

examples.ko: 제가 한국어를 잘 못해서요, 천천히 말해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jega hangugeoreul jal motaeseoyo, cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo.

examples.ko: 죄송하지만 조금만 더 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요? 잘 못 알아들어서요.

entries.nuance: A learner's lifeline: ask the speaker to slow down. 천천히 = slowly; the benefactive 주세요 makes it 'do it for me'. Polite default is 말해 주세요; formal/upward becomes 말씀해 주시겠어요?, where 말씀하다 is the honorific 'to speak'. The classic mistake is using 느리게 instead of 천천히 — 느리다 means slow as in low-speed/sluggish (a slow car, slow internet), and 느리게 말하다 sounds like you want them to drag each word oddly; for 'speak at a slower pace' Koreans say 천천히. Pair it with 조금/조금만 ('a little') to sound less demanding. Another trap is leaving off 주세요 and saying just '천천히 말해요', which sounds like you're describing or commanding flatly. Mentioning you're a learner ('한국어를 잘 못해서요') almost always gets a warm, slower response.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '느리게 말해 주세요'.
느리다 means low-speed/sluggish and sounds off for speech pace. The natural word is 천천히: '천천히 말해 주세요.'
Dropping 주세요: '천천히 말해요'.
Without the benefactive it sounds flat or like a statement. Keep '말해 주세요' so it's a request done for you.
Using plain 말해 to a stranger or elder.
That's curt/반말. Raise it: '천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?' with the honorific 말씀하다.

entries.explanation: "Please say that again" — that is 다시 한번 말해 주세요 (dasi hanbeon malhae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 다시 한번 말해 주세요 ("Please say that one more time"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.en: Please say that one more time
usagePhrases.note: 존댓말; ask someone to repeat what they said
반말; to a friend

usagePhrases.en: Could you say that again, please?
usagePhrases.note: 격식/honorific; 말씀하다 for a stranger, elder, or on the phone
natural alternative; the quick everyday 'come again?'

examples.ko: 네? 다시 한번 말해 주세요.
examples.romanization: ne? dasi hanbeon malhae juseyo.
examples.en: Sorry? Please say that again.
examples.note: '네?' with rising tone signals you didn't catch it, then the request

examples.ko: 잘 못 들었어요. 다시 한번 말해 주세요.
examples.romanization: jal mot deureosseoyo. dasi hanbeon malhae juseyo.
examples.en: I didn't hear well. Please say it again.
examples.note: '잘 못 들었어요' politely explains why you need a repeat

examples.ko: 죄송한데 성함을 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: joesonghande seonghameul dasi hanbeon malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, could you tell me your name once more?
examples.note: asking specifically (성함=name) is clearer than a vague 'again'

entries.nuance: Your repair tool when you miss what someone said. 다시 = again, 한번 = once (here softening, 'one more time'). Polite default 말해 주세요; upward/formal 말씀해 주시겠어요?. The very common spoken alternative is 뭐라고요? / 뭐라고 하셨어요? ('sorry, what?'), which is quick and natural; 다시 한번 말해 주세요 is a fuller, calmer request — the dividing line is that 뭐라고요? reacts in the moment, while 다시 한번… explicitly asks for a repeat. English speakers sometimes say '한 번 더' literally as 'one more' but forget 다시 or 주세요, or they say '리피트' / translate 'repeat' as 반복하다 — 반복하다 means repeat as in do-over/loop (drills, processes), not 'say it again', so it sounds robotic. Stick with 다시 한번 말해 주세요. Saying 'sorry' (죄송한데) first makes it gracious.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 반복하다: '반복해 주세요'.
반복하다 = repeat an action/loop (e.g., a drill). To re-say something use '다시 한번 말해 주세요.'

structuredNuance.t: Your repair tool when you miss what someone said. 다시 = again, 한번 = once (here softening, 'one more time'). Saying 'sorry' (죄송한데) first makes it gracious.

The very common spoken alternative is 뭐라고요? / 뭐라고 하셨어요? ('sorry, what?'), which is quick and natural; 다시 한번 말해 주세요 is a fuller, calmer request — the dividing line is that 뭐라고요? reacts in the moment, while 다시 한번… explicitly asks for a repeat.
Polite default 말해 주세요; upward/formal 말씀해 주시겠어요?.

English speakers sometimes say '한 번 더' literally as 'one more' but forget 다시 or 주세요, or they say '리피트' / translate 'repeat' as 반복하다 — 반복하다 means repeat as in do-over/loop (drills, processes), not 'say it again', so it sounds robotic. Stick with 다시 한번 말해 주세요.

entries.nuance: A close cousin of 다시 한번 말해 주세요, but the particle 만 ('only/just') frames it as 'just this once more' — humble and apologetic, as if you hate to trouble them again. Same register ladder: 말해 줘 (friend) → 말해 주세요 (polite) → 말씀해 주시겠어요? (formal). The dividing line vs. 다시 한번 말해 주세요: 다시 한번 is a neutral 'again', while 한 번만 더 stresses you only need one more pass (often after already asking, or on a fading phone line) and sounds extra modest thanks to 만. A frequent English-speaker error is dropping 만 or putting the spacing wrong: it's 한 번 (counter 번 spaced from 한) and the softener 만 attaches to 번 → 한 번만. Also avoid translating 'one more time' as '한 시간 더' (that's 'one more hour'!) — 번 is the counter for times/occurrences, not 시간 (hours).

시간 = hour; 번 = a time/occurrence. 'One more time' is '한 번 더', so '한 번만 더 말해 주세요.'
Dropping 만 so it loses the 'just once' nuance.
만 = only/just, which makes it modest. '한 번만 더' signals you need exactly one more repeat — keep the 만.

As a counter it's spaced: '한 번' + 만 → '한 번만'. (The fused '한번' means 'sometime/once' in a different sense.)

entries.nuance: The everyday 'how does this work / how do I do this' for machines, forms, apps, kiosks. The -는 거예요? ending (= 'is it the case that…') makes it a natural spoken question, softer than a bare 어떻게 해요?. Casual is 어떻게 하는 거야?. If it's specifically a device, 어떻게 사용해요?/사용하는 거예요? (use 사용하다) is just as good. The nearest alternative 이거 어떻게 써요? uses 쓰다 ('use', casual) and is fine for gadgets, but 쓰다 also means 'write', so context matters. The big English-speaker mistake is translating literally as '이거 어떻게 일해요?' using 일하다 — 일하다 means 'to work' as in a person doing a job, NOT a machine functioning; for 'how does it work' you say 어떻게 하는 거예요? or 어떻게 작동해요? (작동하다 = operate/function, more technical). Also keep 거 (thing) — '어떻게 하는 거예요?' sounds far more natural than bare '어떻게 해요?'.

Using bare '어떻게 해요?' with no 거.
It's understandable but blunt. The natural spoken form keeps 거: '이거 어떻게 하는 거예요?'
Mixing up 쓰다 'use' and 'write'.
'이거 어떻게 써요?' can read as 'how do I write this?'. To be clear about operating it, use '어떻게 하는 거예요?' or '어떻게 사용하는 거예요?'

entries.nuance: The polished, slightly more formal sibling of 잠깐만요 — used when YOU ask someone else to wait, especially in service, on the phone, or at a counter. 잠시 (a moment) is a touch more refined than 잠깐, and the full 기다려 주세요 explicitly says 'please wait (for me)'. Casual is 잠깐만 기다려 줘; very formal service uses 기다려 주시겠어요? or 기다려 주시면 감사하겠습니다. The difference from bare 잠깐만요: 잠깐만요 is a quick 'hold on/coming through' you toss off in any direction, while 잠시만 기다려 주세요 is a complete, courteous request to wait, fitting when you're serving or addressing someone formally. English speakers sometimes command '기다리세요' ('wait!') without 주다, which sounds bossy; the benefactive 기다려 주세요 ('wait for me, please') is the polite form. Don't confuse 기다리다 (wait) with 기대하다 (look forward to/expect).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying '기다리세요' without 주다.
Bare 기다리세요 can sound like an order. The polite request is '기다려 주세요' (wait for me, please).
Confusing 기다리다 and 기대하다.
기다리다 = wait; 기대하다 = look forward to/expect. To ask someone to wait, it's '잠시만 기다려 주세요.'
Using 잠깐만요 when serving a customer formally.
That's casual and clipped. In service, the complete courteous form is '잠시만 기다려 주세요' or '기다려 주시겠어요?'

entries.nuance: An everyday ask for someone to glance at or check something — a form, a screen, a piece of writing. 보다 = look/see; with 주다 it's 'look at it for me', and the -ㄹ 수 있어요? frame makes it a gentle request. Casual is 봐 줄래?; formal/upward is 봐 주시겠어요?. The nearest alternative is 확인해 주실 수 있어요? — the dividing line: 봐 주다 = take a look / glance over (informal check), while 확인하다 = verify/confirm something is correct (a fact, a number, a reservation). English speakers sometimes use 보다's literal 'see' and say odd things like '이것 좀 보세요' as a command ('look at this!'), which sounds like you're pointing something out, not requesting help — keep the benefactive 봐 주다 for 'check this for me'. Also don't overuse 체크하다 (Konglish 'check'); 확인하다 is the natural Korean.

체크하다 is Konglish. The natural verb for verifying is 확인하다: '이것 좀 확인해 주실 수 있어요?'

The benefactive 봐 주다 ('look for me') is what makes it a request done on your behalf. Keep 주다 so it's clearly help, not a command.

entries.explanation: "I don't think I can make it today" — that is 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 (oneul mot gal geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 ("I don't think I can make it today"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 is 못 ('cannot') + 가다 ('to go') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('it seems / I think'), so literally 'it seems I can't go today.' The whole trick is the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge: Korean almost never says a flat 못 가요 ('I can't go') to cancel, because that sounds blunt and final, almost rude. Wrapping it in 같아요 ('I think / it seems') softens it into a gentle, apologetic 'I don't think I can make it' — even when you are 100% sure you can't go, you still say 같아요. This is the single most useful cancel-line a newcomer needs. The near alternative 안 갈 것 같아요 uses 안 ('won't, by choice') instead of 못 ('can't, prevented'), and that difference matters: 못 가요 means something is stopping you (work, illness), which sounds like a valid excuse, while 안 가요 means you simply choose not to go, which can sound like you just don't want to — so for canceling, default to 못. The classic English-speaker pitfall is translating 'I can't make it' word-for-word and dropping the hedge, producing a cold 오늘 못 가요; add 것 같아요 and a 미안한데/죄송한데 opener. Register: 같아요 (polite) for most people, 같습니다 for work/superiors, 같아 only with close friends.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying a flat 오늘 못 가요 to cancel.
Without the hedge it sounds blunt and final, almost like a refusal. Soften it to 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요 — the -ㄹ 것 같다 makes it polite and apologetic even when you're certain.
Using 안 갈 것 같아요 when something is preventing you.
안 = 'won't (by choice)', which can sound like you just don't feel like coming. If circumstances stop you, use 못 ('can't'): 오늘 못 갈 것 같아요.
Mistranslating 'make it' literally with 만들다.
'Make it' here is idiomatic English for 'attend'. 만들다 means 'to build/create' — never 오늘 못 만들어요. Use 못 가요/못 갈 것 같아요.

entries.nuance: 갑자기 일이 생겨서요 is 갑자기 ('suddenly') + 일 ('a matter/thing/work') + 생기다 ('to arise/come up') + -어서 ('because') + 요 (polite ender), i.e. 'because something suddenly came up.' This is the socially perfect vague excuse: 일 is deliberately broad — it can mean work, an errand, a family thing, anything — so you can bow out without disclosing private details, and Koreans accept it without prying. The trailing -서요 (reason + 요, with the main clause left unsaid) is extremely natural and polite; it implies '…so I can't make it' without you having to spell out the blunt part. Watch the verb: it must be 생기다 ('to arise', intransitive), so 일이 생겼어요 ('a matter arose'); learners wrongly use 만들다 ('make') and say 일을 만들었어요, which means 'I created trouble/work' — wrong nuance entirely. Particle trap: it's 일이 (subject) with 생기다, not 일을. Compare 바빠서요 ('because I'm busy'), which is fine but can sound like a weaker brush-off; 일이 생겨서요 implies a concrete unforeseen event and lands as a stronger, more legitimate reason. The 갑자기 ('suddenly') is what signals this wasn't your fault — keep it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 일을 만들었어요 to mean 'something came up'.
만들다 ('make') + 일을 means 'I created work/trouble'. The event-arising verb is 생기다, used with 이: 일이 생겼어요 / 일이 생겨서요.
Wrong particle: 일을 생겨서요.
생기다 is intransitive and takes the subject particle: 일이 생겨서요, not 일을. The thing 'arises' on its own; you don't act on it.

The point of 일이 생겨서요 is its vagueness — Koreans won't pry. Volunteering every detail can sound like over-justifying; the trailing -서요 is enough.

entries.nuance: 약속 취소해도 될까요? is 약속 ('plans/an appointment/a promise') + 취소하다 ('to cancel', Sino-Korean 取消) + -아도 되다 ('is it okay to…') + -ㄹ까요 ('I wonder, may I?'). Framing the cancellation as a permission question — 'would it be okay if…' — is the polite, face-saving move: instead of announcing you ARE canceling, you ask whether you may, handing the other person dignity. Note 약속 is a big, important word: it covers plans to meet, an appointment, AND a promise, so canceling 약속 carries a slight weight of breaking your word — which is exactly why you ask so gently. The near alternative 약속 취소할게요 ('I'll cancel our plans', with -ㄹ게요) just DECLARES the cancellation and can feel one-sided/abrupt for plans with another person; reserve 취소할게요 for impersonal bookings (a reservation, a delivery). The negative-question variant 취소하면 안 될까요? ('would it be a problem if I canceled?') sounds even more pleading and apologetic — handy when you feel bad. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) saying 약속을 깨다 ('break the appointment') — 깨다 is harsh, literally 'shatter the promise', and sounds like a serious betrayal; use 취소하다 for a normal cancel. (2) Treating 약속 as only 'a promise' and avoiding it for plans — it's the right word for 'our plans to meet'.

깨다 ('break/shatter') sounds like betraying a serious promise. For ordinary plans use 취소하다: 약속 취소해도 될까요?
Declaring 약속 취소할게요 to a person.
-ㄹ게요 announces your decision and can feel abrupt for plans involving someone else. Ask permission instead: 취소해도 될까요? Save 취소할게요 for bookings/reservations.
Confusing 약속 with only 'a promise'.
약속 also means 'plans/an appointment to meet'. 'Cancel our plans' is 약속 취소하다 — it's the correct everyday word, not just for breaking a vow.

entries.nuance: 약속 시간 좀 바꿔도 될까요? is 약속 시간 ('meeting time') + 좀 (softener) + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). Crucial distinction from the previous card: this CHANGES the time but KEEPS the plan, whereas 취소 cancels it — and Koreans much prefer rescheduling to canceling, so this is the friendlier ask. 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for 'change/swap'; the Sino-Korean 변경하다 means the same but is more formal and shows up in business/official contexts (변경하다 a flight, a meeting, a reservation). If you specifically want it LATER, the precise verb is 미루다 or 늦추다 ('postpone/push back'); if EARLIER, 당기다 ('move up'). The 좀 here is a politeness lubricant, not 'a little' — though you can add 조금만 ('just a little') for a small shift: 시간 조금만 바꿔도 될까요?. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using 바꾸다 with the wrong particle pattern — say 시간을 바꾸다 ('change the time'), and to swap A for B it's A를 B로 바꾸다 (e.g. 3시를 5시로 바꾸다, 'change 3 to 5'); learners drop the -로 on the new time. (2) Saying 시간을 옮기다 — 옮기다 ('move/relocate') is more for physically moving things or moving a date/venue (날짜를 옮기다 works), but for the clock time, 바꾸다/미루다 is more natural.

To replace A with B you mark the new value with -로: 3시를 5시로 바꿔도 될까요? ('change 3 to 5'). Without -로 it's incomplete.
Using formal 변경하다 with a close friend.
변경하다 is Sino-Korean and sounds official/business-like. With friends use the everyday 바꾸다: 시간 좀 바꿔도 돼?
Saying 시간을 옮기다 for the clock time.
옮기다 ('move/relocate') fits dates or venues (날짜를 옮기다) better than the time of day. For the time, prefer 바꾸다 or, for 'later', 미루다/늦추다.

entries.nuance: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? is 다른 날 ('another day') + -로 (direction particle, 'to') + 미루다 ('to postpone/put off') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). 미루다 is THE verb for postponing — pushing an event to a later point — and it's the heart of polite rescheduling. The particle -로 on 다른 날 ('to another day') is essential and exactly where learners slip: you move it TO a day, so 다른 날로, 다음 주로, 주말로; dropping the -로 (saying 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요) sounds off. Two contrasts to know: (1) 미루다 vs. 취소하다 — 미루다 keeps the plan alive for later (much preferred socially), 취소하다 kills it; reach for 미루다 whenever you can still meet, just not now. (2) 미루다 vs. 연기하다 — 연기하다 (Sino-Korean 延期) means the same 'postpone' but is formal/official (postponing an event, a wedding, a match: 경기가 연기됐다); for casual plans use 미루다, for official announcements use 연기하다/연기되다. English-speaker pitfall: 미루다 can also mean 'to procrastinate/keep putting off' (일을 자꾸 미루다 = 'keep putting work off'), so in the right frame it's neutral 'reschedule', but be aware tone — paired with a reason and 다른 날로 it clearly means 'postpone to another day', not 'I'm lazily delaying'. Don't confuse 미루다 with 밀다 ('to push physically').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -로: 다른 날 미뤄도 될까요?
You postpone something TO a day, so the target takes -로: 다른 날로 미뤄도 될까요? Without -로 the destination is unmarked and sounds incomplete.
Using 연기하다 for casual plans with a friend.
연기하다 is formal/official ('postpone an event'). For everyday plans say 미루다: 다른 날로 미뤄도 돼? Save 연기되다 for matches/ceremonies.
Confusing 미루다 with 밀다.
밀다 is 'to push (physically)' or 'to shove'. 'Postpone' is 미루다. 약속을 밀다 isn't the idiom — say 약속을 미루다 / 다른 날로 미루다.

entries.nuance: 다음에 봬요 is 다음에 ('next time / another time') + 봬요 (the contracted polite form of 뵈어요, from 뵙다, the humble verb 'to see/meet someone respectfully'). This is the gentle sign-off that softens a cancellation — by promising a future meeting, it signals 'no hard feelings, we'll still get together.' The spelling/sound is a notorious trap: 봬요 (= 뵈어요) is correct, NOT 뵈요; in speech both sound like 'bwae-yo', but 뵈요 is a misspelling — many natives get this wrong too. Register nuance: 뵙다 is humble (you lower yourself before the person you're meeting), so 봬요/뵐게요 is warmer and more respectful than the plain 봐요/볼게요 (from 보다). To an elder, boss, or someone you respect, 다음에 뵐게요 is lovely; among peers 다음에 봬요 or casual 다음에 봐 is fine. The near alternative 다음에 만나요 (from 만나다 'to meet') is also correct and a bit more neutral/direct, but 봬요 carries that humble politeness. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) writing 뵈요 instead of 봬요. (2) Treating 'next time' literally and pinning a date — 다음에 is intentionally vague ('sometime'), a friendly soft promise, not a commitment to a specific next meeting; if you DO want a real plan, say 다음에 언제 볼까요? ('when shall we meet next?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Writing or saying 뵈요 instead of 봬요.
봬요 is the contraction of 뵈어요; 뵈요 is a misspelling. When in doubt, expand it: 뵈어요 → 봬요. (Same logic as 돼요 from 되어요.)
Using plain 봐요 to an elder/superior.
보다's plain 봐요 is fine among peers, but for respect use the humble 뵙다: 다음에 뵐게요/봬요 lowers yourself politely before them.
Reading 다음에 as a firm commitment.
다음에 봬요 is a warm, vague 'sometime'. It doesn't fix a date. To actually schedule, follow up with 언제 볼까요? or 날짜 정해요.

entries.explanation: "I think I'll be a little late" — that is 조금 늦을 것 같아요 (jogeum neujeul geot gatayo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 조금 늦을 것 같아요 ("I think I'll be a little late"). entries.nuance: 조금 늦을 것 같아요 is 조금 ('a little') + 늦다 ('to be late') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('I think / it seems'). This isn't a cancel — it's the polite running-late heads-up, and in Korea sending it the moment you know is basic courtesy. Again the -ㄹ 것 같다 hedge does the politeness work, but here it also genuinely means 'I expect to be late' (a prediction), so 같아요 is doubly natural. The verb is the adjective 늦다 ('to be late'); learners confuse it with 늦추다 ('to delay/push back something'), which is transitive — you 늦추다 a meeting, but YOU yourself 늦다. So 'I'll be late' = 늦을 것 같아요, never 늦출 것 같아요. Pair it with a number (5분/10분 늦을 것 같아요) and a reason (길이 막혀서 'because of traffic', 차가 막혀서 'traffic's jammed') to be considerate. The near alternative 늦어요 (flat 'I'm late') sounds abrupt and after-the-fact; 늦을 것 같아요 is a forward-looking, apologetic warning. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) confusing 늦다 (be late) with 느리다 ('to be slow' in speed) — 'I'll be late' is 늦다, not 느려요. (2) Forgetting that Koreans expect the proactive text; silently arriving late is read as rude — fire off 조금 늦을 것 같아요 early.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 늦출 것 같아요 to mean 'I'll be late'.
늦추다 is transitive ('delay something', e.g. a meeting). For your own lateness use the adjective 늦다: 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
Confusing 늦다 with 느리다.
느리다 = 'slow (in speed)'; 늦다 = 'late (in time)'. 'I'll be late' is 늦을 것 같아요, not 느릴 것 같아요.
Just showing up late with no message.
In Korea a proactive heads-up is expected courtesy. Text 조금 늦을 것 같아요 (ideally with minutes + reason) as soon as you know, rather than arriving silently late.

The engine is 말고, which means 'not X (but rather)' and is the natural way to say 'instead of': X 말고 Y = 'Y instead of X'. This card teaches you to COUNTER-PROPOSE rather than just cancel — far more cooperative, and Koreans appreciate it. Key contrast: 말고 vs. 아니고. Both can translate 'not… but…', yet 말고 is for choosing/substituting between options ('give me this 말고 that', 'tomorrow 말고 today'), while 아니고 corrects a fact ('he's not a teacher 아니고 a student'). For swapping a day, you want 말고. The synonym 대신(에) ('instead, in place of') also works and is slightly more formal: 오늘 대신 내일. 어때요? is the friendly 'how about?'; to a superior, raise it to 어떠세요?. (2) Calquing 'instead of' as 대신에 everywhere including casual chat, which can sound stiff — among friends 말고 is breezier. (3) Forgetting 어때요 already means 'how about', so don't add extra words like 어떻게 생각해요 ('what do you think') unless you want a fuller opinion.

entries.nuance: 혹시 시간 되세요? is 혹시 ('by any chance / perhaps') + 시간 ('time') + 되다 ('to work out / be available') + -세요 (honorific). When you're rearranging plans, you first need to find a slot that suits the other person, and this is the courteous way to ask 'are you free?'. Two pieces matter. First, 혹시 ('by any chance') is a politeness softener that makes any request tentative and non-pushy — Koreans sprinkle it before favors and questions; here it signals 'no pressure if not'. Second, 시간(이) 되다 is an idiom: 되다 literally 'to become/work out', so 시간 돼요? = 'does the time work (for you)?' = 'are you free?'. Don't translate 'have time' with 가지다 ('to possess') — 시간을 가지다 is unidiomatic for availability; Koreans say 시간(이) 되다 or 시간(이) 있다. The honorific is 시간 되세요? (raising the other person); plain polite is 시간 돼요?; 반말 is 시간 돼?. Near alternative 시간 있으세요? ('do you have time?') is also perfectly natural and interchangeable; 시간 되세요? leans slightly toward 'does it work out schedule-wise', 있으세요? toward 'do you have any free time' — both fine. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping 혹시 and asking a bare 시간 있어요?, which is fine but a touch more direct/demanding; 혹시 cushions it. (2) Using 가지다 for 'have time'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 시간을 가지고 있어요? for 'do you have time?'.
가지다 ('possess') doesn't fit availability. Use the idiom 시간(이) 되다 or 시간(이) 있다: 혹시 시간 되세요? / 시간 있으세요?
Omitting 혹시 so it sounds demanding.
혹시 ('by any chance') softens the ask and signals no pressure. 혹시 시간 되세요? is gentler than a bare 시간 돼요? before requesting a favor.
Confusing 되세요 (honorific of 되다) with 데세요.
It's 시간 되세요? from 되다 ('to work out'). 데다 ('to get burned') is unrelated — mind the 되/데 spelling so it stays 되세요.

entries.nuance: 일정이 안 맞을 것 같아요 is 일정 ('schedule/itinerary', Sino-Korean 日程) + -이 + 안 ('not') + 맞다 ('to fit/match') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('I think'). This is the graceful way to decline a proposed time without blaming anyone — instead of 'I can't', you say 'the schedules don't line up', which is face-saving and blame-free. The verb 맞다 here means 'to fit/coincide', so 일정이 맞다 = 'schedules match', 일정이 안 맞다 = 'they don't match'; the subject is 일정이 (use 이/가, not 을/를 — 맞다 in this sense is intransitive). 일정 is the formal/neutral word for one's schedule; the loanword 스케줄 is more casual-conversational, and 약속(들) ('appointments') is more concrete. A stronger, more formal way to state a clash is 일정이 겹치다 ('schedules overlap/collide'), common in work emails. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using 맞다 with 을/를 — say 일정이 안 맞아요, not 일정을 안 맞아요. (2) Confusing this 맞다 ('fit/be correct') with 맞추다 ('to adjust/coordinate, make things fit') — 일정을 맞추다 means 'to coordinate schedules (actively)', a different, useful phrase ('let's coordinate our schedules'), whereas 일정이 안 맞다 is the passive 'they don't fit'. (3) The 것 같아요 hedge again keeps it soft; a flat 일정이 안 맞아요 is fine but blunter for declining.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Marking 일정 with 을/를: 일정을 안 맞아요.
In the 'fit/match' sense 맞다 is intransitive and takes 이/가: 일정이 안 맞아요. Use 을/를 only with 맞추다 ('to coordinate'): 일정을 맞추다.
Confusing 맞다 with 맞추다.
일정이 안 맞다 = 'schedules don't fit' (passive). 일정을 맞추다 = 'coordinate schedules' (active). Don't say 일정이 안 맞춰요 — that mixes them up.
Using formal 일정 with very casual friends only via that word.
일정 is fine but a bit formal; chatting with friends, 스케줄 안 맞아 or 그날 시간 안 돼 sounds more natural. Match the word to the register.

entries.nuance: 약속 시간 다시 잡을까요? is 약속 시간 ('meeting time') + 다시 ('again') + 잡다 ('to grab/set/fix') + -ㄹ까요? ('shall we?'). The idiom is 약속(을) 잡다 / 시간(을) 잡다 — literally 'to grab a time', meaning 'to set/arrange an appointment'; 다시 잡다 = 'set it again' = 'reschedule'. This is the positive, forward-moving phrase that turns a cancellation into a new plan, and -ㄹ까요? ('shall we?') invites the other person to decide together, which is collaborative and polite. 잡다 is wonderfully idiomatic for scheduling (약속 잡다 'make plans', 날짜 잡다 'set a date', 회의 잡다 'set up a meeting'); a close synonym is 정하다 ('to decide/fix'), used more for the date/number itself (날짜를 정하다 'fix the date'). English-speaker pitfalls: (1) translating 'set up a meeting' with 만들다 ('make') — 약속을 만들다 is unnatural; the verb is 잡다 (or 정하다). (2) Reaching for the Sino-Korean 재조정하다 ('readjust/reschedule') — it exists but is bureaucratic; everyday speech is 다시 잡다. (3) Particle: it's 약속을 잡다 (object + 잡다); in casual speech the 을 often drops (약속 잡다), which is fine, but don't swap in a wrong particle. -ㄹ까요? specifically suggests doing it together; if you want to state YOU'll set it, use 다시 잡을게요 ('I'll reschedule it').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약속을 만들다 for 'make plans / set up'.
만들다 ('build/create') doesn't collocate with 약속. The verb is 잡다: 약속(을) 잡다, 시간 잡다, 다시 잡을까요?
Using bureaucratic 재조정하다 in casual talk.
재조정하다 sounds like office jargon. For everyday rescheduling say 다시 잡다: 약속 다시 잡을까? / 시간 다시 잡을까요?
Confusing -ㄹ까요? with -ㄹ게요.
-ㄹ까요? ('shall we?') asks the other person to decide together. -ㄹ게요 ('I'll…') declares your own action. To re-set jointly: 다시 잡을까요?; to take charge: 다시 잡을게요.

entries.nuance: 급한 일이 생겨서 못 갈 것 같아요 combines three building blocks you've met: 급한 ('urgent', from 급하다) + 일이 생기다 ('something came up') + -어서 ('so') + 못 갈 것 같아요 ('I don't think I can go'). It's the heavyweight cancellation — adding 급한 ('urgent') signals the matter is serious and genuinely unavoidable, which makes your cancel sound legitimate rather than flaky, especially to a boss or for an important event. The whole phrase is a model of natural Korean excuse-structure: vague-but-serious reason (급한 일이 생겨서) + softened inability (못 갈 것 같아요). 급하다 means 'to be urgent/in a hurry'; common collocations are 급한 일 ('urgent matter'), 급한 약속 ('urgent appointment'), 급해요 ('I'm in a hurry / it's urgent'). The connector -어서 ('because/so') links cause to result and is the right choice for giving a reason that leads to a consequence; learners sometimes use -니까, but -어서 is more natural and softer for apologetic reasons (and crucially, -어서 cannot attach to imperative/suggestion endings, which is fine here since we end in a statement). English-speaker pitfalls: (1) saying 바쁜 일 ('busy matter') — wrong; 바쁘다 describes a person being busy, not a matter; the matter is 급한 일 ('urgent'). (2) Over-detailing the emergency; 급한 일 is enough and respects Korean discretion. (3) Confusing 급하다 ('urgent') with 빠르다 ('fast in speed') — an urgent matter is 급한 일, not 빠른 일.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 바쁜 일이 생겨서 for 'something urgent'.
바쁘다 describes a busy person, not a matter. An urgent matter is 급한 일: 급한 일이 생겨서 못 갈 것 같아요.
Confusing 급하다 with 빠르다.
급하다 = 'urgent / in a hurry'; 빠르다 = 'fast (speed)'. The reason is 급한 일 ('urgent matter'), never 빠른 일.
Using -니까 instead of -어서 for the apologetic reason.
For excuses leading to 'so I can't go', -어서 sounds softer and more natural: 생겨서 못 갈 것 같아요. -니까 can feel more assertive/justifying here.

entries.shortExplanation: 혹시 약속 미뤄도 괜찮을까요? is a practical expression meaning "Would it be alright if we postponed our plans?".
entries.explanation: "Would it be alright if we postponed our plans?" — that is 혹시 약속 미뤄도 괜찮을까요? (hoksi yaksong mirwodo gwaenchaneulkkayo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 혹시 약속 미뤄도 괜찮을까요? ("Would it be alright to postpone our plans?"). entries.nuance: 혹시 약속 미뤄도 괜찮을까요? layers up the politeness: 혹시 ('by any chance') + 약속 ('plans') + 미루다 ('postpone') + -아도 괜찮다 ('is it okay to…') + -ㄹ까요 ('I wonder if…'). This is the most deferential reschedule request — you'd use it when you feel bad about asking, or with someone you want to be extra careful with. The difference between -아도 괜찮을까요? and -아도 될까요? (from the earlier card) is subtle: both ask permission, but 괜찮을까요? ('would it be alright / would you mind') foregrounds the other person's comfort and feels a touch warmer and more apologetic, while 될까요? ('would it be possible / may I') is a hair more neutral/practical — for a delicate cancel, 괜찮을까요? is lovely. Stacking 혹시 at the front and -ㄹ까요 at the end is a classic Korean politeness sandwich: tentative opener + 'I wonder' ender. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) translating 'is it okay' as 괜찮아요? in statement-form rather than the questioning -ㄹ까요?, losing some softness — 괜찮을까요? is gentler than 괜찮아요?. (2) Over-stacking honorifics incorrectly — to a superior, 괜찮으실까요? (with the subject-honorific -시-) is right because you're asking about THEIR feeling; learners drop the -시- or misplace it. (3) Remember 미루다 keeps the plan (good!), so pair it with a goodwill follow-up like 다음 주는 언제든 괜찮아요 ('I'm free anytime next week') to show you really do want to meet.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 약속 미뤄도 괜찮아요? (flat) to be polite.
The statement-form 괜찮아요? is okay but less soft. The questioning -ㄹ까요 is gentler and more deferential: 미뤄도 괜찮을까요?
Dropping -시- with a superior: 괜찮을까요? where 괜찮으실까요? fits.
When you ask about the OTHER person's comfort and they outrank you, add subject-honorific -시-: 괜찮으실까요? It honors them.
Forgetting to offer goodwill after asking to postpone.
Since 미루다 keeps the plan alive, a Korean speaker softens the ask with a follow-up like 다음 주는 언제든 괜찮아요. Just asking to postpone without it can feel one-sided.

structuredNuance.t: Layers up the politeness: 혹시 ('by any chance') + 약속 ('plans') + 미루다 ('postpone') + -아도 괜찮다 ('is it okay to…') + -ㄹ까요 ('I wonder if…'). This is the most deferential reschedule request — you'd use it when you feel bad about asking, or with someone you want to be extra careful with. Stacking 혹시 at the front and -ㄹ까요 at the end is a classic Korean politeness sandwich: tentative opener + 'I wonder' ender. Remember 미루다 keeps the plan (good!), so pair it with a goodwill follow-up like 다음 주는 언제든 괜찮아요 ('I'm free anytime next week') to show you really do want to meet.

The difference between -아도 괜찮을까요? and -아도 될까요? is subtle: both ask permission, but 괜찮을까요? ('would it be alright / would you mind') foregrounds the other person's comfort and feels a touch warmer and more apologetic, while 될까요? ('would it be possible / may I') is a hair more neutral/practical — for a delicate cancel, 괜찮을까요? is lovely.

(1) Translating 'is it okay' as 괜찮아요? in statement-form rather than the questioning -ㄹ까요?, losing some softness — 괜찮을까요? is gentler than 괜찮아요?. (2) Over-stacking honorifics incorrectly — to a superior, 괜찮으실까요? (with the subject-honorific -시-) is right because you're asking about THEIR feeling; learners drop the -시- or misplace it.

entries.nuance: 그날은 선약이 있어서요 is 그날 ('that day') + 은 (topic particle) + 선약 ('a prior engagement', Sino-Korean 先約, lit. 'earlier-promise') + 이 있다 ('to have') + -어서요 ('because…'). This is the dignified way to decline a proposed date: 선약 specifically means 'a previously-made commitment', so it conveys 'I'd love to, but I'm already booked' — a polite, blame-free no that doesn't reveal what the other plan is. It sounds a bit more formal/elegant than the plain 이미 약속이 있어요 ('I already have plans'), which is perfectly fine in casual speech; 선약 is great for work or when you want to sound gracious. The topic particle on 그날은 ('as for that day') is important — it isolates that specific day as the problem, implying other days might be fine, which softly opens the door to rescheduling. The trailing -어서요 leaves '…so I can't' unsaid, politely. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) saying 약속을 가지고 있어요 (calque of 'I have an appointment') — use 약속이 있어요 (있다 = 'to exist/have'), never 가지다 for appointments. (2) Marking it 선약을 있어요 — 있다 takes 이/가, so 선약이 있어요. (3) Forgetting the topic 은 on the day and saying 그날 선약이 있어요 flatly — it's understandable, but 그날은 nicely frames 'that particular day' and hints you're open to alternatives. Always good manners to follow with 다른 날은 어때요? ('how about another day?').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 약속을 가지고 있어요 for 'I have plans'.
Appointments use 있다 ('exist/have'), not 가지다 ('possess'): 선약이 있어요 / 약속이 있어요. 가지고 있어요 is a calque of English 'have'.
Marking 선약 with 을/를: 선약을 있어요.
있다 takes the subject particle 이/가: 선약이 있어요. There's no 을/를 with 있다.
Treating 선약 as casual everyday speech.
선약 is a touch formal/refined. Among close friends, 이미 약속 있어 / 다른 약속 있어 sounds more natural; save 선약 for polite or work contexts.

entries.nuance: 다음 기회로 미룰 수 있을까요? is 다음 기회 ('next opportunity/time') + -로 ('to') + 미루다 ('postpone') + -ㄹ 수 있을까요 ('would it be possible to…?'). This is the elegant Korean equivalent of taking a rain check: rather than a hard cancel, you postpone to an unspecified 'next opportunity', which warmly keeps the relationship and the door open. 다음 기회 ('next chance') is a set, graceful phrase — softer and more gracious than naming a concrete reschedule — and pairs beautifully with declining an invitation you genuinely regret missing. The -로 on 다음 기회 ('to the next chance') is the same direction-particle as in 다른 날로; don't drop it. The construction -ㄹ 수 있을까요? ('would it be possible?') is more tentative and humble than -아도 될까요? ('may I?'), fitting for this softer, wistful tone. A more literary synonym is 다음을 기약하다 ('to pledge a future time'), lovely but a bit formal/poetic. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) trying to translate 'rain check' literally — there's no rain involved in Korean; the idiom is 다음 기회로 미루다 / 다음 기회에. (2) Confusing 기회 ('opportunity/chance') with 기대 ('expectation') or 기약 ('a promised time') — for 'next time' it's 다음 기회. (3) Because this keeps things warm, add a sincere 꼭 ('definitely') or 아쉽다 ('what a pity') so it reads as genuine regret, not a brush-off; without warmth, even 다음 기회로 can sound like a polite blow-off.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'rain check' literally with 비/rain words.
Korean has no rain metaphor here. Say 다음 기회로 미룰 수 있을까요? or 다음 기회에 봬요 to mean 'rain check'.
Dropping -로: 다음 기회 미룰 수 있을까요?
You postpone TO the next chance, so it takes -로: 다음 기회로 미루다. Without -로 the destination is unmarked.
Confusing 기회 with 기대 or 기약.
기회 = 'opportunity/chance' (다음 기회 'next time'); 기대 = 'expectation'; 기약 = 'a pledged time'. For a rain check use 다음 기회.

entries.english: I'm so sorry to cancel on you so suddenly
entries.shortExplanation: 갑자기 취소하게 돼서 정말 죄송해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm so sorry to cancel on you so suddenly".
entries.explanation: "I'm so sorry to cancel on you so suddenly" — that is 갑자기 취소하게 돼서 정말 죄송해요 (gapjagi chwisohage dwaeseo jeongmal joesonghaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 갑자기 취소하게 돼서 정말 죄송해요 ("I'm really sorry to cancel so suddenly"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 갑자기 취소하게 돼서 정말 죄송해요 is 갑자기 ('suddenly') + 취소하다 ('cancel') + -게 되다 ('to end up …ing', circumstances forced it) + -어서 ('so') + 정말 죄송해요 ('I'm really sorry'). The masterstroke is -게 되다: it frames the cancellation as something that HAPPENED TO you / you ended up having to do, rather than a deliberate choice — 취소하게 됐어요 ('it came about that I have to cancel') sounds far more apologetic and less culpable than the bald 취소했어요 ('I canceled'). That nuance — 'circumstances made me' — is deeply polite and exactly what you want when you feel bad. This is the full apology that should accompany any last-minute cancellation; in Korea, bailing without a proper 죄송해요/미안해 can damage a relationship, so saying it sincerely matters. Register: 죄송해요/죄송합니다 is the apology to non-intimates and superiors, while 미안해/미안 is for close friends — mixing them up (saying 미안 to your boss, or stiff 죄송합니다 to a buddy) is a classic register error. Stack 정말/너무/진짜 ('really/so') for sincerity. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) skipping the -게 되다 and saying 갑자기 취소해서 죄송해요 — grammatical and fine, but -게 돼서 adds that 'it was beyond my control' softness Koreans prefer for apologies. (2) Using 미안하다 to a superior — too casual; use 죄송하다. (3) Calquing 'cancel on you' with an object like 당신을 취소하다 — you cancel the plan/appointment (약속을 취소하다), not the person.

entries.nuance: 시간 좀 당겨도 될까요? is 시간 ('time') + 좀 (softener) + 당기다 ('to pull / move up') + -아도 될까요 ('may I…?'). This is the essential OPPOSITE of 미루다: where 미루다/늦추다 pushes an event LATER, 당기다 (or the fuller 앞당기다, lit. 'pull forward') moves it EARLIER. Newcomers learn 'postpone' first and then get stuck when they actually need it sooner — so this pairs directly with the 미루다 card. 당기다 literally means 'to pull (toward you)', and the time sense is exactly that: pulling the appointment closer in time. 앞당기다 ('front-pull') is even more unambiguous and very common for schedules (회의를 앞당기다 'move the meeting earlier'). The 좀 is a politeness softener (not 'a little'), though you can add a concrete amount: 한 시간 당겨도 될까요? ('move it up an hour?'). English-speaker pitfalls: (1) there's no single everyday English verb pair, so learners often only know 'later' and clumsily say 더 일찍 만날 수 있어요? — that's understandable ('can we meet earlier?') but 시간 당기다/앞당기다 is the crisp, idiomatic way. (2) Confusing 당기다 ('pull / move up') with 댕기다 (dialect) or 땅기다 ('feel taut', e.g. skin) — for scheduling it's 당기다. (3) Direction mix-up: don't say 미루다 when you mean earlier — 미루다 is always later; 당기다 is always earlier. Register: 될까요? polite, 돼? casual, 앞당겨도 괜찮으실까요? extra-deferential.

Confusing 당기다 with 땅기다.
땅기다 means 'to feel tight/taut' (피부가 땅긴다 'skin feels tight'). For moving a time up it's 당기다 / 앞당기다.
Only knowing 'later' and saying 더 일찍 만날 수 있어요? awkwardly.
It's understandable, but the idiomatic verb is 당기다: 시간 좀 당겨도 될까요? sounds far more natural for 'make it earlier'.

entries.explanation: 정해지면 다시 연락드릴게요 (jeonghaejimyeon dasi yeollakdeurilgeyo) means "I'll get back to you once it's settled". What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 정해지면 다시 연락드릴게요 is 정해지다 ('to get decided/settled', the passive of 정하다 'to decide') + -면 ('once/if') + 다시 ('again') + 연락드리다 (humble 'to contact', = 연락 + 드리다 'to give/do for a superior') + -ㄹ게요 ('I'll…'). When rescheduling, you often can't fix a new date on the spot, and this is the polite way to keep the plan alive without ghosting: 'once it's settled, I'll reach out.' Two key pieces. First, 정해지다 (passive) means the date 'gets settled' — learners wrongly use the active 정하다 and say 정하면 ('once I decide'), which is fine if YOU alone decide, but 정해지면 ('once it's settled') is more natural when the timing depends on circumstances/both of you. Second, 연락드리다 is the humble form: 드리다 lowers you and elevates the listener, so 연락드릴게요 is more polite than the plain 연락할게요 — use 드리다 with anyone you'd treat with respect (a senior, a new contact), and plain 연락할게 only with close friends. The -ㄹ게요 ('I'll') commits YOU to the follow-up, which is reassuring. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) translating 'get back to you' literally with 돌아가다 ('go back') — totally wrong; the idiom is 다시 연락드리다 ('contact you again'). (2) Skipping 드리다 with someone senior and sounding under-polite — say 연락드릴게요, not 연락할게요, to a boss or stranger. (3) Saying it and then actually never following up — in Korea this phrase is a real soft commitment, so flaking on it reads as rude; mean it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'get back to you' as 다시 돌아갈게요.
돌아가다 ('go/return back') is physical movement. 'Get back to you' = contact again: 다시 연락드릴게요.
Using plain 연락할게요 with a senior or new contact.
For politeness use the humble 드리다: 연락드릴게요 (lowers you, honors them). Save 연락할게 for close friends.
Saying 정하면 when timing depends on circumstances.
Active 정하면 = 'once I decide' (you alone). When it gets settled by circumstances/both sides, the passive 정해지면 ('once it's settled') is more natural.

entries.nuance: 저기요 is 저기 ('over there') + 요, an attention-getter that literally gestures away from the speaker, which makes it feel slightly softer and more tentative than 여기요 — that indirectness is exactly why Koreans reach for it constantly. It is polite-neutral and extremely versatile: it calls a waiter, stops a stranger who dropped something, or opens a question to a clerk. The dividing line from 여기요 is range and directness: 여기요 ('right here') is pointed and almost exclusively for service/seated situations, while 저기요 also works out in the world to address someone you don't know. To raise the formality with a stranger, shift to 저, 실례지만… ('um, pardon me, but…'). The classic English-speaker error is treating 저기요 as literally 'that place over there' and getting confused — in this set phrase it is purely a polite 'excuse me', the location meaning is bleached out. Don't pair it with a name; it stands alone.

entries.nuance: 메뉴 좀 주세요 is 메뉴 ('menu') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 (the honorific 'please give'), the bread-and-butter way a customer asks for the menu. The 좀 here is NOT 'a little'; it is a politeness lubricant that turns a bare order into a gentle request, so dropping it (메뉴 주세요) is grammatical but blunter. Note 메뉴 means the menu as a concept/list, while 메뉴판 specifically names the physical board or booklet — both are natural here, with 메뉴판 slightly clearer when you want the object in hand. To go more formal/deferential, swap 주세요 for 주시겠어요? ('would you give…?'), which phrases it as a question and sounds extra courteous. The English-speaker trap is over-translating 'can I get' as 제가 받을 수 있어요? — Korean expresses 'can I have X' simply as 'please give X' with 주세요; the 'can I' is already baked into the polite request. With family at the table you'd drop to 메뉴 좀 줘.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

It's understandable but blunt. The softener 좀 makes it polite and natural; keep it: 메뉴 좀 주세요.
Using 메뉴판 when you mean the food choices.
메뉴판 is the physical menu board/booklet; 메뉴 can mean the dishes/options. To ask 'what's good on the menu', say 메뉴 추천, not 메뉴판 추천.

entries.nuance: 주문할게요 is 주문하다 ('to order', from Sino-Korean 注文) in the -ㄹ게요 form, which announces YOUR OWN intention as a courteous heads-up: 'I'm going to order (now).' That -ㄹ게요 is the natural register a customer uses — polite but not stiff. The dividing line from 주문 좀 받아 주세요 ('please take our order') is direction: 주문할게요 declares what you will do, while 받아 주세요 asks the server to do something (come and take it); use 주문할게요 when the server is already there, and 받아 주세요 to summon them. For upscale or very formal places you can elevate to 주문하겠습니다. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'I would like to order' and producing 주문하고 싶어요 — grammatically 'I want to order', which sounds oddly like expressing a desire rather than doing it; Koreans simply say 주문할게요. Also don't confuse 주문 ('an order of food/goods') with 명령 ('a command') — only 주문 fits a restaurant.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

That means 'I want to order' and sounds like stating a wish. To actually place the order, announce it with 주문할게요.

시키다 ('to order/make someone do') is fine among friends (뭐 시킬까?) but to the server the cleaner verb is 주문하다. Say 주문할게요 to staff.
Over-formalizing every time with 주문하겠습니다.
합쇼체 can sound overly formal in a casual eatery. Default to 주문할게요; reserve 주문하겠습니다 for upscale or business settings.

entries.nuance: 이거 주세요 is 이거 (the spoken contraction of 이것, 'this thing') + 주세요 ('please give'), the point-and-order workhorse for any item you can indicate. Crucially, 이거 ('this, near me') belongs to a set — 그거 ('that, near you'), 저거 ('that, away from both') — so pick by where the thing is on the menu or table. A subtle but important alternative is 이걸로 주세요 (이거 + -로, 'with/by this'): use 이걸로 when you are CHOOSING among options ('I'll go with this one'), and plain 이거 when you simply want the object itself; menus and cafés very often hear 이걸로. The English-speaker mistake is forcing the object particle and saying 이것을 주세요 in speech — natives contract to 이거 and usually drop the particle. Another is using 이거 for a person; 이거 is for things only, so never point at someone and say 이거. Add 하나/둘 for quantity: 이거 둘 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이것을 주세요 in conversation.
The full 이것을 is bookish; spoken Korean contracts to 이거 and drops the particle: 이거 주세요. The written form sounds stiff at a table.
Using 이거 when the item is near the server or far away.
이거 is for what's near you. If you're pointing at something across the room, it's 저거; near the listener, 그거. The wrong one confuses which dish you mean.
Confusing 이거 주세요 with 이거 뭐예요.
주세요 orders the item; 뭐예요 only asks what it is. If you want to buy it, say 이거 주세요, not just 이거 뭐예요 (which means 'what is this?').

examples.en: Excuse me, could we get more water? We've run out.
examples.note: 더 for a refill, with a reason

entries.nuance: 물 좀 주세요 is 물 ('water') + 좀 (politeness softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). In Korea water is normally free and self-serve or brought on request, so this is one of the most-used lines in any eatery. Again 좀 is NOT 'a little' — it cushions the request; 물 주세요 without it is correct but curt. For a refill you insert 더 ('more'): 물 좀 더 주세요. To sound extra polite, especially to an older owner, use 물 좀 주시겠어요? as a question. The English-speaker trap is asking 'can I have water' as a literal ability question (물 마실 수 있어요? = 'am I able to drink water?') — that asks about permission/capacity, not a request; Koreans say 'please give water'. Also, tap vs. bottled rarely needs specifying since restaurant water is just 물; don't over-explain with 수돗물 ('tap water') unless you truly mean it.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 물 마실 수 있어요? to request water.
That means 'am I able to drink water?' — a question about permission/ability, not an order. To get water, say 물 좀 주세요.
Saying 물 좀 주세요 expecting it to mean 'a little water'.
좀 is a softener, not a quantity. It doesn't limit the amount; it just makes the request polite. For a small amount, say 조금만.
Forgetting 더 when you want a refill.
물 좀 주세요 asks for water generally; for more of what you already had, add 더: 물 좀 더 주세요. Without 더 the server may think you have none yet.

entries.explanation: "Could you recommend something?" — that is 추천 좀 해 주세요 (chucheon jom hae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 추천 좀 해 주세요 ("Could you recommend something?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.en: Could you recommend something?

examples.en: What's good here? Could you recommend something?
examples.note: Pair with 뭐가 맛있어요 to invite their pick
