examples.note: 처음 왔다 ('first visit') makes the ask natural

entries.nuance: 추천 좀 해 주세요 is 추천 ('recommendation', Sino-Korean 推薦) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The 해 주세요 (해 주다 = 'do as a favor') is what makes it a request for the server's help, not just a statement; the 좀 softens it further. It's the polite go-to when you can't decide and want the staff's pick. The nearest alternatives are content questions: 뭐가 맛있어요? ('what's tasty?') and 뭐가 제일 잘 나가요? ('what sells best?') — these ask for specific info, while 추천 좀 해 주세요 invites them to choose for you; the dividing line is that the recommendation request leans on the server's judgment. The English-speaker error is using 추천하다 without 주다 and saying 추천하세요 — that commands the server TO recommend (like ordering them), which is too blunt; the favor verb 해 주세요 keeps it courteous. Also note 추천 is a 하다-noun, so it needs the verb 하다: with the softener it's 추천 좀 해 주세요, and without it the joined 추천해 주세요 — but never 추천 주세요, since you can't 'give' a recommendation directly.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 추천하세요 to the server.
Bare 추천하세요 is an imperative ('you, recommend!') and sounds bossy. The polite favor form is 추천 좀 해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Saying 추천 주세요 without 하다.
추천 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it directly. It needs the verb 하다 plus the favor 주다: 추천 좀 해 주세요.
Over-literal 'recommend me' as 저를 추천해 주세요.
저를 추천해 주세요 means 'please recommend ME (to someone)'. To get a suggestion, drop the object: 추천 좀 해 주세요, or specify 메뉴 추천.

entries.explanation: 안 맵게 해 주세요 (an maepge hae juseyo) = "Could you make it not spicy?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 안 맵게 해 주세요 ("Please make it not spicy"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.romanization: an maepge hae juseyo.
examples.en: Make it not spicy, please.

examples.en: I can't handle spicy well, so please make it not spicy.

examples.en: Could you possibly make the tteokbokki less spicy?

entries.nuance: 안 맵게 해 주세요 is 안 ('not') + 맵게 (the adverbial form of 맵다 'to be spicy', so 'spicily') + 해 주세요 ('please make it for me'). The -게 turns the adjective into a manner ('in a not-spicy way'), and 해 주다 asks the cook to make it that way as a favor. The key distinction is 안 맵게 ('not spicy at all') vs. 덜 맵게 ('less spicy'): use 덜 when you still want some heat — many English speakers overshoot with 안 and then find the dish bland. Korean 맵다 is an adjective conjugated irregularly (맵다 → 매워요, but 맵게 for the adverb), and a common error is saying 맵지 않게 — which is actually fine and natural too, just longer; 안 맵게 is the crisp spoken default. Another trap is treating 맵다 like a verb and saying 안 매워 주세요 — you need the adverb 맵게 before 해 주세요, not the conjugated 매워. To check feasibility first, ask 안 맵게 돼요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 매워 주세요.
맵다 is an adjective; before 해 주세요 you need its adverb form 맵게, not the conjugated 매워. Correct: 안 맵게 해 주세요.
Using 안 맵게 when you actually want mild, not bland.
안 맵게 removes the spice entirely. If you want some heat reduced, say 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ('less spicy'), which keeps flavor.
Putting the negative on the wrong word: 맵게 안 해 주세요.
맵게 안 해 주세요 oddly negates the whole 'make' action. The natural placement negates 맵다: 안 맵게 해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 계산해 주세요 is 계산 ('calculation/reckoning', Sino-Korean 計算) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'), so literally 'please do the reckoning' — the standard 'check, please.' In Korea you usually pay at the front counter (계산대) on the way out, not at the table, so this is often said while standing to leave or handed to whoever's at the register. The near-twin 계산할게요 ('I'll pay') is the version YOU say announcing your own action at the counter, while 계산해 주세요 asks the staff to ring it up; both are common. A more casual synonym is 얼마예요? ('how much is it?'), which can double as 'let me pay' when said at the register. The English-speaker error is asking for 'the bill/check' as a physical object — 영수증 주세요 means 'give me the RECEIPT', which you get AFTER paying, not the request to pay; to settle up, say 계산해 주세요. Don't confuse 계산 with 영수증.

계산 is 'calculation/the bill'; 계좌 is a 'bank account'. They sound similar but 계좌 has nothing to do with paying at a restaurant.

examples.en: Please ring us up separately — just mine first.

entries.nuance: 따로 계산해 주세요 is 따로 ('separately, apart') + 계산해 주세요 ('please ring up'), used when each person in a group pays their own. The cashier will often ask 같이 계산하시겠어요, 따로 하시겠어요? ('together or separate?'), and this is your answer. Note Korean culture historically leans toward one person treating (한턱 내다) or paying together (같이 계산), so splitting evenly per item is less automatic than in the West — but 따로 계산 (separate) and Dutch-pay (더치페이) are now common among younger people. The dividing line: 따로 계산 means each pays for what they had / their own check, while 같이 계산 (or N분의 1, 'split into N') means one combined bill. The English-speaker error is saying 'split the bill' as 나눠 주세요 ('please divide it'), which is vague and can confuse the cashier; the clear request is 따로 계산해 주세요 (separate) or, for an even split, 1/n로 해 주세요. Don't forget 따로 modifies 계산, so keep the order 따로 계산.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 나눠 주세요 to mean 'split the bill'.
나누다 ('to divide') is vague here and can sound like dividing the food. For separate checks say 따로 계산해 주세요; for an even split say 1/n(분의 일)로 해 주세요.
Assuming separate checks are the default.
Many Korean places expect one payment; one person often treats or pays together. Always state 따로 계산해 주세요 explicitly if you want to split.
Misplacing 따로 as 계산 따로 해 주세요.
The natural adverb order is 따로 계산해 주세요. 계산 따로 is understandable but sounds reordered; lead with 따로.

entries.nuance: 잘 먹겠습니다 is 잘 ('well') + 먹다 ('to eat') + -겠습니다 (a formal future/intention ending), literally 'I will eat well' — the set phrase Koreans say BEFORE eating to thank whoever cooked or is paying. It's the eating-time counterpart to a host's 맛있게 드세요 ('enjoy your meal'): the eater says 잘 먹겠습니다, the host says 드세요. The register here is formal-polite (-습니다); soften to 잘 먹을게요 with someone close, or drop to 잘 먹을게 in 반말 with friends/family. The dividing line from 잘 먹었습니다 is tense: 먹겠습니다 (future) before the meal, 먹었습니다 (past) after — mixing them is the classic learner slip. The English-speaker error is staying silent (since English has no pre-meal phrase) or saying 감사합니다 alone — 잘 먹겠습니다 is the expected, almost obligatory line when someone feeds or treats you; skipping it can read as ungrateful. Don't say it about food you bought entirely for yourself with no host present.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘 먹었습니다 before the meal.
먹었습니다 is past tense ('I ate well') — that's the after-meal line. Before eating, use the future 잘 먹겠습니다.
Skipping it because English has no equivalent.
When someone cooks for or treats you, 잘 먹겠습니다 is socially expected. Silence or a bare 감사합니다 can feel cold; say the set phrase.
Saying it about food you bought just for yourself.
잘 먹겠습니다 thanks a cook or host. Eating your own solo lunch with no one treating, you wouldn't announce it to a stranger; it's directed at the provider.

entries.nuance: 잘 먹었습니다 is 잘 ('well') + 먹다 + -었습니다 (formal past), literally 'I ate well' — the standard thank-you AFTER a meal, said to the cook, the host who paid, or even called out to restaurant staff as you leave. It pairs with the pre-meal 잘 먹겠습니다; the only difference is tense (past vs. future), and swapping them is the most common learner error. Register: -습니다 is formal-polite; everyday speech often uses 잘 먹었어요, and friends say 잘 먹었어. A warmer version adds praise: 맛있게 잘 먹었습니다. The dividing line from a plain 감사합니다 ('thank you') is specificity — 잘 먹었습니다 thanks specifically FOR the food/meal, so after eating it's the precise phrase, while 감사합니다 is generic. The English-speaker error, again, is silence (no English habit of thanking after eating) or mistranslating as 'I ate well' in the dietary sense; it's a courtesy formula, not a comment on nutrition. Saying it to the server on your way out is normal and gracious in Korea.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘 먹겠습니다 after finishing.
먹겠습니다 is future ('I will eat'), said before the meal. After eating, use the past 잘 먹었습니다.
Reading it as a literal 'I ate well (healthily)'.
It's a set courtesy meaning 'thank you for the meal', not a comment on how nutritious it was. Treat it as a fixed thank-you formula.
Using only 감사합니다 after someone feeds you.
감사합니다 is generic 'thank you'; the meal-specific, expected phrase is 잘 먹었습니다. Pair them if you like: 잘 먹었습니다, 감사합니다.

entries.nuance: 리필 돼요? is the loanword 리필 ('refill') + 되다 ('to be possible') in polite question form: 'is a refill possible?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility — and importantly, whether it's free — which matters because in Korea side dishes (반찬) are frequently refilled at no charge, while drinks may or may not be. Once you know it's possible, you ask 리필 좀 해 주세요 ('please refill it'). The dividing line from 추가 ('an additional order') is cost: 리필 implies topping up (often free, same item), while 추가 (추가요 / 추가해 주세요) means ordering MORE as a paid add-on — mixing these can surprise you with a charge. The English-speaker error is using the verb 'refill' as if Korean had a native verb and saying 다시 채워 주세요 ('please fill it again'), which is understandable but unidiomatic; 리필 돼요? is what people actually say. For free banchan specifically, 반찬 리필 돼요? or 반찬 좀 더 주세요 both work.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Assuming 리필 is always free.
리필 often is for banchan, but drinks may cost extra. If unsure, ask 리필 돼요? 무료예요? or whether it's 추가 (a paid add-on).
Confusing 리필 with 추가.
리필 = topping up the same item (often free); 추가 = ordering an additional paid portion. Say 리필 돼요? to top up, 추가요 to order more for a charge.
Saying 다시 채워 주세요 for a refill.
It's understandable but not idiomatic. Koreans use the loanword: 리필 돼요? to ask, 리필 좀 해 주세요 to request.

entries.nuance: 여기 화장실 어디예요? is 여기 ('here') + 화장실 ('restroom', Sino-Korean 化粧室, lit. 'grooming room') + 어디 ('where') + 예요 (polite copula). 화장실 is the standard polite word for a toilet — never the crude 변소. The 여기 ('here') scopes the question to this establishment, useful since Korean restroom may be inside, down the hall, or in a shared building corridor that needs a 비밀번호 (door code). A fuller variant is 화장실이 어디 있어요? ('where is the restroom located?'), using the existence verb 있다. The dividing line: 화장실 어디예요? asks location, while 화장실 좀 쓸게요 ('I'll use the restroom') announces you're going (a heads-up, not a location question) — don't swap them. The English-speaker error is over-politely asking 'may I use the bathroom?' as 화장실 가도 돼요? to a server when you really need directions — in a public restaurant you don't need permission to go, you need the location, so ask 어디예요?. Also keep the copula attached: 어디예요, not 어디 이에요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 변소 instead of 화장실.
변소 is crude and dated. The neutral polite word for a public toilet is 화장실: 화장실 어디예요?
Asking 화장실 가도 돼요? when you want directions.
That asks permission ('may I go?'), not location. In a restaurant you don't need permission; ask where it is: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Saying 어디 이에요 separately.
The copula fuses: 어디 + 예요 → 어디예요. Writing 어디 이에요 is unnatural; say 화장실 어디예요?

entries.explanation: "For how many?" — that is 몇 명이요? (myeon myeongiyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 몇 명이요? ("How many people?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

entries.nuance: 몇 명이요? is 몇 ('how many') + 명 (the counter for people) + 이요 (polite particle), the question staff ask at the door — 'for how many?'. As a customer you mostly ANSWER it, with 숫자 + 명 + 이요: 한 명이요, 두 명이요, 세 명이요. Note the counter 명 is the plain word for counting people, while 분 is its honorific; staff politely ask 몇 분이세요? (using 분 + the honorific copula 세요), but YOU refer to your own group with humble/plain 명, never elevating yourselves with 분. That asymmetry is the key learner point. Native Korean numbers are used with 명 (한, 두, 세, 네…), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — a frequent slip. The dividing line from 몇 사람? is register: 명 is the standard counter; 사람 ('person') as a counter sounds blunter and less polite in service. The English-speaker error is answering with Sino-Korean numbers (이 명) or honorifically calling their own party 분 — both sound off. Just say 두 명이요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Counting your own party with the honorific 분.
분 honors others; for your own group use plain 명: 두 명이요. Saying 우리 두 분이요 wrongly elevates yourselves.
Using Sino-Korean numbers with 명.
명 takes native numbers: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 — not 일 명, 이 명. So 'two people' is 두 명이요, never 이 명이요.
Answering 몇 명이요? with just a bare number.
A bare '둘' can sound abrupt; attach the counter and polite 요: 두 명이요. It's the natural, complete answer.

entries.nuance: 이거 안 시켰는데요 is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 시켰- (past of 시키다 'to order') + -는데요, a soft sentence-ender that signals 'just so you know…' and invites the listener to respond. The dividing line from a blunt 이거 안 시켰어요 ('we didn't order this') is tone — the -는데요 version is softer and less confrontational, which matters when correcting staff. The English-speaker error is omitting -는데요 and stating a flat negative, which can sound like an accusation, or misusing 시키다 vs. 주문하다 register. Another trap: don't say 이거 틀렸어요 ('this is wrong/incorrect') — that's for wrong answers, not a mis-delivered dish; for a mix-up, say you didn't order it or name what you did order.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping -는데요 and saying flat 이거 안 시켰어요.
The bare negative can sound accusatory. The soft ender -는데요 raises it gently: 이거 안 시켰는데요? lets the server fix it without feeling blamed.

틀리다 means 'to be incorrect (like a wrong answer)'. A mis-delivered dish isn't 'wrong' that way; say 이거 안 시켰는데요 or name what you ordered.

entries.explanation: 예약했는데요 (yeyakaenneundeyo) means "I have a reservation". Say it as one set phrase — for example 예약했는데요 ("I have a reservation (just so you know)"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: The walk-in version when you have no booking

examples.ko: 안녕하세요, 예약했는데요.
examples.romanization: annyeonghaseyo, yeyakaenneundeyo.
examples.en: Hi, I have a reservation.
examples.note: The standard check-in line right after greeting

examples.ko: 세 시에 예약했는데요. 이름은 김민수예요.
examples.romanization: se sie yeyakaenneundeyo. ireumeun gimminsuyeyo.
examples.en: I booked for three o'clock — the name is Kim Minsu.
examples.note: Add the time and name so they find your booking

examples.romanization: jeogiyo, neibeoro yeyakaenneundeyo. hwagin jom hae juseyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, I booked through Naver — could you check?
examples.note: 네이버 예약 (Naver booking) is how most Koreans reserve salons

entries.nuance: 예약했는데요 is 예약(을) 하다 ('to make a reservation', Sino-Korean 豫約) in the past tense plus the soft ender -는데요, which means roughly 'I booked, so…(I'm here / please check)'. That -는데요 is the politeness engine: it hands the situation to the staff and invites them to look you up, rather than barking a flat fact. You say it in 존댓말 to salon staff the moment you arrive; with a friend you'd drop to 예약했어, but never use 반말 to the receptionist. The near-twin is plain 예약했어요, which is fine but a hair blunter and less inviting than the -는데요 form. The classic English-speaker trap is translating 'I have a reservation' literally with the verb 있다 and saying 예약이 있어요 — that is grammatical but sounds like you're just informing them a booking exists somewhere; Koreans naturally use the verb 하다 (예약했는데요 / 예약했어요) to mean 'I (have) made a booking.' Another pitfall is the particle: it's 예약을 하다, so the object is 예약, and you don't say 예약에 했어요. In Korea most salon bookings happen through the Naver app, so 네이버로 예약했어요 is extremely common.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 예약이 있어요 to check in.
It's grammatical but means 'a reservation exists', which sounds detached. Koreans use the verb 하다: 예약했는데요 / 예약했어요 ('I made a booking').
Dropping -는데요 to a flat 예약했어요 and stopping there.
It works but is blunter and doesn't invite the staff to respond. -는데요 softens it and signals 'so please check me in': 예약했는데요.
Using 반말 예약했어 with the receptionist.
예약했어 is 반말, far too casual for staff you don't know. Keep 존댓말: 예약했는데요 or 예약했어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 커트만 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "Just a cut, please".
entries.explanation: "Just a cut, please" — that is 커트만 할게요 (keoteuman halgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 커트만 할게요 ("I'll just get a cut"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.ko: 오늘은 커트만 할게요.
examples.romanization: oneureun keoteuman halgeyo.
examples.en: Today I'll just get a cut.
examples.note: 오늘은 ('today') frames it as today's choice

examples.ko: 펌은 안 하고 커트만 할게요.
examples.romanization: peomeun an hago keoteuman halgeyo.
examples.en: No perm — just a cut, please.
examples.note: Contrast 안 하다 (not doing) with what you do want

examples.romanization: keoteuman halgeyo. eolmayeyo?

examples.note: Pair with 얼마예요 to confirm the price upfront

entries.nuance: 커트만 할게요 is 커트 (the loanword 'cut') + -만 ('only') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 form of 하다, announcing your own intention politely). The -만 is doing the real work: it tells the stylist you want ONLY a haircut and no extras like perm or dye, which matters because salons often upsell or assume add-ons. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the friendly customer register — polite but not stiff. Note the spelling/sound: Koreans write and say 커트 for a haircut (헤어컷 also appears in menus), and the verb is 머리(를) 자르다 ('to cut hair') in everyday speech — so 커트하다 and 머리 자르다 are interchangeable, with 커트 sounding more salon-technical. The dividing line from 머리 자르려고요 ('I came to get a cut') is that 커트만 할게요 actively EXCLUDES other services via 만, while 자르려고요 just states your purpose. The English-speaker trap is putting 만 in the wrong slot or using the wrong verb: saying 커트 할게요만 is broken word order (만 attaches to the noun: 커트만), and translating 'just' as 그냥 (그냥 커트 할게요) means 'just casually a cut', a different nuance. Also don't confuse 커트 with 컷 used for editing/film; for hair it's 커트.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Misplacing 만 as 커트 할게요만.
만 ('only') attaches to the noun, not the sentence end. Correct: 커트만 할게요.
Using 그냥 to mean 'just a cut'.
그냥 커트 할게요 means 'I'll just casually get a cut' (no strong reason). To mean 'only a cut, nothing else', use 만: 커트만 할게요.
Saying 머리 컷 주세요 like ordering an object.
A haircut isn't 'given' like a dish. Use the verb: 커트만 할게요 or 머리 좀 잘라 주세요.

entries.explanation: 다듬어 주세요 (dadeumeo juseyo) = "Just tidy it up / trim it, please". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 다듬어 주세요 ("Please just trim/tidy it"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.romanization: girineun geudaero, dadeumeoman juseyo.
examples.en: Keep the length — just tidy it up.
examples.note: 길이는 그대로 ('length as is') signals no real shortening

examples.ko: 끝이 좀 상했어요. 다듬어 주세요.
examples.romanization: kkeuchi jom sanghaesseoyo. dadeumeo juseyo.
examples.en: The ends are a bit damaged — please trim them.
examples.note: 상하다 ('to be damaged') gives the reason for a trim

examples.romanization: mani jareuji malgo geunyang dadeumeo juseyo.
examples.en: Don't cut much — just tidy it up.
examples.note: 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much') protects your length

entries.nuance: 다듬어 주세요 is 다듬다 ('to trim, neaten, tidy up') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form ('please do for me'). This is the single most useful salon word for someone who does NOT want a dramatic change: 다듬다 means cleaning up the shape and trimming the ends while keeping essentially the same length and style. The crucial contrast is with 자르다 ('to cut'): 자르다 implies actually shortening / removing length, while 다듬다 implies light maintenance — if you say 잘라 주세요 the stylist may take off more than you wanted, so for 'just a trim' always reach for 다듬다. To be extra safe, stack 끝만 살짝 ('just the tips, lightly') or 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much'). The English-speaker trap is exactly this verb choice — 'trim' gets mistranslated as 자르다, producing a real haircut when you wanted maintenance. Another pitfall is the irregular conjugation: 다듬다 keeps the ㅁ, so it's 다듬어 (not 다듬워 or 다듬아); and the favor form needs 주세요 — bare 다듬으세요 would oddly command the stylist to trim their OWN hair. Register stays 존댓말 with staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 잘라 주세요 when you only want a trim.
자르다 ('cut') means shortening/removing length. For a light cleanup that keeps the length, use 다듬다: 다듬어 주세요.
Conjugating it as 다듬아 주세요 or 다듬워 주세요.
다듬다 is a regular verb keeping ㅁ: the form is 다듬어 주세요, not 다듬아/다듬워.
Saying 다듬으세요 to the stylist.
Bare 다듬으세요 is a command to the listener to trim (their own) hair. The favor form 다듬어 주세요 means 'please trim mine for me'.

structuredNuance.t: 다듬어 주세요 is 다듬다 ('to trim, neaten, tidy up') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form ('please do for me'). This is the single most useful salon word for someone who does NOT want a dramatic change: 다듬다 means cleaning up the shape and trimming the ends while keeping essentially the same length and style. To be extra safe, stack 끝만 살짝 ('just the tips, lightly') or 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much'). Register stays 존댓말 with staff.

The crucial contrast is with 자르다 ('to cut'): 자르다 implies actually shortening / removing length, while 다듬다 implies light maintenance — if you say 잘라 주세요 the stylist may take off more than you wanted, so for 'just a trim' always reach for 다듬다.
Note the conjugation: 다듬다 keeps the ㅁ, so it's 다듬어 (not 다듬워 or 다듬아); and the favor form needs 주세요 — bare 다듬으세요 would oddly command the stylist to trim their OWN hair.
The English-speaker trap is exactly this verb choice — 'trim' gets mistranslated as 자르다, producing a real haircut when you wanted maintenance.

entries.nuance: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 is 너무 ('too') + 짧다 ('to be short') in the -지 않게 form ('in a way that is NOT…') + 해 주세요 ('please make it'). The structure -지 않게 해 주세요 = 'please make it so that it's not ~', a hugely useful frame for setting limits on any service. Here it caps the haircut: cut, but don't overshoot into 'too short'. The natural alternative is 너무 짧게 자르지 마세요 ('don't cut it too short') with the prohibitive -지 마세요 — both are correct; the -지 않게 version softens by describing the desired result, while -지 마세요 directly forbids the action. The English-speaker trap is the double-negative word order: learners produce 너무 안 짧게 (wrong placement of 안) or 짧지 않게 너무, scrambling it — the fixed order is 너무 + 짧지 않게. Another pitfall is using 작다 ('small in size') instead of 짧다 ('short in length') — hair is 짧다, never 작다. Also 너무 literally skews negative ('excessively'), so it fits perfectly with limits; don't replace it with 많이 ('a lot') here, since 많이 짧지 않게 sounds off. Keep 해 주세요 to make it a request to the stylist, not a self-command.

작다 means 'small in size'. Hair length is 짧다 ('short'). Say 너무 짧지 않게, not 너무 작지 않게.
Dropping 해 주세요 and saying just 너무 짧지 않게.
Without the verb it's an incomplete fragment. Finish it: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 (or … 잘라 주세요).

entries.nuance: 앞머리 내려 주세요 is 앞머리 ('front hair / bangs / fringe', lit. 'front-head') + 내리다 ('to lower, bring down') in the favor form. 앞머리 is the fixed Korean word for the fringe over your forehead, and 내리다 means to wear it DOWN over the forehead (as opposed to swept back). The essential contrast is 까다: 앞머리(를) 까다 means to push the bangs UP/BACK off the forehead — so 내려 주세요 (down/forward) and 까 주세요 (back/up) are opposites you must not swap, since they produce completely different looks. The English-speaker trap starts with the vocabulary: there is no single word 'bangs' in their head-to-Korean map, so they describe it ('the hair in front') and confuse the stylist; just learn 앞머리. Another pitfall is the verb — learners reach for 자르다 thinking 'bangs = cut bangs', but 내리다 is about how you WEAR them, and to actually create/trim bangs you'd say 앞머리 만들어 주세요 ('make bangs') or 앞머리 다듬어 주세요 ('trim the bangs'). Also note 머리 alone means 'head/hair' generally; the front fringe specifically is 앞머리. Keep 존댓말 with the stylist.

To make bangs say 앞머리 만들어 주세요; to keep them worn down say 앞머리 내려 주세요. Plain 자르다 just means 'cut' and is ambiguous here.

entries.nuance: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is 이 사진 ('this photo') + -처럼 ('like, as') + 해 주세요 ('please do it for me'). Showing a reference photo is the single most reliable way to communicate a hairstyle across a language gap, and -처럼 ('like ~') is the particle that attaches to the noun to mean 'in the manner of this photo'. The key grammar point is that -처럼 fuses directly onto the noun with no spacing issues: 사진처럼, never 사진 같이 처럼 or 사진를 처럼. A close synonym is 사진같이 (사진 + 같이, 'same as the photo'), which is also natural; -처럼 and 같이 are near-interchangeable here, with -처럼 feeling a touch more standard in this request. The English-speaker trap is over-building the sentence with the verb 보이다 ('to look') — saying 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 ('make it LOOK like this photo') is understandable but wordier than natives need; plain 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is what people say. Another pitfall is forgetting to actually verify realism, so Koreans often append 가능해요? or 될까요? ('is it possible?') because a photo of someone else's hair may not suit yours. Keep 존댓말; the favor verb 해 주세요 keeps it a polite request, not a command.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Adding a particle before 처럼, like 사진을 처럼.
-처럼 attaches straight to the noun with no object particle: 사진처럼 해 주세요, not 사진을 처럼.
Saying 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 every time.
It's correct but wordy. Natives simply say 이 사진처럼 해 주세요; the 보이게 ('so it looks') is usually unnecessary.
Confusing 처럼 ('like/similar') with 때문에 ('because').
처럼 means 'in the manner of'. Don't swap in 때문에; 이 사진 때문에 해 주세요 would wrongly mean 'do it because of this photo'.

entries.explanation: "Please add some layers" — that is 층 내 주세요 (cheung nae juseyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 층 내 주세요 ("Please put layers in"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.note: 답답해 보이다 ('looks heavy/stuffy') is why you want layers

examples.note: Pair with 숱 치다 ('thin out the volume')

entries.nuance: 층 내 주세요 is 층 ('layer', Sino-Korean 層, the same word as a building 'floor') + 내다 ('to produce, bring out') in the favor form. The set salon collocation is 층(을) 내다 = 'to put layers in / create a layered cut', so the verb you need is specifically 내다, not 만들다 or 하다. The opposite request is 층 안 나게 해 주세요 ('keep it without layers') for a blunt one-length cut, using the intransitive 층이 나다 ('layers form'). A related but different ask is 숱 치다 ('to thin out the volume/density') — 층 is about creating stepped lengths for movement, while 숱 치기 is about reducing thickness; English speakers often conflate 'layers' and 'thinning', so keep them separate. The English-speaker trap is vocabulary again: 'layers' has no obvious Korean cognate, so learners invent 레이어 (the loanword exists in salon menus but plain 층 is what people say) or describe it clumsily. Another pitfall is the verb pairing — 층을 만들어 주세요 ('make layers') is understandable but unidiomatic; the natural verb is 내다 (transitive, you ask the stylist) vs. 나다 (intransitive, layers appear). Keep 존댓말; 내 주세요 = 'please bring them out for me'.

Confusing 층 내기 (layers) with 숱 치기 (thinning).
층 내다 creates stepped lengths for movement; 숱 치다 reduces thickness/density. They're different — say what you actually want.
Pronouncing/writing it as 칭 or mixing with 청.
It's 층 (cheung, 'layer/floor'). Don't confuse it with similar-sounding syllables; the request is 층 내 주세요.

entries.shortExplanation: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please thin it out a bit".
entries.explanation: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 (sut jom chyeo juseyo) = "Please thin it out a bit". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 ("Please thin it out a bit"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

examples.en: My hair's too thick, so please thin it out.
examples.note: 머리숱이 많다 ('hair is thick/dense') is the reason

examples.romanization: witbubuneun dugo araejjongman sut chyeo juseyo.

examples.note: Target it: 아래쪽만 ('only the bottom part')

examples.note: 조금만 ('just a little') caps the amount

entries.nuance: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 is 숱 ('the amount/density of hair', i.e. how thick your head of hair is) + 좀 (softener) + 치다 ('to strike', here the set verb 'to thin out') in the favor form. The fixed collocation is 숱(을) 치다 = 'to thin the hair out' with thinning shears, reducing bulk without changing length much. The crucial vocabulary is 숱 itself: 머리숱이 많다 = 'to have thick/dense hair', 숱이 적다 = 'thin/sparse hair' — note this is about DENSITY, not length or the 'thin/fat' of 얇다/두껍다. The English-speaker trap is exactly that confusion: 'thin out my hair' gets mistranslated with 얇게 ('thinly', about width of strands) producing 머리 얇게 해 주세요, which is wrong — you want 숱(을) 치다 for density. Another pitfall is the verb 치다: it has many meanings ('hit, play, count'), so learners doubt it, but 숱 치다 is the standard salon phrase. Also don't confuse 숱 with 술 ('alcohol') — one consonant apart but totally different. Distinguish from 층 내다 (layering for movement): you can thin without layering and vice versa. Keep 존댓말; 쳐 주세요 = 'please thin it for me', and 좀 keeps it gentle.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 머리 얇게 해 주세요 to mean 'thin it out'.
얇다 is about the width of each strand, not density. To reduce bulk, say 숱(을) 쳐 주세요 ('thin out the volume').
Using a different verb like 숱 줄여 주세요.
The idiomatic collocation is 숱(을) 치다. 줄이다 ('reduce') is understandable but unnatural here; say 숱 좀 쳐 주세요.

숱 = hair density; 술 = alcohol. Keep the ㅌ: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요, not 술 좀 쳐 주세요.

entries.nuance: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요 is 옆 ('side') + -이랑 ('and') + 뒤 ('back') + 는 (topic marker) + 짧게 (adverb of 짧다 'short') + 해 주세요. Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 짧은 해 주세요.

It's understandable but choppy. The natural phrasing groups them: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 감겨 주세요 is the CAUSATIVE of 감다 ('to wash one's own hair'): 감다 → 감기다 ('to wash someone ELSE'S hair') → 감겨 주다 ('to wash someone's hair for them as a favor'). This causative shift is the whole point and the #1 learner trap. When YOU wash your own hair, it's 머리(를) 감다. But at the salon, the staff wash YOUR hair, so from your mouth as the customer asking them to do it, you need the causative 감기다 → 감겨 주세요 ('please wash [my hair] for me'). If you mistakenly say 머리 감아 주세요 using the plain stem, it's a common error that sounds like you're asking the stylist to wash THEIR own hair as a favor — natives will understand from context, but 감겨 주세요 is the correct causative. Compare 머리 감았어요 ('I washed my hair', plain, about yourself) vs. 머리 감겨 주세요 ('please wash my hair', causative, staff do it). The English-speaker trap is that English uses the same verb 'wash' regardless of who does it, so the 감다/감기다 distinction is invisible to them. Also note 머리(를) 감다 specifically means washing HAIR; washing your face is 세수하다 and washing the body is 씻다 — don't generalize 감다. Keep 존댓말 at the basin.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 머리 감아 주세요 to the stylist.
감다 is washing your OWN hair. To ask staff to wash yours, use the causative 감기다: 감겨 주세요 ('wash my hair for me').
Using 씻겨 주세요 for hair.
씻다/씻기다 is for washing the body or objects. Hair specifically takes 감다/감기다: 머리 감겨 주세요.
Confusing 감다 (wash hair) with 감다 (close eyes / wind).
감다 is a homonym (also 'close the eyes', 'wind up'). In the salon it means washing hair; context and 머리 make it clear: 머리 감겨 주세요.

entries.nuance: 드라이까지 해 주세요 is 드라이 (the loanword 'dry', meaning a blow-dry / styling with a dryer and brush) + -까지 ('even, up to, including') + 해 주세요. The key particle is -까지 ('up to and including'), which here means 'go all the way through to the blow-dry/styling too' — implying it's an additional step on top of the cut. In Korean salons 드라이 specifically refers to professionally blow-drying and styling your hair (often a paid add-on), not merely removing water — so 드라이 받다 ('get a blow-out') can be a service in itself. The English-speaker trap is the word 드라이: 'dry' in English is just the opposite of wet, but Korean 드라이 means a styled blow-out, so don't be surprised it may cost extra or be its own menu item. Another pitfall is the particle nuance: -까지 ('including/even') vs. -도 ('also') — 드라이도 해 주세요 means 'do the blow-dry as well' (listing it as another item), while 드라이까지 emphasizes completing the process through to styling; both work, with -까지 sounding like 'finish it off with a blow-dry'. Also note the verb is 드라이하다 / 드라이(를) 해 주세요, treating 드라이 as a 하다-noun. To decline, say 드라이 안 해도 돼요 ('no need to blow-dry'). Keep 존댓말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 드라이 just means 'dry it off'.
In Korean salons 드라이 means a styled blow-out (often a paid service), not merely removing water. It may be an extra menu item.
Saying 드라이 해 주세요만 with 만 at the end.
만 attaches to the noun: 드라이만 해 주세요 ('only a blow-out'). Tacked onto the sentence end it's broken.
Confusing -까지 ('including') with -부터 ('from/starting').
-까지 means 'up to/including' the blow-dry. -부터 ('from') would wrongly mean 'starting from the blow-dry'. Use 드라이까지.

entries.explanation: 펌하고 싶은데요 (peomhago sipeundeyo) means "I'd like to get a perm". Say it as one set phrase — for example 펌하고 싶은데요 ("I'd like to get a perm"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.en: I'd like a perm today — how long does it take?
examples.note: Perms take hours; ask 시간 얼마나 걸려요

examples.note: 자연스러운 ('natural') + asking for advice

examples.note: 손상 안 되게 ('without damage') voices a real concern

entries.nuance: 펌하고 싶은데요 is 펌 (the loanword 'perm', from 'permanent') + 하고 싶다 ('to want to do') + the soft ender -는데요. Note the spelling: Koreans say and write 펌 (not 파마... though 파마 is the older colloquial form still heard) — younger salon usage strongly favors 펌. The -는데요 ender again softens and invites a response, perfect for opening a consultation: 'I'd like a perm, so… (what do you suggest?)'. The English-speaker trap here is the want-construction: learners overuse 하고 싶어요 in blunt isolation, but pairing it with -는데(요) makes it sound like a natural lead-in rather than a flat demand. Another pitfall is register/word choice: saying 파마 isn't wrong but sounds slightly dated; 펌 is current. Distinguish the directions: 펌하고 싶어요 ('I want to perm') states desire, while 펌하려고 왔어요 ('I came to perm') states purpose — both are good openers. Beware that 펌 covers many styles (셋팅펌 setting perm, 열펌 digital/hot perm, 볼륨매직 volume magic), so the stylist will ask which; be ready with 자연스러운 펌 ('a natural perm') or to ask 추천 좀 해 주세요. Keep 존댓말, and remember a perm is a long, pricey service, so confirming 시간 ('time') and 가격 ('price') upfront is normal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 펌 주세요 like ordering a product.
A perm is a service you 'do', not 'receive' like an object. Use 펌하고 싶은데요 or 펌하려고요, not 펌 주세요.
Defaulting to 파마 thinking it's the only word.
파마 is older/colloquial; current salon Korean prefers 펌. Both are understood, but 펌하고 싶은데요 sounds more natural now.
Dropping -는데요 to a blunt 펌하고 싶어요 and stopping.
It's fine but abrupt as a conversation opener. -는데요 invites the stylist's input: 펌하고 싶은데요 (어떤 게 좋을까요?).

structuredNuance.t: 펌하고 싶은데요 is 펌 (the loanword 'perm', from 'permanent') + 하고 싶다 ('to want to do') + the soft ender -는데요. The -는데요 ender again softens and invites a response, perfect for opening a consultation: 'I'd like a perm, so… (what do you suggest?)'. Beware that 펌 covers many styles (셋팅펌 setting perm, 열펌 digital/hot perm, 볼륨매직 volume magic), so the stylist will ask which; be ready with 자연스러운 펌 ('a natural perm') or to ask 추천 좀 해 주세요. Keep 존댓말, and remember a perm is a long, pricey service, so confirming 시간 ('time') and 가격 ('price') upfront is normal.

Note the word choice: 파마 isn't wrong but sounds slightly dated; 펌 is current — younger salon usage strongly favors 펌. Distinguish the directions too: 펌하고 싶어요 ('I want to perm') states desire, while 펌하려고 왔어요 ('I came to perm') states purpose — both are good openers.
The English-speaker trap here is the want-construction: learners overuse 하고 싶어요 in blunt isolation, but pairing it with -는데(요) makes it sound like a natural lead-in rather than a flat demand.

entries.nuance: 염색하고 싶은데 색 추천해 주세요 chains 염색(을) 하다 ('to dye hair', Sino-Korean 染色) + 하고 싶다 ('want to') + -는데 ('and so…') + 색 ('color') + 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend'). It's a complete, natural consultation opener: state the goal (dye), then ask for guidance (color). The connector -는데 links your wish to the request smoothly — a more advanced but very Korean way to speak than two choppy sentences. Vocabulary to lock in: 염색 = coloring/dyeing; 뿌리 염색 = root touch-up (just the regrowth); 탈색 = bleaching (lightening, often needed before bright colors); 새치 염색 / 흰머리 염색 = covering gray. The English-speaker trap is over-relying on the loanword 컬러 — while 컬러 appears in salon menus, the verb for the act is 염색하다, so 'I want to color my hair' is 염색하고 싶어요, not 컬러하고 싶어요 (which sounds off). Another pitfall is particle/connector overload: keep 색 추천해 주세요 simple (you can drop the object particle), and don't say 색을 추천 주세요 (추천 needs the verb 하다: 추천해 주세요). Also distinguish 염색 (adding color) from 탈색 (removing color/bleaching) — asking for a light color may trigger 탈색해야 돼요? ('do we need to bleach?'). Keep 존댓말 throughout.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 컬러하고 싶어요 for 'dye my hair'.
The verb is 염색하다. 컬러 is a noun in menus, but 'I want to dye it' is 염색하고 싶어요, not 컬러하고 싶어요.
Saying 색 추천 주세요 without 하다.
추천 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. It needs 하다: 색 추천해 주세요.
Confusing 염색 (dye) with 탈색 (bleach).
염색 adds color; 탈색 strips it to lighten. For a bright shade you may need 탈색 first — ask 탈색해야 돼요?, not just 염색해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요 is 원래 ('original, originally', Sino-Korean 元來) + 머리색 ('hair color') + -으로 ('to/into', the particle of result/direction) + 해 주세요. The 'change it INTO' meaning needs the particle -(으)로: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요. -을/를 marks an object, not a result.

원래 머리색 = 'original hair color'. 원해 is from 원하다 ('to want'). Don't write 원해 머리색.

Natural hair may be dark brown, not pure black. For your real shade say 원래 머리색으로; 검은색 ('black') forces full black, which can look unnatural.

entries.nuance: 커트 얼마예요? is 커트 ('a haircut') + 얼마 ('how much (in price)') + 예요 (polite copula), the direct way to ask a service's cost. The key word is 얼마, which asks specifically about PRICE/amount of money — distinct from 얼마나 ('how much/long', about extent or duration). This is the #1 confusion for the previous phrase: 얼마예요? = 'how much does it cost?', while 얼마나 걸려요? = 'how long does it take?' — one consonant-cluster apart but completely different questions, so never mix them. Salons in Korea often price by gender and length (남자 커트 vs. 여자 커트, with long hair costing more), and add-ons like 펌 and 염색 are billed separately, so asking upfront avoids surprises. The English-speaker trap is the copula attachment: 얼마 fuses with the polite ending as 얼마예요 (not 얼마 이에요), and you don't need a particle on 커트 — bare 커트 얼마예요? is natural, whereas 커트가 얼마예요? is also fine but slightly heavier. Another pitfall is using 가격 ('price') awkwardly as 커트 가격 얼마예요? — understandable, but natives just say 커트 얼마예요?. To ask a range, use -부터 ('from'): 펌은 얼마부터예요? ('perms start from how much?'). Keep 존댓말 with staff; drop to 얼마야? only with friends.

structuredNuance.t: 커트 얼마예요? is 커트 ('a haircut') + 얼마 ('how much (in price)') + 예요 (polite copula), the direct way to ask a service's cost. The key word is 얼마, which asks specifically about PRICE/amount of money. Salons in Korea often price by gender and length (남자 커트 vs. 여자 커트, with long hair costing more), and add-ons like 펌 and 염색 are billed separately, so asking upfront avoids surprises. To ask a range, use -부터 ('from'): 펌은 얼마부터예요? ('perms start from how much?'). Keep 존댓말 with staff; drop to 얼마야? only with friends.

얼마 is distinct from 얼마나 ('how much/long', about extent or duration). This is the #1 confusion: 얼마예요? = 'how much does it cost?', while 얼마나 걸려요? = 'how long does it take?' — one consonant-cluster apart but completely different questions, so never mix them.

The English-speaker trap is the copula attachment: 얼마 fuses with the polite ending as 얼마예요 (not 얼마 이에요), and you don't need a particle on 커트 — bare 커트 얼마예요? is natural, whereas 커트가 얼마예요? is also fine but slightly heavier. Another pitfall is using 가격 ('price') awkwardly as 커트 가격 얼마예요? — understandable, but natives just say 커트 얼마예요?.

entries.nuance: 얼마나 걸려요? is 얼마나 ('how much, to what extent') + 걸리다 ('to take time / be required') in polite question form. The verb 걸리다 is the standard way Korean expresses 'time is taken' — it's intransitive, so time is the SUBJECT, not the object: 한 시간 걸려요 ('it takes an hour'), literally 'one hour is taken'. This matters because perms and dyes can run two to three hours, so asking upfront is essential, especially if you have later plans. The English-speaker trap is the verb frame: learners model on 'take' as a transitive verb and say 시간을 얼마나 걸려요? (wrongly marking 시간 as object with 을) or invent 얼마나 걸어요? — but 걸다 ('to hang/make a call') is a different verb; the time verb is 걸리다, used as 얼마나 걸려요?. Another pitfall is mixing up 얼마나 ('how much/long', for extent) with 얼마 ('how much', for price): 얼마예요? asks the cost, 얼마나 걸려요? asks the duration — don't swap them. To soften, add 시간 and -ㄹ까요: 시간 얼마나 걸릴까요? ('I wonder about how long'). Keep 존댓말 with staff.

걸리다 is intransitive; time is the subject, not the object. Say 시간(이) 얼마나 걸려요? or simply 얼마나 걸려요?.

걸다 ('hang / make a phone call') is a different verb. The time-taking verb is 걸리다: 얼마나 걸려요?.

얼마예요? asks the price; 얼마나 걸려요? asks the duration. To ask time, use 얼마나, not 얼마.

entries.nuance: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? combines 마음에 들다 (the IDIOM 'to be to one's liking', lit. 'to enter the heart') negated as 마음에 안 들다 ('to not be to my liking') + -는데 ('and so…') + 다시 ('again') + 해 주시다 (honorific favor) + -ㄹ 수 있어요? ('are you able to…?'). This is the diplomatic, face-saving way to say you're unhappy and request a redo — vital because complaining about service is delicate. The core idiom 마음에 들다 is the natural Korean for 'to like (a thing/result)'; you do NOT use 좋아하다 here, which is for liking people/activities in general — saying 이거 안 좋아해요 about a haircut sounds wrong. That's the #1 English-speaker trap: 'I don't like it' must be 마음에 안 들어요, not 안 좋아해요. The honorific 해 주시다 (with -시-) respectfully asks the stylist, and phrasing the request as an ability question (-ㄹ 수 있어요?) rather than a command keeps it soft and non-confrontational. Another pitfall is the particle in the idiom: it's 마음'에' 들다 (locative 에), so never 마음을 들다 or 마음이 안 들다. Always lead with a softener (죄송한데 'sorry, but…' or a reason like 생각했던 거랑 달라서) before asking for the redo. Keep 존댓말; this is staff-facing.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이거 안 좋아해요 to mean 'I don't like this haircut'.
좋아하다 is for general liking of people/activities. For not liking a result, use the idiom 마음에 안 들어요.
Getting the particle wrong: 마음을 안 들어요 or 마음이 안 들어요.
The idiom takes locative 에: 마음에 안 들어요 ('it doesn't enter my heart'). Not 을/를 or 이/가 on 마음.
Demanding a redo bluntly: 다시 하세요.
다시 하세요 is a command and sounds rude to staff. Ask as an ability question with honorific 시: 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?, and lead with 죄송한데.

entries.nuance: 출석 불렀어요? is 출석 ('attendance', Sino-Korean 出席) + 불렀어요 (past of 부르다 'to call'). Calling roll is literally 출석을 부르다 ('to call attendance'), so this asks 'have they called the roll yet?' — the thing a latecomer most wants to know. It's the polite -어요 form you'd use with a classmate you don't know well; with a friend it drops to 출석 불렀어?. The everyday near-synonym is 출석 체크했어요? (출석 + the loanword 체크 'check'), which is interchangeable in casual academy talk. The key contrast is direction: 출석 불렀어요? asks a peer whether it happened, while 출석 체크해 주세요 asks the TEACHER to mark you present — don't say 출석 불러 주세요 to mean 'mark me', because 부르다 means the act of reading names aloud, not recording you. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'take attendance' word-for-word with 가지다 ('to take/hold') — 출석을 가져요 is meaningless; Korean uses 부르다 ('call') or 체크하다. Also note 출석 is the opposite of 결석 ('absence'); don't mix them up.

Saying 출석 가졌어요? for 'did you take attendance?'.
'Take attendance' is not 가지다 ('to hold/take an object'). Korean says 출석을 부르다 ('call the roll') or 출석 체크하다. Ask 출석 불렀어요? or 출석 체크했어요?

부르다 is reading names aloud, not recording you. To be marked present, say 출석 (체크) 해 주세요 — 출석 불러 주세요 sounds like 'please call out the roll.'

출석 is attendance at class/school; 출근 is 'going to work / clocking in.' Say 출석 for the classroom, not 출근.

entries.shortExplanation: 오늘 결석할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I won't be coming to class today".
entries.explanation: "I won't be coming to class today" — that is 오늘 결석할게요 (oneul gyeolseokalgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 오늘 결석할게요 ("I'll be absent today"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.ko: 선생님, 저 오늘 결석할게요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnim, jeo oneul gyeolseokalgeyo.
examples.en: Teacher, I'll be absent today.
examples.note: A heads-up message before class starts

examples.ko: 몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요. 죄송합니다.
examples.romanization: momi an joaseo oneul gyeolseokalgeyo. joesonghamnida.
examples.en: I'm not feeling well, so I'll miss today. Sorry.
examples.note: Give a reason (몸이 안 좋다) then apologize

examples.ko: 내일 일이 생겨서 결석하게 됐어요. 미리 말씀드려요.
examples.romanization: naeil iri saenggyeoseo gyeolseokage dwaesseoyo. miri malsseumdeuryeoyo.
examples.en: Something came up tomorrow so I'll be absent. Telling you in advance.
examples.note: 결석하게 됐어요 ('it turned out I'll be absent') sounds less willful

entries.nuance: 오늘 결석할게요 is 오늘 ('today') + 결석 ('absence', Sino-Korean 缺席) + -할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 ending that announces your own intention as a courteous notice). It's how you tell a teacher or academy you won't attend. Register matters a lot here: to the teacher you keep -할게요 or go more formal, and you almost always add a reason + 죄송합니다, because announcing an absence bluntly can feel rude. The softer, blame-deflecting variant is 결석하게 됐어요 ('it came to be that I'll be absent'), which frames it as circumstance, not choice — very useful for sounding polite. The everyday plain alternative is 오늘 못 가요 ('I can't come today'). The contrast to watch: 결석 is the neutral/formal word for a missed class, while 빠지다 ('to skip/drop out of') as in 오늘 수업 빠질게요 is more casual and can hint you're choosing to skip — fine with friends, a bit loose to a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'be absent' tempts 있다/없다, but you cannot say 결석이에요 for a planned absence to the teacher; use the verb 결석하다. Also avoid 'skip class' as 점프하다 (a 직역 trap) — that's nonsense in Korean.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 오늘 결석이에요 to announce you'll miss class.
The copula 이에요 states a fact/label, not an action you're doing. To tell the teacher, use the verb: 오늘 결석할게요 (or 못 가요).
Translating 'skip class' as 수업 점프해요 / 스킵해요.
직역 of 'skip/jump' doesn't work. Korean uses 결석하다 (formal) or 수업 빠지다 (casual): 오늘 수업 빠질게요.
Announcing the absence with no reason or apology.
A bare 결석할게요 can sound abrupt to a teacher. Add a reason and 죄송합니다: 몸이 안 좋아서 오늘 결석할게요, 죄송합니다.

entries.shortExplanation: 숙제가 뭐예요? is a practical expression meaning "What's the homework?".
entries.explanation: 숙제가 뭐예요? (sukjega mwoyeyo?) = "What's the homework?". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 숙제가 뭐예요? ("What's the homework?"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

Checking whether any was assigned at all

examples.ko: 숙제가 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: sukjega mwoyeyo?
examples.en: What's the homework?
examples.note: Asked at the end of class or to a friend later

examples.ko: 오늘 숙제 있어요? 있으면 뭐예요?
examples.romanization: oneul sukje isseoyo? isseumyeon mwoyeyo?
examples.en: Is there homework today? If so, what is it?
examples.note: Two-step: check existence, then content

examples.ko: 저 어제 결석해서 그런데, 숙제가 뭐였어요?
examples.romanization: jeo eoje gyeolseokaeseo geureonde, sukjega mwoyeosseoyo?
examples.en: I was absent yesterday — what was the homework?
examples.note: Past 뭐였어요 for homework already assigned

entries.nuance: 숙제가 뭐예요? is 숙제 ('homework', Sino-Korean 宿題) + 가 (subject particle) + 뭐예요 ('what is it?'). It's the basic ask for an assignment, fine to the teacher or a classmate. 숙제 is the standard schoolwork word; in a university/academy context you'll also hear 과제 ('assignment/task', 課題), which sounds more formal and is used for bigger projects, essays, and reports, whereas 숙제 is everyday practice work — using 숙제 for a major term paper sounds a little childish, and 과제 for tiny daily exercises sounds stiff, so match the size of the task. A frequent practical variant is 숙제 어디까지예요? ('how far does the homework go?'), since Korean classes often assign by page range. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: many learners drop it or use 을/를 (숙제를 뭐예요 is wrong) — with 뭐예요 you use the subject 가, or just drop the particle in speech (숙제 뭐예요?). Another trap is treating 숙제 as a verb; it's a noun, so 'do homework' is 숙제하다 / 숙제를 하다, not 숙제다. If you missed a day, switch to past tense: 숙제가 뭐였어요?
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 숙제를 뭐예요?
With 뭐예요 ('what is…?') the noun takes the subject particle 가, not the object 를. Say 숙제가 뭐예요?, or in speech just 숙제 뭐예요?
Using 숙제 for a big essay/report.
숙제 is everyday practice work; a major paper or project is 과제. Calling a term paper 숙제 sounds childish — say 과제 for serious assignments.
Treating 숙제 like a verb (숙제다 / 숙제어요).
숙제 is a noun. 'Do homework' is 숙제하다 or 숙제를 하다. To say you finished it: 숙제 다 했어요, not 숙제했다 as a state.

entries.explanation: 숙제 언제까지예요? (sukje eonjekkajiyeyo?) means "When is the homework due?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 숙제 언제까지예요? ("When is it due?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

examples.ko: 숙제 언제까지예요?
examples.romanization: sukje eonjekkajiyeyo?
examples.en: When's the homework due?
examples.note: Asked right after homework is assigned

examples.ko: 이 과제 언제까지 내야 돼요?
examples.romanization: i gwaje eonjekkaji naeya dwaeyo?
examples.en: By when do I have to submit this assignment?
examples.note: 내야 돼요 ('have to submit') makes the duty explicit

examples.ko: 다음 주 월요일까지예요? 아니면 수업 전까지예요?
examples.romanization: daeum ju woryoilkkajiyeyo? animyeon sueop jeonkkajiyeyo?
examples.en: Is it due next Monday, or before class?
examples.note: Pinning down the exact cutoff with 까지

entries.nuance: 숙제 언제까지예요? is 숙제 + 언제 ('when') + 까지 ('until/by') + 예요. The particle 까지 is doing the heavy lifting: it means 'by (a deadline)', so 언제까지 = 'by when'. This is the natural way to ask a due date, far more idiomatic than 언제 ('when') alone — 숙제 언제예요? sounds like asking when homework happens, not when it's due, so 까지 is essential. For formal assignments the word 마감 ('deadline', lit. 'closing') appears: 과제 마감 언제예요?. The contrast to know: -까지 means 'by/up to and including that point' (a deadline you must meet), while -까지는 or 동안 ('during') express duration — don't confuse 'due by Monday' (월요일까지) with 'until Monday' in the sense of an ongoing period. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 까지 and just asking 언제 (which loses the 'deadline' sense), or using 'submit' as 제출하다 in casual speech when 내다 ('to hand in') is more natural: 언제까지 내야 돼요?. Also, 'due' has no single Korean word — you express it with 까지 + 내다/제출하다, not a 직역.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking 숙제 언제예요? for the deadline.
언제 alone asks 'when (does it happen)?' To ask a due date, add 까지 ('by'): 숙제 언제까지예요?
Looking for one word for 'due'.
Korean has no single 'due'. Express it with 까지 + a verb: 언제까지 내야 돼요? ('by when must I hand it in?'). Don't invent 듀하다.
Overusing 제출하다 in casual class talk.
제출하다 ('to submit') is formal/written. In everyday speech, 내다 ('to hand in') is more natural: 숙제 언제까지 내요?

-까지 means 'by/up to and including that point' (a deadline you must meet), while -까지는 or 동안 ('during') express duration — don't confuse 'due by Monday' (월요일까지) with 'until Monday' in the sense of an ongoing period.
Dropping 까지 and just asking 언제 (which loses the 'deadline' sense); or using 'submit' as 제출하다 in casual speech when 내다 ('to hand in') is more natural: 언제까지 내야 돼요?.

entries.nuance: 숙제 다 했어요 is 숙제 + 다 ('all') + 했어요 (past of 하다 'to do'). The little word 다 means 'all/completely' and is what turns 'I did homework' into 'I finished it all' — it's the natural completion marker, more idiomatic than 완성했어요 ('completed', which sounds like finishing a painting or building) for everyday homework. The negative is the crucial pair: 'I didn't do it' splits into 안 했어요 (didn't do it — chose not to / just didn't) vs. 못 했어요 (couldn't do it — tried but failed / had no time). To a teacher, 다 못 했어요 ('couldn't finish') sounds more sympathetic than 안 했어요 ('didn't do it'), so pick deliberately. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 안/못 distinction: saying 숙제 안 했어요 when you mean you ran out of time makes you sound like you blew it off. Another trap is placing 다 wrong — it goes before the verb (다 했어요), not after. For a major 과제, 끝냈어요 ('finished/wrapped up') sounds better than 했어요.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 숙제 안 했어요 when you ran out of time.
안 했어요 = 'didn't do it (chose not to).' If you tried but couldn't finish, say 못 했어요 ('couldn't'): 숙제 다 못 했어요 — it sounds far less like you blew it off.
Using 완성했어요 for finishing homework.
완성하다 ('to complete') fits a painting, building, or big creation. For homework, the natural word is 다 했어요 (or 끝냈어요 for a project).
Putting 다 after the verb: 했어요 다.
다 ('all') comes before the verb: 다 했어요. 했어요 다 is unnatural word order.

entries.nuance: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 is 한 번 ('one time') + 더 ('more') + 설명하다 ('to explain', 說明) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The favor verb 주세요 is essential — it asks the teacher to explain FOR your benefit, which is polite; bare 설명하세요 would be an order ('you, explain!') and sounds rude to a teacher. 한 번 더 ('one more time') is the crisp, natural way to ask for a repeat; the near-synonym 다시 ('again') also works (다시 설명해 주세요), the difference being that 한 번 더 stresses 'one additional time' while 다시 stresses 'from the start/over again' — both fine in class. To sound more deferential to a teacher you respect, swap 말하다 for the humble-honorific 말씀하다: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?. The English-speaker pitfall is omitting 주다 and commanding 설명하세요, or 직역-ing 'one more time' as 한 더 번 (wrong order — the counter sequence is number + 번, so 한 번 + 더). Also, to say you didn't understand, use 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't get understood'), not 나는 이해하지 않아요, which sounds like you refuse to understand.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 설명하세요 to the teacher.
Bare -세요 here is a command ('explain!') and sounds bossy. Use the favor form: 한 번 더 설명해 주세요 ('please explain for me').
Word order 한 더 번 / 더 한 번.
The counter pattern is number + counter, then 더: 한 번 더. 한 더 번 is wrong; 더 한 번 sounds off in this request.
Saying 이해하지 않아요 for 'I don't understand'.
That sounds like 'I refuse to understand.' Natural Korean is 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood') or 잘 모르겠어요.

entries.nuance: 질문 있어요 is 질문 ('question', 質問) + 있어요 ('there is/I have'). It's the simple, correct way to signal you want to ask something. The polite upgrade for a teacher is the humble verb 여쭤보다 ('to ask (up)'), used when YOU ask a SUPERIOR: 여쭤봐도 돼요? ('may I ask?'). The key verb contrast English speakers must learn: 물어보다 is the plain 'to ask' (asking a peer or someone below you), while 여쭤보다 is its humble form for asking someone above you — using 물어봐도 돼요? to a respected teacher isn't wrong but 여쭤봐도 돼요? sounds more polished. A softer way to open is 질문 있는데요 (with -는데요, the gentle 'just so you know…' ender that invites the teacher to say 'go ahead'). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb 'have': don't say 질문 가지고 있어요 (직역 of 'have', sounds like physically holding a question) — Korean uses 있다 ('there is'): 질문 있어요. Another trap is 질문하다 vs. 질문 있다 — 질문하다 means the act of questioning ('to pose a question'), so 'I have a question' is 질문 있어요, while 'I'll ask' is 질문할게요.

물어보다 is plain 'ask (a peer).' To a teacher, the humble 여쭤보다 is more polished: 여쭤봐도 돼요?

질문하다 = the act of asking; 질문 있다 = having a question. To flag one, say 질문 있어요, not 질문해요 (which announces you're asking now).

("Did you register for classes?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.en: Did you register for courses?

examples.romanization: ibeon hakgi sugang sincheong da haesseoyo?
examples.en: Did you finish registering this semester?
examples.note: 이번 학기 ('this semester') + 다 했어요 ('done it all')

entries.nuance: 수강 신청했어요? is 수강 신청 ('course registration': 수강 受講 'taking a class' + 신청 申請 'application') + 했어요 ('did'). This is THE word for signing up for university/academy courses each term — it's the act of choosing which classes to take. Crucially, distinguish it from 등록 ('enrollment/registration', 登錄), which in Korean school contexts means officially enrolling and PAYING tuition (등록금 = tuition). So 수강 신청 = picking your courses; 등록 = paying/enrolling as a student — they're separate steps and not interchangeable, which trips up English speakers who lump both under 'register.' Another near-term is 신청하다 alone ('to apply'), which needs an object (장학금 신청 'scholarship application', 휴학 신청 'leave-of-absence application'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 등록하다 when you mean course sign-up: saying 수업 등록했어요? is understandable but slightly off — natives say 수강 신청했어요?. Also, the verb attaches via 하다: 수강 신청하다 / 수강 신청을 하다, never 수강 신청이다. Korean university 수강 신청 is famously a fast, competitive click-race (often called 수강 신청 전쟁, 'registration war'), so 자리 없어서 못 했어요 ('couldn't, no seats') is a common lament.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 등록하다 to mean 'register for a course'.
등록 in school = enrolling/paying tuition (등록금). Picking courses is 수강 신청. Say 수강 신청했어요?, not 수업 등록했어요?
Saying 수강 신청이에요 instead of the verb.
수강 신청 is a noun that takes 하다: 수강 신청했어요 / 수강 신청을 했어요. The copula 이에요 doesn't express the action of signing up.

structuredNuance.t: 수강 신청했어요? = 수강 신청 ('course registration') + 했어요 ('did'). This is THE word for signing up for university/academy courses each term — the act of choosing which classes to take. The verb attaches via 하다: 수강 신청하다 / 수강 신청을 하다, never 수강 신청이다. Korean university 수강 신청 is famously a fast, competitive click-race (often called 수강 신청 전쟁, 'registration war'), so 자리 없어서 못 했어요 ('couldn't, no seats') is a common lament.

Distinguish it from 등록 ('enrollment/registration', 登錄), which in Korean school contexts means officially enrolling and PAYING tuition (등록금 = tuition). So 수강 신청 = picking your courses; 등록 = paying/enrolling as a student — separate steps, not interchangeable. Another near-term is 신청하다 alone ('to apply'), which needs an object (장학금 신청 'scholarship application', 휴학 신청 'leave-of-absence application').
수강 신청 = 수강 受講 ('taking a class') + 신청 申請 ('application').
Using 등록하다 when you mean course sign-up: saying 수업 등록했어요? is understandable but slightly off — natives say 수강 신청했어요?. English speakers lump both 수강 신청 and 등록 under 'register.'

entries.nuance: 시험 언제예요? is 시험 ('exam', 試驗) + 언제 ('when') + 예요. Simple and correct. The crucial collocation to learn is the verb for 'taking' an exam: 시험을 보다 (lit. 'to see an exam') or 시험을 치다 — NOT 시험을 하다 or 가지다. So 'I take a test' is 시험 봐요, 'I have a test next week' is 다음 주에 시험 봐요. Closely related study words: 범위 ('range/scope' — which chapters are covered), 중간고사 ('midterm', 中間考査), 기말고사 ('final exam', 期末考査). The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'do a test' or 'have a test' tempts 시험을 해요 / 시험이 있어요 — while 시험이 있어요 ('there's a test') is actually fine for 'I have a test', the act of taking it is 시험을 보다, so 'I'm taking the test now' is 시험 보고 있어요, never 시험 하고 있어요. Another distinction: 시험 본다 ('take the exam', as a student) vs. 시험 친다 (same, regional/also common) vs. 시험 출제하다 ('to set/write the exam', what a teacher does) — as a student you 보다, not 출제하다. Don't confuse 시험 ('exam') with 실험 ('experiment'), which sound alike but mean very different things.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 시험을 해요 for 'take a test'.
The verb for sitting an exam is 보다 (or 치다): 시험을 봐요. 시험을 하다 is not idiomatic for taking one.

시험 = exam/test; 실험 = experiment. 실험 언제예요? would ask when the lab experiment is — say 시험 for a school test.

출제하다 ('to set questions') is what the teacher does. A student says 시험 봤어요 ('I took the test'), not 출제했어요.

entries.nuance: 시험 범위가 어디까지예요? is 시험 범위 ('exam scope': 시험 + 범위 範圍 'range') + 가 + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 예요. 범위 is the standard school word for 'what's on the test' — the chapters/pages covered. The phrase 어디까지 ('up to where') pairs with the deadline-style 까지 ('up to/until') to ask the END point of coverage; combine with 부터 ('from') to state a span: 3과부터 7과까지 ('from lesson 3 to lesson 7'). A more casual equivalent is 시험에 뭐 나와요? (lit. 'what comes out on the test?'), where 나오다 ('to come out/appear') is the idiomatic verb for material APPEARING on an exam — a high-frequency collocation worth memorizing. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'cover' literally with 덮다 ('to cover with a lid') — 시험이 덮어요 is nonsense; Korean expresses coverage with 범위 + 까지 or with 나오다 ('appears'). Another trap is the counter for lessons: textbook units are counted with 과 (제3과 / 3과, 'lesson 3'), so 'up to lesson 7' is 7과까지, not 7 레슨까지. Also note 범위 vs. 분야 ('field/area') — 범위 is the test's span; 분야 is a subject field, not interchangeable here.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'cover' as 덮다.
덮다 means physically covering (with a lid/blanket). Exam coverage is 범위 + 까지, or use 나오다: 시험에 뭐 나와요? ('what's on the test?').
Saying 7 레슨까지 for textbook lessons.
Korean counts textbook units with 과: 7과까지 ('up to lesson 7'). 레슨 is rarely used for school chapters.
Using 분야 instead of 범위.
분야 = a field/discipline (e.g., 의학 분야 'the medical field'). The test's span is 범위. Ask 시험 범위가 어디까지예요?

examples.note: 오늘 배운 거 ('what I learned today') as the object

entries.nuance: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 is 복습 ('review (of learned material)', 復習) + 좀 (softener) + 해야겠어요 (해야겠다 = 'I'd better do', expressing a self-directed resolution). The -아/어야겠어요 ending is a nice way to say 'I really ought to' about yourself. The essential pair to learn: 복습 ('review' — going over what you ALREADY learned, 復 'again' + 習 'study') vs. 예습 ('preview' — studying ahead BEFORE class, 豫 'beforehand' + 習) — Korean neatly splits these into two words, where English just says 'review/prepare,' so English speakers must pick the right one: after class you 복습, before class you 예습. Don't confuse either with 연습 ('practice', 練習) — that's drilling a skill (피아노 연습 'piano practice'), not going over lessons. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'review' as 다시 보다 ('to look again') — while 다시 보다 can work casually, the precise academic word is 복습하다. Another trap: 복습 is a noun needing 하다 (복습하다 / 복습을 하다), not 복습이다. The verb 까먹다 ('to forget', colloquial) in the example is the everyday spoken word, vs. the neutral 잊어버리다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Confusing 복습 with 예습.
복습 = reviewing what you already learned (after class); 예습 = previewing ahead (before class). Don't say 예습 when you mean to go back over today's lesson — say 복습.
Mixing up 복습 and 연습.
연습 ('practice') is drilling a skill (연습 문제 'practice problems', 발음 연습 'pronunciation practice'). Going over lessons is 복습. They're different 習 words.
Saying 복습이에요 instead of 복습하다.
복습 is a noun and needs 하다: 복습해요 / 복습을 해요. 복습이에요 just labels something as 'review,' not the act of reviewing.

structuredNuance.t: 복습 좀 해야겠어요 = 복습 ('review of learned material', 復習) + 좀 (softener) + 해야겠어요 (해야겠다 = 'I'd better do', a self-directed resolution). The -아/어야겠어요 ending is a nice way to say 'I really ought to' about yourself. The verb 까먹다 ('to forget', colloquial) in the examples is the everyday spoken word, vs. the neutral 잊어버리다.

The essential pair: 복습 ('review' — going over what you ALREADY learned) vs. 예습 ('preview' — studying ahead BEFORE class) — Korean neatly splits these into two words, where English just says 'review/prepare,' so pick the right one: after class you 복습, before class you 예습. Don't confuse either with 연습 ('practice', 練習) — that's drilling a skill (피아노 연습 'piano practice'), not going over lessons. Also 복습 is a noun needing 하다 (복습하다 / 복습을 하다), not 복습이다.
복습 = 復 'again' + 習 'study'; 예습 = 豫 'beforehand' + 習; 연습 練習 ('practice'). They are different 習 words.
직역-ing 'review' as 다시 보다 ('to look again') — while 다시 보다 can work casually, the precise academic word is 복습하다.

entries.nuance: 잘 모르겠어요 is 잘 ('well') + 모르다 ('to not know') + -겠- + 어요. Counterintuitively, 잘 모르겠어요 is SOFTER and more natural than plain 몰라요 ('I don't know'): the -겠- adds a hedging, tentative feel ('I'm afraid I don't quite know'), and 잘 ('well') means 'I don't know it WELL' rather than a flat blank — so this is the polite, humble way to admit you're lost in class, while bare 몰라요 can sound curt or even dismissive ('dunno'). The contrast: 몰라요 = flat 'I don't know'; 잘 모르겠어요 = gentle 'I'm not really sure' (preferred to a teacher). For 'I don't understand' specifically, 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't come to be understood') is the natural phrasing, NOT 이해하지 않아요 (which sounds like refusing to understand). The English-speaker pitfall is using 몰라요 everywhere and sounding blunt, or 직역-ing 'I can't understand' as 이해할 수 없어요 — that's overly strong ('it's impossible to understand'), whereas 잘 모르겠어요 / 이해가 안 돼요 is the right register for class. Also, 모르겠어요 with -겠- is not future tense here; it's a softening device, a frequent confusion.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying flat 몰라요 to the teacher.
몰라요 ('dunno') can sound curt. The softer, humbler 잘 모르겠어요 ('I'm not quite sure') is the polite classroom version.
Saying 이해하지 않아요 for 'I don't understand'.
That implies you refuse to understand. Use 이해가 안 돼요 ('it doesn't get understood') or 잘 모르겠어요.
Reading -겠- in 모르겠어요 as future.
Here -겠- softens the statement, not future tense. 잘 모르겠어요 means 'I'm not sure (right now),' not 'I will not know.'

entries.nuance: 다음 시간에 봬요 is 다음 시간 ('next time/period' — 시간 here means the class period) + 에 ('at') + 봬요 (contraction of 뵈어요, the humble form of 보다 'to see', used when seeing a SUPERIOR). The key point is the humble verb: to a teacher you don't say 봐요 (plain 'see'), you say 봬요 / 뵈어요 (humble), because 뵈다/뵙다 is 보다 elevated for meeting someone above you — using plain 다음 시간에 봐요 to a teacher is understandable but less respectful. The spelling 봬요 vs 뵈요 confuses even Koreans: the correct contraction of 뵈어요 is 봬요. At the very end of class, the expected set phrase to the teacher is 수고하셨습니다 ('you've worked hard'), a courtesy you say to someone who did the work/effort — note you generally say it to peers, juniors, or in service contexts, and to a clearly senior teacher 감사합니다 ('thank you') is safer, since 수고하셨습니다 can feel slightly evaluative coming from below. The English-speaker pitfall is using plain 봐요 to the teacher, or 직역-ing 'see you' as 너를 봐요 ('I see YOU' with an object) — the set goodbye drops the object: just 다음 시간에 봬요. The extra-formal 뵙겠습니다 ('I will see you') is even more deferential.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다음 시간에 봐요 to the teacher.
봐요 is plain 'see.' To a teacher use the humble 봬요 / 뵈어요 (from 뵈다, 'to see a superior'): 다음 시간에 봬요.
Adding an object: 선생님을 봐요.
The goodbye drops the object. Just say 다음 시간에 봬요, not 선생님을 봐요 (which sounds like reporting that you see the teacher).
Saying 수고하셨습니다 to a much-senior teacher.
From a student to a clearly senior teacher, 수고하셨습니다 can feel evaluative. 감사합니다 ('thank you') is safer; use 수고하셨습니다 with peers/juniors.

entries.shortExplanation: 환불돼요? is a practical expression meaning "Can I get a refund (on the tuition)?".
entries.explanation: "Can I get a refund (on the tuition)?" — that is 환불돼요? (hwanbuldwaeyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 환불돼요? ("Can I get a refund?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

examples.romanization: sueom mot deureul geot gateunde hwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: I don't think I can attend — can I get a refund?

examples.romanization: han beondo an naganneunde jeonae kwanbuldwaeyo?
examples.en: I never attended even once — can I get a full refund?
examples.note: 전액 ('full amount') + 환불 for a complete refund

entries.nuance: 환불돼요? is 환불 ('refund', 還拂) + 되다 ('to be possible') in polite question form: 'is a refund possible?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility/policy — exactly what you want when asking an academy about getting your money back. For academies (학원) this is a real and common need: tuition is 수강료 or 학원비, a full refund is 전액 환불, and the rules are 환불 규정. Once you know it's possible, you request it with 환불해 주세요 ('please refund it') or 환불받고 싶어요 ('I'd like to get a refund'). The verb contrast: 환불하다 is what the academy does (issue the refund), while 환불받다 ('receive a refund') is what YOU do — so as the customer, 환불받고 싶어요 is more accurate than 환불하고 싶어요 (which sounds like you'll be giving the refund). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 하다/받다 direction confusion, plus 직역-ing 'get my money back' as 돈 다시 가져가요 ('I'll take the money again'), which is unidiomatic — say 환불돼요? or 환불받을 수 있어요?. Korea has legally mandated 학원 refund schedules (you generally get more back the earlier you cancel), so asking 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is smart and normal.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 환불하고 싶어요 as the customer.
환불하다 (issue a refund) is what the academy does. You RECEIVE one: 환불받고 싶어요 ('I'd like to get a refund').
직역-ing 'get my money back' as 돈 다시 가져가요.
That's unidiomatic. Use 환불: 환불돼요? ('can I get a refund?') or 환불받을 수 있어요?
Confusing 환불 with 할인.
환불 = a refund (money back on something paid). 할인 = a discount (lower price). Asking 할인돼요? requests a price cut, not your money back.

entries.nuance: 보강 가능해요? is 보강 ('make-up class / supplementary lesson', 補講 — 補 'supplement' + 講 'lecture') + 가능하다 ('to be possible') in polite question form. 보강 is the specific academy word for a class held to make up for one you missed (or one the teacher had to reschedule). This is essential vocabulary for academy life that English handles with the loose phrase 'make-up class' — Korean has the precise term 보강. To request one you say 보강하다 / 보강 신청하다 ('to apply for a make-up') or 보강 받다 ('to receive a make-up'). The contrast to know: 보강 is making up a MISSED session, while 복습 ('review') is going over material on your own, and 추가 수업 ('extra/additional class') is a bonus lesson beyond the schedule — don't say 추가 수업 when you mean making up an absence. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'make-up class' as 화장 수업 (since 화장 also means 'makeup' cosmetics!) — a real and embarrassing false-friend trap; the correct word is 보강, never 화장. Another trap is the particle with 가능하다: it pairs with 이/가 or stands alone (보강 가능해요?), not 보강을 가능해요. Also 보강 vs 보충 (補充): 보충 수업 also means supplementary class and is common in schools, near-synonymous; academies tend to say 보강.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 화장 수업 for 'make-up class'.
False friend! 화장 = cosmetics makeup. A make-up (supplementary) class is 보강. Ask 보강 가능해요?, never 화장 수업.
Using 추가 수업 to mean making up an absence.
추가 수업 = an extra/bonus class beyond schedule. Making up a MISSED class is 보강. Say 보강 가능해요? for what you missed.
Saying 보강을 가능해요.
가능하다 takes 이/가 or no particle: 보강(이) 가능해요. 보강을 가능해요 is ungrammatical — drop 을 or use 보강할 수 있어요.

entries.nuance: 진도 어디까지 나갔어요? is 진도 ('progress through material', 進度) + 어디까지 ('up to where') + 나갔어요 (past of 나가다 'to go out/advance'). This is the natural, idiomatic way to ask how far a class has gotten through the curriculum — vital when you've missed a session and need to catch up. The crucial collocation is 진도가 나가다 (lit. 'progress goes out/advances'): Korean uses the motion verb 나가다 to express a class MOVING FORWARD through material, which is non-obvious to English speakers. So 'we covered a lot' is 진도가 많이 나갔어요, 'the class is slow' is 진도가 느려요. The contrast: 진도 ('how far through the syllabus') vs. 범위 ('exam scope') vs. 복습 ('review') — 진도 is about the curriculum's forward motion, not the test or self-study. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'how far did we go' as 우리 얼마나 멀리 갔어요? (sounds like physical distance traveled!) — the idiom is 진도 어디까지 나갔어요?. Another trap is using 가다 instead of 나가다 (진도 갔어요 sounds off; the set verb is 나가다). For a lighter, simpler ask, 오늘 어디 했어요? ('what part did you do today?') also works among classmates.

examples.romanization: siheom jal bwasseoyo?

entries.nuance: 시험 잘 봤어요? is 시험 ('exam') + 잘 ('well') + 봤어요 (past of 보다 — recall that 'to take an exam' is 시험을 보다). So literally 'did you SEE the exam well?' meaning 'did it go well / did you do well?'. This reuses the key collocation 시험(을) 보다, now in the past to ask about RESULTS, which makes it the natural conversational follow-up to 시험 언제예요?. The opposite reply is 시험 망쳤어요 ('I ruined the test') — 망치다 ('to spoil/ruin') is THE everyday verb for bombing an exam, far more idiomatic than a 직역 like 나빴어요 ('it was bad'). Score vocabulary: 점수 ('score', 點數), 점 (the counter for points — 90점 '90 points'), and the collocation 점수가 나오다 / 점수를 받다 ('a score comes out / to get a score'). The contrast: 시험 잘 봤어요? asks how it WENT (the experience/outcome), while 시험 결과 언제 나와요? asks specifically WHEN the graded results are released — don't merge them. The English-speaker pitfall is 직역-ing 'do well' as 잘 했어요? — 시험 잘 했어요? sounds slightly off because the set verb is 보다, not 하다, so keep 시험 잘 봤어요?. Another trap: a low score uses 틀리다 ('to be wrong') for mistakes, not 잘못하다 ('to do wrong/misbehave') — you got an answer 틀렸어, you didn't 잘못했어.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 시험 잘 했어요? for 'did you do well?'.
The verb for an exam is 보다, not 하다. The idiomatic ask is 시험 잘 봤어요? — 시험 했어요 sounds off.
Saying 시험이 나빴어요 for 'I did badly'.
직역 of 'bad' is unnatural here. Koreans say 시험 망쳤어요 ('I bombed it', from 망치다) or 시험 못 봤어요 ('didn't do well').
Using 잘못했어요 for wrong test answers.
잘못하다 = to misbehave / do wrong (an act). A wrong answer is 틀리다: 두 문제 틀렸어요 ('I got two wrong'), not 잘못했어요.

examples.romanization: mianhande noteu jom billyeojul su isseoyo?
examples.en: Sorry, could you lend me your notes?
examples.note: 미안한데 ('sorry, but…') softens the favor

examples.ko: 어제 결석해서요, 필기한 거 사진 찍어도 돼요?
examples.romanization: eoje gyeolseokaeseoyo, pilgihan geo sajin jjigeodo dwaeyo?
