examples.note: 필기한 거 ('what you wrote down') + 사진 찍다

examples.ko: 노트 빌려주면 오늘 안에 돌려줄게요.
examples.romanization: noteu billyeojumyeon oneul ane dollyeojulgeyo.
examples.en: If you lend me your notes, I'll return them today.
examples.note: 돌려주다 ('to return') reassures you'll give it back

entries.nuance: 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? is 노트 ('notes/notebook', from English) + 좀 (softener) + 빌려주다 ('to lend') + ㄹ 수 있어요 ('can you…?'). The make-or-break vocabulary here is the borrow/lend pair, which English speakers constantly mix up because English uses different words too: 빌리다 = 'to BORROW' (you take it), 빌려주다 = 'to LEND' (they give it to you). When asking a classmate to give you THEIR notes, you must say 빌려주다 ('lend to me') — 노트 빌려줄 수 있어요? — not 빌릴 수 있어요? from their perspective; saying 노트 빌릴 수 있어요? is actually fine too ('can I borrow?'), but the favor framing 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?') is warmer and clearer. The related word 필기 ('lecture notes / written-down content', 筆記) is what's actually on the page — 필기 보여줄 수 있어요? ('can you show me your notes?'). The English-speaker pitfall is using one verb for both directions: don't say 빌려주다 when you mean you'll borrow (빌리다), or vice versa. Another trap: in practice Koreans often just photograph notes, so 사진 찍어도 돼요? ('may I take a photo?') is a super common, low-imposition alternative. Add 돌려줄게요 ('I'll return it') to be courteous about giving it back.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Mixing up 빌리다 and 빌려주다.
빌리다 = you borrow (take); 빌려주다 = they lend (give). To ask a classmate to give you their notes, say 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?') — or 빌릴 수 있어요? ('can I borrow?'), but never use them backwards.
Saying 노트 줄 수 있어요? when you'll give it back.
주다 ('give') implies keeping it. To borrow and return, use 빌려주다 ('lend'): 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요?

structuredNuance.t: 노트 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? = 노트 ('notes/notebook', from English) + 좀 (softener) + 빌려주다 ('to lend') + ㄹ 수 있어요 ('can you…?'). The related word 필기 ('lecture notes / written-down content', 筆記) is what's actually on the page — 필기 보여줄 수 있어요? ('can you show me your notes?'). In practice Koreans often just photograph notes, so 사진 찍어도 돼요? ('may I take a photo?') is a super common, low-imposition alternative. Add 돌려줄게요 ('I'll return it') to be courteous about giving it back.

The make-or-break pair is borrow/lend, which English speakers constantly mix up: 빌리다 = 'to BORROW' (you take it), 빌려주다 = 'to LEND' (they give it to you). When asking a classmate to give you THEIR notes, say 빌려주다 ('lend to me') — 노트 빌려줄 수 있어요?. Saying 노트 빌릴 수 있어요? ('can I borrow?') is fine too, but the favor framing 빌려줄 수 있어요? ('can you lend?') is warmer and clearer.
Using one verb for both directions: don't say 빌려주다 when you mean you'll borrow (빌리다), or vice versa.

entries.nuance: 얼마예요? is the single most useful shopping phrase, said by a customer to a seller to ask a price; 얼마 means 'how much/how many' and 예요 is the polite copula, so it literally asks 'it is how much?'. The politeness sits at the everyday 해요체 level — perfectly polite for markets, shops and taxis — and you drop to 얼마야? only with a friend, or rise to 얼마입니까? in a formal counter or on the phone. The nearest alternative, 가격이 어떻게 돼요? ('what's the price?'), is a touch softer and more common for services or quotes, while 얼마예요? is the blunt, direct market question; the dividing line is that 얼마예요? names a number you expect right now. The classic English-speaker mistake is writing 얼마에요 — the copula after a vowel is 예요, not 에요 — and saying 얼마이에요, which is over-spelled; native spelling is 얼마예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Spelling it 얼마에요.
After a noun ending in a vowel the polite copula is -예요, not -에요. The correct, natural spelling is 얼마예요?
Asking 얼마 많아요? thinking 많다 means 'much'.
많다 is 'many/a lot' (quantity), not price. Price uses the fixed word 얼마, so it is 얼마예요?
Using 얼마야? with a shop clerk you don't know.
얼마야? is 반말 and sounds rude to a stranger. To any seller use 얼마예요? or 얼마입니까?

entries.nuance: 이거 얼마예요? is the pointing version of the price question, said by a customer holding or gesturing at one specific item right in front of them; 이거 is the spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing'), so it means 'this — how much?'. It stays at polite 해요체, the default for shops; with a friend's stall you can say 이거 얼마야?, and in a formal showroom 이것은 얼마입니까?. The key three-way distance system is 이거 (this, near me) / 그거 (that, near you) / 저거 (that, far from both), and English speakers, who only have 'this/that', constantly mix up 그거 and 저거. The nearest alternative is just 얼마예요? with a point, but adding 이거 removes all ambiguity about which item — useful when several sit side by side. The typical mistake is saying 이것 얼마예요? in speech: in conversation Koreans almost always shorten 이것 to 이거, and they attach no particle (not 이거가/이거를) before 얼마예요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이것 얼마예요? in conversation.
이것 is the written form; spoken Korean contracts it to 이거. Natural speech is 이거 얼마예요?
Adding a particle: 이거를 얼마예요?
얼마예요 takes no object; the thing is simply named as the topic. Say 이거 얼마예요? with no 를/가.
Using 저거 for an item right in your hand.
저거 means 'that, far away'. For something you're holding use 이거. Pick the right distance word.

entries.nuance: 좀 깎아 주세요 is a customer's haggling request at a place where bargaining is normal — traditional markets (시장), street stalls, some electronics alleys — but NOT department stores, franchises or convenience stores, where it falls flat. 깎다 literally means 'to shave/whittle down', so you ask the seller to 'shave a bit off (the price)'; 좀 ('a little') is the softener that makes it polite rather than pushy, and 주세요 makes it a request 'for me'. It sits at polite 해요체; drop to 깎아 줘 only with a friend, and soften upward with 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? ('couldn't you take some off?'). The nearest alternative, 싸게 해 주세요 ('make it cheap for me'), asks for a lower price in general, while 깎아 주세요 specifically asks to reduce THIS quoted number — the dividing line is that 깎다 acts on an already-stated price. English speakers translate 'discount' as the loanword 디스카운트 or say 할인해 주세요 (할인 is the store's own 'sale', odd to demand by hand), which sounds unnatural at a market; the native haggle is 깎아 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 디스카운트 주세요 or 할인해 주세요 to haggle.
할인 is a store-set sale, not something you request face to face; the loanword sounds off. The market verb is 깎다: 좀 깎아 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and just saying 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without 좀 it sounds blunt, almost like an order. 좀 softens it into a polite request, so include it.
Trying to haggle in a department store or chain.
깎아 주세요 only works where bargaining is expected (markets, stalls). In fixed-price shops it just confuses the clerk.

entries.nuance: 입어 봐도 돼요? is a customer asking a clothing clerk for permission to try a garment on; it is built from 입다 ('to wear/put on') + the -아/어 보다 'try doing' pattern + -아도 돼요? 'is it okay to...?', so literally 'is it okay if I try wearing it?'. The crucial point is that Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 for clothes on the torso/legs (shirts, pants, dresses), 신다 for shoes/socks on the feet, 쓰다 for hats/glasses, 끼다 for gloves/rings — so this exact phrase is only for clothes you 입다. ('can I take a look?'), only asks to look, not to put on — 입어 봐도 돼요? specifically asks to wear it. English speakers literally translate 'try on' and may say 시도해 봐도 돼요? (시도 = 'attempt', wrong here) or use 입어 for shoes; both miss. Use 입어 for tops, 신어 for shoes.

The polite form of 되다 here is 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요. Correct: 입어 봐도 돼요?

entries.nuance: 신어 봐도 돼요? is the shoe-shop twin of 입어 봐도 돼요?: a customer asks a clerk to try footwear on. 신다 is the verb specifically for putting on shoes and socks (things on your feet), combined with -아 보다 'try' and -아도 돼요? entries.nuance: 다른 색 있어요? is a customer asking a clerk whether an item comes in a different color; 다른 means 'other/different', 색 is the short spoken form of 색깔 ('color'), and 있어요? is 'is there / do you have?'. Politeness is everyday 해요체; casual is 다른 색 있어?, and a slightly softer poll is 다른 색깔도 있나요?. The verb of stock/availability in Korean is always 있다 ('to exist/have'), so 'do you have X?' becomes 'X 있어요?' — there is no separate verb 'to have' like English; this trips up beginners who hunt for a 'have' verb. The nearest alternative, 다른 거 있어요? ('do you have a different one?'), asks for a different item generally, while 다른 색 있어요? pins it to color specifically. entries.nuance: 더 큰 거 있어요? is a customer asking for a larger size or larger item; 더 means 'more', 큰 is the adjective 크다 ('big') in its noun-modifying form, 거 is the spoken 것 ('thing/one'), and 있어요? is 'do you have?'. ('another size?'), is vaguer, while 더 큰 거 specifies the direction. The big English-speaker trap is the adjective form: 크다 becomes 큰 before a noun (큰 거), NOT 크는 거 — descriptive adjectives use -ㄴ/은, not -는, to modify nouns; saying 크는 거 is a classic error. entries.nuance: 이거 세일해요? is a customer checking whether an item is discounted; 세일 is the English loanword 'sale' and 하다 makes it a verb, so 'does this do a sale / is this on sale?'. This is the everyday store word (department stores, franchises) — the opposite setting from 깎아 주세요 at a market. Politeness is 해요체; casual 세일해?, softer 세일 중인가요?. The native synonym is 할인 (割引, 'discount'): 할인해요? / 할인되는 거예요? mean the same and sound a touch more formal or written; the dividing line is register, not meaning — 세일 is breezy and spoken, 할인 is the word on signs and receipts. English speakers often say 온 세일 ('on sale') copying English, but Korean treats 세일 as a verb with 하다, so it's 세일해요?, not 온 세일이에요. Another error is confusing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (available to buy) — Korean 세일 only means discounted; 'is this for sale?' would be 이거 파는 거예요?.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 온 세일이에요? copying English 'on sale'.
Korean uses 세일 as a 하다-verb. Ask 이거 세일해요? — there is no 'on' construction.
Mixing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (available).
세일 = discounted only. To ask if something is purchasable, say 이거 파는 거예요?, not 세일.
Treating 세일 and 할인 as different deals.
They mean the same; 할인 is just more formal/written. Either 세일해요? or 할인돼요? works.

entries.nuance: 환불돼요? asks a clerk whether a refund (money back) is possible; 환불 is Sino-Korean 還拂 ('return-pay'), and 되다 here means 'to be possible/to work', so 'is a refund doable?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 환불돼?, more formal 환불 가능한가요?. The crucial contrast is 환불 (refund — money back) vs 교환 (exchange — swap for another item); Korean keeps these strictly separate, and English speakers who say 'return' blur them — decide whether you want your money (환불) or a different item (교환). You ask 환불돼요? to learn if it's allowed, and 환불해 주세요 to actually demand it. The spelling trap is 돼요 vs 되요: the polite form is 되 + 어 = 돼요, so 환불돼요, never 환불되요. entries.nuance: 교환돼요? asks whether you can swap an item for a different size or color (or different item), said by a customer to a clerk; 교환 is Sino-Korean 交換 ('exchange/swap') and 되다 = 'to be possible', so 'is an exchange doable?'. entries.nuance: 영수증 주세요 is a customer asking the cashier for the receipt; 영수증 is Sino-Korean 領收證 ('proof of receiving payment') and 주세요 is the polite 'please give (me)'. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 영수증 좀 주시겠어요?. In Korea the cashier often asks 영수증 드릴까요? ('shall I give you the receipt?') and many shops won't process a refund/exchange without it, so keeping it matters. Don't confuse 영수증 (paper receipt, proof of purchase) with 현금영수증 (a separate cash-receipt registered to your phone number for tax deduction) — Koreans are often asked 현금영수증 해 드릴까요?. The nearest related verb is just 주세요 ('please give'), with 영수증 as the thing; note no particle is needed (not 영수증을 주세요 in casual speech, though 영수증을 is also correct and slightly fuller). A common English-speaker mistake is mispronouncing/misspelling it as 영수정 or 영수즁; it's 영수증. Also, 주세요 already means 'give me', so don't add 저에게 ('to me') — it's understood.

영수증 = the purchase receipt; 현금영수증 = a tax cash-receipt tied to your number. Different things; ask for the one you need.
Adding 저에게: 저에게 영수증 주세요.
주세요 already means 'give me'. Just say 영수증 주세요 — the 'to me' is built in.

The correct word is 영수증 (證, 'proof'). Get the final 증 right.

entries.shortExplanation: 그냥 둘러볼게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm just looking around".
entries.explanation: 그냥 둘러볼게요 (geunyang dulleobolgeyo) means "I'm just looking around". Say it as one set phrase — for example 그냥 둘러볼게요 ("I'm just looking around"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

반말 to a friend
구경 = browsing/sightseeing, very common
Shortest polite brush-off

examples.ko: 그냥 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: geunyang dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: I'm just looking around.
examples.note: Bare reply when a clerk asks if you need help

examples.ko: 아, 괜찮아요. 그냥 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: a, gwaenchanayo. geunyang dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: Oh, it's okay. I'm just browsing.
examples.note: 괜찮아요 softens the refusal of help

examples.ko: 도움 필요하시면 부를게요. 일단 그냥 둘러볼게요.
examples.romanization: doum piryohasimyeon bureulgeyo. ildan geunyang dulleobolgeyo.
examples.en: I'll call you if I need help. For now I'm just looking.
examples.note: Polite and friendly; 일단 = for now

entries.nuance: 그냥 둘러볼게요 is what a customer says to a clerk who offers help, to signal 'no need, I'm just browsing'; 그냥 means 'just/for no particular reason', 둘러보다 is 'to look around', and -ㄹ게요 expresses the speaker's intention ('I'll...'). It politely declines assistance without buying pressure. Politeness is 해요체; casual 그냥 둘러볼게, and a very common equivalent is 구경 좀 할게요 (구경 = 'looking/browsing'). The phrase 둘러보다 (look around a space) vs 구경하다 (look at things for fun) overlap heavily here; both are natural, with 구경 sounding lighter. The nuance of -ㄹ게요 is 'I will (for my part)', which fits declining help; using the plain -아요 (둘러봐요) would sound like a statement of fact, not a polite intention, so the -ㄹ게요 ending is what makes it gracious. English speakers translate 'just looking' as 그냥 보고 있어요 ('I'm just watching'), which is understandable but flatter; the idiomatic brush-off is 그냥 둘러볼게요. Spelling: 둘러볼게요, pronounced with a tense 께, but written 게.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 그냥 보고 있어요 for 'just looking'.
That literally means 'I'm just watching' and feels flat. The natural browse-and-decline phrase is 그냥 둘러볼게요 or 구경 좀 할게요.
Using 둘러봐요 instead of 둘러볼게요.
둘러봐요 is a flat statement; -ㄹ게요 adds the polite 'I'll...' intention that fits declining help. Use 둘러볼게요.
Spelling it 둘러볼께요.
Although pronounced tense (께), the correct spelling of the -ㄹ게요 ending is 게: 둘러볼게요.

entries.shortExplanation: 이걸로 할게요 is a practical expression meaning "I'll take this one".
entries.explanation: "I'll take this one" — that is 이걸로 할게요 (igeollo halgeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이걸로 할게요 ("I'll take this one"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

반말 to a friend
Formal 합쇼체 at a counter
Same decision, asking to be handed it

examples.ko: 이걸로 할게요.
examples.romanization: igeollo halgeyo.
examples.en: I'll take this one.
examples.note: Bare decision, pointing at your choice

examples.ko: 고민했는데 이걸로 할게요. 계산해 주세요.
examples.romanization: gominhaenneunde igeollo halgeyo. gyesanhae juseyo.
examples.en: I thought about it — I'll take this one. Please ring it up.
examples.note: 고민하다 = to mull over; 계산 = checkout

examples.ko: 둘 다 예쁜데 이걸로 할게요. 이거 하나만 주세요.
examples.romanization: dul da yeppeunde igeollo halgeyo. igeo hanaman juseyo.
examples.en: Both are pretty, but I'll take this one. Just this one, please.
examples.note: Choosing between options; 하나만 = just one

entries.nuance: 이걸로 할게요 is how a customer announces their final choice to buy; 이걸로 is 이것으로 ('with/by this one') contracted, and 하다 here means 'to go with / decide on', plus -ㄹ게요 'I'll', so 'I'll go with this one'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 이걸로 할게, formal 이걸로 하겠습니다. The particle 으로/로 ('with/by means of') is doing the selection work — Korean marks the chosen option with 으로/로, which is why it's 이걸로 (이것 + 으로), and English speakers who say 이거 할게요 (without 로) sound slightly off, though understandable. The near-twin 이걸로 주세요 ('give me this one') is interchangeable at checkout; 할게요 stresses your decision, 주세요 stresses the request to hand it over. The -ㄹ게요 ending again signals personal intention, perfect for committing to a purchase. A common mistake is using 이것을 할게요 (object particle 을) — selection takes 으로/로, not 을/를, so it's 이걸로. Spelling: 할게요, not 할께요.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 이것을 할게요 with the object particle.
Choosing an option uses 으로/로, not 을/를. The natural form is 이걸로 할게요 (이것으로).
Dropping the 로 and saying 이거 할게요.
Selection is marked with 으로/로. 이걸로 할게요 sounds complete; bare 이거 할게요 is a bit off.
Spelling it 할께요.
Despite the tense pronunciation, the -ㄹ게요 ending is spelled 게: 할게요.

entries.shortExplanation: 포장해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "Please wrap it up / pack it".
entries.explanation: 포장해 주세요 (pojanghae juseyo) = "Please wrap it up / pack it". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 포장해 주세요 ("Please wrap it up"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite request to staff
반말 to a friend
Softer, extra-polite request
Asking specifically for gift wrapping

examples.ko: 이거 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: igeo pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: Please wrap this up.
examples.note: Bare request handing over the item

examples.ko: 선물할 거라서요, 예쁘게 포장해 주세요.
examples.romanization: seonmulhal georaseoyo, yeppeuge pojanghae juseyo.
examples.en: It's a gift, so please wrap it nicely.
examples.note: Reason plus 예쁘게 = prettily

examples.ko: 따로따로 포장해 주세요. 선물할 거예요. 리본도 돼요?
examples.romanization: ttarottaro pojanghae juseyo. seonmulhal geoyeyo. ribondo dwaeyo?
examples.en: Please wrap them separately. They're gifts. Can you add a ribbon too?
examples.note: Detailed request; 따로따로 = separately

entries.nuance: 포장해 주세요 asks staff to wrap or pack an item, said by a customer; 포장 is Sino-Korean 包裝 ('wrapping/packaging'), 하다 makes it a verb, and 주세요 is 'please (do) for me', so 'please wrap it for me'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 포장해 줘, softer 포장 좀 해 주시겠어요?. Be careful: 포장 has a second meaning in restaurants — 'takeout/to go' (포장이요 = 'to take away'), the opposite of 먹고 갈게요 ('I'll eat here'). In a shop it means gift/parcel wrapping; for gifts specify 선물 포장 ('gift wrap'). The -아/어 주세요 pattern ('do X for me') is the workhorse request frame, and you stack adverbs before it: 예쁘게 포장해 주세요, 따로 포장해 주세요. English speakers literally translate 'wrap' as 싸다/싸 주세요 (싸다 = to wrap/bundle, also 'cheap' — confusing) which exists but sounds informal; the clean store word is 포장해 주세요. Another error is forgetting 주세요 and just saying 포장해요, which sounds like a statement, not a request.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 포장해요 without 주세요.
포장해요 is a flat statement ('it wraps / wraps it'). To request, use the -아 주세요 frame: 포장해 주세요.
Using 싸 주세요 for store gift-wrapping.
싸다 works but is informal and overlaps with 싸다 'cheap'. The clear word for wrapping is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Forgetting 포장 also means 'takeout' in restaurants.
In a café/restaurant 포장이요 means 'to go'. For wrapping a purchased item it means gift/parcel wrapping — context decides.

entries.nuance: 봉투 주세요 asks the cashier for a bag, said by a customer; 봉투 means 'bag/envelope' (for shopping it's the carry bag) and 주세요 is 'please give me'. entries.nuance: 교통카드 is 교통 ('transportation', Sino-Korean 交通) + 카드 ('card'), the generic word for the rechargeable tap card you use on every Korean subway and bus. In real life most people say the brand name 티머니 (T-money) — and 캐시비/Cashbee is the other big one — but 교통카드 is the safe umbrella term any clerk understands. You buy them at any convenience store (편의점) for a few thousand won, then load cash onto them. The key thing for English speakers: you do NOT buy single paper tickets for daily travel the way you might elsewhere — Koreans tap a reusable card, so asking for a 표 ('ticket') at a convenience store will confuse the clerk; ask for a 교통카드. Note also that 카드 alone often means a credit/debit card, so in a money context say 교통카드 in full to be clear. The polite default 주세요 is fine to a clerk; you would not use 반말 with a stranger behind a counter.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Asking for a 표 (ticket) to ride daily.
표 means a paper ticket, used for single-journey tokens or intercity buses — not everyday city travel. For tapping on/off the subway and bus, you buy a reusable 교통카드.
Saying just 카드 주세요 at a convenience store.
Bare 카드 is ambiguous and often means a credit card. To buy a transit card say the full 교통카드 주세요 (or 티머니 주세요).
Assuming the card is free or refundable like a deposit.
The plastic 교통카드 itself costs money (a few thousand won) and isn't refunded. Only the loaded cash balance is yours to spend; budget for the card price.

entries.nuance: 충전 is the Sino-Korean word (充電) literally meaning 'to charge (a battery)', but for a transit card it means 'to load cash onto it' — top it up. You say 충전해 주세요 to a convenience-store clerk, who taps your card on a pad and adds the cash you hand over; subway stations also have self-serve 충전 machines (교통카드 충전기). The natural order is amount + 충전해 주세요: 만 원 충전해 주세요 ('load 10,000 won'). For English speakers the trap is thinking 충전 means battery-charging only — it covers loading money, phone data, and gift balances too, so trust it here. Don't confuse 충전 (load money on) with 결제 ('payment/settling a charge') or 환불 ('refund'); they're different actions. Also note T-money is prepaid cash, so you must 충전 before the balance runs out — if it's empty the gate won't open. Use 주세요 (polite) with the clerk; the clerk uses honorific 드릴까요 ('shall I do for you?') back to you.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Thinking 충전 only means charging a phone/battery.
충전 also means loading money onto a transit card, phone, or gift balance. 교통카드 충전해 주세요 correctly means 'top up my transit card' — it's the standard verb.
Putting the amount after the verb: 충전해 주세요 만 원.
Korean states the amount first: 만 원 충전해 주세요. Tacking 만 원 on the end sounds out of order; lead with the number + 원.
Confusing 충전 (load money) with 결제 (pay) or 환불 (refund).
결제 is settling a payment; 환불 is getting money back. To add balance to your card you 충전 — say 충전해 주세요, not 결제해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 잔액 is Sino-Korean (殘額) meaning 'remaining amount / balance'. (subject marker 이), not 잔액을 — you're not doing anything to the balance, you're stating that 'the balance is how much?'. entries.nuance: 호선 is the counter for numbered subway lines: 1호선 (Line 1), 2호선 (Line 2), and so on, where 호 (號) means 'number' and 선 (線) means 'line'. Crucially, line numbers use SINO-KOREAN numbers — 일, 이, 삼, 사… — so it's 이 호선 (2호선), NOT 두 호선; this is the single biggest learner slip because many counters take native numbers, but 호선 does not. You ask 몇 호선이에요? to learn which line a station is on, or 몇 호선 타야 돼요? to learn which to board. The particle for 'toward a line' is -으로/-로: 2호선으로 가요 ('go toward Line 2'). English speakers also tend to say 'Line number 2' literally as 라인 2 — Koreans never say 라인 for the subway; it's always 호선. Note named lines exist too (신분당선, 경의중앙선), which don't use 호선; for those you say the full name. To a stranger or station agent, keep it polite with -이에요/-예요; you wouldn't drop to 반말 asking directions.

entries.nuance: 이거 시청역 가요? is 이거 ('this one') + the destination + 가요? ('does it go?'), the everyday way to confirm a train or bus is heading where you want before you commit. The 가요 here is intransitive 'go (to)', and Korean often drops the destination particle in speech, so 시청역 가요? sounds natural without -에/-까지. For buses you swap 이거 for 이 버스, and the same frame works. The big subway-specific issue is DIRECTION: a single line runs both ways, so even on the right 호선 you can board the wrong way — that's why 방향 ('direction') questions like 강남 방향이에요? are so useful. English speakers tend to over-build this with 'go to' as 가는 거예요? or add 에 awkwardly (시청역에 가요?, which is fine but stiffer in this snap question); the crisp spoken form is just 시청역 가요?. Ask a fellow passenger, the driver, or a station agent — all polite -요 form; don't use 반말 with strangers. Note 가요? (does it go) differs from 내려요? (do I get off) — keep them distinct.

가요 asks the destination; 서요 (from 서다 'to stop') asks whether it stops at a place. For 'does this stop at City Hall?' say 시청역 서요?, not 가요?

entries.nuance: 어디서 내려요? is 어디서 ('at where', 어디 + the location-of-action particle 서) + 내려요 ('get off', from 내리다). This is the core question for not missing your stop. The particle 서 matters: getting off HAPPENS AT a place, so it's 어디서 내려요?, and 'get off here' is 여기서 내려요 — using 어디에 (static location) here is a classic English-speaker error, because 내리다 is an action that needs the dynamic 에서/서, not 에. The opposite verb is 타다 ('to get on/board'), and the pair 타다/내리다 is essential: you 타다 a vehicle and 내리다 from it. On buses, since stops aren't always announced clearly, 내릴 때 알려 주세요 ('tell me when it's my stop') asked to the 기사님 (driver) or a neighbor is genuinely useful. To confirm a specific stop, 여기서 내리면 돼요? ('is here where I get off?'). Keep it polite -요; you're addressing strangers or staff. Don't confuse 내리다 (get off a vehicle) with 떨어지다 ('to fall/drop') — only 내리다 fits exiting transit.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 에 instead of 서: 어디에 내려요?
Getting off is an action at a location, so it takes 에서/서: 어디서 내려요?, 여기서 내려요. 어디에 내려요 sounds wrong because 에 marks static existence, not the place of an action.
Mixing up 타다 (get on) and 내리다 (get off).

structuredNuance.t: 어디서 내려요? is 어디서 ('at where', 어디 + the location-of-action particle 서) + 내려요 ('get off', from 내리다). This is the core question for not missing your stop. On buses, since stops aren't always announced clearly, 내릴 때 알려 주세요 ('tell me when it's my stop') asked to the 기사님 (driver) or a neighbor is genuinely useful. To confirm a specific stop, 여기서 내리면 돼요? ('is here where I get off?'). Keep it polite -요; you're addressing strangers or staff.

The opposite verb is 타다 ('to get on/board'), and the pair 타다/내리다 is essential: you 타다 a vehicle and 내리다 from it. Don't confuse 내리다 (get off a vehicle) with 떨어지다 ('to fall/drop') — only 내리다 fits exiting transit.

The particle 서 matters: getting off HAPPENS AT a place, so it's 어디서 내려요?, and 'get off here' is 여기서 내려요 — using 어디에 (static location) here is a classic English-speaker error, because 내리다 is an action that needs the dynamic 에서/서, not 에.

entries.nuance: 다음 역이 어디예요? is 다음 ('next') + 역 ('station', Sino-Korean 驛) + 이 어디예요? ('is where/what?'). A subtle but crucial distinction trips up English speakers: 이번 역 means the station ARRIVING RIGHT NOW (announcements say 이번 역은… 'this stop is…'), while 다음 역 is the one AFTER that. So if you want the stop you're pulling into, ask 이번 역이 어디예요?; for the following one, 다음 역. Mixing them up makes you get off one stop early or late. Polite -요 is right for strangers and staff; this is a question you'd ask anyone nearby.

entries.nuance: 환승 is Sino-Korean (換乘) meaning 'to change/transfer (vehicles)', the everyday word for switching between subway lines, or between bus and subway. 환승하려면 어디로 가요? uses -려면 ('if you intend to / in order to') + 어디로 ('to where', with the direction particle 로) + 가요? — 'in order to transfer, where do I go?'. A huge practical point unique to Korea: if you tap your same 교통카드 when you switch within about 30 minutes, you get a 환승 할인 (transfer discount) and often pay little or nothing extra — but ONLY if you TAP OUT and TAP IN with the same card; paying cash or using a different card forfeits it. English speakers under-use 환승 and try literal phrases like 갈아타다 (also correct and very natural! 'to change and ride') — both 환승하다 and 갈아타다 work, with 환승 sounding a touch more 'system/official' and 갈아타다 more colloquial. The direction particle is 로/으로 (어디로 가요), not 에 — you're asking which way to head. Use polite -요 with agents and strangers.

Both work. 갈아타다 ('to change and board') is very natural and colloquial: 2호선으로 갈아타요. Don't force the Sino-Korean 환승 everywhere; 갈아타다 is just as common in speech.

entries.nuance: 갈아타다 is the native-Korean verb for transferring: 갈아 (from 갈다 'to change/replace') + 타다 ('to ride'), literally 'change and ride'. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? = 'is it okay to change here?' / 'do I transfer here?', using -면 돼요? ('is it okay if…?'), the standard way to confirm a correct action. This is the colloquial twin of 환승하다 (Sino-Korean); both are common, but 갈아타다 is what you'll hear most in casual speech and from helpful strangers. The particle on the place is 서 (여기서, 사당역에서) because the changing HAPPENS AT that station — an action, so 에서/서, not static 에. The line you switch TO takes 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타요. English speakers sometimes invent 바꾸다 ('to change/exchange an object') here — 기차를 바꾸다 wrongly means swapping the physical train like an item; the correct verb for switching what you ride is 갈아타다. Polite -요 for strangers; 갈아타세요 (honorific imperative) is what staff say to you, 갈아타 is 반말 to a friend.

Marking the place with 에 instead of 서: 여기에 갈아타요.
Transferring happens AT a station, an action, so use 에서/서: 여기서 갈아타요, 사당역에서 갈아타요. Static 에 is wrong for the place of the action.
Using 로/으로 wrong for the target line.
The line you switch to takes 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타요 ('change to Line 4'). Saying 4호선에 갈아타요 misuses the particle; 으로 marks the new line you board.

entries.nuance: The verb for tapping a transit card is 찍다 — literally 'to stamp/press/dot' — so 'tap your card' is 카드(를) 찍다, and the reader is the 단말기. This is THE word; English speakers often reach for 대다 ('to touch/put against', also heard: 카드를 대다) which is acceptable, but 찍다 is the idiomatic default everyone uses. Critically, on Korean city buses you tap TWICE: once boarding (front door) and AGAIN when getting off (back door) — the tap-out (하차 태그) is what preserves your 환승 할인 and charges the correct distance-based fare. Forgetting to tap out can cost you the transfer discount or a penalty fare next ride, so 내릴 때도 찍어야 돼요? ('do I tap getting off too?') — yes. The honorific 찍으셨어요? (with 시) is how a driver or elder addresses you; you'd answer plainly 찍었어요. Don't confuse 찍다 here with its other meanings (take a photo 사진을 찍다, dip food 찍어 먹다) — context makes it clear, but the action on the reader is 찍다. Buses also accept the same 교통카드 as the subway; you don't need a separate 'bus card'.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Forgetting to tap out (하차 태그) when getting off the bus.
Korean buses require tapping AGAIN at the back-door reader when you exit. Skipping the tap-out can void your 환승 할인 and trigger a penalty fare next time. Always 내릴 때 카드 찍으세요.
Using a verb other than 찍다/대다 for tapping.
The idiomatic verb is 찍다 (or 대다): 카드 찍으세요. Don't invent 누르다 ('to press a button') or 터치하다; 찍다 is what Koreans say for tapping the reader.
Thinking you need a separate 'bus card'.
The same 교통카드 (T-money/Cashbee) works on buses and subways alike. There's no special bus-only card to buy; tap the same card you use underground.

entries.nuance: 현금 is Sino-Korean (現金) for 'cash', and 현금도 돼요? = 'does cash work too?' (되다 'to be possible' + the particle 도 'also/too'). You ask this mainly on BUSES, because a real-life gotcha is that paying cash on a Korean city bus often gives NO change (거스름돈) — you drop the exact fare in the box, and overpaying is simply lost. Subways take cash via ticket machines that DO give change, but buses typically don't, so 거스름돈 줘요? ('do I get change?') is a smart follow-up. The particle 도 ('too/also') implies 'cash, in addition to card' — natural when card is the default and you're checking the alternative; if you just ask 현금 돼요? (with no 도) that's also fine. To say HOW you'll pay, use 으로: 현금으로 낼게요 ('I'll pay by cash'), 카드로 낼게요 ('by card'). English speakers misuse 돈 ('money') for 'cash' — 돈 is money in general; specifically physical cash is 현금. Don't say 돈으로 돼요? when you mean cash; say 현금으로. Polite -요 with the driver.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Expecting change when paying cash on a city bus.
Korean buses usually give NO 거스름돈 (change) for cash — you pay the exact fare or lose the difference. Prepare exact coins, or better, use a 교통카드. Subway machines do give change.
Using 돈 instead of 현금 for 'cash'.
돈 means money in general (including cards, balance). Physical cash specifically is 현금: 현금도 돼요? Say 현금으로 낼게요 ('pay by cash'), not 돈으로.
Mixing up the particle: 현금에 낼게요.
'Pay BY cash' uses the means particle 으로: 현금으로 낼게요, 카드로 낼게요. 현금에 is wrong; 으로 marks the method of payment.

entries.nuance: 정류장 (停留場, 'stopping place') is the word for a BUS STOP — distinct from 역, which is a subway/train station. Newcomers constantly conflate them, but you wait for a bus at a 정류장 (or 버스 정류장 / 버스 정류소, the same thing) and board a train at a 역. To find one, ask 정류장이 어디예요? with the subject particle 이 ('the stop is where?'). Korean buses are identified by NUMBER, and you ask which one with 몇 번 버스 ('what-number bus') — note 번 ('number') for routes uses Sino-Korean numbers: 146번 is 백사십육 번. To say at which stop you board, use 에서 (the action-location particle): 이 정류장에서 타요 ('I board at this stop'), because boarding is an action. A common English-speaker pitfall is asking 'where is the bus' (버스 어디예요?) when they mean the STOP — that asks for the vehicle's current position, not the waiting place; ask 정류장 어디예요? for the stop. Polite -요 with strangers. Also, 정류장 vs 종점: 종점 is the final terminus/last stop, not a regular stop.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Calling a bus stop a 역.
역 is a subway/train station. A bus stop is a 정류장 (or 버스 정류장). Ask 정류장이 어디예요? for a bus stop; reserve 역 for the subway.
Asking 버스 어디예요? when you mean the stop.
That asks where the bus (vehicle) currently is. To find the waiting place, ask for the stop: 정류장이 어디예요? or 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Using native numbers for bus route numbers.
Bus numbers are Sino-Korean: 146번 is 백사십육 번, 7016번 is 칠천십육 번. Don't say 일곱 번 for bus No. 7 — route numbers read like figures, not counted items.

entries.nuance: 이 버스 자주 와요? is 이 버스 ('this bus') + 자주 ('often/frequently') + 와요? ('does it come?'), a casual, friendly way to gauge how long you'll wait. The more 'official' phrasing is 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? — 배차 (配車, 'dispatching vehicles') + 간격 ('interval'), literally 'what's the dispatch interval?', the term used on signs and apps. Practically, most newcomers should just check a real-time app (카카오맵, 네이버 지도, or the stop's electronic sign showing 'arriving in N분'), but knowing 자주 와요? and 언제 와요? lets you ask a human. 자주 ('often') is an adverb of frequency — don't confuse it with 빨리 ('quickly/fast'), which is speed; 자주 와요 asks about how OFTEN, 빨리 와요 would oddly ask if it comes fast. English speakers also misuse 많이 ('a lot/much') for frequency — 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'do many buses come?' (quantity), whereas 자주 ('often') is the right frequency word. Polite -요 with fellow passengers. The reply you'll hear is often a 분 ('minute') count: 한 10분 와요 ('about 10 minutes').
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 빨리 (fast) when you mean 자주 (often).
자주 asks frequency ('comes often'); 빨리 asks speed ('comes fast'). For 'does it come frequently?' say 자주 와요?, not 빨리 와요?
Using 많이 for frequency: 버스 많이 와요?
많이 means 'a lot (in quantity)', so this sounds like 'do many buses come?'. For how OFTEN one bus runs, use 자주: 이 버스 자주 와요?
Saying 배차 (dispatch) without 간격 (interval).
배차 간격 together means the gap between buses. 배차 alone is incomplete for asking wait time; say 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? or just 자주 와요?

structuredNuance.t: 이 버스 자주 와요? is 이 버스 ('this bus') + 자주 ('often/frequently') + 와요? ('does it come?'), a casual, friendly way to gauge how long you'll wait. Practically, most newcomers should just check a real-time app (카카오맵, 네이버 지도, or the stop's electronic sign showing 'arriving in N분'), but knowing 자주 와요? and 언제 와요? lets you ask a human. Polite -요 with fellow passengers. The reply you'll hear is often a 분 ('minute') count: 한 10분 와요 ('about 10 minutes').

The more 'official' phrasing is 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? — 배차 (配車, 'dispatching vehicles') + 간격 ('interval'), literally 'what's the dispatch interval?', the term used on signs and apps. 자주 ('often') is an adverb of frequency — don't confuse it with 빨리 ('quickly/fast'), which is speed; 자주 와요 asks about how OFTEN, 빨리 와요 would oddly ask if it comes fast.
English speakers misuse 많이 ('a lot/much') for frequency — 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'do many buses come?' (quantity), whereas 자주 ('often') is the right frequency word.

entries.explanation: 막차 몇 시예요? (makcha myeot siyeyo?) means "What time's the last train/bus?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 막차 몇 시예요? ("What time's the last one?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: 막차 is 막 ('last/final') + 차 ('vehicle/train/bus'), 'the last train or bus of the day' — a survival word in Korea, where the subway typically stops around midnight and missing it means an expensive late-night taxi or 심야버스 (night bus). Its opposite is 첫차 ('first train/bus' of the morning). You ask 막차 몇 시예요? ('what time is the last one?') with 시 ('o'clock'). The verb for service ENDING is 끊기다 ('to be cut off'): 막차 끊겼어요? ('has the last one already gone?') — note 끊기다 here doesn't mean a phone call dropping; it means the line/service has stopped for the night. To say you MISSED it, use 놓치다 ('to miss/let slip'): 막차 놓쳤어요 ('I missed the last train'). English speakers tend to say 마지막 기차 ('the final train') — understandable and not wrong, but the idiomatic, compact word is 막차; likewise 막차 is more natural than spelling out 마지막 버스. Time uses 시 with NATIVE numbers for the hour (열두 시 'twelve o'clock'), but minutes use Sino-Korean — a frequent learner mix-up. Polite -요 with staff.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 마지막 차/기차 instead of 막차.
마지막 차 is understandable but the natural, idiomatic word is 막차 (and 첫차 for the first). Ask 막차 몇 시예요?, not 마지막 기차 몇 시예요?
Using 끊기다 wrong or reaching for 끝나다.
막차 끊겼어요? means 'has the last one ended (for the night)?'. 끝나다 ('to finish') is more about an event ending; for transit service stopping, 끊기다 is idiomatic: 지하철 끊겼어요?
Mixing number systems for the time.
Hours with 시 use native numbers (열두 시 = 12:00), but minutes use Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min). So 'twelve thirty' is 열두 시 삼십 분 — don't say 십이 시 for the hour.

entries.shortExplanation: 이 자리 비었어요? is a practical expression meaning "Is this seat free?".
entries.explanation: "Is this seat free?" — that is 이 자리 비었어요? (i jari bieosseoyo?). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 이 자리 비었어요? ("Is this seat free?"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; checking if a seat is taken
Asking permission to sit
Asking if space is available
Checking if the spot is occupied by someone

examples.ko: 이 자리 비었어요?
examples.romanization: i jari bieosseoyo?
examples.en: Is this seat free?
examples.note: Asked to a nearby passenger before sitting

examples.ko: 여기 사람 있어요? — 아니요, 앉으세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi saram isseoyo? — aniyo, anjeuseyo.
examples.en: Is anyone here? — No, please sit.
examples.note: Common exchange; 앉으세요 ('please sit') invites you

examples.ko: 죄송한데, 여기 노약자석이에요.
examples.romanization: joesonghande, yeogi noyakjaseogieyo.
examples.en: Sorry, but this is a priority seat.
examples.note: 노약자석 ('elderly/disabled seat') — leave it for those who need it

entries.nuance: 이 자리 비었어요? is 이 자리 ('this seat') + 비었어요? (past of 비다 'to be empty'), literally 'is this seat empty?' — the polite way to check before sitting. The most natural alternatives are 여기 사람 있어요? ('is anyone here?', checking for an occupant) and 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?', asking permission). A cultural must-know: Korean subways/buses have 노약자석 (priority seats for the elderly, pregnant, disabled) usually at the car ends, and 임산부 배려석 (pink pregnant-passenger seats) — even if empty, a young able-bodied person is strongly expected NOT to sit there, so 이 자리 비었어요? doesn't override that etiquette. The verb 비다 ('be empty') here is intransitive; English speakers sometimes use 자유 ('freedom') literally for 'free' (이 자리 자유예요?) which is nonsense in Korean — 'free/vacant' for a seat is 비다 (empty) or 'no one here' (사람 없어요). Also 비었어요 (empty/vacant) vs 없어요 ('there isn't'): 자리 없어요 means 'there are no seats (all full)', a different statement. Polite -요 with strangers; you'd never use 반말.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Translating 'free' literally with 자유: 이 자리 자유예요?
자유 means 'freedom/liberty', not 'vacant'. A free/empty seat is 비다: 이 자리 비었어요? or check the occupant: 여기 사람 있어요?
Sitting in 노약자석 or 임산부 배려석 when able-bodied.
Priority seats (노약자석) and pink pregnant-passenger seats (임산부 배려석) should be left empty for those who need them, even on an empty train. Sitting there as a young, healthy rider draws real disapproval.
Confusing 자리 비었어요 with 자리 없어요.
비었어요 ('it's empty/free') asks if THIS seat is open; 없어요 ('there isn't') means no seats are available at all. They're nearly opposite — keep them straight.

entries.shortExplanation: 좀 지나갈게요 is a practical expression meaning "Let me through, please".
entries.explanation: 좀 지나갈게요 (jom jinagalgeyo) = "Let me through, please". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 좀 지나갈게요 ("Let me through / coming through"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.

usagePhrases.note: Polite; squeezing past to reach the door
Said to make people step aside briefly
Announcing you need to exit, so people move
More direct request to clear the way

examples.ko: 저기요, 좀 지나갈게요.
examples.romanization: jeogiyo, jom jinagalgeyo.
examples.en: Excuse me, let me through.
examples.note: Pushing toward the door on a crowded train

examples.ko: 잠깐만요, 내릴게요!
examples.romanization: jamkkanmanyo, naerilgeyo!
examples.en: One sec — I'm getting off!
examples.note: 잠깐만요 + 내릴게요 to part a packed crowd at your stop

examples.ko: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요. 다음에 내려요.
examples.romanization: joesonghamnida, jom jinagalgeyo. daeume naeryeoyo.
examples.en: Sorry, coming through — I get off next.
examples.note: Apologize, state you're passing, give the reason

entries.nuance: 좀 지나갈게요 is 좀 (softener) + 지나가다 ('to pass by/through') + -ㄹ게요 (announcing your own action politely), 'I'm going to pass through (so excuse me)'. On a packed Seoul subway this is the phrase that gets you to the door in time. The single most useful crowd word is actually 잠깐만요 ('just a moment'), said to make people shift aside — it's gentler than a command. To announce you're EXITING so people clear the path, say 내릴게요 ('I'm getting off!'), which is hugely effective at your stop. A more direct option is 좀 비켜 주세요 ('please step aside'), slightly stronger. English speakers wrongly use 실례합니다 ('pardon the intrusion') here — it's understandable but stiff/formal for a quick squeeze; Koreans say 잠깐만요 or 좀 지나갈게요. Also don't translate 'excuse me' as 미안해요 (an apology for wrongdoing) when you just need to pass — though 죄송합니다 can accompany the squeeze. The -ㄹ게요 ending signals intent and courtesy at once. Keep it polite -요; you're brushing past strangers, so the softener 좀 and the -요 ending matter a lot.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례합니다 to squeeze past on a crowded train.
실례합니다 is formal and a bit stiff for a quick crowd-squeeze. Koreans say 잠깐만요 ('one moment') or 좀 지나갈게요 ('coming through') to part the crowd.
Staying silent and physically pushing to the door.
Without a word, shoving past feels rude and you may miss your stop. Announce it: 잠깐만요! or 내릴게요! — people will reliably step aside when you say you're getting off.
Saying 미안해요 alone when you mean 'excuse me, let me by'.
미안해요 apologizes but doesn't signal you need to pass. Pair an apology with the action: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요, or just say 잠깐만요 to get people to move.

entries.shortExplanation: 이거 급행이에요? is a practical expression meaning "Is this the express train?".
entries.explanation: 이거 급행이에요? (igeo geupaengieyo?) means "Is this the express train?". Say it as one set phrase — for example 이거 급행이에요? ("Is this the express?"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

usagePhrases.note: Crucial: express skips many stations

examples.ko: 이거 급행이에요?
examples.romanization: igeo geupaengieyo?
examples.en: Is this the express?
examples.note: Asked on the platform before boarding a 1호선 train

examples.ko: 급행 타면 우리 역 안 서요?
examples.romanization: geupaeng tamyeon uri yeok an seoyo?
examples.en: If I take the express, won't it stop at our station?
examples.note: 안 서요 ('doesn't stop') — the express skips it

examples.ko: 급행 놓쳤는데 다음 일반 열차 언제 와요?
examples.romanization: geupaeng notchyeonneunde daeum ilban yeolcha eonje wayo?

examples.note: 일반/완행 ('all-stop') as the slower alternative

entries.nuance: 급행 is Sino-Korean (急行) meaning 'express', a train that skips many stations to run faster — found on lines like 1호선, 9호선, 경의중앙선, and 수인분당선. Its opposite is 완행 or, more commonly said, 일반 (열차) ('regular/all-stop train'). The make-or-break point for newcomers: a 급행 will BLOW PAST your station if it's not an express stop, so before boarding you ask 이거 급행이에요? and, vitally, 급행 우리 역 서요? ('does the express stop at my station?'). The verb for stopping is 서다 (서요 / 안 서요), distinct from 가다 ('to go') — 급행이 안 서요 means 'the express doesn't stop (here)', which is exactly what catches people out. 9호선 in particular runs 급행 and 일반 on the same tracks, and tourists routinely overshoot. English speakers sometimes call it the 'express' in English to staff or reach for 빠른 기차 ('fast train') — the correct term is 급행; 빠른 기차 isn't how the system is labeled. Signs and announcements mark trains 급행 vs 일반, so learn to recognize 급행. Polite -요 with staff and passengers.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.

structuredNuance.t: 급행 means 'express', a train that skips many stations to run faster — found on lines like 1호선, 9호선, 경의중앙선, and 수인분당선. The make-or-break point for newcomers: a 급행 will BLOW PAST your station if it's not an express stop, so before boarding you ask 이거 급행이에요? and, vitally, 급행 우리 역 서요? ('does the express stop at my station?'). The verb for stopping is 서다 (서요 / 안 서요), distinct from 가다 ('to go') — 급행이 안 서요 means 'the express doesn't stop (here)', which is exactly what catches people out. 9호선 in particular runs 급행 and 일반 on the same tracks, and tourists routinely overshoot. Signs and announcements mark trains 급행 vs 일반, so learn to recognize 급행. Polite -요 with staff and passengers.
Its opposite is 완행 or, more commonly said, 일반 (열차) ('regular/all-stop train').
급행 is Sino-Korean (急行) meaning 'express'.
English speakers sometimes call it the 'express' in English to staff or reach for 빠른 기차 ('fast train') — the correct term is 급행; 빠른 기차 isn't how the system is labeled.

entries.nuance: 벨 is the loanword 'bell' — the STOP-REQUEST BUTTON on a Korean city bus (formally 하차벨, 하차 'alighting' + 벨), and 벨 눌러 주세요 = 'please press the bell', using 누르다 ('to press') + the favor 주세요. This is essential because Korean buses do NOT stop at every stop automatically: if no one has pressed the bell AND no one is waiting at the stop, the driver drives straight past. So you must press the red 벨 in advance (미리) when your stop is coming. The verb is 누르다 ('to press a button'), conjugating 눌러요/눌러 주세요 (르-irregular) — don't use 찍다 (that's for tapping the card) or 치다 ('to hit') here; you 누르다 a button. If you're not near a button on a crowded bus, you can ask a fellow passenger 벨 좀 눌러 주세요. English speakers sometimes say 버튼 ('button'), which is understood, but the bus stop-request is idiomatically the 벨/하차벨. Note this is bus-specific — subways stop at every station, so there's no 벨 underground. Polite -요/주세요 with strangers; among friends 벨 눌러 (반말).
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Assuming the bus stops at every stop without pressing the bell.
Korean buses skip a stop if no one pressed the 벨 and no one is waiting there. To get off, press the 하차벨 in advance (미리), or the bus drives past your stop.
Using 찍다 or 치다 for pressing the bell.
찍다 is for tapping the card; 치다 means 'to hit/strike'. Pressing a button is 누르다: 벨 눌러 주세요. The verbs aren't interchangeable.
Pressing the bell too late, right as the stop arrives.
The driver needs warning to pull over safely, so press 미리 ('ahead of time') as the previous stop passes. Pressing at the last second may mean overshooting your stop.

entries.nuance: This is the opening line you say to a taxi driver as you get in and show or read an address, customer-to-driver, and the politeness is plain 존댓말 (가 주세요 = 'please go'), which is exactly right for any stranger providing a service. To sound warmer or more formal add 기사님 ('driver, sir/ma'am') at the front and use 가 주시겠어요? The 반말 form 가 줘 is only for a friend who happens to be driving you. The nearest alternative is 여기로 가 주세요 ('go to here'), which you use when pointing at a map pin rather than reading out a full street address — 이 주소 names the written address, 여기 points at a spot. The classic English-speaker mistake is dropping the helper verb and saying 이 주소 가요, which sounds like you are narrating your own plan ('I'm going to this address') rather than requesting the driver to take you there; the 주세요 ('do it for me') is what makes it a polite request.

Calling the driver 아저씨 ('mister') to get his attention — it's not rude but sounds rough; 기사님 is the respectful, standard term.

entries.nuance: You say this to tell the driver where you intend to get out, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말. The -ㄹ게요 ending signals your own intention/decision ('I'll go ahead and get off'), which is softer and more natural here than barking a command. The 반말 form is 내릴게; the formal/격식 form 내리겠습니다 suits a very stiff or business-car setting. The dividing line with 여기서 세워 주세요 is who the verb is about: 세워 주세요 commands the driver to stop the car, while 내릴게요 describes your own action of getting off — Koreans often pair them ('저 앞에서 세워 주세요' to command, '저 앞에서 내릴게요' to announce). The English-speaker mistake is translating 'I want to get off' as 내리고 싶어요, which is grammatically fine but sounds like a child stating a desire; the adult, situation-appropriate form is the intention ending 내릴게요. Also note 저 앞 ('that spot ahead, away from us') versus 이 앞 ('right in front of us') — 저 is what you point to a short distance forward.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.

Using 타다 or 떨어지다 — 타다 is 'to get ON', 떨어지다 is 'to fall'; getting OUT of a vehicle is 내리다.
Saying 이 앞에서 when the spot is some meters ahead — 이 앞 is right at your position; for a point further forward use 저 앞.

entries.nuance: This asks the driver how much time the ride will take, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말. The verb 걸리다 here means 'to take (time)' and is the fixed phrase for durations — 얼마나 걸려요? is THE way to ask 'how long'. Make it tentative with 얼마나 걸릴까요? (inviting a guess); 반말 is 얼마나 걸려? Do not confuse this with 얼마예요? ('how much is it?'), which asks about money — 걸려요 is time, 예요 is price. The English-speaker mistake is mapping 'how long' onto length and saying 얼마나 길어요?, which literally asks about physical length and is wrong for duration; time always pairs with 걸리다. Another trap is 시간 얼마나 있어요?, which asks 'how much time do you have', a totally different meaning. Add the destination with 까지 (e.g. 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요?).

Confusing it with price: 얼마예요? asks the cost, not the time; keep 걸려요 strictly for duration.
Marking the destination with 에 (공항에 얼마나 걸려요) — duration to a place uses 까지, so 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요?.

entries.nuance: You say this to urge the driver to speed up, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말, and the little word 좀 ('a bit/please') is essential — without it 빨리 가 주세요 can sound like a curt order. For extra courtesy use 서둘러 주시겠어요? or attach a reason ('시간이 없어서요'); 반말 is 빨리 가 줘. The nearest alternative is 서둘러 주세요 ('please hurry'), which focuses on haste in general, while 빨리 가 주세요 specifically means drive faster — both are fine, but Koreans soften either with 좀. The English-speaker mistake is the bare imperative 빨리 가요 or even 빨리!, which to a stranger is rude; you need 좀 ... 주세요 to make it a polite request, and prefacing with 죄송한데 makes pressing him feel considerate. Be aware drivers can only do so much in traffic, so Koreans frame it as a request, not a demand.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying just 빨리! or 빨리 가요 — to a stranger that's an abrupt order; add 좀 and 주세요: 좀 빨리 가 주세요.
Using 빠르게 instead of 빨리 — 빠르게 is more written/technical; the everyday spoken adverb for 'quickly' is 빨리.
Dropping the reason — Koreans usually justify a hurry ('시간이 없어서요'); without it the push feels demanding even with 주세요.

entries.nuance: This asks whether the taxi takes card payment, customer-to-driver, in casual 존댓말. entries.shortExplanation: 잔돈은 괜찮아요 is a practical expression meaning "Keep the change.".
entries.explanation: 잔돈은 괜찮아요 (jandoneun gwaenchanayo) means "Keep the change.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 잔돈은 괜찮아요. ("The change is fine (keep it)."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.

entries.nuance: You say this to let the driver keep the leftover change, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말. 잔돈 = 'change/small money', and 괜찮아요 here means 'it's fine (don't bother returning it)'. The topic particle 은 on 잔돈 nicely sets 'as for the change...'. Formal is 괜찮습니다; 반말 잔돈은 됐어. The nearest alternative is 그냥 가지세요 ('just keep it'), which is more direct, while 잔돈은 괜찮아요 is the softer, indirect way Koreans usually phrase a tip. Note tipping is NOT customary in Korean taxis — this is mainly used to round up a fare or skip tiny coins, not to add a percentage. The English-speaker mistake is inventing a literal 'keep the change' as 변화를 지켜요, mistranslating 'change' as 변화 (transformation) and 'keep' as 지키다 (guard) — the money sense is 잔돈, and you decline it with 괜찮아요. Another error is using 거스름돈 wrongly; 거스름돈 is fine too but 잔돈 is the everyday word.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 변화를 지켜요 — that's 'keep (guard) the transformation'; money-change is 잔돈, and you wave it off with 괜찮아요.
Marking 잔돈 with 를 (잔돈을 괜찮아요) — 괜찮다 is descriptive and takes 은/는 or no particle here; say 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
Expecting to tip a percentage — Korean taxis don't use tipping; this phrase just rounds the fare up, so don't over-explain a 'tip'.

entries.nuance: You say this so the driver pops the trunk for your luggage, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말, and 좀 ('a bit/please') softens the imperative into a courteous request. The fuller polite form is 열어 주시겠어요?; 반말 is 열어 줘. 트렁크 is the standard loanword for a car trunk/boot; the verb is 열다 ('open'), with 열어 주세요 = 'open it for me'. There isn't a close competing phrase — this is simply the fixed taxi request — but you can lead with the reason (짐이 있어서요 / 캐리어가 있어서요) to make it feel natural. The English-speaker mistake is using the British word literally or saying 트렁크 열어 ('open trunk') with no helper verb, which sounds like a bare command; you need 좀 ... 주세요. Another error is the causative confusion — say 열어 주세요 ('open it for me'), not 열려 주세요, since 열리다 is the intransitive 'to be opened'.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 트렁크 열려 주세요 — 열리다 is 'to be opened (by itself)'; you want the driver to open it, so use the transitive 열다: 열어 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and 주세요 (트렁크 열어) — to a stranger that's a blunt command; add 좀 ... 열어 주세요.
Calling it 부트 (boot) or other English — in Korean the universally understood word is 트렁크.

entries.nuance: In a taxi this most often runs driver-to-customer ('please buckle up'), but you'd use the same line for anyone in your car; it's plain 존댓말. The verb for putting on a seatbelt is 매다 ('to tie/fasten'), so 안전벨트 매 주세요 = 'please fasten the seatbelt'. The official/격식 wording on signs and announcements is 착용해 주세요 (착용하다 = 'to wear/don'); 반말 is 안전벨트 매. The dividing line is register only: 매다 is the everyday spoken verb, 착용하다 is formal/written. The English-speaker mistake is reaching for 입다 ('to wear clothes') or 하다 and saying 안전벨트 입어요 / 안전벨트 해요 — a seatbelt is fastened (매다) or worn (착용하다), never 입다, which is only for garments you put your body into. Another trap is 묶다 ('to tie up a bundle'), which is wrong for a belt; the collocation is 벨트를 매다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안전벨트 입어 주세요 — 입다 is only for clothing; a seatbelt is fastened with 매다, so 안전벨트 매 주세요.
Using 묶다 — that's tying a rope/bundle; the fixed collocation is 벨트를 매다, so 매 주세요.
Confusing the formal verb: 착용하다 is for signs/announcements; in casual speech use 매다, not a mix like 착용해.

entries.nuance: This asks the starting/flag-fall fare of the taxi, customer-to-driver (or anyone), in plain 존댓말. 기본요금 = 'base/basic fare' (기본 'basic' + 요금 'fee'), and you pair it with 얼마예요? ('how much is it?'). The subject particle 이 ('기본요금이') is correct because 기본요금 is the thing being asked about; softer is 얼마인가요?, 반말 is 얼마야?. Another error is dropping the particle and over-relying on word order; while casual speech can drop 이, the clean form is 기본요금이 얼마예요? examples.en: Please just follow the GPS, and don't take a detour.
examples.note: Real situation asking him to stick to the navigation route

entries.nuance: You say this to ask the driver not to pad the route (and the fare) by going the long way, customer-to-driver, in careful 존댓말. The verb 돌아가다 means 'to go around / take a roundabout way', and 말아 주세요 is the polite negative request ('please don't ~'). Softer is 말아 주시겠어요?; 반말 is 돌아가지 마. A more tactful positive alternative is 지름길로 가 주세요 ('take the shortcut') or 내비대로 가 주세요 ('go by the GPS'), which make the same point without sounding accusatory — the dividing line is tone: the negative 돌아가지 마세요 implies suspicion, the positive versions are friendlier. The English-speaker mistake is forming the negative as 안 돌아가 주세요, which is ungrammatical for a request; the prohibitive uses -지 말다, so 돌아가지 말아 주세요. Also note 돌아가다 can mean 'to return/go back' or even 'to pass away', so context (a taxi route) is what fixes the 'detour' reading.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 안 돌아가 주세요 — negative requests use -지 말다, not 안 + verb; the correct form is 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
Using 돌아오다 instead of 돌아가다 — 돌아오다 is 'to come back (here)'; taking a roundabout route away from you is 돌아가다, so 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
Over-bluntly saying 돌아가지 마! to a driver — that sounds accusatory; soften with 주세요 or flip to the positive 지름길로 가 주세요.

entries.nuance: This announces that the trip has reached (or nearly reached) the destination; in a taxi either the driver says it to you or you say it to signal 'this is the place', in plain 존댓말. Literally 다 ('all') + 왔어요 ('have come') = 'we've come all the way', i.e. arrived — note it uses 오다 (come) in the past, a fixed expression, even though you might expect 가다 (go). Formal/격식 is 다 왔습니다; 반말 is 다 왔어; not-quite-there is 거의 다 왔어요. The nearest alternative is 도착했어요 ('have arrived'), which is more neutral/formal, while 다 왔어요 is the warm, everyday spoken version. The English-speaker mistake is using the present 와요 or saying 다 가요 — arrival is expressed with the past 왔어요 (the coming is completed), and the verb is 오다 here, not 가다. Another trap is treating it as literally 'all came' for people; it's an idiom for 'we've arrived'.

Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 다 가요 — arrival idiom uses 오다 in the past: 다 왔어요, not 가다.
Using present 다 와요 — the arriving is complete, so it's past tense 왔어요.
Reading it literally as 'everyone came' — 다 왔어요 is a set phrase meaning 'we've arrived / we're here'.

entries.nuance: This is the set farewell you give a taxi driver (and many service workers) as you get out, customer-to-worker, in 존댓말. 감사합니다 = 'thank you', and 수고하세요 literally tells someone 'keep up the hard work / take care with your labor' — a uniquely Korean send-off acknowledging their job. A warm alternative is 안전 운전하세요 ('drive safe'). The key cultural/English-speaker mistake is saying 수고하세요 to someone OF HIGHER STATUS (a boss, a much older person, a professor) — it can sound condescending, as if praising their effort from above; with a driver it's perfectly normal, but never say it to your superior. Also, don't translate 'take care' as 조심하세요 ('be careful'), which warns of danger rather than thanking effort.

entries.nuance: You say this to ask a staff member (hotel desk, restaurant, building security) to phone for a taxi on your behalf, customer-to-staff, in 존댓말 with softening 좀. 부르다 here means 'to call/summon', so 택시 불러 주세요 = 'please summon a taxi for me'. More formal is 택시 한 대 불러 주시겠어요?; 반말 is 불러 줘. The nearest alternative is 택시 잡아 주세요, where 잡다 ('to catch/grab') means flagging one down on the street — the dividing line is method: 부르다 = phone/app a cab to come, 잡다 = hail a passing one. The English-speaker mistake is translating 'call' as 전화하다 and saying 택시한테 전화해 주세요 ('please phone to the taxi'), which is odd because you summon the service, not ring a specific cab; the verb is 부르다. Another trap is omitting 좀, which makes the request feel curt.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 택시한테 전화해 주세요 — you summon a cab with 부르다, not 전화하다; say 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
Confusing 부르다 and 잡다 — 부르다 is call/summon (by phone/app), 잡다 is hail on the street; pick by method.
Dropping 좀 — without the softener 택시 불러 주세요 sounds abrupt; add 좀: 택시 좀 불러 주세요.

entries.nuance: You ask this to a driver about the route to a place you're showing, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말, often opening with 기사님 to address him respectfully. 어떻게 = 'how', 가요 = 'do (we) go', so 여기 어떻게 가요? = 'how do we get here?'. A softer, indirect version is 여기 어떻게 가는지 아세요? ('do you know how to get here?'); 반말 is 여기 어떻게 가?. The nearest alternative is 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 ('please tell me the way'), which directly requests directions, whereas 어떻게 가요? asks the method more openly — both are natural. The English-speaker mistake is calquing 'how can I get there' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which over-uses the ability form and sounds stilted; Koreans simply say 어떻게 가요? Another error is 어디 가요? ('where are we going?'), which asks the destination, not the route.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? — the ability form is unneeded; the natural route question is just 어떻게 가요?.
Confusing 어떻게 (how) with 어디 (where) — 어디 가요? asks the destination; for the route use 어떻게 가요?.
Using 오다 (여기 어떻게 와요) when you mean traveling there — for going to the spot use 가다: 여기 어떻게 가요?.

entries.nuance: 감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' you can say to literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never be wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝). To go down in formality, switch to 고마워요 (still polite, warmer) or plain 고마워 (반말, only for friends and people clearly younger/closer); to go UP toward 격식, use 대단히 감사합니다 or 감사드립니다 in speeches and writing. The nearest alternative is 고맙습니다, which is pure native Korean and feels a touch warmer; the dividing line is mostly tone, not rank — both are equally polite. The classic English-speaker mistake is to thank for a noun with the wrong glue: you cannot say '도움 감사합니다' as if stacking words; to thank for an action you attach ~아/어 주셔서 (도와주셔서 감사합니다). Another is over-using 고마워 with strangers, which sounds rude.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 고마워 to a stranger, clerk, or anyone older — that is 반말 and sounds rude; default to 감사합니다 or at least 고마워요.
Trying to thank for an action by just naming it ('도와 감사합니다') — Korean needs ~아/어 주셔서: 도와주셔서 감사합니다.
Writing 감사 합니다 with a space — 감사합니다 is one word; the space is wrong.

entries.nuance: 고맙습니다 is the native-Korean twin of 감사합니다 and is equally polite — many Koreans feel it sounds a little warmer and more personal, while 감사합니다 feels slightly more formal/standard. You say it to anyone in 존댓말; drop to 고마워요 (gently polite) or 고마워 (반말) as closeness rises and age/rank falls. The dividing line versus 감사합니다 is feel and origin (native vs Sino-Korean), NOT politeness level — never think 고맙습니다 is 'less polite'. English speakers stumble on the verb stem: the dictionary form is 고맙다, so the polite ending is 고맙습니다 (with ㅂ), and the 반말 is 고마워 (the ㅂ becomes 워), never 'goma' or '고맙어'. Another pitfall is reaching only for 감사합니다 in every situation; sprinkling 고맙습니다 to people you know sounds more human.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Conjugating 반말 as 고맙어 — 고맙다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 고마워, never 고맙어.
Assuming 고맙습니다 is less polite than 감사합니다 and avoiding it with seniors — both are fully polite; the difference is warmth, not rank.
Saying 고마워요 to your boss in a formal setting — prefer 고맙습니다 or 감사합니다; 고마워요 can feel a touch too casual upward.

entries.nuance: 천만에요 is the dictionary answer to 'thank you', but in real life it sounds a little formal or even old-fashioned, so Koreans more often say 아니에요, 별말씀을요, or 별거 아니에요 to wave off thanks. The literal sense is '(that's) ten million [words]', i.e. 'far from it, not at all'. Register: 천만에요 is polite; the 반말 brush-off is 뭘 or 아니야; the most 격식 form is 천만의 말씀입니다. The dividing line versus 별말씀을요 is that 별말씀을요 is gentler and more humble (used when a senior or customer thanks you), while 천만에요 can feel slightly textbook. The English-speaker mistake is treating 천만에요 like the constant, reflexive 'you're welcome' of English; Koreans often answer thanks with 네 + a smile or 아니에요, and over-firing 천만에요 sounds stilted.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 천만에요 reflexively after every thanks like English 'you're welcome' — it sounds stiff; 아니에요 or 별말씀을요 is more natural.
Saying 천만에요 to a close friend — too formal; use 뭘 or 아니야 in 반말.
Misspelling it 천만애요 — it is 천만에요 (에, not 애).

entries.nuance: 별말씀을요 is a humble, polite way to wave off thanks OR praise, literally '(what) unusual words (you say)' — i.e. 'you needn't say such a thing'. It is the go-to when someone above you (a customer, a senior, an elder) thanks you and you want to sound modest, softer than 천만에요. Register: polite/humble by default; the 격식 expansion is 별말씀을 다 하십니다; casually you might hear a clipped 별말을. The dividing line versus 천만에요 is humility and direction — 별말씀을요 leans 'I'm too humble to accept this thanks' and works beautifully upward, while 천만에요 is more neutral-textbook. English speakers mis-segment it: the 말씀 is the honorific word for 'words/speech', and the ending is 을요 (often written 별말씀을요), not '별 말씀 이요'. Also, do not use it to a close friend — it is too formal; say 뭘 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 별말씀을요 with a close friend — it is humble/formal; in 반말 just say 뭘 or 아니야.
Breaking it into 별 말씀 with a space or writing 별말씀이요 — the set phrase is 별말씀을요.
Thinking it only answers thanks — it also gracefully deflects praise ('you flatter me').

entries.nuance: 죄송합니다 is the higher-courtesy 'I'm sorry', from Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I've committed a fault/I'm fearful before you'. Because it carries that deferential nuance, it is the apology you give to strangers, seniors, customers, and your boss. The 반말 partner is 미안해 (from 미안하다), used downward/among close friends; the gentler polite form is 미안해요; the 격식 upgrade is 대단히 죄송합니다 or 죄송스럽습니다. The dividing line versus 미안하다 is deference: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is safer upward, while 미안하다 is more horizontal and personal. The English-speaker mistakes: (1) attaching the reason wrong — to apologize for doing X you use X-아/어서 죄송합니다 (늦어서 죄송합니다), not '늦은 것 죄송'; (2) using 미안해 to a boss, which is far too casual; (3) confusing it with 실례합니다, which is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not a real apology.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 미안해 to a boss, teacher, or stranger — that is 반말; use 죄송합니다 (or at least 미안해요) for a real apology upward.
Forming the reason wrong, e.g. '늦은 거 죄송' — use the ~아/어서 connector: 늦어서 죄송합니다.
Swapping in 실례합니다 to apologize for a real mistake — 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor intrusion, not an apology for fault.

entries.nuance: 미안해요/미안하다 is the warmer, more horizontal 'sorry' — used downward or sideways: to friends, peers, your kids, people younger or close to you. From 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease (in my heart)'. The ladder is 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward/格式). The key dividing line versus 죄송하다: 미안하다 does NOT lower you, so it can feel too casual or even slightly presumptuous toward a senior or customer — for them choose 죄송합니다. English speakers wrongly treat 미안해요 and 죄송해요 as interchangeable 'sorry'; using 미안해요 to your boss sounds under-deferential, while using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds oddly stiff and distant. Also note: a quick 'sorry, excuse me' to squeeze past a stranger is NOT 미안해요 but 실례합니다 / 잠시만요.

Using 미안해요 to a boss, customer, or elder for a real fault — it isn't deferential enough; say 죄송합니다.
Using 미안하다 to brush past someone in a crowd — Koreans say 실례합니다 or 잠시만요, not 미안해요, for that.
Saying 미안해 to someone you've just met — too familiar; with strangers use 미안합니다/죄송합니다.

structuredNuance.t: 미안해요/미안하다 is the warmer, more horizontal 'sorry' — used downward or sideways: to friends, peers, your kids, people younger or close to you. The ladder is 미안해 (반말) → 미안해요 (gently polite) → 미안합니다 (firmer polite) → 죄송합니다 (deferential, upward/격식).
The key dividing line versus 죄송하다: 미안하다 does NOT lower you, so it can feel too casual or even slightly presumptuous toward a senior or customer — for them choose 죄송합니다.
From 미안(未安), literally 'not at ease (in my heart)'.

English speakers wrongly treat 미안해요 and 죄송해요 as interchangeable 'sorry'; using 미안해요 to your boss sounds under-deferential, while using 죄송합니다 to a close friend sounds oddly stiff and distant. Also note: a quick 'sorry, excuse me' to squeeze past a stranger is NOT 미안해요 but 실례합니다 / 잠시만요.

entries.nuance: 괜찮아요 does triple duty: 'it's okay / don't worry about it' (accepting an apology), 'I'm fine' (about your state), and crucially 'no, thank you' (politely declining an offer). The decline meaning trips up English speakers most: when a host offers food or a refill and you say 괜찮아요, you are turning it DOWN, not accepting — so to accept you must say 네, 주세요, not 괜찮아요. Register: 괜찮아 (반말) → 괜찮아요 (polite) → 괜찮습니다 (firmer/격식). The nearest relatives are 됐어요 (also 'I'm good/no need', but can sound curt) and 아니에요 ('no, it's nothing'); 괜찮아요 is the soft, safe choice. The standard mistake is hearing '괜찮아요?' as merely 'are you okay?' and missing that a flat 괜찮아요 to an offer means 'no thanks' — leaving learners unfed at Korean tables.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Answering an offer of food/drink with 괜찮아요 expecting MORE — it means 'no, I'm fine'; to accept, say 네, 주세요.
Using 괜찮아 with a stranger or senior — that is 반말; say 괜찮아요/괜찮습니다.
Confusing 괜찮아요 with 됐어요 in tone — 됐어요 can sound blunt/annoyed; 괜찮아요 stays gentle.

entries.nuance: 실례합니다 is 'excuse me' for a minor social intrusion — getting a stranger's attention, asking a question, passing by, or entering a space. From Sino-Korean 실례(失禮), literally 'I'm committing a breach of etiquette'. It is NOT an apology for a real fault (that's 죄송합니다) and NOT just 'sorry'. Register: 실례합니다 is polite; the 격식 form is 실례하겠습니다 / 실례하지만; you almost never say it in 반말 (a clipped 실례 sounds odd). The nearest alternatives are 저기요 and 잠시만요/잠깐만요: 저기요 hails a server or stranger casually, 잠시만요 means 'one moment / let me through', while 실례합니다 is the more polished, formal opener. English speakers misuse it as an all-purpose 'sorry' or 'pardon?' — to ask someone to repeat, you say 네? or 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요?, not 실례합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례합니다 as 'sorry' for a real mistake — for fault use 죄송합니다; 실례합니다 is only for a small intrusion.
Saying 실례합니다 to mean 'pardon? / say again?' — to ask for a repeat use 네? or 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Hailing a waiter with 실례합니다 every time — Koreans more often call 저기요 or 여기요 in casual eateries.

entries.nuance: 실례지만 is the polite 'excuse me, but…' you put in FRONT of a question that might intrude — asking a stranger's name, age, whether a seat is taken, or for directions. It is 실례(失禮) 'breach of etiquette' + 지만 'but', i.e. 'it's rude of me, but…'. It softens nosy or imposing questions, especially personal ones, where Korean expects cushioning. Register: 실례지만 is polite; 실례하지만 and 실례합니다만 are slightly more 격식; a softer/casual variant is 실례인데. The nearest alternative is 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), which leans more apologetic; the dividing line is that 실례지만 frames a social intrusion ('this question is a bit forward'), while 죄송하지만 frames asking a favor/imposition. English speakers either drop the cushion entirely (firing 나이가 어떻게 되세요? cold, which feels blunt) or mistranslate it as a standalone 'excuse me' — but 실례지만 must attach to a following clause, it can't end a sentence by itself.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 실례지만 alone like English 'excuse me' — it needs a following clause (실례지만, 누구세요?); to stand alone use 실례합니다.
Asking personal questions (age, name, marital status) with no cushion — Korean expects 실례지만/혹시 in front to soften.
Swapping it freely with 죄송하지만 — 실례지만 frames an intrusive question; 죄송하지만 leans toward asking a favor.

entries.nuance: 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges effort — 'you've worked hard, thank you' — said when a task, shift, meeting, or service is finished. It's the standard workplace sign-off and also what you say to a delivery driver or staff who just did something for you. Register: 수고했어 (반말, downward) → 수고하셨어요 (softer polite) → 수고하셨습니다 (polite) → 고생 많으셨습니다 / 고생하셨습니다 (warmer, more 격식). The crucial social rule English speakers miss: 수고하세요/수고하셨습니다 is best used SIDEWAYS or DOWNWARD (to peers and juniors); saying 수고하셨습니다 to a clear superior (your boss, a much older person, a professor) can sound slightly presumptuous, as if you're evaluating their effort. To a superior, prefer 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 said carefully. Also, the present 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work') is for someone still working, while 수고하셨습니다 (past) is for when it's done — don't mix the tenses.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 수고하셨습니다 to your boss or a much older superior — it can sound like you're grading them; use 감사합니다 (or 고생 많으셨습니다) instead.
Using 수고했어 with someone older or a stranger — that is 반말; say 수고하셨습니다/수고하셨어요.
Mixing tenses — say 수고하세요 to someone still working, 수고하셨습니다 only after the work is finished.

entries.nuance: 덕분 means 'thanks to (your) help/grace/virtue' (德分), so 덕분에 / 덕분이에요 credits another person for a good result — it's gratitude that says 'because of you, things went well'. entries.nuance: 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 thanks someone for the care, attention, or trouble they took on your behalf — for worrying about you, asking after you, or quietly handling something. 신경(을) 쓰다 literally means 'to use one's nerves', i.e. 'to pay attention / take pains / fret over'. The polite engine is the favor pattern ~아/어 주셔서 ('because you kindly did…') + 감사합니다. Register: 신경 써 줘서 고마워 (반말) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사합니다 (polite) → 신경 써 주셔서 감사드립니다 (격식). The nearest alternative is the plainer 도와주셔서 감사합니다 ('thanks for helping'); the dividing line is that 신경 써 주셔서 specifically thanks for the emotional care/attention and effort, not just a concrete action. English-speaker mistakes: writing 신경써 with no space (it's 신경(을) 쓰다, so 신경 써), and using plain 신경 써서 (no 주다), which drops the gratitude-for-a-favor nuance and sounds like you're just describing that they worried.
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Dropping 주다 → '신경 써서 감사합니다' — without ~아/어 주셔서 it loses the 'kindly did me a favor' nuance; keep 신경 써 주셔서.
Writing 신경써 with no space — the verb is 신경(을) 쓰다, so it is 신경 써 (주셔서).
Using it to a close friend in full 존댓말 — too stiff; say 신경 써 줘서 고마워.
